source: Plain-English versions written for DKLA by an agent swarm and checked by a legal checker; they explain the narrative, they are not the court's words.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Tompkins claimed longstanding open use made him a licensee entitled to ordinary care.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Tompkins said that because people had openly walked this path for years, he was there with the railroad’s tacit permission (a “licensee”), not trespassing. If so, the railroad owed him ordinary, reasonable care, and it would be liable if it had simply been careless.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Erie, a New York corporation, argued that Pennsylvania decisions treated users of a longitudinal railroad path as trespassers, owed only protection against willful or wanton harm while undiscovered.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Erie, a New York corporation, argued that Pennsylvania’s courts treated people walking along the tracks (a “longitudinal” path, as opposed to crossing them) as trespassers. Until a railroad noticed a trespasser, it only had to avoid “willful or wanton” harm, meaning deliberate or reckless injury, not mere carelessness.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: He further argued that without a Pennsylvania statute, railroad duty was general law on which a federal court could exercise independent judgment.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Tompkins also argued that, because no Pennsylvania statute covered the railroad’s duty, the question was “general law” under Swift v. Tyson. On such questions a federal court could use its “independent judgment,” deciding for itself what care the railroad owed instead of following Pennsylvania’s court decisions.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The issue was whether a diversity court could bypass authoritative state decisions on a substantive state-created claim.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The question was whether a “diversity court” (a federal court hearing a case only because the parties are from different states) could ignore authoritative decisions of the state’s courts. The claim was “substantive,” meaning it concerned the parties’ actual rights and duties, and state law itself created it.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Tompkins disputed that reading and its application, including a contention that he was struck at a transverse crossing.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Tompkins disputed that reading of Pennsylvania law and how it applied to him. He said, among other things, that he was hit at a “transverse crossing,” a place where a path crosses the tracks rather than running alongside them, which might be treated differently.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Tompkins filed a diversity tort suit in the Southern District of New York.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Tompkins filed a “diversity” tort suit: a suit for a civil injury, brought in federal court because he (from Pennsylvania) and Erie (a New York company) were citizens of different states. He filed in the federal trial court in Manhattan, the Southern District of New York.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Jurisdiction itself was not the issue; the dispute concerned which source supplied substantive rights.
cp-erie-decision.plain: “Jurisdiction,” the federal court’s power to hear the case, was not in dispute. The fight was over which source of law, federal judges’ own view or Pennsylvania’s, supplied the “substantive rights,” meaning what the railroad actually owed Tompkins.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The Second Circuit affirmed, treating railroad negligence as general jurisprudence.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The Second Circuit, the federal appeals court over New York, affirmed (upheld) the verdict. It treated railroad “negligence,” meaning carelessness that causes harm, as a matter of “general jurisprudence” that federal judges could decide for themselves.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: It used ordinary care for permissive path users and allowed jury consideration of negligence and contributory negligence without resolving the parties’ competing state-law authorities.
cp-erie-decision.plain: It held the railroad owed “ordinary care” (reasonable care) to people using the path with its permission. It let the jury decide whether Erie was guilty of “negligence” and whether Tompkins’s own carelessness (“contributory negligence”) barred recovery, without resolving which side’s Pennsylvania cases were right.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The Court heard argument on January 31, 1938, and reconsidered Swift v. Tyson, the precedent permitting independent federal formulation of rules in fields categorized as general law.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The Court heard argument on January 31, 1938, and used the case to re-examine Swift v. Tyson. That 1842 precedent let federal judges make up their own rules in fields labeled “general law.”

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Justice Brandeis explained that Swift had read § 34 of the Judiciary Act, the Rules of Decision Act, to include statutes, local usages, and fixed local matters while leaving broader commercial and common-law questions open to federal judgment.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Justice Brandeis explained how Swift had read § 34 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, known as the Rules of Decision Act, which tells federal courts to follow state “laws.” Swift read “laws” to cover only state statutes, local customs (“local usages”), and fixed local matters like land titles. That left broader commercial and common-law (judge-made) questions to federal judges’ own judgment.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Historical research into the original Act supported reading “laws” to include written and unwritten state law except where federal law governed.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Historical research into how the original 1789 Act was drafted supported reading “laws” to include both written state law (statutes) and unwritten state law (court decisions). The only exception was where federal law governed.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The same transaction inside one State could have different legal consequences depending on access to federal court.
cp-erie-decision.plain: So the “same transaction,” such as one deal or accident inside one State, could have different legal results depending on whether a party could get into federal court.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The Taxicab litigation illustrated the consequence: a Kentucky business reincorporated in Tennessee and obtained federal enforcement of an exclusive arrangement Kentucky common law would invalidate.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The Taxicab case showed the result. A Kentucky company “reincorporated” (re-formed itself as a corporation) in Tennessee so it could sue in federal court as an out-of-stater. There it enforced an “exclusive arrangement,” a deal giving it sole rights, that Kentucky common law would have struck down.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Diversity’s response to possible local bias had become access to a distinct substantive law.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Federal courts hear cases between citizens of different states to protect out-of-staters from possible local bias. Under Swift, though, that access had become a way to reach a different “substantive law,” meaning different rules about the parties’ actual rights.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Law governing state-created relationships derived authority from the State whether made by legislature or judiciary; it was not an independent body of universal principles federal judges could discover differently with equal authority.
cp-erie-decision.plain: State law includes both state statutes and state court decisions. There is no separate 'general' common law above the states that federal judges can work out on their own with equal authority.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Drawing on Field and Holmes dissents, the majority extended respect for state autonomy to authoritative state judgments as well as statutes.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Drawing on earlier dissents by Justices Field and Holmes, the majority held that respect for state independence covers authoritative state court “judgments” (decisions), not just state statutes.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The earlier practice represented an unconstitutional assumption of power over matters reserved to States.
cp-erie-decision.plain: By making their own rules in areas the Constitution leaves to the states, federal courts had been exercising power they never had.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: It rejected a general power to prescribe state substantive common law merely because a lawsuit was federal, not every possible law grounded in distinct federal authority.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The Court rejected any general federal power to make up state “substantive” common law (rules about rights and duties) just because a “lawsuit” is in federal court. It did not reject every law that rests on a separate federal source of authority, such as the Constitution or a federal statute.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: That distinction mattered because the separate opinions questioned the necessity and procedural propriety of the constitutional discussion.
cp-erie-decision.plain: That distinction, that the fault lay in how judges applied Swift and not in any unconstitutional statute, mattered because the separate “opinions” of other Justices attacked the constitutional discussion. They doubted it was necessary, and doubted it was procedurally proper when the parties had not argued it.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The statute’s reference to state law included state decisions, which was sufficient to overrule Swift.
cp-erie-decision.plain: In Justice Reed’s view, the “statute” (the 1789 law’s reference to state “laws”) already included state court decisions. That alone was enough to “overrule” Swift, meaning to formally declare it no longer good law.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Federal power over procedure was unquestioned, while the substance-procedure boundary was difficult.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Reed noted that federal power over court procedure was unquestioned. But the “substance-procedure” line, between procedure (how a case is run) and substance (the parties’ actual rights, which come from state law), was hard to draw.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The Judiciary Article and Necessary and Proper Clause might support legislation relevant to these questions.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Reed thought the “Judiciary Article” (Article III of the Constitution, on federal courts) and the Necessary and Proper Clause (Congress’s power to pass laws needed to carry out its other powers) might let Congress legislate on these questions.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: In his view, declaring Congress unable to prescribe the longstanding rule effectively invalidated § 34 as previously understood, calling for United States participation under the 1937 intervention statute.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Justice Butler argued that saying Congress could not have enacted Swift’s longstanding rule effectively “invalidated” (struck down) § 34 as courts had long read it. That, he said, called for the United States to take part under the 1937 “intervention statute,” a law letting the federal government join cases challenging a federal statute’s constitutionality.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Butler would nevertheless reverse Tompkins’s judgment for contributory negligence under the governing law as he understood it.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Butler would still “reverse” (overturn) Tompkins’s “judgment,” the lower courts’ final decision in his favor. He thought that under the governing law, as he understood it, Tompkins’s own carelessness (contributory negligence) barred recovery.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: The Supreme Court chose neither party’s final interpretation, left the crossing contention open, and did not enter judgment absolving Erie.
cp-erie-decision.plain: The Supreme Court adopted neither party’s final reading of Pennsylvania law and left open whether Tompkins was hit at a crossing. It did not “enter judgment” (issue a final ruling) clearing Erie of liability; it sent the case back to the Second Circuit to apply Pennsylvania law.

cp-erie-decision.sentence: Later cases such as York, Byrd, and Hanna would develop federal-state procedural conflicts; this decision removed the unauthorized general-law foundation for Tompkins’s judgment.
cp-erie-decision.plain: Later Supreme Court cases such as York, Byrd, and Hanna would work out conflicts between federal procedure and state law. This decision removed the unauthorized “general law” foundation for Tompkins’s “judgment,” his win in the lower courts.

cp-garcia.sentence: Hilton moved to dismiss because Garcia had not expressly alleged publication to another person and because the accusation was conditionally privileged.
cp-garcia.plain: Hilton “moved to dismiss,” asking the court to throw the case out, for two reasons. Garcia’s complaint never expressly “alleged” (formally claimed) publication, meaning that the accusation was communicated to someone else, which defamation requires. And Hilton said the accusation was “conditionally privileged,” protected by a limited privilege covering some good-faith statements.

cp-garcia.sentence: Hilton therefore had to assert conditional privilege as an affirmative defense rather than obtain dismissal merely because it might be available.
cp-garcia.plain: So Hilton had to raise “conditional privilege” as an “affirmative defense,” a defense it must plead and prove itself in its answer. The mere chance that the privilege might apply was not enough to win “dismissal” at the start of the case.

cp-garcia.sentence: Alternatively, it asked to strike paragraphs 5–8, which described the labor proceeding, and to require a more definite statement.
cp-garcia.plain: In the alternative, Hilton asked the court to “strike” (delete) paragraphs 5–8, which described the labor-department proceeding. It also asked for a “more definite statement,” an order making Garcia state his claim more clearly.

cp-garcia.sentence: Under the liberal pleading approach applied in 1951, Rule 8(a) called for a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief rather than the older formula of facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action.
cp-garcia.plain: Under the “liberal pleading approach” (forgiving rules for complaints) used in 1951, Rule 8(a) required only a “short and plain statement” showing the plaintiff deserved relief. That replaced the older demand for facts sufficient to make out a “cause of action,” meaning a legally recognized claim.

cp-garcia.sentence: Drawing on Dioguardi, a decision favoring an opportunity to develop an imperfectly expressed claim, Roberts asked whether evidence within this complaint’s framework could establish relief.
cp-garcia.plain: Following Dioguardi, a decision that gave a plaintiff the chance to develop a poorly written claim, Judge Roberts asked whether evidence fitting this complaint’s framework could show Garcia was entitled to “relief” (a legal remedy).

cp-garcia.sentence: Nevertheless, the alleged discharge accompanied by a false and slanderous accusation conveyed a publication claim Hilton could understand, and Garcia might prove publication at trial.
cp-garcia.plain: Still, the “alleged” (claimed) firing together with a false and “slanderous” accusation (spoken defamation) told Hilton clearly enough that Garcia claimed “publication,” meaning that others heard it. Garcia might prove that publication at trial.

cp-garcia.sentence: Unlike absolute privilege, it could be lost through abuse or actual malice.
cp-garcia.plain: Unlike “absolute privilege,” which gives full protection, this conditional privilege could be lost if the speaker abused it or spoke with actual malice, such as spite or knowing falsehood.

cp-garcia.sentence: Courts elsewhere similarly protected communications to bodies exercising quasi-judicial powers.
cp-garcia.plain: Courts elsewhere similarly protected statements made to bodies with “quasi-judicial” powers, meaning government agencies that hear and decide disputes much like courts.

cp-garcia.sentence: That policy and the statute’s coverage of legally authorized proceedings supported absolute privilege here; malice could not defeat it.
cp-garcia.plain: That policy of letting people speak freely in labor enforcement, plus the “statute” covering proceedings authorized by law, supported “absolute privilege” (full protection) for Hilton’s statements at the hearing. Even malice could not defeat it, so Garcia could not sue over those statements.

cp-garcia.sentence: Roberts struck paragraphs 5–8 as redundant, including the surrounding account of the labor claim and compromise.
cp-garcia.plain: Judge Roberts “struck” (deleted) paragraphs 5–8 as “redundant,” meaning unnecessary to any valid claim, including their account of the labor claim and its compromise (settlement).

cp-garcia.sentence: The protected repetition did not retroactively turn the original discharge accusation into a statement made in the official hearing.
cp-garcia.plain: Repeating the accusation at the protected hearing did not “retroactively” (after the fact) turn the original accusation made at the firing into a statement made in the official hearing. So the firing accusation stayed outside the absolute privilege.

cp-garcia.sentence: Roberts granted the Rule 12(e) request for a more definite statement requiring that information.
cp-garcia.plain: Judge Roberts “granted” (approved) Hilton’s Rule 12(e) request for a “more definite statement.” He ordered Garcia to supply the missing details: the substance of the words spoken and the facts showing publication.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Those circumstances were later held sufficient to establish fraud and illegality at issuance.
brief-CP-140.plain: Courts later decided that these facts (one bond handed to the county judge as a 'gratuity', and the courthouse never built) proved the bonds were issued through fraud and illegally. So the county did not have to pay just anyone who held them.

brief-CP-140.sentence: A holder seeking payment therefore had to show protected acquisition for value before maturity rather than rely solely on possession of the instruments.
brief-CP-140.plain: Because of that defect, a “holder” (a person holding the bonds) could not collect just by possessing the “instruments,” meaning the bonds and coupons as written promises to pay. He had to prove protected “acquisition for value” before maturity: that he paid real value before they came due, making him an innocent buyer the law protects.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Cromwell’s later action was not a motion to reopen the lost coupon claims.
brief-CP-140.plain: Cromwell’s later “action” (lawsuit) was not a “motion” (a request within an existing case) to reopen the coupon claims Smith had lost. He was suing on different bonds and coupons.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Cromwell sought Supreme Court review by writ of error, raising both the scope of the prior adjudication and the use of evidence identifying him as the first suit’s beneficial litigant.
brief-CP-140.plain: Cromwell sought Supreme Court review by “writ of error,” the old way of asking a higher court to correct legal errors. He argued the first judgment decided less than the trial court thought, and objected to evidence showing he was the first suit’s beneficial “litigant,” the person Smith had really sued for.

brief-CP-140.sentence: A final merits judgment on the same claim settled the whole demand, including grounds of recovery or defense available but omitted.
brief-CP-140.plain: A “final merits judgment,” a final decision on the substance of a claim, settles that whole claim for good. Any ground for “recovery” (winning money) or defense that a party could have raised but didn’t is lost too; this is claim preclusion.

brief-CP-140.sentence: A party generally could not reopen a judgment on a promissory note by later presenting payment, forgery, or lack of consideration.
brief-CP-140.plain: So a “party” who lost a suit on a promissory note (a written promise to pay) generally cannot “reopen” that judgment later by raising payment, “forgery” (a faked signature), or lack of consideration (getting nothing in return for the promise). Those defenses belonged in the first suit.

brief-CP-140.sentence: When a later suit involved a different claim, only matters actually litigated and determined as a basis of the first judgment were conclusive.
brief-CP-140.plain: But when a later suit involves a different claim, the first judgment is binding only on matters “actually litigated” (fought over) and decided as a basis for that judgment. This narrower rule is issue preclusion.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Potential relevance to earlier pleadings was insufficient.
brief-CP-140.plain: It was not enough that an issue might have been relevant under the first case’s “pleadings,” the papers in which each side stated its claims and defenses. The issue had to have been actually decided.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Conversely, a general verdict resting on several possible counts might not settle the validity of a contract appearing in only one.
brief-CP-140.plain: On the other hand, a “general verdict,” where a jury just names a winner, may rest on any of several “counts” (separate claims in one lawsuit). So it might not settle whether a contract that appeared in only one count was valid, since no one can tell which count the jury relied on.

brief-CP-140.sentence: The first judgment established the fraudulent or illegal issuance and the need for protected holder status.
brief-CP-140.plain: What the first “judgment” did settle for good was that the bonds were issued through fraud or illegality. So anyone seeking payment needed protected “holder” status: he had to show he was an innocent buyer who paid value before maturity.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Failure to prove acquisition for value of the first instruments did not even presumptively establish nonpayment for all others.
brief-CP-140.plain: Smith’s failure to prove “acquisition for value” (that he paid for) the first coupons did not, even “presumptively” (as a starting assumption open to disproof), show that no one paid for all the others. Each purchase was a separate fact.

brief-CP-140.sentence: A bona fide holder who acquired these particular instruments for value before maturity could enforce them despite the original defect.
brief-CP-140.plain: A “bona fide holder,” meaning an honest buyer without notice of the problem, who paid value for these particular “instruments” (the bonds and coupons) “before maturity” (before they came due) could collect on them. That was true despite the defect in their original issuance.

brief-CP-140.sentence: An earlier finding that Smith held and owned the coupons established legal title sufficient to maintain that suit, but was compatible with Cromwell holding the equitable or beneficial interest.
brief-CP-140.plain: The first court’s finding that Smith held and owned the coupons showed only that he had the legal title (formal ownership) needed to bring that suit. That fit with Cromwell holding the “equitable or beneficial interest,” meaning he was the real owner who would get the money.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Thus the real-party connection and the reach of the adjudication were separate.
brief-CP-140.plain: So two questions were distinct: whether Cromwell was the real party behind Smith's suit, and which issues that suit actually decided. Answering the first did not widen the second.

brief-CP-140.sentence: Justice Clifford first stated that the original evidence of irregularity should not have overcome the usual presumption that a bearer acquired negotiable obligations for value.
brief-CP-140.plain: Justice Clifford, dissenting, first said the original court got it wrong. Someone holding “negotiable obligations” payable to the bearer (bonds that pass by simple handover) is usually presumed to have paid value for them, and the evidence of irregularity should not have overcome that presumption.

brief-CP-140.sentence: A mistaken strategy about the burden should have been addressed by objection or a new-trial request.
brief-CP-140.plain: In Clifford’s view, if Smith made a strategic mistake about who bore the burden of proving payment, the fix was an “objection” at trial or a request for a new trial. It was not saving proof for later lawsuits.

brief-CP-140.sentence: The result illustrated the distinction between a bar on repeating the same claim and the narrower preclusion of actually decided issues in another claim.
brief-CP-140.plain: The result shows the difference between a “bar” on suing again on the same claim (claim preclusion) and a narrower rule for a different claim. In the second situation, a party is bound only by issues actually decided before (issue preclusion).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Connecticut Retirement Plans and Trust Funds purchased Amgen stock and sought to represent other purchasers under § 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act and Securities and Exchange Commission Rule 10b-5.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Connecticut Retirement Plans and Trust Funds, a pension fund, bought Amgen stock and sued for securities fraud under § 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act and Securities and Exchange Commission Rule 10b-5, the main federal anti-fraud provisions. It asked to represent all other buyers as a class action.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Basic Inc. v. Levinson, the governing fraud-on-the-market precedent, permitted a rebuttable inference of reliance because an efficient market incorporated public material information into price.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Basic Inc. v. Levinson set the “fraud-on-the-market” rule: investors need not each prove they read and believed a lie. Because an efficient market builds public “material information” (facts important to investors) into the stock price, buyers at that price are presumed to have relied on it. The presumption is “rebuttable,” meaning the company can try to disprove it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: It was a method of proving reliance in individual as well as class cases, not elimination of other fraud elements.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: The presumption only helps prove reliance. Investors still must prove the other parts of fraud, such as a false statement that mattered and that caused their loss.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: The district court certified a Rule 23(b)(3) class of purchasers between the first alleged misrepresentation and last alleged corrective disclosure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) certified a Rule 23(b)(3) class, a class action seeking money damages. It covered everyone who bought Amgen stock between the first alleged misrepresentation and the last alleged “corrective disclosure,” the announcement said to have revealed the truth.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Amgen argued that the fund had to prove materiality first and that the court should consider its evidence that public information already rendered the statements immaterial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Amgen argued the fund had to prove “materiality” first, meaning that the statements were important to a reasonable investor, before the class could be certified. It also asked the court to consider its evidence that the truth was already public, so the statements could not have mattered.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: The Ninth Circuit permitted an interlocutory appeal under Rule 23(f) and affirmed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: The Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, allowed an “interlocutory appeal” under Rule 23(f): an appeal of the certification ruling right away, before the case ended. It then “affirmed” (upheld) the certification.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Courts must rigorously apply Rule 23 and may examine merits bearing on its requirements, but cannot turn certification into an unrestricted preliminary merits trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Courts must rigorously apply Rule 23, the class-action rule, and may look at the “merits” (who should ultimately win) when that bears on its requirements. But they cannot turn “certification,” the decision to let a case proceed as a class action, into an unlimited early trial of the merits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: The question was whether proving materiality was necessary to decide predominance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: The question was whether the fund had to prove materiality to establish “predominance,” the requirement that questions common to the whole class outweigh questions about individual members.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Materiality objectively asked what a reasonable investor would consider significant in the total mix of information, making it a common issue independent of particular investors’ subjective reactions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Materiality is an objective test: what a “reasonable investor” would find significant in the “total mix of information,” meaning everything publicly available. Because it does not depend on what each actual investor thought, it is a common issue with the same answer for the whole class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Failure would therefore produce a common merits defeat, not many surviving individual claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: So if the fund failed to prove materiality, the whole class would lose together on the “merits” (the substance of the claim). That would not leave many individual claims still alive, so it was no reason to refuse class treatment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: By contrast, an inefficient market or nonpublic statement could defeat the presumption while leaving direct-reliance claims viable, potentially making individual inquiries significant.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: It is different with an “inefficient market” (one that does not reliably build public information into price) or a statement that was not public. Then the presumption fails, but some investors could still pursue “claims” by proving they personally relied on the lie, so individual questions could become significant.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: A materiality minitrial could duplicate later proceedings, while denial of certification would not bind absent investors against another attempt.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: A mini-trial on materiality at certification could duplicate what later proceedings would decide. And denying certification would not bind “absent investors” (class members not personally in court) against another attempt to certify, so it would not even settle the issue.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Later adjustment was ordinary certification flexibility; elimination of formally conditional certification did not remove the authority to alter or amend certification before final judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Changing things later was ordinary certification flexibility. Although the rule no longer labels certification “conditional,” a court still has power to alter or “amend” (change) a certification before final judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Even conclusive immateriality would defeat all claims together without undermining predominance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Even if Amgen fully proved the statement did not matter, that would sink everyone's claims at once. It would not show that individual issues dominate.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: This evidence therefore belonged at summary judgment or trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: So Amgen’s evidence belonged at “summary judgment,” where a court decides whether there is any real factual dispute needing a trial, or at trial itself, not at the certification stage.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Justice Thomas, joined throughout by Kennedy and except I-B by Scalia, required proof of all predicates before reliance became common.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Justice Thomas dissented, “joined” (agreed with) throughout by Justice Kennedy and by Justice Scalia except for Part I-B. Thomas would have required proof of every condition of the Basic presumption, including materiality, before reliance could be treated as common to the class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.sentence: Materiality remained essential to eventual liability and to the presumption, but proof before certification and this materiality rebuttal were unnecessary to establish predominance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-343.plain: Materiality is still essential to final “liability” (legal responsibility) and to the reliance “presumption.” But the fund did not need to prove it before certification, and Amgen’s rebuttal evidence was not needed to decide “predominance.”

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Only Cole’s Rule 12(b)(2) motion was decided here, after March 3, 2021 argument.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: The only issue decided was Cole’s Rule 12(b)(2) motion, a request to dismiss because the Michigan federal court lacked “personal jurisdiction” (power over her as a defendant). The court ruled after hearing argument on March 3, 2021.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Plaintiffs relied on knowledge, effects, and a suggestion that a Vancouver publication targeted nearby American consumers, including southeastern Michigan, because they had held Toronto workshops.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: The plaintiffs argued Michigan could hear the case because Cole knew they were in Michigan and the harm was felt there. They also suggested that the Vancouver publication was aimed at nearby American readers, including southeastern Michigan, because they had held workshops in Toronto.
As a backup, they asked the court to move the case to Arizona, where Cole lives, instead of dismissing it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Judge Gershwin Drain required reasonably particular prima facie facts on written submissions, favoring plaintiffs rather than accepting Cole’s conflicting account.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: Judge Gershwin Drain decided on written papers, so the plaintiffs needed only reasonably specific “prima facie” facts, meaning facts that, if true, would support jurisdiction. Where Cole’s account conflicted, he took the plaintiffs’ version rather than hers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Michigan’s long-arm reach was treated as coextensive with due process; its individual general-jurisdiction provision did not apply.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: Michigan’s “long-arm” statute (its law on suing out-of-state people) was treated as “coextensive with due process,” meaning it reaches as far as the Constitution allows. Michigan’s general-jurisdiction provision for individuals, which would let them be sued there on any claim, did not apply to Cole.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Specific jurisdiction required purposeful forum conduct or consequences, a related claim, and a substantial reasonable connection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: “Specific jurisdiction,” power over a defendant for claims tied to her conduct, required three things. Cole must have purposely acted in, or caused consequences in, the “forum” (the state where the suit was filed); the claim must arise from that conduct; and the connection must be substantial enough to make suit there reasonable.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Calder involved developed forum focus, sources, and circulation; Walden required the defendant’s connection rather than residence and injury supplied by plaintiffs.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: In Calder, the writers had a developed focus on the “forum” state (California), used California sources, and the story circulated widely there. Walden held that what counts is the defendant’s own connection to the state, not the plaintiff’s “residence” there or injury the plaintiff suffered there.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Michigan readers’ reactions and cancellations also were third-party choices, not Cole-created contacts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: Michigan readers’ reactions and canceled contracts were “third-party” choices, made by other people. They were not Cole-created “contacts,” meaning ties to Michigan that Cole herself formed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Even assuming she knew plaintiffs’ location, despite her disputed claim of learning it only through Vice, foreseeable injury there was insufficient.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: Cole made a disputed “claim” that she learned the plaintiffs’ location only through Vice. Even assuming she knew they were in Michigan, the fact that injury there was “foreseeable” (predictable) was not enough for jurisdiction.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Drain recognized interest-of-justice transfer despite missing jurisdiction, discussing §§ 1631 and 1406(a), though the application paragraph later referred to § 1404(a) without explanation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: Judge Drain recognized that a court lacking jurisdiction may still make an “interest-of-justice transfer,” moving the case to a proper court instead of dismissing it. He discussed §§ 1631 and 1406(a), federal transfer statutes, though his paragraph applying the rule later cited § 1404(a) without explanation.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: Here the explicit threat to burden distant critics supported apparent bad faith in choosing Michigan.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: Here, the plaintiffs’ open threat to make distant critics bear the costs of fighting in Michigan supported apparent “bad faith,” meaning an improper motive, in choosing Michigan as the place to sue.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.sentence: The suit was young, plaintiffs identified no prejudice from dismissal, and no limitations obstacle was suggested.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES.plain: The suit was at an early stage, the plaintiffs identified no “prejudice” (unfair harm) from dismissal, and no one suggested a “limitations obstacle,” meaning a filing deadline that would stop them from suing again elsewhere.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: The lease-purchase required eighty-four monthly $281.16 payments beginning by the first day of the month after Telerent completed its work, followed by a nominal purchase option.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: The “lease-purchase” deal (a lease that ends with a chance to buy) required eighty-four monthly payments of $281.16, about seven years. They began by the first day of the month after Telerent finished its work, followed by a “purchase option” to buy the equipment for a token price.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Telerent returned it and demanded the larger amount within five days, threatening acceleration and removal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: Telerent sent Patel’s reduced payment back and demanded the larger amount within five days. It threatened “acceleration,” making the entire remaining balance due at once, and removal of the equipment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Telerent obtained replevin possession of twenty-two sets with radios, twenty-two locking pedestals, and the alarm system.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: Through “replevin,” a court action to recover specific property, Telerent took possession of twenty-two TV sets with radios, twenty-two locking pedestals (stands), and the alarm system.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: It did not assert the replevin judgment precluded Patel’s breach defense.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: Telerent did not argue that its “replevin” judgment (winning the repossession case) barred Patel from defending on the ground of “breach,” meaning that Telerent itself broke the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: The county judge found failure of the typed tap-and-amplifier requirement, timely rejection and abandonment, and a notice failure, denying relief December 22, 1986.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: The county judge found that Telerent failed the typed requirement to replace room taps and provide an amplifier. He also found “timely rejection” (Patel refused the system in time) and abandonment of it, plus a notice failure. On December 22, 1986, he denied Telerent any “relief” (remedy).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: The circuit court, acting on appeal, applied North Carolina law and treated certificates and engraving the motel name on sets as acceptance; it found ineffective rejection and rendered judgment for Telerent.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: The “circuit court,” acting as the first appeals court, applied North Carolina law. It treated Patel’s signed completion “certificates” and the engraving of the motel’s name on the sets as “acceptance” of the goods, so his rejection was ineffective, and it entered judgment for Telerent.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Presiding Justice Hawkins’s Supreme Court opinion treated the nominal-option lease-purchase as functionally a sale under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: Presiding Justice Hawkins’s “opinion” (written decision) for the state Supreme Court looked past the “lease” label. Because this was a “nominal-option” lease-purchase, letting Patel buy the sets for a token price at the end, it functioned as a sale of goods under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Relevant Mississippi and North Carolina provisions were identical, so no conflicting-state rule had to be chosen.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: The relevant Mississippi and North Carolina provisions were identical, since both states use the same Uniform Commercial Code rules. So the court did not have to choose between conflicting state rules.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Substantial evidence and absence of manifest error required deference, with supporting necessary findings assumed; a correct ground could sustain the result even if the trial judge gave another explanation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: Because the county judge’s findings had “substantial evidence” (solid support in the record) and no “manifest error” (obvious mistake), the higher court had to defer to them, assuming any necessary supporting findings. It could “sustain” (uphold) the result on any correct ground, even one the trial judge did not give.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Under the Code, a buyer notifying the seller could deduct breach damages from the price owed under that same contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: Under the Code (the Uniform Commercial Code), a buyer who notifies the seller may deduct the damages caused by the seller’s breach from the price still owed under that same contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: The court also invoked written demands for adequate assurance and commercially reasonable suspension when the agreed return had not been received.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: The court also relied on two Code tools for a party that has not received what it bargained for. It may demand in writing “adequate assurance” that the other side will perform, and it may suspend its own performance, such as payments, in a commercially reasonable way meanwhile.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: Acceptance and use of defective goods did not necessarily waive price offsets or continuing obligations.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: “Acceptance” and use of defective goods did not necessarily “waive” (give up) the buyer’s right to deduct damages from the price, or end the seller’s continuing obligations.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.sentence: The Supreme Court therefore sustained the county court through material breach, withholding, and recoupment without adopting every rejection-and-abandonment characterization.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-068.plain: So the state Supreme Court “sustained” (upheld) the county court on three grounds: Telerent’s “material breach” (a serious failure to perform), Patel’s right to withhold payment, and “recoupment,” meaning subtracting his damages from what he owed under the same contract. It did not adopt every “rejection-and-abandonment” finding about whether Patel properly refused the goods.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Assignment in specified transactions required delivery of an undertaking binding the assignee to Famous’s obligations.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: “Assignment” here means transferring the contract to another company. In certain specified deals, Famous could assign only by delivering an “undertaking,” a written promise binding the new company (the assignee) to Famous’s obligations.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Material default required a written specification and thirty days without cure.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: A material (serious) default counted only after the complaining side specified the problem in writing and thirty days passed without “cure,” meaning without the other side fixing it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: It restricted Contemporary’s assignments but not Famous’s, while paragraph 12 denied power to create obligations in the other party’s name.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: The contract restricted Contemporary’s right to assign (transfer) it, but not Famous’s. Paragraph 12 said neither party had power to create obligations in the other party’s name.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Famous did not challenge the instruction that assigning Virgin without ABC’s written undertaking breached that clause.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Famous did not challenge the judge’s instruction to the jury that assigning the Virgin contract to ABC without ABC’s written “undertaking” (a promise to perform Famous’s duties) breached that clause.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Contemporary cross-appealed exclusion of projected royalty evidence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Contemporary “cross-appealed,” meaning it brought its own appeal in the same case, challenging the judge’s exclusion of its evidence projecting the extra royalties it would have earned.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Judge Meskill, joined by Judge Mansfield, held the exclusive Virgin grant also implied reasonable national promotion under Wood v. Lucy.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Judge Meskill, joined by Judge Mansfield (making his view the majority), held that the exclusive grant of rights to Virgin also “implied” an unwritten promise to promote it reasonably nationwide. He followed Wood v. Lucy, which reads such a duty into exclusive deals.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: An amendment permitting cessation when promotion lost effectiveness and profitability required a good-faith determination, not arbitrary discretion; none was shown.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: An “amendment” (contract change) let Famous stop promoting once promotion stopped being effective and profitable. But that required a “good-faith” (honest) determination, not arbitrary “discretion,” and none was shown.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Assuming without deciding that Martell-linked promotion was delegable, delegation did not discharge Famous.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: The court was “assuming without deciding” (accepting for argument’s sake, without ruling) that the Martell-linked promotion duties were “delegable,” meaning they could be handed to another company. Even so, delegating them to ABC did not free Famous from them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Contemporary showed nobody performed after the sale; it need not prove ABC’s independently actionable repudiation or disprove an unpleaded performance defense.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Contemporary showed that nobody performed after the sale. It did not have to prove a separately “actionable” repudiation by ABC (a refusal to perform that could itself be sued on), or disprove an “unpleaded” defense of performance, one Famous never raised in its court papers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: The cure provision was not a pleading trap, and Famous’s disposal of its division left it unable to cure.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: The contract’s cure provision (written notice and thirty days to fix) was not a “pleading” trap for defeating claims on technicalities. And Famous, having sold off its record division, was unable to cure the problem anyway.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Contemporary’s claim that assignment was void did not estop recovery on Famous’s own outstanding duty.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Contemporary argued the “assignment” to ABC was void (legally ineffective). That position did not “estop” it, meaning legally block it, from recovering for Famous’s own unmet duty.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: New York distinguished certainty of loss from precision of amount.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: New York law separates “certainty of loss” from precision of amount. A plaintiff must show with reasonable certainty that a loss happened, but need not prove its exact size.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Missing information about speed of ascent, performer reputation, and promotion affected weight rather than basic relevance, with contrary proof available.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Gaps in the statistics made them less persuasive but did not make them irrelevant, and Famous could offer evidence pointing out those gaps.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: Federal Rule of Evidence 403 permitted exclusion where unfair prejudice, confusion, or misleading force substantially outweighed probative value.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: Federal Rule of Evidence 403 lets a judge exclude relevant evidence when its “probative value” (how much it helps prove something) is substantially outweighed by “unfair prejudice,” confusion, or the risk of misleading the jury.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.sentence: The district court relied on Freund’s substantive certainty rule without that balance; the majority remanded for the judge to perform it and determine whether Contemporary should receive a new damages trial.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-027.plain: The district court (the trial court) had excluded the evidence under Freund’s “substantive certainty rule,” a New York rule against speculative damages, without doing that Rule 403 weighing. The “majority” of the appeals panel sent the case back for the judge to do it and decide whether Contemporary should get a new trial on damages.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: Kel Kim promised continuous public liability insurance with responsible, solvent insurers: at least $500,000 for one person and $1 million for a single accident in the aggregate.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: Kel Kim promised to keep continuous “public liability insurance” (coverage for injuries to members of the public) with responsible, “solvent” (financially sound) insurers. Coverage had to be at least $500,000 for one person and $1 million “in the aggregate” (in total) for a single accident.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: In November 1985 its insurer said the policy would expire January 6, 1986 without renewal because a reinsurer’s finances were uncertain under court-appointed administration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: In November 1985, Kel Kim’s insurer said the “policy” would expire January 6, 1986, without renewal. The reason was that a “reinsurer” (a company that insures the insurer) was under court-appointed administration, making its finances uncertain.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: Kel Kim and its individual guarantors sought a declaration excusing the insurance obligation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: Kel Kim and its individual “guarantors,” the people who had personally promised to back its lease obligations, asked the court for a declaration (a ruling on their rights) excusing the insurance requirement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: Special Term instead granted the landlords summary judgment, nullified the lease and ordered vacatur.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: Special Term, the motion part of New York’s trial court, instead granted the landlords “summary judgment,” a ruling without a trial. It nullified (ended) the lease and ordered Kel Kim to vacate (move out).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: Its impossibility rule required objective impossibility from destruction of the subject matter or means of performance through an event that could neither be foreseen nor guarded against by contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: New York’s “impossibility” rule excuses performance only when it becomes objectively impossible, meaning impossible for anyone. That requires destruction of the subject matter or of the means of performance, by an event that could neither be foreseen nor guarded against in the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: Inability to obtain that insurance was a contingency the parties could foresee and address.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: Being unable to get that insurance was a “contingency,” a possible future event, that the parties could have foreseen and addressed in the lease. So it was no excuse.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: The general similar-causes language stayed bounded by the listed events affecting daily operations, rather than reaching every difficulty beyond control.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: The catch-all phrase 'similar causes' covers only events like those listed, things that disrupt day-to-day operations, not every problem outside the tenant's control.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.sentence: On December 21, 1987, the unsigned memorandum affirmed with costs.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-058.plain: On December 21, 1987, New York’s highest court “affirmed” (upheld) the decision in a short unsigned opinion (a memorandum), with costs, meaning Kel Kim also had to pay the landlords’ court costs.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.sentence: The movers sued on an account annexed for the fair value of services rendered through the fire.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.plain: The movers sued on an “account annexed,” an itemized bill attached to the complaint, for the “fair value” (reasonable worth) of the work they did up to the fire.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.sentence: The owner pleaded nonperformance and alleged that the movers’ negligence had caused the destruction.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.plain: The owner “pleaded” (stated in his formal answer) that the movers had not performed the job, and “alleged” (claimed) that their “negligence,” meaning carelessness, caused the building’s destruction.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.sentence: The owner challenged the refusal and instructions by exceptions; the allegation of negligence was therefore not an established cause of the fire.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.plain: The owner challenged the judge’s refusal and jury instructions by “exceptions,” formal objections that let a higher court review them. Because the jury found for the movers, the claim of “negligence” was never established as the cause of the fire.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.sentence: Massachusetts precedent recognized an implied obligation to pay for what either party properly did before that condition failed, treating the services as performed at the other’s request.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.plain: Massachusetts “precedent” (earlier cases) recognized an “implied obligation”: when the “condition” a contract depends on fails, such as the building continuing to exist, each “party” must pay for what the other properly did before then. The work is treated as done at the other side’s request.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.sentence: Excuse from completing the relocation did not eliminate payment for their proper partial performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.plain: Being excused from finishing the move did not wipe out the movers’ right to be paid for their proper “partial performance,” the work they had correctly done.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.sentence: On June 20, 1900, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court overruled the owner’s exceptions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-064.plain: On June 20, 1900, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, the state’s highest court, overruled (rejected) the owner’s “exceptions,” his formal objections. So the verdict for the movers stood.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: After a Massachusetts arrest for operating under the influence in 2006, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) personally served him May 31 with a document charging removability for overstay.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: After a 2006 Massachusetts arrest for operating (driving) under the influence, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) personally handed Pereira a document on May 31. It charged “removability,” meaning he could be deported, for “overstay”: staying past the end of his visa.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: He missed the hearing, was ordered removed in absentia, and did not know of the order.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: The hearing notice was mailed to the wrong address, so he missed the hearing and was ordered removed (deported) “in absentia,” meaning in his absence. He did not know of the order.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: He sought cancellation of removal based in part on more than ten years’ continuous physical presence.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: He sought “cancellation of removal,” a discretionary form of relief that lets some noncitizens stay. He relied in part on having more than ten years of “continuous physical presence,” meaning living in the U.S. without a break.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: The 1996 immigration legislation authorized discretionary cancellation for certain nonpermanent residents meeting conditions including ten years of continuous physical presence before application.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: The 1996 immigration law authorized “discretionary cancellation,” meaning the government may, but need not, cancel deportation. It covers certain “nonpermanent residents” (noncitizens without green cards) who meet conditions, including ten years of “continuous physical presence” before applying.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: Section 1229b(d)(1)(A) stopped accrual upon service of a notice to appear under § 1229(a).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Section 1229b(d)(1)(A), the “stop-time” rule, stopped the ten-year clock from running (“accrual”) once the person was served with a “notice to appear” under § 1229(a), the section that says what that notice must contain.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) dismissed his appeal under Matter of Camarillo, which treated the cross-reference as identifying a document category without importing all content requirements.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), the agency’s appeals body, dismissed his appeal under its own earlier decision, Matter of Camarillo. Camarillo read the cross-reference to § 1229(a) as just naming a type of document, without requiring all the contents that section lists.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: The First Circuit found ambiguity and deferred under Chevron, the then-governing agency-interpretation precedent.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: The First Circuit, the federal appeals court, found the statute ambiguous (unclear) and “deferred under Chevron,” accepting the agency’s reasonable reading. Chevron was the governing “precedent” at the time on how courts treat agency interpretations.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: Paragraph (1) described a notice to appear that specified hearing time and place; those particulars were essential to stop time.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Paragraph (1) of § 1229(a) describes a notice to appear as one that specifies the hearing’s time and place. Those details were essential, so a paper lacking them did not stop the clock.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: The same statutory term ordinarily meant the same thing for both that protection and stop time.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: A term in a statute usually means the same thing each time it appears, so 'notice to appear' must include the hearing time and place for the clock rule too.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: The word “under” could vary by context, but here linked the trigger to compliance with substantive criteria.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: The word “under” can mean different things in different contexts. Here, a notice “under” § 1229(a) meant one that actually meets that section’s “substantive” criteria, its required contents.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: Administrative practice could not supersede clear statutory requirements.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Administrative practice, here the government’s habit of leaving dates off these notices, could not override clear “statutory” requirements, meaning what the law’s text demands.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: Because the text was clear, the majority did not proceed to Chevron deference.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Because the statute’s text was clear, the “majority” never reached “Chevron deference,” the rule that courts accept an agency’s reasonable reading when a statute is ambiguous.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: That was a separate invitation, not a majority overruling in 2018.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Kennedy’s suggestion to reconsider Chevron in a future case was a separate invitation. It was not an “overruling” (formal abandonment) of Chevron by the majority in 2018.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: He agreed notices were required to contain time and place but distinguished that duty from whether a defective notice still stopped time.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Justice Alito agreed the notice must state the time and place, but argued that a notice missing them could still stop the clock.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.sentence: Treating the document primarily as a charging instrument was a permissible functional choice, and Chevron in his view required deference.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-010.plain: Alito thought the agency could permissibly treat the document mainly as a “charging instrument,” the paper that brings the charges, as a practical choice. In his view Chevron required “deference,” meaning courts had to accept that reasonable agency reading.

cp-grable.sentence: The Government then conveyed its interest to purchaser Darue by quitclaim deed.
cp-grable.plain: The Government then “conveyed” (transferred) its interest in the land to the buyer, Darue, by “quitclaim deed,” a deed that passes whatever interest the seller has without promising the title is good.

cp-grable.sentence: Five years later Grable sued Darue in state court to quiet title, claiming its own title superior because 26 U.S.C. § 6335(a) required personal service of seizure notice.
cp-grable.plain: Five years later Grable sued Darue in state court “to quiet title,” asking the court to declare who owns the land. Grable claimed its own “title” (ownership) was superior because 26 U.S.C. § 6335(a), a federal tax statute, required personal service of the seizure notice, not mail.
Darue used “federal-question removal,” moving the case from state court to federal court on the ground that it raised a question of federal law.

cp-grable.sentence: The district court denied Grable’s request to return to state court because the title claim necessarily raised federal notice law even without a federal private quiet-title remedy against the purchaser.
cp-grable.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) refused Grable’s request to send the case back to state court. Grable’s “title” claim necessarily raised federal notice law, even though federal law gave Grable no “private quiet-title remedy,” meaning no federal right of its own to sue the buyer to settle ownership.

cp-grable.sentence: It then granted Darue summary judgment, reading the statute to require personal service but allowing substantial compliance.
cp-grable.plain: The court then “granted” Darue summary judgment, ruling for it without a trial. It read the statute to require personal service, but held that “substantial compliance” (coming close enough, here by certified mail) was enough.

cp-grable.sentence: Justice Souter’s unanimous opinion asked whether this state claim could originally fit 28 U.S.C. § 1331.
cp-grable.plain: Justice Souter’s “unanimous” opinion (all Justices agreeing) asked whether this state-law claim could have been filed in federal court originally under 28 U.S.C. § 1331, the statute giving federal courts power over cases “arising under” federal law.

cp-grable.sentence: Such jurisdiction required a necessary, actually disputed, substantial federal question and compatibility with Congress’s division of state and federal judicial work.
cp-grable.plain: Such “jurisdiction” over a state claim required a “substantial federal question” that is necessary to the claim, actually disputed, and important beyond this case. It also had to fit the division of work Congress set between state and federal courts.

cp-grable.sentence: Government had an interest in a federal forum testing its administrative acts, and taxpayers and purchasers could benefit from federal tax experience.
cp-grable.plain: The Government had an interest in a federal “forum” (court) testing whether its tax-collection steps were valid. Taxpayers and buyers of seized property could also benefit from federal judges’ tax experience.

cp-grable.sentence: Congress’s omission of a remedy mattered as evidence of intent, not an automatic veto.
cp-grable.plain: Congress’s choice not to create a federal “remedy” (a right to sue) mattered as “evidence” of what Congress intended. But it was not an automatic veto on federal jurisdiction.

cp-grable.sentence: In Merrell Dow, federal jurisdiction whenever state negligence relied on a federal standard threatened to shift a large body of traditional tort work.
cp-grable.plain: In Merrell Dow, allowing federal jurisdiction whenever a state negligence claim relied on a federal standard would have shifted a large body of traditional “tort” work (suits over injuries) into federal court.

cp-grable.sentence: That suggestion did not replace the Court’s four-part embedded-issue test or decide whether certified mail complied.
cp-grable.plain: Thomas’s suggestion (limiting § 1331 to claims federal law itself creates) did not replace the Court’s four-part “embedded-issue” test for state claims with a federal issue built in. Nor did the Court decide whether certified mail complied with the statute.

cp-scott.sentence: The claim reviewed by the Supreme Court alleged excessive force constituting an unreasonable Fourth Amendment seizure; other claims and defendants remained outside review.
cp-scott.plain: The claim the Supreme Court reviewed “alleged” (claimed) excessive force: that pushing Harris’s car off the road was an unreasonable seizure under the Fourth Amendment. Other claims and defendants were outside the Court’s “review.”

cp-scott.sentence: The district court denied Scott’s qualified-immunity summary-judgment motion.
cp-scott.plain: The district court (the trial court) denied Scott’s “motion” for summary judgment on qualified-immunity grounds. Qualified immunity shields officers from suit unless they violated clearly established law.

cp-scott.sentence: On interlocutory appeal, the Eleventh Circuit agreed a jury could find unconstitutional deadly force and sufficiently established unlawfulness to defeat immunity.
cp-scott.plain: On “interlocutory appeal,” an immediate appeal before the case ended, the Eleventh Circuit agreed a jury could find Scott used unconstitutional deadly force. It also held the unlawfulness was clearly established enough to defeat his “immunity.”

cp-scott.sentence: For that motion, they accepted an account of fast but controlled driving, little actual danger to others, and a largely clear roadway at intervention.
cp-scott.plain: For deciding that “motion,” the lower courts accepted Harris’s account: fast but controlled driving, little actual danger to others, and a largely clear road when Scott intervened.

cp-scott.sentence: Under the then-mandatory Saucier sequence, the Supreme Court addressed constitutional violation first.
cp-scott.plain: Under the “Saucier sequence,” then mandatory, courts first had to decide whether the officer violated the Constitution, and only then whether the law was clearly established. So the Supreme Court addressed the constitutional violation first.

cp-scott.sentence: Justice Scalia’s eight-Justice opinion reaffirmed favorable treatment of a nonmovant’s evidence and reasonable inferences.
cp-scott.plain: Justice Scalia’s “opinion” for eight Justices reaffirmed the usual summary-judgment rule. The court views the evidence of the “nonmovant” (the side opposing the motion) favorably and draws “reasonable inferences” (sensible conclusions from the evidence) in its favor.

cp-scott.sentence: An account plainly contradicted by the record so that no reasonable jury could believe it need not govern.
cp-scott.plain: But if one side’s account is so plainly contradicted by the record, here the video, that no “reasonable jury” could believe it, the court need not accept that account.

cp-scott.sentence: After selecting supportable facts and inferences, it treated constitutional reasonableness as legal.
cp-scott.plain: After picking out the facts and “inferences” the record could support, the Court treated whether Scott’s action was constitutionally reasonable as a legal question for judges.

cp-scott.sentence: Scott conceded a seizure because he deliberately terminated movement by hitting Harris’s car.
cp-scott.plain: Scott conceded a “seizure” under the Fourth Amendment, because he deliberately stopped Harris’s movement by hitting Harris’s car. So the question was whether that seizure was reasonable.

cp-scott.sentence: The Court rejected treating that label as a mechanical trigger.
cp-scott.plain: The Court refused to treat the “deadly force” label as a mechanical trigger for Tennessee v. Garner’s strict requirements, such as necessity and warning. The question remained whether the force was reasonable.

cp-scott.sentence: He proposed ending mandatory Saucier sequencing because unnecessary constitutional decisions could consume resources, rest on poor records, or evade review when immunity still protected defendants.
cp-scott.plain: Justice Breyer proposed ending mandatory “Saucier sequencing” (deciding the constitutional question first). Unnecessary constitutional rulings could waste resources, rest on poor records, or “evade review,” escaping appeal, when immunity still protected the “defendants.”

cp-scott.sentence: He agreed flight deserved punishment but thought those facts did not establish potentially lethal intervention’s necessity as a matter of law.
cp-scott.plain: Justice Stevens, dissenting, agreed Harris’s flight deserved punishment. But he thought the facts did not establish “as a matter of law” (so clearly that no jury could disagree) that potentially lethal intervention was necessary.

cp-scott.sentence: The result rested on no constitutional violation, not a separate conclusion excusing an established violation through qualified immunity.
cp-scott.plain: Scott won because the Court found no constitutional violation at all. It did not separately conclude that “qualified immunity” excused an established violation.

cp-walmart.sentence: Under Title VII, they claimed both disparate impact from discretionary practices and disparate treatment through the company’s awareness and failure to control them.
cp-walmart.plain: Under Title VII, the federal job-discrimination law, the women claimed “disparate impact”: that letting managers decide pay and promotions freely hurt women disproportionately. They also claimed “disparate treatment” (intentional discrimination), because the company knew of this and failed to control it.

cp-walmart.sentence: The district court certified the class under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(a) and Rule 23(b)(2), which concerns injunctive or declaratory relief.
cp-walmart.plain: The district court (the trial court) certified the class under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(a), the basic class requirements, and Rule 23(b)(2). That type of class seeks injunctive relief (court orders) or “declaratory relief” (court declarations of rights) for the whole group.

cp-walmart.sentence: It found a common question about corporate policies and allowed backpay claims because monetary relief did not predominate over prospective relief.
cp-walmart.plain: The appeals court found a common question about corporate policies. It allowed “backpay” (lost wages) claims because “monetary relief” did not “predominate,” meaning money was not the main relief sought compared with forward-looking changes.

cp-walmart.sentence: It also accepted possible use of sample claims and extrapolation to calculate classwide relief.
cp-walmart.plain: It also accepted possible use of “sample claims,” deciding some claims and extrapolating (projecting) the results, to calculate “classwide” relief for everyone.

cp-walmart.sentence: Scalia, joined on commonality by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, required a common contention whose resolution would answer an issue central to every member’s claim.
cp-walmart.plain: Scalia, joined on commonality by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, required a common contention (a shared question). Its answer had to resolve an issue central to every member’s claim at once.

cp-walmart.sentence: Plaintiffs had to affirmatively establish the certification requirements through rigorous analysis, even when that analysis overlapped with the merits.
cp-walmart.plain: Plaintiffs had to affirmatively prove the class-action requirements were met, and the court had to apply “rigorous analysis” to them. That held even when the analysis overlapped with “the merits,” meaning the discrimination claims themselves.

cp-walmart.sentence: His evidence was inadequate even assuming admissibility; the Court questioned the refusal to apply Daubert at certification but did not decide that evidentiary issue.
cp-walmart.plain: Even assuming “admissibility” (that the court could consider it), the sociologist’s “evidence” did not prove a common policy. The Court doubted the refusal to apply Daubert, the test for reliable expert testimony, at certification, but did not decide that evidentiary question.

cp-walmart.sentence: The majority said employee differences defeated the proposed common answer, rather than importing the separate predominance requirement of Rule 23(b)(3).
cp-walmart.plain: The “majority” said differences among employees defeated any proposed common answer for all the women. It was not importing the separate “predominance” requirement of Rule 23(b)(3), the stricter damages-class test that common issues outweigh individual ones.

cp-walmart.sentence: That provision concerns an indivisible injunction or corresponding declaration benefiting the class together.
cp-walmart.plain: Rule 23(b)(2) concerns an “indivisible” injunction, a single court order that cannot be split up among members, or a matching declaration that benefits the class all together.

cp-walmart.sentence: Individual monetary claims required the protections of Rule 23(b)(3), including predominance, superiority, notice, and an opportunity to opt out.
cp-walmart.plain: Individual money claims required the protections of Rule 23(b)(3), the damages-class rule. Those include predominance (common issues outweigh individual ones), “superiority” (a class action is the best method), notice to members, and a chance to “opt out,” or leave the class.

cp-walmart.sentence: Sampling and extrapolation could not replace those proceedings and eliminate a substantive defense right consistently with the Rules Enabling Act.
cp-walmart.plain: Sampling and “extrapolation” (deciding some claims and projecting the results to everyone) could not replace individual proceedings. That would wipe out Wal-Mart’s “substantive” right to raise individual defenses, a right court procedure rules cannot take away under the Rules Enabling Act.

cp-walmart.sentence: Emphasizing the district court’s findings, she accused the majority of demanding too much at the commonality stage and confusing that threshold with Rule 23(b)(3)’s more demanding inquiries.
cp-walmart.plain: Relying on the district court’s findings, Ginsburg accused the majority of demanding too much at the “commonality” stage (whether the class shares a common question). She said it confused that threshold with the more demanding inquiries of Rule 23(b)(3), the damages-class rule.

dixon.sentence: They alleged on information and belief that the home’s value exceeded the balance and arrears.
dixon.plain: The Dixons “alleged” (claimed in their complaint) “on information and belief,” meaning they believed it but lacked firsthand proof, that the home was worth more than the loan balance plus “arrears,” the missed payments.

dixon.sentence: The claimed injury arose from entering default in reliance before honest consideration occurred.
dixon.plain: Their harm was that, trusting the bank, they stopped paying and fell into default, and the bank then never honestly considered them for a modification.

dixon.sentence: Wells Fargo removed on March 4 and moved to dismiss on April 11.
dixon.plain: Wells Fargo “removed” the case (moved it from state court to federal court) on March 4. It “moved to dismiss,” asking the judge to throw the case out, on April 11.

dixon.sentence: At a May 9 hearing, Judge William G. Young denied remand and dismissed the insufficiently pleaded ordinary contract claim.
dixon.plain: At a May 9 “hearing,” Judge William G. Young denied “remand” (sending the case back to state court). He dismissed the ordinary breach-of-contract claim because it was not adequately “pleaded,” meaning stated in the complaint.

dixon.sentence: He reserved promissory estoppel and the Home Owners’ Loan Act preemption defense for supplemental briefing.
dixon.plain: He “reserved” (put off deciding) two issues for “supplemental briefing,” more written arguments from the parties. One was promissory estoppel, enforcing a promise because someone reasonably relied on it; the other was the bank’s defense that the federal Home Owners’ Loan Act preempted (overrode) that state-law claim.

dixon.sentence: The federal pleading question was plausibility, leaving promise, reasonable reliance, and injury for proof.
dixon.plain: Under federal “pleading” rules, the question was “plausibility”: whether the complaint described a believable claim. Whether the Dixons could prove the promise, their reasonable reliance, and their injury would come later.

dixon.sentence: The bank contended that an indefinite agreement to agree supplied no obligation and, independently, that federal banking regulation displaced any state claim.
dixon.plain: The bank argued that an “indefinite” agreement to agree, a vague promise to make a deal later, created no obligation. Separately, it argued federal banking “regulation” displaced (overrode) any state-law claim.

dixon.sentence: Massachusetts decisions including Loranger Construction and Rhode Island Hospital Trust v. Varadian treated reliance enforcement as contractual, requiring contract elements apart from consideration.
dixon.plain: Massachusetts decisions, including Loranger Construction and Rhode Island Hospital Trust v. Varadian, treated enforcing a promise because of reliance as contractual. It requires the usual contract “elements,” such as a real commitment, but not “consideration,” meaning something given in exchange.

dixon.sentence: Ordinarily, unresolved essential terms made an agreement to agree unenforceable because courts lacked a standard to know the final bargain and parties retained freedom to reject it.
