dixon.plain: Usually, leaving “essential terms” unresolved makes an “agreement to agree” (a promise to make a deal later) unenforceable. Courts have no standard to know what the final “bargain” would have been, and each side remains free to reject it.

dixon.sentence: This remained a federal prediction, not a new high-court state holding.
dixon.plain: This was only a “federal prediction,” a federal judge’s forecast of how Massachusetts’s highest court would rule. It was not a new holding by that state court, so it does not bind Massachusetts courts.

dixon.sentence: The Dixons would have to prove the claim by a preponderance.
dixon.plain: The Dixons would have to prove their claim by a “preponderance” of the evidence, meaning show it is more likely true than not.

dixon.sentence: Wachovia’s status brought the then-applicable Office of Thrift Supervision regulation, 12 C.F.R. § 560.2, into the Home Owners’ Loan Act analysis.
dixon.plain: Because Wachovia, the original lender, was a federal savings bank, the then-applicable Office of Thrift Supervision regulation, 12 C.F.R. (Code of Federal Regulations) § 560.2, entered the Home Owners’ Loan Act analysis. That federal rule limited state laws affecting such banks’ lending.

dixon.sentence: The regulation occupied specified lending fields, including credit terms and servicing, while allowing contract and tort rules incidentally affecting lending.
dixon.plain: That rule pushed aside state laws regulating lending matters such as loan terms and servicing, but left in place ordinary contract and injury law that only indirectly touches lending.

dixon.sentence: Young found this claim enforced the bank’s voluntary undertaking rather than prescribed loan terms or generally required modifications.
dixon.plain: Judge Young found this claim enforced the bank’s own voluntary “undertaking” (promise). It did not impose state-prescribed loan terms or generally require loan “modifications,” so the federal rule did not block it.

feinberg.sentence: Employment remained at will: she promised no further service, and the company could discharge her.
feinberg.plain: Her employment stayed “at will,” meaning either side could end it at any time. She promised no further service, and the company could fire her.

feinberg.sentence: The parties waived a jury in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis.
feinberg.plain: The “parties” waived (gave up) a jury, letting a judge alone decide the case in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis.

feinberg.sentence: Missouri’s review statute required the appellate court to review law and evidence and enter the judgment that should have been entered.
feinberg.plain: Missouri’s review statute required the “appellate court” (the appeals court) to review both the law and the evidence itself. It then had to enter the judgment that should have been “entered” at trial, rather than only checking for legal mistakes.

feinberg.sentence: The completed thirty-seven years explained corporate gratitude but could not have been exchanged for a later promise.
feinberg.plain: Her past years of work explained why the company was grateful, but work already done cannot be the 'price' paid for a new promise, so it was not consideration.

feinberg.sentence: Feinberg could retire immediately, the board merely hoped she would stay, and she undertook no reciprocal service obligation.
feinberg.plain: She never promised anything in return, so there was no bargain that made the pension a contract.

feinberg.sentence: The court instead applied First Restatement § 90: a promise becomes binding when the promisor should reasonably expect definite and substantial action or forbearance, it actually induces that response, and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice.
feinberg.plain: The court instead applied § 90 of the First Restatement of Contracts (an influential summary of contract law), the rule of promissory estoppel. A promise binds when the “promisor” (the one promising) should reasonably expect definite and substantial action or “forbearance” (refraining from acting), it actually “induces” (brings about) that response, and only enforcement avoids injustice.

feinberg.sentence: Missouri decisions had variously called induced conduct consideration, estoppel, or an implied return promise; § 90 and promissory estoppel best explained this enforcement without a bargain.
feinberg.plain: Earlier Missouri decisions had called “induced” conduct (action a promise brought about) by different names: consideration, estoppel, or an “implied” (unstated) return promise. The court said § 90 and promissory estoppel best explained enforcing this promise without a “bargain,” an exchange.

feinberg.sentence: Commissioner Doerner recommended affirmance, and the court adopted his opinion per curiam on March 17, 1959.
feinberg.plain: Commissioner Doerner, a court officer who drafted opinions, recommended “affirmance” (upholding the judgment). On March 17, 1959, the court adopted his opinion per curiam, as the court’s own unsigned opinion.

feinberg.sentence: The subsequently reproduced Second Restatement permits relief limited as justice requires; that wording was not part of the First Restatement rule this court quoted and applied.
feinberg.plain: The later Second Restatement, reproduced after the opinion, lets courts limit relief “as justice requires,” awarding less than the full promise when fairness calls for it. That wording was not part of the First Restatement rule this court quoted and applied.

ford.sentence: He alleged strict liability for defective design and failure to warn, as well as negligence, and requested compensatory and punitive damages.
ford.plain: Lucero “alleged” (claimed) strict liability, meaning responsibility without proof of fault, for defective design and failure to warn, plus “negligence” (carelessness). He sought compensatory damages for the losses and “punitive damages,” extra money meant to punish Ford.

ford.sentence: Ford sought dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction: its Montana activities, Ford argued, had not generated this claim about a vehicle originally sold in Washington.
ford.plain: Ford sought dismissal for lack of “personal jurisdiction,” the court’s power over Ford as a defendant. It argued its Montana activities had not produced this claim about a vehicle first sold in Washington.

ford.sentence: Ford then asked the Montana Supreme Court to exercise supervisory control, overturn the ruling, and direct dismissal while the tort suit remained pending.
ford.plain: Ford then asked the Montana Supreme Court to use “supervisory control,” an extraordinary power to correct a lower court mid-case. It wanted the court to overturn the trial judge’s “ruling” and order dismissal while the “tort” suit (the injury lawsuit) was still pending.

ford.sentence: That route of review explains the trial court’s appearance in the caption; Lucero remained the claimant in the underlying action.
ford.plain: That route of review explains why the trial court appears in the “caption” (the case title). Lucero was still the “claimant,” the person suing, in the “underlying action,” the original lawsuit.

ford.sentence: At this dismissal stage, Bandemer needed a prima facie jurisdictional showing, and the court accepted the complaint’s allegations and supporting affidavits as true under the governing standard.
ford.plain: At this “dismissal” stage, Bandemer needed only a “prima facie” showing of jurisdiction: facts that, if true, would support it. Under the governing standard, the court accepted as true the “complaint” (his initial court filing) and supporting “affidavits,” sworn written statements.

ford.sentence: Minnesota’s long-arm statute reached the federal due-process boundary.
ford.plain: Minnesota’s “long-arm statute,” its law on suing out-of-state defendants, reached the “federal due-process boundary,” meaning as far as the U.S. Constitution allows.

ford.sentence: Both Minnesota appellate courts left Bandemer’s alternative registered-agent consent theory undecided because specific jurisdiction was sufficient.
ford.plain: Both Minnesota “appellate courts” left undecided Bandemer’s alternative theory of “consent”: that Ford agreed to be sued there by registering an agent to receive legal papers. They did not need it because “specific jurisdiction,” based on the claim’s link to Ford’s activities in the state, was enough.

ford.sentence: These were appeals through the state-court systems, not federal diversity cases, and consolidation did not merge the separate accidents or claims.
ford.plain: These were “appeals” that came up through the state-court systems, not federal “diversity cases” (federal suits between citizens of different states). Deciding them together (consolidation) did not merge the separate accidents or “claims.”

ford.sentence: The parties agreed that Ford was ordinarily at home in Delaware and Michigan and was not subject to general, all-purpose jurisdiction in Montana or Minnesota.
ford.plain: The “parties” agreed Ford was “at home” in Delaware, where it is incorporated, and Michigan, its headquarters. It was not subject to “general, all-purpose jurisdiction” in Montana or Minnesota, meaning it could not be sued there on any claim at all.

ford.sentence: International Shoe required purposeful contacts, an adequate relationship between those contacts and the litigation, and consistency with fair play and substantial justice.
ford.plain: International Shoe, the basic test, required three things: “contacts” the defendant purposely made with the state, an adequate relationship between those contacts and the lawsuit, and consistency with “fair play and substantial justice,” meaning basic fairness.

ford.sentence: The dispute concerned whether the claims had to be caused by Ford’s forum activities to “arise out of or relate to” them.
ford.plain: The dispute was whether Ford’s activities in the state had to have caused the “claims” for the claims to “arise out of or relate to” those activities, or whether a close connection was enough.

ford.sentence: She gave separate work to both parts of “arise out of or relate to.”
ford.plain: Justice Kagan gave each half of the phrase “arise out of or relate to” its own separate meaning.

ford.sentence: The first addresses causation; the second allows some sufficiently close relationships without proving that forum conduct caused the claim.
ford.plain: The first part (“arise out of”) addresses “causation,” whether the defendant’s in-state activity caused the claim. The second (“relate to”) allows some close enough relationships without proof that the defendant’s conduct in the “forum” (the state where the suit is filed) caused the claim.

ford.sentence: The person’s unilateral move did not supply Ford’s contacts; Ford’s established activities in the destination market did.
ford.plain: What counts is Ford's own business in the state, not the car owner's personal choice to move there.

ford.sentence: Kagan acknowledged that the discussion was dictum, then explained that Keeton, Burger King, Goodyear, the O’Connor opinion in Asahi, and Daimler had endorsed the principle.
ford.plain: Kagan admitted World-Wide Volkswagen’s discussion was “dictum,” a statement not needed to decide that case and so not binding. But she explained that later cases had endorsed the principle: Keeton, Burger King, Goodyear, Justice O’Connor’s “opinion” in Asahi, and Daimler.

ford.sentence: Plaintiff connections could help describe that relationship but could not substitute for defendant-created contacts.
ford.plain: The plaintiffs' ties to the state can help show how the claim relates to it, but cannot replace the defendant's own contacts.

ford.sentence: Convenience could not cure absent contacts or absent relatedness.
ford.plain: Convenience could not make up for missing “contacts” (the defendant’s own ties to the state) or missing “relatedness” (a connection between those ties and the claim).

ford.sentence: Alito objected to parsing a judicial phrase like statutory language to create two distinct jurisdictional categories.
ford.plain: Alito objected to parsing a phrase from judicial opinions as if it were statutory language, creating two distinct “jurisdictional” categories (separate grounds for a court’s power over a defendant).

ford.sentence: Extensive business may be insufficient for the former under Goodyear, Daimler, and BNSF while supporting the latter for an appropriately related injury.
ford.plain: Under Goodyear, Daimler, and BNSF, extensive business in a state may not be enough for the former, general jurisdiction (being sued there on any claim). But it can support the latter, specific jurisdiction, for an injury properly related to that business.

hadley.sentence: The millers’ declaration originally had two counts.
hadley.plain: The millers’ declaration, the old name for a plaintiff’s formal written complaint, originally had two “counts,” meaning separate claims.

hadley.sentence: The surviving count alleged failure to use due care and diligence to deliver within a reasonable time.
hadley.plain: The surviving “count” (claim) alleged that the carriers failed to use “due care” and diligence, meaning reasonable care and effort, to deliver within a reasonable time.

hadley.sentence: The carriers paid £25 into court as satisfaction; the millers said that was insufficient.
hadley.plain: The carriers paid £25 “into court,” depositing it with the court as full satisfaction of what they owed. The millers said that was not enough.

hadley.sentence: At the Gloucester Assizes, Justice Crompton left damages generally to the jury despite the carriers’ objection that lost profits were too remote.
hadley.plain: At the Gloucester Assizes, the traveling trial court for the county, Justice Crompton left “damages” (the money award) generally to the jury. He did so despite the carriers’ objection that lost profits were too “remote,” too far-removed a result of the delay to count.

hadley.sentence: The carriers obtained a rule nisi asking for a new trial because of the instruction.
hadley.plain: The carriers got a provisional order (a 'rule nisi') requiring the millers to show why there should not be a new trial, arguing that the judge had instructed the jury wrongly.

hadley.sentence: Recoverable loss must fairly and reasonably arise naturally in the usual course from breach, or have been reasonably contemplated by both parties at formation as its probable result.
hadley.plain: “Recoverable” loss, the kind a breaching party must pay for, must fairly and reasonably arise naturally, in the usual course of things, from the breach. Otherwise it must have been reasonably “contemplated” (expected) by both parties, when they made the contract, as the probable result of a breach.

hadley.sentence: Communication of special circumstances could make their ordinary consequences recoverable.
hadley.plain: Telling the other side about “special circumstances,” unusual facts about one’s situation, could make the ordinary consequences of those circumstances recoverable.

hadley.sentence: Notice gave parties an opportunity to arrange special terms for increased risk.
hadley.plain: Being told gives the other side a chance to charge more, take extra care, or refuse the bigger risk.

hadley.sentence: Causation therefore did not establish that profits were within recoverable contractual risk.
hadley.plain: “Causation,” the fact that the delay really caused the lost profits, therefore did not show the profits were within the contractual risk the carriers took on. So they were not “recoverable.”

hadley.sentence: The Court of Exchequer made the rule absolute and ordered a new trial.
hadley.plain: The Court of Exchequer, an English common-law court, made the rule absolute, turning its provisional order (the rule nisi) into a final one, and ordered a new trial.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Section 6(b)(5), addressing toxic substances and harmful physical agents, directed the Secretary of Labor to provide the most adequate assurance, to the extent feasible and on the best available evidence, against material impairment over a working lifetime.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Section 6(b)(5), on toxic substances and harmful physical agents, directed the Secretary of Labor to set the standard that most adequately assures workers against material impairment (serious health harm) over a working lifetime. That duty runs “to the extent feasible,” meaning as far as achievable, and on the best available evidence.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: In 1976 it identified benzene as a human carcinogen and recommended one part per million (ppm), based on detection limits and background exposure rather than a demonstrated safe threshold or feasibility evaluation.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: In 1976 the federal workplace-health research agency identified benzene as a human “carcinogen” (a cancer-causing substance) and recommended a limit of one part per million (ppm). That figure rested on detection limits and background exposure, not on a proven safe level or a “feasibility” study of whether it was achievable.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: The Secretary presumed no safe cancer threshold unless industry proved one.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: The Secretary presumed there is no safe level of exposure to a cancer-causing substance unless industry proved one.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Before issuing a permanent standard, the Secretary had to find a significant risk of material impairment under existing conditions and a prospect that the new standard would eliminate or reduce it.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Before issuing a “permanent standard” (a lasting rule, as opposed to an emergency one), the Secretary had to find a significant risk of material impairment under existing conditions. He also had to find that the new standard would likely eliminate or reduce that risk.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Stevens required clearer congressional authorization for that breadth and invoked constitutional avoidance because such open-ended power could raise delegation problems.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Stevens required clearer authorization from Congress for power that broad. He invoked “constitutional avoidance,” reading a statute to avoid serious constitutional doubts, because such open-ended power could raise “delegation problems”: concerns that Congress handed its lawmaking power to an agency.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: That was a statutory construction reinforced by constitutional concern, not a holding invalidating the Act.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: That was a “statutory construction” (an interpretation of the statute) reinforced by constitutional concern. It was not a “holding” that struck down the Act.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: In Part III–D, joined only by Burger and Stewart, Stevens placed the substantial-evidence burden on the agency instead of requiring industry to prove safety.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: In Part III–D, joined only by Burger and Stewart, Stevens put the “substantial-evidence” burden on the agency: it had to support its risk finding with solid evidence. Industry did not have to prove benzene was safe.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Judicial review could not invent a rationale or findings the Secretary had not used.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: “Judicial review” (courts checking the agency’s action) could not invent a rationale or “findings” the Secretary had not actually used.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: He also expressly reserved whether an alternative statutory interpretation would violate nondelegation, despite joining Part III–B.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Powell also expressly “reserved” (left undecided) whether an alternative “statutory interpretation” would violate “nondelegation,” the principle that Congress cannot hand its lawmaking power to an agency. He did so even though he joined Part III–B of Stevens’s opinion.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Justice Rehnquist concurred in the judgment on nondelegation grounds.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Justice Rehnquist “concurred in the judgment,” meaning he agreed with the result but not the reasoning. His ground was nondelegation: Congress had unconstitutionally handed its own lawmaking job to the agency.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Congress had not supplied the political decision, intelligible administrative guidance, or standards for judicial review.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Congress had not made the basic political decision itself, given the agency intelligible guidance, or supplied standards for “judicial review,” meaning for courts to check the agency’s work.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: Rehnquist supplied the fifth vote for the judgment without converting Stevens’s plurality interpretation into a majority opinion or invalidating the statute for the Court.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Rehnquist’s vote made five for the “judgment” (the outcome). But it did not turn Stevens’s “plurality” reading, the view of the largest group short of a majority, into a majority opinion, and it did not strike down the “statute” on behalf of the Court.

lrs-i-benzene.sentence: He rejected the industry argument that “material” excluded low-probability harms: the words concerned material impairment, not material risk of impairment.
lrs-i-benzene.plain: Marshall rejected the industry argument that “material” excluded unlikely harms. The statute speaks of “material impairment,” so “material” describes how serious the harm is, not how likely; it does not say material risk of impairment.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: That statute broadly waived federal sovereign immunity for specified injuries caused by employees acting within the scope of employment when a private person would be liable under the law of the place of the conduct.
lrs-k-raila.plain: That “statute,” the Federal Tort Claims Act, broadly waived the federal government’s “sovereign immunity,” its usual protection from being sued. It covers specified injuries caused by federal employees acting within the “scope of employment” (on the job), whenever a private person would be liable under the law of the place where the conduct happened.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: But 28 U.S.C. §2680(b) retained immunity for claims arising from loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.
lrs-k-raila.plain: But 28 U.S.C. §2680(b) kept the government’s “immunity” for claims arising from the loss, “miscarriage” (misdelivery), or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: On February 26, 2003, District Judge Covello agreed and dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
lrs-k-raila.plain: On February 26, 2003, District Judge Covello agreed and “dismissed” the case for lack of subject-matter “jurisdiction,” meaning the court had no power to hear this kind of claim against the government.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: The Second Circuit heard argument on November 6, 2003, and reviewed the jurisdictional ruling and statutory interpretation anew, accepting the allegations and favorable reasonable inferences.
lrs-k-raila.plain: The Second Circuit heard argument on November 6, 2003. It “reviewed” the jurisdictional “ruling” and the statute’s interpretation “anew,” deciding them fresh without deferring to the trial judge. It accepted the Railas’ “allegations” as true and drew “reasonable inferences” in their favor.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: Its opinion used the then-prevailing no-set-of-facts formulation for dismissal.
lrs-k-raila.plain: Its “opinion” used the “no-set-of-facts” test then in force for dismissal: a case could be dismissed only if no set of facts the plaintiffs could prove would support their claim.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: It assessed ambiguity within the whole statutory scheme rather than treating a dictionary definition in isolation.
lrs-k-raila.plain: The court judged “ambiguity” (whether the words were unclear) by reading them within the whole “statutory scheme,” the law as a whole, rather than relying on a dictionary definition in isolation.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: Read alongside them, negligent transmission addressed the same kind of postal mishap, not every common-law injury inflicted while delivering mail.
lrs-k-raila.plain: Read alongside “loss” and “miscarriage,” “negligent transmission” addressed the same kind of postal mishap: harm to, or failure of, the mail itself. It did not cover every “common-law” injury (an ordinary judge-made tort such as negligence) caused while delivering mail.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: The postal exception instead enumerated particular wrongs.
lrs-k-raila.plain: The “postal exception” instead listed particular wrongs, rather than using broad language covering everything postal workers do.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: It found the contrasting results an absurd consequence supporting the narrower reading.
lrs-k-raila.plain: The court found those contrasting results, treating similar injuries differently depending on whether mail was involved, an “absurd consequence.” That supported reading the exception narrowly.

lrs-k-raila.sentence: The panel declined to select an immunity rule by forecasting caseload; its task was to interpret Congress’s words and intent, and Congress could amend the statute.
lrs-k-raila.plain: The panel refused to pick an “immunity” rule by forecasting how many lawsuits would follow. Its task was to interpret Congress’s words and intent, and Congress could “amend” (change) the statute if it disliked the result.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: After the union filed an unfair-labor-practice charge, the administrative law judge found the dealership a successor employer, carrying a bargaining obligation and a rebuttable presumption of continuing majority support.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: After the union filed an “unfair-labor-practice” charge (a complaint that the employer broke labor law), the “administrative law judge,” the agency’s hearing judge, found the dealership a “successor employer” that took over the old business and workforce. So it had a “bargaining” obligation (a duty to negotiate with the union) and faced a “rebuttable presumption” of continuing “majority support,” meaning the union was presumed to keep most workers’ backing unless the employer showed otherwise.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: He found compliance with polling safeguards but insufficient objective reasonable doubt beforehand.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: The judge found the vote itself was run fairly, but said the employer lacked enough solid evidence beforehand to justify holding it.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: The National Labor Relations Board adopted that conclusion and ordered recognition and bargaining.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: The National Labor Relations Board, the federal labor agency, adopted that conclusion. It ordered the dealership to recognize the union and begin “bargaining” (negotiating) with it.
A divided D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court in Washington, enforced the Board’s order, making it legally binding.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: The historical framework permitted a Board election, withdrawal of recognition, or internal poll, using the same good-faith reasonable-doubt threshold for the challenged alternatives.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: Under the historical framework, an employer doubting union support could seek a Board election, withdraw “recognition” (stop dealing with the union), or poll its own workers. The two challenged options, withdrawal and polling, used the same “good-faith reasonable-doubt” threshold: an honest doubt based on objective evidence.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: Justice Scalia’s Part II majority acknowledged awkwardness but sustained the standard.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: Justice Scalia’s Part II majority admitted the rule was awkward but “sustained” (upheld) the standard.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: Scalia’s Parts III and IV asked whether a reasonable factfinder could conclude that Allentown lacked genuine, reasonable uncertainty.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: Scalia’s Parts III and IV asked whether a reasonable “factfinder,” the body deciding the facts, could conclude that Allentown lacked genuine, “reasonable uncertainty” about the union’s majority support.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: Objective evidence meant material outside subjective impressions supporting uncertainty, not conclusive proof that the union lacked a majority.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: 'Objective' evidence meant actual facts, such as what workers said, that gave reason to doubt, not proof that the union had lost its majority.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: It could not use continuity to impose bargaining while disregarding it entirely for contrary evidence.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: The Board could not use workforce continuity to impose bargaining while entirely ignoring it when it supported contrary “evidence,” such as a report that workers opposed the union.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: Fair treatment of this circumstantial record therefore required a finding of reasonable doubt.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: Fair treatment of this “circumstantial” record (indirect evidence, from which conclusions must be inferred) therefore required a “finding” that Allentown had reasonable doubt.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: Reasoned decisionmaking governs adjudication as well as rulemaking; covert changes in substance or proof burden confuse hearing judges, frustrate review, and conceal policy choices.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: “Reasoned decisionmaking,” honest and logical explanation of decisions, governs an agency’s adjudication (deciding individual cases) as well as its “rulemaking” (making general rules). Secretly changing the substance of a standard or the burden of proof confuses the agency’s “hearing” judges, frustrates court review, and hides policy choices.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: Substantial-evidence review already deferred by asking what a reasonable factfinder could find; an extra layer of deference to an eccentric evidentiary understanding would erase review.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: “Substantial-evidence” review already gives deference by asking only what a reasonable “factfinder” could find. An extra layer of “deference” to the Board’s eccentric understanding of evidence would erase review altogether.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: He thought the application question outside the certiorari grant and Supreme Court intervention in substantial-evidence review unusually unwarranted.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: Breyer thought the question of how the standard applied here fell outside the “certiorari” grant, the specific question the Court agreed to review. He also thought Supreme Court intervention in ordinary “substantial-evidence” review of agency factfinding was unusually unwarranted.

lrs-n-allentown-mack.sentence: The Supreme Court reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded with instructions to deny enforcement of the bargaining order.
lrs-n-allentown-mack.plain: The Supreme Court “reversed” (overturned) the D.C. Circuit and “remanded” (sent the case back). It instructed that court to deny “enforcement of the bargaining order,” refusing to make the Board’s order to negotiate legally binding.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: The Fair Labor Standards Act generally requires overtime pay but exempts bona fide administrative employees as defined by Department of Labor regulations.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: The Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal wage law, generally requires overtime pay. But it “exempts” (excludes) bona fide administrative “employees,” genuine administrative workers, as defined by Department of Labor “regulations,” its binding rules.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: In 2004 the Department revised its regulations through notice and comment.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: In 2004 the Department revised its “regulations” (binding rules) through notice and comment, publishing a proposal and taking public comments first.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: In 2010 an Administrator’s Interpretation changed position again.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: In 2010 an Administrator’s Interpretation, an official guidance document from the head of the agency’s wage division, changed the agency’s position again.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: The Mortgage Bankers Association, or MBA, challenged the 2010 interpretation under the Administrative Procedure Act, or APA, on both procedural and arbitrary-and-capricious grounds.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: The Mortgage Bankers Association, or MBA, challenged the 2010 interpretation under the Administrative Procedure Act, or APA, the law governing how federal agencies act. It argued both that the agency used the wrong procedure and that the decision was “arbitrary-and-capricious,” meaning unreasonable or unexplained.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: Applying the D.C. Circuit’s Paralyzed Veterans doctrine, it found no substantial and justifiable reliance sufficient to require notice and comment for the change.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: Applying the D.C. Circuit’s Paralyzed Veterans doctrine, the trial court asked whether people had substantially and justifiably relied on the old interpretation. It found no reliance strong enough to require notice and comment for the change.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: It held that a significant revision of a definitive regulatory interpretation required notice and comment even without reliance, and the Department conceded a prior conflicting interpretation.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: The D.C. Circuit held that a significant revision of a definitive (settled) “regulatory” interpretation, an agency’s reading of its own regulation, required notice and comment even without reliance. The Department admitted it had earlier taken a conflicting interpretation.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: Section 553 generally requires notice and comment but exempts interpretive rules, general policy statements, and rules of organization, procedure, or practice, subject to notice or hearing independently required by another statute.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: “Section 553” of the APA generally requires notice and comment before agencies issue rules. It exempts “interpretive rules” (guidance explaining existing law), general policy statements, and rules of organization, procedure, or practice, unless another “statute” independently requires “notice or hearing.”

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: Legislative rules carry the force and effect of law; interpretive rules advise the public how an agency understands the statutes and regulations it administers and lack independent legal force.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: “Legislative rules” carry the “force and effect of law,” meaning they bind like a statute. Interpretive rules only tell the public how an agency understands the “statutes” and regulations it administers, and have no legal force of their own.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: Vermont Yankee had established that courts cannot add procedural requirements to those the APA prescribes because they consider them desirable administration.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: Vermont Yankee, an earlier Supreme Court case, held that courts cannot add procedural steps beyond those the APA requires just because they think the steps would make for better administration.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: The D.C. Circuit’s doctrine nevertheless imposed a judicially created notice-and-comment condition on an expressly exempt class and therefore conflicted with the APA.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: The D.C. Circuit’s doctrine nevertheless imposed a court-made notice-and-comment requirement on a class of rules the APA expressly exempts. So it conflicted with the APA.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: MBA also invoked Auer deference to an agency’s understanding of its own regulation.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: MBA also invoked “Auer deference,” the rule that courts defer to an agency’s reading of its own regulation. It suggested that this deference gives such readings the force of binding rules.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: Even assuming it had not waived the point below, MBA omitted it from its certiorari opposition contrary to Supreme Court Rule 15.2.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: Even assuming MBA had not “waived” (given up) the argument “below,” in the lower courts, it left the point out of its brief opposing “certiorari” (Supreme Court review). Supreme Court Rule 15.2 requires such points to be raised there, so MBA lost the argument.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: He thought APA § 706 assigns interpretation to courts, which should independently decide the meaning of agency regulations.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: Justice Scalia thought APA § 706, which tells reviewing courts to decide questions of law, gives interpretation to courts. So courts should independently decide what agency regulations mean, rather than defer to agencies.

lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.sentence: He traced its origins and expansion, questioned transferring Article III interpretive responsibility to executive officials, and emphasized independent judicial judgment and the checking function.
lrs-n-perez-mortgage-bankers.plain: Justice Thomas traced the deference doctrine’s origins and expansion. He questioned handing executive officials the interpretive duty that Article III, the Constitution’s judiciary article, gives courts, and he stressed “independent judicial judgment” and the courts’ role in checking the other branches.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: In 2001, the Band asked the Secretary of the Interior to acquire the Bradley Property in Wayland Township, Michigan, in trust under §5 of the Indian Reorganization Act, then codified at 25 U.S.C. §465.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: In 2001, the Band asked the Secretary of the Interior to acquire the Bradley Property in Wayland Township, Michigan, “in trust,” meaning the United States would own it for the tribe’s benefit. It relied on §5 of the Indian Reorganization Act, a 1934 law then codified (placed in the U.S. Code) at 25 U.S.C. §465.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: Federal trust ownership could satisfy the land requirements of the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: Federal “trust ownership,” the U.S. holding land for a tribe, could satisfy the land requirements for a casino under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: An injunction preventing acquisition was consequently moot, but everyone agreed that Patchak’s continuing suit effectively sought to divest the government of title.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: Once the government took title, an “injunction” (court order) to prevent the purchase was “moot,” meaning too late to matter. But everyone agreed that Patchak’s continuing suit effectively sought to “divest” the government of title, taking ownership away from it.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: The Supreme Court subsequently decided Carcieri, holding that the Secretary’s acquisition authority depended on a tribe’s being under federal jurisdiction in 1934.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: The Supreme Court then decided Carcieri, holding that the Secretary’s power to acquire land depended on the tribe having been under federal “jurisdiction” (authority) in 1934.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: It held that his interests fell outside the acquisition statute’s zone of interests.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: The trial court held that Patchak’s interests fell outside the acquisition statute’s zone of interests: they were not the kind of interests that law protects or regulates, so he could not sue under it.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: APA §702 generally waived federal sovereign immunity for suits seeking nonmonetary relief against official action, but withheld that waiver where another consent-to-suit statute expressly or impliedly forbade the requested relief.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: APA §702 generally “waived” (gave up) federal sovereign immunity for suits seeking nonmonetary relief, such as court orders, against official action. But the waiver did not apply where another “consent-to-suit” statute, a law allowing suits against the government, expressly or impliedly forbade the relief requested.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: That statute permitted certain suits involving competing property interests while excluding trust or restricted Indian lands.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: That “statute,” the Quiet Title Act, allowed certain suits over competing property claims against the government, but excluded “trust” or restricted Indian lands, land the U.S. holds for tribes.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: The majority distinguished the kind of claim from the practical consequence of relief.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: The “majority” separated the kind of claim from the practical result of “relief” (what the plaintiff would get by winning).

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: An adverse owner could not evade the Indian-lands exception by calling a quiet-title suit an APA action.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: An “adverse owner,” someone claiming to own the land against the government, could not get around the Indian-lands exception by relabeling a “quiet-title suit” (a suit to settle ownership) as an APA action.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: The majority described the APA zone-of-interests test as relatively undemanding: a plaintiff’s interest need only arguably fall within interests the allegedly violated statute protected or regulated.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: The “majority” called the APA zone-of-interests test relatively undemanding. A “plaintiff’s” interest need only arguably fall within the interests that the “allegedly” violated statute (the law the plaintiff says was broken) protects or regulates.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: Patchak’s alleged economic, environmental, and aesthetic injuries made a foreseeably affected neighbor a reasonable challenger to the statutory limits on that acquisition.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: Patchak’s “alleged” (claimed) economic, environmental, and aesthetic injuries made him, a neighbor “foreseeably” (predictably) affected by the casino, a reasonable challenger to the “statutory” limits on the government’s power to acquire the land.

lrs-n-standing-patchak.sentence: She read APA §702’s exception as concerned with forbidden relief: Patchak sought divestiture of Indian trust land, precisely the consequence Congress had restricted through the Quiet Title Act.
lrs-n-standing-patchak.plain: Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, read the exception in APA §702 as concerned with forbidden “relief.” Patchak sought “divestiture,” taking the Indian trust land away from the government, which was precisely the result Congress had restricted through the Quiet Title Act.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: Willful violations permitted actual damages or $100–$1,000 statutory damages, fees and costs, and potentially punitive damages.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: For “willful” violations (knowing or reckless), a person could recover actual damages or “statutory damages” of $100–$1,000, a fixed amount set by the law without proving loss. Fees and costs, and possibly punitive damages, were also available.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: The Court assumed Spokeo qualified as a consumer reporting agency solely for this opinion.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: Solely for this “opinion,” the Court assumed without deciding that Spokeo was a “consumer reporting agency,” the kind of business the credit-reporting law covers.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: The district court initially declined jurisdictional dismissal, reconsidered, and dismissed with prejudice for inadequate injury in fact.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: The district court first refused a “jurisdictional” dismissal, then reconsidered. It “dismissed with prejudice” (for good, barring refiling) because Robins had not adequately shown “injury in fact,” a real harm to himself, which standing to sue requires.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: A named plaintiff proposing a class still had to plead his own concrete and particularized, actual or imminent injury, along with traceability and likely redressability.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: A “named plaintiff” proposing a class still had to “plead” (state in his complaint) his own injury that was “concrete” (real) and particularized, and actual or “imminent” (about to happen). He also needed “traceability” (Spokeo caused it) and likely “redressability” (a court ruling could fix it).

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: Particularization asks whether harm affects the person individually; the Ninth Circuit’s own-rights and individualized-data discussion addressed that.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: “Particularization” asks whether the harm affects the person individually. The Ninth Circuit’s discussion of Robins’s own rights and his individualized data addressed that requirement.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: Concreteness separately asks whether a real rather than abstract injury exists.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: 'Concrete' asks a separate question: is the harm real, or only on paper?

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: For statutory intangible interests, the Court looked to a close relationship with harms traditionally supporting English or American lawsuits and to Congress’s judgment.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: For intangible (non-physical) interests created by statute, the Court looked to whether the harm closely resembles harms that traditionally supported lawsuits in English or American courts. It also considered Congress’s “judgment” about which harms matter.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: A bare procedural violation disconnected from concrete harm was not enough merely because legislation supplied a cause of action.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: A bare procedural violation, one disconnected from any “concrete” (real) harm, was not enough just because a statute supplied a “cause of action,” a right to sue.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: On May 16, 2016, it vacated and remanded rather than affirming the district court’s dismissal.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: On May 16, 2016, the Court “vacated” (canceled) the Ninth Circuit’s ruling and remanded, rather than “affirming” (approving) the district court’s “dismissal.” The case went back for the correct test to be applied, without deciding who wins.

lrs-n-standing-spokeo.sentence: Invasion of one’s property, contract, or other private right could support suit without separately proved damages, while private enforcement of public duties ordinarily needed special individual injury, subject to his preserved qui tam exception.
lrs-n-standing-spokeo.plain: Justice Thomas said invasion of a person’s own property, “contract,” or other “private right” could support suit without separately proved “damages” (losses). But a private person enforcing duties owed to the public ordinarily needed a special individual injury, apart from his preserved exception for “qui tam” suits, where private citizens sue on the government’s behalf.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: In 1971, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) adopted a consensus limit of fifty parts per million (ppm) averaged over eight hours.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: In 1971, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) adopted a “consensus limit,” taken from existing private safety standards, of fifty parts per million (ppm) averaged over eight hours.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: By June 1984, OSHA prepared an unpublished final draft with a one-ppm eight-hour permissible exposure limit, or PEL, and a ten-ppm short-term exposure limit, or STEL, averaged over fifteen minutes.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: By June 1984, OSHA had an unpublished final draft with two limits. One was a one-ppm “permissible exposure limit,” or PEL, the most a worker may be exposed to averaged over an eight-hour day. The other was a ten-ppm “short-term exposure limit,” or STEL, a cap on exposure averaged over fifteen minutes.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: Under Executive Order 12,291, OSHA sent the draft to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
lrs-o-tyson.plain: Under Executive Order 12,291, a presidential directive requiring review of major rules, OSHA sent the draft to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the White House budget office.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: Public Citizen Health Research Group attacked the STEL refusal and alleged unlawful surrender of agency decisionmaking to OMB; members of Congress supported that argument as amici.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: Public Citizen Health Research Group attacked OSHA’s refusal to adopt the STEL (the short-term limit). It “alleged” (claimed) the “agency” had unlawfully surrendered its decisionmaking to OMB, the White House budget office, and members of Congress backed that argument as amici, outside “friends of the court.”

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: Section 6(f) required substantial evidence on the record as a whole.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: Section 6(f) of the statute required “substantial evidence,” enough that a reasonable mind could accept it, considering the “record as a whole,” meaning everything before the agency.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: OSHA’s hybrid rulemaking mixed findings, legislative judgments, and scientific predictions.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: OSHA's rulemaking combined factual findings, policy choices, and scientific predictions.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: The Benzene decision, Industrial Union Department v. American Petroleum Institute, required an evidentiary foundation for significant risk while permitting scientifically supported conservative estimates at the frontiers of knowledge.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: The Benzene decision, Industrial Union Department v. American Petroleum Institute, required real evidence showing a significant risk. But it permitted cautious, scientifically supported estimates where knowledge runs out.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: For risk, OSHA extrapolated from the Bushy Run rat study using a linear no-threshold model and animal-to-human conversion.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: To estimate risk, OSHA extrapolated (projected) from the Bushy Run rat study using a “linear no-threshold” model, which assumes any exposure carries some risk in proportion to the dose. It then converted the rat results to humans.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: OSHA assumed eight-hour compliance captured virtually all STEL benefits, but that required information about actual exposure patterns.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: OSHA assumed that meeting the eight-hour limit would capture virtually all the benefits of a STEL (a short-term limit). But that assumption required information about how exposure actually happens in workplaces.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: OSHA made no adequate findings showing that real workplace patterns caused PEL compliance to subsume the STEL.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: OSHA made no adequate “findings” that real workplace exposure patterns meant compliance with the PEL (the eight-hour limit) would subsume, or fully cover, the protection of a STEL.

lrs-o-tyson.sentence: Because statutory review supplied a remand, the court declined the constitutional questions about OMB.
lrs-o-tyson.plain: Because ordinary “statutory” review already justified a “remand” (sending the issue back to the agency), the court declined to decide the constitutional questions about the role of OMB.

parker.sentence: It also said Fox need not use her services but must pay the guarantee subject to the agreement’s terms.
parker.plain: The contract also said Fox did not have to actually use her services, but had to pay the guaranteed amount, subject to the agreement’s terms.

parker.sentence: Fox admitted the contract’s validity, her compliance and readiness to perform, and its own anticipatory repudiation.
parker.plain: Fox admitted the contract was valid, that she had complied and was ready to perform, and its own “anticipatory repudiation”: announcing, before performance was due, that it would not keep the contract.

parker.sentence: Its only defense was that she unreasonably failed to mitigate by rejecting Big Country.
parker.plain: Fox’s only “defense” was that she unreasonably failed to “mitigate,” meaning reduce her losses, by turning down the lead role in Big Country.

parker.sentence: Though she had not begun Bloomer Girl, the parties stipulated for the motion that she had been discharged so wrongful-discharge damages principles applied.
parker.plain: Although she had not started work on Bloomer Girl, the parties “stipulated” (formally agreed) for this motion that she had been discharged (fired). So the damages rules for “wrongful-discharge” cases applied.

parker.sentence: The trial court awarded Parker $750,000 plus interest on summary judgment.
parker.plain: The trial court ruled for Parker without a trial, awarding her the $750,000 guarantee plus interest, because it found no real factual dispute.

parker.sentence: The governing procedure required adequate moving evidence and no genuine material dispute, with strict construction of the movant’s affidavits and doubts favoring trial.
parker.plain: Under the governing summary-judgment procedure, Parker as “movant” (the party asking for judgment without trial) needed adequate supporting “evidence” and no “genuine material dispute,” no real disagreement about an important fact. Her sworn statements were read strictly, and any doubts favored holding a trial.

parker.sentence: An opponent’s admissions could establish facts, but a party’s own conclusory pleading could not substitute for proof.
parker.plain: An opponent’s “admissions” could establish facts. But a party’s own “conclusory” pleading, a bare conclusion in its court papers without supporting facts, could not substitute for proof.

parker.sentence: Before unaccepted work can reduce recovery, however, the employer must establish comparable or substantially similar employment.
parker.plain: Before a job the worker turned down can reduce her “recovery” (what she is owed), the employer must prove the job was “comparable or substantially similar employment,” work of the same kind and quality.

parker.sentence: Fox’s declarations calling the offer comparable and not inferior were conclusions about undisputed terms, not facts creating a triable issue.
parker.plain: Fox’s sworn statements calling the “offer” comparable and not inferior were just conclusions about terms nobody disputed. They were not facts creating a “triable issue,” a factual dispute that needs a trial.

parker.sentence: Recognizing loss of approval rights required neither entertainment expertise nor judicial notice.
parker.plain: Seeing that losing her approval rights made the offer worse required neither film-industry expertise nor “judicial notice,” a court’s acceptance of a fact as common knowledge without proof.

parker.sentence: He also criticized the trial court’s judicial notice of entertainment practices without the opportunity to be heard required by Evidence Code section 455.
parker.plain: Justice Sullivan, dissenting, also faulted the trial court for taking “judicial notice” of entertainment-industry practices (treating them as known without proof). It did so without the “opportunity to be heard” that California’s Evidence Code section 455 requires.

parker.sentence: The agreement’s guarantee therefore was not adjudicated as a general waiver of mitigation.
parker.plain: So the court never “adjudicated” (decided) whether the agreement’s pay guarantee was a “general waiver” of mitigation, meaning that Parker never had to try to reduce her losses at all.

seaver.sentence: It gave Judge Beman lifetime use of the house, with the remainder to the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.
seaver.plain: The will gave Judge Beman “lifetime use” of the house, the right to use it until he died. The “remainder,” the ownership that takes effect after the lifetime use ends, went to the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.

seaver.sentence: He was also residuary legatee and executor.
seaver.plain: He was also the “residuary legatee,” the person who receives whatever is left after the will’s specific gifts, and the executor, the person who manages the estate.

seaver.sentence: Judge Beman offered to rewrite it, but his wife feared she would die before executing a new instrument.
seaver.plain: Judge Beman offered to rewrite the will, but his wife feared she would die before “executing” (signing in the legally required way) a new “instrument,” meaning a new legal document.

seaver.sentence: The trial court reasoned that Beman obtained property through his promise to provide the niece $6,000, the house’s value, and that equity impressed his property with a trust.
seaver.plain: The trial court reasoned that Beman obtained property through his promise to provide the niece $6,000, the house’s value. So “equity,” the branch of law based on fairness, impressed his property with a “trust,” treating it as held for her benefit.

seaver.sentence: The Appellate Division affirmed instead because Seaver could enforce a contract made for her benefit.
seaver.plain: The Appellate Division, the middle-level appeals court, affirmed for a different reason. Seaver could enforce a “contract” made for her benefit, even though the promise was made to someone else.

seaver.sentence: Beman’s executors appealed, contesting her relationship to the promise, the availability of specific performance, and the asserted trust.
seaver.plain: Beman’s “executors,” the people managing his estate, appealed. They disputed her relationship to the promise, whether “specific performance” (a court order to actually carry out the promise) was available, and whether any trust existed.

seaver.sentence: A legatee who receives property by promising to apply it to the testator’s stated purpose may hold that property in trust.
seaver.plain: A “legatee” (someone who receives property under a will) who gets property by promising to use it for the “testator’s” stated purpose (the will-maker’s wish) may hold that property in “trust” for that purpose.

seaver.sentence: Mrs. Beman’s execution of the will in the requested form supplied consideration; this was not an unsupported gift promise made directly to her niece.
seaver.plain: Mrs. Beman’s signing of the will in the form her husband requested “supplied consideration,” the thing he got in exchange for his promise. So this was not an unsupported promise of a gift made directly to her niece.

seaver.sentence: Pound reviewed the historical privity rule and American movement toward intended-beneficiary enforcement.
seaver.plain: Judge Pound reviewed the historical “privity” rule, under which only the parties to a contract may sue on it. He also reviewed the American trend toward letting an intended beneficiary enforce a promise.

seaver.sentence: The childless aunt’s desire to provide for this dependent, favored niece therefore supported enforcement without an existing debt or mandated testamentary provision.
seaver.plain: So the childless aunt’s wish to provide for this dependent, favored niece supported enforcement. No existing debt or legally required “testamentary” provision (a gift the law compels in a will) was needed.

seaver.sentence: Acceptance would make him personally liable even if the house proved worth less: the testatrix would effectively have bequeathed a promise.
seaver.plain: If Beman had received the house on condition of paying Seaver, “acceptance” would make him personally “liable” (legally responsible) to pay, even if the house proved worth less. The “testatrix” (the woman making the will) would in effect have “bequeathed” (left by will) his promise.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: The district court dismissed as unripe, but the Ninth Circuit found finality and no adequate California compensation remedy for temporary regulatory takings at the relevant time.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: The district court dismissed the case as “unripe,” filed too early. The Ninth Circuit disagreed: the City’s decision was final, and California then offered no adequate “remedy” for getting paid for a temporary regulatory taking, so the suit could proceed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: On remand, takings and equal protection went to a jury while the judge retained substantive due process.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: “On remand,” back in the trial court, the takings and “equal protection” (unequal treatment) claims went to a jury. The judge kept for himself the “substantive due process” claim, that the City acted arbitrarily.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: The jury could find a taking from loss of all economically viable use or failure of the final 190-unit denial substantially to advance a legitimate public purpose.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: The jury could find a taking in either of two ways: the City left the land with no economically viable use, or the final denial of the 190-unit plan did not substantially advance a “legitimate public purpose,” a proper government goal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: Section 1983’s reference to an action at law did not itself create a statutory jury guarantee.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: Section 1983 says a wrongdoer is liable in “an action at law,” but those words did not themselves create a “statutory” right to a jury. Any jury right had to come from the Constitution.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: Five Justices instead treated a § 1983 claim for legal relief as tort-like under the Seventh Amendment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: Five Justices instead treated a § 1983 claim for legal relief (money damages) as “tort-like,” resembling the traditional injury suits that were tried to juries. So the Seventh Amendment’s jury guarantee applied.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: Only four Justices joined Kennedy’s Part IV-A-2 comparing historical tort and quasi-contract remedies for uncompensated property interference with an ordinary condemnation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: Only four Justices joined Justice Kennedy’s Part IV-A-2, so its reasoning is not binding. That section compared this case with historical “tort” and quasi-contract (implied-payment) “remedies” for interfering with property without paying, rather than with an ordinary condemnation, a routine government land-taking case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: Justice Scalia preferred the general § 1983 tort-like cause of action over a new historical analogue for each constitutional right.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: Justice Scalia preferred to treat every § 1983 suit as one general tort-like “cause of action” (type of lawsuit). He opposed hunting for a new “historical analogue,” an old-fashioned matching lawsuit, for each constitutional right.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: Damages through that vehicle implicated the Seventh Amendment, though a purely equitable request did not acquire a jury simply from the tort analogy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: In his view, “Damages” sought through § 1983 brought in the Seventh Amendment’s jury guarantee. But a purely “equitable” request, such as an injunction (a court order), did not get a jury just because § 1983 resembles tort law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: The Court reserved ordinary inverse-condemnation jury rights and precise allocation across broader zoning or regulatory challenges.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: The Court “reserved” (left undecided) “jury rights” in ordinary inverse-condemnation suits, where owners sue the government for payment for a taking. It also left open exactly how to divide judge and jury roles in broader zoning or regulatory challenges.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: He considered direct condemnation the closest analogue because both proceedings enforced compensation, and direct condemnation historically lacked a constitutional jury entitlement.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: Justice Souter considered “direct condemnation,” an ordinary eminent-domain case in which the government takes property and pays for it, the closest analogue, since both proceedings enforce compensation. Direct condemnation historically carried no constitutional right to a jury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: His proposed remand need not retry facts: the district judge could treat the verdict as advisory and make independent findings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: Souter’s proposed “remand” (sending the case back) would not require the court to “retry” the facts. The “district judge” could treat the “verdict as advisory,” mere advice, and make independent “findings” of fact.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.sentence: On May 24, 1999, the Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit five to four, sustaining submission of this particular § 1983 damages claim to the jury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-419.plain: On May 24, 1999, the Court “affirmed” (upheld) the Ninth Circuit five to four, “sustaining” (approving) the decision to let the jury decide this particular § 1983 damages claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: By 1907, Slocum had borrowed the full $2,360 policy reserve.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: By 1907, Slocum had borrowed the full $2,360 “policy reserve,” the cash value built up inside his life insurance policy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: It therefore could not fund continued or paid-up insurance after default.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: So the reserve could not fund continued coverage or “paid-up insurance” (a smaller policy needing no further premiums) after he missed a payment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: She argued that the agent’s acceptance extended coverage or that the company ratified his action; reserve-based continuation was another asserted theory.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: The executrix, who handled Slocum’s estate, argued that the agent’s “acceptance” of the check extended coverage, or that the company “ratified” (later approved) the agent’s action. Continuing the policy through its “reserve-based” value was another theory she raised.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: The check mattered only with a valid adjustment or waiver, and someone aware of an agent’s restricted authority could not bind the principal through an unauthorized act.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: The check mattered only if there was a valid adjustment of terms or a “waiver” (the company giving up its rights). And someone who knew the agent’s authority was restricted could not bind the “principal,” the company the agent worked for, through an act the agent was not authorized to do.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: The blue note’s terms were substantive.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: The blue note’s terms were “substantive.” The blue note was the signed note the company required for a payment extension, and its terms were the real conditions of that extension, not a mere formality.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: The Seventh Amendment’s Reexamination Clause constrained the federal court regardless of state procedure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: The Seventh Amendment’s Reexamination Clause, which limits how courts may re-examine facts a jury has found, bound the federal court no matter what Pennsylvania “procedure” allowed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: Historical English common law, not one State’s practice, supplied the relevant modes of reexamination: a trial court could grant a new trial, or an appellate court could order one for legal error.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: Historical English “common law,” not one State’s practice, defined the permitted ways to re-examine a jury’s findings. A trial court could grant a new trial, or an “appellate court” (an appeals court) could order one for “legal error,” a mistake about the law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: Sufficiency determined whether the judge should direct a verdict but did not dispense with a verdict or authorize an appellate final disposition of factual issues.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: “Sufficiency” of the evidence decided whether the judge should “direct a verdict,” telling the jury how it must rule. But it did not let the court skip a verdict altogether, or let an “appellate” court finally decide the factual issues itself.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: The right to jury trial followed material factual issues in the pleadings, distinct from the legal sufficiency of the evidence presented.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: The right to jury trial attached to the material (important) factual issues raised in the “pleadings,” the parties’ formal court papers. That is separate from the “legal sufficiency” of the evidence at a particular trial, meaning whether it was enough as a matter of law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: Historical judgment notwithstanding the verdict and arrest of judgment addressed deficiencies appearing in the pleadings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: Historically, “judgment notwithstanding the verdict” (a judgment contrary to the jury’s verdict) and arrest of judgment (blocking judgment on a verdict) dealt with defects appearing in the “pleadings” themselves, not with weak trial evidence.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: Pennsylvania’s procedure preserved the law-fact distinction because judgment remained unavailable where conflicting evidence on a material issue prevented binding instructions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: In the dissent’s view, Pennsylvania’s procedure kept the line between law and fact. “Judgment” was unavailable whenever conflicting evidence on a “material” (important) issue meant the judge could not give “binding instructions,” directions telling the jury how it must decide.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: Hughes read common-law demurrers to evidence as allowing final judgment when every favorable fact and inference was admitted but still legally insufficient; the modern device performed that function more simply.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: Hughes read the “common-law” demurrer to evidence (a request that the court rule the evidence fails as a matter of law) as allowing “final judgment” when, even admitting every favorable fact and “inference,” the evidence was still legally insufficient. Pennsylvania’s modern “device” did the same job more simply.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.sentence: On April 21, 1913, the Supreme Court modified the Third Circuit’s judgment by removing its instruction to enter judgment for the insurer and substituting a new-trial direction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-436.plain: On April 21, 1913, the Supreme Court modified the Third Circuit’s judgment. It removed the instruction to “enter judgment” (issue a final ruling) for the insurer and directed a new trial instead.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: A separate government antitrust suit against Paramount and other film companies produced a 1946 decree prohibiting existing film-franchise performance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: In a separate “antitrust” case (under competition law), the federal government sued Paramount and other film companies. It produced a 1946 “decree,” a court order, barring performance of their existing film-franchise deals.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Partmar refused to leave, and Paramount brought a diversity action in federal California court for possession and a declaration of valid termination.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: When Partmar refused to leave, Paramount brought a “diversity action” in federal court in California, allowed because the companies were citizens of different states. It sought possession of the theatre and a declaration that it had validly ended the lease.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Partmar and its parent defended and counterclaimed for treble antitrust damages, alleging an industry conspiracy enabled excessive fees and lease terms, including payment of half the theatre’s net receipts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: Partmar and its parent company defended and “counterclaimed,” suing Paramount back, for treble (triple) antitrust damages. They alleged an industry “conspiracy,” an illegal agreement among the studios, let Paramount impose excessive fees and lease terms, including payment of half the theatre’s net receipts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Before that trial, the Supreme Court reversed the franchise-related portion of the government decree: franchises were not necessarily illegal for every theatre regardless of size.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: Before that trial, the Supreme Court “reversed” (overturned) the franchise-related part of the government “decree.” It held franchises were not necessarily illegal for every theatre regardless of size.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Final judgment preserved the lease and franchise and rejected unlawful detainer, while dismissing treble-damage counterclaims with prejudice without their promised separate trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: The final judgment kept the lease and “franchise” (the film-supply deal) in place and rejected Paramount’s “unlawful detainer” claim, its suit to evict. But it also dismissed Partmar’s “treble-damage” counterclaims with prejudice (for good), without the separate trial promised for them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Justice Reed distinguished claim preclusion from issue preclusion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: Justice Reed distinguished “claim preclusion,” which bars suing again on the same claim, from issue preclusion, which bars re-arguing a specific issue already decided, even in a different claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: The counterclaims asserted a cause of action not previously adjudicated as such, but a matter actually litigated and essential to final judgment could bind in another claim.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: Partmar’s counterclaims asserted a “cause of action” (a claim) never “adjudicated” (decided) as such. But a matter “actually litigated” (fought over) and essential to the “final judgment” in the first trial could bind Partmar in another claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Once the principal action conclusively settled the necessary issue, repeating it would defeat preclusion; on that account, no due-process violation occurred.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: Once the main case had conclusively “settled” the necessary issue, trying it again would defeat “preclusion,” the rule against relitigating decided issues. On that reasoning, Partmar suffered no “due-process” violation, no denial of fair procedure.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Partmar argued that a counterclaim trial would allow the government judgment as prima facie conspiracy evidence under Clayton Act § 5.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: Partmar argued that a separate “counterclaim” trial would let it use the government’s “judgment” against the studios as prima facie (initial, rebuttable) proof of conspiracy, as Clayton Act § 5 allows.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: The earlier franchise-specific finding had been reversed, and the final Paramount decree did not determine that these particular agreements resulted from the industry conspiracy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: But the earlier finding against franchises had been reversed, and the final Paramount “decree” (court order) in the government case never found that these particular agreements resulted from the industry conspiracy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: Consented separate trials meant failure of proof in Paramount’s case was not fair adjudication of Partmar’s reserved affirmative claim.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: For Chief Justice Warren, dissenting, the key was that the parties had consented to “separate trials.” So Paramount’s failure of proof in its own case was not a fair decision on Partmar’s “reserved” affirmative claim, the counterclaim saved for later.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: On February 8, 1954, the Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit’s judgment sustaining dismissal with prejudice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: On February 8, 1954, the Court “affirmed” (upheld) the Ninth Circuit’s “judgment,” which had sustained dismissal of the counterclaims with prejudice (permanently).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.sentence: The holding depended on the majority’s particular account of a necessary, actually determined issue, not a blanket bar on reserved counterclaims or unrestricted appeals by successful parties.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524.plain: The holding rested on the majority’s particular view that this issue was necessary and actually decided. It did not create a blanket bar on “reserved” counterclaims (ones saved for a later trial) or a rule that winning “parties” may always appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: California Packing Corporation alleged that it drew a draft on Kelly Storage and Distributing Company, which accepted it for valuable consideration.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.plain: California Packing Corporation “alleged” (claimed) that it drew a “draft,” a written order directing Kelly Storage and Distributing Company to pay. It said Kelly accepted (agreed to pay) the draft for “valuable consideration,” meaning in exchange for something of value.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: California Packing used its complaint and an accompanying affidavit to obtain a warrant of attachment in the contract action.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.plain: California Packing used its complaint and an accompanying “affidavit” (sworn statement) to get a “warrant of attachment,” a court order seizing Kelly’s property to secure any judgment, in its “contract” lawsuit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: Phoenix and Third National Bank of Lexington, Kentucky, a third party, moved under Code of Civil Procedure § 682 to vacate the attachment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.plain: Phoenix and Third National Bank of Lexington, Kentucky, a “third party” not in the lawsuit, moved under Code of Civil Procedure § 682 to “vacate” (cancel) the attachment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: California Packing obtained permission to appeal with three certified questions: could the bank move, did the consideration allegation state fact or legal conclusion, and did the papers sufficiently show a cause of action?
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.plain: California Packing got “permission to appeal” to New York’s highest court with three “certified questions,” specific questions the court was asked to answer. Could the bank make the motion? Was the consideration “allegation” a statement of fact or a mere “legal conclusion,” and did the papers sufficiently show a “cause of action” (a valid claim)?

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: The First Department had repeatedly treated valuable consideration as a conclusion requiring more detail, whereas the Third Department considered a detailed recital unnecessary.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.plain: New York’s First Department, one of its regional intermediate appeals courts, had repeatedly treated “valuable consideration” as a bare conclusion requiring more detail. The Third Department considered a detailed “recital” (spelling out what was exchanged) unnecessary.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: Section 519 required liberal construction toward substantial justice, and established common-law forms allowed pleading a transaction’s legal effect.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.plain: Section 519 of the procedure code required “liberal construction” of pleadings, reading them generously to achieve substantial justice. And established “common-law” forms allowed a plaintiff to plead a transaction’s legal effect without every detail.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-044.sentence: Precedent accepted value received on a nonnegotiable note; a litigant could rely on that settled form without inventing an elaborate recital.
