lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.sentence: Scalia read the Administrator’s judgment as a condition for mandatory regulation, not an unconditional obligation to make an endangerment determination whenever someone petitioned.
lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.plain: Scalia read the Administrator’s judgment as a "condition" (a trigger): once EPA judges a danger exists, regulation becomes mandatory. It is not an unconditional duty to make an "endangerment determination" whenever someone petitions.

lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.sentence: Because the Act did not separately define air pollution, he would have deferred under the then-operative Chevron framework to EPA’s distinction between global greenhouse effects and ordinary ambient-air pollution.
lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.plain: Because the Act did not separately define "air pollution," Scalia would have deferred under the "Chevron framework" then in force, which accepts an agency's reasonable reading of an unclear statute. He would have accepted EPA's distinction between global greenhouse effects and ordinary "ambient-air" pollution, the air around us.

lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.sentence: The four complete standing notes, pages 1239–1243, explore a possible public-action/SCRAP reading without eliminating the concrete-injury requirement; whether the review provision supplies the relevant procedural right; comparisons to Spokeo and TransUnion; and whether existing harm or increased future risk does the work.
lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.plain: The four standing notes, pages 1239–1243, ask whether the case reads like a public-action or SCRAP-style loosening without dropping the "concrete-injury" requirement, and whether the review provision supplies the relevant procedural right. They compare later standing cases, Spokeo and TransUnion, and ask whether existing harm or increased future risk does the work.

lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.sentence: The final standing note compares proprietary, sovereign, and quasi-sovereign interests.
lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.plain: The last "standing" note compares a state's three kinds of interest: "proprietary" (as a property owner), sovereign (as a government with lawmaking power), and "quasi-sovereign" (as protector of its people's general welfare).

lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.sentence: In the last comparison, the five-Justice rulemaking/enforcement rationale differs from the three-Justice concurrence’s criticism of special solicitude.
lrs-n-massachusetts-epa.plain: In the last comparison, United States v. Texas, the five-Justice majority's reasoning about "rulemaking" versus enforcement choices differs from a three-Justice "concurrence" (a separate opinion agreeing with the result). That concurrence criticized "special solicitude," the extra leniency on standing given to states.

lucy.sentence: Zehmer prepared a second version saying that “we” agreed to sell the Ferguson Farm complete for $50,000, with title satisfactory to the buyer.
lucy.plain: Zehmer wrote a second version saying "we" (he and his wife) agreed to sell the Ferguson Farm complete for $50,000, with "title" (legal ownership) satisfactory to the buyer, meaning free of problems the buyer would object to.

lucy.sentence: The two Lucys filed a bill in equity in the Circuit Court of Dinwiddie County asking for specific performance: a decree requiring the Zehmers to convey the farm under the signed agreement.
lucy.plain: The two Lucys filed a "bill in equity" (a request for a non-money court order) in the Circuit Court of Dinwiddie County. They asked for "specific performance": an order requiring the Zehmers to "convey" (transfer ownership of) the farm under the signed agreement, rather than just pay damages.

lucy.sentence: They contended that the exchange was a jest, relied on the drinking, disputed formal delivery of the paper, and asked the equity court to withhold the requested remedy.
lucy.plain: The Zehmers argued the deal was a joke, relied on their drinking, and disputed formal "delivery" of the paper (that it was properly handed over as a binding document). They asked the "equity court" to refuse the "remedy" the Lucys sought, a forced sale.

lucy.sentence: The appellate question therefore concerned both whether the communicated acts formed a contract and whether the record justified the particular equitable remedy the buyers sought.
lucy.plain: The "appellate" question therefore had two parts: whether the words and acts the parties exchanged formed a contract, and whether the record justified the particular "equitable" remedy the buyers sought, a court order forcing the sale.

lucy.sentence: A privately intended meaning does not displace the reasonable meaning conveyed to the other party unless that party knows of the special meaning.
lucy.plain: A secret meaning, like 'I was only joking', does not count unless the other person knew about it.

lucy.sentence: These later acts corroborated his actual, reasonably grounded understanding; they did not substitute for assent missing at the time of formation.
lucy.plain: Lucy's later acts confirmed that he actually and reasonably believed there was a deal. But they could not replace "assent" (agreement) that was missing at "formation," the moment the contract was supposedly made.

lucy.sentence: Defense counsel conceded at oral argument that the evidence established capacity to contract.
lucy.plain: "Defense counsel," the Zehmers' own lawyer, admitted at "oral argument" before the appeals court that the "evidence" showed Zehmer had capacity to contract, meaning he was sober enough to make a contract.

lucy.sentence: On November 22, 1954, the Supreme Court of Appeals reversed the dismissal and remanded with instructions to enter a decree requiring the Zehmers to perform.
lucy.plain: On November 22, 1954, the Supreme Court of Appeals, Virginia's highest court, reversed the trial court's "dismissal" of the suit. It remanded with instructions to enter a "decree" (a court order) requiring the Zehmers to go through with the sale.

lucy.sentence: Its reasoning requires separate attention to communicated assent, capacity, and the conditions for equitable relief.
lucy.plain: The reasoning calls for three separate questions: was there outwardly communicated "assent" (agreement), did each party have capacity (the mental ability to contract), and are the conditions met for "equitable relief," a court order forcing performance?

walgreen.sentence: After an evidentiary hearing, the district court found breach and permanently barred Sara Creek from leasing the anchor premises to Phar-Mor until Walgreen’s lease ended.
walgreen.plain: After an "evidentiary hearing" (a hearing where evidence is taken), the district court found a "breach" of the lease. It permanently barred Sara Creek, the landlord, from renting the "anchor premises," the big main store space, to Phar-Mor until Walgreen's lease ended.

walgreen.sentence: Sara Creek’s expert thought Walgreen’s loss readily estimable, but Walgreen employees disputed that and emphasized hard-to-value goodwill.
walgreen.plain: Sara Creek’s expert said Walgreen's loss could easily be estimated in money. Walgreen's employees disagreed and stressed lost "goodwill," customer loyalty and reputation that are hard to put a price on.

walgreen.sentence: It did not pursue the antitrust objection raised below, so the appellate court did not decide that question.
walgreen.plain: The landlord did not pursue on appeal the antitrust (competition-law) objection it raised "below," meaning in the trial court. So the "appellate court" did not decide that question.

walgreen.sentence: Similar exclusivity cases had measured lost profits or lost leasehold value.
walgreen.plain: In similar "exclusivity" cases, about lease promises not to rent to a competitor, courts measured damages as lost profits or the lost value of the "leasehold," the tenant's interest in its lease.

walgreen.sentence: For a preliminary injunction, irreparable injury concerns harm a later final judgment cannot repair.
walgreen.plain: For a "preliminary injunction," a temporary court order before trial, "irreparable injury" means harm that a later "final judgment" could not repair.

walgreen.sentence: A permanent injunction ordinarily is that judgment, making inadequacy of damages the appropriate inquiry.
walgreen.plain: A "permanent injunction" ordinarily is itself that final judgment. So the right question is simply whether money damages would be inadequate.

walgreen.sentence: But injunctions can demand continuing supervision, harm outsiders, or create a bilateral monopoly: only Walgreen could sell the necessary waiver, and only Sara Creek could buy it for this transaction.
walgreen.plain: But "injunctions" (court orders to do or not do something) have costs. Courts may have to keep supervising, outsiders may be harmed, and they can create a "bilateral monopoly": only Walgreen could sell the needed "waiver" (permission to give up its right), and only Sara Creek could buy it for this deal, which can make bargaining hard.

walgreen.sentence: Damages would require forecasts of revenues and costs, isolation of Phar-Mor’s competitive effect, and discounting to present value.
walgreen.plain: Figuring damages would require forecasting Walgreen's revenues and costs, separating out Phar-Mor's competitive effect, and "discounting to present value," converting future losses into today's dollars.

walgreen.sentence: Phar-Mor was already a party; its benefit could appear in the rent it offered Sara Creek, which could then offer Walgreen payment for waiver.
walgreen.plain: Phar-Mor was already a party. Its benefit from the space could show up in the rent it offered Sara Creek, and Sara Creek could then offer Walgreen money for a "waiver," Walgreen giving up its right.

walgreen.sentence: Judge Kanne joined Posner; Senior Judge Harlington Wood, Jr., separately concurred, expressly joining both the affirmance and analysis without announcing an additional rule.
walgreen.plain: Judge Kanne "joined" (signed on to) Judge Posner's opinion. Senior Judge Harlington Wood, Jr., "concurred" separately, expressly agreeing with both the "affirmance" (upholding the trial court) and the analysis, without adding any new rule.

walgreen.sentence: The court recognized but left undecided a possible presumption favoring injunctions for shopping-center exclusivity clauses.
walgreen.plain: The court noted, but left undecided, a possible "presumption" (a default starting point) in favor of injunctions to enforce "exclusivity clauses" in shopping-center leases, the promises not to rent to a competitor.

wood-lucy.sentence: Lady Duff-Gordon challenged the legal sufficiency of that complaint through the New York pleading procedure described as a demurrer and a motion for judgment on the pleadings.
wood-lucy.plain: Lady Duff-Gordon challenged whether the complaint was legally sufficient, using the New York "pleading" procedure called a "demurrer" and a "motion for judgment on the pleadings." Both argue that, even if everything Wood said is true, his complaint states no valid legal claim.

wood-lucy.sentence: For that purpose, her challenge accepted the well-pleaded allegations and argued that the writing created no enforceable obligation supporting her promises.
wood-lucy.plain: For that purpose, her challenge accepted the "well-pleaded allegations" (the facts Wood properly stated) as true. She argued only that the writing created no "enforceable" (legally binding) duty on Wood to support her promises.

wood-lucy.sentence: Because the agreement did not expressly require him to procure any transaction, that court found no mutuality or consideration and granted judgment on the pleadings to Lady Duff-Gordon.
wood-lucy.plain: The agreement did not expressly require Wood to procure (bring about) any deal. So the intermediate appeals court found no "mutuality" (a two-way exchange of binding promises) and no consideration (something given in return), and it granted judgment on the pleadings, a win without trial, to Lady Duff-Gordon.

wood-lucy.sentence: The question before that court was whether the complete writing implied an enforceable reasonable-efforts undertaking, so that the exclusivity promise had consideration and Wood’s complaint stated a contract claim.
wood-lucy.plain: The question for the highest court was whether the whole writing implied an enforceable "reasonable-efforts" promise by Wood to try reasonably hard. If so, that promise was the "consideration" (the return promise) for her grant of "exclusivity" (sole rights), and Wood's "complaint" stated a valid contract claim.

wood-lucy.sentence: Wood’s acceptance of that exclusive position therefore carried an undertaking to make reasonable efforts to operate the channel.
wood-lucy.plain: Wood's "acceptance" of that exclusive position therefore carried an implied promise to make reasonable efforts to run the channel, that is, to market her endorsements and designs.

wood-lucy.sentence: Cardozo’s interpretation drew on the business-efficacy reasoning associated with The Moorcock and New York exclusive-agency cases.
wood-lucy.plain: Cardozo's reading drew on "business-efficacy" reasoning, the idea that courts supply terms needed to make a business deal work, associated with "The Moorcock," an English case. He also drew on New York "exclusive-agency" cases about agents given sole rights.

wood-lucy.sentence: It answered the intermediate court’s focus on the absence of an express procurement sentence by explaining the commitment conveyed by the agreement as a whole.
wood-lucy.plain: The "intermediate court" (the middle-level appeals court) focused on the lack of an express sentence requiring "procurement," that is, requiring Wood to bring in deals. Cardozo answered that the agreement as a whole conveyed that commitment anyway.

wood-lucy.sentence: On December 4, 1917, a four-judge Court of Appeals majority reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term, with costs in both appellate courts.
wood-lucy.plain: On December 4, 1917, four judges of the Court of Appeals, New York's highest court, formed a majority. They reversed the Appellate Division (the middle-level appeals court) and affirmed Special Term, the trial-level ruling letting Wood's suit proceed, awarding Wood costs in both "appellate courts."

wood-lucy.sentence: Wood’s claim could proceed because the implied reasonable-efforts promise supplied consideration.
wood-lucy.plain: Wood's "claim" could go forward because the "implied reasonable-efforts promise," his unstated but understood promise to try reasonably hard, supplied consideration, making the contract binding.

wucherpfennig.sentence: Donald owned an undivided two-thirds of the quarter containing the farmstead; Elizabeth and Louise each owned one-sixth.
wucherpfennig.plain: Donald owned an "undivided two-thirds" of the quarter-section with the farmstead: a two-thirds share in the whole property, not a specific piece of it. His sisters Elizabeth and Louise each owned a one-sixth share.

wucherpfennig.sentence: He then asked Elizabeth to state the exact amount she expected for her land interest and whether she would sign an agreement concerning Special Use Valuation, requesting answers on both matters.
wucherpfennig.plain: The estate's lawyer then asked Elizabeth to state the exact amount she expected for her land interest. He also asked whether she would sign an agreement on "Special Use Valuation," a federal estate-tax rule for valuing farmland, and requested answers on both points.

wucherpfennig.sentence: Donald sued Elizabeth for specific performance, which would require conveyance of her share, and alternatively for partition of the co-owned property.
wucherpfennig.plain: Donald "sued" Elizabeth for "specific performance," a court order forcing "conveyance" (transfer) of her share to him. In the alternative he asked for "partition," a court division of the co-owned property.

wucherpfennig.sentence: By consent, the parties tried specific performance first.
wucherpfennig.plain: By consent of both sides, the court tried the "specific performance" claim (the request to force the sale) first, before the partition claim.

wucherpfennig.sentence: The North Dakota Supreme Court addressed acceptance and, finding that ground sufficient, expressly left the others undecided.
wucherpfennig.plain: The North Dakota Supreme Court addressed only acceptance. Finding that ground enough to uphold the result, it expressly left the other grounds undecided.

wucherpfennig.sentence: Justice Sand applied North Dakota Century Code § 9-03-21 and precedents requiring absolute, unequivocal, unconditional acceptance.
wucherpfennig.plain: Justice Sand applied North Dakota Century Code § 9-03-21, a state statute, and "precedents" (earlier cases) requiring that an acceptance be absolute, "unequivocal" (clear, with no hedging), and unconditional.

wucherpfennig.sentence: Cooke v. Blood Systems, Grossman v. McLeish Ranch, Greenberg v. Stewart, and the Minnesota decisions Markmann and Minar supplied formulations requiring assent to the same bargain with an intention that the response itself create the contract.
wucherpfennig.plain: Cooke v. Blood Systems, Grossman v. McLeish Ranch, Greenberg v. Stewart, and the Minnesota cases Markmann and Minar stated the test. An acceptance must show "assent" (agreement) to the very same "bargain," and be meant, by itself, to create the contract.

wucherpfennig.sentence: The holding did not require labeling the February letter a definite counteroffer; continued negotiation sufficed to explain why it was no acceptance.
wucherpfennig.plain: The holding did not require calling the February letter a definite "counteroffer" (a new offer on different terms). It was enough that the letter showed continued negotiation, which explained why it was no "acceptance."

wucherpfennig.sentence: Restatement §§ 59 and 61 describe that distinction between conditional assent and an acceptance accompanied by a request.
wucherpfennig.plain: Restatement §§ 59 and 61 (sections of the Restatement of Contracts) describe that difference. "Conditional assent" ("I accept only if...") is not an acceptance, while an acceptance that comes with a request ("I accept; could you also...") still is.

wwvw.sentence: The record treated Seaway and World-Wide as independent corporations whose relationships with one another and with Audi and Volkswagen were contractual only.
wwvw.plain: The record treated Seaway (the dealer) and World-Wide (the regional distributor) as independent "corporations." Their ties to each other and to Audi and Volkswagen were by contract only, not by ownership.

wwvw.sentence: The Robinsons brought a manufacturers’ products-liability action in the District Court for Creek County, Oklahoma.
wwvw.plain: The Robinsons brought a "products-liability" suit, a claim that a defective product caused injury, against the manufacturers and others in the District Court for Creek County, Oklahoma, a state trial court.

wwvw.sentence: World-Wide and Seaway made special appearances contesting personal jurisdiction and submitted evidence of their businesses’ geographic limits.
wwvw.plain: World-Wide and Seaway made "special appearances," coming to court only to challenge personal jurisdiction (the court's power over them). They submitted "evidence" that their businesses were limited to New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut.

wwvw.sentence: The companies’ papers also mentioned venue of the subject matter, and they took depositions touching the merits.
wwvw.plain: The companies' papers also mentioned "venue" (whether this was the right place for the case), and they took "depositions," pretrial questioning under oath, that touched the merits (the substance of the claims).

wwvw.sentence: The Robinsons later claimed waiver, but the trial court classified the appearances as special and Oklahoma’s Supreme Court addressed jurisdiction.
wwvw.plain: The Robinsons later argued "waiver," meaning the companies had given up their objection by doing those things. But the "trial court" classified the appearances as special, and Oklahoma’s Supreme Court went on to address "jurisdiction."

wwvw.sentence: They requested prohibition ordering Judge Charles Woodson to stop exercising personal jurisdiction over them before the products-liability trial.
wwvw.plain: They asked for a writ of prohibition, an order forbidding Judge Charles Woodson, the trial judge, from exercising "personal jurisdiction" (power) over them before the "products-liability" trial.

wwvw.sentence: On October 10, 1978, the Oklahoma Supreme Court assumed original jurisdiction but denied the writ.
wwvw.plain: On October 10, 1978, the Oklahoma Supreme Court took "original jurisdiction," hearing the request directly rather than on appeal, but denied the "writ" (the order the companies asked for).

wwvw.sentence: Section 1701.03(a)(3), concerning an in-state act causing tortious injury, did not suffice because the alleged design and distribution acts occurred elsewhere.
wwvw.plain: Section 1701.03(a)(3), covering an act in Oklahoma that causes "tortious" (legally wrongful) injury, did not apply. The "alleged" (claimed) design and distribution acts happened outside Oklahoma.

wwvw.sentence: The underlying tort action remained pending; this was review of adjudicatory power, not a products-liability judgment.
wwvw.plain: The underlying "tort" action, the injury suit itself, was still pending. This was review of "adjudicatory power" (whether Oklahoma courts could hear the case against these companies), not a "products-liability" judgment.

wwvw.sentence: Pennoyer expressed that limit through territorial authority; International Shoe framed corporate jurisdiction through minimum contacts consistent with fair play and substantial justice.
wwvw.plain: "Pennoyer," the older case, expressed that limit as territorial: a state's power stopped at its borders. "International Shoe" framed corporate "jurisdiction" as requiring minimum contacts with the state, consistent with "fair play and substantial justice," meaning that hearing the case there is fair.

wwvw.sentence: Under Hanson, purposeful availment supplies an act connecting the defendant with the forum’s benefits and protections.
wwvw.plain: Under "Hanson," an earlier case, "purposeful availment" means the defendant itself did something deliberate connecting it with the forum’s benefits and protections, that is, with the state where it is sued.

wwvw.sentence: The relevant foreseeability is whether the defendant’s own conduct gives reasonable notice of possible suit there.
wwvw.plain: What matters is not whether a car might foreseeably end up in Oklahoma, but whether the defendant's own actions should lead it to expect being sued there.

wwvw.sentence: Hess v. Pawloski involved a nonresident’s own use of forum roads, coupled with statutory appointment of a service official for claims arising from that driving.
wwvw.plain: "Hess v. Pawloski" involved a nonresident’s own driving on the roads of the "forum" (the state where he was sued). A "statutory" provision named a state official to receive the lawsuit papers for "claims" arising from that driving.

wwvw.sentence: Adequacy of notice was uncontested, and the Court decided neither defect, causation, damages, venue, governing law nor those other defendants’ liabilities.
wwvw.plain: No one disputed that notice of the suit was adequate. The Court decided nothing about defect, "causation" (whether the car caused the injuries), damages, venue, which law governs, or the other defendants’ liabilities.

www-associates.sentence: The buyer would pay $25,000 on signing, $225,000 at closing, and deliver a $500,000 purchase-money mortgage payable two years later.
www-associates.plain: The buyer would pay $25,000 on signing and $225,000 at "closing" (the final transfer). It would also give the sellers a $500,000 "purchase-money mortgage," a loan from the sellers secured by the land, due two years later.

www-associates.sentence: If the litigation delayed closing, closing would be adjourned until it ended.
www-associates.plain: If the litigation delayed closing, the closing would be "adjourned" (postponed) until the suit ended.

www-associates.sentence: On June 2, the sellers canceled and tendered the down payment, which the buyer refused.
www-associates.plain: On June 2, the sellers canceled the deal and "tendered" (formally offered back) the down payment, which the buyer refused.

www-associates.sentence: A notice of pendency had raised concerns about construction financing and related title insurance for the senior housing project, despite assurances that the underlying suit lacked merit.
www-associates.plain: A "notice of pendency," a public filing warning that a lawsuit concerned the land, raised worries about construction loans and related title insurance for the senior housing project. That was so even though the buyer had been assured the underlying suit lacked merit.

www-associates.sentence: The buyer argued that it could waive a condition for its sole benefit and compel the sale.
www-associates.plain: The buyer argued that it could "waive a condition" (give up a contract term) that existed only for its own benefit, here the cancellation clause, and force the sale.

www-associates.sentence: The Appellate Division adopted the buyer’s affidavit account, searched the record, and ordered specific performance for the buyer.
www-associates.plain: The Appellate Division, the middle-level appeals court, accepted the account in the buyer's "affidavit" (sworn written statement). It searched the record, which let it grant judgment to a party that had not moved for it, and ordered "specific performance" (a forced sale) for the buyer.

www-associates.sentence: Judge Kaye’s Court of Appeals opinion accepted the general rule allowing the sole beneficiary of a condition to waive it.
www-associates.plain: Judge Kaye’s opinion for the Court of Appeals, New York's highest court, accepted the general rule: the "sole beneficiary of a condition," the only party it protects, may waive (give up) that condition.

www-associates.sentence: Ambiguity was a legal question for the court.
www-associates.plain: "Ambiguity," whether contract words are unclear, was a legal question for the court to decide, not a factual question for trial.

www-associates.sentence: Once the sellers showed entitlement to judgment, the buyer needed admissible evidence raising a genuine issue or an acceptable explanation for its absence.
www-associates.plain: Once the sellers showed they were entitled to "judgment," the buyer had to offer "admissible evidence" (proof a court can consider) raising a "genuine issue" of fact, a real dispute, or give an acceptable reason why it could not.

www-associates.sentence: The vice-president’s report of what the broker said a seller had said was conclusory and insufficient, even under the more generous treatment afforded a summary-judgment opponent.
www-associates.plain: The buyer's vice-president reported what a broker said a seller had said. That account was "conclusory" (a bare claim without supporting facts) and not enough, even under the more generous reading given to a party opposing "summary-judgment."

www-associates.sentence: The court did not decide after trial that the sellers had diligently defended the underlying litigation; it found no triable issue in this record.
www-associates.plain: The court did not find, after a trial, that the sellers had diligently defended the underlying lawsuit. It found only that this record showed no "triable issue," no real factual dispute worth sending to trial.

www-associates.sentence: On December 27, 1990, the unanimous seven-member Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division with costs, granted the sellers’ summary-judgment motion, and dismissed the complaint.
www-associates.plain: On December 27, 1990, the Court of Appeals, New York's highest court, ruled 7-0 and reversed the Appellate Division with costs. It "granted" the sellers' "summary-judgment" motion, ruling for them without trial, and "dismissed" (threw out) the buyer's complaint.

alaska-packers.sentence: The full report describes payments and releases under the original arrangements, but the appellate decision did not independently resolve whether those releases defeated recovery.
alaska-packers.plain: The full report says the workers were paid under the original agreements and signed releases (papers giving up further claims). But the "appellate" decision did not itself decide whether those releases blocked the workers' "recovery" of the extra pay.

alaska-packers.sentence: The workers sued in admiralty, where they were called libelants and the Association the respondent.
alaska-packers.plain: The workers sued in "admiralty," the court system for maritime cases. There the suing side is called the "libelants" and the Association, the side being sued, the "respondent," instead of plaintiff and defendant.

alaska-packers.sentence: Because pay partly depended on the catch, genuinely deficient equipment could have changed the employer’s performance and the crew’s obligations.
alaska-packers.plain: Because the crew's pay depended partly on the catch, truly deficient nets could have changed the employer's "performance" (whether it was doing its part). That, in turn, could have changed what the crew owed in return.

alaska-packers.sentence: He assumed both that the new agreement was made and that the superintendent had authority, then asked whether consideration supported it.
alaska-packers.plain: Judge Ross gave the workers the benefit of the doubt: he assumed the new pay deal was really made and that the superintendent was allowed to make it. He then asked whether the company got anything in return for its promise of more pay, since without that exchange ('consideration') a promise is not enforceable.

alaska-packers.sentence: That sufficient legal issue left actual authority undecided.
alaska-packers.plain: That "legal issue," lack of consideration, was enough to decide the case. So the court left undecided whether the superintendent had "actual authority," real power from the company, to change the contracts.

alaska-packers.sentence: Avoiding disruption had obvious practical value to the Association, but did not supply a newly bargained-for legal benefit under the rule applied.
alaska-packers.plain: Avoiding disruption obviously had practical value to the Association. But under the rule applied, getting only what was already promised is not a new "bargained-for" legal benefit, something given in exchange, so it could not support a new promise.

alaska-packers.sentence: The rejected net contention mattered: consideration analysis proceeded on an unjustified refusal to perform, not a finding that the employer had disabled performance.
alaska-packers.plain: The rejected claim about bad nets mattered. The consideration analysis rested on the crew's unjustified refusal to perform work it owed, not on a finding that the employer had disabled "performance" by supplying bad equipment.

alaska-packers.sentence: Performing an existing duty therefore supplied no consideration for the additional wage promise.
alaska-packers.plain: Performing a duty one already has supplied no "consideration," meaning nothing new given in exchange, for the company's promise of extra wages. So that promise was not enforceable.

alaska-packers.sentence: The record did not support voluntary rescission and substitution or waiver merely from his apparent assent.
alaska-packers.plain: The record did not show "rescission" (the company freely canceling the old contracts) and substitution of new ones. Nor did it show "waiver" (knowingly giving up its rights) just from the superintendent's apparent "assent," his seeming agreement to the demand.

alaska-packers.sentence: The court used King v. Railway Co. to reject estoppel based on eventually completing the work.
alaska-packers.plain: The court relied on King v. Railway Co. to reject estoppel, a doctrine that can bind a party to a promise someone relied on. The workers' eventually finishing the job did not create such reliance.

alaska-packers.sentence: A worker who extracts an additional promise by unjustifiably refusing an existing obligation cannot turn later performance of that obligation into protected reliance barring the consideration defense.
alaska-packers.plain: A worker who extracts an extra promise by wrongly refusing work already owed cannot turn his later "performance" of that work into protected reliance. Such reliance is not a ground barring the company's "defense" that it got no consideration, because the work was owed anyway.

alaska-packers.sentence: On May 26, 1902, the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded with directions to enter judgment for the Association with costs.
alaska-packers.plain: On May 26, 1902, the Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, reversed the workers' win and "remanded" (sent the case back) with directions to "enter judgment" for the Association, with costs.

alaska-packers.sentence: Lack of consideration was the operative ground; coercive circumstances explained why apparent assent and completed work did not establish a voluntary replacement or protected reliance.
alaska-packers.plain: "Lack of consideration," the company getting nothing new for its promise, was the deciding ground. The "coercive" circumstances (the crew's pressure) explained why the superintendent's apparent "assent" and the finished work did not show a freely made replacement contract or reliance the law should protect.

alaska-packers.sentence: Later Restatement § 89 can support some modifications without new consideration, but replacement difficulty alone does not establish unforeseen circumstances supporting a fair adjustment, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every performance of an existing duty.
alaska-packers.plain: Restatement § 89, a later rule, can make some contract "modifications" (changes) binding without new consideration if fair and caused by "unforeseen circumstances," events nobody expected. Difficulty finding replacement workers alone does not qualify, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every "performance" of a duty already owed.

alaska-packers.sentence: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove consideration objections to qualifying signed modifications without supplying authority or eliminating duress.
alaska-packers.plain: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove "consideration" objections (that nothing new was exchanged) to qualifying signed, written "modifications" of a contract. But it does not give someone authority he lacked, and it does not cure duress, meaning improper pressure.

alaska-packers.sentence: Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209 applies to goods modifications; a crew’s services contract is not a goods sale merely because its employer sells salmon.
alaska-packers.plain: Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209, which allows contract changes without new consideration, applies to sales of goods. A crew's contract for services is not a sale of goods just because the employer sells salmon.

bollinger.sentence: Their claim was that the paper failed to record a bargain already reached, rather than that an accurately recorded provision should be disregarded merely because they had not read it.
bollinger.plain: The Bollingers' "claim" was that the paper failed to record a "bargain" (deal) already reached. They were not arguing that a correctly recorded term should be ignored just because they had not read it.

bollinger.sentence: The landowners brought an equity action to reform the document by adding the omitted paragraph and to enforce the corrected agreement.
bollinger.plain: The landowners asked a court using its equity (fairness) powers to rewrite the contract to include the missing topsoil promise, and then to make the company follow it.

bollinger.sentence: After testimony, the chancellor found the heavy burden of proving the shared understanding met through corroborating conduct and granted relief.
bollinger.plain: After hearing "testimony," the chancellor (the equity judge) found the heavy "burden of proving" that both sides shared the understanding was met, through "corroborating" conduct, meaning actions that backed up the Bollingers' story. He "granted" relief by ordering the correction.

bollinger.sentence: Justice Musmanno explained that equity could reform written evidence of a contract to match the parties’ actual agreement, but the mistake had to be mutual.
bollinger.plain: Justice Musmanno explained that "equity" (the courts' power to do fairness) can reform, meaning correct, the written "evidence" of a contract to match the parties’ actual agreement. But the mistake had to be mutual, shared by both sides.

bollinger.sentence: A party’s later denial did not itself defeat a finding that the shared bargain had mistakenly been omitted.
bollinger.plain: A party’s later denial in court, here the company's, did not by itself defeat a finding that the shared "bargain" (the topsoil term) had been left out of the paper by mistake.

bollinger.sentence: Failure to understand what one signed was not enough; reformation required proper evidence of an actual shared mistake rather than a hypothetical or contrived claim.
bollinger.plain: Not understanding what one signed was not enough. "Reformation" (a court correcting a written contract) required proper "evidence" of a real shared mistake, not a hypothetical or made-up "claim."

bollinger.sentence: The court was correcting an instrument that failed to record the agreement, not first accepting a fully accurate writing and then adding a separate oral promise.
bollinger.plain: The court was correcting an "instrument" (the written document) that failed to record the agreement. It was not accepting a fully accurate writing and then adding a separate "oral promise" (a spoken side term), which the rules on written contracts usually forbid.

bollinger.sentence: After the decree nisi, the company requested rehearing based on purportedly after-discovered evidence.
bollinger.plain: After the "decree nisi" (a provisional order that becomes final unless successfully challenged), the company asked for "rehearing." It claimed to have "after-discovered evidence," evidence found only after trial.

bollinger.sentence: The Supreme Court assumed without deciding that the material qualified as newly discovered.
bollinger.plain: The state Supreme Court "assumed without deciding" that the material qualified as "newly discovered," meaning it accepted that point only for argument's sake and did not rule on it.

bollinger.sentence: On May 24, 1967, the Court affirmed the decree with costs against the contractor.
bollinger.plain: On May 24, 1967, the state Supreme Court "affirmed" (upheld) the decree correcting and enforcing the contract, and ordered the contractor to pay the court costs.

brief-CP-100.sentence: On November 26, 1943, he sued the two tug owners, individually and as partners, and the railroad under the Jones Act.
brief-CP-100.plain: On November 26, 1943, Hickman sued the two tug owners, both personally and as business partners, and the railroad. He sued under the Jones Act, a federal law letting families of seamen killed at work sue for negligence.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Number 38 sought copies of written witness statements and detailed accounts of oral statements; supplemental questions sought reports and memoranda.
brief-CP-100.plain: Question 38 asked the owners to hand over copies of written statements their lawyer had taken from witnesses, and to describe in detail what witnesses told him out loud. Follow-up questions asked for his reports and notes.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Fortenbaugh described how he obtained the material during proceedings on objections; no express production demand was made during his informal deposition.
brief-CP-100.plain: The owners' lawyer, Fortenbaugh, explained how he got the statements during the hearings on objections. But during his informal "deposition" (questioning under oath), no one made an express "production demand," a direct request that he hand them over.

brief-CP-100.sentence: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania, sitting en banc, found no privilege and ordered the written statements, disclosure of oral-interview facts, and production or judicial submission of memoranda to separate factual portions.
brief-CP-100.plain: The Eastern District of Pennsylvania, the federal trial court, sitting "en banc" (all its judges together), found no "privilege" (legal protection) for the material. It ordered "production" of the written statements and disclosure of facts from oral interviews, and ordered the lawyer's notes handed over or given to the court to separate out the factual parts.

brief-CP-100.sentence: The owners and Fortenbaugh refused, received contempt orders, and faced imprisonment until compliance.
brief-CP-100.plain: The owners and their lawyer, Fortenbaugh, refused. The court issued contempt orders (punishment for disobeying the court), and they faced jail until they complied.

brief-CP-100.sentence: The Third Circuit en banc reversed on lawyer-work-product grounds.
brief-CP-100.plain: The Third Circuit, the federal appeals court sitting with all its judges, "reversed" that order. It held that a lawyer's "work product," material he prepares for a case, was protected.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Rule 33 interrogatories directed to the owners did not authorize compulsory production by their nonparty lawyer under the rules then in force, and there was no proper Rule 34 motion.
brief-CP-100.plain: Rule 33 "interrogatories" (written questions) sent to the owners did not allow "compulsory production," forcing documents to be handed over, by their "nonparty" lawyer under the rules then in force. And no proper Rule 34 motion, the tool for demanding documents, was ever made.

brief-CP-100.sentence: A deposition and subpoena to counsel would pose the question through a different mechanism.
brief-CP-100.plain: A "deposition" (questioning under oath) of the owners' "counsel" (lawyer) and a subpoena, an order to bring documents, would have raised the question through a different procedure.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Because the substantive issue would recur, the Court did not rest only on that defect.
brief-CP-100.plain: Because the "substantive" issue, the real question about lawyers' files, would come up again, the Court did not rest only on that procedural defect.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Discovery broadly revealed facts and narrowed issues, and a general “fishing expedition” objection was insufficient.
brief-CP-100.plain: "Discovery," the pretrial exchange of information, is meant broadly to bring out facts and narrow the issues. So a general objection that the other side is on a "fishing expedition" was not enough to refuse.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Attorney-client privilege did not cover third-party witness accounts, and counsel’s legal theories and working papers required a different justification.
brief-CP-100.plain: "Attorney-client privilege," which protects lawyer-client conversations, did not cover accounts from "third-party" witnesses (outsiders). Protection for the legal theories and working papers of counsel (the lawyer) had to rest on a different justification.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Protection arose from adversarial preparation itself: collecting and selecting facts, evaluating theories, recording impressions, and planning strategy.
brief-CP-100.plain: The protection came from adversarial preparation itself, the lawyer's work getting ready for a contested case: collecting and choosing facts, weighing theories, recording impressions, and planning strategy.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Hickman therefore demanded another lawyer’s collection and organization of accessible facts without establishing need.
brief-CP-100.plain: So Hickman was asking for the opposing lawyer's work collecting facts Hickman could get himself, without showing any real need for it.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Materiality and absence of attorney-client privilege alone, the district court’s grounds here, did not meet it.
brief-CP-100.plain: The district court’s grounds here were "materiality" (the statements were relevant) and the absence of attorney-client privilege. Those alone did not meet the test; Hickman had to show real need.

brief-CP-100.sentence: Direct questioning or deposition would obtain the witness’s account and permit meaningful impeachment.
brief-CP-100.plain: Hickman could question the witnesses directly or take their "deposition" (questioning under oath before trial). That would get their accounts and allow meaningful "impeachment," attacking their credibility if their stories changed.

brief-CP-100.sentence: On January 13, 1947, the Supreme Court affirmed the Third Circuit’s reversal of production and contempt.
brief-CP-100.plain: On January 13, 1947, the Supreme Court "affirmed" (upheld) the Third Circuit’s "reversal" of the orders. The lawyer did not have to produce the materials, and the "contempt" penalties for refusing fell.

brief-CP-100.sentence: The later express work-product rule was not yet the text the Court interpreted.
brief-CP-100.plain: The later written "work-product rule," which expressly protects lawyers' trial-preparation materials and was based on this case, did not yet exist. So it was not the text the Court was interpreting.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: The defendants filed a thirty-five-paragraph response, repeatedly saying they neither admitted nor denied the allegations and demanding strict proof.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: The defendants filed a thirty-five-paragraph answer that kept saying they neither "admitted" nor denied the "allegations" (the plaintiff's stated claims) and "demanded strict proof," instead of giving one of the responses the rules allow.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: He counted thirty affected paragraphs, including material incorporated by reference.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: Judge Shadur counted thirty paragraphs with this problem, including some "incorporated by reference," meaning they adopted the improper responses by pointing back to earlier paragraphs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: Rule 8(b) permitted admission, denial, or a statement that the defendant lacked knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about the allegation’s truth.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: Rule 8(b) allowed only three responses to each allegation: admit it, deny it, or state that the "defendant" lacks knowledge or information enough to form a belief about whether it is true.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: The last response operated as a denial when made with the objective and subjective good faith required by Rule 11.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: The last response ("we don't know enough") counts as a denial, but only if made in "good faith," both objectively reasonable and honestly believed, as Rule 11 requires of court filings.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: A plaintiff’s ordinary burden to prove contested facts did not create a fourth response option, and a demand for strict proof did not itself put the allegation in dispute.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: The plaintiff's normal burden to prove disputed facts did not create a fourth response option. And a demand for "strict proof" ("prove it") did not itself put the "allegation" in dispute.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: Those observations explained his choice to apply the admission consequence here.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: Those comments explained why he chose to apply the "admission consequence" here, treating the improper non-answers as admissions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: Historical Rule 8(d) treated allegations requiring an answer as admitted if not denied, except allegations about the amount of damages.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: Rule 8(d), as it then read, said allegations that require an "answer" are treated as admitted if not denied. The one exception was allegations about the amount of "damages," the money claimed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: On June 17, 1998, Shadur applied that provision to the improper responses and directed the action to proceed on that basis.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: On June 17, 1998, Judge Shadur applied that rule to the improper responses, treating those allegations as admitted, and ordered the case to go forward on that basis.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.sentence: His warning of similar treatment for future violations did not impose a monetary sanction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-289.plain: He warned that future violations would be treated the same way, but he did not impose a money "sanction" (a fine or penalty).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: The district court distinguished general-view signs from messages it considered potentially directed at the family.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: The "district court" (the federal trial court) separated signs stating the church's general views from messages it thought might be aimed at the Snyder family itself.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Diversity supplied jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: "Diversity" jurisdiction let the federal court hear the case: the two sides were citizens of different states.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Before trial, Judge Richard D. Bennett granted defendants summary judgment on defamation and publicity of private life: the online statements were religious opinion rather than the required defamatory communication, and the personal information was public.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: Before trial, Judge Richard D. Bennett granted the defendants "summary judgment" (a ruling without trial) on two claims. Defamation failed because the online post was religious opinion, not the false factual statement defamation requires; "publicity of private life" failed because the personal information was already public.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Intentional infliction of emotional distress, intrusion on seclusion, and civil conspiracy remained.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: Three claims remained for trial: "intentional infliction of emotional distress" (deliberately causing severe emotional harm), intrusion on seclusion (invading private grief), and "civil conspiracy" (agreeing together to commit those wrongs).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: The venire exceeded one hundred, more than triple the usual civil pool.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: The "venire," the pool of potential jurors called, exceeded one hundred, more than three times the usual size for a civil case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Defendants sought judgment as a matter of law, reconsideration, a new trial, reduction, relief from judgment, and stays.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: After the verdict, the defendants sought judgment as a matter of law (a ruling for them despite the verdict), "reconsideration" of earlier rulings, a new trial, reduction of damages, "relief from judgment" (undoing it), and stays pausing enforcement.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Applying Rule 47(a)’s broad trial-court discretion and focus on impartiality, Bennett found the questionnaire and extensive individual follow-up adequate to expose publicity bias.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: Applying Rule 47(a), which gives trial judges broad discretion over juror questioning as long as the jury is impartial, Judge Bennett found the written questionnaire plus extensive individual follow-up questions enough to expose bias from news coverage.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Bennett explained that the challenged comments occurred outside the jury’s presence and arose from trial evidence, without the deep antagonism required by judicial-bias precedent.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: Judge Bennett explained that the challenged comments were made outside the jury's presence and responded to trial evidence. They lacked the deep hostility that judicial-bias "precedent" (past cases) requires before a judge counts as biased.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: He treated Albert and the funeral as private and declined to turn an obituary into voluntary entry into public controversy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: He treated Albert Snyder and the funeral as private. He refused to treat publishing an obituary as voluntarily entering a "public controversy," which would have made Albert's claims much harder to win.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: He distinguished general views from signs and online statements a jury could read as targeting the family, and rejected religious belief as automatic immunity from generally applicable tort responsibility.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: He separated general views from signs and online statements a jury could read as targeting the family. He also rejected the idea that religious belief gives automatic "immunity" (exemption) from "tort" law, the ordinary injury law that applies to everyone.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Conspiracy required one of the underlying torts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: The conspiracy claim required one of the underlying "torts" (civil wrongs), such as intrusion or emotional distress, to have actually been committed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: For the separate new-trial motion, Bennett could weigh evidence and credibility rather than apply only the judgment-as-a-matter-of-law standard.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: On the separate new-trial motion, Judge Bennett could weigh the evidence and decide whom to believe. He was not limited to the stricter "judgment-as-a-matter-of-law" standard, which views the evidence in the winner's favor.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: He found no result against the clear weight or miscarriage of justice; false evidence was not alleged.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: He found the verdict was not against the "clear weight" of the evidence and not a miscarriage of justice (grossly unjust), and no one "alleged" (claimed) that false evidence was used.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Following Gasperini, the Supreme Court precedent governing federal review of state-law excessiveness, Bennett used Maryland substantive standards within federal motion procedure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: Following Gasperini, the Supreme Court "precedent" on federal "review" of "excessiveness" (whether damages on a state claim are too high), Judge Bennett used Maryland's "substantive" standards (its legal test) within federal "motion" procedure.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: He declined the state noneconomic cap because controlling intermediate appellate law excluded intentional torts, rejected certification and requests to disregard that decision, and found $2.9 million supported by testimony and medical proof.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: He refused to apply Maryland's "noneconomic cap" (a limit on damages for pain and emotional harm), because binding intermediate "appellate" law excluded "intentional torts." He rejected certifying the question to Maryland's highest court or ignoring that ruling, and found the $2.9 million supported by "testimony" and medical proof.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: For punitive damages, he applied constitutional guideposts and state considerations.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: For the "punitive damages," money meant to punish, he applied the "constitutional guideposts" (the Supreme Court's tests for when such awards are unconstitutionally large) plus Maryland's own factors.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: He distinguished Philip Morris’s concern about punishment for past harm to nonparties from counsel’s argument for deterring future conduct.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: The Philip Morris case forbids punishing a defendant for past harm to "nonparties," people outside the case. The judge said counsel's argument was different: it urged deterring future conduct.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Compensation remained joint and several.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: The compensation award remained "joint and several": Albert could collect the full amount from any one defendant or from all together, but no more than the total.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Because reduction rested on constitutional as well as state grounds, he did not give Albert the new-trial option associated with ordinary discretionary remittitur.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: Usually, when a judge cuts damages, the plaintiff may choose a new trial instead. Because this cut was required by the Constitution, not just the judge's discretion, Albert got no such choice.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: On February 4, 2008, Bennett retained liability, denied Rule 60 relief for lack of a specified basis, and granted reduction motions only as to punishment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: On February 4, 2008, Judge Bennett kept the finding of liability (legal responsibility). He denied Rule 60 relief from the judgment because no specific basis was given, and "granted" the reduction motions only as to the punitive (punishment) damages.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.sentence: Stays pending the posttrial motions became moot; a stay pending appeal awaited a bond or other security.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-429.plain: "Stays" (pauses in collecting the judgment) pending the post-trial motions became moot once he decided them. A "stay pending appeal" would require a bond or other security guaranteeing payment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: Her state complaint alleged intentional fraud and malicious conversion, and separately alleged that Grimes transferred an $18,000 Petty-built dragster to his wife to frustrate creditors.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Miller's state "complaint" "alleged" intentional "fraud" and malicious "conversion," meaning wrongfully taking her property. It also claimed Grimes moved an $18,000 Petty-built dragster into his wife's name to "frustrate creditors," keeping it from people he owed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: After default, Judge McConnell found intentional, willful, malicious, fraudulent conversion: the Pinto’s value had fallen from $6,500 to $150.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: After Grimes's default (his failure to answer the suit), Judge McConnell found intentional, "willful" (deliberate), malicious, fraudulent "conversion" of Miller's property. The Pinto’s value had fallen from $6,500 to $150.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: He awarded $6,350 loss and $5,000 punitive damages and authorized execution against Grimes’s person if property execution failed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: He awarded $6,350 for the loss and $5,000 in "punitive damages" (money to punish). He also authorized "execution" (enforcing the judgment) against Grimes's person, meaning arrest and jail, if seizing his property failed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: He made no finding on the alleged transfer to the wife; her case was dismissed without prejudice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: He made no "finding" on the "alleged" (claimed) transfer to Grimes's wife. The case against her was "dismissed without prejudice," meaning it could be brought again later.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: Property execution was unsatisfied, and body-execution writs issued January 15 and May 23, 1975.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: "Execution" against Grimes's property did not satisfy the debt, so "body-execution" writs, orders to arrest him, were issued on January 15 and May 23, 1975.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: A lawyer eventually acted without a fee, unsuccessfully sought habeas relief, and then petitioned for an insolvent’s oath.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: A lawyer eventually took the case without a fee. He first sought "habeas" relief (an order freeing someone held unlawfully), which failed, and then "petitioned" for an "insolvent’s oath," a sworn statement that the debtor has no property, which could lead to release.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: The three-judge Middle District of North Carolina court rejected his standing to challenge prejudgment arrest because he had experienced only postjudgment execution.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: The three-judge federal court for the Middle District of North Carolina said Grimes lacked "standing" (the right to sue) to challenge "prejudgment arrest," arrest before any judgment. He had faced only "postjudgment" execution, arrest after a judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: That challenge remained live despite release: other debts created a reasonable recurrence risk, and short detention could evade review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: That challenge stayed live even though he had been released. His other debts made it reasonably likely he would be jailed again, and short jailings could "evade review," ending before courts could decide the issue.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: With no pending state case or relevant ambiguity, abstention was unwarranted.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: With no pending state case and no relevant "ambiguity" (unclear state law), abstention, a federal court stepping back to let state courts act first, was not justified.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: On that construction it rejected substantive due-process, equal-protection, and Eighth Amendment challenges; wealthy concealers could also remain confined.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Reading the law that way, the court rejected "substantive due-process" (basic fairness), equal-protection (unequal treatment of the poor), and Eighth Amendment (cruel and unusual punishment) challenges. Wealthy debtors who hid assets could also stay jailed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: Without more, jail would punish wrongdoing without criminal protections.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Jailing someone just for a civil wrong would be punishment without the safeguards of a criminal trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: Before detention, the court required additional probable-cause facts showing impending flight to avoid creditors, fraudulent concealment or diversion of assets, or a risk of such conduct unless immediate detention occurred.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Before jailing a debtor, the court required additional "probable-cause" facts, meaning good reason to believe: that the debtor was about to flee to avoid creditors, was fraudulently hiding or moving assets, or would do so unless jailed right away.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: The federal court acknowledged that it could not authoritatively construe state law and was predicting a saving construction by North Carolina’s highest court.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: The federal court admitted it could not authoritatively "construe" (give the final word on the meaning of) state law. It was predicting that North Carolina's highest court would adopt a "saving construction," a narrow reading that keeps the law constitutional.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: The twenty-day creditor-notice rule was unconstitutional insofar as it barred preliminary release, even for someone plainly assetless.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Making a jailed debtor wait twenty days for creditors to be notified before any release was unconstitutional, at least for someone who obviously had nothing.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: Preliminary release was not final statutory discharge: creditors could investigate and pursue later confinement for fraudulent concealment until full disclosure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Early release was not the final "statutory" discharge of the debt that the law provides. Creditors could still investigate and seek to jail the debtor again for "fraudulent concealment" (dishonestly hiding assets) until he fully disclosed them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: Miller had acted in good faith under the existing scheme and could not reasonably anticipate the new construction, so damages were denied.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: Miller had acted "in good faith" (honestly) under the law as it then stood and could not reasonably have predicted the court's new reading, so "damages" (money) against her were denied.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.sentence: It dismissed the prejudgment challenge, denied classes, an injunction, and statutory attorney fees, and assigned each side its own costs.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-486.plain: The court dismissed the "prejudgment" arrest challenge. It refused to certify classes, to grant an "injunction" (an order stopping officials), or to award statutory "attorney fees" to Grimes, and each side paid its own costs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: When Consumers Union refused, Bose sued for product disparagement in federal court under diversity jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: When Consumers Union, the magazine's publisher, refused to retract, Bose sued it for product disparagement, false statements harming a product. It sued in federal court under "diversity jurisdiction," available because the companies were from different states.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: The judge treated that discrepancy as a false, disparaging factual assertion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: The judge treated the words 'about the room' as a false statement of fact that unfairly hurt the product.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: The question of culpability therefore centered on Seligson’s state of mind when he wrote the report or checked the article.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: So the question of "culpability" (legal fault) centered on the engineer Seligson's state of mind, what he knew or believed, when he wrote the report or checked the article.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: From that disbelief and the mismatch between words and perception, the court inferred that Seligson knew the statement was inaccurate when published.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Because the judge did not believe Seligson, and the words did not match what he heard, the judge concluded Seligson must have known the statement was wrong when it was published.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: The court found actual malice by clear and convincing evidence.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: The judge found, by the demanding standard of clear and convincing proof, that the magazine published knowing the statement was false or seriously doubting it ('actual malice').

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: It assumed without deciding that the words were false factual statements rather than opinion and accepted their disparaging character.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: The appeals court "assumed without deciding" (accepted for argument's sake, without ruling) that the words were false statements of fact rather than opinion. It also accepted that they disparaged, or harmed, Bose's product.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: It did not reassess demeanor, but independently examined actual malice and concluded that imprecise wording did not clearly establish knowing falsity or reckless disregard.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: It did not reassess "demeanor" (how Seligson came across on the stand). But it independently reviewed actual malice and found that imprecise wording did not clearly prove knowing falsity or "reckless disregard," meaning serious doubt about the truth that he ignored.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Bose did not contest the determination that it was a public figure or the use of the New York Times v. Sullivan standard, which protects expression absent the constitutionally required level of fault.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Bose did not dispute that it counted as a public figure, so it had to meet the strict New York Times v. Sullivan test: speech is protected unless the speaker knew it was false or recklessly ignored serious doubts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: The Supreme Court took the case to determine whether Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a), which governs clearly erroneous review of bench-trial findings, controlled the actual-malice determination.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: The Supreme Court took the case to decide whether Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a) controls the actual-malice finding. That rule requires appeals courts to accept facts found in a "bench-trial" (a trial with no jury) unless "clearly erroneous," clearly wrong.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Bose argued that knowledge at a particular time was a historical fact, especially deserving deference when based on credibility.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Bose argued that what Seligson knew at a particular time was a "historical fact," a plain question of what happened. It said such a finding especially deserves deference when it rests on the trial judge's judgment of credibility.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Consumers Union invoked appellate responsibility to examine the record before a judgment placed expression outside First Amendment protection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Consumers Union pointed to "appellate" judges' duty to examine the "record" themselves before a "judgment" places speech outside First Amendment protection.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Justice Stevens, joined by Justices Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, and Powell, held that appellate judges must independently determine whether evidence establishes actual malice with convincing clarity in a case governed by Sullivan.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Justice Stevens, "joined by" Justices Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, and Powell, held that in a case "governed by Sullivan" (the actual-malice rule), "appellate" judges must decide for themselves whether the evidence proves actual malice with convincing clarity.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: An ordinary fact does not lose deferential review merely because it affects the outcome or is called an ultimate fact.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: An ordinary fact does not lose "deferential review," where appeals judges accept the trial court's finding, just because it decides the outcome or is called an "ultimate fact."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: But the rule does not insulate legal error embedded in a mixed determination, and constitutional sufficiency cannot simply be delegated to the trial judge or jury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: But the deference rule does not shield a "legal error" buried in a mixed finding of fact and law. And constitutional "sufficiency," whether the evidence meets a constitutional standard, cannot simply be left to the trial judge or jury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: If actual malice is established, reversal still requires another legal error or a clearly erroneous factual finding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: If actual malice is proven, the appeals court can reverse only for some other "legal error" or a "clearly erroneous" (clearly wrong) factual finding.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Rejecting a later rationalization permitted the judge to disregard that explanation; it did not itself affirmatively prove the opposite state of mind at the earlier publication date.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Disbelieving Seligson's after-the-fact explanation let the judge ignore it. But disbelief is not proof that he actually knew the statement was false when it was published.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Chief Justice Burger concurred in the judgment without explaining his reasoning, making the judgment 6–3 but leaving five Justices in the majority opinion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Chief Justice Burger "concurred in the judgment" (agreed with the result) without explaining why. That made the "judgment" 6–3, but only five Justices joined the "majority opinion" and its reasoning.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Justice White agreed with Justice Rehnquist that actual knowledge of falsity was a historical fact, although White did not characterize reckless disregard the same way.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Justice White agreed with Justice Rehnquist that "actual knowledge" of falsity was a "historical fact," a plain question of what happened. White did not describe reckless disregard the same way.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.sentence: Because the district judge had found actual knowledge, White would have returned the case to the First Circuit for review under the proper deferential standard.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-531.plain: Because the "district judge" (the trial judge) had found "actual knowledge," White would have sent the case back to the First Circuit to review that finding under the proper "deferential standard," accepting it unless clearly wrong.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Johnson initially relied on Texas citizenship and injury there.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: At first, Johnson relied on his Texas "citizenship" and on being harmed there as the reason a Texas court could hear the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Johnson appealed, emphasizing website features and alternatively seeking jurisdictional discovery.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: Johnson appealed, stressing HuffPost's website features. As a fallback, he asked for "jurisdictional discovery," a chance to gather evidence about HuffPost's Texas contacts before the court ruled on its power.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Judge Jerry E. Smith, joined by Judge King, reviewed de novo with uncontroverted nonconclusory allegations accepted and the burden on Johnson.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: Judge Jerry E. Smith, "joined by" Judge King, "reviewed" the question "de novo" (afresh). He accepted as true Johnson's "uncontroverted" (not contradicted), specific factual allegations, but the burden of showing the court's power was on Johnson.
Johnson conceded that "general jurisdiction," power to hear any claim against HuffPost because it is "at home" in Texas, was unavailable.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Specific jurisdiction required purposeful contacts, a claim arising out of or relating to them, and fairness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: "Specific jurisdiction," power over this particular claim, required three things: HuffPost's purposeful contacts with Texas, a claim arising out of or relating to them, and fairness.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Interactivity initiated rather than completed Internet-libel analysis; Calder’s story-and-harm connection still mattered.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: A website's interactivity only began the Internet-libel analysis; it did not end it. Under Calder, the connection between the story itself and the harm felt in the state still mattered.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: A New York store’s compensated referral to a visiting Texan would not alone allow another Texan’s unrelated tort suit in Texas.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: By comparison, a New York store paid for a referral of a visiting Texan could not, for that alone, be sued in Texas by another Texan over an unrelated "tort" (civil wrong).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Using unrelated contacts would collapse specific into general jurisdiction and disregard other states’ authority over the publisher at home.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: Counting unrelated "contacts" (ties to Texas) would merge claim-specific jurisdiction into all-purpose general jurisdiction. It would also ignore the authority of the states where the publisher is at home.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: The majority accepted that Ford rejected strict causation, but its local sales, marketing, and servicing concerned the same vehicle models involved in injury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: The majority accepted that the Ford case rejected strict "causation," so a claim need not be directly caused by the in-state activity. But in Ford, the local sales, marketing, and servicing involved the same car models that caused the injuries.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Keeton’s regular magazine shipments represented affirmative forum distribution; mere national website accessibility did not, as pleaded, establish equivalent targeting.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: In Keeton, regular monthly magazine shipments were deliberate distribution into the "forum" (the state where the suit was filed). A website merely reachable nationwide did not, as Johnson "pleaded" (stated) his case, show the same kind of targeting.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Keeton’s circulation route differed from Calder’s effects test for individual writers or editors; the National Enquirer itself had not contested jurisdiction in Calder.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: Keeton's route, based on a publisher circulating in a state, differed from Calder's "effects test" for individual writers or editors who aim a story there. The National Enquirer itself had not contested "jurisdiction" in Calder.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Requiring the ad itself to cause libel restored an improper strict-causation rule.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: In her view, the majority was demanding that the Texas ads themselves cause the defamation, reviving the strict cause-and-effect test the Ford case rejected.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Johnson needed specific likely jurisdiction-establishing facts, but requested only the extent of contacts the majority already considered legally insufficient.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: To get extra fact-gathering, Johnson had to point to specific facts likely to prove jurisdiction. He only wanted to learn how many Texas contacts HuffPost had, and the court had already held such contacts did not count.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.sentence: Haynes would vacate and remand under her publication-focused reading without deciding defamation merits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-JOHNSON-HUFFPOST.plain: Judge Haynes, dissenting, would "vacate" (cancel) the dismissal and remand (send the case back) under her reading focused on the publication. She would not decide the defamation merits, whether the article was actually defamatory.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Avianca removed on federal-question grounds under the Montreal Convention and later sought dismissal under that treaty’s limitations period.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Avianca "removed" the case, moving it to federal court, because it raised a federal question under the Montreal Convention, a treaty on international flights. It later sought dismissal under that treaty's limitations period, its two-year deadline to sue.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Steven Schwartz of Levidow, Levidow & Oberman had handled the state case but was not admitted in the Southern District of New York.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Steven Schwartz of Levidow, Levidow & Oberman handled the state case. But he was "not admitted in" (not licensed to practice before) the federal court for the Southern District of New York.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: After encountering limited federal access through the firm’s Fastcase subscription, Schwartz treated ChatGPT as a search engine and requested cases supporting tolling during a bankruptcy stay.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: With only limited access to federal cases through the firm's Fastcase subscription, Schwartz used ChatGPT as a search engine. He asked for cases supporting "tolling" (pausing the deadline to sue) during a "bankruptcy stay," the automatic freeze on lawsuits in bankruptcy.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: On March 1, 2023, LoDuca signed and filed Schwartz’s opposition affirmation with a declaration under penalty of perjury.
