brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: On March 1, 2023, LoDuca signed and filed Schwartz's opposition affirmation, a sworn written response opposing dismissal, with a declaration under penalty of perjury that it was true.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: LoDuca obtained an extension by falsely saying he was on vacation when Schwartz was away.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: LoDuca got more time by falsely telling the court he was on vacation; in fact Schwartz was the one away.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: A May 4 show-cause order addressed LoDuca’s opposition and attachments.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: A May 4 "show-cause order" required LoDuca to explain why he should not be sanctioned (punished) over his opposition filing and its attachments.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: A May 26 supplemental order added Schwartz and the firm and addressed notarization.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: A May 26 supplemental order added Schwartz and the firm to the inquiry and raised questions about notarization, the official witnessing, of a sworn filing.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2) required reasonable inquiry supporting legal contentions in existing law or a nonfrivolous proposal to change it.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2) requires a lawyer to make a reasonable inquiry before filing. Each legal argument must be supported by existing law or be a "nonfrivolous" (serious, not baseless) argument for changing it.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Failure to correct after discovering unsupported contentions could constitute continued advocacy.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Leaving a false argument in place after learning it was unsupported counts as continuing to make it.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Rule 11(c)(3) allowed a specifically described court-initiated inquiry after notice and an opportunity to respond.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Rule 11(c)(3) allows a "court-initiated" inquiry, one the judge starts on her own, if it specifically describes the conduct. The lawyers must get "notice and an opportunity to respond."

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Responsibility could reach Schwartz despite his neither signing nor appearing, and the firm was jointly responsible absent exceptional circumstances.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Schwartz could be punished even though he never signed or formally appeared, and the law firm shared responsibility unless there were exceptional circumstances.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Under the Second Circuit precedent governing this court-initiated process, subjective bad faith was required, a higher standard than objective unreasonableness ordinarily associated with an adversary’s motion and twenty-one-day safe harbor.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Under binding Second Circuit precedent for this "court-initiated" process, the judge had to find subjective bad faith. That is stricter than the "objective unreasonableness" standard usually used when an "adversary" (the opposing side) moves for sanctions, which comes with a 21-day "safe harbor" to withdraw the filing.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Inherent-authority sanctions also required bad faith and restraint.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: "Inherent-authority" sanctions, punishment based on a court's built-in power over its own proceedings, also required bad faith and had to be used with restraint.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Knowing falsehood or conscious avoidance of a recognized high probability could qualify; negligence, confusion, foolishness, or sloppy research alone could not.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Knowingly stating a falsehood, or "conscious avoidance" (deliberately not confirming something one recognizes is highly likely), could count as bad faith. "Negligence" (carelessness), confusion, foolishness, or sloppy research alone could not.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: The court distinguished Braun v. Zhiguo Fu, where innocent reliance on another person gave the lawyer no reason to suspect falsehood.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: The court "distinguished" (explained why it differs from) Braun v. Zhiguo Fu. In that case, a lawyer innocently relied on another person and had no reason to suspect anything was false.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: For Schwartz, failed searches, Avianca’s warning, and the court’s orders established awareness of a high probability of fabrication.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: For Schwartz, his own failed searches, Avianca’s warning that the cases could not be found, and the court's orders showed he was aware of a high probability that the cases were fabricated.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: The firm accepted responsibility and identified corrections but showed no exceptional circumstances excusing Rule 11(c)(1) joint responsibility.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: The firm accepted responsibility and described corrective steps. But it showed no exceptional circumstances excusing it from joint responsibility under Rule 11(c)(1), which normally holds a law firm responsible along with its lawyers.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: The court declined an independent sanction under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 because it had not found dilatory tactics or delay of the kind addressed by unreasonable and vexatious multiplication.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: The court declined a separate "sanction" under 28 U.S.C. § 1927, a statute aimed at lawyers who needlessly drag out cases. It found no "dilatory tactics" (stalling) or delay of the kind that law targets as unreasonable and "vexatious" (harassing) multiplying of proceedings.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Rule 11 and, alternatively, inherent authority supplied the grounds.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: The sanctions rested on Rule 11 and, as an alternative ground, on the court's "inherent authority," its built-in power over its own proceedings.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Discussion of 18 U.S.C. § 505 illustrated the concern with counterfeit judicial authority, but no forged signature or seal appeared, so the respondents had not violated that criminal statute.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: The discussion of 18 U.S.C. § 505, the federal crime of forging a judge's signature or court seal, showed the concern with fake judicial authority. But no forged signature or seal appeared, so the "respondents" (the lawyers and firm) had not violated that criminal "statute."

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: Remorse, embarrassment, clean disciplinary histories, absence of financial gain or personal animus, and low repetition risk mitigated consequences without negating violations.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: Remorse, embarrassment, clean disciplinary records, no financial gain or personal "animus" (spite), and a low risk of repeating the conduct lightened the consequences. They did not erase the violations.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: On June 22, 2023, the court imposed one $5,000 penalty, jointly and severally payable by LoDuca, Schwartz, and the firm to the court registry within fourteen days—not $5,000 each or compensation to Avianca.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: On June 22, 2023, the court imposed one $5,000 penalty, paid into the "court registry" (the court's own account) within fourteen days. LoDuca, Schwartz, and the firm were liable "jointly and severally," each responsible for the whole, but it was paid once, not $5,000 each, and none went to Avianca.

brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.sentence: It resolved sanctions rather than Mata’s substantive claim or the merits of Avianca’s limitations defense.
brief-CP-SUP-MATA-SANCTIONS.plain: The decision resolved only "sanctions" (punishment of the lawyers). It did not decide Mata's "substantive" injury claim or "the merits" of Avianca’s "limitations defense," its argument that he sued too late.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: Halston moved to dismiss the mental-anguish cause as legally insufficient.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: Halston "moved to dismiss" (asked the court to throw out) the mental-anguish claim as legally insufficient, meaning that even if her account were true, the law gives no money for it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: The court considered her account favorably for that motion; it did not try and resolve each alleged defect.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: For that "motion," the court viewed her account favorably, assuming it true. It did not hold a trial or decide whether each "alleged" (claimed) defect in the dress was real.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: He nevertheless applied the general rule against recovering mental-suffering damages for breach of contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: Judge Sherman nevertheless applied the general rule against "recovering" "damages" (money) for mental suffering caused by a breach of contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: The authorities he cited recognized a few exceptions involving fiduciary or quasi-fiduciary contractual relationships, such as hotel and guest, carrier and passenger, or amusement park and patron, coupled with tortious conduct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: The "authorities" (earlier cases) he cited allowed a few exceptions for "fiduciary" or near-fiduciary relationships of special trust, such as hotel and guest, "carrier" (a transport company) and passenger, or amusement park and patron. Those cases also involved "tortious" conduct, a wrong beyond just breaking the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: Sherman also invoked the contract-damages principle associated with Hadley: recovery is limited to natural and probable consequences reasonably foreseeable at formation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: Sherman also relied on the contract-damages rule from Hadley: recovery covers only the "natural and probable consequences" of a breach that were reasonably foreseeable at "formation," when the contract was made.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: On October 3, 1977, the Civil Court of the City of New York, Special Term, New York County, dismissed the first cause of action for mental suffering and directed judgment accordingly.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: On October 3, 1977, the Civil Court of the City of New York, Special Term, New York County, "dismissed" Levin's first "cause of action" (legal claim), for mental suffering. It "directed judgment" accordingly, ordering judgment entered on that claim.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.sentence: The separately pleaded deposit claim was outside the disposition described in this opinion.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-020.plain: Her separately "pleaded" (stated) claim for return of the deposit was outside the "disposition" (outcome) described in this "opinion," so it was not decided here.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The ordinance covered employees working on or under the authority of a City service contract, provided compensated time off, and required contractors to accept civil enforcement by aggrieved employees.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The "ordinance" (city law) covered employees working on or under a City service contract and required paid time off. It also required contractors to accept "civil enforcement" by aggrieved employees, meaning affected workers could sue them directly.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The court certified production and stockroom workers employed at both facilities from July 1, 1999 through June 30, 2003, and Hayward intervened.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The court certified a class, letting the case proceed for all production and stockroom workers at both plants from July 1, 1999 through June 30, 2003. The City of Hayward "intervened," joining the lawsuit.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: After the Private Attorneys General Act, or PAGA, became effective, the employees amended to seek additional penalties.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: After the Private Attorneys General Act, or PAGA, took effect, the employees "amended" their complaint to seek added penalties. PAGA lets workers sue for penalties that only the state could collect before.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The trial court rejected an early extraterritoriality challenge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The trial court rejected an early "extraterritoriality" challenge, Cintas's argument that Hayward could not regulate work done outside city limits.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: On September 23, 2005, it ruled on cross-motions for summary judgment or adjudication that the ordinance was constitutional, enforceable, applicable to all hours of covered employees, and violated by Cintas.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: On September 23, 2005, ruling on cross-motions (both sides asking for a decision without trial), the court held the "ordinance" constitutional and "enforceable." It held that the law covered all hours of covered employees and that Cintas violated it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: It found no willfulness justifying enhanced or waiting-time penalties.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: It found no willfulness, no deliberate refusal to pay, so the enhanced penalties and "waiting-time penalties" (extra pay owed when wages are not paid on time) did not apply.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: An appeal-facilitating stipulation produced judgment for the employees and City, later corrected in form.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: A "stipulation" (formal agreement) between the parties, made to allow an appeal, produced a judgment for the employees and the City; its form was later corrected.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Presiding Justice McGuiness, joined by Justices Pollak and Jenkins, distinguished Hayward’s proprietary contracting authority from general territorial regulation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Presiding Justice McGuiness, joined by Justices Pollak and Jenkins, separated Hayward's power as a contracting customer setting terms for its own contracts (its "proprietary" role) from general regulation of businesses within its territory.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Employee enforcement and fines did not transform the condition into regulation of every outside employer.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Letting employees sue and imposing fines did not turn the contract condition into "regulation" (a law) governing every outside employer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Its context and remedial purpose answered the vagueness challenge, and economic regulation allowed more flexibility than penal law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The law's context and "remedial purpose" (protecting workers) answered the "vagueness challenge," the claim that it was too unclear. Economic "regulation" may also be less precise than "penal law," criminal law that punishes.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: City officials’ testimony on statutory meaning was inadmissible legal opinion, even when given by a designated knowledgeable deposition representative.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: City officials' testimony about what the law means was "inadmissible" (not allowed as evidence), because that is legal opinion for the judge. That held even when given by a "designated knowledgeable deposition representative," the City's official spokesperson at a deposition.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The claim that they served only their employer was waived and inconsistent with the text.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Cintas's claim that its workers served only Cintas was "waived" (lost because raised too late) and also conflicted with the law's text.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Neither wages nor leave carried a City-minutes limitation, and there was no de minimis exception.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Neither the wage nor the leave requirement was limited to City-minutes, the time spent on City items. And there was no "de minimis" exception for tiny amounts of covered work.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Wage-law precedents and unequal access to proof justified requiring Cintas to identify workers who did no covered work.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Earlier wage-law "precedents" and the fact that Cintas, not the workers, held the records justified requiring Cintas to identify which workers did no covered work.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Civil Code § 1559 allowed nonparties to enforce contracts expressly made for their benefit where that intent appeared in the terms.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Civil Code § 1559 lets "nonparties" (people who did not sign) enforce a contract expressly made for their benefit, where that intent appears in its terms.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: They were intended beneficiaries entitled to sue for breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The workers were "intended beneficiaries," people Cintas's promise to the City was meant to benefit, so they could sue Cintas for breach.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Contract recovery remained a separate inquiry from any statutory private-action question.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Recovery for breach of contract was a separate question from whether the "statutory" ordinance itself gave workers a private right to sue.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: PAGA allowed employees to pursue existing penalties previously collectible by the Labor Commissioner.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: PAGA let employees sue for existing penalties that before could be collected only by the state's wage enforcer, the Labor Commissioner.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: That new standing did not change the legal consequences of past underpayments.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: That new "standing," the workers' new right to bring the suit, did not change the legal consequences of past underpayments. So PAGA could be applied to earlier violations.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The amendments related back because they concerned the same underpayments and injuries, despite the newly available legal theory.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The "amendments" (added claims) "related back," meaning they were treated as filed on the original date, because they concerned the same underpayments and injuries, even though the legal theory was newly available.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: A good-faith legal or factual defense could negate willfulness even if rejected.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: A "good-faith" (honest and reasonable) legal or factual "defense" could show the violation was not willful, even if the court rejected it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Its first-impression ordinance arguments were substantial rather than frivolous.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Cintas's arguments about the "ordinance" raised questions of first impression, never decided before, and were substantial rather than "frivolous" (baseless).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Cintas violated Labor Code § 223 by certifying required-scale payment to Hayward while secretly paying less; concealment could be from the contracting or enforcement party even if workers knew their actual wages.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Cintas violated Labor Code § 223, a state wage law, by certifying to Hayward that it paid the required wage scale while secretly paying less. The "concealment" (hiding the truth) could be from the contracting or enforcing "party," here the City, even if workers knew their actual wages.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Repetition did not automatically turn the second payday into a subsequent violation at twice the rate; notice that conduct violated the law marked that transition.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The higher penalty for 'repeat' violations did not start just because underpayment continued to a second payday. It started only once Cintas was told its conduct broke the law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Base penalties were mandatory, subject to PAGA’s power to reduce a maximum that would be unjust, arbitrary and oppressive, or confiscatory under its criteria.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The base penalties were mandatory. But PAGA’s rules let a court reduce the maximum if, under PAGA's criteria, it would be unjust, arbitrary and oppressive, or "confiscatory," so large it amounts to taking the business's property.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The court respected the Labor Commissioner’s persuasive interpretation about notice and pay periods, but rejected an informal policy excusing all penalties in good-faith disputes as contrary to statute.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The court followed the Labor Commissioner’s persuasive reading on notice and pay periods. But it rejected the agency's informal policy of excusing all penalties in "good-faith" (honest) disputes, because that conflicted with the statute.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Most legal questions received de novo review; good-faith factual findings received substantial-evidence review, and penalty reduction and fee enhancement were discretionary questions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: Most legal questions got "de novo" "review" (decided afresh). The finding of good faith got substantial-evidence review, upheld if reasonable evidence supports it, and penalty reduction and fee "enhancement" (raising the fee) were left to the trial judge's discretion.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The appellate court therefore left unresolved whether identical interest could be awarded on unpaid-wage restitution under unfair-competition law; deciding it would provide no effective relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The "appellate court" therefore left open whether the same interest could be "awarded" on "restitution" (repayment) of unpaid wages under unfair-competition law. The workers already got that interest on their contract claim, so deciding it would give no effective "relief."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: The trial court had awarded $1,199,550 in fees, using a $727,000 lodestar and 1.65 multiplier, plus $60,611 for the fee motion.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: The trial court had awarded $1,199,550 in fees. It used a $727,000 "lodestar" (reasonable hours times reasonable rates) raised by a 1.65 multiplier, plus $60,611 for the "fee motion," the work of requesting fees.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: They could not recover $65,641.28 in other expenses, including experts, without statutory authority; Olson had disapproved the sole precedent they invoked.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: They could not recover $65,641.28 in other expenses, including "experts" (expert-witness fees), without a statute allowing it. The California Supreme Court in Olson had "disapproved" (rejected) the only "precedent" they cited.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.sentence: Rehearing was denied July 2 and California Supreme Court review September 10; those later denials added no reasoned merits holding.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-074.plain: "Rehearing" (reconsideration by the appeals court) was denied July 2, and the California Supreme Court denied "review" September 10. Those later refusals added no reasoned ruling on the "merits."

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: It called for final binding arbitration in Honolulu under the Federal Arbitration Act and American Arbitration Association procedures for employment and termination claims, presented within two years after actual or constructive awareness.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: It required final, binding arbitration (a private decision-maker instead of a court) in Honolulu under the Federal Arbitration Act and American Arbitration Association rules. Claims had to be raised within two years after actual or "constructive awareness," meaning when the employee knew or should have known of them.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: It described the handbook as information rather than an employment contract, said guidelines were not conditions of employment, and reserved the company’s right to change the handbook at any time without notice.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: It described the handbook as information, not an employment contract, and said its guidelines were not conditions of employment. It also "reserved" (kept) the company's right to change the handbook at any time without notice.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Douglass filed an administrative discrimination complaint in May 2002, received a September 25 right-to-sue letter, and sued in circuit court December 17.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Douglass filed a discrimination complaint with a government agency in May 2002 and got a "right-to-sue letter" (the agency's permission to sue) on September 25. He sued in "circuit court," the state trial court, on December 17.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Following a deposition, the parties stipulated on September 11, 2003, to dismiss the negligent-training and supervision claims with prejudice.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: After a "deposition" (pretrial questioning under oath), the parties "stipulated" (formally agreed) on September 11, 2003, to "dismiss" the negligent-training and supervision claims "with prejudice," meaning permanently.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Pflueger moved to stay and compel arbitration December 1.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: On December 1, Pflueger moved to "stay" (pause) the lawsuit and to compel arbitration, asking the court to order Douglass into arbitration.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: At the December 29 hearing, the judge reasoned that someone accepting contractual benefits should not disavow another contract provision.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: At the December 29 "hearing," the judge reasoned that someone who accepts the benefits of a "contractual" deal, here the job, should not reject another term of that contract, the arbitration clause.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Chief Justice Moon first distinguished at-will employment from no contract at all.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Chief Justice Moon first explained that "at-will" employment, a job either side can end at any time, is still a contract; it is not the same as no contract at all.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: The majority then rejected an absolute right to disaffirm that agreement because of minority.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: The "majority" then rejected an absolute right to "disaffirm" (cancel) the agreement because of "minority," Douglass being under 18 when he made it.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: It recognized the protective common-law infancy doctrine and the exception for necessaries, but nobody argued this job was a necessary.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: The court recognized the protective "common-law" (judge-made) infancy rule letting minors cancel contracts, and its exception for "necessaries," basic needs such as food or shelter. But nobody argued this job was a necessary.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Instead, the majority inferred from Hawaii’s child-labor scheme that statutory protections made employment agreements binding.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Instead, the majority inferred from Hawaii's child-labor laws that their "statutory" protections for working minors meant the legislature intended job agreements with minors to be binding.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: The court reviewed formation de novo under the summary-judgment evidentiary standard.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: The court "reviewed" formation, whether an arbitration agreement was made, "de novo" (afresh, without deferring to the trial judge). It applied the same evidence standard used for "summary-judgment," deciding without a trial.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: A policy favoring arbitration could not replace agreement.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: The law's general preference for arbitration cannot force arbitration on someone who never agreed to it.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Brown v. KFC National Management Co., an earlier arbitration-formation case, required writing, unambiguous intent to arbitrate, and bilateral consideration.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Brown v. KFC National Management Co., an earlier case on forming arbitration agreements, required a writing, an "unambiguous" (clear) intent to arbitrate, and bilateral consideration, binding promises from both sides.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Former chapter 658 governed; chapter 658A’s later effective date did not reach this September 2001 agreement.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Former chapter 658, Hawaii's older arbitration statute, governed. Chapter 658A's later "effective date" (when it took effect) came after this September 2001 agreement, so it did not apply.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: But the informational acknowledgment, contractual disclaimers, and absence of arbitration from the signature page defeated a showing of unambiguous assent.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: But the signature page called the handbook information, disclaimers said it was not a contract, and the signature page never mentioned arbitration. Together these defeated any showing of "unambiguous" (clear) assent to arbitrate.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: The majority preserved the usual rule that someone knowingly entering a contract cannot escape merely by failing to read it.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: The "majority" kept the usual rule that someone who knowingly enters a contract cannot escape it just by failing to read it.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Even assuming assent, the majority found no binding reciprocal consideration.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Even assuming "assent" (that Douglass agreed), the majority found no binding reciprocal consideration: the company was not really bound to anything in return.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: It could revoke its obligation while insisting the employee remain bound.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: The company could take back its own promise to arbitrate whenever it liked while holding Douglass to his, so its promise was empty.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: A severable standalone agreement might survive a power to amend handbook policies.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: A severable, standalone arbitration agreement, one separate from the handbook, might survive even if the employer kept power to "amend" (change) handbook policies.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: With no valid agreement, the majority did not decide whether disputed formation facts independently required a trial or whether Pflueger waived arbitration through litigation conduct.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: With no valid agreement, the "majority" did not decide whether disputed facts about "formation" (whether an agreement was made) required a trial. Nor did it decide whether Pflueger "waived" (gave up) arbitration by litigating in court.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Employment was not established as a necessary, and permission to hire a minor did not abolish disaffirmance.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Justice Acoba said employment was not shown to be a necessary (a basic need), and laws allowing employers to hire minors did not abolish "disaffirmance," a minor's right to cancel a contract.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Arbitration policy and equal treatment of adult and minor employees could not eliminate a minor’s distinct capacity defense.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Favoring arbitration, and treating adult and minor employees equally, could not erase a minor's separate "capacity defense," the rule that a minor lacks full legal capacity to be bound by contracts.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Douglass also sought statutory and tort remedies, not employment-contract benefits while rejecting burdens.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Douglass was also seeking "statutory" remedies (under anti-discrimination laws) and tort "remedies" for personal wrongs such as assault. He was not taking job-contract benefits while rejecting its burdens.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Alternatively, Acoba would read the whole handbook’s conflicting binding and nonbinding messages against Pflueger as drafter, making arbitration directory rather than compulsory.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Alternatively, Acoba would read the handbook's conflicting binding and nonbinding messages against Pflueger "as drafter," the party that wrote it. That would make arbitration "directory" (an optional suggestion) rather than compulsory.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: He shared the illusory-promise concern but criticized requiring employees to decipher typography, boxes, and placement within a document declaring itself noncontractual.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: He shared the "illusory-promise" concern, that the company's promise bound it to nothing. But he criticized requiring employees to decode fonts, boxes, and placement within a document that declares itself not a contract.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: On May 25, 2006, the Hawaii Supreme Court vacated the December 30 stay and arbitration order and remanded for further proceedings.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: On May 25, 2006, the Hawaii Supreme Court "vacated" (canceled) the December 30 order granting a "stay" (pause of the lawsuit) and compelling arbitration. It remanded, sending the case back for further proceedings.

brief-CT-CB-0450.sentence: Moon, Levinson, Nakayama, and Duffy joined the court’s reasoning; Acoba concurred only in the result.
brief-CT-CB-0450.plain: Justices Moon, Levinson, Nakayama, and Duffy joined the court's reasoning. Justice Acoba "concurred" only in the result, agreeing with the outcome but not the reasoning.

cp-byrd.sentence: If the contracted work was part of its own business, Byrd could be its statutory employee despite his immediate employment by Bouligny, making compensation the exclusive remedy and barring negligence recovery.
cp-byrd.plain: If the contracted work was part of Blue Ridge's own business, Byrd could be its "statutory employee," treated by law as its employee even though Bouligny directly hired him. Workers' compensation would then be his "exclusive remedy" (only remedy), barring a negligence suit against Blue Ridge.

cp-byrd.sentence: Blue Ridge’s manager described prior construction by company crews, but cross-examination left its extent uncertain.
cp-byrd.plain: Blue Ridge's manager testified that company crews had done such construction before. But on "cross-examination" (questioning by Byrd's lawyer) it stayed unclear how much.

cp-byrd.sentence: An earlier dismissal on asserted nonprofit immunity had been reversed.
cp-byrd.plain: The case had earlier suffered a "dismissal" (been thrown out) on a claim of "nonprofit immunity," the idea that a nonprofit could not be sued. That ruling was "reversed," meaning a higher court overturned it.

cp-byrd.sentence: That reading made evidence of internal construction insufficient, and he struck the defense.
cp-byrd.plain: Under that reading, evidence that Blue Ridge built its own lines could not be enough, so the judge "struck" (removed from the case) Blue Ridge's workers'-compensation defense.

cp-byrd.sentence: A jury then found for Byrd on negligence; it never decided statutory employment.
cp-byrd.plain: The jury found Blue Ridge negligent (careless) and ruled for Byrd. It never decided "statutory employment," meaning whether the statute treated Byrd as Blue Ridge's employee.

cp-byrd.sentence: The Fourth Circuit rejected the trial judge’s South Carolina interpretation, assessed the existing evidence, and directed judgment for Blue Ridge.
cp-byrd.plain: The Fourth Circuit, the federal appeals court, rejected the trial judge's reading of South Carolina law. It weighed the existing evidence itself and ordered judgment for Blue Ridge without a new trial.

cp-byrd.sentence: Justice Brennan explained that Byrd had no reason to rebut a defense the trial court considered legally unavailable.
cp-byrd.plain: Justice Brennan explained that Byrd had no reason to "rebut" (offer evidence against) a defense the trial judge had already ruled could not legally apply, so it was unfair to fault him for not doing so.

cp-byrd.sentence: Sufficient proof to keep a defense in the case did not compel its acceptance, and even credited historical construction involved a question of degree about Blue Ridge’s business.
cp-byrd.plain: Having enough evidence to let a jury consider the defense does not mean the jury must accept it. Even if Blue Ridge's crews had built lines before, whether that made such work part of its business was a matter of degree.

cp-byrd.sentence: Byrd’s motion to strike did not waive a responsive evidentiary opportunity when its legal premise proved wrong.
cp-byrd.plain: By asking the judge to strike the defense, Byrd did not "waive" (give up) his chance to answer it with evidence once the judge's legal view turned out to be wrong.

cp-byrd.sentence: For a possible retrial, Blue Ridge relied on South Carolina’s Adams v. Davison-Paxon decision assigning statutory-employment facts to a judge.
cp-byrd.plain: Looking ahead to a possible "retrial" (new trial), Blue Ridge relied on a South Carolina case, Adams v. Davison-Paxon, saying a judge, not a jury, decides the facts on whether someone is a statutory employee.

cp-byrd.sentence: It argued that Erie required the same federal allocation.
cp-byrd.plain: Blue Ridge argued that under the Erie rule, which makes federal courts follow state law in state-law cases, a federal judge also had to decide that question instead of the jury.

cp-byrd.sentence: The Supreme Court first asked whether that choice of decisionmaker defined the compensation relationship itself.
cp-byrd.plain: The Supreme Court first asked whether South Carolina's choice of judge over jury was part of the workers' compensation relationship itself, rather than just a way of running trials.

cp-byrd.sentence: The state precedent drew from judicial review of the Industrial Commission’s jurisdiction, where judges had traditionally found relevant facts.
cp-byrd.plain: The state "precedent" (earlier ruling) came from "judicial review" of the Industrial Commission’s power, that is, courts checking whether the state compensation agency could hear a case. There judges had traditionally decided the facts.

cp-byrd.sentence: Nothing explained why extending that practice to an affirmative negligence defense was integral to substantive rights.
cp-byrd.plain: Nothing explained why using that judge-decides practice for an affirmative defense in a negligence suit was an essential part of the "substantive rights," meaning the actual legal rights and duties, that the state law created.

cp-byrd.sentence: State-law immunity remained controlling, but its factfinding mechanism did not necessarily follow.
cp-byrd.plain: The state-law "immunity" (the rule shielding employers from being sued) still controlled. But the state's way of "factfinding," deciding the disputed facts, did not automatically come with it.

cp-byrd.sentence: York’s concern with practical outcomes meant a procedural label was insufficient: judges and juries can reach different results, giving uniformity weight.
cp-byrd.plain: "York’s concern" with practical outcomes (from Guaranty Trust Co. v. York) meant calling a rule "procedural" was not enough to ignore it. Judges and juries can reach different results, so matching state-court outcomes mattered.

cp-byrd.sentence: Against it stood the federal system’s essential judge–jury allocation, operating under the Seventh Amendment’s influence.
cp-byrd.plain: On the other side was the federal system's essential division of work between judge and jury, shaped by the Seventh Amendment’s guarantee of a civil jury trial, under which juries decide disputed facts.

cp-byrd.sentence: Herron had protected a federal judge’s role against a state allocation to juries; the institutional principle therefore did not simply favor more jury power in every case.
cp-byrd.plain: In an earlier case (Herron), the Court protected a federal judge's power against a state rule giving juries more say. So the principle was about preserving the federal system's own division of labor, not always favoring juries.

cp-byrd.sentence: Using a jury did not guarantee a different result as ignoring a limitations bar might.
cp-byrd.plain: Using a jury was not sure to change the result, unlike ignoring a "limitations bar" (a state filing deadline that ends a late suit), which plainly would.

cp-byrd.sentence: Federal judges could comment on evidence and credibility and grant a new trial against the weight of evidence.
cp-byrd.plain: Federal judges also have tools to guide juries: they may "comment on evidence" and witness credibility, and they may grant a new trial when a verdict is "against the weight" of the evidence.

cp-byrd.sentence: Given that qualified risk and a strong federal structural interest, the state method did not displace federal practice.
cp-byrd.plain: Given that limited risk of a different outcome and a strong "structural" federal interest (in how federal courts divide work between judge and jury), the state method did not override federal practice.

cp-byrd.sentence: The Court expressly reserved whether the Seventh Amendment itself independently guaranteed that outcome for this issue.
cp-byrd.plain: The Court expressly "reserved" (left undecided) whether the Seventh Amendment, the constitutional right to a civil jury, by itself required a jury on this issue.

cp-byrd.sentence: The analysis considered connection to substantive entitlements, probable outcome effects, and the particular federal interest rather than stopping at a substance-procedure label.
cp-byrd.plain: The Court weighed whether the state rule was tied to the rights themselves, whether ignoring it would likely change outcomes, and how strong the federal interest was. It did not stop at a "substance-procedure" label.

cp-byrd.sentence: In his view, the compensation scheme gave the Industrial Commission exclusive jurisdiction over covered claims, with judges deciding its boundary.
cp-byrd.plain: Justice Whittaker thought the compensation law gave the Industrial Commission, the state agency, sole power over covered "claims" (injury cases), with judges deciding which cases fall inside that power.

cp-byrd.sentence: On May 19, 1958, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded to the Fourth Circuit, seven votes to two; Part II received six votes to three.
cp-byrd.plain: On May 19, 1958, the Supreme Court "reversed" the Fourth Circuit (overturned its ruling) and sent the case back, seven votes to two. Part II, on judge versus jury, drew only six votes to three.

cp-byrd.sentence: Unless those made further trial unnecessary, it would return the case for a new trial of directed issues.
cp-byrd.plain: Unless Blue Ridge's other arguments on appeal ended the case, the appeals court would send it back for a new trial on the issues identified.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Attribution of the local conduct to the international organization therefore required separate proof; shared union affiliation did not itself establish the defendant’s responsibility.
cp-gibbs.plain: To hold the "international organization" (the national union) responsible for what the local did, Gibbs needed separate proof. Belonging to the same union did not by itself prove the defendant’s responsibility.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Gibbs sued the international union in federal district court under § 303 of the Labor Management Relations Act, alleging prohibited secondary pressure, and under Tennessee law for an unlawful conspiracy interfering with his employment and hauling arrangements.
cp-gibbs.plain: Gibbs sued the "international union" in federal court under § 303 of the Labor Management Relations Act, alleging illegal "secondary pressure" on companies outside the dispute. He also claimed under Tennessee law that it conspired to wreck his job and hauling contract.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The federal labor claim supplied the asserted original jurisdiction.
cp-gibbs.plain: The federal labor claim was the claimed basis for "original jurisdiction," the federal court's power to hear the case in the first place.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The Tennessee theory had no independent jurisdictional basis.
cp-gibbs.plain: The Tennessee claim had no "independent jurisdictional basis": it could not have been brought in federal court on its own.

cp-gibbs.sentence: On post-trial motions, the judge set aside the hauling award for insufficient support and rejected federal liability for the employment loss because the pressure arose in a primary labor dispute rather than the secondary activity § 303 covered.
cp-gibbs.plain: On "post-trial motions" the judge "set aside" (threw out) the hauling "award" for lack of evidence. He rejected federal "liability" for the job loss because the pressure came from a "primary labor dispute" with the employer itself, not the "secondary activity" § 303 covers.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The court nevertheless retained a reduced recovery under Tennessee law.
cp-gibbs.plain: Still, the judge let Gibbs keep a smaller "recovery" (damages award) under the Tennessee claim.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Justice Brennan rejected an excessively formal distinction associated with Hurn v. Oursler between two grounds for one cause of action and two separate causes.
cp-gibbs.plain: Justice Brennan discarded an overly technical test from Hurn v. Oursler, which asked whether the claims were two "grounds" for one "cause of action" (one legal claim) or two separate causes.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Modern procedure’s treatment of related disputes illustrated why, although procedural rules could not themselves enlarge judicial power.
cp-gibbs.plain: Modern court rules, which encourage trying related claims together, showed why the old test made little sense. But "procedural rules" alone cannot expand "judicial power," meaning what federal courts may constitutionally hear.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Pendent power existed when a substantial federal claim supported original jurisdiction, federal and state claims shared a common nucleus of operative fact, and their relationship made joint trial ordinarily expected.
cp-gibbs.plain: "Pendent" power exists when a substantial federal claim supports original jurisdiction, both claims share a "common nucleus of operative fact" (the same basic events), and you would normally expect to try them together.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Separate theories or remedies did not necessarily divide a constitutional case.
cp-gibbs.plain: Different legal theories or "remedies" (kinds of relief) do not necessarily split one "constitutional case," the single dispute a federal court has power to hear.

cp-gibbs.sentence: A claim that ultimately failed after trial differed from a purported federal claim so insubstantial that jurisdiction never existed.
cp-gibbs.plain: A federal claim that loses after trial is different from one so baseless that "jurisdiction," the court's power over the case, never existed.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Brennan separated Article III power from discretion to use it.
cp-gibbs.plain: Brennan separated Article III power (the Constitution's grant of power to hear the state claim) from "discretion" to use it. Judges may choose not to.

cp-gibbs.sentence: State questions might predominate in proof, breadth, or remedy, and combining theories might confuse a jury or make trial unfair.
cp-gibbs.plain: A judge might decline if state issues "predominate" (dominate) in the evidence, the scope of the case, or the "remedy" sought, or if combining the theories might confuse a jury or make the trial unfair.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Federal claims disappearing before trial ordinarily called for dismissal of the accompanying state claims.
cp-gibbs.plain: If the federal claim drops out early, the judge should usually dismiss the state claims too, so state courts can decide them.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Here the claims were tried together over the same conduct, federal liability failed only after trial, and federal labor preemption directly affected the state theory.
cp-gibbs.plain: Here both claims were tried together over the same conduct, federal "liability" failed only after trial, and federal labor "preemption" (federal law overriding state law) directly limited the state claim.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The district court could have declined jurisdiction, but retaining it was not an abuse of discretion.
cp-gibbs.plain: The "district court" (federal trial court) could have declined "jurisdiction" over the state claim, but keeping it was not an "abuse of discretion," meaning not an unreasonable choice.

cp-gibbs.sentence: States could regulate labor-dispute violence and threats, but that authority did not permit damages for every effect of peaceful conduct regulated by federal labor law.
cp-gibbs.plain: States may "regulate" (make rules about) violence and threats in labor disputes. But that power does not let them award damages for every effect of peaceful conduct that federal labor law governs.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The decisive problem concerned § 6 of the Norris-LaGuardia Act.
cp-gibbs.plain: The deciding problem was § 6 of the Norris-LaGuardia Act, a federal labor law limiting when unions are responsible for their members' acts.

cp-gibbs.sentence: It required clear proof that the international union actually participated in, authorized, or knowingly ratified the unlawful acts.
cp-gibbs.plain: Gibbs had to show by clear proof that the "international union" actually took part in the unlawful acts, authorized them in advance, or knowingly "ratified" them, meaning approved them afterward.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Continuation of legitimate union activity could not, on this record, be treated as ratification of violence.
cp-gibbs.plain: "On this record" (based on the evidence actually presented), continuing lawful union activity could not count as "ratification" (after-the-fact approval) of the violence.

cp-gibbs.sentence: He regarded the broader preemption discussion as unnecessary.
cp-gibbs.plain: He thought the majority's broader discussion of "preemption" (how far federal labor law displaces state law) was unnecessary.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The failure was proof of international-union responsibility under federal law, not absence of pendent judicial power.
cp-gibbs.plain: Gibbs lost because he could not prove the national union was responsible under federal law, not because the court lacked pendent "judicial power" to hear the state claim.

cp-gibbs.sentence: The later statutory supplemental-jurisdiction regime discussed in Allapattah must be read through its own language and restrictions.
cp-gibbs.plain: Congress later wrote these rules into a statute, discussed in the Allapattah case, and that statute's own words now control.

cp-gibbs.sentence: Gibbs supplies the common-fact conception of a constitutional case and the distinction between having power and choosing to exercise it.
cp-gibbs.plain: Gibbs supplies two lasting ideas: claims from the same core facts form one "constitutional case" a federal court can hear, and having that power is different from choosing to use it.

cp-ingraham.sentence: It awarded Jocelyn $750,000 for her losses, including loss of her daughter’s society.
cp-ingraham.plain: The court awarded Jocelyn $750,000 for her losses, including "loss of her daughter’s society," meaning the companionship and relationship she would have had with her daughter.

cp-ingraham.sentence: Yet the government never invoked that statute in its pleadings or during either trial.
cp-ingraham.plain: Yet the government never invoked the cap "statute" in its "pleadings" (its written papers setting out its position) or at either trial.

cp-ingraham.sentence: After the Ingraham judgment, the government filed a notice of appeal and then raised the cap in a motion under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b).
cp-ingraham.plain: After the Ingraham judgment, the government filed a "notice of appeal." Only then did it raise the cap, in a "motion" (formal request) under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b), which lets a court reopen a final judgment.

cp-ingraham.sentence: The district court denied the motion; the government did not separately appeal that denial.
cp-ingraham.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) denied the motion, and the government never separately appealed that denial.

cp-ingraham.sentence: In Bonds, even the government’s initial Rule 59 motion to amend the judgment omitted the cap.
cp-ingraham.plain: In Bonds, even the government's first Rule 59 motion to "amend" (change) the judgment did not mention the cap.

cp-ingraham.sentence: Because the Rule 59 period had expired, the Fifth Circuit treated that later request as a Rule 60 motion; its caption did not supply a separate procedural vehicle.
cp-ingraham.plain: The Rule 59 deadline to change the judgment had passed, so the Fifth Circuit treated the later request as a Rule 60 motion to reopen a final judgment. Its title did not create a separate "procedural" vehicle, a different kind of request.

cp-ingraham.sentence: The government sought reductions under the cap and also preserved two independent objections to the Bonds damages.
cp-ingraham.plain: The government asked for reductions under the cap and also kept alive two separate "objections" (complaints) to the Bonds "damages," the money awarded.

cp-ingraham.sentence: Judge Politz, writing for a panel that also included Chief Judge Clark and Judge Rubin, held that the cap was an affirmative defense under Rule 8(c).
cp-ingraham.plain: Judge Politz, writing for a "panel" (three-judge group) that also included Chief Judge Clark and Judge Rubin, held that the cap is an "affirmative defense" under Rule 8(c): a point the defendant must raise itself in its answer.

cp-ingraham.sentence: That rule covered both its enumerated defenses and other matters constituting an avoidance.
cp-ingraham.plain: The rule covers the defenses it lists plus any other argument that defeats or limits recovery even if the plaintiff proves the claim.

cp-ingraham.sentence: Classification was a federal-law question, though state decisions could provide guidance.
cp-ingraham.plain: Whether the cap counts as an affirmative defense is decided by federal law, though state cases can help.

cp-ingraham.sentence: It supplied an additional statutory reason to deny full recovery even after those elements were proved.
cp-ingraham.plain: The cap gives an extra "statutory" reason (one from a statute) to deny full recovery, even after the plaintiff proves the "elements," the required parts, of the claim.

cp-ingraham.sentence: The court accepted those lost opportunities as concrete unfair surprise without deciding the constitutional questions.
cp-ingraham.plain: The court accepted those lost chances to prepare as real "unfair surprise" (being caught off guard by a late defense), without deciding whether the cap was constitutional.

cp-ingraham.sentence: The government’s failure to raise the cap before judgment therefore waived it in these cases.
cp-ingraham.plain: Because the government did not raise the cap before judgment, it "waived" it (lost the right to use it) in these cases.

cp-ingraham.sentence: The court distinguished Lucas v. United States, an earlier decision allowing an unpleaded cap raised during trial through an effective amendment without unfair surprise.
cp-ingraham.plain: The court "distinguished" (explained why it did not control here) Lucas v. United States, which allowed an "unpleaded" cap, one left out of the answer, because it was raised during trial by an effective "amendment" without unfair surprise.

cp-ingraham.sentence: Rule 8(c) protected a fair opportunity to respond; it did not make every omission from an initial answer incurable.
cp-ingraham.plain: Rule 8(c) protects a fair chance to respond. It does not make every defense left out of the first answer impossible to add later.

cp-ingraham.sentence: Liberal construction of a notice of appeal did not sweep in a distinct determination knowingly omitted from it.
cp-ingraham.plain: "Liberal construction" (generous reading) of a "notice of appeal" does not stretch it to cover a separate ruling the government knowingly left out of it.

cp-ingraham.sentence: A district court could consider that motion despite the pending appeal, and its denial could be separately appealed.
cp-ingraham.plain: The "district court" could decide that "motion" even while the appeal was pending, and the government could have appealed its denial separately.

cp-ingraham.sentence: State law supplied the components and measure of damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act, while the trial judge’s determination of amount was a factual finding reviewed for clear error under Rule 52(a).
cp-ingraham.plain: Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, state law decides what kinds and measure of damages apply. The trial judge's dollar amount is a factual finding, reviewed under Rule 52(a) only for "clear error," meaning overturned only if clearly wrong.

cp-ingraham.sentence: The final findings and judgment controlled.
cp-ingraham.plain: What the judge wrote in the final findings and judgment, not his earlier remarks, is what counts.

cp-panamerican.sentence: It sought interpleader against potential claimants, restrictions on other proceedings, and adjudication in one action, depositing a $100,400 bond; the additional $400 apparently covered costs.
cp-panamerican.plain: The insurer sought "interpleader" (making all potential "claimants" fight over the fund in one suit), limits on other suits, and one decision. It deposited a $100,400 bond; the extra $400 apparently covered costs.

cp-panamerican.sentence: It disclaimed an interest in the fund but denied liability.
cp-panamerican.plain: The insurer "disclaimed" any interest in the fund (said none of the money was its own), but still denied "liability," meaning that its insured was legally at fault.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Counsel explained that surrendering a claim to the money did not concede the insured’s negligence and expose the insured to uninsured liability.
cp-panamerican.plain: "Counsel" (its lawyer) explained that giving up any "claim" to the money did not admit its insured's "negligence" (carelessness), which could leave the insured personally liable beyond the policy.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Complete diversity between insurer and claimants supported ordinary diversity jurisdiction for Rule 22.
cp-panamerican.plain: "Complete diversity" (the insurer was from a different state than every claimant) supplied ordinary diversity jurisdiction for interpleader under Rule 22.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Diversity among claimants supported statutory interpleader, and the fund exceeded the then-applicable ordinary diversity amount and statutory interpleader’s $500 minimum.
cp-panamerican.plain: "Diversity" among the claimants themselves (some from different states) supported statutory interpleader. The fund also exceeded both the then-required ordinary "diversity amount" and the statute's $500 minimum.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Judge Wright therefore did not need to settle competing treatments of an interested stakeholder’s citizenship.
cp-panamerican.plain: So Judge Wright did not need to settle the competing views on how an "interested stakeholder's" citizenship counts, meaning a fund holder that also disputes the claims.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Traditional strict interpleader involved a disinterested holder, while a bill in the nature of interpleader could involve contested claims.
cp-panamerican.plain: Traditional strict interpleader involved a "disinterested" holder who claimed none of the money. A "bill in the nature of interpleader" allowed the holder to contest the claims.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Exposure to multiple litigation over one insufficient fund supplied equitable justification without an additional special ground.
cp-panamerican.plain: Facing "multiple litigation" (many suits) over one fund too small to pay everyone was enough "equitable" justification, a fairness reason courts accept, without any further special ground.

cp-panamerican.sentence: A policy cap did not defeat potential multiple liability; the possibility of excessive payment was enough.
cp-panamerican.plain: A policy limit did not rule out "multiple liability" (being made to pay more than once or more than the limit); the possibility of paying too much was enough.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Different amounts or legal sources did not remove adversity, because each recovery reduced the money available for others.
cp-panamerican.plain: Different amounts or legal bases did not remove "adversity" (the claimants being opponents), because each "recovery" (award) reduced the money left for the others.

cp-panamerican.sentence: The court rejected unclean hands.
cp-panamerican.plain: The court rejected "unclean hands," the argument that the insurer's own wrongdoing barred it from asking for fairness-based relief.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Louisiana’s description of insurer and insured as joint tortfeasors served prescription rules and did not establish that Pan American caused the accident.
cp-panamerican.plain: Louisiana calls insurer and insured "joint tortfeasors" (wrongdoers sharing liability) only for its prescription rules, meaning filing deadlines. That did not show Pan American caused the accident.

cp-panamerican.sentence: The tort claims need not already be liquidated judgments.
cp-panamerican.plain: The "tort" (injury) claims did not need to be "liquidated judgments," meaning already decided and fixed in amount.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Four deaths and many injuries reasonably supported anticipating claims over $100,000, and Louisiana direct-action law allowed claims against the insurer without prior judgments against its insured.
cp-panamerican.plain: Four deaths and many injuries reasonably suggested claims over $100,000. Louisiana's "direct-action law" also let victims sue the insurer without first winning "judgments" against its insured.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Equitable interpleader also need not eliminate jury rights: negligence and damages could go to a jury, with the court retaining allocation of an inadequate fund under separate-issue procedures.
cp-panamerican.plain: Interpleader did not take away jury trials: a jury could decide fault and damages, and the judge would then divide the money if it fell short.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Section 2361 expressly authorized injunctions within the Anti-Injunction Act’s exception for congressional authorization.
cp-panamerican.plain: Section 2361 of the interpleader statute expressly allows "injunctions" (orders stopping other suits). That fits the Anti-Injunction Act’s exception for stays Congress has authorized.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Rule 22 alone lacked that express power.
cp-panamerican.plain: Interpleader under Rule 22 alone did not carry that express power to stop other suits.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Wright favored, while acknowledging doubt about, a possible injunction under the separate necessary-in-aid-of-jurisdiction exception, but the actual decree rested on statutory interpleader.
cp-panamerican.plain: Wright favored, though with doubt, an injunction under the separate "necessary-in-aid-of-jurisdiction" exception, for protecting the court's own case. But the actual "decree" (order) rested on "statutory interpleader."

cp-panamerican.sentence: Wells’s Wisconsin citizenship prevented a common defendant-residence venue in Louisiana under Rule 22, leaving the insurer’s Texas domicile, with service ordinarily confined to the forum state.
cp-panamerican.plain: Wells's Wisconsin "citizenship" ruled out "venue" (the proper place to sue) in Louisiana under Rule 22, which needed a district where all defendants resided. That left Texas, the insurer's home, the "forum state" where papers could ordinarily be served.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Statutory interpleader allowed venue where a claimant lived and nationwide service.
cp-panamerican.plain: "Statutory interpleader" allows venue wherever any claimant lives and service of papers anywhere in the country.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Without Wells’s waiver and appearance or Louisiana presence, only the statute maintained this suit there.
cp-panamerican.plain: Unless Wells gave a "waiver" by appearing in the case, or was found in Louisiana, only the statute kept this "suit" in Louisiana.

cp-panamerican.sentence: Pan American remained a party because it still owed a contractual duty to resist claims.
cp-panamerican.plain: Pan American remained a "party" in the case because it still owed a "contractual" duty, under its policy, to defend against the claims.

cp-panamerican.sentence: The court directed injunctions against pending and future accident suits against both insurer and insured, required claims by answer within thirty days of notice, provided a joint jury trial on timely demand, and reserved allocation if aggregate verdicts exceeded coverage.
cp-panamerican.plain: The court ordered "injunctions" stopping pending and future crash suits against both "insurer" and insured, required claims within thirty days of notice, and offered one joint jury trial on timely demand. It "reserved" (put off) dividing the money if "aggregate" (total) verdicts exceeded the "coverage."

cp-pimentel.sentence: The Republic of the Philippines and its Presidential Commission on Good Government, or PCGG, claimed Philippine law vested assets derived from abuse of public office in the Republic from the moment of misappropriation.
cp-pimentel.plain: The Republic of the Philippines and its Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) claimed Philippine law made assets gained by abusing public office the Republic's property from the moment of "misappropriation," when they were wrongly taken.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Frozen assets later went into escrow at the Philippine National Bank, or PNB, pending a forfeiture action begun in 1991 in the Sandiganbayan, the Philippines’ special corruption court.
cp-pimentel.plain: The frozen assets later went into "escrow" (held by a neutral party) at the Philippine National Bank (PNB), awaiting a forfeiture case filed in 1991 in the Sandiganbayan, the Philippines’ special anticorruption court.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Instead, at District Judge Manuel Real’s direction, Merrill Lynch filed statutory interpleader under 28 U.S.C. § 1335 in Hawaii, naming the sovereigns, Arelma, PNB, the victims, and others as competing defendants.
cp-pimentel.plain: Instead, at District Judge Manuel Real’s direction, Merrill Lynch filed "statutory interpleader" under 28 U.S.C. § 1335 in Hawaii, asking the court to decide who gets the money. It named the governments, Arelma, PNB, the victims, and others as rival "defendants."

cp-pimentel.sentence: Real had presided by designation over the human-rights case, but interpleader was a new stakeholder action.
cp-pimentel.plain: Judge Real had presided over the Marcos human-rights case "by designation" (on special assignment), but "interpleader" was a new case brought by the "stakeholder," the money holder.

cp-pimentel.sentence: The Republic and Commission invoked the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and sought dismissal because the case could not proceed without them.
cp-pimentel.plain: The Republic and the Commission invoked the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, which generally bars suing foreign nations in U.S. courts. They sought "dismissal" because the case could not go on without them.

cp-pimentel.sentence: On the first appeal the Ninth Circuit held them immune and required parties under Rule 19(a), and stayed the case pending the Sandiganbayan.
cp-pimentel.plain: On the first appeal, the Ninth Circuit held them immune and required parties under Rule 19(a), meaning they should be in the case. It paused the case to await a ruling by the Sandiganbayan.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Though the sovereigns were required, it predicted failure of their claims, chiefly under a supposed New York six-year misappropriation limitation.
cp-pimentel.plain: Though the governments were required parties, the court predicted their claims would fail, mainly under a supposed New York six-year "misappropriation limitation," a filing deadline for wrongful-taking claims.

cp-pimentel.sentence: The class argued that entities dismissed on immunity could not appeal.
cp-pimentel.plain: The victims argued that parties dismissed from the case because they were immune had no right to appeal.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Their request to vacate the entire judgment supplied a stake even without a petition attacking substantive rejection of their individual ownership claims.
cp-pimentel.plain: Asking to "vacate" (cancel) the whole judgment gave Arelma and PNB a stake in the appeal, even without a petition attacking the "substantive" rejection of their own ownership claims, meaning the loss on the merits.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Parties generally may raise Rule 19(b), and courts may address absent required parties themselves.
cp-pimentel.plain: Parties generally may raise Rule 19(b), the rule on whether a case must be dismissed when a required party is missing, and courts may raise absent required parties on their own.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Rule 19(a) identifies people to join if feasible.
cp-pimentel.plain: Rule 19(a) identifies people who must be joined (brought into the case) if "feasible," meaning if possible.

cp-pimentel.sentence: When they cannot be joined, subdivision (b) asks whether equity and good conscience allow proceeding, considering prejudice, ways to reduce it, adequacy of a judgment, and the plaintiff’s alternative remedy.
cp-pimentel.plain: When they cannot be joined, subdivision (b) asks whether "equity and good conscience" (basic fairness) allow going on. Courts weigh "prejudice" (harm) to the absent party, ways to reduce it, whether a judgment would be adequate, and whether the plaintiff could sue elsewhere.

cp-pimentel.sentence: The 2007 replacement of “necessary” with “required” and removal of “indispensable” were stylistic, not substantive; required status alone does not always compel dismissal.
cp-pimentel.plain: The 2007 change from "necessary" to "required" and the removal of "indispensable" were style changes, not "substantive" ones that change meaning. Being a required party alone does not always force dismissal.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Justice Kennedy’s opinion reserved the precise appellate review standard: equitable judgment suggests some deference, but the legal errors required reversal under any appropriate standard.
cp-pimentel.plain: Justice Kennedy’s "opinion" left open the exact "appellate" review standard. An "equitable judgment" (fairness call) suggests some "deference" to the trial judge, but the legal errors required reversal under any proper standard.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Immunity protects comity, equality, and sovereign dignity beyond absence from a caption.
cp-pimentel.plain: Foreign "sovereign" immunity protects comity (mutual respect among nations), their equality, and their dignity, not just keeping a nation's name off the case caption.

cp-pimentel.sentence: The Ninth Circuit effectively adjudicated a consequential sovereign interest without consent by predicting a limitations defeat.
cp-pimentel.plain: By predicting a "limitations defeat" (losing because the claim came too late), the Ninth Circuit in effect decided an important "sovereign" interest of the Philippines without its consent.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Earlier governmental-immunity decisions supported dismissal where an immune required sovereign advances nonfrivolous claims and adjudication threatens injury.
cp-pimentel.plain: Earlier "governmental-immunity" cases supported dismissal where an "immune" required government raises "nonfrivolous" (serious, not baseless) claims and going ahead threatens to harm it.

cp-pimentel.sentence: A Philippine ownership decree might let the Republic act for Arelma on breach of the brokerage contract, accruing upon refusal to deliver, or seek enforcement of a foreign judgment.
cp-pimentel.plain: A Philippine ruling on ownership might let the Republic sue for Arelma for breach of the brokerage contract, a claim arising only when Merrill Lynch refused to hand over the assets. Or it might seek "enforcement of a foreign judgment" in U.S. courts.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Adequacy also meant the public interest in settling the whole controversy, not simply satisfying victims.
cp-pimentel.plain: An 'adequate' judgment means one that settles the whole dispute, not just one that pays the victims.

cp-pimentel.sentence: The sovereigns would not be bound, so distribution would leave their claims unresolved.
cp-pimentel.plain: Since the Philippines was not in the case, it would not be bound by the result and could still claim the money.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Yet in later piecemeal suits it could try joining the sovereigns and invoking Rule 19(b) if immunity persisted, a likely defense rather than a guarantee.
cp-pimentel.plain: In later "piecemeal suits" (separate cases one at a time), Merrill Lynch could try joining the governments and, if their immunity held, invoke Rule 19(b). That was a likely "defense," not a guarantee.

cp-pimentel.sentence: On June 12, 2008, the Court reversed and remanded with instructions to order dismissal, not simply rebalancing.
cp-pimentel.plain: On June 12, 2008, the Court "reversed" and sent the case back with instructions to order dismissal, not simply to reweigh the factors.

cp-pimentel.sentence: Stevens joined only the threshold standing discussion.
cp-pimentel.plain: Justice Stevens joined only the opening discussion of "standing," meaning who had a right to bring the appeal.

cp-tashire.sentence: It deposited $20,000 in federal court in Oregon and invoked statutory interpleader to bring competing claimants to the limited fund into one proceeding.
cp-tashire.plain: State Farm deposited $20,000 in federal court in Oregon and invoked "statutory interpleader" to bring all rival "claimants" to that "limited fund" (money too small to pay everyone) into one case.

cp-tashire.sentence: State Farm sought to require every claimant to proceed in Oregon against Clark and the insurer, and to obtain discharge from policy obligations, including its defense duties.
cp-tashire.plain: State Farm wanted every "claimant" to sue Clark and the "insurer" only in Oregon, and wanted a "discharge" (release) from its policy obligations, including its "defense duties" to defend Clark.

cp-tashire.sentence: Alternatively, it asserted an exclusion and sought return of the deposit.
cp-tashire.plain: As a backup, it relied on an "exclusion" (a policy clause leaving this accident out of coverage) and asked for its deposit back.

cp-tashire.sentence: On interlocutory appeal, the Ninth Circuit ordered dissolution of the injunction and dismissal.
cp-tashire.plain: On "interlocutory appeal" (one taken before the case ended), the Ninth Circuit ordered the "injunction" against other suits dissolved and the case dismissed.

cp-tashire.sentence: It reasoned that, without a state direct-action right, tort victims were not claimants against the insurer until they obtained judgments against its insured.
cp-tashire.plain: It reasoned that, without a state "direct-action right" to sue the insurer directly, injury victims were not "claimants" against State Farm until they won judgments against its "insured," Clark.

cp-tashire.sentence: Justice Fortas’s opinion first addressed diversity, an issue the Court raised itself.
cp-tashire.plain: Justice Fortas’s "opinion" first addressed diversity of citizenship, an issue the Court raised on its own.

cp-tashire.sentence: Section 1335 required minimal diversity: at least two adverse claimants had to differ in citizenship, even if other rival claimants shared citizenship.
cp-tashire.plain: Section 1335 requires only minimal diversity: at least two "adverse claimants" (rivals) must differ in "citizenship," even if other rival claimants share a state.

cp-tashire.sentence: Strawbridge, the earlier complete-diversity decision, had interpreted a statute rather than fixed Article III’s outer limit.
cp-tashire.plain: Strawbridge, the earlier complete-diversity decision, had only interpreted a statute. It did not set the outer limit of Article III’s grant of federal power, so Congress could require less.

cp-tashire.sentence: Early interpleader protected both the insurer and competing claimants, even though their substantive entitlement was still contingent.
cp-tashire.plain: Early interpleader protected both the "insurer" and rival "claimants," even though their "substantive" right to the money was still "contingent," meaning it depended on future judgments.

cp-tashire.sentence: State Farm could require enforcement against it of judgments against Clark to occur through the interpleader proceeding.
cp-tashire.plain: State Farm could require that any "judgments" against Clark be collected from it only through the interpleader case.

cp-tashire.sentence: Section 2361 did not give a relatively small stakeholder control over all claimants’ choice of forum for separate claims.
cp-tashire.plain: Section 2361 did not let a fairly small "stakeholder" control all "claimants’" choice of court for their separate "claims" against others, such as Clark.

cp-tashire.sentence: Congress had not made interpleader a general mechanism for centralizing mass-tort litigation.
cp-tashire.plain: Congress had not made interpleader a general tool for gathering all "mass-tort" litigation, suits from one accident injuring many people, into one court.

cp-tashire.sentence: The deposit did not extinguish Clark’s possible personal liability or determine anyone’s ultimate entitlement to the money.
cp-tashire.plain: The deposit did not "extinguish" (end) Clark's possible personal "liability" beyond the policy, or decide who was ultimately entitled to the money.

cp-tashire.sentence: The policy and applicable state law required a judgment or agreed settlement before suing the insurer.
cp-tashire.plain: The policy and the applicable state law required a judgment or agreed settlement against Clark before anyone could sue the "insurer."

cp-tashire.sentence: The Court left other questions unresolved: service on Canadian claimants, their asserted indispensability, and the reach or exclusivity of § 2361’s service provisions.
cp-tashire.plain: The Court left open how to serve papers on Canadian claimants, their claimed "indispensability" (whether the case could go on without them), and the reach or "exclusivity" of § 2361's nationwide service provisions.

dg-stout.sentence: For liquor supplier Bacardi Imports, organized outside Indiana and operating primarily from Miami, General had distributed its products in Northern Indiana at will for more than thirty-five years.
dg-stout.plain: For Bacardi Imports, a liquor supplier organized outside Indiana and run mainly from Miami, General had distributed products in Northern Indiana "at will" (either side could end it anytime) for over thirty-five years.

dg-stout.sentence: The account later viewed favorably to General on summary judgment described Stout disclosing a contemplated sale and Bacardi emphatically promising to stay, without a duration.
dg-stout.plain: Taking General's account as true, as courts do on "summary judgment" (deciding without a trial), Stout told Bacardi of a possible sale, and Bacardi emphatically promised to stay, without saying for how long.

dg-stout.sentence: General sued Bacardi in Indiana federal court under diversity, seeking loss in sale value through promissory estoppel.
