dg-stout.plain: General sued Bacardi in Indiana federal court under "diversity" (parties from different states). It sought its lost sale value through "promissory estoppel," which can enforce a promise someone reasonably relied on.

dg-stout.sentence: Judge Miller granted summary judgment because the open-ended at-will assurance did not support the claimed reliance under Indiana law.
dg-stout.plain: Judge Miller "granted" summary judgment, ending the case, because under Indiana law an open-ended promise in an "at-will" relationship (one Bacardi could end anytime) could not support the claimed reliance.

dg-stout.sentence: Cudahy, joined by Posner and Flaum, applied Indiana’s Section 90 principle: a promise inducing foreseeable action or forbearance can warrant enforcement necessary to avoid injustice, with relief tailored accordingly.
dg-stout.plain: Judge Cudahy, joined by Posner and Flaum, applied Indiana’s version of the Section 90 principle: a promise "inducing" foreseeable action or "forbearance" (holding back from acting) can be enforced when needed to avoid injustice, with the "relief" (remedy) fitted to the harm.

dg-stout.sentence: At-will status supplied no fixed future term or guaranteed stream of Bacardi profits, but did not necessarily defeat reliance costs.
dg-stout.plain: "At-will" status (Bacardi could leave anytime) gave General no fixed future term or guaranteed Bacardi profits. But it did not necessarily rule out recovering costs General suffered by relying on the promise.

dg-stout.sentence: The court compared indefinite employment promises, where no future wage term is guaranteed but moving costs or wages surrendered in preparation may be protected.
dg-stout.plain: By comparison, someone promised an at-will job is not guaranteed future pay, but may recover moving costs or pay from a job given up to take it.

dg-stout.sentence: National already sold a competing rum and assumed it would not retain Bacardi, so the decline reflected lost bargaining leverage and a going-concern alternative, not simply capitalization of future Bacardi earnings.
dg-stout.plain: National already sold a competing rum and assumed it would not keep Bacardi. So the price drop reflected General's lost bargaining leverage and its lost "going-concern" option (selling as an operating business), not simply the value of future Bacardi profits.

dg-stout.sentence: The reasonable reliance period, promise, causation, and amount nevertheless required trial.
dg-stout.plain: Still, how long "reasonable reliance" lasted, whether there was a promise, "causation" (whether the promise caused the loss), and the amount all had to be decided at trial.

dg-stout.sentence: On remand Judge Miller made Rule 52(a) findings after trial.
dg-stout.plain: "On remand" (back in the trial court), Judge Miller held a trial and made formal findings of fact under Rule 52(a), the rule for trials decided by a judge.

dg-stout.sentence: Those findings differed from the summary-judgment version without eliminating the applicable legal rule.
dg-stout.plain: Those trial "findings" of fact differed from the "summary-judgment" version assumed earlier, but the same legal rule still applied.

dg-stout.sentence: The court found actual, reasonable, definite, substantial reliance despite lack of notice of this particular negotiation.
dg-stout.plain: The court found actual, reasonable, definite, and substantial reliance by General, despite Bacardi's "lack of notice" (not knowing) of this particular sale negotiation.

dg-stout.sentence: Five years of eight-percent simple prejudgment interest applied to the $291,000 portion calculable without discretionary valuation, adding $116,400.
dg-stout.plain: The court added "prejudgment interest" (interest for the time before judgment) at eight percent simple interest for five years on the $291,000 part of the loss that could be calculated without "discretionary" valuation, a judgment call. That added $116,400.

dg-stout.sentence: The final result compensated proven changed-position losses, not an assumed perpetual distributorship or all differences between the headline sale prices.
dg-stout.plain: General got back what it proved it lost by relying on the promise, not profits from a distributorship assumed to last forever, and not the full gap between the two sale prices.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: The Environmental Protection Agency selected the best adequately demonstrated system of emission reduction while considering cost, nonair health and environmental effects, and energy requirements.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: The Environmental Protection Agency picks the "best adequately demonstrated system of emission reduction," the best proven method of cutting pollution, while considering cost, health and environmental effects not involving air, and energy needs.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Performance standards reflected reductions achievable through that system.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: "Performance standards" (each plant's emission limits) reflect the cuts that best system could achieve.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: For existing sources under § 111(d), EPA established the degree of reduction and states supplied implementing plans; this program filled gaps left by other pollution programs.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: For existing plants under § 111(d), EPA set how much pollution must be cut and states wrote plans to carry it out. This program filled gaps left by other pollution programs.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: EPA modeled moving coal’s share from thirty-eight percent in 2014 to twenty-seven percent by 2030 and derived caps existing coal plants could not meet without that shift.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: EPA modeled coal's share of U.S. electricity falling from thirty-eight percent in 2014 to twenty-seven percent by 2030. It set limits existing coal plants could not meet without that shift, such as by producing less, investing in cleaner power, or buying credits.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: None was a finding that an enforced Plan had produced those results: it never took effect.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: None of these figures was a "finding" (an established fact) that an enforced Plan produced those results, because the Plan never took effect.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: After an administration change, EPA repealed it in 2019, interpreting § 111 to permit only systems applicable at individual facilities.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: After a change of President, EPA repealed the Plan in 2019, reading § 111 to allow only systems applied at each individual plant.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: The D.C. Circuit concluded EPA misunderstood its authority, vacated repeal and replacement, and remanded.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: The D.C. Circuit held that EPA misread its authority. It "vacated" (cancelled) both the repeal and the replacement rule and "remanded" (sent the matter back) to EPA.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Following another administration change, EPA obtained a partial stay of the mandate to prevent the old Plan returning while it wrote a new rule.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: After another change of President, EPA got a "partial stay" of the "mandate" (a pause on part of the appeals court's order taking effect), so the old Plan would not return while EPA wrote a new rule.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: State petitioners had appellate standing because the judgment purported to restore requirements that they regulate plant emissions more stringently; reversal would redress that burden.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: The state "petitioners" had "standing" to appeal because the "judgment" would bring back requirements that they regulate plant emissions more strictly. A "reversal" would remove that burden.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: EPA’s later nonenforcement intentions implicated mootness.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: EPA's later plan not to enforce the old rule raised "mootness," the question whether a live dispute was still left for the Court to decide.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Under voluntary-cessation principles the government bore the burden, continued defending generation-shifting authority and disclaimed no future use.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Under "voluntary-cessation" principles (a party that stops on its own must show it will not start again), the government "bore the burden." It still defended its "generation-shifting" power and did not rule out using it.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Decisions including Brown & Williamson, Utility Air and Gonzales involved extraordinary agency claims whose history, breadth and economic or political importance warranted more than an ordinary plausible reading.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Earlier cases, including Brown & Williamson, Utility Air and Gonzales, involved extraordinary agency claims whose history, breadth, and economic or political importance required more than an ordinary plausible reading of the statute.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Separation of powers and legislative intent required clear congressional authorization.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: "Separation of powers" (Congress, not agencies, makes major policy) and likely legislative intent required "clear congressional authorization" for such power.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Trading to satisfy a cap derived from source-level controls differed from using generation shifting itself to set the cap.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Letting plants trade credits to meet a limit based on what each plant can do itself differs from using "generation shifting" (moving power production from coal to cleaner sources) to set the limit.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Repeated unsuccessful congressional attempts at comparable carbon cap-and-trade legislation reinforced skepticism, though those failures were not themselves an enacted prohibition.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Congress's repeated failed attempts to pass a similar carbon "cap-and-trade" law (a pollution limit with tradable credits) added to the Court's doubt, though failed bills are not an "enacted" ban.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: System was broad enough linguistically to include generation shifting, but that possibility did not clearly authorize this extraordinary power.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: The word 'system' could cover generation shifting, but that was not clear enough permission for such a big power.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: The Court rejected this particular best system under § 111(d), while declining to decide whether every lawful system must stay inside the individual plant’s pollution performance.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: The Court rejected this particular "best system" under § 111(d), but declined to decide whether every lawful system must stay within measures at the individual plant.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Justice Gorsuch, joined by Justice Alito, treated the doctrine as a clear-statement safeguard for Article I, democratic accountability, federalism and fair notice.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Justice Gorsuch, "joined by" Justice Alito, treated the major questions doctrine as a "clear-statement safeguard" protecting Congress's Article I lawmaking role, democratic accountability, "federalism" (the states' role), and fair notice.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: Those lists and constitutional explanations belonged to a two-Justice concurrence, not mandatory separate elements adopted by the Court.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Those lists and constitutional explanations came from a two-Justice "concurrence" (a separate opinion agreeing with the result), not required separate "elements" adopted by the Court.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: For her, broad authorization was not vague authorization.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: In her view, when Congress gives an agency broad power, that grant is still clear.

lrs-i-west-virginia.sentence: She also questioned discretionary review of a defunct rule while conceding the majority might be right under strict mootness law.
lrs-i-west-virginia.plain: Justice Kagan also questioned the Court's "discretionary review" (choosing to hear the case) of a dead rule, while conceding the "majority" might be right under strict "mootness" law.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: At a January 11, 1974 hearing he conceded that he had overstayed and was deportable.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: At a January 11, 1974 "hearing" he admitted he had overstayed his visa and was "deportable," meaning he could legally be removed.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The judge adjourned the hearing so he could apply for suspension of deportation.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The judge "adjourned" (paused) the hearing so he could apply for "suspension of deportation," a form of relief letting him stay.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Even satisfying those criteria left a discretionary decision.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Even meeting all those requirements left a "discretionary" decision: officials could still choose whether to grant relief.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Section 244(c)(2) allowed either chamber to disapprove during the session in which a suspension was reported or before the end of the following session.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Section 244(c)(2) let either the House or the Senate alone disapprove a suspension during the session in which it was reported or before the end of the next session.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Without timely disapproval, the statute provided for cancellation of deportation proceedings and adjustment of status.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Without "timely" disapproval, the "statute" ended the deportation case and gave "adjustment of status," meaning the person became a lawful permanent resident.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The resolution was discharged from committee; it had not been printed for members, and it passed without debate or a recorded vote.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The "resolution" was pulled from committee without its usual review. It had not been printed for members, and it passed with no debate and no "recorded vote" showing who voted how.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Under the statute, that one chamber’s action nevertheless changed the legal consequence of the agency decision: Chadha now had to be deported unless another basis for relief intervened.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Under the "statute," that one chamber's vote still changed the legal effect of the "agency" decision: Chadha now had to be deported unless some other ground for relief applied.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The judge considered himself without power to invalidate an Act of Congress and entered a deportation order on November 8, 1976.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The immigration judge believed he had no power to strike down an Act of Congress, and he ordered Chadha deported on November 8, 1976.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The INS agreed that the one-House veto was unconstitutional but said it would carry out the order unless a court restrained it.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The INS agreed that the "one-House veto" was unconstitutional, but said it would carry out the deportation "order" unless a court stopped it.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The INS appealed to the Supreme Court under the then-applicable 28 U.S.C. § 1252, while the House and Senate separately petitioned for certiorari to defend the statute.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The INS appealed to the Supreme Court under 28 U.S.C. § 1252, a statute then in force, while the House and Senate separately "petitioned" for certiorari (asked the Court to hear the case) to defend the law.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The Court granted their petitions, postponed its decision on the INS’s appeal jurisdiction, and heard argument on February 22, 1982, followed by reargument on December 7, 1982.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The Court "granted" their petitions and put off deciding whether the INS’s appeal was proper. It heard argument on February 22, 1982, and then "reargument" (a second round) on December 7, 1982.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The INS can appeal despite agreeing with the constitutional ruling because the lower court’s judgment prevents it from executing the statutory command.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The INS could appeal despite agreeing the law was unconstitutional, because the "lower court" judgment stopped it from carrying out the "statutory" command to deport.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Article III adversity remains because Chadha faces enforcement and Congress defends the veto; the INS’s agreement does not turn the case into an advisory opinion.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Article III "adversity" (a real clash between sides) remained, because Chadha faced deportation and Congress defended the veto. The INS’s agreement did not make the case an "advisory opinion," legal advice with no real dispute.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Nor is this an unreviewable political question.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Nor was this an "unreviewable" political question, the kind of issue the Constitution leaves entirely to Congress or the President, which courts stay out of.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Severability is another threshold problem, considered next: if removing the veto destroyed the authority to suspend deportation, invalidating the veto would not simply preserve Chadha’s relief.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: "Severability," whether the veto could be cut out of the law alone, was another threshold problem. If removing the veto also destroyed the power to suspend "deportation," striking the veto would not save Chadha's relief.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The clause creates a presumption that invalidating one provision leaves the remainder standing; the inquiry is whether Congress would have wanted that remainder to operate.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The law's severability clause creates a presumption that striking one part leaves the rest "standing" (still in force). The question is whether Congress would have wanted the rest to work without the invalid part.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Section 7 requires passage by both Houses and presentment to the President, subject to the constitutional veto and override process.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Article I, Section 7 requires passage by both Houses and "presentment" (sending the bill to the President) to sign or veto, with Congress able to override a veto.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Clause 3 prevents Congress from evading presentment merely by calling legislative action an order, resolution, or vote instead of a bill.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Clause 3 stops Congress from avoiding "presentment" just by calling its lawmaking an order, "resolution," or vote instead of a bill.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Expediency, the popularity of legislative vetoes, and their long use cannot add an unwritten exception.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: That legislative vetoes were convenient, popular, and long used did not create an exception the Constitution does not contain.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The resolution altered the legal rights, duties, and relations of Chadha, the Attorney General, and other people outside the legislative branch.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The House "resolution" changed the legal rights, duties, and relations of Chadha, the Attorney General, and other people outside the legislative branch.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: That external alteration was legislative in character and therefore required the Article I procedure.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Because it changed the legal position of people outside Congress, it was lawmaking in character, so it had to follow the "Article I procedure": passage by both chambers and presentment to the President.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The earlier enactment of § 244 through both chambers and presentment could not authorize a later exercise of legislative power that dispensed with those same constitutional steps.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Passing § 244 itself through both "chambers" and presentment (its "enactment") could not authorize a later use of "legislative power" that skipped those same constitutional steps.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The Court distinguishes executive action under delegated authority.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The Court "distinguishes" (treats as different) action by the executive branch under "delegated authority," meaning power Congress has given an agency by law.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The classification of this congressional intervention is doing the work.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: What matters is that this was Congress itself acting with legal effect, which made it lawmaking.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: He sees the House as deciding whether six identified people met statutory criteria: a function ordinarily entrusted to adjudication.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Justice Powell saw the House as deciding whether six identified people met the "statutory" criteria, a job normally given to adjudication, meaning decisions by courts or agency judges in individual cases.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Do not attribute his reasoning to the six-Justice majority or convert his discussion of adjudication into a separate majority holding under the Bill of Attainder Clause.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Justice Powell's reasoning, including his view of the House's act as adjudication, was his alone, not the six-Justice "majority" opinion's. It is not a separate "holding" (binding ruling) that the veto was a law punishing named people under the Bill of Attainder Clause.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Justice White sees the legislative veto as a practical accommodation between broad delegations to the Executive and congressional responsibility for policy.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Justice White saw the legislative veto as a practical "accommodation" (compromise) between broad "delegations" of power to the Executive and Congress's responsibility for policy.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: On his account, changing Chadha’s status permanently required the Executive’s approval and the absence of objection from either chamber.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: In his view, making Chadha's status permanent always required both the Executive’s approval and no objection from either chamber.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The veto preserved the statutory status quo instead of independently legislating a new rule.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: So the veto just kept the "statutory" status quo (things as the law already left them) rather than making a new rule.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: He disputes the idea that the veto necessarily aggrandizes Congress at the Executive’s expense when it operates as a limit on a power Congress could have withheld.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: He denied that the veto necessarily "aggrandizes" Congress (expands its power) at the Executive’s expense, since it limits a power Congress could have refused to give at all.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: Burger’s opinion has six votes; Powell supplies a seventh vote for the judgment on his narrower ground.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Chief Justice Burger's opinion had six votes. Justice Powell supplied a seventh vote for the "judgment" (the result for Chadha) on his narrower ground.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: The later comparison in the full brief separates this case from Whitman and Gundy: those cases address which choices Congress may delegate and how it must constrain administrators.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: The full brief later separates this case from Whitman and Gundy, which address what choices Congress may "delegate" (hand to agencies) and what limits it must set on administrators.

lrs-s-chadha.sentence: A lawful delegation does not itself authorize a one-House override.
lrs-s-chadha.plain: Even a lawful delegation of power to an agency does not by itself allow a one-House override of the agency's decision.

naval-institute.sentence: One provision conveyed those exclusive rights, and another began the license term on the agreement’s date.
naval-institute.plain: One clause gave Berkley the sole paperback rights, and another said the license began on the day the agreement was signed.

naval-institute.sentence: A separate covenant prohibited publication before October 1985.
naval-institute.plain: A separate "covenant" (a binding promise in the contract) barred publication of the paperback before October 1985.

naval-institute.sentence: In its 1989 Naval I decision, the Second Circuit reversed on contract liability and remanded for appropriate relief.
naval-institute.plain: In its 1989 Naval I decision, the Second Circuit reversed on contract liability, holding Berkley broke the contract, and "remanded" (sent the case back) for appropriate "relief," the remedy.

naval-institute.sentence: On remand the district court treated the conduct as copyright infringement.
naval-institute.plain: "On remand" (back in the trial court), the district court treated Berkley's early sales as copyright infringement, not just a contract breach.

naval-institute.sentence: Berkley cross-appealed, arguing that an exclusive licensee could not infringe its own rights, that Naval abandoned contract damages, and that the lost-profit estimate was speculative.
naval-institute.plain: Berkley "cross-appealed" (appealed too). It argued an "exclusive licensee" cannot "infringe" (violate) its own rights, that Naval had "abandoned" (given up) contract damages, and that the lost-profit estimate was "speculative," mere guesswork.

naval-institute.sentence: The panel would review factual damage calculations for clear error; established breach remained law of the case.
naval-institute.plain: The panel would "review" factual damage figures only for "clear error," overturning them only if clearly wrong. The earlier breach ruling stayed settled as "law of the case," binding for the rest of the case.

naval-institute.sentence: Judge Kearse, writing for a panel with Judges Winter and Altimari, concluded that an exclusive license transfers the conveyed rights’ ownership.
naval-institute.plain: Judge Kearse, writing for a "panel" (three-judge group) with Judges Winter and Altimari, held that an exclusive license transfers ownership of the rights it conveys.

naval-institute.sentence: Because Berkley owned the paperback rights when it sold early, it breached its promise without infringing Naval’s ownership of those already-conveyed rights.
naval-institute.plain: Because Berkley already owned the paperback rights when it sold early, it "breached" (broke) its contract promise without "infringing" Naval's copyright in rights Naval had already handed over.

naval-institute.sentence: Copyright Act § 504(b)’s infringer-profit remedy could not survive merely because Berkley violated a contract.
naval-institute.plain: The Copyright Act § 504(b) remedy of taking an infringer's profits could not survive just because Berkley broke a contract.

naval-institute.sentence: Ownership did not excuse the contractual timing duty.
naval-institute.plain: Owning the rights did not excuse Berkley's contract "duty" about when to publish.

naval-institute.sentence: Naval I had nevertheless established entitlement to relief for breach, and Berkley had not sought reargument on abandonment.
naval-institute.plain: But Naval I had already held Naval entitled to "relief" (a remedy) for the breach, and Berkley had not sought "reargument" (asked that court to reconsider) on whether Naval abandoned it.

naval-institute.sentence: That determination governed as law of the case.
naval-institute.plain: That ruling controlled as "law of the case," meaning it was binding for the rest of the case.

naval-institute.sentence: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(c) generally requires a nondefault judgment to award relief to which a party is entitled even if not specifically demanded.
naval-institute.plain: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(c) generally requires a "judgment" in a contested (nondefault) case to give each "party" the relief it is entitled to, even if it did not ask for that exact relief.

naval-institute.sentence: Naval had accepted substantial royalties and renounced rescission, so damages supplied suitable relief on its successful contract theory.
naval-institute.plain: Naval had accepted substantial "royalties" (its share of paperback sales) and given up "rescission" (cancelling the contract), so money damages were suitable "relief" on its winning contract claim.

naval-institute.sentence: Ordinary contract damages compensate the promisee’s loss.
naval-institute.plain: Ordinary contract damages pay back the "promisee’s" loss, meaning the loss of the party who was promised performance, not the breaching party's gain.

naval-institute.sentence: Awarding all those gains would detach compensation from the injury caused by breach.
naval-institute.plain: "Awarding" Naval all of Berkley's gains would cut the money off from the actual harm the "breach" caused.

naval-institute.sentence: The remaining uncertainty concerned how much loss, not an absence of any causal basis.
naval-institute.plain: The remaining uncertainty was about how much Naval lost, not whether there was any "causal" link between the breach and a loss.

naval-institute.sentence: Some uncertainty created by a breacher’s alteration of events could be resolved against that party.
naval-institute.plain: When the breaching party's own conduct makes losses hard to measure, doubts can be resolved against it.

naval-institute.sentence: The agreement selected New York law, which supplied prejudgment interest on successful contract damages to compensate delayed payment.
naval-institute.plain: The contract chose New York law, which adds "prejudgment interest" (interest for the time before judgment) to contract damages to make up for the delay in payment.

naval-institute.sentence: With infringement rejected, the Copyright Act no longer supported fees, and ordinary contract law supplied no comparable entitlement.
naval-institute.plain: With "infringement" rejected, the Copyright Act no longer supported an award of lawyers' fees, and ordinary contract law gave no similar right to fees.

sullivan.sentence: Sullivan sued separately for breach of the result promise and negligence and demanded a jury trial.
sullivan.plain: Sullivan "sued" on two separate claims: "breach" of the "result promise" (the doctor's promise of a specific result) and negligence (carelessness). She "demanded a jury" trial.

sullivan.sentence: The jury found for Sullivan on contract and for O’Connor on negligence.
sullivan.plain: The jury found for Sullivan on "contract" (the doctor broke his promise) and for O’Connor on "negligence" (he was not careless).

sullivan.sentence: O’Connor excepted to allowing anything beyond expenditures, specifically challenging disfigurement and the extra operation’s suffering.
sullivan.plain: O'Connor "excepted" (formally objected) to letting the jury award anything beyond her expenses, especially for disfigurement (her worsened looks) and the pain of the extra operation.

sullivan.sentence: His directed-verdict objection to liability was not pressed on appeal; the Supreme Judicial Court also said it could not succeed.
sullivan.plain: His "objection" that a directed verdict for him on liability was required was not pursued on appeal. The Supreme Judicial Court, the state's highest court, also said it could not have succeeded.

sullivan.sentence: She offered to waive her exceptions if her verdict stood.
sullivan.plain: She offered to "waive" (drop) her own exceptions if her "verdict," the jury's award, was left standing.

sullivan.sentence: That condition left the court reviewing the common ground supporting the existing award rather than every difference between damages theories.
sullivan.plain: So the court only had to check whether the award could be justified under the damages measures, not choose among them.

sullivan.sentence: Massachusetts therefore allowed result-promise actions with clear proof and close scrutiny.
sullivan.plain: So Massachusetts allows "result-promise" suits, where a doctor is sued for breaking a promise of a specific result, but requires clear proof and close scrutiny of whether a real promise was made.

sullivan.sentence: Once established, however, that promise was not rewritten as merely a duty of care.
sullivan.plain: But once proven, that promise was not rewritten as merely a "duty of care," the ordinary duty to be careful.

sullivan.sentence: Restitution returns benefits received by the physician, most obviously a paid fee.
sullivan.plain: One way to measure damages, 'restitution', gives back what the doctor received, such as the fee.

sullivan.sentence: Reliance seeks to undo detrimental changes caused by undertaking the agreement, potentially including hospital payments and a worsened bodily condition.
sullivan.plain: Another, 'reliance', puts the patient back where she was before the deal, covering costs like hospital bills and harm to her body.

sullivan.sentence: Expectation compares the actual condition with the promised result.
sullivan.plain: A third, 'expectation', gives her the difference between the nose she got and the nose she was promised.

sullivan.sentence: Reimbursement of all expenditures is not necessarily restitution when some payments enriched third parties rather than the physician.
sullivan.plain: Paying back all her expenses is not necessarily restitution (returning what the doctor gained), because some payments went to "third parties" such as the hospital, not the physician.

sullivan.sentence: Using Hawkins’s promised-result approach, expectation would encompass both failure to improve and actual deterioration.
sullivan.plain: Under the promised-result approach of Hawkins’s "hairy hand" case, expectation damages (putting her where the promise would have) would cover both the improvement she did not get and her actual worsening.

sullivan.sentence: Unpaid fees also must be accounted for to avoid putting the patient above the performance position.
sullivan.plain: Any unpaid fees must also be subtracted, so the patient does not end up better off than her position had the doctor's "performance" (the promised result) occurred.

sullivan.sentence: Those policy observations did not establish an exclusive reliance rule for every medical contract.
sullivan.plain: Those policy thoughts did not set a rule that reliance is the only measure of damages for every medical "contract."

sullivan.sentence: She also waived a potential reliance claim treating the first two operations’ suffering as wasted expenditure of bodily effort.
sullivan.plain: She also "waived" (gave up) a possible reliance claim treating the pain of the first two operations as a wasted spending of bodily effort.

sullivan.sentence: What remained—actual deterioration and an additional operation’s suffering—was compensable under either expectation or restoration to the earlier position.
sullivan.plain: What remained, her actual worsening and the pain of the extra operation, was "compensable" (could be paid for) under either expectation or restoration to her earlier position.

sullivan.sentence: Combining generous pieces of different measures without checking the resulting counterfactual would overcompensate.
sullivan.plain: Combining the most generous parts of different measures without checking the resulting "counterfactual" (the imagined position the award puts her in) would overpay the patient.

sullivan.sentence: On May 9, 1973, the Supreme Judicial Court overruled O’Connor’s exceptions and treated Sullivan’s exceptions as waived.
sullivan.plain: On May 9, 1973, the Supreme Judicial Court overruled O’Connor’s exceptions (rejected his objections) and treated Sullivan's exceptions as "waived," as she had offered.

sullivan.sentence: Both justified the challenged items actually preserved for review.
sullivan.plain: Either measure supported the challenged parts of the award that were actually preserved for "review" (properly raised for the appeals court).

wassermans.sentence: The signed contract also required 25% of average annual gross receipts over the preceding three complete fiscal years, a term absent from the solicitation.
wassermans.plain: The signed "contract" also required a payment of 25% of average annual "gross receipts" (total sales) over the three prior complete fiscal years, a term not in the "solicitation," the Township's invitation for bids.

wassermans.sentence: In 1973 it sold the business and sublet to Rocco Laurino doing business as Jo-Ro, Inc., for $1,850 monthly, agreeing how to allocate cancellation proceeds.
wassermans.plain: In 1973 Wasserman's sold the business and "sublet" (rented the space onward) to Rocco Laurino, "doing business as" (operating under the name) Jo-Ro, Inc., for $1,850 a month, agreeing how to split any cancellation payment.

wassermans.sentence: On cross-motions for summary judgment, the Law Division upheld the lease and provision, later entering a reported $346,058.44 judgment plus 10% prejudgment interest.
wassermans.plain: On "cross-motions for summary judgment" (both sides asking for a ruling without trial), the Law Division, the trial court, upheld the lease and clause. It later entered a reported $346,058.44 "judgment" plus 10% "prejudgment interest."

wassermans.sentence: It continued to argue that officials lacked authority to add the gross-receipts provision and that changing the solicitation violated public-contract requirements.
wassermans.plain: The Township kept arguing that its officials had no power to add the "gross-receipts" payment term, and that changing the terms of the "solicitation" broke public-contract rules.

wassermans.sentence: Justice Pollock’s unanimous New Jersey Supreme Court opinion applied the statute in force when the parties signed, New Jersey Statutes Annotated section 40:60-42,, which did not require bidding for this private lease.
wassermans.plain: Justice Pollock’s "unanimous" New Jersey Supreme Court "opinion" applied the "statute" in force when the "parties" signed, New Jersey Statutes Annotated section 40:60-42. It did not require public bidding for this private lease.

wassermans.sentence: Voluntary advertising did not import an inapplicable bidding regime.
wassermans.plain: Advertising the lease anyway did not make the bidding rules apply.

wassermans.sentence: Belated invalidation also risked contract-clause concerns, although the court did not decide a constitutional violation.
wassermans.plain: Striking the lease down years later also risked "contract-clause" concerns (the Constitution limits states impairing existing contracts), though the court did not decide that there was a constitutional violation.

wassermans.sentence: The court nevertheless tested the revenue-based payment for reasonableness as compensation rather than punishment.
wassermans.plain: Still, the court checked whether the sales-based payment was a reasonable estimate of losses or an unenforceable penalty.

wassermans.sentence: Difficulty estimating damages informed that inquiry instead of operating as a mechanically separate requirement.
wassermans.plain: How hard it was to estimate "damages" when signing was part of judging reasonableness, not a mechanically separate test.

wassermans.sentence: Commercial stipulations between parties of comparable bargaining power were presumptively reasonable, with production and persuasion burdens on the challenger.
wassermans.plain: Commercial "stipulations" (agreed terms) between parties of similar "bargaining power" were presumed reasonable. The challenger bore the burden of production and the "persuasion burdens," meaning it had to offer evidence and convince the court.

wassermans.sentence: Consumer contracts were reserved, and unfairness or unconscionability could still matter.
wassermans.plain: The court left consumer contracts for another day, and unfairness or "unconscionability" (terms so one-sided they shock the conscience) could still matter.

wassermans.sentence: A revenue formula could reimburse saved expenses or create a windfall, but no rule made every percentage of receipts invalid.
wassermans.plain: A sales-based formula could pay back expenses the tenant saved by ending early, or create a "windfall" (more than its real loss). But no rule made every percentage of receipts invalid.

wassermans.sentence: Tax and economic losses differ, but those figures raised a serious question if they reflected actual performance.
wassermans.plain: Tax losses and "economic losses" (real business losses) differ. But the tiny reported profits and a loss raised a serious question about the $290,310.18 claim if they reflected the store's actual "performance."

wassermans.sentence: Enforceability was legal, but necessary underlying facts were missing.
wassermans.plain: Whether the clause is enforceable is for the judge to decide, but the judge needed more facts to decide it.

wassermans.sentence: The Township retained the burden of proving unreasonableness.
wassermans.plain: The Township still bore the "burden of proving" the payment unreasonable.

wassermans.sentence: The Supreme Court affirmed the lease’s validity and the $55,748.27 improvement award, reversed in part, and remanded for the necessary damages proceedings.
wassermans.plain: The Supreme Court "affirmed" (upheld) the lease and the $55,748.27 improvement "award," reversed in part, and "remanded" (sent back) for the needed proceedings on "damages" under the sales-based payment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: The suits invoked the Alien Tort Act, 28 U.S.C. section 1350, the Torture Victim Protection Act, general federal-question jurisdiction, and supplemental state claims, seeking compensatory and punitive damages and other relief.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: The suits relied on the Alien Tort Act, 28 U.S.C. section 1350 (foreigners may sue over violations of international law), the Torture Victim Protection Act, general federal-question jurisdiction, and "supplemental state claims." They sought compensatory and "punitive damages" (to punish) and other "relief."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: He understood human-rights liability to require state action, considered Srpska insufficiently established as a state, and treated possible future recognition and head-of-state immunity as reasons against proceeding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: The judge thought human-rights "liability" required "state action" (conduct by a government), doubted Srpska was a state, and saw possible future recognition, with "head-of-state immunity" for Karadzic, as reasons not to proceed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Chief Judge Newman, joined by Judges Feinberg and Walker, held that the Alien Tort Act required an alien’s tort claim actually satisfying a treaty or law-of-nations norm, not merely a colorable invocation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Chief Judge Newman, joined by Judges Feinberg and Walker, held the Alien Tort Act requires a foreigner's claim that actually violates a treaty or international-law rule, not merely a "colorable" (plausible-sounding) appeal to one.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Congress’s criminal implementation disclaimed a new private action but did not implicitly repeal the preexisting Alien Tort Act.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Congress's law making genocide a crime said it created no new private "action" (right to sue). But it did not "implicitly repeal" (silently cancel) the older Alien Tort Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Independent claims under the norms considered here required official action or color of law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Stand-alone "claims" under the rules considered here, such as torture, required official action or "color of law," meaning acting with government authority.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Analogies to joint action and substantial state assistance under section 1983 explained possible color of law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Comparisons to "joint action" with officials and substantial state help under "section 1983" (the U.S. civil-rights law) showed how Karadzic might have acted under "color of law" if, as alleged, he acted with officials of the former Yugoslavia.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: The Torture Victim Protection Act expressly supplied a remedy for official torture and extrajudicial killing, subject to adequate available local-remedy exhaustion and limitations.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: The Torture Victim Protection Act directly provides a remedy for official torture and "extrajudicial killing" (killing without legal process). It requires "exhaustion" of adequate local remedies first, and a filing deadline.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Personal service on an individual physically present ordinarily satisfied service rules and personal-jurisdiction due process.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Handing papers to a person physically present in the state ordinarily satisfies the service rules and the due-process limits on "personal-jurisdiction," the court's power over him.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Applying Baker’s political-question criteria, the panel found manageable international norms and congressional authorization.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Courts avoid 'political questions' that belong to Congress or the President. Using the test from Baker v. Carr, the court found this was not one: international law gave workable standards, and Congress had authorized such suits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.sentence: Conditions in Bosnia and inadequate Serbia alternatives also left no suitable forum shown for forum-non-conveniens dismissal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-094.plain: Conditions in Bosnia and inadequate options in Serbia meant no suitable other "forum" (court) was shown, as a "forum-non-conveniens" dismissal (sending a case to a more convenient court elsewhere) requires.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.sentence: At 5 p.m. on September 21, the district court denied relief and declined certification for a discretionary interlocutory appeal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.plain: At 5 p.m. on September 21, the "district court" denied relief and declined to certify a "discretionary" interlocutory appeal, an early appeal the appeals court may choose to hear.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.sentence: The officials sought dismissal because denial of a temporary restraining order ordinarily is not appealable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.plain: The officials sought "dismissal" of the appeal because denial of a "temporary restraining order" (a short emergency order) ordinarily is not "appealable" right away.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.sentence: Drawing on Cohen and related precedents construing finality practically, the majority held that an order deciding substantial rights irreparably lost through delayed review could be immediately reviewed under 28 U.S.C. §1291.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.plain: Relying on Cohen and related "precedents" reading finality practically, the majority held that an order settling important rights that would be lost forever by waiting could be appealed at once under 28 U.S.C. §1291, which allows appeals from final decisions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.sentence: Under the Supreme Court’s Leiter Minerals decision, the majority understood the statutory prohibition as inapplicable to suits by the United States, without limiting that principle to property disputes or civil state proceedings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.plain: Under the Supreme Court's Leiter Minerals decision, the majority read the "statutory" ban on federal courts halting state proceedings as not applying to suits by the United States, and did not limit that to property disputes or civil cases.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.sentence: But the district court’s reliance on Douglas v. City of Jeannette and ordinary discretion to avoid state criminal proceedings did not answer this authorized enforcement claim.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.plain: But the "district court’s" reliance on Douglas v. City of Jeannette and its ordinary "discretion" to avoid interfering with state criminal cases did not answer this enforcement "claim" Congress had authorized.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.sentence: Section 1971(d) required jurisdiction without exhaustion of other remedies, and Congress had rejected language making that exercise permissive.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-US-WOOD.plain: Section 1971(d) required federal courts to take jurisdiction without "exhaustion" of other remedies (trying them first), and Congress had rejected wording that would have made hearing these cases optional.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.sentence: Nicholas would give an unlimited guarantee, secured through both spouses’ charge over their home.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.plain: Nicholas promised to repay all of the company's bank debts, with no cap, if the company did not. To back that promise, both spouses gave the bank a legal claim on their jointly owned house (like a mortgage), so it could take the house if the debt went unpaid.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.sentence: Scott L.J. discussed both agency and a special equity for vulnerable sureties in influential relationships.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.plain: Scott L.J. (Lord Justice Scott) discussed two theories: "agency" (Nicholas acting for the bank, so his lie counted against it), and a "special equity," a fairness-based protection, for vulnerable "sureties" who guarantee a loved one's debts.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.sentence: A surety first needed a legal or equitable basis against the principal debtor, such as misrepresentation or undue influence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.plain: First, the "surety" (the wife guaranteeing the debt) needed a "legal or equitable" ground against the "principal debtor," her husband, to escape the deal, such as "misrepresentation" (lying) or undue influence (improper pressure).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.sentence: The equity then bound the creditor through agency or actual or constructive notice.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.plain: That "equity" (her fairness-based right) then bound the "creditor" bank only through agency, or through actual notice or "constructive notice," meaning the bank knew or is treated as knowing of the wrongdoing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.sentence: A transaction facially offering the wife no financial advantage, with substantial risk of spousal wrongdoing in transactions of that type, put the bank on inquiry without proof it knew an actual lie.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.plain: A deal "facially" (on its face) giving the wife no financial benefit, of a type with a real risk of a husband's wrongdoing, put the bank "on inquiry": on alert to take reasonable steps, even without proof it knew of an actual lie.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.sentence: Instead it merely witnessed signature, giving it constructive notice of the misrepresentation and her resulting equity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-051.plain: Instead the bank only watched her sign, so it had "constructive notice" (is treated as knowing) of the husband's "misrepresentation" and her resulting "equity," her right to escape the deal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.sentence: Justice Cantil-Sakauye rejected the claim that conformity to buyer specifications displaced merchantability.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.plain: Justice Cantil-Sakauye rejected the argument that "conformity" to the buyer's specifications displaced "merchantability," the implied promise that goods are fit for their ordinary purpose.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.sentence: Even assuming another express warranty, California Uniform Commercial Code section 2317 made reasonably consistent warranties cumulative.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.plain: Even assuming the specifications were another "express warranty" (a stated promise), California Uniform Commercial Code section 2317 makes warranties cumulative where reasonably consistent, so one does not cancel the other.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.sentence: Its selective, incomplete evidence presentation forfeited substantial-evidence review and failed on the merits.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.plain: Its selective, incomplete description of the evidence forfeited "substantial-evidence" review (an appeal claiming the evidence could not support the finding), and the challenge also failed "on the merits."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.sentence: Under section 2715(2)(a), Mao Shun needed reason at contracting to know requirements and potential loss, not foresight of the precise hidden flaw.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.plain: Under section 2715(2)(a), Mao Shun needed reason, when it made the contract, to know Garlock's requirements and possible losses, not foresight of the exact hidden flaw.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.sentence: Mao Shun failed to link earlier purchases to particular damages, defeating its four-year limitation objection without decision of Garlock’s discovery-accrual alternative.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.plain: Mao Shun did not tie earlier purchases to particular damages, which defeated its "objection" under the four-year filing deadline. So the court did not decide Garlock's "discovery-accrual" argument that the clock started only when it found the problem.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.sentence: Implied contractual indemnity arose from contractual responsibilities and breach foreseeably causing third-party loss, allocated according to contractual equities.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-092.plain: "Implied contractual indemnity" (an unwritten duty to reimburse) arises from contract duties when a breach foreseeably causes "third-party" loss, such as money owed to Rockwell, divided according to fairness under the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.sentence: Such losses were neither an immediate and necessary consequence of the clothing breach nor shown to be within the parties’ contemplation at formation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.plain: Those losses were neither an immediate and necessary result of the clothing breach nor shown to be within the "parties’ contemplation" (what both sides had in mind) when the contract was formed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.sentence: Under the foreseeability reasoning associated with Hadley, predictable disappointment did not by itself make that intervening choice chargeable to him.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.plain: Under the "foreseeability" reasoning of Hadley (damages for losses both sides could foresee), predictable disappointment did not make the bride's "intervening choice" to call off the wedding chargeable to the supplier.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.sentence: Nominal damages alone would prevent dismissal of an otherwise adequate claim.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.plain: "Nominal damages" (a token award for a breach with no provable loss) alone would prevent "dismissal" of an otherwise adequate claim.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.sentence: A treatise’s broader dispute about wholly executory consideration did not need resolution because Coppola had made an actual payment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-006.plain: A "treatise" (legal textbook) questioned whether a "wholly executory" deal, made only of unperformed promises, supports damages. The court did not need to decide that, because Coppola had made an actual payment.

brief-CT-CB-0074.sentence: The Court of Common Pleas directed a nonsuit: the family relationship and later promise supplied no sufficient consideration.
brief-CT-CB-0074.plain: The Court of Common Pleas, the trial court, directed a "nonsuit" (ended the case without a verdict): the family relationship and the later promise were not enough "consideration," something given in exchange.

brief-CT-CB-0074.sentence: Parker examined their usual examples: promises to pay debts barred by limitations, obligations incurred during infancy, and debts discharged in bankruptcy.
brief-CT-CB-0074.plain: Judge Parker examined the usual examples: promises to pay debts "barred" by time limits, obligations made during "infancy" (while a minor), and debts "discharged in bankruptcy" (cancelled).

brief-CT-CB-0074.sentence: The later promise removed or waived an impediment to enforcing an obligation that already possessed that underlying basis.
brief-CT-CB-0074.plain: In those cases the later promise removed or "waived" (gave up) an obstacle to enforcing a debt that already had that original basis of a fair exchange.

brief-CT-CB-0074.sentence: Instruments under seal and certain negotiable commercial instruments had historically recognized formal or mercantile treatment; those exceptions did not turn an ordinary reimbursement letter into such an instrument.
brief-CT-CB-0074.plain: "Instruments" under seal and some "negotiable commercial instruments" (like promissory notes) historically got special formal or "mercantile" (merchant-law) treatment. Those exceptions did not make an ordinary letter promising repayment into one.

brief-CT-CB-0074.sentence: But liability required facts and an adjudication absent here: the needy person’s legally relevant settlement and likelihood of becoming chargeable to a town, the relative’s ability to provide support, and a judgment entered after an opportunity to be heard.
brief-CT-CB-0074.plain: But "liability" under the support law required facts and a ruling absent here: Levi's legal "settlement" (which town was responsible), his likelihood of needing town support, the father's ability to pay, and a "judgment" after an "opportunity to be heard."

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.sentence: The contract allowed acceleration, notice and possession remedies, made payment timing essential, preserved use after full accelerated payment and contained a nonwaiver term.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.plain: The contract allowed demanding the full balance, giving notice, and taking "possession" of the sign. It made on-time payment essential, let the Harrisons keep the sign after full payment, and had a "nonwaiver" term: Walker kept its rights even if it sometimes did not enforce them.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.sentence: The Harrisons defended and sought recoupment, claiming Walker’s prior material breach justified termination and damages.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.plain: The Harrisons defended and sought "recoupment" (cutting what they owed by their own damages), claiming Walker's earlier "material breach" (a serious failure to perform) justified ending the contract and damages.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.sentence: The Supreme Court accepted that a material breach can justify repudiation but stressed the risk of judging materiality incorrectly.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.plain: The Supreme Court accepted that a "material breach" can justify "repudiation" (refusing to keep performing), but stressed the risk of judging "materiality" wrongly and becoming the party in breach.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.sentence: It considered substantial benefit remaining, adequate compensation, performance already rendered, termination hardship, the character of misconduct and uncertainty of future performance.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0128.plain: To decide whether a breach is serious, the court asked how much of the bargain the customer still got, whether money could make up the shortfall, how much had been performed, how hard ending the deal would be on Walker, whether Walker acted in bad faith, and how likely future performance was.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.sentence: It treated the grant as voidable, rather than void from inception, and proposed setting it aside while permitting temporary operation and reopening the comparison.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.plain: The FCC treated the license grant as "voidable" (valid until cancelled), not "void" from the start. It proposed cancelling it while allowing temporary operation and reopening the comparison of applicants.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.sentence: WHDH also received a demerit for unapproved transfers of de facto control when its president changed.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.plain: WHDH also got a demerit because, when its president changed, "de facto control" (actual control) of the station shifted without FCC approval.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.sentence: It characterized use of new-applicant criteria as an unlawful forfeiture and argued that ignoring stability violated due process and legitimate expectations.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.plain: WHDH called the use of new-applicant criteria an unlawful "forfeiture" (taking away of its license), and argued that ignoring its stability violated due process and its legitimate expectations.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.sentence: Warning signs could justify intervention when an agency failed to take a hard look or make a reasoned decision.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.plain: Warning signs could justify a court stepping in when an agency failed to take a "hard look" (seriously consider the key issues) or to make a "reasoned decision" it explained rationally.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.sentence: A discernible path could survive imperfect clarity, and immaterial errors could be harmless, but a reviewing court could not invent missing findings or reasons.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.plain: A followable path of reasoning can survive imperfect clarity, and "immaterial" errors that did not affect the result can be "harmless." But a "reviewing court" cannot invent "findings" or reasons the agency never gave.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.sentence: Diversification was a permissible public-interest criterion because independently selected editorial subjects and reportorial attention mattered even with fairness regulation.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-078.plain: "Diversification" of ownership was a permissible public-interest factor, because independent choices of editorial subjects and news coverage mattered even with "fairness regulation" requiring balanced coverage.

carnival.sentence: The Ninth Circuit considered Washington solicitation a but-for cause of the trip and injury sufficient for contacts.
carnival.plain: The Ninth Circuit treated Carnival's advertising in Washington as a "but-for cause" of the trip and injury (without it, neither would have happened), which was enough contact with the state.

carnival.sentence: An intermediate procedural step mattered: the Ninth Circuit withdrew its 1988 opinion while certifying the Washington long-arm statute question to the State Supreme Court.
carnival.plain: An in-between "procedural" step mattered: the Ninth Circuit withdrew its 1988 "opinion" and asked the Washington State Supreme Court whether Washington's "long-arm statute" (its law on suing out-of-state defendants) reached Carnival.

carnival.sentence: The Bremen had enforced a forum clause in an individually negotiated international towage agreement between sophisticated corporations.
carnival.plain: The Bremen had enforced a "forum clause" (a clause choosing the court) in a one-on-one negotiated international "towage" (ship-towing) contract between sophisticated "corporations."

carnival.sentence: Former 46 U.S.C. App. § 183c barred passenger terms relieving negligence liability or weakening trial rights in a competent court.
carnival.plain: Former 46 U.S.C. App. § 183c barred passenger ticket terms excusing a ship owner's "negligence" (carelessness) liability or weakening a passenger's right to trial in a proper court.

carnival.sentence: The Court therefore enforced a location provision, not an exculpation.
carnival.plain: So the Court enforced a clause choosing where to sue, not an "exculpation," a clause freeing Carnival from liability.

carnival.sentence: Traditional admiralty and adhesion-contract scrutiny considered unequal bargaining, weak assent, and deterrence of negligence.
carnival.plain: Traditional "admiralty" (maritime law) and adhesion-contract scrutiny of take-it-or-leave-it terms looked at unequal bargaining, weak "assent" (real agreement), and reduced deterrence of "negligence."

channel-home.sentence: Baker Investment was equitable owner, Equitable Life held title, and closing was anticipated in February 1985.
channel-home.plain: Baker Investment was the "equitable owner" (it had agreed to buy, giving it ownership rights in fairness), Equitable Life "held title" (legal ownership), and closing was expected in February 1985.

channel-home.sentence: Without advance notice, the judge consolidated it with trial under Rule 65(a)(2), denied relief, and on March 26 entered judgment against Channel for lack of intent, consideration, and compliance with the lease statute of frauds.
channel-home.plain: Without "advance notice," the judge merged the hearing with trial under Rule 65(a)(2) and denied relief. On March 26 he "entered judgment" against Channel, finding no intent, no consideration, and no compliance with the lease "statute of frauds," which requires a signed writing.

channel-home.sentence: With no square Pennsylvania decision, the panel predicted that an express agreement to negotiate could be enforced if intent, definiteness, and consideration were established.
channel-home.plain: With no Pennsylvania case directly on point, the panel predicted an "express agreement" to negotiate could be enforced if intent to be bound, "definiteness" (clear enough terms), and consideration were shown.

channel-home.sentence: The lease statute of frauds therefore did not answer the narrower obligation to withdraw the premises and negotiate exclusively in good faith.
channel-home.plain: So the lease "statute of frauds" did not defeat the narrower promise to take the premises off the market and negotiate only with Channel "in good faith," meaning honestly.

channel-home.sentence: The theory did not rest solely on expenditures, and the court did not reach unilateral-contract or promissory-estoppel alternatives.
channel-home.plain: The claim did not rest only on Channel's spending, and the court did not reach the backup "unilateral-contract" theory (accepting an offer by acting) or promissory estoppel (enforcing a relied-on promise).

cp-celotex.sentence: Its majority read Rule 56 and Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co., an earlier summary-judgment decision, to require evidence affirmatively negating exposure before Catrett had to respond.
cp-celotex.plain: The appeals court majority read Rule 56, the summary-judgment rule, and Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co., an earlier Supreme Court case, to require Celotex to offer evidence disproving exposure before Catrett had to respond.

cp-celotex.sentence: After adequate discovery, failure to show an essential element on which a party bears the trial burden can justify summary judgment.
cp-celotex.plain: After adequate "discovery" (the pretrial exchange of evidence), "summary judgment" (ending a case without trial) can be proper if a "party" cannot show an "essential element" on which it bears the "trial burden," the duty to prove that point at trial.

cp-celotex.sentence: The moving party still had an initial responsibility: identify the basis of its motion and the record supporting the absence of a genuine material dispute.
cp-celotex.plain: The "moving party" still had a first duty: explain the basis of its "motion" and point to the parts of the record showing no genuine dispute about a "material" (important) fact.

cp-celotex.sentence: Once a motion was properly made and supported, the opponent had to designate specific facts beyond the complaint’s allegations.
cp-celotex.plain: Once a "motion" was properly made and supported, the other side had to point to specific facts, beyond the complaint's allegations, showing a real issue for trial.

cp-celotex.sentence: The question included whether the identified substance could become admissible proof at trial.
cp-celotex.plain: The question included whether the evidence identified could become "admissible" (usable) proof at trial, for example through live testimony.

cp-celotex.sentence: He distinguished the initial production burden from the ultimate burden of establishing entitlement to judgment.
cp-celotex.plain: Justice Brennan separated the initial "production burden" (coming forward with evidence) from the "ultimate burden" of showing entitlement to "judgment," which stays with the moving party.

cp-celotex.sentence: When the opponent bore the trial burden, a movant could negate an element or demonstrate the insufficiency of existing proof; the latter method required engagement with favorable record evidence.
cp-celotex.plain: When the opponent bore the "trial burden," a moving party could disprove an "element" or show the opponent's existing proof falls short. The second way required dealing with helpful evidence already in the record.

cp-daimler.sentence: They instead invoked general jurisdiction, which would allow unrelated claims, by attributing a United States distributor’s California business to the German parent.
cp-daimler.plain: Instead the plaintiffs invoked "general jurisdiction," which would allow even unrelated "claims," by counting a United States distributor's California business as the German parent's own.

cp-daimler.sentence: Daimler had not contested MBUSA’s own California general jurisdiction below, so the Supreme Court assumed the distributor was at home there for this case.
cp-daimler.plain: Daimler had not disputed in the lower courts that MBUSA itself was subject to "general jurisdiction" in California, so the Supreme Court assumed the distributor was "at home" there for this case.

cp-daimler.sentence: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(k)(1)(A) ordinarily incorporated state jurisdictional limits, and California’s long-arm statute reached the constitutional boundary.
cp-daimler.plain: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(k)(1)(A) ordinarily adopts the state's "jurisdictional" limits, and California's "long-arm statute" (its law on reaching out-of-state defendants) goes as far as the Constitution allows.

cp-daimler.sentence: Following International Shoe, specific jurisdiction expanded through the connection among defendant, forum, and dispute, leaving general jurisdiction a narrower role.
cp-daimler.plain: After International Shoe, specific jurisdiction, based on links among the defendant, the forum state, and the dispute, expanded, leaving "general jurisdiction" (suit on any claim) a narrower role.

cp-daimler.sentence: Incorporation and principal place of business were clear paradigm homes, not an exclusive two-place list.
cp-daimler.plain: "Incorporation" (where a company is legally formed) and its principal place of business (headquarters) are the clear model homes, not an exclusive two-place list.

cp-daimler.sentence: The Court noted that Kiobel’s extraterritoriality treatment of the Alien Tort Statute and Mohamad’s restriction of Torture Victim Protection Act defendants to natural persons had undermined the asserted federal claims.
cp-daimler.plain: The Court noted that Kiobel’s limit on the Alien Tort Statute's reach to conduct abroad, and Mohamad’s holding that Torture Victim Protection Act defendants must be "natural persons" (individuals, not companies), had undermined the federal claims.

cp-hancock.sentence: The oil companies then sought interpleader.
cp-hancock.plain: The oil companies then sought "interpleader," asking the court to make the rival claimants fight over the money so the companies would pay only once.

cp-hancock.sentence: The trial court sustained them without leave to amend because a tenant could not deny the landlord’s title as it existed when the tenancy began.
cp-hancock.plain: The trial court upheld the objections "without leave to amend" (no chance to fix the complaint), because a tenant may not deny the landlord's "title" (ownership) as it stood when the "tenancy" began.

cp-hancock.sentence: Justice Edmonds’s majority began with traditional equitable interpleader requirements: claims to the same thing, debt, or duty; a common source; a disinterested stakeholder; and no independent liability to a claimant.
cp-hancock.plain: Justice Edmonds’s "majority" began with traditional interpleader requirements: claims to the same thing, debt, or duty; a "common source" for the claims; a disinterested stakeholder; and no "independent liability" to any "claimant."

cp-hancock.sentence: If the partnership instead sought reasonable use value, mesne profits, or waste damages, it would assert a different obligation unsuitable for this interpleader.
cp-hancock.plain: If the partnership instead sought reasonable use value, "mesne profits" (money for wrongful occupation of land), or damages for waste (harm to the land), that would be a different obligation, unsuitable for this interpleader.

cp-hancock.sentence: Removing the common-source restriction undermined the associated common-law obstacle to tenant interpleader.
cp-hancock.plain: Dropping the "common-source" requirement weakened the related "common-law" (judge-made) bar against tenants using interpleader against their landlords.

cp-hancock.sentence: He preferred requiring the adverse claimant to seek an injunction or receiver and furnish security for the landlord if the claim failed.
cp-hancock.plain: The dissent preferred making the "adverse claimant" (the rival) seek an "injunction" or a receiver (a neutral manager) and post security for the landlord if its claim failed.

cp-hancock.sentence: The complaint survived general demurrer; even if uncertainty required clarification, denying leave to amend was an abuse of discretion.
cp-hancock.plain: The complaint survived general demurrer (an objection that it states no claim). Even if parts needed clarifying, denying "leave to amend" was an "abuse of discretion," an unreasonable choice.

cp-kroger.sentence: Impleader requires possible liability to the defendant for the plaintiff’s claim, rather than merely liability directly to the plaintiff.
cp-kroger.plain: "Impleader" (a defendant bringing in a third party) requires that the third party may be liable to the defendant for the plaintiff's claim, not merely liable directly to the plaintiff.

cp-kroger.sentence: Because corporate citizenship included the principal place of business as well as incorporation, both remaining litigants were Iowa citizens.
cp-kroger.plain: Because "corporate citizenship" includes the "principal place of business" (headquarters) as well as the state of "incorporation," both remaining "litigants," Owen and the widow, were Iowa citizens.

cp-kroger.sentence: The Eighth Circuit sustained ancillary jurisdiction because the claims shared operative facts and approved retention after finding that Owen had concealed its Iowa citizenship.
cp-kroger.plain: The Eighth Circuit upheld ancillary (tag-along) jurisdiction because the claims shared the same facts, and approved keeping the claim after finding that Owen had hidden its Iowa "citizenship."

cp-kroger.sentence: Rule 14 allowed a plaintiff to plead a related claim against an impleaded party, but a procedural rule could not itself supply subject-matter jurisdiction.
cp-kroger.plain: Rule 14 let a plaintiff assert a related claim against an impleaded party. But a "procedural rule" cannot itself supply "subject-matter jurisdiction," the court's power to hear that kind of case.

cp-kroger.sentence: The diversity statute, § 1332, required complete diversity under its settled interpretation, which Congress had repeatedly left intact.
cp-kroger.plain: The diversity statute, § 1332, has long been read to require complete diversity (no plaintiff sharing a state with any defendant), and Congress had repeatedly left that reading in place.

cp-kroger.sentence: Otherwise, plaintiffs could sue diverse defendants and wait for them to bring in nondiverse tortfeasors.
cp-kroger.plain: Otherwise, plaintiffs could sue out-of-state defendants and wait for them to bring in "nondiverse" (same-state) wrongdoers, dodging the rule.

cp-kroger.sentence: This was an absence of power, not an abuse of discretion in retaining a permissible claim.
cp-kroger.plain: This was a lack of power to hear the claim, not an "abuse of discretion" in keeping a claim the court could hear.

cp-tellabs.sentence: The court then dismissed with prejudice: the allegedly misleading statements were sufficiently specified, but the facts did not adequately plead scienter.
cp-tellabs.plain: The court then "dismissed with prejudice" (for good): the allegedly misleading statements were identified well enough, but the facts did not adequately "plead" scienter, intent to deceive.

cp-tellabs.sentence: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act imposed separate pleading duties: identify each misleading statement and why it was misleading, and allege particular facts supporting a strong inference of the required mental state.
cp-tellabs.plain: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act sets separate "pleading" duties: identify each misleading statement and why it misled, and "allege" particular facts giving a "strong inference" of the required mental state.

cp-tellabs.sentence: Justice Ginsburg, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer, held that the scienter inference must be cogent and at least as compelling as any plausible opposing inference from the alleged facts.
cp-tellabs.plain: Justice Ginsburg, "joined by" Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer, held that the "inference" of "scienter" (intent to deceive) must be convincing and at least as compelling as any plausible innocent explanation.

cp-tellabs.sentence: The court must accept factual allegations as true and consider them collectively, along with incorporated documents and matters properly subject to judicial notice under Rule 12(b)(6).
cp-tellabs.plain: Under Rule 12(b)(6), on a motion to dismiss, the court accepts factual "allegations" as true and views them together, with documents the complaint relies on and facts proper for "judicial notice" (undisputed public facts).

cp-tellabs.sentence: Comparing explanations while assuming pleaded facts true differed from proving fraud at trial by a preponderance of the evidence.
cp-tellabs.plain: Comparing explanations while assuming the "pleaded" facts true differs from proving fraud at trial by a "preponderance of the evidence," meaning more likely than not.

cp-wild-oats.sentence: It would trigger the forum-defendant restriction on removal, but Lively’s thirty-day objection period had expired.
cp-wild-oats.plain: Being a Californian would trigger the "forum-defendant" rule (a defendant from the state where suit was filed cannot remove it to federal court). But Lively's thirty-day period to object had expired.

cp-wild-oats.sentence: The judge treated that restriction as jurisdictional and remanded under § 1447(c).
cp-wild-oats.plain: The judge treated that rule as "jurisdictional" (limiting the court's basic power, so it cannot be waived) and sent the case back to state court under § 1447(c).

cp-wild-oats.sentence: The then-§ 1441(b) barred diversity removal by a properly joined and served forum citizen.
cp-wild-oats.plain: The then-§ 1441(b) barred removal based on diversity by a forum-state citizen who was "properly joined and served," meaning correctly named and given the papers.

cp-wild-oats.sentence: Under Thermtron and later cases, subsections (c) and (d) operated together: the bar protected remands within statutory authority, not every order invoking the section.
cp-wild-oats.plain: Under Thermtron and later cases, subsections (c) and (d) work together: the ban on appealing remands protects only remands the statute authorizes, not every order citing the section.

cp-wild-oats.sentence: Mandatory sua sponte remand after waiver could defeat both parties’ preference and the plaintiff’s choice.
cp-wild-oats.plain: A required "sua sponte" remand (one on the judge's own initiative) after the objection was waived could override both "parties’" preference, including the plaintiff's choice.

cp-wild-oats.sentence: The District Court therefore exceeded § 1447(c) by remanding on its own, allowing appellate review of that unauthorized order.
cp-wild-oats.plain: So the District Court went beyond § 1447(c) by remanding on its own, and that unauthorized "order" was open to "appellate" review.

doe-great-expectations.sentence: Under the statute as applied, a contract charging more than $25 had to promise a specified certain number of referrals per month.
