doe-great-expectations.plain: Under the "statute" as applied, a dating contract costing more than $25 had to promise a specified number of referrals (introductions) each month.

doe-great-expectations.sentence: That finding supported full restitution as actual damages and substantial justice in the small-claims cases.
doe-great-expectations.plain: That "finding" (that the customers would not have signed had they known their rights) supported full "restitution" (returning everything paid) as actual damages and "substantial justice" (a fair result) in these small-claims cases.

doe-great-expectations.sentence: The judge distinguished older decisions treating noncompliant contracts as automatically void on public-policy grounds.
doe-great-expectations.plain: The judge "distinguished" (set aside as different) older cases that treated contracts breaking this law as automatically "void" (unenforceable from the start) on public-policy grounds.

lefkowitz.sentence: The store relied on decisions treating advertisements as invitations for customers to make offers, asserted that its proposal could be withdrawn without notice, and invoked its house rule.
lefkowitz.plain: The store argued that ads are normally just invitations for customers to make offers (not offers that can be accepted), that it could withdraw its deal at any time, and that its women-only policy applied.

lefkowitz.sentence: It was sufficiently definite to leave no further negotiation and gave a customer power to complete the bargain through the requested acts.
lefkowitz.plain: The ad was "sufficiently definite" (specific enough) to leave nothing to negotiate, so a customer could complete the "bargain" (form a binding deal) just by doing what it asked.

lefkowitz.sentence: The merchant could modify an outstanding offer before acceptance, but could not impose a new or arbitrary condition after formation.
lefkowitz.plain: The store could change an open offer before acceptance, but could not add a new or arbitrary condition after "formation" of the contract.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: Hobby Lobby held the unaccommodated mandate inconsistent with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) for the closely held corporate objectors there.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: Hobby Lobby held that the mandate, without an accommodation (workaround), violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) for the "closely held" (family-owned, few-owner) companies objecting there.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: In 2017, the agencies issued two immediately effective interim final rules, invoking good cause to proceed without advance comment while also soliciting comments.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: In 2017 the agencies issued two "interim final rules" that took effect at once. They claimed good cause to skip inviting public comment first, while also asking for comments.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: The Supreme Court rejected the circuit’s demand for independent appellate standing from the Little Sisters: the government had standing and both requested the same dissolution.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: The Supreme Court rejected the circuit's demand that the Little Sisters show their own "appellate" "standing" (a right to appeal): the government had standing, and both sought the same lifting of the court order.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: Ignoring RFRA entirely could overlook an important aspect of the problem and expose a rule to arbitrary-and-capricious review.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: Ignoring RFRA entirely could miss an important aspect of the problem and expose a rule to "arbitrary-and-capricious" review, under which courts strike down unreasoned agency action.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: Under Vermont Yankee and Perez, courts cannot add procedures beyond the statute.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: Under Vermont Yankee and Perez, courts cannot require agencies to follow procedures beyond what the "statute" requires.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: Existing exceptions undermined the asserted compelling interest, and less restrictive alternatives remained even if the interest were compelling.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: In Justice Alito's view, existing exemptions undercut the claimed "compelling interest" (a goal vital enough to justify burdening religion), and less restrictive options remained even if it were compelling.

lrs-n-little-sisters.sentence: Justice Kagan, joined by Justice Breyer, agreed on procedural validity and the judgment but found statutory authority through the then-applicable Chevron deference framework.
lrs-n-little-sisters.plain: Justice Kagan, "joined by" Justice Breyer, agreed the rules were procedurally valid and agreed with the "judgment," but found "statutory authority" only through the then-applicable "Chevron deference" rule of deferring to reasonable agency readings of unclear laws.

lrs-s-arthrex.sentence: Inter partes review permits adversarial reconsideration of an issued patent’s novelty and nonobviousness.
lrs-s-arthrex.plain: "Inter partes review" (a Patent Office proceeding between two sides) allows adversarial "reconsideration" of whether an issued patent's invention was new and showed "nonobviousness," meaning it was not an obvious step.

lrs-s-arthrex.sentence: The Federal Circuit held that APJs were principal officers because neither the Secretary nor the Director could review their decisions or remove them at will.
lrs-s-arthrex.plain: The Federal Circuit held APJs (administrative patent judges) were principal officers, needing Senate-approved appointment, because neither the Secretary nor the Director could review their decisions or fire them freely.

lrs-s-arthrex.sentence: The Appointments Clause’s principal-officer process assigns public responsibility through presidential nomination and Senate confirmation; its exception for inferior appointments still requires genuine subordination.
lrs-s-arthrex.plain: The Appointments Clause’s principal-officer process (presidential nomination and Senate confirmation) makes clear who is publicly responsible. Its exception for inferior (lower-level) appointments still requires real subordination to a superior.

lrs-s-arthrex.sentence: Under the Court’s existing public-rights treatment of inter partes review, these adjudications exercised executive power despite their judicial form.
lrs-s-arthrex.plain: Under the Court's existing "public-rights" view of "inter partes review" (patents are rights the government grants), these court-like proceedings were an exercise of executive power.

lrs-s-arthrex.sentence: The remedial holding made § 6(c) unenforceable only insofar as it barred the Director from independently reviewing final Board decisions.
lrs-s-arthrex.plain: The "remedial" holding (the fix) made § 6(c) "unenforceable" only to the extent it barred the Director from independently reviewing the Board's final decisions.

lrs-s-edmond.sentence: The specific-over-general principle did not apply because the two provisions did not conflict.
lrs-s-edmond.plain: The "specific-over-general" principle (a specific law beats a general one) did not apply, because the two provisions did not conflict.

lrs-s-edmond.sentence: A Judge Advocate General was neither the President, a department head, nor a court of law, so Congress could not entrust that official with appointing even inferior officers.
lrs-s-edmond.plain: A Judge Advocate General (a top military lawyer) is not the President, a department head, or a "court of law," so Congress could not let that official appoint even "inferior officers."

lrs-s-edmond.sentence: The Court accepted those powers but explained that significant federal authority distinguished officers from employees, not principal from inferior officers.
lrs-s-edmond.plain: The Court accepted those powers, but explained that significant federal authority separates officers from mere employees, not principal officers from "inferior officers."

lrs-s-edmond.sentence: Generally, inferior officers’ work was directed and supervised at some level by officers appointed through presidential nomination and Senate consent.
lrs-s-edmond.plain: In general, "inferior officers" are those whose work is directed and supervised at some level by officers appointed by the President with "Senate consent."

lrs-s-freytag.sentence: In the catchall category they could hear evidence and prepare proposed findings and an opinion, but a regular Tax Court judge had to enter the decision.
lrs-s-freytag.plain: In the "catchall" category of other cases, special judges could hear "evidence" and prepare "proposed findings" and an "opinion," but a regular Tax Court judge had to enter the decision.

lrs-s-freytag.sentence: The majority regarded the objection as nonjurisdictional but structural and, drawing on Glidden’s treatment of tribunal validity, exercised discretion to consider a serious challenge to the very proceeding under review.
lrs-s-freytag.plain: The majority saw the objection as "nonjurisdictional" (not about the Court's basic power) but structural. Following Glidden’s treatment of a tribunal's validity, it used its "discretion" to consider a serious challenge to the very proceeding under "review."

lrs-s-freytag.sentence: An amicus offered the ground the majority accepted: “courts of law” under the Appointments Clause need not be Article III courts.
lrs-s-freytag.plain: An "amicus" (a nonparty filing a brief) offered the theory the majority adopted: "courts of law" under the Appointments Clause need not be Article III courts with life-tenured judges.

lrs-s-freytag.sentence: Consent cannot legalize unconstitutional conduct, but forfeiture can bar a particular remedy and protect orderly trials, developed review, and avoidance of strategic silence.
lrs-s-freytag.plain: Consent cannot make unconstitutional conduct lawful. But "forfeiture" (losing a point by not raising it in time) can bar a particular "remedy," keeping trials orderly, letting issues develop for review, and stopping parties from holding objections in reserve.

lrs-s-freytag.sentence: Five entertained the otherwise unpreserved objection and upheld appointment by a court of law; four preferred forfeiture and, alternatively, appointment by an executive-department head.
lrs-s-freytag.plain: Five Justices considered the "unpreserved" objection (one not raised in time) and upheld appointment by a court of law. Four preferred "forfeiture" and, alternatively, would have upheld it as appointment by an executive-department head.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: For primary standards, § 109(b)(1) directed the Administrator to use the air-quality criteria, allow an adequate margin of safety, and select a level requisite to protect public health.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: For "primary standards" (health-based limits), § 109(b)(1) told the Administrator to use the air-quality criteria, allow an adequate "margin of safety" (an extra cushion), and set a level "requisite" to protect public health.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: On nondelegation, however, the panel concluded that the EPA had interpreted the section to confer discretion without an intelligible principle.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: On "nondelegation," though, the panel held the EPA had read the section to give it "discretion" without an "intelligible principle," a clear guiding standard from Congress.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: The opinion’s image of Congress not hiding elephants in mouseholes expressed that inference from statutory design.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: The "opinion's" image of Congress not hiding "elephants in mouseholes" (big changes in small, vague provisions) expressed that "inference" from how the statute is built.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: But avoidance selects among legally available interpretations; it cannot contradict an unambiguous statutory direction.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: But constitutional avoidance only chooses among legally possible readings. It cannot contradict an "unambiguous" (clear) statutory command.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: An agency cannot repair Congress’s failure to constrain power by deciding voluntarily how little of that power it will use.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: If Congress failed to set limits, an agency can't cure that by promising to use less power.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: Requisite meant sufficient, but no more stringent than necessary, to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: "Requisite" meant strict enough, but no stricter than necessary, to protect public health with an adequate "margin of safety" (an extra cushion).

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: Finality concerned whether the agency had finished deciding; ripeness concerned whether judicial review at that time was suitable and useful.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: Finality asked whether the agency had finished deciding. Ripeness asked whether "judicial review" (a court stepping in) at that time was suitable and useful.

lrs-s-whitman.sentence: Later still, Loper Bright, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), overruled Chevron and required independent judicial judgment about statutory meaning, while recognizing that statutes can confer agency discretion.
lrs-s-whitman.plain: Later, Loper Bright, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), "overruled" Chevron (deference to reasonable agency readings of unclear laws) and required "independent judicial judgment" about what statutes mean, while recognizing statutes can give agencies discretion.

brief-CP-149.sentence: The FAA and Fairchild argued that Herrick had virtually represented Taylor.
brief-CP-149.plain: The FAA and Fairchild argued that Herrick had "virtually represented" Taylor, meaning stood in for him in the first case, so Taylor should be bound by Herrick's loss though never a party.

brief-CP-149.sentence: The district court granted summary judgment on preclusion, and the D.C. Circuit affirmed under a test requiring aligned interests and adequate representation plus some connection such as close relationship, substantial participation, or tactical maneuvering.
brief-CP-149.plain: The "district court" granted summary judgment on "preclusion" (being bound by Herrick's loss). The D.C. Circuit affirmed, using a test of aligned interests, adequate representation, and some further link such as a close relationship, heavy participation, or tactical maneuvering.

brief-CP-149.sentence: Claim and issue preclusion protect against repetition and inconsistent results, but ordinarily a person retains a claim if absent from the earlier litigation.
brief-CP-149.plain: The rules against relitigating claims and issues exist to stop repeat lawsuits and conflicting results. But normally someone who was not a party to the earlier case keeps the right to bring their own claim.

brief-CP-149.sentence: Preclusion was an affirmative defense that the FAA and Fairchild had to plead and prove.
brief-CP-149.plain: Preclusion was an "affirmative defense," so the FAA and Fairchild had to "plead" it (raise it in their papers) and prove it; Taylor did not have to disprove it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-367.sentence: Discoverable information need not itself be admissible.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-367.plain: "Discoverable" information (what can be requested in pretrial discovery) need not itself be "admissible," meaning usable as evidence at trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-367.sentence: Independently, Federal Rule of Evidence 407 admissibility was a different question from discovery relevance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-367.plain: Separately, admissibility under Federal Rule of Evidence 407, which bars using later safety improvements to prove fault, is a different question from relevance in discovery.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-528.sentence: It resolved factual issues favorably to Google but deemed the use legally unfair and directed a damages trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-528.plain: The appeals court resolved the factual issues in Google's favor but held the use unfair as a matter of law, and ordered a trial on "damages," how much Google owed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-528.sentence: The majority found that reimplementation transformative despite the same basic task-calling function.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-528.plain: The majority held that putting the familiar commands to work in a new smartphone setting added something new (it was 'transformative'), even though the commands did the same basic job of calling up tasks.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.sentence: These were allegations on dismissal motions, not findings after trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.plain: These were "allegations" (claims taken as true) on motions to dismiss, not "findings" made after a trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.sentence: Justice Kennedy separated plausible constitutional wrongdoing from judicial authority to imply damages.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.plain: Justice Kennedy separated plausible constitutional wrongdoing from whether courts have authority to "imply damages," meaning create a right to sue for money that Congress did not provide.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.sentence: A context was new if it differed meaningfully from those Supreme Court settings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.plain: A claim counts as a 'new context' if it differs in any meaningful way from the three Supreme Court cases that allowed damages suits against federal officers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.sentence: Assuming truth and adequate pleading, the Court granted qualified immunity to all petitioners.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ZIGLAR-ABBASI.plain: Assuming the claims were true and the "pleading" adequate, the Court granted qualified immunity to all "petitioners" (the officials appealing). That shield protects officials unless clearly established law told them their conduct was illegal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.sentence: Strict liability went to the jury, which returned a defense verdict.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.plain: The strict liability claim (that the board was a dangerously defective product, which needs no proof of carelessness) went to the jury, which returned a "defense verdict," finding for Anthony.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.sentence: Assumption of risk instead required discovery of the defect, actual understanding of its danger, and voluntary, unreasonable encounter with it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.plain: The defense that does bar recovery, 'assumption of risk', requires that the plaintiff actually knew about the defect, understood its danger, and still chose, voluntarily and unreasonably, to face it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.sentence: The Sheehans still had to prove an unreasonably dangerous defect proximately causing injury.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-071.plain: At the new trial, the Sheehans would still have to prove that the board had a defect making it unreasonably dangerous and that the defect actually and directly caused the injury.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.sentence: The Uniform Commercial Code writing requirement was not otherwise satisfied.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.plain: The Uniform Commercial Code requirement of a signed writing for a sale of goods this large was not otherwise met by any document here.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.sentence: But § 2-201(3)(c) allowed enforcement for goods with payment made and accepted.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.plain: But UCC § 2-201(3)(c) made an exception: an oral sale can be enforced for goods for which payment has been made and accepted.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.sentence: Its purpose and acceptance needed trial, so the sales claim survived without a formation ruling.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-001.plain: What the payment was for, and whether Amax gave "acceptance" of it, needed a trial. So the sales claim went forward without a ruling on "formation," whether a contract was actually made.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-048.sentence: The trial court sustained a demurrer without leave to amend and dismissed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-048.plain: The trial court sustained a "demurrer" (an objection that, even taking the complaint as true, there is no legal claim) without leave to amend, refusing to let Odorizzi rewrite it, and dismissed the case.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-048.sentence: Duress and menace required unlawful acts or threats.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-048.plain: To undo a contract for duress or 'menace' (threats), the pressure must involve unlawful acts or threats of unlawful harm.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-048.sentence: Mistake also failed because participants knew the material circumstances and principally predicted consequences.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-048.plain: His claim of mistake failed because everyone knew the relevant facts; he had merely guessed wrong about what would happen next.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-054.sentence: The parties had stipulated that remedies would await liability.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-054.plain: The parties had "stipulated" (formally agreed) that remedies, what the court would order, would wait until liability was decided.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-054.sentence: Past liability and a need for future restraints were distinct questions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-054.plain: Past "liability" (whether someone broke the law) and the need for future restraints (an order to stop it happening again) were separate questions.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-054.sentence: The limitation was remedial relief rather than a penalty assessment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-054.plain: The limit was that the order be "remedial" relief, repairing the wrong by taking away ill-gotten gains, rather than a penalty that punishes.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.sentence: Remaining preliminary objections were joined to the merits.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.plain: Kenya's remaining preliminary objections were "joined to the merits," meaning put off to be decided together with the main dispute.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.sentence: An illegal transaction might still have proprietary consequences where title could be shown independently, but no such separate claim was pleaded.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.plain: An illegal deal might still have "proprietary consequences" (effects on who owns property) where ownership could be shown without relying on the deal, but no such separate claim was pleaded.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.sentence: Bribery of the other party’s agent made the contract voidable at the principal’s option, not necessarily void from inception.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.plain: Bribing the other "party’s" agent made the contract voidable at the option of the "principal" (Kenya, for whom the agent acted), not necessarily "void" (invalid) from the start.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.sentence: Positive avoidance was required and informed affirmation could defeat it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.plain: The innocent side had to take a clear step to cancel the contract, and it would lose that right if it confirmed the contract after learning of the bribe.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.sentence: Continued dealings without knowledge established no affirmation, waiver, or estoppel.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-036.plain: Kenya's continued dealings before it knew of the bribe were no affirmation (confirming the contract), "waiver" (giving up the right to cancel), or estoppel (being barred from cancelling).

brief-CT-CB-0304.sentence: Uber moved to confirm in September.
brief-CT-CB-0304.plain: In September Uber asked the court to confirm the arbitrator's award, turning it into an enforceable court judgment.

brief-CT-CB-0304.sentence: Section 12(a)(5) allowed no-agreement vacatur only if that issue had not already been adversely decided in compulsion proceedings and participation was not without objection.
brief-CT-CB-0304.plain: Section 12(a)(5) allowed "vacatur" (cancelling an award) for lack of an arbitration agreement only if a court had not already rejected that point when compelling arbitration, and the party had not taken part without objecting.

brief-CT-CB-0304.sentence: Reconsideration was an abuse of discretion.
brief-CT-CB-0304.plain: "Reconsideration" of the arbitration order at that late stage was an "abuse of discretion," an unreasonable use of the judge's judgment.
Uber proved neither that users had reasonable notice of the terms nor that clicking showed agreement to them.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0129.sentence: The Court nevertheless explained that exceeding compensatory damages does not alone make a penalty excessive.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0129.plain: The Court explained, though, that exceeding "compensatory damages" (the amount of the actual loss) does not by itself make a penalty excessive.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0129.sentence: Making proved damages an automatic ceiling would erase that distinction.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0129.plain: If proved loss automatically capped the penalty, the penalty would be no different from ordinary damages.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-025.sentence: Only one of three captioned dockets remained; the others were moot.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-025.plain: Only one of the three "dockets" (cases listed in the heading) remained live; the others were "moot," meaning no real dispute was left.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-025.sentence: Broad discretion also risked subjective content discrimination.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-025.plain: Broad "discretion" for the FCC also risked subjective "content discrimination," officials favoring or punishing speech based on what it says.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-064.sentence: Feasible meant capable of accomplishment, not worthwhile after a separate health-cost comparison.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-064.plain: 'Feasible' means capable of being done, not 'worth doing' after weighing health benefits against costs.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-064.sentence: Courts could not search the record to construct that missing explanation.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-064.plain: Courts could not "search the record" (dig through the agency's files) to build the explanation the agency itself never gave.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-064.sentence: Justice Rehnquist, joined by Chief Justice Burger, instead saw an unlawful delegation.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-064.plain: Justice Rehnquist, joined by Chief Justice Burger, instead saw an "unlawful delegation": the statute handed the agency a basic policy choice Congress itself should have made.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-085.sentence: The Act permits specified tort claims against the Government but preserves enumerated exceptions.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-085.plain: The Federal Tort Claims Act allows certain injury claims against the Government, but keeps "enumerated exceptions," a listed set of cases where it cannot be sued.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-085.sentence: It moved under Rule 12(b)(1) to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-085.plain: The government moved under Rule 12(b)(1) to dismiss for "lack of subject-matter" jurisdiction, arguing that because of the mail exception the court had no power to hear the case.

cp-bechtel.sentence: Bright requested remand and asserted he now wanted to litigate only state withholding.
cp-bechtel.plain: Bright asked for a "remand" (sending the case back to state court) and said he now wanted to "litigate" (challenge in court) only the state-tax withholding.

cp-bechtel.sentence: Pendent jurisdiction survived dismissal of the federal claim because both deductions arose from the same operative facts: the federal direction activated California’s rule.
cp-bechtel.plain: "Pendent jurisdiction" over the state claim survived dismissal of the federal claim because both deductions arose from the same "operative facts": the federal directive triggered California's rule.

cp-bechtel.sentence: The $3,300 district fee award was permissible deterrence, not a finding of tax underpayment.
cp-bechtel.plain: The $3,300 "fee award" by the district court (making Bright pay Bechtel's lawyer fees) was permissible "deterrence" to discourage such suits, not a finding that he underpaid his taxes.

cp-mcgee.sentence: International received registered-mail process at its principal Texas office.
cp-mcgee.plain: International received "registered-mail process" (the lawsuit papers sent by registered mail) at its main office in Texas.

cp-mcgee.sentence: It did not make International answerable in California for unrelated disputes.
cp-mcgee.plain: The ruling did not mean International could be sued in California over matters unrelated to this policy.

cp-moore.plain: Lawyer fees were "reserved" (put off) to be decided on later motions.

cp-moore.sentence: Allowing that amendment and award was an abuse of discretion.
cp-moore.plain: Allowing that "amendment" (adding Sidney's claim for her own support) and the award was an "abuse of discretion," an unreasonable use of the trial court's judgment.

cp-mosley.sentence: Judge Ross’s panel applied abuse-of-discretion review.
cp-mosley.plain: Judge Ross’s "panel" (three-judge group) applied abuse-of-discretion "review," overturning only an unreasonable ruling.

cp-mosley.sentence: Rules 20(b) and 42(b) supplied protective measures and separate trials.
cp-mosley.plain: Rules 20(b) and 42(b) supplied protective measures and separate trials if trying everything together became unfair or confusing.

cp-pennoyer.sentence: Execution instead enforces a judgment already entered.
cp-pennoyer.plain: Seizing and selling property after judgment ('execution') only collects on a judgment that already exists; it does not by itself give the court the power over the defendant that it needed when it entered that judgment.

cp-pennoyer.sentence: Pennoyer brought a writ of error to the Supreme Court.
cp-pennoyer.plain: Pennoyer brought a "writ of error" (the old procedure for asking a higher court to correct legal errors) to the Supreme Court.

cp-pennoyer.sentence: This is a collateral attack on the first judgment.
cp-pennoyer.plain: This is a "collateral attack" on the first judgment: Neff challenged Mitchell's old judgment in a separate lawsuit rather than appealing it directly.

cp-pennoyer.sentence: The Oregon personal default judgment, entered against an absent nonresident without personal service or appearance, could not authorize the execution sale.
cp-pennoyer.plain: The Oregon personal "default judgment" (entered because Neff never responded) was entered against an absent "nonresident" without personal service or "appearance" in the case. It could not authorize the "execution sale" (sheriff's sale) of his land.

cp-wyman.sentence: The defect concerned acquisition of personal jurisdiction, not a later procedural irregularity.
cp-wyman.plain: The defect concerned gaining "personal jurisdiction" (power over Newhouse) in the first place, not a later "procedural irregularity," a mistake in how the case was run.

cp-wyman.sentence: The assigned caption records denial of certiorari in 1938.
cp-wyman.plain: The assigned case heading records that the Supreme Court denied "certiorari" (declined to review the case) in 1938.

lawrence-fox.sentence: The Superior Court at General Term affirmed.
lawrence-fox.plain: The Superior Court at General Term, a panel of judges of the same New York City court hearing the appeal, “affirmed,” meaning it upheld the judgment for Lawrence.

lawrence-fox.sentence: Lawrence therefore did not need an equitable interest in a particular fund.
lawrence-fox.plain: So Lawrence did not need an “equitable interest” in a particular fund, meaning an ownership-like right in a specific pot of money of the kind a trust beneficiary holds.

lrs-i-mead-note.sentence: They ordinarily required public availability, not initial notice and comment.
lrs-i-mead-note.plain: The letters generally had to be made public, but Customs did not first have to publish proposals and take public comments.

lrs-i-mead-note.sentence: Under the then-governing Chevron doctrine, mandatory acceptance of a reasonable agency answer depended on Congress delegating authority to make rules with legal force and the agency exercising that authority in the interpretation at issue.
lrs-i-mead-note.plain: Under the “Chevron doctrine” then in force, a court had to accept an agency’s reasonable reading of a statute only if Congress was “delegating” to the agency power to make rules with legal force, and the agency was using that power when it adopted the reading.

lrs-i-mead-note.sentence: Transaction-specific binding effect and usefulness as precedent were insufficient.
lrs-i-mead-note.plain: That a ruling letter bound Customs for one transaction, and could serve as “precedent” (a guide for deciding later matters), was not enough to give it the force of law.

lrs-i-mead-note.sentence: Mead’s threshold for mandatory Chevron treatment therefore describes the former system.
lrs-i-mead-note.plain: Since the Supreme Court overruled Chevron in 2024, Mead's test for when Chevron deference applied describes a system that no longer exists.

lrs-n-overton-park.sentence: The Supreme Court stayed construction and expedited review.
lrs-n-overton-park.plain: The Supreme Court “stayed” construction, meaning it ordered it paused, and granted “expedited review,” meaning it fast-tracked the case.

lrs-n-overton-park.sentence: Section 701(a)(2)’s exception for action committed to agency discretion was narrow, and these statutes contained a prohibition with defined exceptions: no feasible and prudent alternative and all possible harm-minimizing planning.
lrs-n-overton-park.plain: Section 701(a)(2) of the APA bars court review of action “committed to agency discretion,” meaning left entirely to the agency’s judgment, but that exception is narrow. These statutes set a clear ban with defined exceptions: parkland could be used only if there was no feasible and prudent alternative and all possible planning had been done to minimize harm.

lrs-n-overton-park.sentence: Those requirements supplied law for a court to apply.
lrs-n-overton-park.plain: Those conditions gave a court a legal standard to measure the Secretary's decision against, so the decision could be reviewed.

lrs-n-overton-park.sentence: A presumption of regularity excused none of those inquiries.
lrs-n-overton-park.plain: The “presumption of regularity,” the usual assumption that officials do their jobs properly, did not excuse the court from any of these checks.

lrs-o-cafeteria-workers.sentence: A divided appellate panel initially reversed, but its opinion was withdrawn on rehearing.
lrs-o-cafeteria-workers.plain: At first a divided “appellate” panel (three appeals judges, split in their vote) “reversed,” ruling for her, but its “opinion” (written decision) was withdrawn when the court agreed to rehear the case.

lrs-o-cafeteria-workers.sentence: The en banc D.C. Circuit affirmed with four dissenters.
lrs-o-cafeteria-workers.plain: The D.C. Circuit, sitting “en banc” (all its active judges together rather than a three-judge panel), “affirmed,” upholding the ruling against her. Four judges were “dissenters,” meaning they disagreed with the result.

lrs-o-marbury.sentence: Keeping those steps distinct explains why two favorable conclusions produced no writ.
lrs-o-marbury.plain: Separating the three questions explains how Marbury won the first two (he had a right, and the law gave a remedy) but still got no writ of mandamus ordering Madison to deliver his commission.

lrs-o-marbury.sentence: On February 24, 1803, the operative order discharged the show-cause rule.
lrs-o-marbury.plain: On February 24, 1803, the Court’s actual order “discharged the show-cause rule,” cancelling its earlier order directing Madison to show cause, that is, to explain why he should not be ordered to deliver the commission.

lrs-o-marbury.sentence: The assigned editors call the earlier ministerial discussion technically dicta because the Court ultimately lacked original jurisdiction.
lrs-o-marbury.plain: The casebook editors call the earlier discussion of Madison’s “ministerial” duty (a routine duty with no room for choice) to deliver the commission technically “dicta,” remarks not needed for the decision. That is because the Court ultimately held it lacked “original jurisdiction,” the power to hear the case first rather than on appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: Every plaintiff was a Pennsylvania citizen; Anskis was a New Jersey citizen, supplying diversity jurisdiction over that suit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: Every “plaintiff” (the people suing) was a Pennsylvania citizen, and Anskis was a New Jersey citizen. That supplied “diversity jurisdiction,” the power of federal courts to hear state-law cases between citizens of different states, over that suit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: On April 1, 1957, Anskis defaulted for failure to appear, plead or defend.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: On April 1, 1957, Anskis was held in default because he failed to appear, plead or defend, meaning he never showed up or answered the lawsuit. A default generally lets the court treat the claims against him as admitted.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: The district court dismissed on the Danners’ motion, finding no proper Rule 13(g) crossclaim and no independent federal jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: On the Danners’ “motion” (formal request), the “district court” (the federal trial court) dismissed the Weintraubs’ claim against them. It found the claim was not a proper Rule 13(g) crossclaim against a party on the same side, and that there was no independent federal “jurisdiction,” or power, to hear it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: Anskis’s default had not created a claim against the Weintraubs to which their proposed crossclaim responded.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: Anskis’s default did not mean anyone had made a claim against the Weintraubs. So their proposed “crossclaim” (a claim against a party on their own side) against the Danners was not responding to any claim against them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: But he understood the device as ancillary to a claim already asserted against the crossclaimant: a defendant could claim against a codefendant, and a plaintiff facing a counterclaim could claim against a coplaintiff about that counterclaim’s transaction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: Judge Maris understood the Rule 13(g) “device” as an add-on to a claim already made against the “crossclaimant” (the party bringing the crossclaim). A defendant could claim against a “codefendant,” and a plaintiff facing a “counterclaim” (a claim back by the defendant) could claim against a “coplaintiff” about the same transaction as that counterclaim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: The court connected that reading to Rule 82’s jurisdictional limits: joining Pennsylvania plaintiffs against a New Jersey defendant did not create federal authority over a separate controversy between those Pennsylvania parties.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: The court tied that reading to Rule 82, which says the procedural rules cannot widen federal courts’ jurisdiction. Joining Pennsylvania “plaintiffs” together against a New Jersey “defendant” did not give the federal court power over a separate dispute between those Pennsylvania “parties,” who are citizens of the same state.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: Independently brought, the proposed claim lacked diversity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: If the Weintraubs had brought the proposed “claim” against the Danners as a separate case, both sides would be from Pennsylvania, so it would lack diversity of citizenship and the federal court could not hear it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: The Third Circuit declined to decide that ground because procedure and jurisdiction sufficed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: The Third Circuit, the federal appeals court, declined to decide whether the claim was filed too late, because the procedural and jurisdictional problems were enough to uphold the dismissal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: It observed that more than two years had passed before crossclaim service and that, if the dismissal were reversed, the Danners could plead limitations under Rule 12.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: The court noted that more than two years had passed before the crossclaim was served. If the “dismissal” were reversed, the Danners could “plead limitations” under Rule 12, meaning formally raise the defense that the deadline for suing (the statute of limitations) had run out.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.sentence: Later textbook questions about collusion and supplemental jurisdiction were not holdings of this court.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-317.plain: Later casebook questions about “collusion” (parties secretly cooperating to manufacture a federal case) and supplemental jurisdiction (federal power to hear related claims) go beyond what this court actually held.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: The trial judge recognized apparent bias but concluded that Colorado Rule of Evidence 606(b) barred the affidavits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: The “trial judge” saw that the juror appeared biased, but concluded that Colorado Rule of Evidence 606(b), which forbids jurors from testifying about deliberations, barred the “affidavits” (the jurors’ sworn written statements).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: The rule ordinarily excludes juror testimony about deliberative statements and mental processes, allowing exceptions for extraneous prejudicial information, outside influence, and a mistaken verdict-form entry.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: The rule normally bars juror testimony about statements in deliberations and jurors’ “mental processes” (how they reached their decision). The exceptions are “extraneous prejudicial information” (harmful information from outside the trial), outside influence on the jury, and a mistake in filling out the verdict form.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Colorado treated those decisions as supporting application of the no-impeachment rule despite the asserted constitutional injury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: Colorado’s courts read those Supreme Court decisions as supporting the “no-impeachment rule,” the rule against using juror testimony to attack (impeach) a verdict, even though Peña-Rodriguez asserted a constitutional injury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: The majority began with the substantial reasons for protecting deliberations: candid discussion, protection against posttrial harassment, finality, and avoidance of routine litigation over jurors’ mental processes.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: The majority began with the substantial reasons for protecting “deliberations,” the jury’s private discussion: frank talk, protection from “posttrial” (after-trial) harassment, finality of verdicts, and avoiding routine lawsuits over jurors’ “mental processes,” meaning their thinking.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Earlier decisions had left room for exceptional cases in which excluding evidence would itself violate basic principles of justice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: Past Supreme Court cases had suggested that, in rare situations, refusing to hear evidence of juror misconduct could itself be fundamentally unjust.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: The majority held that the Sixth Amendment requires the no-impeachment rule to yield when a juror makes an overt statement showing serious racial bias that casts serious doubt on the verdict’s fairness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: The “majority” held that the Sixth Amendment’s right to an impartial jury requires the “no-impeachment rule” to give way when a juror makes an overt (clear) statement showing serious racial bias that casts serious doubt on the verdict’s fairness. Then the court may consider jurors’ testimony about it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Evidence must tend to establish that racial animus was a significant motivating factor in the vote to convict.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: The evidence must tend to show that “racial animus” (racial hostility) was a significant motivating factor in the juror’s vote to “convict,” meaning to find the defendant guilty, not merely a stray remark.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: H.C.’s reported comments met that threshold because they linked stereotypes directly to guilt and urged other jurors to reason the same way.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: H.C.'s reported remarks were serious enough to qualify, because he tied a stereotype about Mexican men directly to his view that the defendant was guilty and urged other jurors to think the same way.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: It expressly left open the procedures for investigating and hearing a resulting motion and the standard for deciding when evidence requires setting aside a verdict.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: The Court expressly left open how trial courts should investigate such claims and run the “hearing” on the resulting “motion” (request to set aside the verdict), and how strong the evidence must be before a verdict is thrown out.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Peña-Rodriguez therefore won access to consideration of the evidence, not an immediate new trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: So Peña-Rodriguez won the right to have the court consider the jurors’ “evidence” about the biased juror, not an immediate new trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Thomas argued that neither the Sixth Amendment’s original understanding nor the understanding associated with the Fourteenth Amendment included a right to impeach a verdict through juror testimony.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: Justice Thomas argued that neither the original understanding of the Sixth Amendment’s jury-trial right, nor the understanding when the Fourteenth Amendment applied it to the states, included a right to “impeach” (attack) a verdict with juror testimony.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Like other legal privileges that exclude relevant evidence to protect institutional relationships, jury secrecy protects candid discussion and durable verdicts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: Justice Alito compared jury secrecy to legal privileges, such as lawyer-client confidentiality, that keep out “relevant evidence” (evidence that bears on the case) to protect important relationships. Jury secrecy likewise protects frank discussion and lasting verdicts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.sentence: Ambiguous comments and posttrial questioning might encourage harassment or coercion and chill deliberations.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-449.plain: Alito worried that “ambiguous” (unclear) comments, plus “posttrial” questioning of jurors, could encourage harassment or “coercion” (pressuring jurors) and chill future “deliberations,” making jurors afraid to speak openly.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.sentence: Avista filed document 105 asking the court to designate the location for a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.plain: Avista filed document 105 asking the court to choose where a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition would take place. In that kind of deposition, an organization must send someone prepared to answer questions on its behalf.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.sentence: It did not describe the underlying insurance claims, identify competing preferred locations or adjudicate substantive liability.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.plain: The order did not describe the underlying insurance “claims,” identify the “locations” each side preferred, or decide “substantive liability,” meaning who was actually legally responsible.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.sentence: It meant review by the issuing district judge, not an appeal described as going to a circuit court.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.plain: The “review” it mentioned meant review by the same “district judge” who issued the order, Judge Presnell, not an appeal to a “circuit court,” the higher federal appeals court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.sentence: Its limited case-management command preserved timing, location and judicial-review constraints, with no separate writing or footnote.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-015.plain: This limited “case-management” order (an order handling the logistics of the lawsuit) kept limits on timing, location and the judge’s power to review, and it had no separate written opinion or footnote.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Marrese filed a similar separate action, which was stayed pending Treister’s appeal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Marrese filed his own similar separate “action” (lawsuit), which was “stayed,” meaning paused, until Treister’s appeal was decided.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: The Illinois Appellate Court directed dismissal of Treister’s complaint, reasoning that Academy membership was not an economic necessity, and the Illinois Supreme Court declined review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: The Illinois Appellate Court ordered “dismissal” of Treister’s “complaint” (the document starting his lawsuit), reasoning that Academy membership was not an economic necessity. The Illinois Supreme Court “declined review,” refusing to hear a further appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Their amended complaint alleged that the Academy possessed monopoly power and excluded them to discourage competition, creating a boycott prohibited by § 1 of the Sherman Act.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Their “amended complaint” alleged that the Academy had “monopoly power” (it dominated its field) and excluded them to discourage competition. They alleged this was a group boycott prohibited by § 1 of the main federal antitrust law, the Sherman Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: The Academy sought dismissal because the state actions concerned the same events and ended with prejudice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: The Academy sought dismissal because the doctors’ state lawsuits involved the same events and ended “with prejudice,” meaning dismissals that barred suing again on those claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: The district court denied claim-preclusion dismissal, reasoning that state courts lacked jurisdiction over federal antitrust claims and could not bar them.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) refused a “claim-preclusion dismissal,” meaning it would not throw out the case on the ground that the earlier state suits already covered it. It reasoned that state courts “lacked jurisdiction” (had no power) over federal antitrust claims, so the state judgments could not “bar” (block) them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: A plurality stressed the available, materially similar Illinois antitrust theory; another judge proposed requiring related claims within a reasonable time, through concurrent suits or a federal action with pendent state claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: A “plurality” of the appeals judges (the largest group, but not a majority) stressed that the doctors could have brought a materially similar Illinois antitrust claim in state court. Another judge would have required related claims to be brought within a “reasonable time,” either in concurrent (parallel) suits or in one federal action with “pendent state claims,” meaning state-law claims added alongside the federal ones.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: The district court initially refused to certify its denial of dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), but later certified the preclusion question while the contempt appeal was pending.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Normally a case cannot be appealed until it ends, but 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b) lets a trial judge approve an early appeal on a key legal question. The district court first refused to do that for its denial of dismissal, but later “certified the preclusion question” (approved an early appeal on whether the state cases barred this one) while the separate appeal from its contempt ruling, a penalty for disobeying a court order, was pending.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: An appeal ordinarily transfers control over the aspects involved in it, but criminal contempt separately vindicates judicial authority.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Once an appeal is filed, the trial court usually loses power over the issues being appealed. But the contempt finding was a separate matter about enforcing the court's authority, so appealing it did not take the whole case away from the trial court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1738, federal courts ordinarily gave state judgments the preclusive effect they received under the rendering state’s law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1738, a federal statute, federal courts ordinarily give a state-court judgment the same “preclusive effect” (power to block later lawsuits) it would have under the law of the “rendering state,” meaning the state whose court issued the judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Exclusive federal jurisdiction over Sherman Act claims did not excuse that first inquiry.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: “Exclusive federal jurisdiction” over Sherman Act claims, meaning only federal courts may hear them, did not excuse that first inquiry. The federal court still had to start by asking what effect Illinois law gives its own judgments.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Only if Illinois law produced a bar should the court consider whether the Sherman Act expressly or impliedly displaced § 1738.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Only if Illinois law would produce a bar (block the claim) should the court ask a second question: whether the Sherman Act, the main federal antitrust law, expressly or impliedly displaced § 1738, that is, created an exception to the usual rule of respecting state judgments.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: A state court might decide an issue important to a later exclusively federal claim, allowing issue preclusion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: A state court might still decide an issue that matters to a later “exclusively federal claim” (one only federal courts can hear). That ruling could then bind the parties through “issue preclusion,” which stops them from relitigating an issue already decided.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Claim preclusion posed a different problem when the first tribunal lacked power over the omitted theory or remedy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: “Claim preclusion,” which blocks a whole claim that could have been raised earlier, posed a different problem when the first “tribunal” (court) lacked power over the omitted theory or remedy. In that situation the plaintiff had no chance to raise it there.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: The Seventh Circuit suggested federal courts could give the state judgments stronger preclusive effect than Illinois would.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: The Seventh Circuit, the federal appeals court covering Illinois, had suggested that federal courts could give the state judgments stronger preclusive effect, blocking more, than Illinois courts themselves would.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: The earlier Migra decision, which remanded to determine the rendering state’s rule, foreclosed that approach.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: The earlier Migra decision ruled out that approach. There the Supreme Court “remanded” (sent the case back) so the lower court could determine the rule of the “rendering state,” the state whose court issued the judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: It distinguished claim-splitting rules between limited and general courts in a single system and observed the usual understanding that litigation under an analogous state statute did not bar a later federal claim outside the state court’s jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: The Court distinguished “claim-splitting” rules, which forbid dividing one claim across lawsuits, as dealing with limited and general courts inside a single system, where the plaintiff could have used a court with full power. It also noted the usual understanding that suing under an analogous (similar) state statute does not bar a later federal claim outside the state court’s “jurisdiction,” its power to hear cases.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: If a virtually identical state cause offered the same theory and remedy, he questioned whether lack of jurisdiction over the federal label necessarily preserved another suit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: Chief Justice Burger questioned whether the state court’s “lack of jurisdiction” (no power) over a claim labeled federal antitrust necessarily preserved the doctors’ right to another suit, if a virtually identical state cause of action offered the same theory and remedy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: Burger favored considering a federal rule, if Illinois law remained ambiguous, asking whether the doctors had a full and fair opportunity to pursue equivalent rights.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: If Illinois law remained “ambiguous” (unclear), Chief Justice Burger favored considering a “federal rule,” a test made by federal courts. It would ask whether the doctors had already had a “full and fair opportunity” to pursue essentially equivalent rights in state court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.sentence: On March 4, 1985 all seven participating Justices reversed and remanded, leaving Illinois law’s application to the district court first.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MARRESE-SC.plain: On March 4, 1985, all seven participating Justices “reversed” (overturned the appeals court) and remanded (sent the case back). That left the district court, the trial court, to work out how Illinois law applied first.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: Mavrix sued Brand and its chief executive, Brad Mandell, in the Central District of California, requesting an injunction and actual and statutory copyright damages.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: Mavrix sued Brand and its chief executive, Brad Mandell, in the Central District of California, the federal trial court in Los Angeles. It asked for an “injunction” (a court order stopping further use of its photos) and for money: actual damages (its proven losses) or “statutory” damages, fixed amounts the copyright law allows without proof of loss.
Brand, an Ohio company, challenged “personal jurisdiction,” arguing that a California court had no power over it at all.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: Reviewing the dismissal anew, the panel required only a prima facie jurisdictional showing because the motion had been decided on written materials.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: The appeals panel was “reviewing” the dismissal “anew,” deciding the question fresh without deferring to the trial judge. Because the “motion” to dismiss had been decided on written materials, not a live hearing, Mavrix needed only a “prima facie” showing: facts that, if true, would support jurisdiction.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: Uncontroverted allegations and disputed facts favored Mavrix at this stage, although bare allegations could not overcome contradicting affidavits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: At this stage, “uncontroverted allegations” (claims Brand did not dispute) were taken as true, and disputed facts were resolved in Mavrix’s favor. But bare allegations, unsupported claims in the complaint, could not overcome contradicting “affidavits,” which are sworn written statements.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: With no applicable federal statute independently authorizing jurisdiction, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(k)(1)(A) pointed to California's long-arm law, which reached the limits of federal due process.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: No applicable federal statute independently gave the court jurisdiction over Brand, so Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 4(k)(1)(A) pointed to California’s “long-arm law,” the state law on reaching out-of-state defendants. That law reaches as far as federal due process allows, so the only question was whether the Constitution permitted jurisdiction.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: General jurisdiction would allow claims unrelated to Brand's California contacts and therefore required a much stronger affiliation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: “General jurisdiction” would let Brand be sued in California on any “claims,” even ones unrelated to its California “contacts” (its activities and ties there). So it required a much stronger affiliation, close to Brand being at home in the state.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: The panel also rejected using the website-interactivity scale associated with Zippo as a substitute for general-jurisdiction analysis.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: The panel also refused to use the website-interactivity scale associated with Zippo, an earlier decision that rates sites by how interactive they are, as a substitute for general-jurisdiction analysis, which asks whether Brand could be sued in California on any claim at all.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: Specific jurisdiction required purposeful direction or availment, a claim arising from or relating to forum activity, and reasonableness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: “Specific jurisdiction,” which covers only claims tied to the defendant’s activity in the state, required three things. Brand must have purposefully directed activity at, or availed itself of, the “forum” (California); the claim must arise from or relate to that activity; and there must be “reasonableness,” meaning hearing the case there is fair.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: Mavrix bore the first two burdens; Brand then had to show a compelling case of unreasonableness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: Mavrix bore the “burdens” (the duty to prove) on the first two points. Brand then had to present a compelling case of “unreasonableness,” showing that being sued in California would be unfair.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: For the tort-like copyright claim, the court used Calder's effects framework: an intentional act, express aiming at the forum, and harm the defendant knew was likely there.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: Because a copyright claim is “tort-like” (similar to a civil wrong such as defamation), the court used Calder’s “effects” test. It asked whether the “defendant” committed an intentional act, engaged in “express aiming” at the “forum” (specifically targeted California), and caused harm it knew was likely to be suffered there.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: Express aiming required more than Internet accessibility; even a passive site might qualify with additional targeted conduct, while passive publication alone would not.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: “Express aiming” required more than a site being reachable on the Internet in California. Even a passive site, one that just displays content, might qualify if the owner also did something targeted at California, but passive publication alone would not.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: The court compared Keeton, where Hustler magazine's deliberate, regular distribution supported jurisdiction over a claim about published content even though those sales did not support general jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: The court compared Keeton, where Hustler magazine’s deliberate, regular distribution of copies in a state supported “jurisdiction” there over a claim about what it published. Those sales still did not support “general jurisdiction,” the power to hear any claim at all against the magazine.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: California-directed advertisements supported an inference that Brand actually or constructively knew of and commercially exploited those users.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: Advertisements aimed at Californians supported an “inference” (a reasonable conclusion from the evidence) that Brand actually knew, or “constructively knew” (should have known), about its California users and commercially exploited them by making money from them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: The court therefore found foreseeable and jurisdictionally significant California injury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: The court therefore found the injury to Mavrix in California “foreseeable” (something Brand could expect) and jurisdictionally significant, meaning it counted toward letting California courts hear the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.sentence: On August 8, 2011, the unanimous panel held that Mavrix had made the prima facie showing necessary for specific jurisdiction over Brand, though general jurisdiction was lacking.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MAVRIX.plain: On August 8, 2011, the “unanimous” panel (all judges agreeing) held that Mavrix had made the “prima facie” showing, enough at this early stage, needed for “specific jurisdiction” over Brand on the photo claim. But “general jurisdiction,” which would allow any claim against Brand in California, was lacking.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Although AT&T customers appeared in the original complaint and AT&T remained in the caption, the operative complaint’s five representatives had been charged Sprint fees.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: AT&T customers appeared in the original complaint, and AT&T remained in the “caption” (the case title listing the parties). But the five named representatives in the operative complaint, the version then in force, had all been charged Sprint fees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Specified claims in California’s Ayyad litigation were excluded, but the release otherwise covered a broad range of fee-related claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Under the “release,” the part of the settlement in which class members give up claims, a broad range of fee-related claims was surrendered. Specified claims in California’s separate Ayyad litigation were excluded.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: The District of New Jersey preliminarily approved the agreement and conditionally certified a Rule 23(b)(3) class in December 2008.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: In December 2008 the District of New Jersey, the federal trial court there, gave the agreement preliminary approval. It also “conditionally certified” (tentatively allowed) a Rule 23(b)(3) class, the type of class action seeking money for members with common claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: The court explained that difficulty identifying everyone did not excuse failing to identify reasonably accessible subsets and ordered another plan.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Being unable to find every class member did not excuse failing to find the groups who could reasonably be located, so the court ordered a new notice plan.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Nevertheless, on January 15, 2010 the district court approved certification and settlement, described notice as robust, and found no antagonism between representatives and class.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Nevertheless, on January 15, 2010, the district court (the trial court) gave final approval to class certification and the settlement. It described the notice as robust and found no antagonism (conflict) between the named representatives and the class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Judge Jordan, joined by Chief Judge McKee and Judge Fuentes, explained that Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires individual notice to every member identifiable through reasonable effort.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Judge Jordan, “joined by” Chief Judge McKee and Judge Fuentes (meaning they signed on to his opinion), explained the notice rule. Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires individual notice to every class member who can be identified through reasonable effort, not just a general published notice.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Although certification and settlement approval receive abuse-of-discretion review, legal error, clearly erroneous findings, or improper application of law can constitute abuse.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Certification and settlement approval get “abuse-of-discretion” review, meaning appeals courts usually defer to the trial judge. But legal error, “clearly erroneous” (plainly mistaken) findings of fact, or improper application of the law can count as an abuse.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: The panel assumed Rice’s declaration was admissible without deciding evidentiary objections or whether those objections had been waived.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: The panel assumed that Rice’s declaration, a sworn statement estimating the cost of searching Sprint’s records, was admissible as evidence. It did not decide the “objections” (challenges) to it or whether those objections had been “waived,” meaning given up by not being raised properly.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Oppenheimer addressed allocation of identification costs rather than eliminating the obligation to obtain available information.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: The Oppenheimer case decided who pays to identify class members; it did not excuse anyone from using records that could identify them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Electronic-discovery proportionality supplied an analogy, not a substitute for Rule 23: the value of identifying absent members was already apparent.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Electronic-discovery “proportionality,” where courts weigh the cost of searching records against the benefit, offered an analogy but not a substitute for Rule 23’s notice rule. The value of identifying absent class members was already apparent.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Adequacy requires both freedom from conflicting interests and the ability and incentive to represent the class vigorously.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: “Adequacy” of the named representatives requires both freedom from interests that conflict with the class and the ability and incentive to represent the class vigorously.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Qualified counsel did not answer that question; counsel’s own adequacy was separately governed by Rule 23(g).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Having qualified “counsel” (lawyers) did not answer whether the named representatives were adequate. The lawyers’ own adequacy was a separate question governed by Rule 23(g).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: The panel did not finally find the representatives inadequate: the objection had been less clearly developed below, and waiver was debatable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: The panel did not finally find the representatives inadequate. The objection had been less clearly developed “below” (in the trial court), and whether it had been “waived,” or given up, was debatable.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: Another objector, Jessica Hall, alleged a reverse auction and challenged charging renewed notice expenses to the fund.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: Another objector, Jessica Hall, “alleged” (claimed, without proof yet) a “reverse auction,” meaning Sprint had settled with whichever class lawyers would accept the least. She also challenged charging the cost of the renewed notice to the class’s settlement fund.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.sentence: The January 15 certification-and-settlement order was vacated and the case remanded; neither Sprint’s underlying liability nor any individual payment was finally adjudicated.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-180.plain: The January 15 certification-and-settlement “order” was vacated (wiped out) and the case “remanded,” or sent back to the trial court. Neither Sprint’s underlying “liability” (whether it broke the law) nor any individual payment was finally “adjudicated,” meaning decided by a court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: In 1954, Hutchinson, Kansas, began condemnation in Reno County district court for street opening, widening, and extension over Lee Walker’s land.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: In 1954 the city of Hutchinson, Kansas, “began condemnation” in the Reno County district court, a proceeding to take Lee Walker’s land for opening, widening, and extending a street. Condemnation is the government’s power to take private property for public use, so long as it pays fair compensation.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: The court appointed three commissioners to value the land and other appropriation damage.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: The court appointed three “commissioners,” people charged with valuing the land and any other “appropriation damage,” meaning loss the taking itself caused Walker.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: He later sought equitable relief, alleging no notice or knowledge until that period expired and requesting restraint against City entry and other appropriate relief.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: Walker later sought “equitable relief,” a court order rather than money. He alleged he had no notice or knowledge of the proceeding until the time to appeal had expired, and asked for “restraint” (an order stopping the City from entering his land) and any other appropriate relief.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: The United States Supreme Court heard the appeal under the then-applicable § 1257(2).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: The United States Supreme Court heard the appeal under the then-applicable § 1257(2), a law then in force that gave a right of appeal when a state’s highest court upheld a state statute against a federal constitutional challenge.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: The majority inferred that the state court treated the pleading as adequately alleging monetary harm from lack of compensation notice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: The majority inferred that the Kansas court had treated Walker’s “pleading” (his written complaint) as adequately “alleging” money harm from the lack of “compensation notice,” meaning notice of the hearing on how much he would be paid.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: Applying Mullane, the earlier decision requiring notice reasonably calculated to inform affected persons, the Court rejected a fixed formula for every circumstance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: The Court applied Mullane, the earlier decision requiring notice “reasonably calculated” to actually inform the people affected. It rejected any fixed formula for every circumstance: what notice is enough depends on the situation.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: The Court reserved how far Mullane had undermined Huling.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: The Court “reserved,” meaning it left undecided, how far its Mullane decision had undermined the older Huling case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: Governmental condemnation did not reduce the owner’s hearing right, and meaningful compensation notice need not obstruct orderly acquisition.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: “Governmental condemnation,” a taking by the government itself, did not reduce the owner’s right to a “hearing” (a chance to be heard). And meaningful notice about compensation need not “obstruct” (block or delay) the orderly acquisition of land.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: A general irreparable-harm allegation following threatened entry did not establish monetary shortfall.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: Walker’s general “irreparable-harm” allegation, a claim that the threatened entry would cause harm that could not be undone, did not establish a monetary shortfall, meaning that he had been paid too little.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: His appendix reproduced the complete amended petition, whose specific prayer sought immediate and permanent restraint and whose general prayer sought other equitable relief.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: Justice Frankfurter’s appendix reproduced Walker’s complete “amended petition” (his revised complaint). Its specific request sought immediate and permanent “restraint” (an order keeping the city off the land), and its “general prayer,” a catch-all request, sought other “equitable relief,” meaning any other fair court-ordered remedy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: Article III demanded an actual particular injury, not abstract constitutional review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: “Article III,” the part of the Constitution that sets up federal courts, demanded an actual, particular injury to the party. It did not allow abstract review of whether a law is constitutional.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: A state could take before payment if adequate compensation arrangements existed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: A state may take land before paying, so long as there is an adequate way for the owner to get compensated.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.sentence: The order did not award more money, void the condemnation, or require the requested permanent injunction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-347.plain: The order did not award Walker more money, “void the condemnation” (cancel the city’s taking), or require the “permanent injunction” he had asked for, a court order keeping the city off his land forever.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: These allegations were assumed true on demurrer.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Foley’s “allegations” (his claims of fact) were assumed true on “demurrer,” the employer’s request to dismiss on the ground that, even if everything Foley said were true, he had no legal claim.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Foley sought compensatory and punitive damages through discharge contrary to public policy, breach of an implied agreement requiring good cause, and tortious breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Foley sought compensatory damages (money for his losses) and “punitive damages” (money to punish) on three theories: discharge contrary to public policy; breach of an “implied agreement,” not put into words, requiring good cause to fire; and tortious breach of the “implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing,” the fairness duty built into every contract, treated as a tort rather than a mere breach.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: The trial court sustained demurrers without leave to amend, and the Court of Appeal affirmed all three.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: The trial court sustained the demurrers, ruling all three claims legally insufficient, “without leave to amend,” meaning Foley could not rewrite his complaint. The Court of Appeal, the intermediate appeals court, affirmed all three rulings.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Chief Justice Lucas explained that Labor Code § 2922’s at-will presumption did not authorize violations of fundamental public policy.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Chief Justice Lucas explained that Labor Code § 2922 creates an “at-will” presumption: a worker can be fired for any reason or none. But that presumption did not authorize firings that violate a fundamental public policy.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Tameny recognized an independent legal duty, exemplified by refusing an employer’s demand to commit a crime, without requiring a job-security contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: The Tameny case recognized an “independent legal duty” on employers, one that exists apart from any contract, for example not to fire a worker for refusing the employer’s demand to commit a crime. No job-security contract was required.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Foley invoked an employee-agent’s duty to relay material business information.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Foley invoked an employee-agent’s duty, as someone acting for the company, to relay “material” (important) business information to it, arguing that firing him for doing so violated public policy.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Parties could agree to dispense with adverse-background reporting about colleagues but could not contract around prohibitions such as perjury or antitrust violations.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Parties to employment could agree to dispense with reporting adverse background information about colleagues, which showed that duty was private. But they could not “contract around” (sign away by agreement) prohibitions such as those against “perjury,” lying under oath, or antitrust violations, which protect the public.
