brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: The job-security allegation was more accurately implied in fact than an express oral promise: Foley relied on conduct and representations rather than particular words establishing good cause.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Foley’s job-security “allegation” was more accurately a contract “implied in fact,” one shown by conduct, than an “express” oral promise made in words. He relied on the company’s conduct and “representations” (statements) rather than particular words establishing that he could be fired only for “good cause.”

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Section 2922 supplied a presumption, not a prohibition on implied discharge limits.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Section 2922 supplied only a “presumption,” a starting assumption that employment is at will. It did not prohibit “implied discharge limits,” unspoken agreements that firing requires good cause.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Services could support multiple promises, including wages and protection against arbitrary dismissal; separate consideration was not invariably necessary.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Foley’s services could support multiple promises from the employer, including his wages and protection against “arbitrary dismissal” (firing for no good reason). Separate consideration, something extra given in exchange for job security, was not invariably necessary.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Postemployment competition and information commitments supplied additional evidence of a continuing relationship, though indispensable extra consideration was not required.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Foley’s commitments about postemployment competition and handing over information were further evidence of a continuing relationship. But extra consideration for job security was not “indispensable,” meaning it was not required.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Civil Code § 1624 applied only where the terms made performance within one year impossible.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Civil Code § 1624, California’s rule that certain contracts must be in writing, applied only where the contract’s terms made “performance” (carrying it out) within one year impossible. A job of indefinite length could end within a year, so an unwritten promise could still be enforced.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: The Court of Appeal’s reliance on Newfield confused anticipated duration and differing termination rights with that test.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: The Court of Appeal, the intermediate appeals court, had relied on an earlier case, Newfield. It confused how long the job was expected to last, and the parties’ differing rights to end it, with the real test: whether the contract could possibly be performed within a year.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: The implied covenant applied to employment contracts, but the majority declined to carry over insurance law’s exception allowing tort damages.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: The “implied covenant” of good faith and fair dealing applied to employment contracts. But the “majority” refused to carry over insurance law’s exception, which allows tort damages, such as punitive damages, for bad-faith breach.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Seaman’s narrow tort involving bad-faith denial of a contract’s existence did not extend to disputes about good cause under an acknowledged agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Seaman’s narrow tort, which covered denying in bad faith that a contract exists at all, did not extend to disputes about whether there was good cause to fire under an admitted agreement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Cleary and related decisions were disapproved insofar as they authorized tort remedies for employment-covenant breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: Cleary and related decisions were “disapproved,” meaning the court rejected them, to the extent they allowed tort damages for “breach” of the good-faith covenant in employment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: On December 29, 1988, the court affirmed the public-policy and tortious-covenant dismissals, reversed the implied-contract dismissal, and remanded.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: On December 29, 1988, the court “affirmed” (upheld) the “dismissals” of the public-policy and tortious-covenant claims. It reversed the dismissal of the implied-contract claim and “remanded” it, sending it back for further proceedings.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.sentence: Prospective versus retroactive application remained reserved because it was neither briefed nor argued.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-094.plain: “Prospective versus retroactive application,” whether the new limit applies only to future cases or also to past ones, was left undecided. No one had “briefed” it (addressed it in written arguments) or argued it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Their output exceeded consultants’ work in bulk, but bulk did not establish which tasks legally constituted engineering.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Amato's team produced more drawings than the licensed consultants, but the amount of paper did not show which tasks counted as 'engineering' under the licensing law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Town Planning sued on the express agreement and alternatively an account annexed for $30,388 calculated under the contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Town Planning sued on the “express agreement” (the written contract) and, as a backup, on an “account annexed,” a simplified Massachusetts claim for money owed on an itemized bill, for $30,388 calculated under the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Amesbury asserted misrepresentation, unsatisfactory work, illegality, and failure of consideration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Amesbury’s defenses were “misrepresentation” (being misled), unsatisfactory work, “illegality” (that the contract or work broke the law), and failure of consideration, meaning it did not get what it bargained for.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: A Superior Court auditor recommended recovery and rejection of repayment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: A Superior Court auditor, a fact-finder appointed by the trial court, recommended “recovery” (payment) for Town Planning and rejection of Amesbury’s demand to get its earlier payment back.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: The Supreme Judicial Court took direct review after appeal was sought in the Appeals Court.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: The Supreme Judicial Court, Massachusetts’s highest court, took direct review after appeal was sought in the Appeals Court, the intermediate court, so it heard the case first.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: The trial judge allowed missing registration as rebuttable evidence of inadequate qualifications or lack of good-faith performance, not conclusive proof of defects.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: The trial judge let Amato’s missing engineering “registration” (license) be used as rebuttable evidence of inadequate qualifications or lack of “good-faith” performance, meaning other evidence could overcome it. It was not conclusive proof that the work was defective.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: General Laws chapter 112, § 81T generally required registration for engineering practice; § 81R(f) permitted corporate practice with a registered engineer or surveyor in charge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: General Laws chapter 112, § 81T, a Massachusetts statute, generally required “registration” (a license) to practice engineering. Section 81R(f) let a corporation practice engineering if a registered engineer or surveyor was in charge.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Amesbury bore the illegality burden without a serious expert effort to classify tasks.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Amesbury bore the burden of proving “illegality,” yet it made no serious expert effort to classify which tasks counted as engineering.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: The contract’s terms were lawful; the assumed problem concerned performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: The contract’s terms were lawful. The assumed problem concerned “performance,” the way the work was actually carried out.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: The scheme protected public safety and made violations misdemeanors, but did not expressly forfeit compensation, unlike the real-estate-broker statute.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: The licensing scheme protected public safety and made violations “misdemeanors” (minor crimes). But unlike the real-estate-broker statute, it did not expressly “forfeit” compensation, meaning take away an unlicensed firm’s right to be paid, so the court had to decide whether to add that penalty itself.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Registration was neither optional nor merely revenue-producing, and lawful contract wording did not categorically immunize illegal performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Registration was neither optional nor merely “revenue-producing,” a rule that exists only to raise fees; it protected the public. And a contract written in lawful words did not automatically shield illegal “performance,” the way the work was actually done.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Total nonpayment would confer a substantial unearned benefit.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: If Town Planning got nothing, Amesbury would keep valuable work for free.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: With material illegality circumstances substantially undisputed, the judge could decide their civil consequences as law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Because the important facts about the “illegality” (the licensing problem) were substantially undisputed, the judge could decide their civil consequences, such as whether they barred payment, as a question of law rather than leaving it to the jury.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.sentence: Reduced quantum meruit could sometimes fit illegality too serious for full contract recovery but insufficient to bar all relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-042.plain: Sometimes a court allows reduced “quantum meruit,” recovery of the fair value of the work instead of the full contract price, where the illegality is too serious for full contract recovery but not serious enough to “bar” (block) all relief.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Gerardus gave a promissory note payable on demand, and Louisa endorsed it at his request as security for the old debt.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Gerardus gave Strong a “promissory note,” a signed written promise to pay, payable whenever Strong demanded. At Gerardus’s request, Louisa endorsed it (signed the back) “as security” for the old debt, making herself answerable if it went unpaid.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: The only asserted new consideration for her undertaking was Strong’s collection arrangement.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: For Louisa’s “undertaking” (her promise to answer for the debt) to bind her, she needed “new consideration,” something given in exchange now. The only thing claimed was Strong’s arrangement about how he would handle collection.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: He appealed under a stipulation permitting judgment absolute against him if that reversal was affirmed.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Strong appealed under a “stipulation,” an agreement between the parties, that if the appeals court affirmed the “reversal” of his win, final judgment would be entered against him instead of a new trial.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Chief Judge Andrews explained that negotiable form did not supply the missing exchange between these original parties.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Chief Judge Andrews explained that the note’s “negotiable form,” meaning it was a transferable commercial document, did not supply the missing bargain between these “original parties,” Strong and Louisa, who had made the deal directly.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Rules protecting a later bona fide holder for value before maturity were irrelevant.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Special rules protect a later “bona fide holder for value,” someone who buys a note in good faith and pays for it before it is due. Those rules were irrelevant because Strong was the original holder.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: A binding promise to delay collection of a presently due debt could support another person’s undertaking for it.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: A binding promise by the creditor to delay collecting a debt that is already due could be the exchange that supports another person’s “undertaking,” or promise, to answer for that debt.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Alternatively, a debtor’s request could invite actual forbearance: if a third party’s undertaking was exchanged for reasonable delay performed in reliance on it, consideration could exist without a binding advance promise by the creditor.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Alternatively, the debtor’s request could invite actual “forbearance” (real waiting): if a third party’s undertaking was given in exchange for a reasonable delay that the creditor actually performed in reliance on it, “consideration,” the required exchange, could exist without the creditor’s binding promise in advance.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Strong expressly reserved collection whenever he wanted the money, leaving no room to imply even a reasonable waiting period.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Strong expressly “reserved,” meaning kept for himself, the right to collect whenever he wanted the money. That left no room for the court to imply even a promise to wait a reasonable time.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: He could sue immediately without breach: that act would merely demonstrate that he wanted payment.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: Strong could sue immediately without any “breach” of his promise, because suing would merely show that he now wanted payment. So he had promised nothing real in exchange.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Interest might indicate expected indulgence but barred no immediate suit on either note or original debt.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: The note carried interest, which might suggest “expected indulgence,” meaning Strong expected to give Louisa time. But interest barred no immediate suit on either the note or the original debt.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Strong’s actual two-year wait did not convert this exchange into a different request-for-performance arrangement.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: That Strong in fact waited two years did not turn the deal into a different kind of bargain, one in which Louisa's promise was given in exchange for actual waiting.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Consideration depended on their chosen agreement rather than Strong’s later discretionary restraint.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: “Consideration,” the required exchange, depended on the agreement the parties chose at the time, not on Strong’s later “discretionary” restraint, meaning the two-year wait he chose freely but never promised.

brief-CT-CB-0098.sentence: Later Uniform Commercial Code treatment of antecedent debt was separate doctrinal development, not an authority Andrews applied.
brief-CT-CB-0098.plain: The later Uniform Commercial Code treats an “antecedent debt” (one that already exists) as enough to support some obligations on notes. That was a separate, later development in the law, not authority Andrews applied.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Dickinson wanted time to decide and gave nothing in exchange for the promise to keep it open.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Dickinson paid nothing for Dodds's promise to hold the offer open, so the promise was not a binding option and Dodds could still withdraw it.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Dickinson sought specific performance against Dodds, an injunction preventing conveyance to Allan, and, if conveyance occurred, an order treating Allan as trustee and requiring him to convey to Dickinson.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Dickinson sought “specific performance,” an order making Dodds complete the sale, and an “injunction” forbidding “conveyance” (transfer of the property) to Allan. If Allan already had it, he asked the court to treat Allan as a “trustee,” holding it for Dickinson, and order him to convey it to Dickinson.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Each demand depended on an enforceable right preceding Allan’s.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Every remedy Dickinson wanted depended on his having an “enforceable” right, one a court would uphold, that came before Allan’s.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: He considered acceptance within the stated period effective and related it back to the original date, so Dodds’s intervening agreement could not defeat Dickinson’s equitable interest.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: The trial judge treated Dickinson’s acceptance within the stated period as effective and as counting from the offer’s original date. So Dodds’s intervening deal with Allan could not defeat Dickinson’s “equitable interest,” a right in the property that a court of equity would protect.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: The additional promise of time lacked consideration.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Dodds’s additional promise to give Dickinson time lacked “consideration,” because Dickinson gave nothing in exchange for it, so the promise was not binding.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: The £800 would support a sale if acceptance occurred while the offer remained open; it did not separately purchase the opportunity to accept until Friday.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: The £800 would support a sale if “acceptance” occurred while the offer was still open. It did not separately buy Dickinson a right to accept until Friday.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Once Dickinson had information equivalent to withdrawal, the messenger’s lack of authority to revoke did not preserve the offer.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Once Dickinson actually knew that Dodds had agreed to sell to someone else, that knowledge worked like a withdrawal of the offer, even though the man who told him, Berry, had no authority from Dodds to revoke it.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Without an enforceable option, the deadline marked the outside time for accepting a continuing offer; it did not protect the offer against earlier withdrawal.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Without an “enforceable option,” a paid-for promise to keep the offer open, the deadline only marked the latest time for “accepting” a continuing offer. It did not protect the offer against earlier “withdrawal” by Dodds.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: His horse-sale and death-of-offeror analogies illustrated that conclusion; his application repeatedly depended on knowledge, rather than a rule that unknown intervening conduct automatically extinguished an offer.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Mellish illustrated his point with examples, such as a horse sale and the death of the person making an offer. But his reasoning kept turning on what Dickinson knew, not on a rule that a sale ends an offer even when the other side has not heard of it.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Mellish explained that a signed land offer could in principle become binding against its signer through verbal acceptance satisfying the Statute of Frauds.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: A sale of land normally needs a signed writing under the Statute of Frauds. Mellish explained that Dodds’s signed offer could in principle bind Dodds, as signer, even if Dickinson’s “acceptance” was only spoken.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: Because Dickinson never formed a binding sale contract, the court did not need to decide priority between two binding purchasers.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: Because Dickinson never formed a binding sale contract, the court did not need to decide “priority,” meaning which of two buyers with binding contracts for the same land wins.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: The Court of Appeal reversed Bacon’s decree and dismissed Dickinson’s bill with costs.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: The Court of Appeal reversed Bacon’s “decree” (the trial judge’s order) and dismissed Dickinson’s bill, his suit, with costs, meaning he had to pay the other side’s legal costs.

brief-CT-CB-0242.sentence: The reporter’s tentative broader suggestion that a sale alone could revoke without notice did not supply the operative holding.
brief-CT-CB-0242.plain: The reporter’s tentative broader suggestion, by the editor who published the case, that a sale to someone else alone could revoke an offer without notice was not the court’s operative holding.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: The terms, updated in May 2013, required binding arbitration of agreement- or service-related disputes, with small-claims and specified intellectual-property exceptions.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: Uber’s terms, updated in May 2013, required binding arbitration, decided by a private arbitrator instead of a court, of disputes about the agreement or the service. Small-claims cases and certain intellectual-property disputes were exceptions.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: They waived jury and class or representative proceedings and chose American Arbitration Association rules.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: Users “waived jury” trial, meaning they gave up that right, and gave up class or representative proceedings, in which one person sues for a group. They also chose the rules of the American Arbitration Association, a major private arbitration organization.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: The district court denied his dismissal motion, later joined Uber as necessary, and discovery began.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) denied Kalanick’s “dismissal motion,” his request to throw out the case. It later added Uber as a necessary party, one the case could not fairly proceed without, and “discovery,” the exchange of evidence, began.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: The court denied their motions for insufficient notice and assent without deciding waiver from litigation conduct or Kalanick’s nonsignatory position.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: The court denied the defendants’ “motions” to compel arbitration, finding Meyer lacked sufficient notice of the terms and did not give “assent” (agreement). It did not decide “waiver,” whether they gave up arbitration by litigating in court, or Kalanick’s position as a “nonsignatory,” someone who did not sign the contract.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: Defendants appealed under FAA § 16, and the action was stayed.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: Defendants appealed under FAA § 16, the part of the Federal Arbitration Act allowing an immediate appeal when a court refuses arbitration. The action was “stayed,” meaning paused, while the appeal went forward.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: An unaware person was not bound by inconspicuous terms whose contractual character was unapparent, but reasonable inquiry notice plus unambiguous conduct could bind without actual reading.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: An unaware person was not bound by “inconspicuous” (hard-to-notice) terms that did not look like a contract. But “reasonable inquiry” notice, terms shown clearly enough that a reasonable person would look, plus “unambiguous” (clear) conduct showing agreement could bind someone who never read them.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: A compel motion used summary-judgment-like treatment of admissible evidence and favorable reasonable inferences for the resisting party.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: A motion to compel arbitration is treated much like summary judgment: the court relies on “admissible evidence” (evidence a court may properly consider) and draws “reasonable inferences” in favor of the “party” resisting arbitration.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: Genuine formation disputes could require a § 4 trial.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: A genuine dispute over whether an arbitration agreement was formed could require a § 4 trial, a trial on that question under section 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: Here no evidentiary trial had resolved contested evidence; screenshots and registration facts were undisputed, so their legal sufficiency received de novo review.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: Here no “evidentiary” trial, one hearing witnesses and evidence, had resolved contested facts. The screenshots and registration facts were undisputed, so their “legal sufficiency” to form a contract received de novo “review,” meaning the appeals court decided it fresh.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: The court also held Kalanick could enforce as a protected employee or disclosed agent of the contracting entity despite not personally signing.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: The court also held that Kalanick could enforce the arbitration agreement, despite not signing it personally, as a protected “employee” or disclosed agent (someone known to act for) of Uber, the contracting company.

brief-CT-CB-0314.sentence: Although other arbitration-waiver issues might go to an arbitrator under cited precedent, a district judge could decide waiver from participation in court proceedings.
brief-CT-CB-0314.plain: Under cited “precedent” (earlier decisions), some arbitration-waiver issues might go to an arbitrator. But a district judge could decide whether a party waived arbitration by participating in court proceedings.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: They gave Dominion Federal a $600,000 secured note.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: They gave Dominion Federal a $600,000 “secured note,” a written promise to repay the loan backed by the property through a mortgage, so the lender could take it if they did not pay.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: A December 30 deed conveyed fee-simple ownership, recited love and respect for the university, identified the mortgage, and expressly required the grantee to assume payment and hold the grantors harmless.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: A December 30 deed conveyed “fee-simple” (full) ownership to the Association and recited love and respect for the university. It identified the mortgage and expressly required the “grantee,” the Association, to assume payment and “hold the grantors harmless,” meaning protect Langman and Stowe from any loss on it.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Langman testified she read it carefully, understood assumption differed from taking subject to debt, and would not donate equity without that protection.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: Langman “testified” (said under oath) that she read the deed carefully and understood that assumption, a promise to pay the mortgage, differed from “taking subject to debt,” taking property the bank could foreclose on while she stayed liable. She would not “donate equity” (give her ownership value) without that protection.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: When the Association denied responsibility, she cured while reserving rights and sued for a declaration.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: When the Association denied responsibility for the mortgage, Langman cured the default (paid what was overdue) while “reserving rights,” making clear she was not giving up her claims. She then sued for a declaration, a court ruling stating who owed the debt.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: After a three-day hearing, the trial court found no knowing acceptance of contractual conditions, mistaken insertion by an unidentified draftsman, and sufficient repudiation.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: After a three-day “hearing,” the trial court found that the Association never knowingly accepted the deed’s contractual “conditions,” meaning the duty to pay. It found the clause was inserted by mistake by an unidentified draftsman, and that the Association had made a sufficient “repudiation” (rejection) of it, so there was no binding “acceptance.”

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Langman appealed use of parol evidence and attempted rejection after more than two years of ownership.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: Langman “appealed,” asking a higher court to review two rulings: the trial court’s use of “parol evidence,” outside evidence offered to contradict a clear written document, and its acceptance of the Association’s attempted rejection after more than two years of ownership.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Its gift recital did not contradict payment: an encumbered portion supplied consideration through assumption, while unencumbered equity could be donated.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: The deed’s gift “recital” (its stated reason) did not contradict payment. The “encumbered portion,” the part of the value tied up in the mortgage, was paid for through “assumption” of the debt, while the unencumbered equity, the value above the debt, could be a gift.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: The error was contradicting an unambiguous instrument through extrinsic intent, not excluding every challenge to validity.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: The trial court’s error was contradicting an “unambiguous” (clear) written instrument through “extrinsic intent,” evidence from outside the document about what people meant. It was not that every challenge to the deed’s validity, such as fraud or mistake, was excluded.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Acceptance could be behavioral, and a beneficial conveyance was presumed accepted absent renunciation.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: “Acceptance” of a deed could be shown by behavior, such as acting as owner. And a beneficial “conveyance,” a transfer that helps the recipient, was presumed accepted unless the recipient renounced (rejected) it.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Those facts could not support timely renunciation of the whole deed while claiming its benefits.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: Those facts could not support a “timely” renunciation, one made soon enough, of the whole deed while the Association kept claiming its benefits.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Virginia Code § 11-2(4) required a signed writing for a promise to answer for another’s default.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: Virginia Code § 11-2(4), part of Virginia’s statute of frauds, required a signed writing for a promise to answer for another person’s “default,” meaning to pay someone else’s debt if they fail to.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: It received a direct benefit and made an original undertaking, rather than merely guaranteeing someone else’s payment.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: The Association received a direct benefit, the property, and made an “original undertaking,” a promise to pay for its own sake, rather than merely guaranteeing someone else’s payment. So no signed writing was needed.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Conflicting proof did not clearly and convincingly establish all elements of actual or constructive fraud.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: The conflicting proof did not “clearly and convincingly,” a demanding standard of proof, establish all the “elements” (required parts) of actual fraud or of “constructive fraud,” which is misleading conduct without intent to deceive.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: Mutual mistake required a shared error.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: “Mutual mistake,” a ground for undoing a contract, required a shared error, meaning both sides were wrong about the same basic fact.

brief-CT-CB-0400.sentence: The trial court had credited Langman’s knowing understanding of assumption, a supported finding defeating mutuality.
brief-CT-CB-0400.plain: The trial court had itself credited Langman’s testimony that she knowingly understood the assumption clause. That was a supported “finding” of fact, and it defeated mutuality: the mistake was not shared by both sides.

cp-lexecon.sentence: That litigation went to Arizona for coordinated pretrial work under 28 U.S.C. § 1407, the multidistrict-litigation statute.
cp-lexecon.plain: That litigation was sent to Arizona for coordinated pretrial work under 28 U.S.C. § 1407, the multidistrict-litigation statute, which lets related federal cases be gathered before one judge for their early stages.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Lexecon then filed a diversity action in the Northern District of Illinois against plaintiff-side law firms Milberg Weiss and Cotchett, Illston & Pitre, alleging malicious prosecution, abuse of process, tortious interference, commercial disparagement, and defamation.
cp-lexecon.plain: Lexecon then filed a “diversity action,” a federal suit allowed because the parties were from different states, in the Northern District of Illinois against plaintiff-side law firms Milberg Weiss and Cotchett, Illston & Pitre. Alleging malicious prosecution, “abuse of process” (misusing court procedures), tortious interference with its business, “commercial disparagement” (false statements hurting its business), and defamation, it sought damages.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Lexecon repeatedly asked Roll to suggest remand to Illinois.
cp-lexecon.plain: Under the Panel’s practice, the Arizona judge first recommends returning a case to its home court. Lexecon repeatedly asked Judge Roll to “suggest remand,” meaning recommend sending the case back to Illinois.

cp-lexecon.sentence: The firms opposed and instead requested that he transfer the action under § 1404(a) to his own Arizona court for trial.
cp-lexecon.plain: The firms opposed and instead asked Judge Roll to transfer the action under § 1404(a), the general transfer statute, to his own Arizona court so he could hold the trial himself.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Cotchett received a separate Rule 54(b) judgment.
cp-lexecon.plain: Cotchett received a separate Rule 54(b) judgment, a final judgment entered on its claims right away even though other claims in the case were still pending.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Lexecon sought Ninth Circuit mandamus to undo self-assignment and secure remand.
cp-lexecon.plain: Lexecon sought “mandamus” from the Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, an extraordinary order directing the judge to undo his “self-assignment” (keeping the case for himself) and to “remand,” or send it back, to Illinois.

cp-lexecon.sentence: It objected to a trial district the MDL statute did not permit the receiving judge to retain over a preserved objection.
cp-lexecon.plain: Lexecon objected to a trial district that the MDL (multidistrict litigation) statute did not let the “receiving judge,” the judge who got the cases for pretrial work, keep over a “preserved objection,” one Lexecon properly raised and kept raising.

cp-lexecon.sentence: But § 1407(a) authorized coordinated or consolidated pretrial transfer and required the Panel to remand every uncompleted action to its original district at or before pretrial proceedings ended.
cp-lexecon.plain: But § 1407(a) authorized transfer only for coordinated or “consolidated” (combined) pretrial work. It required the Panel to “remand,” or send back, every unfinished action to its original district at or before the end of “pretrial proceedings.”

cp-lexecon.sentence: The firms’ attempt to distinguish the Panel’s duty from the judge’s power allowed one statutory actor to disable another’s mandatory obligation.
cp-lexecon.plain: The firms tried to separate the Panel’s duty to send cases back from the judge’s power to keep them. That reading would let one “statutory” actor, someone acting under the statute, disable another’s mandatory obligation.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Lexecon had not waived protection by requesting the judge’s remand suggestion rather than moving directly before the Panel.
cp-lexecon.plain: Lexecon had not “waived” (given up) its protection by asking for the judge’s “remand suggestion” instead of moving directly before the Panel, because that was the expected procedure.

cp-lexecon.sentence: The statute instead referred to termination of the civil action, as by dismissal or summary judgment, not a change of venue label.
cp-lexecon.plain: The “statute” instead referred to termination of the “civil action,” meaning the lawsuit actually ending, for example by dismissal or summary judgment. A change of venue label, relabeling the case as transferred, did not count.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Section 1407(h) expressly authorized trial as well as pretrial transfer for certain Clayton Act actions.
cp-lexecon.plain: Section 1407(h) expressly authorized transfer for trial, not just pretrial work, for certain Clayton Act antitrust actions. That showed Congress knew how to allow trial transfers and did not do so generally.

cp-lexecon.sentence: An ordinary § 1404 transfer after remand might be possible, but ordinary venue limits—unlike § 1407’s broader transfer rules—would still govern.
cp-lexecon.plain: After remand, an ordinary § 1404 transfer to another court might be possible. But ordinary “venue” limits, the rules on where a case may be heard, would still govern, and those are narrower than § 1407’s broader transfer rules.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Milberg urged harmless error because Lexecon could initially have sued in Arizona and identified no independent trial mistake.
cp-lexecon.plain: Milberg urged “harmless error,” meaning the mistake did not affect the result, because Lexecon could have sued in Arizona originally and identified no separate mistake at trial.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Letting the impermissible trial justify itself would erase a substantial statutory venue interest despite a continuously preserved objection.
cp-lexecon.plain: Letting the forbidden trial justify itself would erase a substantial statutory right to have the case tried in its original venue, even though Lexecon kept a “preserved objection,” one it raised continuously throughout.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Caterpillar involved an improper-removal jurisdictional defect cured before judgment.
cp-lexecon.plain: Caterpillar involved an “improper-removal” defect, a case wrongly moved from state to federal court without jurisdiction, that was “cured” (fixed) before judgment. Here the error lasted through trial.

cp-lexecon.sentence: Cotchett’s Rule 54(b) dismissal remained because it was a proper pretrial merits disposition.
cp-lexecon.plain: Cotchett’s Rule 54(b) dismissal, a final judgment entered separately, remained in place because it was a proper pretrial decision on the “merits,” the substance of the claims, which the Arizona judge was allowed to make.

cp-swanson.sentence: The district court dismissed discrimination claims, relying heavily on Latimore v. Citibank, a decision addressing evidence required at summary judgment.
cp-swanson.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) dismissed the discrimination claims, relying heavily on Latimore v. Citibank. That decision addressed the evidence required at summary judgment, a later stage, not what a complaint must say.

cp-swanson.sentence: It initially allowed a generously construed fraud theory, then dismissed that too because the statements were indefinite and reliance unreasonable.
cp-swanson.plain: The court first allowed a fraud theory, “construed” (read) generously from her complaint, then dismissed that too. It said the bank’s statements were too indefinite and her “reliance unreasonable,” meaning she should not have trusted them.

cp-swanson.sentence: She also named Routen as plaintiff and appellant, but as an unrepresented litigant she could not represent her husband.
cp-swanson.plain: Swanson also named her husband, Routen, as a “plaintiff” and appellant. But as an “unrepresented litigant,” someone without a lawyer, she could represent only herself, not her husband.

cp-swanson.sentence: Judge Wood, joined by Chief Judge Easterbrook, recognized that the Supreme Court’s Twombly decision had displaced the notion that any imaginable supporting facts would suffice.
cp-swanson.plain: Judge Wood, “joined by” Chief Judge Easterbrook (he signed on to her opinion), recognized that the Supreme Court’s Twombly decision had displaced the old idea that a complaint survives if any imaginable supporting facts would suffice.

cp-swanson.sentence: But Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8 still required a short, plain statement.
cp-swanson.plain: But Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8, the basic pleading rule, still required only a short, plain statement of the claim, not a detailed account.

cp-swanson.sentence: Erickson emphasized fair notice; Rule 9 and particular statutes separately imposed heightened requirements.
cp-swanson.plain: Erickson emphasized that a complaint must give the defendant fair notice of the claim. Rule 9, which covers claims like fraud, and particular statutes separately imposed “heightened requirements,” meaning extra detail, for some claims.

cp-swanson.sentence: The Court had not silently revived old code fact pleading.
cp-swanson.plain: The Court had not silently revived old code “fact pleading,” the strict system that required complaints to plead detailed facts.

cp-swanson.sentence: Plausibility did not require choosing the most likely account or deciding truth.
cp-swanson.plain: To be 'plausible,' a claim need not be the most likely explanation; at this stage the court is not deciding what really happened.

cp-swanson.sentence: Latimore’s evidentiary requirement nevertheless could not simply become a pleading requirement.
cp-swanson.plain: Latimore’s evidentiary requirement, what a plaintiff must prove at summary judgment, nevertheless could not simply become a “pleading” requirement, something demanded in the complaint at the start.

cp-swanson.sentence: Concerns about costly, asymmetric discovery did not authorize replacing Rule 8 through judicial interpretation; formal rulemaking had a role.
cp-swanson.plain: Concerns about costly, asymmetric discovery, which burdens defendants more, did not authorize judges to replace Rule 8 through interpretation; “formal rulemaking had a role,” meaning changing the rule is a job for the official rule-amending process.

cp-swanson.sentence: Rule 9(b) and substantive fraud law required information that Swanson had not supplied.
cp-swanson.plain: Rule 9(b), which requires fraud to be pleaded with detail, and substantive fraud law, which requires an actual loss from relying on the false statement, demanded information that Swanson had not supplied.

cp-swanson.sentence: He read Iqbal to require examination of obvious innocent explanations in simple as well as complex cases.
cp-swanson.plain: Judge Posner read Iqbal to require judges to weigh obvious innocent explanations for what happened, in simple cases as well as complex ones, when deciding whether a claim is plausible.

cp-swanson.sentence: Each side bore its own appellate costs.
cp-swanson.plain: Neither side had to pay the other's court costs for the appeal.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: Swierkiewicz sued for national-origin discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and age discrimination under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA).
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: Swierkiewicz sued for “national-origin discrimination,” being treated worse because of his Hungarian origin, under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. He also sued for age discrimination under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA).

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: The Second Circuit affirmed under precedent requiring allegations establishing protected-group membership, qualification for the job, an adverse employment action, and circumstances suggesting discrimination.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: The Second Circuit, the federal appeals court, affirmed under its own “precedent” (earlier decisions). That precedent required a complaint to allege membership in a protected group, qualification for the job, an “adverse employment action” (a serious negative job decision, such as firing), and circumstances suggesting discrimination.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: The Supreme Court granted review to resolve a conflict among the circuits over that requirement.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: The Supreme Court “granted review,” agreeing to hear the case, to resolve a conflict among the federal appeals courts (the circuits) over that requirement.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: Its prima facie showing created an evidentiary inference; the Court had not made every component a prerequisite to pleading.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: McDonnell Douglas’s “prima facie” showing, a basic case that, once proved with evidence, lets a court infer discrimination, is a rule about evidence. The Court had not made each part of it a prerequisite for “pleading,” meaning something every complaint must contain.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: Direct evidence could establish discrimination without every element of that framework, and a plaintiff might find such evidence only in discovery.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: “Direct evidence,” such as a boss’s statement of bias, could establish discrimination without every “element” (required part) of that framework. And a “plaintiff” might find such evidence only in discovery, the exchange of evidence after the complaint is filed.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: Requiring more at pleading than might be necessary at trial would be incongruous.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: Requiring more at the “pleading” stage, in the complaint, than a worker might need to prove at trial would be incongruous, meaning it would make no sense.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: The Court applied Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2), requiring a short and plain statement, together with Conley’s then-used fair-notice formulation.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: The Court applied Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2), which requires only a “short and plain statement” of the claim. It paired that with Conley’s then-used formula that a complaint must give the defendant fair notice of the claim and its grounds.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: Rule 9(b) specified fraud and mistake for heightened particularity; employment discrimination and municipal liability under §1983 were not listed.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: Rule 9(b) lists only fraud and mistake as claims needing heightened particularity (extra detail). Employment discrimination and “municipal liability” under §1983, civil-rights suits against cities and other local governments, were not listed.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: Rule 12(e) allowed a more definite statement where needed, and Rule 56 addressed claims lacking merit.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: Rule 12(e) let a defendant ask for a “more definite statement” when a complaint was too vague. Rule 56, the summary-judgment rule, addressed claims lacking merit later in the case.

cp-swierkiewicz.sentence: A new particularity rule had to come through the rule-amendment process.
cp-swierkiewicz.plain: A new “particularity rule” demanding more detail had to come through the “rule-amendment process,” the formal procedure for changing the federal rules, not from judges.

fera.sentence: The developers defaulted, Bank of the Commonwealth took a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and Schostak Brothers managed the property.
fera.plain: The developers “defaulted” (failed to pay their loan). Bank of the Commonwealth took a “deed in lieu of foreclosure,” meaning it accepted ownership of the property instead of going through foreclosure, and Schostak Brothers managed the property.

fera.sentence: The Court of Appeals nevertheless ordered a new damages trial, treating anticipated profits as improper for a new business and this proof as speculative.
fera.plain: The Court of Appeals, Michigan’s intermediate appeals court, nevertheless ordered a new trial on “damages” (the amount of money). It treated expected profits as improper for a new business and this proof as “speculative,” meaning guesswork.

fera.sentence: Chief Justice Kavanagh’s opinion held that a new business could recover anticipated profits if evidence provided a reasonable basis for estimating the loss.
fera.plain: Chief Justice Kavanagh’s “opinion” for the Michigan Supreme Court held that a new business could recover anticipated profits if the evidence gave a reasonable basis for estimating the loss.

fera.sentence: Older distinctions between new and interrupted businesses reflected different proof: an established operation usually had a predictive history, while a new one faced greater difficulty.
fera.plain: Old rules treating new businesses differently from established ones really reflected proof: an existing business has a track record to predict profits from, while a new one does not.

fera.sentence: Uncertainty described the evidence, not an inherently unrecoverable category of profit.
fera.plain: Uncertainty described the “evidence,” which was harder to assemble for a new business. It did not make new-business profit an inherently “unrecoverable” category, one the law forbids.

fera.sentence: Contradictions and impeachment did not eliminate all probative value of the Feras’ evidence.
fera.plain: Contradictions and “impeachment,” attacks on the credibility of the Feras’ witnesses, did not eliminate all “probative value,” meaning the power to help prove a fact, of their evidence.

fera.sentence: The Supreme Court acknowledged that its members might themselves have found the Feras unpersuasive as jurors, but that differed from concluding no reasonable minds could disagree or that the trial judge abused discretion by submitting the issue and denying a new trial.
fera.plain: The Supreme Court admitted its members might themselves have found the Feras unpersuasive as jurors. But that differed from concluding that no reasonable minds could disagree, or that the trial judge abused his discretion by sending the issue to the jury and denying a “new trial.”

fera.sentence: Once some injury was established, inability to measure it precisely did not necessarily defeat recovery, especially when the defendant’s conduct contributed to imprecision.
fera.plain: Once it is clear the plaintiff was harmed, difficulty measuring exactly how much does not bar recovery, especially when the defendant's own wrong made it hard to measure.

fera.sentence: She endorsed the earlier remedy proposed by appellate Judge O’Hara: affirm only if the Feras agreed within thirty days to remit the award above $60,000; otherwise order a new trial.
fera.plain: Justice Coleman endorsed the remedy earlier proposed by appellate Judge O’Hara: “affirm” the verdict only if the Feras agreed within thirty days to “remit the award” (give up the part) above $60,000, or else order a new trial.

fera.sentence: Coleman concurred in part and dissented in part; Levin and Ryan did not participate.
fera.plain: Coleman “concurred in part and dissented in part,” agreeing with some of the decision and disagreeing with some. Levin and Ryan “did not participate,” meaning they took no part in the case.

hassler.sentence: Paragraph C called the restrictions negotiated and reasonable and directed courts to substitute the maximum reasonable restrictions if a term failed.
hassler.plain: The contract declared the limits fair and told any court that found them too broad to rewrite them to the broadest limits the law would allow.

hassler.sentence: On cross-motions for summary judgment, the district court reduced the covenant from twenty-four to twelve months and from seven counties to Natrona and Converse, found Hassler in breach of the revised restriction, and awarded $94,742.10 in projected profit.
hassler.plain: On “cross-motions for summary judgment,” where both sides asked the judge to decide without a trial, the district court shrank the “covenant” (the noncompete promise) from twenty-four to twelve months and from seven counties to Natrona and Converse. It found Hassler in “breach” of the narrowed version and awarded Circle C $94,742.10 in projected profit.

hassler.sentence: Employers could protect legitimate interests against unfair competition, but not suppress ordinary competition.
hassler.plain: Employers could protect “legitimate interests,” such as trade secrets and customer relationships, against unfair competition. But they could not suppress ordinary competition from former employees.

hassler.sentence: Noncompetes were prima facie invalid; employers bore the burden to establish a written employment covenant, reasonable consideration, reasonable time and territory, and consistency with public policy.
hassler.plain: Noncompetes were prima facie invalid, meaning presumed invalid at the outset. The employer “bore the burden” to prove a written employment covenant, reasonable consideration (fair value given for it), a “reasonable time” and territory, and consistency with “public policy,” the public interest.

hassler.sentence: The court distinguished invalidation, deletion of severable language that left a coherent agreement, and substantive rewriting into reasonable restrictions.
hassler.plain: The court distinguished three things: striking the whole noncompete, deleting “severable” language (words that can be cut while leaving a coherent agreement), and “substantive” rewriting into new, reasonable restrictions.

hassler.sentence: Assured judicial narrowing encouraged overbreadth: broad terms deterred mobility, while litigation could still produce an enforceable narrower covenant.
hassler.plain: Guaranteed judicial narrowing encouraged “overbreadth,” noncompetes broader than needed. Broad terms scared workers from changing jobs, while litigation could still produce an “enforceable” narrower covenant, so employers lost nothing by overreaching.

hassler.sentence: Paragraph C could not appoint courts to manufacture a reasonable bargain.
hassler.plain: Paragraph C, the clause directing courts to substitute the maximum reasonable restrictions, could not appoint courts to manufacture a reasonable “bargain” the parties never made.

hassler.sentence: Those defects justified overruling Hopper’s liberal blue-pencil rule.
hassler.plain: Those defects justified “overruling” (expressly abandoning) Hopper’s liberal “blue-pencil” rule, which had let judges freely trim and rewrite unreasonable noncompetes.

hassler.sentence: With those restrictions undisputedly unreasonable and judicial redrafting unavailable, the noncompete was void on public-policy grounds.
hassler.plain: Because the restrictions were undisputedly unreasonable and judicial redrafting was no longer available, the noncompete was void on “public-policy” grounds, meaning unenforceable because it harmed the public interest.

hassler.sentence: Rule 56 therefore permitted relief on the newly dispositive ground.
hassler.plain: Rule 56, the summary-judgment rule, therefore permitted “relief” (a ruling) for Hassler on this newly “dispositive” ground, one that decides the case.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: A vehicle standard controlled the car as manufactured for sale; an equipment standard governed an accessory without necessarily assuring installation in every car.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: A rule for vehicles tells carmakers what every new car must have; a rule for equipment only sets requirements for add-on parts, without ensuring that every car gets one.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: The Automotive Service Industry Association (ASIA) intervened in consolidated review.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: The Automotive Service Industry Association (ASIA) “intervened,” meaning it joined the case as a party, in the consolidated review, where several challenges to the rule were combined.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: In direct court review they also demanded formal Administrative Procedure Act hearings.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: In direct “court review” of the rule, the challengers also demanded formal, trial-like hearings under the Administrative Procedure Act.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Judge McGowan’s unanimous panel identified serious preservation concerns but decided the question because the Government defended the merits and administration of the new law involved a public interest.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: Judge McGowan’s “unanimous” panel (all judges agreeing) identified serious “preservation concerns,” because the objection had not been raised before the agency first. It decided the question anyway, because the Government defended the merits and administering the new law involved a public interest.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Formal §§ 556–557 procedures attach under § 553 when a statute requires rules on the record after an agency hearing.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: Under § 553, the formal, trial-like procedures of §§ 556–557 apply only when a statute requires rules to be made “on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.” Otherwise ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking is enough.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Calling standards “orders” did not turn future general policy into adjudication.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: Even though the statute called the safety standards 'orders,' they were general rules for the future, not case-by-case decisions about particular parties.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Petitioners argued that filing the agency record in court, judicial review, and remand for more evidence required a formal evidentiary hearing.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: “Petitioners,” the challengers, argued that filing the “agency record” (the documents behind the rule) in court, “judicial review,” and remand for more evidence together required a formal evidentiary hearing.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Section 706(2)(E)’s substantial-evidence provision applied to the formal proceedings its text identified, not automatically whenever this statute authorized review.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: Section 706(2)(E)’s “substantial evidence” test applied to the formal, trial-type proceedings its text names. It did not apply automatically whenever this statute authorized court review.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Other § 706 grounds still permitted searching, strict examination of appropriate legislative materials.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: Other § 706 grounds, the APA’s remaining review standards, still allowed a searching, strict examination of the appropriate legislative materials, meaning the rulemaking record.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: APA § 553(c) also required a concise general statement of basis and purpose.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: APA § 553(c) also required a “concise general statement” of the rule’s basis and purpose, a short explanation of why the agency adopted it.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: Reasons need not address every submission or make formal findings on every issue, but must expose major policy choices and why they were made.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: The agency’s reasons need not answer every submitted comment or make “formal findings” on every issue. But they must expose the major policy choices and why the agency made them.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: These were contemporaneous agency reasons supplied through promulgation and reconsideration, not new litigation rationalizations.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: These were contemporaneous agency reasons, given through “promulgation” (issuing the rule) and reconsideration. They were not “litigation rationalizations,” explanations invented later by lawyers for the lawsuit.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: McGowan criticized the inconsistency with their earlier support and demand for speed but also decided the merits alternatively.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: McGowan criticized the challengers for inconsistency with their earlier support for head restraints and their demand for speed. But he also decided “the merits,” the substance of their objections, as an alternative ground.

lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.sentence: On December 27, 1968, Chief Judge Bazelon and Judges McGowan and Robinson unanimously denied the petitions, leaving Standard No. 202 operative.
lrs-n-automotive-parts-boyd.plain: On December 27, 1968, Chief Judge Bazelon and Judges McGowan and Robinson “unanimously” denied the “petitions” for review, the challenges to the rule. That left Standard No. 202, the head-restraint standard, in force.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) could regulate vehicle pollutants reasonably anticipated to endanger health or welfare under Clean Air Act § 202(a)(1), while § 202(a)(2) required time for development and application of necessary technology.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: Under Clean Air Act § 202(a)(1), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) could “regulate” vehicle pollutants reasonably anticipated to “endanger” (threaten) health or welfare. Section 202(a)(2) required giving manufacturers time to develop and apply the necessary technology.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: The final rule retained 0.60 but moved it to 1982 because 1981 certification testing had become impracticable.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: The “final rule” kept the 0.60 grams-per-mile particulate limit but moved it to 1982. “Certification testing,” the EPA testing new models must pass before sale, had become impracticable for 1981.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: EPA incorrectly treated § 202(a)(3)(A)(iii) as a mandatory particulate provision for all light-duty vehicles.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: EPA wrongly treated § 202(a)(3)(A)(iii) as a mandatory particulate (soot) provision covering all light-duty vehicles. That part of the Act actually addressed heavy-duty vehicles.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: Because this administrative record supported that ground, the court declined a remand merely to correct a statutory citation.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: Because the “administrative record,” the documents and evidence before the agency, supported the rule under the correct provision, the court declined a “remand” (sending it back to EPA) just to fix a “statutory” citation.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: Arbitrary-or-capricious review required careful examination of EPA’s explanation without replacing its technical judgment.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: “Arbitrary-or-capricious” review, the test for whether an agency acted unreasonably, required carefully examining EPA’s explanation without replacing the agency’s technical judgment with the court’s.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: Congress contemplated technology forcing: standards could induce advances instead of waiting for completed devices.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: Congress contemplated “technology forcing”: standards could push industry to invent advances instead of waiting until completed “devices,” such as finished pollution traps, already existed.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: Lead time created uncertainty, offered opportunity to make theoretical solutions practical, and allowed later adjustment before irrevocable production commitments.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: “Lead time,” setting the rule years before it took effect, created uncertainty. But it also gave a chance to make theoretical solutions practical, and allowed EPA to adjust the rule before manufacturers made irrevocable production commitments.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: General Motors’ statements that compliance might be possible reinforced, without estopping, its challenge.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: General Motors’ own statements that compliance might be possible reinforced EPA’s position. But they did not end up “estopping” GM, meaning legally barring it from challenging the rule.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: The agency reasonably read the long-term air-quality condition to ask whether a substantial likelihood existed that engines would meet applicable standards after waiver.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: A waiver could not threaten long-term air quality. The “agency” reasonably read that condition to ask whether there was a substantial likelihood the engines would meet the applicable standards after the waiver ended.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: Its deference belongs to the historical 1981 framework.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: The court’s “deference,” its willingness to accept the agency’s reading of the statute, belongs to the historical 1981 framework, which has since changed.

lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.sentence: A separate challenge involving California nitrogen-oxide requirements and the 1982 particulate standard remained in abeyance and was not decided.
lrs-n-nrdc-epa-1981.plain: A separate challenge involving California’s nitrogen-oxide requirements and the 1982 particulate standard remained “in abeyance,” meaning on hold, and was not decided.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: In Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm in 1983, the Supreme Court held the explanation inadequate and required reconsideration.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: In Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm in 1983, the Supreme Court held the agency’s explanation for canceling the automatic-restraint rule inadequate and required “reconsideration,” sending the matter back for the agency to think again.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: The rule also included a contingent rescission provision, called the trap door.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: The rule also included a “contingent rescission” provision, called the trap door: the automatic-protection requirement would be canceled if a condition was met, namely states covering two-thirds of the population passing qualifying seatbelt-use laws.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: It also needed a minimum $25 penalty for each violator, use of violations in mitigation of civil damages, compliance promotion, and evaluation.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: A qualifying state law also needed a minimum $25 fine for each violator and use of violations “in mitigation of civil damages,” meaning courts could reduce an injured person’s damages for not buckling up. It also needed programs promoting compliance and evaluating results.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: They contended that rescission lacked a rational basis: the Department had not adequately considered keeping both state usage laws and federal passive restraints, justified a two-thirds population substitute, or explained the waiver rule.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: They argued that rescission lacked a “rational basis,” a sensible justification. The Department had not adequately considered keeping both state seatbelt-use laws and federal “passive restraints” (automatic protection like airbags), justified the two-thirds population trigger, or explained its waiver rule.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: Judge Starr, joined by Judge Scalia, applied Abbott Laboratories’ inquiry into fitness for judicial decision and hardship from delay.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: Judge Starr, “joined by” Judge Scalia, applied the Abbott Laboratories’ ripeness test: “fitness for judicial decision,” whether the issue was ready for a court to decide, and hardship to the challengers from delay.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: Fitness included finality and legal character but also the value of a concrete setting and whether adjudication might prove unnecessary.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: An issue is fit for decision when the agency's action is final and the question is legal, but courts also consider whether real facts would help and whether the issue may never arise.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: The threatened deaths depended on actual rescission, and petitioners could seek review and a stay if that became imminent.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: The threatened deaths depended on “actual rescission,” the rule really being canceled. If that became “imminent” (about to happen), the petitioners could seek review and a “stay,” an order blocking it.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: Insurers’ uncertainty about lobbying for strong state laws while retaining federal restraints was insufficient planning uncertainty, unlike Abbott’s immediate compliance costs and civil or criminal exposure.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: Insurers’ uncertainty about “lobbying” states for strong seatbelt laws while keeping federal restraints was not enough planning hardship. In Abbott, by contrast, the challengers faced immediate compliance costs and possible civil or criminal penalties.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: A statutory sixty-day filing period required timely petitions but did not require immediate adjudication of unripe issues.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: A “statutory” sixty-day filing period required “timely” petitions, filed within the deadline. But it did not require the court to decide “unripe” issues, ones not yet ready for decision, immediately.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: The majority noted constitutional and prudential roots of ripeness without locating a precise boundary between them.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: The “majority” noted that ripeness has constitutional roots and “prudential” roots (courts’ own good-sense policies), without fixing a precise boundary between them.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: The permitted devices were fixed, needed no further agency action or factual development, and affected current production in the phase-in.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: The challenge to the permitted safety devices was ripe: the choices were fixed, needed no further “agency action” or factual development, and already affected current production in the “phase-in,” the gradual rollout of the requirement.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: Under the Act and Administrative Procedure Act § 706(2)(A), the agency had to connect facts and policy choice through a satisfactory explanation.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: Under the safety Act and Administrative Procedure Act § 706(2)(A), the agency had to connect the facts it found to its policy choice through a satisfactory explanation.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: Courts could not invent reasons or substitute a preferred technology, but could follow a reasonably discernible path.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: Courts could not invent reasons or substitute a technology they preferred. But they could uphold an imperfect explanation if the agency’s “reasonably discernible path” of reasoning could be followed.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: New York proposed solutions, but the court found no clear error of judgment.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: New York proposed alternative solutions, but the court found no “clear error of judgment,” meaning the agency’s choice was not plainly unreasonable.

lrs-n-state-farm-dole.sentence: It dismissed every other petition and the remainder of New York’s as unripe.
lrs-n-state-farm-dole.plain: The court “dismissed” every other “petition,” and the remainder of New York’s, as “unripe,” meaning not yet ready for decision; they could be brought later if the rule were actually canceled.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Existing Part 15 rules allowed some unlicensed devices if emissions lacked significant potential for harmful interference.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Existing Part 15 rules, the FCC’s rules for unlicensed devices, allowed some devices to operate without a license if their emissions lacked significant potential for “harmful interference” with licensed radio users.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Using twenty instead would yield a higher estimated emission level at the regulatory measurement distance.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Using twenty instead would assume signals fade more slowly with distance, yielding a higher estimated emission level at the “regulatory” measurement distance, the distance where the rules measure signals.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: FCC called withheld sections preliminary results or deliberative opinions and denied relying on those portions.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: The FCC called the withheld sections preliminary results or “deliberative opinions,” internal staff views offered while a decision is being made, and denied relying on those portions.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Judge Rogers’s opinion applied Administrative Procedure Act (APA) review, allowing substantial technical deference while requiring a discernible connection between facts and choices.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Judge Rogers’s “opinion” applied Administrative Procedure Act (APA) review. It gave substantial technical “deference” (weight to the agency’s expertise) while still requiring a discernible connection between the facts and the agency’s choices.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Applying Portland Cement’s technical-disclosure precedents under APA § 553, the court reviewed unredacted pages in camera and found test-data summaries, scientific recommendations, and methodology analysis.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Applying Portland Cement’s precedents requiring disclosure of technical studies under APA § 553, the court “reviewed” the unredacted pages “in camera,” privately in chambers. It found test-data summaries, scientific recommendations, and analysis of methods, not mere opinions.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: The League also showed prejudice by identifying useful comments on recommendations and methods, including material about new information urging caution and spectrum tradeoffs.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: The League also showed “prejudice,” meaning the secrecy actually hurt it, by identifying useful comments it could have made on the recommendations and methods, including material about new information urging caution and spectrum tradeoffs.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: EchoStar differed because its study was available before reconsideration and withheld staff thoughts addressed already disclosed evidence without a timely record objection.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: EchoStar came out differently: its study was available before the agency’s “reconsideration,” and the withheld staff thoughts addressed evidence already disclosed, with no “timely” (made in time) objection on the record.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: The Freedom of Information Act’s deliberative-process privilege did not justify blanket secrecy for scientific facts adopted or incorporated into public action.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: The Freedom of Information Act’s deliberative-process privilege, which protects internal opinions and drafts, did not justify blanket secrecy for scientific facts the agency adopted or relied on in its public action.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Rogers treated disclosure as enforcing the selected notice-and-comment process, not an additional procedural device prohibited by Vermont Yankee.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Vermont Yankee bars courts from adding procedures beyond the APA. Rogers treated disclosure as enforcing the “notice-and-comment” process the agency chose, where the public sees a proposal and comments, not an extra procedural “device.”

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Tatel separately relied on APA § 706’s whole-record requirement.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Judge Tatel separately relied on APA § 706’s “whole-record requirement,” which directs courts to review the agency’s entire record, so parts of it cannot be hidden.

lrs-o-american-radio.sentence: Judge Kavanaugh agreed that circuit precedent compelled disclosure but thought Portland Cement lacked § 553 textual support and conflicted with Vermont Yankee’s limits on added judicial procedures.
lrs-o-american-radio.plain: Judge Kavanaugh agreed that “circuit” precedent, earlier decisions of this appeals court, compelled disclosure. But he thought Portland Cement lacked support in § 553’s text and conflicted with Vermont Yankee’s limits on courts adding procedures.
The court “ordered” no vacatur, meaning it did not cancel the rules; they stayed in effect while the FCC fixed the problems.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The Act’s special procedure allowed a district court to certify constitutional questions to the D.C. Circuit sitting en banc, followed by direct Supreme Court appeal.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The Act’s special procedure let the district court (the trial court) certify, or send, constitutional questions to the D.C. Circuit sitting en banc, with all its judges, followed by a “direct Supreme Court appeal.”

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: That ripeness conclusion rested on concrete interests, not elimination of Article III injury.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: That “ripeness” conclusion, that the case was ready for decision, rested on “concrete” (real, specific) interests of the plaintiffs. It did not eliminate Article III’s requirement of actual injury.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Giving money expresses support and association, while translating the contribution into further communication generally involves the recipient’s speech.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: Giving money to a candidate shows support, but it is the candidate who turns that money into speech. So limiting donations restricts the donor's own expression less than limiting spending does.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Preventing actual or apparent quid pro quo corruption was sufficiently important, and these limits were closely drawn.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: Preventing actual or apparent “quid pro quo corruption,” money given in exchange for official favors, was a sufficiently important goal. And the contribution limits were “closely drawn,” meaning tailored narrowly to serve it.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Higher allowances for established committees and the individual annual ceiling served anticircumvention purposes.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The higher allowances for established political committees and the individual $25,000 annual ceiling served “anticircumvention” purposes, stopping donors from evading the per-candidate limits, for example by routing money through others.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The Court construed the independent-spending provision to concern express advocacy of a clearly identified candidate’s election or defeat, avoiding vagueness, but invalidated even that narrowed restriction.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The Court “construed” (interpreted) the independent-spending limit to cover only “express advocacy,” ads explicitly urging a clearly identified candidate’s election or defeat, so it would not be too vague. But it then struck down even that narrowed restriction.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Genuine independence lacked the prearrangement that made coordinated or authorized spending contribution-like; coordinated spending remained subject to contribution limits.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: Genuinely independent spending lacked the prearrangement with a campaign that made coordinated or authorized spending like a donation. So “coordinated spending” remained subject to the “contribution limits,” the caps on donations.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Disclosure survived exacting scrutiny as construed because it informed voters about financial support, exposed potential corruption, and assisted contribution-limit enforcement.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: As narrowly construed, the disclosure rules survived “exacting scrutiny,” a demanding constitutional test. They informed voters about who funded candidates, exposed potential corruption, and helped enforce the contribution-limit rules.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Political committees were construed as candidate-controlled bodies or organizations with candidate nomination or election as their major purpose.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: To avoid vagueness, the Court construed “political committees” to mean groups controlled by a candidate or organizations whose “major purpose” is nominating or electing candidates.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The Court also sustained presidential public financing against the facial challenge.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The Court also “sustained” (upheld) public financing of presidential campaigns against the facial challenge, the claim that the law was unconstitutional in every application.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The Court held that anyone exercising significant federal statutory authority is an officer subject to the Appointments Clause.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The Court held that anyone exercising significant federal “statutory authority,” power given by law, is an officer of the United States. Such a person must be appointed as required by the Appointments Clause.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Principal officers require presidential nomination and Senate advice and consent; Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the President alone, a court of law, or a department head.
