lrs-s-buckley.plain: “Principal officers,” top officials, require nomination by the President and the Senate’s “advice and consent,” its approval. Congress may give appointment of inferior (lower) officers to the President alone, a “court of law,” or a department head.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Four originated with congressional officers who were neither courts nor department heads; the President’s two selections improperly required House confirmation as well as Senate confirmation.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: Four commissioners were picked by congressional officers, who were neither courts nor “department heads,” so they could not appoint officers. The President’s two picks were also improper because they required confirmation by the House as well as the Senate.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The Court distinguished appointment from removal and supervision.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The Court kept two questions apart: who may appoint an official, and who may fire or direct one. This case decided only the first.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Quasi-legislative or quasi-judicial work did not put a federal agency outside the Appointments Clause.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: “Quasi-legislative” work (resembling lawmaking) or quasi-judicial work (resembling judging) did not put a federal agency outside the Appointments Clause; its members still had to be properly appointed.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: Civil-enforcement suits were different: seeking judicial relief to vindicate public rights executed the law.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: “Civil-enforcement” suits were different: seeking judicial “relief” (a court remedy) against violators to vindicate public rights is executing the law, which only properly appointed officers may do.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The mandate issued forthwith except that the judgment affecting Commission powers was stayed for no more than thirty days.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: “The mandate issued” forthwith, meaning the decision took effect immediately. The exception was the “judgment” limiting the Commission’s powers, which was “stayed” (put on hold) for no more than thirty days.

lrs-s-buckley.sentence: The Court accorded de facto validity to past Commission acts and temporarily permitted continued functioning so Congress could reconstitute the agency or establish valid enforcement arrangements.
lrs-s-buckley.plain: The Court gave “de facto validity” to the Commission’s past acts, treating them as valid in practice. It let the “agency” keep working temporarily so Congress could reconstitute it or set up valid enforcement arrangements.

morris-sparrow.sentence: Sparrow filed in chancery for specific performance, and the chancellor ordered Morris to deliver Keno.
morris-sparrow.plain: Sparrow filed in “chancery,” the court of equity, seeking specific performance, an order to hand over the horse itself. The “chancellor,” the equity judge, ordered Morris to deliver Keno.

morris-sparrow.sentence: It found no basis to deem the determination for Sparrow against the preponderance of evidence.
morris-sparrow.plain: The Arkansas Supreme Court found no basis to say the finding for Sparrow went against the “preponderance of evidence,” meaning the greater weight of the evidence.
Entitlement, whether Sparrow was owed the horse, and “remedy,” what the court should order to fix the broken promise, remained separate questions.

morris-sparrow.sentence: Justice Robinson accepted that damages ordinarily remedied a promise to deliver personal property but found special circumstances.
morris-sparrow.plain: Justice Robinson accepted that “damages” (money) were the ordinary remedy for a broken promise to deliver “personal property,” movable things like a horse. But he found “special circumstances” justifying an order to deliver Keno himself.

morris-sparrow.sentence: Arkansas Statutes § 68-1468 further authorized equity to order delivery of specific or ascertained goods when appropriate.
morris-sparrow.plain: Arkansas Statutes § 68-1468, a sales statute, further let “equity” courts order delivery of “specific or ascertained goods,” meaning particular, identified items, when appropriate.

morris-sparrow.sentence: Accord and satisfaction required acceptance of a proposed settlement, not merely words on a check divorced from context.
morris-sparrow.plain: “Accord and satisfaction,” settling a dispute by accepting a payment offered as full settlement, required actual acceptance of the proposed settlement. Words on a check, read apart from their context, were not enough.

morris-sparrow.sentence: The court acknowledged that a disputed money amount knowingly tendered and accepted in full settlement could differ.
morris-sparrow.plain: If the amount of money owed had been disputed and Sparrow knowingly accepted a check offered as full settlement, the result might have been different.

xlo.sentence: X.L.O. sued for breach, account stated, and unjust enrichment.
xlo.plain: X.L.O. sued for breach of contract, “account stated” (that Rivergate had accepted the bill as correct and owed it), and unjust enrichment, meaning Rivergate would unfairly profit from unpaid work.

xlo.sentence: Rivergate asserted an antitrust defense and counterclaim under New York’s Donnelly Act, a Sherman Act damages counterclaim, and contractual fees and costs.
xlo.plain: Rivergate raised an antitrust defense and a “counterclaim” (its own claim back against X.L.O.) under New York’s Donnelly Act, a state antitrust law. It also sought “damages” in a Sherman Act counterclaim and contractual fees and costs.

xlo.sentence: X.L.O. moved to dismiss the first two counterclaims as untimely; Rivergate cross-moved to dismiss the complaint.
xlo.plain: X.L.O. “moved to dismiss” the first two “counterclaims” as untimely, filed too late. Rivergate “cross-moved,” asking in turn to dismiss X.L.O.’s “complaint.”

xlo.sentence: The Appellate Division reinstated the complaint and counterclaims to the extent of its demand.
xlo.plain: The Appellate Division, the intermediate appeals court, reinstated X.L.O.’s “complaint” and let Rivergate’s counterclaims proceed only up to the amount X.L.O. demanded, as an offset against it.

xlo.sentence: Kelly and related antitrust precedents warned against giving buyers completed performance for nothing.
xlo.plain: Kelly and related antitrust precedents warned against letting buyers keep completed “performance,” finished work, for nothing just by raising an antitrust defense.

xlo.sentence: The boundary was whether judgment would enforce the precise prohibited conduct or merely a lawful obligation collateral to it.
xlo.plain: The line was whether a “judgment” for X.L.O. would enforce the precise prohibited conduct itself, or merely a lawful obligation collateral to it, meaning only connected to it.

xlo.sentence: A trial had to determine whether payment was an indivisible component effectuating the conspiracy so that enforcement would consummate the forbidden restraint.
xlo.plain: A trial had to decide whether payment was an “indivisible” component, an inseparable part, that carried out the “conspiracy,” so that enforcing it would complete the “forbidden restraint” on competition.

xlo.sentence: An inflated, discriminatory price caused by suppressed competition might mean that collecting the promise implemented the restraint rather than merely followed it.
xlo.plain: If suppressed competition produced an inflated, discriminatory price, collecting on the promise might mean the court “implemented the restraint,” carrying out the illegal scheme rather than merely following it.

xlo.sentence: Further proceedings also needed to address forfeiture and unjust enrichment, the parties’ comparative culpability, knowledge, and bargaining power, and whether denying contractual recovery would still allow quantum meruit for reasonable value.
xlo.plain: Further proceedings also had to address “forfeiture” (X.L.O. losing all payment) and unjust enrichment; the parties’ comparative blame, knowledge, and “bargaining power”; and whether denying “contractual” recovery would still allow “quantum meruit,” payment of the work’s reasonable value.

xlo.sentence: The substantial policy against the Club operated alongside statutory remedies and the Attorney General’s direct enforcement authority, reducing the need for automatic total forfeiture in every related collection action.
xlo.plain: The strong policy against the Club worked alongside “statutory” remedies and the Attorney General’s direct enforcement power. That reduced the need for automatic total “forfeiture” of payment in every related “collection action,” a suit to collect money owed.

xlo.sentence: The court affirmed the Appellate Division order with costs and answered the certified question affirmatively.
xlo.plain: The court “affirmed” (upheld) the Appellate Division “order,” with costs. It answered “yes” to the “certified question,” the legal question the lower court had sent up for review.

brief-CP-148.sentence: The Eleventh Circuit reversed, concluding that nonparties’ claims could not be barred simply because the decisions implemented earlier judgments.
brief-CP-148.plain: The Eleventh Circuit, the federal appeals court, reversed. It concluded that “nonparties’” claims could not be “barred” (blocked) simply because the city’s decisions carried out earlier “judgments” in a case they were not part of.

brief-CP-148.sentence: Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justices White, O’Connor, Scalia, and Kennedy, began with the ordinary rule that an in personam judgment does not bind a nonparty.
brief-CP-148.plain: Chief Justice Rehnquist, “joined by” Justices White, O’Connor, Scalia, and Kennedy, began with the ordinary rule that an “in personam” judgment, one against particular people, does not bind a “nonparty,” someone who was not part of the case.

brief-CP-148.sentence: Appropriate representation and special statutory proceedings can supply recognized exceptions, but mere knowledge and an opportunity to intervene do not.
brief-CP-148.plain: Proper representation by a party and special statutory proceedings can supply recognized exceptions. But merely knowing about a lawsuit and having the chance to “intervene” (join it as a party) do not.

brief-CP-148.sentence: Litigants seeking to bind affected people ordinarily had to secure joinder under the applicable rules.
brief-CP-148.plain: “Litigants,” the parties, who want to bind affected people ordinarily must secure their “joinder,” formally bringing them into the case as parties under the applicable rules.

brief-CP-148.sentence: Simply describing decree compliance as substantive justification rather than preclusion did not cure a rule that defeated an otherwise valid claim solely through another person’s judgment.
brief-CP-148.plain: Calling obedience to the decree a “substantive” defense on the merits, instead of “preclusion” (being barred by an earlier judgment), changed nothing. Either way, a valid claim was defeated solely through another person’s judgment.

brief-CP-148.sentence: It preserves due process and exceptions including fraud, collusion, transparent invalidity, and absence of subject-matter jurisdiction.
brief-CP-148.plain: The 1991 law still preserves “due process,” constitutional fairness, and allows challenges for fraud, collusion, transparent “invalidity” (a plainly invalid decree), or lack of “subject-matter jurisdiction,” the court’s power to hear that kind of case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.sentence: Notice to him was by publication alone.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.plain: Notice to the husband was “by publication” alone, a notice printed in a newspaper rather than personal delivery.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.sentence: The resident bank’s debt to its nonresident depositor counted as such property.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.plain: A bank deposit is legally a debt the bank owes its depositor. Because the bank was in Ohio, its debt to its “nonresident” depositor, the husband living outside the state, counted as property there that the court could act on.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.sentence: Publication did not confer personal jurisdiction, but attachment or garnishment could apply seized property to an obligation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.plain: Newspaper notice did not give the court “personal jurisdiction,” the power to order the husband himself to pay. But “attachment” or “garnishment,” seizing his property in the state, could apply that property to his obligation.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.sentence: A claim could be contested, unliquidated or inchoate and still be determined as part of the property proceeding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.plain: A claim could be contested, “unliquidated” (of an amount not yet fixed), or inchoate (not yet fully formed) and still be decided as part of the case about the seized property.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.sentence: The opening injunction immobilized the deposit as effectively as conventional garnishment or trustee process; equity could reach property not available to legal attachment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.plain: The opening “injunction,” a court order freezing the deposit, held it as effectively as ordinary garnishment or trustee process. A court of equity could reach property that legal “attachment,” the ordinary seizure procedure, could not.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.sentence: The alimony decree validly charged the deposit but did not create a publication-based personal judgment collectible from the husband’s other assets.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-063.plain: The alimony order could lawfully be paid out of the frozen deposit. But it was not a personal judgment against the husband, so his wife could not collect it from his other property.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: Nixon publicly released edited transcripts of forty-three conversations on April 30, including portions of twenty subpoenaed conversations, but made a special appearance on May 1 to seek to quash the subpoena on executive-privilege grounds.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: On April 30 Nixon publicly released edited transcripts of forty-three conversations, including parts of twenty subpoenaed ones. On May 1 he made a “special appearance,” coming to court only for a limited purpose, seeking to “quash” (cancel) the subpoena on executive-privilege grounds.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: A recipient must refuse compliance, be held in contempt, and appeal that judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: Usually, someone who wants to challenge a subpoena must disobey it, be found in contempt of court, and then appeal that contempt finding, which counts as a final judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: Requiring deliberate disobedience merely to obtain appellate review would generate an unnecessary constitutional confrontation and delay an approaching criminal trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: Requiring the President to deliberately disobey a court order merely to obtain “appellate” review, a hearing by a higher court, would create an unnecessary constitutional clash and delay the approaching criminal trial. So the Court treated the order as appealable now.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: Nixon argued that a disagreement between two Executive Branch officials was not justiciable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: Nixon argued that a disagreement between two Executive Branch officials, the President and his own prosecutor, was not “justiciable,” meaning not the kind of dispute a court can decide.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: Congress had vested criminal litigation authority in the Attorney General, who delegated power through an operative regulation authorizing the Special Prosecutor to seek evidence, contest executive privilege, and exercise substantial independence with special removal protections.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: Congress had given authority over criminal cases to the Attorney General. He delegated power through a binding regulation letting the Special Prosecutor seek evidence, contest executive privilege, and act with substantial independence, backed by special “removal protections” limiting when he could be fired.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: Rule 17(c) obtains evidentiary material before trial; it is not a general criminal-discovery device.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: Rule 17(c) is a tool for obtaining specific evidence before trial. It is not a general “criminal-discovery” device for searching broadly through the other side’s files.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: The materials could include admissible party statements or coconspirator declarations, subject to the requirements for those uses.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: The tapes could include “admissible” (usable at trial) statements by the defendants themselves or “coconspirator declarations,” statements by members of the alleged conspiracy made to further it, if the requirements for those uses were met.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.sentence: The Court held that the trial’s demonstrated evidentiary need prevailed, while expressly reserving civil litigation, congressional demands, and preservation of state secrets.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-499.plain: The Court held that the trial’s demonstrated, specific need for evidence outweighed the President’s general interest in confidentiality. It expressly left open civil lawsuits, demands from Congress, and protection of “state secrets” such as military or national-security information.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: It rejected the claim that Mille Lacs repudiated Race Horse, treated Repsis as binding Herrera through his membership in the Tribe, and also considered the forest occupied.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: The state court on appeal held that Mille Lacs had not rejected Race Horse, that the 1995 Repsis judgment bound Herrera because he was a member of the Tribe that sued, and that the forest was 'occupied' anyway.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: Mille Lacs undermined both: treaty rights could coexist with state sovereignty because necessary, reasonable, nondiscriminatory conservation rules could apply, and abrogation required clear congressional intent or a treaty-specified endpoint.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: Mille Lacs undermined both reasons. Treaty rights could coexist with “state sovereignty” (the state’s own power) because necessary, reasonable, even-handed conservation rules could still apply, and “abrogation” (ending a treaty right) required clear “congressional intent” or an end point set in the treaty itself.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: Mille Lacs had not expressly overruled Race Horse, but the majority found the reasoning irreconcilable and formally repudiated implied extinguishment at statehood.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: Mille Lacs had not expressly overruled Race Horse, but the “majority” found the reasoning irreconcilable. So it formally “repudiated” (rejected) the idea that statehood silently extinguished the treaty right.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: Issue preclusion ordinarily bound actually litigated, resolved, essential issues in a valid judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: “Issue preclusion” ordinarily binds the parties on issues that were actually litigated, decided, and essential to a valid judgment, so they cannot be argued again in a later case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: Bies, Limbach, Sunnen, Montana, and Restatement principles recognized an exception for an intervening change in the governing legal context.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: Bies, Limbach, Sunnen, Montana, and Restatement principles recognized an exception for an “intervening change,” meaning a significant change in the governing law after the earlier ruling.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: It read the judgment below as applying preclusion to statehood alone, considered the alternative question outside the grant, and noted unresolved gateways such as full and fair litigation and possible forfeiture.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: The Court read the state court’s “judgment” as applying “preclusion” only to the statehood issue. It treated the alternative occupied-land question as outside what it agreed to review, and noted unresolved threshold issues, such as whether that question was fully and fairly litigated and whether the argument was forfeited.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: He favored preclusive effect for both independently sufficient grounds, as the First Restatement recommended rather than the Second.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: Justice Alito favored giving “preclusive effect” (binding force in later cases) to both “independently sufficient grounds,” two separate reasons each enough to support the judgment, as the First Restatement recommended rather than the Second.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.sentence: He distinguished preclusion of an offense element from the treaty affirmative defense under Wyoming’s burden framework.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-553.plain: Alito distinguished using preclusion to establish an “offense element,” a fact the prosecution must prove, from using it against Herrera’s treaty defense, an affirmative defense he had to raise, under Wyoming’s rules on who bears the burden.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.sentence: When the 2007 form was adopted, California’s Discover Bank rule made certain adhesive consumer class waivers unconscionable where predictable damages were small and specified circumstances existed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.plain: When the 2007 contract form was adopted, California’s Discover Bank rule made certain “adhesive” (take-it-or-leave-it, fine-print) consumer class-action waivers “unconscionable,” meaning so unfair they were unenforceable, where predictable damages were small and specified circumstances existed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.sentence: In 2011, Concepcion held Discover Bank preempted by the Federal Arbitration Act, or FAA.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.plain: In 2011, Concepcion held that the Discover Bank rule was “preempted,” meaning overridden, by the Federal Arbitration Act, or FAA.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.sentence: It reasoned that parties could choose California law independent of federal preemption and had done so: the specific state-law contingency qualified the general FAA clause, and ambiguity ran against the drafter.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.plain: The state court reasoned that the parties could choose California law apart from federal “preemption,” and had done so. It held the specific state-law “contingency” clause qualified the general FAA clause, and that any “ambiguity” (unclear wording) ran against DIRECTV, which drafted it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.sentence: Second, California contracts incorporated reserved power to change law, and judicial statutory constructions ordinarily applied retroactively; the likely 2007 understanding did not decide the later issue.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.plain: Second, California contracts include the government’s reserved power to change the law, and courts’ “statutory constructions,” rulings interpreting statutes, ordinarily apply “retroactively” to past events. So the likely 2007 understanding did not decide the later issue.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.sentence: Sixth, neither the specific-over-general canon nor the anti-drafter canon established a comparable general reading: the former did not answer what state law meant, and the latter could not be limitless.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.plain: Sixth, neither the “specific-over-general” canon (a specific clause controls a general one) nor the “anti-drafter canon” (read unclear terms against the writer) supported the state court’s reading. The first did not say what “state law” meant, and the second could not be limitless.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.sentence: Her discussion of effective vindication, a 2015 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau study, the FAA’s original commercial setting, and European protections supplied dissenting criticism, not governing holdings or a present comparative-law account.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-598.plain: Justice Ginsburg’s discussion of “effective vindication” (whether consumers can realistically enforce their rights), a 2015 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau study, the FAA’s original business setting, and European protections was dissenting criticism, not governing law or a current comparison of legal systems.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.sentence: The Court of Special Appeals affirmed, using Virginia’s mutuality requirement to deny preclusion and reading the letter as preserving arbitration.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.plain: The Court of Special Appeals, Maryland’s intermediate appeals court, affirmed. It used Virginia’s “mutuality requirement,” which lets only parties to the earlier case use its judgment, to deny “preclusion,” and read the letter as preserving arbitration.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.sentence: These new plaintiffs sought offensive nonmutual preclusion—binding defendants to an issue they lost against different plaintiffs.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.plain: The new plaintiffs wanted to hold the defendants to the issue they had lost in the Virginia case, even though these plaintiffs were not part of that case. This is 'offensive nonmutual preclusion': a newcomer uses a party's earlier loss against it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.sentence: Full faith and credit and Maryland’s own conflicts law required the rendering state’s rules, ordinarily giving its judgment neither greater nor lesser effect.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.plain: “Full faith and credit,” the constitutional duty to respect other states’ judgments, and Maryland’s own “conflicts law” for cases involving other states required applying the “rendering state’s” rules, ordinarily giving its judgment neither more nor less effect than there.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.sentence: Maryland had recognized defensive nonmutual preclusion but had not formally embraced offensive use, and the court declined to do so here.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.plain: Maryland had recognized “defensive nonmutual preclusion,” where a new defendant uses a plaintiff’s earlier loss against that plaintiff. But it had not formally embraced “offensive use,” where a new plaintiff uses a defendant’s earlier loss, and the court declined to do so here.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.sentence: Continued existence was a court question, distinct from scope uncertainty about an admitted existing clause.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.plain: Whether the arbitration agreement still existed at all was a question for the court. That is different from doubt about how far an admittedly existing arbitration clause reaches, which is usually resolved in favor of arbitration.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.sentence: He challenged extending federal full-faith-and-credit precedents to prohibit broader forum preclusion and favored contrary authorities’ reasoning.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ROURKE-AMCHEM.plain: The dissenting judge challenged extending federal “full-faith-and-credit” precedents to forbid broader preclusion by the “forum,” the court now hearing the case, and he favored the reasoning of authorities reaching the opposite result.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: Complete diversity therefore was absent when Hain removed under 28 U.S.C. §1332.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: Complete diversity, every plaintiff being from a different state than every defendant, was therefore absent when Hain “removed” the case (moved it from state to federal court) under 28 U.S.C. §1332.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: After the parents rested, the court granted Hain judgment as a matter of law on every claim for insufficient causation evidence, including whether ingested heavy metals could cause the symptoms and at what levels.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: After the parents “rested,” finishing their evidence, the court “granted” Hain judgment as a matter of law on every “claim,” ruling without the jury. It found the “causation” evidence insufficient, including whether ingested heavy metals could cause the child’s symptoms and at what levels.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis recognized an exception where a defect was properly cured before judgment.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis recognized an exception, letting a judgment stand, where a jurisdictional defect was properly “cured” (fixed) before judgment.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: Ordinary final-judgment and merger rules made it reviewable after the final Hain judgment.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: Ordinary final-judgment and “merger rules,” under which earlier rulings merge into the final judgment, made the dismissal order “reviewable” on appeal after the final Hain judgment.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: A purported cure had to withstand appellate review; otherwise judicial error would enlarge Congress’s jurisdictional grant.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: A “purported cure,” a supposed fix for a jurisdiction problem, had to survive “appellate” review. Otherwise a judge’s error would enlarge the jurisdiction Congress granted federal courts.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: Rule 54(b) partial final judgments and §1292(b) certification might sometimes permit earlier review and reduce that risk, but did not make every joinder ruling immediately appealable.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: Rule 54(b) partial final judgments and §1292(b) certification of key legal questions might sometimes allow earlier review and reduce that risk. But they did not make every “joinder” ruling, on adding or dropping parties, immediately appealable.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: Newman-Green v. Alfonzo-Larrain permitted dismissal of a dispensable nondiverse party in suitable circumstances, with careful attention to prejudice and tactical effects.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: Newman-Green v. Alfonzo-Larrain allowed dismissal of a “dispensable nondiverse party,” a non-essential party from the same state as the other side, in suitable circumstances, with careful attention to “prejudice” (unfair harm) and tactical effects.

brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.sentence: The Court reserved Rule 21 in original federal actions and cases where a nondiverse party was added after proper removal; it did not prohibit all jurisdictional cures under the rule.
brief-CP-SUP-HAIN.plain: The Court “reserved” (left open) how Rule 21 applies in “actions” filed in federal court originally and in cases where a nondiverse party was added after a proper removal. It did not forbid all “jurisdictional cures” under the rule.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.sentence: The solicitors then telegraphed that they agreed to buy for that amount and requested the title deed so they could obtain early possession.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.plain: The “solicitors,” the buyers’ lawyers, then telegraphed that they agreed to buy for that amount and asked for the “title deed,” the document proving ownership, so they could get early possession.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.sentence: They sought an injunction preventing the municipality from taking a conveyance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.plain: They sought an “injunction,” a court order, preventing the municipality, Kingston’s city government, from taking a “conveyance,” a transfer of the property.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.sentence: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council could therefore decide whether a contract existed despite the buyers’ appeal seeking specific relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.plain: So the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the top court for appeals from British colonies, could decide whether any contract existed at all, even though the buyers’ appeal sought specific relief enforcing the sale.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.sentence: Facey’s reply answered that question alone.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.plain: Facey's reply only stated his lowest price; it did not say he would sell to them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.sentence: Their third telegram was accordingly an offer to buy that required his acceptance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.plain: So the buyers' 'we agree to buy' telegram was not an acceptance. It was only an offer to buy, which Facey never accepted, so there was no contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.sentence: Its reasoning distinguishes a price answer from a communicated offer in these exchanges; it does not announce that a price quotation can never be an offer in another context.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-035.plain: The reasoning distinguishes a “price answer,” a reply stating a price, from a communicated offer in these particular messages. It does not announce that a price quotation can never be an offer in another context.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.sentence: The Champaign County circuit court found no ceremonial or common-law marriage.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.plain: The Champaign County “circuit court,” the trial court, found no “ceremonial” marriage (one through a formal ceremony) and no common-law marriage, an informal marriage formed by conduct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.sentence: Because Robert admitted paternity, it said no separate Paternity Act action was needed to determine child support and directed specificity about claimed property.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.plain: Because Robert admitted “paternity” (that he was the children’s father), the court said no separate Paternity Act “action,” or lawsuit, was needed to set child support. It directed Victoria to specify the property she claimed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.sentence: Her amendment asserted an express undertaking and joint efforts, an implied sharing agreement, a trust based on allegedly fraudulent assurances of marriage, and unjust enrichment from reliance and contributions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.plain: Her amendment, the revised complaint, asserted an “express undertaking” (an explicit promise to share) and joint efforts, an implied sharing agreement, a trust based on allegedly fraudulent promises of marriage, and “unjust enrichment” from her reliance and contributions.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.sentence: It was deciding legal enforceability of the pleaded arrangement, not whether a sharing promise had been proved at trial.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.plain: The court was deciding the legal “enforceability” of the arrangement as “pleaded” (described in her complaint), not whether a sharing promise had been proved at trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.sentence: The alleged marital intent, assumed status, and public representation would have fit the former institution; equivalent property effects could indirectly restore what lawmakers abolished.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.plain: The “alleged” intent to be married, assumed married status, and public presentation as married would have fit common-law marriage, which Illinois abolished. Giving them equivalent property effects could indirectly restore what lawmakers abolished.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.sentence: Putative-spouse protection required a ceremony and good-faith belief in validity, ended with knowledge of invalidity, and excluded common-law marriages.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-043.plain: “Putative-spouse” protection, for someone who wrongly but honestly believed they were married, required a ceremony and a “good-faith” belief that the marriage was valid. It ended once the person learned of the “invalidity,” and it excluded common-law marriages.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.sentence: His amended complaint in October 1987 asserted wrongful discharge, promissory estoppel, breach of good faith and fair dealing, defamation, negligent investigation, violation of public policy, and punitive damages.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.plain: His “amended complaint” (revised complaint) of October 1987 asserted “wrongful discharge” (unlawful firing), promissory estoppel, breach of good faith and fair dealing, “defamation” (false statements harming reputation), negligent investigation, and violation of public policy, and it sought punitive damages, money meant to punish.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.sentence: The trial judge directed verdicts for Weirton on wrongful discharge, estoppel and good faith because Dzinglski was employed at will and the discharge violated no public policy.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.plain: The trial judge directed verdicts for Weirton, ruling for it without the jury, on “wrongful discharge,” estoppel, and “good faith.” He did so because Dzinglski was “employed at will,” meaning he could be fired for any lawful reason, and the firing violated no public policy.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.sentence: A lawful discharge therefore does not automatically defeat a claim concerning an abusive manner of discharge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.plain: A lawful discharge therefore does not automatically defeat a “claim” about an abusive manner of firing; an employer with the right to fire may still be liable for how it does it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.sentence: The late amendment was permissible under Rule 15 because the distress theory concerned the investigation already in dispute, caused no unfair prejudice, and could be met by Weirton, which had not requested a discovery continuance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.plain: The “late amendment” adding the distress claim was allowed under Rule 15 because it concerned the investigation already in dispute and caused no “unfair prejudice” (unfair harm) to Weirton. Weirton could meet it and never asked for a continuance, more time, for “discovery,” the exchange of evidence.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.sentence: It also related back: it added a theory about the same conduct, rather than different underlying facts, and was therefore timely.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.plain: The new claim also “related back,” meaning it was treated as filed on the original complaint’s date, because it added a theory about the same conduct rather than different facts. So it was “timely,” not too late.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.sentence: The jury had characterized Weirton’s conduct as wanton, oppressive and reckless, but the court explained that a distress award without physical trauma, based on intentionally outrageous conduct, could itself serve punitive and deterrent purposes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-052.plain: The jury called Weirton’s conduct “wanton” (in reckless disregard of others), oppressive, and reckless. But the court explained that a distress award without physical injury, based on intentionally outrageous conduct, could itself serve to punish and deter, so punitive damages on top would duplicate it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: The banks sought to add conversion and further unfair-practices allegations; the court denied amendment, finally denied class certification, and ordered transfer to Massachusetts Superior Court, describing its earlier rulings as open to reconsideration there.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: The banks sought to add conversion and more “unfair-practices” allegations. The court “denied amendment,” finally refused “class certification” (letting them sue for a group), and ordered “transfer” to Massachusetts Superior Court, a state court, saying its earlier rulings were open to “reconsideration” there.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: Federal jurisdiction had rested on the Class Action Fairness Act’s minimal-diversity provisions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: Federal “jurisdiction,” the court’s power to hear the case, had rested on the Class Action Fairness Act’s minimal-diversity provisions, which let federal courts hear large class actions if any class member and any defendant are from different states.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: Calling rulings without prejudice was not an invitation to cure and refile in the same federal court.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: Calling the court’s “rulings” “without prejudice,” meaning open to being brought again, did not invite the banks to fix and refile the same claims in the same federal court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: Judge Boudin’s opinion for Judges Lipez and Howard applied Massachusetts’s Restatement-based beneficiary rule, which allows contracting parties to exclude third-party enforcement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: Judge Boudin’s “opinion” for Judges Lipez and Howard applied Massachusetts’s Restatement-based “beneficiary” rule. Under it, an outsider a contract was made to benefit may enforce it, but the contracting parties may exclude “third-party” enforcement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: The economic-loss doctrine also barred ordinary negligence because the banks alleged economic loss without personal injury or physical property damage.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: The “economic-loss doctrine” also barred ordinary “negligence” (carelessness) claims, because the banks “alleged” only financial loss, without “personal injury” or physical damage to property.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: Federal Trade Commission standards, complaints, and consent decrees could inform whether prolonged reckless security failures and delayed disclosure were unfair and highly injurious.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: Federal Trade Commission standards, complaints, and “consent decrees” (court-approved settlements) could help show whether long, reckless security failures and delayed disclosure were unfair and highly injurious.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: Under abuse-of-discretion review, the court affirmed denial of amendment without deciding whether Massachusetts conversion covered intangible property or whether hackers’ theft amounted to appropriation by TJX.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: Under “abuse-of-discretion” review, deferring to the trial judge’s reasonable choices, the court “affirmed” the denial of amendment. It did not decide whether Massachusetts conversion, a claim for wrongful taking of property, covers intangible property like card data, or whether the hackers’ theft counted as appropriation by TJX.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.sentence: The accompanying declaration that prior rulings were without prejudice fell with the transfer; the district court could not decide merits and then erase ordinary preclusion consequences.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-082.plain: The statement that earlier rulings were without prejudice fell along with the transfer. The district court could not decide the “merits” (the substance of claims) and then erase the ordinary “preclusion” consequences, the normal binding effect of those decisions.

brief-CT-CB-0195.sentence: The quotation was for immediate acceptance, with a reservation for agency or transportation contingencies, delays, and accidents beyond the seller’s control.
brief-CT-CB-0195.plain: The seller’s “quotation” (price letter) was for immediate acceptance. It included a “reservation,” a stated exception, for “contingencies” (unforeseen events) involving agencies or transportation, delays, and accidents beyond the seller’s control.

brief-CT-CB-0195.sentence: Judge Hobson accepted that price quotations often invite orders the seller can later accept or reject.
brief-CT-CB-0195.plain: Judge Hobson accepted that “price quotations” often only invite customers to place orders, which the seller can later accept or reject.

brief-CT-CB-0195.sentence: Together, context and wording made this a definite offer, and the prompt telegram accepted it before Fairmount could withdraw.
brief-CT-CB-0195.plain: Together, the context and the wording made this letter a definite offer. The buyer’s prompt telegram accepted it, forming a contract before Fairmount could withdraw the offer.

brief-CT-CB-0195.sentence: Under the common-law analysis, a material new condition could matter; the court did not simply excuse changes between merchants.
brief-CT-CB-0195.plain: Under the “common-law” analysis, a “material” (important) new condition in an acceptance could prevent a contract. The court did not simply “excuse” such changes because both sides were merchants.

brief-CT-CB-0195.sentence: Those were authorized performance choices, not further negotiations needing new mutual assent.
brief-CT-CB-0195.plain: Choosing the jar sizes and delivery dates were “performance” choices the offer authorized the buyer to make. They were not further negotiations needing new “mutual assent,” meaning agreement by both sides.

brief-CT-CB-0195.sentence: It treated any pleading defect as cured by judgment and supporting evidence, rather than remanding to see whether an offer might exist.
brief-CT-CB-0195.plain: The court treated any “pleading” defect, a flaw in how the complaint was written, as “cured by judgment” and the supporting evidence. It did not consider “remanding” (sending the case back) to see whether an offer might exist.

brief-CT-CB-0328.sentence: Chief Justice Currie’s opinion adopted Restatement (First) of Contracts § 90 as an affirmative basis for relief.
brief-CT-CB-0328.plain: Chief Justice Currie’s “opinion” adopted Restatement (First) of Contracts § 90, promissory estoppel, as an independent basis for “relief,” meaning a ground for winning a lawsuit, not just a defense.

brief-CT-CB-0328.sentence: A promise must foreseeably induce definite and substantial action or forbearance, actually cause that reliance, and require enforcement to prevent injustice.
brief-CT-CB-0328.plain: A promise must “foreseeably” (as the promisor should expect) induce definite and substantial action or “forbearance,” meaning holding back from acting. It must actually cause that reliance, and enforcement must be needed to prevent injustice.

brief-CT-CB-0328.sentence: Although promissory estoppel sometimes supplied consideration for an otherwise complete gratuitous promise, its role was broader.
brief-CT-CB-0328.plain: Promissory estoppel sometimes substituted for consideration to enforce an otherwise complete “gratuitous” promise, one given for nothing in return. But its role was broader than that.

brief-CT-CB-0328.sentence: A promise of future performance is fraudulent only when made with a present intention not to perform, and the record did not establish such bad faith by Lukowitz.
brief-CT-CB-0328.plain: A promise of future “performance” is fraudulent only if made with a present intention not to keep it, and the record did not establish such “bad faith” by Lukowitz.

brief-CT-CB-0328.sentence: No foreclosure of his equity was shown, and avoiding the loss did not reasonably require another $5,000 commitment after the franchise plan failed.
brief-CT-CB-0328.plain: No foreclosure of his equity, the ownership stake Hoffman’s $1,000 payment had created in the lot, was shown. And avoiding that loss did not reasonably require Hoffman to commit another $5,000 after the franchise plan failed.

brief-CT-CB-0328.sentence: Because the Hoffmans had cross-appealed, they could tax only two-thirds of their costs.
brief-CT-CB-0328.plain: Because the Hoffmans had filed their own cross-appeal, the court let them recover from Red Owl only two-thirds of their court costs.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: On cross-motions for summary judgment, the district court found Article III standing, federal-question jurisdiction under § 1331, and an implied constitutional cause of action.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: On “cross-motions for summary judgment,” where both sides asked for a ruling without trial, the district court found Article III standing (a concrete injury allowing suit), “federal-question” jurisdiction under § 1331, and an “implied constitutional cause of action,” a right to sue drawn from the Constitution itself.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: A congressional demand to a presidential adviser differed from a court’s criminal subpoena, contempt prosecution, habeas petition, or private suit involving congressional process, where individual rights were directly implicated.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: A congressional demand to a presidential adviser differed from a court’s criminal subpoena, a contempt prosecution, a “habeas petition” (a challenge to detention), or a private suit over congressional “process,” such as a subpoena, where individual rights were directly involved.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: The panel stressed nearly two centuries without direct congressional-executive enforcement litigation and political tools including accommodation, appropriations, appointments, bargaining, public pressure, and impeachment.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: The panel stressed nearly two centuries without direct enforcement lawsuits between Congress and the executive branch. Political tools were available instead, including “accommodation” (negotiated compromise), appropriations, appointments, bargaining, public pressure, and impeachment.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: It distinguished circuit cases involving express statutory authority, intervention, or court-managed accommodation, and drew support from § 1365’s Senate-only jurisdiction provision and governmental-privilege exception.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: It “distinguished” (set apart) circuit cases involving “express” statutory authority to sue, intervention, or court-managed “accommodation.” It drew support from § 1365’s Senate-only “jurisdiction” provision for subpoena suits and its exception for governmental privilege.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: Rogers also found an equitable constitutional action, alternatively declaratory relief, and § 1331 jurisdiction.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: Judge Rogers, by contrast, also found an “equitable constitutional action,” a right to sue in equity under the Constitution, or alternatively declaratory relief, and jurisdiction under § 1331, the general federal-question statute.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: With especially rigorous scrutiny for an interbranch case, the court applied injury, traceability, and redressability.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: Applying especially rigorous scrutiny to a dispute between branches, the court applied the three standing tests: injury, “traceability” (the injury was caused by the defendant), and redressability (a court order could fix it).

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: Unlike individual legislators in Raines or one chamber claiming whole-legislature authority in Bethune-Hill, the plaintiff matched the holder of this power.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: Unlike the individual lawmakers in Raines, or the single chamber that tried to speak for the whole legislature in Bethune-Hill, the plaintiff here, a House committee suing with the full House's authorization, was the body that actually holds this investigative power.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.sentence: He also would have rejected a cause of action based on the Senate-specific mechanism, privilege limits, restrictions on implied constitutional remedies, and the merely procedural Declaratory Judgment Act.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-057.plain: Judge Griffith would also have found no “cause of action,” no right to sue, given the Senate-specific statute, privilege limits, restrictions on “implied constitutional remedies,” and the merely procedural Declaratory Judgment Act.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-061.sentence: Texas asked the Supreme Court for leave to file a bill of complaint against Pennsylvania and other states concerning their conduct of elections.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-061.plain: Texas asked the Supreme Court for “leave to file,” meaning permission to file, a bill of complaint, a lawsuit started directly in that Court, against Pennsylvania and other states over how they conducted their elections.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-061.sentence: Texas had not demonstrated a judicially cognizable interest in how another state conducted its elections.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-061.plain: Texas had not shown a "judicially cognizable" interest, meaning a stake that courts recognize as legally protectable, in how another state conducted its own elections.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-061.sentence: Justice Alito, joined by Justice Thomas, stated that the Court had no discretion to deny filing a bill of complaint in a case within its original jurisdiction.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-061.plain: Justice Alito, "joined by" Justice Thomas (meaning Thomas signed on to his opinion), said the Court had no "discretion," or choice, to refuse to let a state file a "bill of complaint," the document that starts a lawsuit brought directly in the Supreme Court. In their view, when a case falls within the Court's original jurisdiction, the Court must allow it to be filed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: With two other judges, they sued Governor John Ashcroft in federal court, invoking the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, or ADEA, and the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: With two other judges, they sued Governor John Ashcroft in federal court, claiming the mandatory retirement age violated the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA), a federal law against age discrimination at work. They also relied on the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause, the Constitution's guarantee that states treat people equally under the law.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: They invoked noscitur a sociis, reading a word by its neighbors: policymakers appeared between personal staff and immediate advisers, suggesting a close working relationship with an elected official that independent judges lacked.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: The judges invoked "noscitur a sociis," Latin for "it is known by its companions," the rule that a word is read in light of its neighbors. Because "policymakers" appeared between personal staff and immediate advisers, it suggested people with a close working relationship with an elected official, which independent judges lack.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: Congress could override state choices within its powers, but uncertain language would not establish disruption of the usual constitutional balance; intent had to be unmistakably clear.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: Congress could override state choices when acting within its powers, but uncertain language would not be read to upset the usual constitutional balance between the federal government and the states. Congress's intent to do that had to be "unmistakably clear" in the law itself.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: Sovereign-immunity and preemption plain-statement principles and political-function cases supported caution.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: Related "plain-statement principles" supported caution: Congress must speak plainly before a law strips a state's "sovereign-immunity" (its protection from being sued) or preempts, meaning displaces, state law. So did "political-function" cases, which let states set qualifications for important government posts.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: The question was clear inclusion, not clear exclusion, and that ambiguity defeated the required statement.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: Because the law had to clearly cover judges, and it was ambiguous, it did not cover them.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: Reconstruction expanded federal power, but political-function precedents and Pennhurst’s caution against inferring an unstated section 5 purpose reinforced the same conclusion under either possible source.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: Reconstruction (the post-Civil War constitutional amendments) did expand federal power over the states. But the "political-function precedents" and Pennhurst’s caution against inferring a purpose Congress never stated under section 5 (the Fourteenth Amendment's grant of power to enforce it) led to the same conclusion, whether Congress acted under its commerce power or under section 5.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: Age was not suspect and no fundamental right to judicial office was asserted, so rational-basis review applied.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: Age was not suspect, meaning it is not a classification (like race) that triggers strict court review, and the judges claimed no fundamental right to hold judicial office. So "rational-basis review" applied: Missouri needed only a rational reason for its rule.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.sentence: He found the rule inconsistent with Garcia, unsupported by alienage cases, uncertain in scope, burdensome in demanding lists, and especially inappropriate for section 5 legislation meant to overcome sovereignty.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-063.plain: He found the Court's clear-statement rule inconsistent with Garcia, unsupported by "alienage" cases (cases about laws treating noncitizens differently), and uncertain in scope. It would burden Congress by demanding lists of covered jobs, and it was especially inappropriate for section 5 legislation, which enforces the Fourteenth Amendment and is meant to overcome state "sovereignty," the states' independent authority.

cp-iqbal.sentence: Supervisory status did not itself create liability.
cp-iqbal.plain: "Supervisory status," meaning simply being the boss of the people who caused the harm, did not by itself make an official liable.

cp-iqbal.sentence: Courts need not presume legal conclusions or unsupported element recitations true.
cp-iqbal.plain: Courts need not presume true a complaint's "legal conclusions," meaning bare legal labels, or recitations that just repeat the elements of a claim without supporting facts.

cp-iqbal.sentence: Plausibility exceeds sheer possibility but does not require probability.
cp-iqbal.plain: "Plausibility," the pleading standard, requires more than a sheer possibility that the defendant acted unlawfully. But it does not require probability, so the plaintiff need not show the claim is more likely true than not.

cp-iqbal.sentence: Accepting that officials detained Arab Muslim men and that these defendants approved restrictive detention pending clearance, the Court found an obvious alternative explanation in the security investigation.
cp-iqbal.plain: Even accepting that officials detained many Arab Muslim men and that these defendants approved harsh detention, the Court saw a more obvious, lawful explanation: a security investigation could naturally sweep in many Arab Muslim men without any intent to discriminate.

cp-iqbal.sentence: The Court rejected limiting Twombly to antitrust: its interpretation of Rule 8 applied across civil actions.
cp-iqbal.plain: The Court refused to limit Twombly, an antitrust case, to antitrust suits. Its interpretation of Rule 8, the federal rule on what a complaint must contain, applies across all civil actions.

cp-iqbal.sentence: Rule 9(b)’s permission to plead mental states generally relaxed the special particularity requirement for fraud or mistake; it did not excuse factual support under Rule 8.
cp-iqbal.plain: Rule 9(b) lets a plaintiff "plead," or allege in the complaint, mental states such as intent or knowledge "generally." That only relaxes the special "particularity" requirement, the extra detail demanded for fraud or mistake; it does not excuse the factual support Rule 8 requires.

cp-surowitz.sentence: Brilliant read and explained the complaint to Surowitz, who verified it partly on information and belief.
cp-surowitz.plain: Brilliant, her son-in-law, read and explained the complaint to Mrs. Surowitz, who then verified it, meaning she swore it was true. She verified it partly "on information and belief," stating that some facts were true based on what she had been told and believed rather than on personal knowledge.

cp-surowitz.sentence: Despite those submissions, the district court treated her verification as false and a nullity and dismissed with prejudice.
cp-surowitz.plain: Despite those submissions, the "district court" (the federal trial court) treated her sworn verification as false and a "nullity," meaning legally void. It dismissed with prejudice, so the case could not be filed again.

cp-surowitz.sentence: The derivative-action verification requirement sought to discourage abusive suits filed without regard to truth to extract settlements from management.
cp-surowitz.plain: The verification (sworn oath) requirement for a "derivative-action," a shareholder suit brought on the company's behalf, aimed to discourage abusive suits. These were suits filed without regard to truth, just to pressure management into paying settlements.

cp-surowitz.sentence: On these facts, former Rule 23(b)’s verification requirement did not justify summary dismissal.
cp-surowitz.plain: On these facts, former Rule 23(b)’s verification requirement, the oath rule as it then stood, did not justify "summary dismissal," meaning throwing out the case quickly without reaching the merits.

cp-surowitz.sentence: It did not excuse counsel from investigation, approve sham pleadings, or decide every question of a nominal shareholder’s adequacy.
cp-surowitz.plain: The decision did not excuse "counsel" (the lawyers) from investigating the facts, or approve "sham pleadings" (fake or baseless complaints). Nor did it decide every question of a "nominal shareholder’s" adequacy, meaning whether the named shareholder bringing the suit is a suitable person to represent the company's interests.

cp-surowitz.sentence: The historical numbering matters: the derivative requirement then appeared in Rule 23(b), the subject now placed by the casebook with Rule 23.1.
cp-surowitz.plain: The historical numbering matters: the "derivative requirement" (the oath rule for shareholder suits on a company's behalf) then appeared in Rule 23(b). The casebook now places that subject with Rule 23.1, so the case is not about today's Rule 23(b), which concerns class actions.

lrs-k-holy-trinity.sentence: The Alien Contract Labor Act of February 26, 1885, prohibited assisting or encouraging alien migration under advance contracts to perform labor or service of any kind.
lrs-k-holy-trinity.plain: The Alien Contract Labor Act of February 26, 1885, made it illegal to assist or encourage the migration of any "alien" (foreigner) to the U.S. under a contract made in advance. The contract could be to perform labor or service of any kind.

lrs-k-holy-trinity.sentence: Justice David J. Brewer conceded literal coverage and the force of the exception-based argument.
lrs-k-holy-trinity.plain: Justice David J. Brewer conceded that the words, read literally, covered the church's contract. He also admitted the force of the "exception-based argument": because Congress listed specific exceptions and ministers were not among them, the law seemed to cover ministers.

lrs-k-holy-trinity.sentence: The church prevailed instead on a claim that this application lay outside legislative intention and the targeted evil.
lrs-k-holy-trinity.plain: The church won because the Court decided that applying the law to a minister went beyond what Congress intended and the problem it meant to fix.

lrs-k-holy-trinity.sentence: The Court identified the mischief as imported cheap unskilled labor depressing existing workers’ wages.
lrs-k-holy-trinity.plain: The Court identified the "mischief," the problem Congress meant to fix, as the import of cheap unskilled labor. Such workers drove down the wages of workers already here.

lrs-k-holy-trinity.sentence: A Senate committee reported it would have preferred “manual labor” or “manual service” but sought passage before adjournment and expected that construction anyway.
lrs-k-holy-trinity.plain: A Senate committee said it would have liked to limit the law to 'manual labor', but did not amend it so the bill could pass quickly, expecting courts to read it that way anyway.

lrs-k-holy-trinity.sentence: That was imaginative reconstruction of a hypothetical legislative response, distinct from the actual committee-report evidence.
lrs-k-holy-trinity.plain: That was "imaginative reconstruction": the Court imagined how Congress would have answered a question it never actually considered. That is different from relying on actual "evidence" of intent, such as the committee report.

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: Under the Clean Air Act, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sets national ambient air-quality standards, while States ordinarily supply State Implementation Plans for implementation, maintenance, and enforcement.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: Under the Clean Air Act, the federal air-pollution law, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sets national ambient air-quality standards, meaning nationwide limits on common pollutants in outdoor air. States ordinarily write State Implementation Plans explaining how they will implement, maintain, and enforce those standards.

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: The Good Neighbor Provision requires plans to prevent emissions significantly contributing to another State’s nonattainment or interfering with maintenance of its standard.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: The Good Neighbor Provision requires each state's plan to prevent emissions that significantly contribute to another state's "nonattainment," meaning its failure to meet the air standard. It also covers emissions that interfere with a downwind state maintaining the standard once it meets it.

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: EPA must approve compliant state plans; a missing or deficient plan can require a Federal Implementation Plan unless the State first cures the defect.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: EPA must approve state plans that comply with the law. If a plan is missing or deficient, EPA can be required to issue a Federal Implementation Plan of its own, unless the state first "cures" the defect, meaning fixes it.

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: EPA defended its severability rationale, disputed preservation of the specific objection, and urged administrative reconsideration first.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: EPA defended its severability reasoning, its statement that the rule could keep working in the remaining states. It "disputed preservation," arguing the challengers had not properly raised this specific objection during the comment period, and urged that they first ask EPA itself for administrative "reconsideration."

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: Under Nken’s stay framework, the Court considered likely success, irreparable injury, injury to others, and public interest.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: Under Nken’s framework for deciding whether to grant a stay (a pause of the rule), the Court weighed four things. It asked about the challengers' "likely success" on the merits, whether they faced irreparable injury (harm that cannot be undone), the injury a stay would cause others, and the public interest.

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: This differed from claiming that a final rule was not a logical outgrowth of its proposal: that objection arises only when the final rule exists and may require reconsideration.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: This differed from claiming that a final rule was not a "logical outgrowth" of its proposal, meaning it went beyond what the proposal gave fair notice of. That objection arises only once the final rule exists, so it may first require asking the agency for "reconsideration."

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: On June 27, 2024, the Court granted the four applications 5–4, staying enforcement against the applicants pending disposition of their D.C. Circuit petitions and any timely certiorari petition.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: On June 27, 2024, the Court granted the four emergency applications by a 5–4 vote, "staying" (pausing) enforcement of the plan against the applicants. The stay lasts pending "disposition," or final decision, of their petitions in the D.C. Circuit (the federal appeals court) and of any "timely" certiorari petition, meaning a request for Supreme Court review filed on time.

lrs-n-ohio-epa.sentence: This was a prediction of likely success on an arbitrary-or-capricious challenge, not a final judgment invalidating the plan or deciding separate state-plan disapprovals.
lrs-n-ohio-epa.plain: This was a prediction of "likely success" on the claim that EPA acted in an "arbitrary-or-capricious" way, meaning unreasonably or without adequate explanation. It was not a "final judgment" striking down the plan, and it did not decide the separate challenges to EPA's disapproval of state-plan submissions.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: The National Firearms Act’s (NFA’s) specialized firearm definition covers short-barreled rifles but generally excludes ordinary pistols.
lrs-o-mock.plain: The National Firearms Act’s (NFA’s) specialized definition of "firearm," used for its strict regulation of especially dangerous weapons, covers "short-barreled rifles." But it generally excludes ordinary pistols.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: Together they challenged statutory authority, invoked lenity and nondelegation, raised Administrative Procedure Act (APA) procedural objections and constitutional objections, and requested an injunction.
lrs-o-mock.plain: Together they challenged ATF's "statutory authority" (whether the statutes gave it this power) and invoked lenity, the rule that unclear criminal laws are read in defendants' favor, and "nondelegation," the limit on Congress handing its lawmaking power to agencies. They raised procedural "objections" under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the law governing how agencies make rules, plus constitutional objections, and requested an "injunction," a court order blocking the rule.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: It regarded ATF as likely authorized, rejected lenity and vagueness arguments, classified the rule as interpretive, and alternatively found the final rule a logical outgrowth of the proposal.
lrs-o-mock.plain: The district court regarded ATF as likely authorized and rejected the lenity (read unclear criminal laws in defendants' favor) and vagueness arguments. It "classified" the rule as interpretive, meaning merely ATF's reading of existing law, and alternatively found the final rule a "logical outgrowth" of the proposal, a foreseeable result of what was proposed.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: ATF answered that it merely interpreted existing statutory coverage and therefore owed no mandatory notice and comment.
lrs-o-mock.plain: ATF responded that its rule only explained how it reads the existing statute, and such interpretive rules do not legally require public notice and comment.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: Acknowledging uncertainty in circuit law, the panel adopted the five-factor approach used in the district court’s Cargill decision to distinguish legislative from interpretive rules: intended legal force, publication in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), invocation of legislative authority, asserted Chevron deference, and significant effects on private interests.
lrs-o-mock.plain: Admitting its own "circuit" precedent was unclear, the "panel" (the three appeals judges) used the five-factor test from the district court’s Cargill decision to tell legislative rules (binding law) from interpretive ones. The factors: whether the agency intended legal force, published the rule in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), invoked legislative authority, asserted Chevron deference (courts deferring to its reading), and whether the rule significantly affects private interests.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: Its language about setting aside or remanding an unlawful rule described a likely APA consequence; the actual appeal still concerned preliminary relief.
lrs-o-mock.plain: Its language about "setting aside" (striking down) or remanding (sending back to the agency) an unlawful rule described a likely consequence under the APA, the law governing agency rules. The actual appeal still concerned only "preliminary relief," a temporary order while the case goes on.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: The panel regarded statutory-authority, lenity, and nondelegation arguments as potentially colorable but unnecessary, and left constitutional issues for later consideration.
lrs-o-mock.plain: The panel regarded the statutory-authority, lenity, and nondelegation arguments as potentially "colorable," meaning plausible enough to take seriously, but did not need to decide them. It left the constitutional issues for later consideration.

lrs-o-mock.sentence: Plaintiffs still had to show irreparable injury, favorable equities, and consistency with the public interest; government and public interests merge when the government is the opponent.
lrs-o-mock.plain: Plaintiffs, the challengers, still had to show "irreparable injury" (harm that cannot be undone), that the equities (the balance of hardships) favored them, and that relief fit the public interest. When the government is the opposing party, its interests and the public interest merge, meaning they are treated as one.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: In Excelsior Underwear, the National Labor Relations Board considered unions’ objections after losing representation elections at two companies that refused to provide employee names and addresses.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: In Excelsior Underwear, an earlier case, the National Labor Relations Board considered objections from unions that lost "representation elections," votes on whether workers would be represented by a union. The two companies involved had refused to give the unions employee names and addresses.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: That prospective limitation, later understood by Justice Black as protecting reliance on previous decisions against compelled disclosure, created the rulemaking-versus-adjudication dispute in Wyman-Gordon.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: That "prospective" limitation, applying the new disclosure rule only to future elections rather than to the companies before the Board, created the rulemaking-versus-adjudication dispute in Wyman-Gordon. Justice Black later understood it as protecting employers who had relied on earlier decisions that did not compel them to disclose names.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: Adjudication could create policy and precedent for later action; that did not automatically create a legislative rule binding the public without further agency action.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: Adjudication, meaning deciding a particular case, could create policy and precedent for the agency's later actions. But that did not automatically create a "legislative rule," one binding the public like a statute, without further agency action.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: Justice Harlan argued that Chenery I’s requirement to review an agency on its own grounds required remand after rejection of its stated premise.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: Justice Harlan argued that Chenery I’s requirement, that courts "review" an agency's action only on the grounds the agency itself gave, meant a "remand" was needed. Once the Board's stated premise was rejected, the case had to be sent back to the Board.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: Under Chenery II, agencies ordinarily choose whether to develop policy through adjudication or rulemaking where both fit.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: Under Chenery II, where both methods fit, agencies ordinarily choose whether to develop policy through "adjudication" (deciding individual cases) or through rulemaking (issuing general rules).

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: Representation certifications were exempt from the APA’s formal adjudication requirements; the pertinent labor-statute procedures governed, so Black was not demanding every APA trial formality for elections.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: "Representation certifications," the Board's official decisions certifying union election results, were exempt from the APA’s formal, trial-like adjudication requirements; the labor statute's own procedures governed instead. So Black was not demanding every APA trial formality for elections.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: Under Chenery I, the regional official’s refusal to reconsider because Excelsior bound him, followed by the Board’s refusal of review, could not be replaced by a court’s confidence about a hypothetical new decision.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: Under Chenery I, a court must judge an agency on the reasons it actually gave. Here the regional official refused to reconsider because he felt bound by Excelsior, and the Board then refused review, so a court could not substitute its own confidence about what a hypothetical new decision would say.

lrs-o-wyman-gordon.sentence: Seven Justices supported that outcome, but only four used Fortas’s invalid-rule/valid-order route; three sustained Excelsior as adjudication.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon.plain: Seven Justices supported enforcing the order, but only four took Fortas’s route: Excelsior was an invalid rule, yet this order was valid. The other three "sustained," or upheld, Excelsior as a proper adjudication, a valid case decision.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: Before it took effect, President Nixon’s August 15, 1971 Executive Order 11615 imposed a ninety-day freeze on prices, rents, wages, and salaries.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: Before the raise took effect, President Nixon’s Executive Order 11615 of August 15, 1971, a directive issued by the President, imposed a ninety-day freeze on prices, rents, wages, and salaries.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: Count I sued Connally and Council officials for declaratory and injunctive relief against the program.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: Count I sued Connally and the Council officials for "declaratory" relief (a court statement that the program was unlawful) and injunctive relief (an order stopping the officials from running it).

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: Equity jurisdiction did not vanish merely because the merits or practical balance might ultimately defeat an injunction.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: "Equity jurisdiction," the court's power to grant remedies such as injunctions, did not vanish merely because "the merits" (who is legally right) or the practical balance of harms might ultimately defeat an injunction.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: The union principally alleged excessive delegation over whether, when, and how broadly to regulate virtually the whole economy, relying on Schechter and Panama Refining.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: The union principally "alleged" excessive delegation: that Congress unconstitutionally handed the President power to decide whether, when, and how broadly to "regulate" virtually the whole economy. It relied on Schechter and Panama Refining, 1935 cases that struck down such broad grants of power.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: Under Yakus and Hampton, the question was whether Congress established basic policy and a sufficiently defined field for Congress, courts, and the public to judge compliance.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: Under Yakus and Hampton, the question was whether Congress set the basic policy and defined the field clearly enough. The field had to be defined well enough for Congress, the courts, and the public to judge whether officials were complying.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) §§ 701–706 permitted appropriate declaratory and injunctive challenges, including pre-enforcement cases satisfying finality, ripeness, direct consequence, and other conditions.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) §§ 701–706, the law's judicial-review sections, allowed appropriate "declaratory" challenges (asking a court to declare agency action unlawful) and injunctive ones (asking it to block the action). These included "pre-enforcement" suits, brought before the rule is enforced against anyone, if they met finality, "ripeness" (a dispute concrete enough to decide), direct consequence, and other conditions.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: The Contracts Clause bound states, so the federal objection sounded in due process.
lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: The Contracts Clause, which bars impairing contracts, binds only the states. So the objection to this federal action "sounded in" due process, meaning its legal basis had to be the due process guarantee.

lrs-s-amalgamated.sentence: Wages and salaries also covered fringe benefits; omission of “other compensation” did not require exclusion in light of prior interpretations and cost-push inflation concerns.
