lrs-s-amalgamated.plain: "Wages and salaries" also covered "fringe benefits" such as pensions and insurance. Leaving out the words "other compensation" did not require excluding them, given prior interpretations and concern about "cost-push inflation," where rising labor costs push prices up.

plante.sentence: Plante did not finish and sought a lien for the unpaid balance and claimed extras; the owners asserted deficient and incomplete work.
plante.plain: Plante did not finish the house and sought a "lien," a legal claim against the property securing payment, for the unpaid balance and for claimed extras. The owners asserted that the work was deficient and incomplete.

plante.sentence: Justice Hallows explained that contract recovery required substantial performance; otherwise the builder would at most have a claim for the reasonable value of services.
plante.plain: Justice Hallows explained that recovery on the contract required "substantial performance," meaning the builder did essentially what was promised despite minor defects. Otherwise the builder would at most have a "claim" for the "reasonable value of services," the fair worth of the work done.

plante.sentence: The nature and scale of each defect mattered, and unreasonable economic waste limited destructive reconstruction.
plante.plain: The nature and scale of each defect mattered. The rule against "unreasonable economic waste" limited awards for tearing out and rebuilding work when that destruction would be wasteful compared with the benefit.

plante.sentence: The trial judge had rejected unproved items, and those findings were not against the great weight and clear preponderance of the evidence.
plante.plain: The trial judge had rejected items the owners did not prove. Those findings stood because they were not against the "great weight and clear preponderance of the evidence," a standard that leaves a trial judge's fact findings in place unless the evidence clearly points the other way.

plante.sentence: Repairing ceiling-plaster cracks, mud jacking and fixing the patio floor, and rebuilding a nonstructural patio wall did not involve unreasonable waste in relation to the house and its cost.
plante.plain: Repairing the ceiling-plaster cracks, mud jacking (raising a sunken slab by pumping material under it) and fixing the patio floor, and rebuilding a nonstructural patio wall did not involve "unreasonable waste." Those costs were reasonable in relation to the house and its cost.

plante.sentence: The applicable diminution measure therefore contemplated leaving the wall where it stood.
plante.plain: The applicable "diminution measure," which awards the drop in the house's value instead of the cost of fixing the defect, therefore assumed the wall would be left where it stood.

psenicska.sentence: They waived participation claims including publicity or likeness, intrusion, prima facie tort, and fraud involving deception or surprise about the film or agreement.
psenicska.plain: They "waived," meaning gave up, claims arising from their participation. These included use of their "publicity or likeness" (their name or image), intrusion on privacy, prima facie tort (intentional harm without justification), and fraud involving deception or surprise about the film or the agreement.

psenicska.sentence: Judge Loretta A. Preska granted all three Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal motions on September 3, 2008, directed closure of the actions, and denied pending motions as moot.
psenicska.plain: Judge Loretta A. Preska granted all three Rule 12(b)(6) "motions" to dismiss on September 3, 2008; that rule ends a case when, even if everything alleged is true, there is no valid legal claim. She also directed that the cases be closed and denied the other pending motions as moot, meaning no longer needing a decision.

psenicska.sentence: Paragraph 5 was a targeted nonreliance provision, not merely a general merger clause: it defeated the attempted fraud-based escape from the releases.
psenicska.plain: Paragraph 5 was a targeted "nonreliance provision," a clause specifically saying the plaintiffs were not relying on statements about the film. It was not merely a general "merger clause," which just says the written contract is the whole deal, so it defeated the attempt to escape the releases by claiming fraud.

psenicska.sentence: Under Danann, the precedent addressing specific nonreliance provisions, a party generally could not base inducement on representations about a subject expressly disclaimed in the contract.
psenicska.plain: Under Danann, the precedent on "specific nonreliance provisions," a party generally could not claim fraudulent "inducement" (being tricked into signing) based on statements about a subject the contract expressly "disclaimed" relying on.

psenicska.sentence: The panel explained that the exception protects against high costs of determining whether an oral assertion is true; it ordinarily does not protect someone able to demand that a deal-breaking assurance be written into the agreement.
psenicska.plain: The exception protects people who could not realistically check whether a statement was true; it generally does not protect someone who could have insisted that a crucial promise be put in writing.

psenicska.sentence: But concealment and disclosure-based theories required reasonable reliance too.
psenicska.plain: But theories based on "concealment" (hiding facts) or a failure to disclose also required reasonable reliance, and that requirement still failed.

bayliner.sentence: His personal speed requirement differed from ordinary trade fitness and from what he conveyed at sale.
bayliner.plain: Crow personally needed a boat that could go about thirty miles per hour, but that is not what boats of this kind ordinarily must do, and he had not made it clear to the dealer. That matters because the warranty claims turned on ordinary standards for such boats or on what the seller knew or said.

bayliner.sentence: He nonsuited the dealer before trial; the final order dismissed the Brunswick negligence claim.
bayliner.plain: Crow "nonsuited" the dealer before trial, meaning he voluntarily dropped his claims against it, and the final order dismissed his negligence claim against Brunswick, the engine maker. That left Bayliner, the boat's maker, still facing his claims.

bayliner.sentence: Following a bench trial the circuit court found Bayliner liable for express warranty, merchantability, and particular-purpose fitness.
bayliner.plain: Following a "bench trial," a trial before a judge without a jury, the Virginia circuit court (the trial court) found Bayliner "liable," or legally responsible, on three warranties. These were an express warranty (a specific promise), the implied warranty of "merchantability" (fitness for ordinary use), and the implied warranty of fitness for Crow's particular purpose.

bayliner.sentence: Justice Barbara Milano Keenan’s Supreme Court of Virginia opinion viewed evidence favorably to Crow and would uphold findings unless plainly wrong or unsupported.
bayliner.plain: In Justice Barbara Milano Keenan’s "opinion" for the Supreme Court of Virginia, the court viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to Crow, who won at trial. It would uphold the trial judge's "findings" of fact unless they were plainly wrong or unsupported by evidence.

bayliner.sentence: Virginia’s Uniform Commercial Code § 2-313 recognizes affirmations, promises, and descriptions relating to the goods and forming the bargain’s basis.
bayliner.plain: Virginia’s Uniform Commercial Code § 2-313, its version of the national sales law, recognizes express warranties created by a seller's "affirmations" (statements of fact), promises, and descriptions relating to the goods. Those statements must form part of the "bargain’s basis," meaning they were part of the deal the buyer agreed to.

bayliner.sentence: Numerical specificity did not promise the same result from Crow’s configuration.
bayliner.plain: The speed charts gave precise numbers, but they described boats with different propellers and much lighter loads. So they were not a promise that Crow's heavier, differently equipped boat would reach those speeds.

bayliner.sentence: It was commendation or opinion under § 2-313(2), not the particular promise claimed.
bayliner.plain: The brochure statement was "commendation," meaning sales praise, or opinion under § 2-313(2), which does not create a warranty. It was not the particular promise Crow claimed he had been given.

bayliner.sentence: For merchantability under § 2-314, Crow supplied no trade standard or evidence that a substantial segment of buyers regarded boats with this capability as unacceptable.
bayliner.plain: To prove a breach of "merchantability" under § 2-314, meaning the boat was not fit for ordinary use, Crow needed proof of a trade standard. He supplied none, and no evidence that a substantial segment of buyers regarded boats with this speed capability as unacceptable.

bayliner.sentence: Section 2-315’s particular-purpose warranty required reason to know Crow’s special purpose and reliance on seller judgment.
bayliner.plain: Section 2-315’s particular-purpose warranty required that the seller had reason to know Crow’s special purpose for the boat. It also required that Crow relied on the seller's "judgment," or skill, to pick suitable goods.

bayliner.sentence: A privately decisive condition did not become communicated merely because the broader activity was known.
bayliner.plain: The dealer knew Crow wanted to fish offshore, but that did not tell the dealer Crow would reject any boat slower than thirty miles per hour. A make-or-break requirement Crow kept to himself could not bind the seller.

bayliner.sentence: It did not remand for Crow to supply missing proof and did not approve the damages method; the amount issues were unnecessary after liability failed.
bayliner.plain: The court did not "remand," or send the case back, for Crow to supply the missing proof, and it did not approve the trial court's damages method. Once liability failed, the questions about the amount of damages were unnecessary.

bloor.sentence: To protect that royalty component, Falstaff promised best efforts to promote and maintain a high sales volume.
bloor.plain: Part of the price was a "royalty," a payment for each barrel of Ballantine beer sold. To protect that royalty, Falstaff promised "best efforts," a duty to try diligently, to promote the brand and maintain a high sales volume.

bloor.sentence: A separate provision called for $1.1 million for each remaining year, including fractions, if Falstaff substantially discontinued distribution during the royalty period, subject to an exception for a governmental restraining order.
bloor.plain: A separate provision required Falstaff to pay $1.1 million for each remaining year of the royalty period, including part-years, if it substantially stopped distributing the brand. The exception was a stop forced by a governmental "restraining order," a government order prohibiting distribution.

bloor.sentence: The high-volume covenant and discontinuance provision created different obligations and remedies.
bloor.plain: The high-volume "covenant" (the contractual promise to push sales) and the discontinuance provision created different obligations. Breaking each one led to different "remedies," the ways the law makes up for a breach.

bloor.sentence: Once the insolvency threat had passed, however, the disproportionate collapse called for commercially reasonable attempts to arrest it without financial disaster.
bloor.plain: Once the threat of "insolvency," being unable to pay its debts, had passed, Ballantine's disproportionate sales collapse called for action. Falstaff had to make "commercially reasonable" attempts, the efforts a sensible business would make, to stop the slide without risking financial disaster.

bloor.sentence: A policy of maximizing companywide profit did not itself fulfill a brand-specific volume promise.
bloor.plain: Trying to make the most money for Falstaff as a whole was not enough, because Falstaff had specifically promised to work at keeping Ballantine's sales high.

bloor.sentence: Their reasoning required attention to the promisor’s capabilities and actual conduct, rather than making disappointing profitability a universal excuse.
bloor.plain: The cases' reasoning looked to the "promisor’s" capabilities and actual conduct, meaning what the party who made the promise could do and actually did. Disappointing profitability was not a universal excuse.

bloor.sentence: Even without express best efforts, that arrangement implied good-faith effort toward substantial sales; the express covenant added a high-volume objective.
bloor.plain: Even without an "express" (written-out) best-efforts promise, a per-barrel payment arrangement carried an "implied" duty, one the law reads in, to make good-faith efforts toward substantial sales. The express "covenant," or promise, added a further high-volume goal.

bloor.sentence: Once Bloor established a permissible inference that Falstaff disregarded volume for overall profit, Falstaff had to show that no significant additional effort was possible without financially disastrous consequences.
bloor.plain: Once Bloor established a "permissible inference," evidence from which a court could reasonably conclude that Falstaff disregarded Ballantine's sales volume for the sake of its overall profit, the burden shifted. Falstaff then had to show that no significant additional effort was possible without financially disastrous consequences.

bloor.sentence: A sufficiently specific objection concerning Schaefer’s losses had not been presented.
bloor.plain: The trial judge estimated damages by comparing Ballantine with similar beers, including Schaefer. Falstaff had not raised a clear, specific objection in time that Schaefer's own losses made it a poor comparison, so that point did not undercut the estimate.

bloor.sentence: Leaving the retail-truck model therefore did not itself trigger the discontinuance clause, especially when the nationwide number of wholesalers carrying Ballantine increased.
bloor.plain: Beer normally reaches stores through independent wholesalers, so Falstaff's ending its own delivery-truck routes did not count as substantially stopping distribution, especially since more wholesalers were carrying Ballantine.

brief-CP-101.sentence: Upjohn invoked attorney-client privilege and work product.
brief-CP-101.plain: Upjohn invoked "attorney-client privilege," which protects confidential communications between a client and its lawyers made to get legal advice, including its employees' talks with company lawyers. It also invoked work product, the protection for materials lawyers prepare with litigation in mind.

brief-CP-101.sentence: The district court adopted a magistrate’s recommendation, including privilege waiver and sufficient governmental need to overcome work product.
brief-CP-101.plain: The "district court," the federal trial court, adopted a magistrate’s recommendation. That recommendation found privilege "waiver," meaning Upjohn had given up its privilege, and found the government's need strong enough to overcome work-product protection.

brief-CP-101.sentence: The Sixth Circuit rejected waiver but restricted corporate privilege to the management group controlling corporate action in response to advice, remanding to identify qualifying interviewees.
brief-CP-101.plain: The Sixth Circuit, the federal appeals court, rejected waiver but limited a corporation's privilege to the management group that controls the company's action in response to legal advice. It was "remanding," sending the case back, to identify which interviewees qualified.

brief-CP-101.sentence: It also held work-product protection unavailable against administrative tax summonses.
brief-CP-101.plain: It also ruled that work-product protection can never be used to resist an IRS summons.

brief-CP-101.sentence: Justice Rehnquist applied Federal Rule of Evidence 501’s development of common-law privilege through reason and experience.
brief-CP-101.plain: Justice Rehnquist applied Federal Rule of Evidence 501, which tells federal courts to develop privileges under "common-law" principles, meaning judge-made law, interpreted in light of reason and experience.

brief-CP-101.sentence: Limiting confidential fact gathering to senior managers could keep counsel ignorant of the very acts generating exposure and discourage knowledgeable employees from answering.
brief-CP-101.plain: Limiting confidential fact gathering to senior managers could keep "counsel," the company's lawyers, ignorant of the very acts that create legal exposure. It could also discourage knowledgeable lower-level employees from answering frankly.

brief-CP-101.sentence: Still, Rule 501 allowed case-specific development, so the Court rejected that restriction without prescribing an exhaustive replacement formula.
brief-CP-101.plain: Because Rule 501 lets privilege law develop case by case, the Court struck down the top-managers-only test without announcing a complete new test to replace it.

brief-CP-101.sentence: The corporate client’s privilege did not establish that counsel personally represented each employee.
brief-CP-101.plain: The privilege belonged to the corporate client, Upjohn itself. It did not establish that "counsel," the company's lawyers, personally represented each employee they talked to.

brief-CP-101.sentence: The Supreme Court distinguished facts from confidential reports of facts.
brief-CP-101.plain: The Supreme Court distinguished the facts themselves from confidential reports of those facts to a lawyer. The privilege protects the communications, so the IRS could still ask employees directly what happened.

brief-CP-101.sentence: The tax-summons statute showed no congressional displacement of the established protection recognized in Hickman, the Supreme Court precedent protecting litigation preparation.
brief-CP-101.plain: The "statute" authorizing IRS tax summonses showed no sign that Congress meant to displace the established protection recognized in Hickman. Hickman is the Supreme Court "precedent," an earlier binding decision, protecting lawyers' litigation-preparation materials.

brief-CP-101.sentence: Civil rules governed enforcement proceedings, and Rule 26(b)(3) incorporated safeguards.
brief-CP-101.plain: The civil procedure rules governed court proceedings to enforce an IRS summons. Rule 26(b)(3), the rule on work product, built in safeguards for materials prepared for litigation.

brief-CP-101.sentence: The Court required a substantially stronger showing than the government made, while reserving whether mental-process material was absolutely protected.
brief-CP-101.plain: The Court required a substantially stronger showing than the government had made. It reserved, or left open, whether "mental-process material," notes revealing a lawyer's own thinking and impressions, is absolutely protected.

brief-CP-130.sentence: They sought injunctions, treble damages, and accountings.
brief-CP-130.plain: They sought "injunctions" (court orders stopping the conduct), treble damages (three times their actual losses, which antitrust law allows), and accountings, meaning court-supervised calculations of money owed.

brief-CP-130.sentence: They did not, but the next day he ordered references on his own initiative, directing a master to receive evidence and report findings of fact and conclusions of law on the general issues.
brief-CP-130.plain: The parties did not agree to a master, but the next day the judge "ordered" references on his own initiative, sending the cases to a master, a court-appointed helper. The master was to receive evidence and report "findings of fact and conclusions of law," meaning what happened and how the law applies, on the general issues.

brief-CP-130.sentence: The parties deposited about $8,000 as security for costs, but all objected and sought vacatur; compliance with the deposit order did not establish consent.
brief-CP-130.plain: The parties deposited about $8,000 "as security" for costs, meaning money held to guarantee the master's expenses would be paid. But all of them objected and sought "vacatur," cancellation of the orders, and complying with the deposit order did not show they consented.

brief-CP-130.sentence: In nonjury cases other than matters of account, it required an exceptional condition.
brief-CP-130.plain: In "nonjury" cases, those tried by a judge alone, the rule allowed a reference to a master only when some exceptional condition justified it. The exception was "matters of account," detailed financial calculations, which did not need that showing.

brief-CP-130.sentence: When La Buy refused to vacate, the parties sought mandamus in the Seventh Circuit under the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1651(a).
brief-CP-130.plain: When Judge La Buy refused to "vacate," or cancel, his orders, the parties sought mandamus in the Seventh Circuit, the federal appeals court. Mandamus is an order commanding a judge to do or stop doing something, and they sought it under the All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1651(a), which lets federal courts issue such orders.

brief-CP-130.sentence: Justice Clark’s opinion held that a court of appeals with eventual appellate jurisdiction could issue mandamus in aid of that jurisdiction in proper exceptional circumstances.
brief-CP-130.plain: Justice Clark’s "opinion" held that a "court of appeals" with eventual "appellate jurisdiction," the power to hear an appeal once the case ends, could issue mandamus in aid of that jurisdiction. It could do so only in proper, exceptional circumstances.

brief-CP-130.sentence: Ordinary review after final judgment did not categorically exclude a writ, but the existence of power did not make every erroneous discretionary order immediately reviewable.
brief-CP-130.plain: The availability of ordinary review after "final judgment," the end of the case, did not categorically rule out a "writ" of mandamus. But having that power did not make every mistaken "discretionary" order, a judgment call left to the trial judge, immediately "reviewable" by the appeals court.

brief-CP-130.sentence: Clark considered the arrangement nearly an abdication of judicial function, depriving the parties of the trial before the court contemplated by the rule.
brief-CP-130.plain: Clark considered the arrangement nearly an "abdication," or abandonment, of the judge's core function of deciding the case. It deprived the parties of the trial before the court that the rule "contemplated," meaning intended.

brief-CP-130.sentence: He distinguished an erroneous exercise of jurisdiction from exceeding or refusing jurisdiction.
brief-CP-130.plain: Justice Brennan distinguished a judge's erroneous exercise of "jurisdiction," the court's power to act, from exceeding that power or refusing to use it. In his view mandamus fits only the latter; ordinary mistakes must wait for a normal appeal.

brief-CP-130.sentence: For Brennan, the All Writs Act protected appellate jurisdiction conferred elsewhere rather than independently authorizing review of otherwise unappealable interlocutory orders.
brief-CP-130.plain: For Brennan, the All Writs Act protected an appeals court's appellate jurisdiction granted by other statutes. It did not independently authorize review of interlocutory (mid-case) orders that were otherwise "unappealable," meaning not yet open to appeal.

brief-CP-130.sentence: Expense and delay were consequences of Congress’s finality policy, not enough to evade it.
brief-CP-130.plain: Expense and delay were consequences of Congress’s "finality policy," its choice that appeals generally wait until the case is over. They were not enough to justify evading that policy.

brief-CP-130.sentence: He feared the majority effectively created discretionary interlocutory appeals without Congress and would worsen congestion through petitions and trial delays.
brief-CP-130.plain: Brennan feared the "majority" (the Justices joining the Court's opinion) had effectively created "discretionary" interlocutory appeals, mid-case appeals allowed whenever an appeals court chooses, without Congress authorizing them. He also feared more petitions and trial delays would worsen court congestion.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Applicants promised no bucket-shop use or redistribution; Western Union’s controlled Gold & Stock Telegraph subsidiary supplied tickers.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: Applicants approved to receive the prices promised not to use them in a "bucket shop," an illegal operation for betting on price movements, and not to redistribute them. The tickers (price-printing machines) came from Gold & Stock Telegraph, a subsidiary Western Union controlled.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Moore, as Odd-Lot’s president, brought a federal antitrust bill alleging interstate dealings, control of national price information, restraint, and monopolization.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: Moore, as Odd-Lot’s president, brought a federal "antitrust bill," a suit in equity under the antitrust laws. It alleged interstate dealings, the exchange's control of national price information, restraint of trade, and monopolization.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: The exchange defended its control and counterclaimed that Odd-Lot obtained quotations unlawfully, directly or through another person, then distributed them to members supplying bucket shops.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: The exchange defended its control and "counterclaimed," suing Odd-Lot back in the same case. It claimed Odd-Lot obtained the "quotations" (price quotes) unlawfully, directly or through another person, and then distributed them to members supplying bucket shops.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: By stipulation it directed final dismissal of the bill and a permanent counterclaim injunction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: By "stipulation," an agreement of the parties, the appeals court directed final "dismissal of the bill," ending Odd-Lot's suit for good. It also directed a permanent injunction on the exchange's "counterclaim," barring Odd-Lot from taking the quotations.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Only ministerial implementation remained, so the Supreme Court treated the decree as final.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: Only "ministerial" implementation remained, meaning routine steps involving no further judgment. So the Supreme Court treated the "decree," the equity court's judgment, as final and ready for review.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Justice Sutherland’s opinion put aside a Federal Trade Commission Act theory because proceedings had to begin before that Commission.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: Justice Sutherland’s "opinion" put aside Odd-Lot's theory under the Federal Trade Commission Act. Claims under that law had to begin with a proceeding before the Commission itself, not a private lawsuit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Selective disposition of the exchange’s own information was treated as private business, with incidental rather than direct or unreasonable effects on interstate trade.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: The Court saw the exchange's choice of who received its price information as its own private business. Any effect on trade between states was indirect, so, in the Court's view then, the antitrust laws were not violated.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: A substantial, nonfrivolous statutory claim gave the court power to decide its sufficiency; only a claim plainly without color of merit would fail at that threshold.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: A substantial, "nonfrivolous" federal statutory claim, meaning a serious one and not obviously baseless, gave the court power to decide whether the claim was sufficient. Only a claim plainly without color of merit, with no plausible basis at all, would fail at that threshold.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Odd-Lot made a serious but insufficient antitrust claim, dismissed on the merits rather than for want of jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: Odd-Lot made a serious but insufficient antitrust claim. It was dismissed on the merits, because it lost, rather than for "want of jurisdiction," meaning lack of the court's power to hear it, so the court kept power over the case, including the counterclaim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Historical Equity Rule 30 required a counterclaim arising from the transaction underlying the suit and separately allowed optional independent equitable claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: Historical Equity Rule 30, from the old federal equity rules, required a defendant to raise any counterclaim arising from the transaction underlying the plaintiff's suit. It separately allowed the defendant to choose to add independent, unrelated equitable claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: The Court expressly reserved the independent-federal-jurisdiction question for the optional category.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: The Court expressly "reserved," meaning left undecided, whether a counterclaim in the optional, unrelated category would need its own independent basis for federal jurisdiction.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.sentence: Extra facts about appropriation did not destroy the logical connection, because complete factual identity would make the transaction rule impractical.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-311.plain: The counterclaim involved some extra facts about how Odd-Lot took the quotes, but the two claims were still logically connected. Requiring identical facts would make the same-transaction rule unworkable.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: Wrongful-death claimants sued the carrier, Korean Air Lines, and their actions were consolidated in the District of Columbia for pretrial proceedings under 28 U.S.C. § 1407, the multidistrict-litigation statute.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: Claimants bringing "wrongful-death" suits, for losses caused by a death, sued the "carrier," Korean Air Lines. Their actions were "consolidated," or combined, in the District of Columbia for "pretrial proceedings" (everything before trial) under 28 U.S.C. § 1407, the multidistrict-litigation statute.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: The plaintiffs sought partial summary judgment declaring that this failure deprived Korean Air Lines of the $75,000 Warsaw/Montreal liability limit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: The "plaintiffs" sought partial summary judgment, a ruling on one issue without a trial. They wanted a declaration that this failure (printing the ticket notice in type smaller than required) cost Korean Air Lines the $75,000 Warsaw/Montreal liability limit, the damages cap set by the Warsaw Convention as raised by the Montreal Agreement.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: Whether the New York actions retained the Second Circuit's interpretation could therefore affect the recoveries available in the same consolidated proceeding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: The Second Circuit, the federal appeals court covering New York, had accepted the plaintiffs' reading. So whether the New York "actions," or lawsuits, kept the Second Circuit's interpretation could change the recoveries available within the same "consolidated" proceeding.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: Montreal was an intercarrier special agreement, not a negotiated amendment of the treaty.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: The Montreal Agreement was an "intercarrier special agreement," a deal among the airlines themselves. It was not a negotiated "amendment" of the treaty by governments.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: Robinson relied on Article XXIII's adherence provision to conclude that the United States and Korea shared treaty obligations at least for the Convention's unamended portions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: Judge Robinson relied on Article XXIII's "adherence provision," the clause on how countries join the treaty. He concluded that the United States and Korea shared treaty obligations at least for the Convention's unamended portions, since Korea had joined the amended version and the United States had not.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: Adding one would alter the bargain that exchanged increased limits for reduced defenses.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: Montreal expressly waived certain airline defenses but contained no express waiver of the liability limit. Adding one would alter the "bargain," the deal in which airlines accepted increased limits in exchange for reduced defenses.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: The district court certified an interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), which the D.C. Circuit permitted.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: The "district court" (the trial court) certified an "interlocutory appeal," an immediate appeal of a mid-case ruling, under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b). The D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court, agreed to hear it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: The plaintiffs relied on Van Dusen v. Barrack, which preserved transferor state law, including choice-of-law rules, after a defendant-initiated convenience transfer of diversity litigation under § 1404(a).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: The "plaintiffs" relied on Van Dusen v. Barrack, which held that after a defendant-initiated convenience transfer under § 1404(a), "transferor state law" still applies. That is the law of the state where the case began, including its choice-of-law rules, in "diversity litigation" (state-law suits in federal court between citizens of different states).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: That rule served the Erie principle that a federal forum should not change the state-law result available where the action began.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: That rule served the "Erie principle": a federal "forum," meaning the court where a case is heard, should not change the state-law result available where the action began.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: It did not give litigants an analogous entitlement to a particular circuit's understanding of one body of federal law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: It did not give "litigants," the parties to a lawsuit, a similar right to keep a particular "circuit's" (regional federal appeals court's) understanding of a single body of federal law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: Federal venue selects a convenient location; it does not create a substantive right to a favorable federal interpretation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: Federal "venue" rules just pick a convenient location for the case. They do not create a "substantive right," a right affecting the outcome, to a favorable interpretation of federal law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: A transferee judge should consider other circuits' decisions carefully, but those decisions do not bind it merely because an action began in those circuits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: A transferee judge, the one who receives transferred cases, should consider other "circuits'" decisions carefully. But those regional appeals courts' decisions do not bind the judge merely because an action began within their territory.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: A prior determination actually precluding the parties also differed from circuit precedent that had never resolved their claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: A prior determination that actually precluded these parties, binding them because it decided their own dispute, also differed from "circuit" precedent. That precedent came from other cases and had never resolved these parties' "claims."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.sentence: The concurrence acknowledged that no controlling decision had settled the interaction of circuit precedent and law of the case.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-KOREAN-AIR-1987.plain: The concurrence, a separate opinion agreeing with the result, acknowledged that no controlling decision had settled how circuit precedent interacts with "law of the case." That doctrine says a ruling made earlier in the same case should generally stand at later stages.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: The appellate court distinguished an appellate law-of-the-case ruling from a trial judge’s revisable decision.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: The "appellate court" distinguished an appellate "law-of-the-case" ruling, an appeals court decision that binds later stages of the same case, from a trial judge’s decision. A trial judge may revise his or her own earlier rulings before the case ends.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Equitable factfinding did not replace jury factfinding on damages claims.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: "Equitable factfinding," the judge's fact-finding on the non-jury equitable claims, did not replace the jury's fact-finding on the claims for money damages.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: The Institute could rely on the Foundation’s jury demand without making another demand.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: The Institute could rely on the Foundation’s "jury demand," its formal request for a jury trial, without filing another demand of its own.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: The first judge had rejected rescission and related restitution; the later summary-disposition ruling found no demonstrated measurement method and regarded the alleged loss as speculative.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: The first judge had rejected "rescission" (undoing the deal) and related "restitution" (returning what was paid). The later "ruling" on summary disposition, decided without trial, found no demonstrated method for measuring damages and regarded the "alleged" loss as speculative, too uncertain to put a number on.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Although a jury generally determines amount, the court determines legal entitlement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: Juries decide how much money is owed, but only after the judge decides that the law allows any recovery at all.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: On the Institute’s cross-appeal, the court applied Michigan’s then-governing standing requirements of concrete injury to a legally protected interest, causation, and likely redressability.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: On the Institute’s "cross-appeal," its own appeal from the same judgment, the court applied Michigan’s then-governing "standing" requirements for who may sue. These required a "concrete" injury (a real harm) to a legally protected interest, "causation" linking it to the defendant, and likely "redressability," meaning a court ruling could probably fix it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: The Attorney General, a co-trustee, or someone with a special interest could enforce such a trust, but the settlor or heirs could not do so merely in that capacity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: The Attorney General, a co-trustee, or someone with a "special interest" (a particular personal stake) could enforce such a charitable trust. But the "settlor," the person who created the trust by giving the money, or the settlor's heirs could not do so merely in that role.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Separately, the court reviewed the unambiguous agreement de novo.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: Separately, the court "reviewed" the agreement "de novo," meaning fresh, without deferring to the trial court, because the contract's words were unambiguous.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Earlier years of contributions could not support a later promise.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: Gifts the Foundation had already given in past years could not count as payment for a new promise; to be enforceable, a promise must be given in exchange for something.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: The court regarded the naming undertaking as gratuitous and unenforceable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: The court regarded the "undertaking" about naming the center as gratuitous, a promise given without anything bargained for in exchange. So it was "unenforceable" in court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Corporate counsel represents the corporation, not its shareholders or agents.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: "Corporate counsel," a company's lawyers, represent the "corporation" itself, not its "shareholders" (owners) or its agents (people who act for it).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: No identified action showed independent representation of the Foundation, and the firm’s agency agreement with the center created no third-party rights.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: No identified action showed the law firm independently representing the Foundation as its own lawyer. And the firm’s "agency" agreement with the center, an agreement to act on the center's behalf, created no "third-party" rights, meaning rights an outsider like the Foundation could enforce.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Fraudulent-concealment tolling required affirmative concealment rather than silence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: Fraudulent-concealment "tolling," which pauses the filing deadline when a defendant hides a claim, required affirmative concealment, meaning active steps to hide it. Mere silence was not enough.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.sentence: Trial-level sanctions were not properly before the appellate court without a cross-appeal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-012.plain: Trial-level "sanctions," penalties for improper litigation conduct, were not properly before the "appellate court" because no "cross-appeal" had been filed. A party wanting them reviewed had to file its own appeal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: On interlocutory appeal, the Court of Appeals directed judgment on most claims, preserving strict liability against Petoseed and one express warranty against Rispens, and treated both seed-price caps as effective in contract and tort.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: On "interlocutory appeal," an appeal taken before the case ended, the Court of Appeals "directed judgment" on most claims, ordering them resolved without trial. It kept only a strict liability (no-fault product) claim against Petoseed and one "express warranty" (specific promise) claim against Rispens, and treated both "seed-price caps," limits on liability to the price of the seed, as effective in "contract" and tort.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Hall Farms sought transfer to restore the broader trial ruling.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: Hall Farms "sought transfer," asking the Indiana Supreme Court to take the case, in order to restore the trial court's broader ruling that had let more claims go forward.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2, whether entirely written statements created warranties was for the court.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: Under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2, the sales law, whether statements that were entirely written created warranties was a question for the court, meaning the judge rather than a jury.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Petoseed’s top-quality description was puffery, but its promise of high vitality, vigor, and germination described performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: Petoseed’s description of its seed as top quality was "puffery," empty sales talk that creates no warranty. But its promise of high vitality, vigor, and germination described "performance," a specific claim about how the seed would grow.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Rispens as movant had not negated material issues; the intermediate court improperly shifted that burden to Hall Farms.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: Rispens, as the "movant" (the party asking for judgment without trial), had not shown the absence of "material" issues, meaning important disputed facts. The "intermediate court," the Court of Appeals, improperly shifted that burden to Hall Farms.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Rispens’s written disclaimer, however, omitted merchantability, was inconspicuous, and appeared on an unsigned reverse side, failing written-disclaimer requirements.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: Rispens’s written "disclaimer," the clause trying to cancel warranties, failed the code's written-disclaimer requirements. It did not mention merchantability, was inconspicuous (not easy to notice), and appeared on an unsigned reverse side.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Trade usage could still modify or exclude the warranty without invariably requiring actual knowledge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: "Trade usage," a regular practice in the industry, could still modify or exclude the warranty. It did not always require proof of the buyer's "actual knowledge" of that practice, though it binds only parties in the trade or who should have known of it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: The majority held that crop loss exceeding seed price and a latent defect did not make that monetary cap fail its essential purpose: limiting exposure was precisely its purpose.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: The "majority" held that a crop loss exceeding the seed price, and a "latent defect" (a hidden flaw), did not make the "monetary cap" fail of its essential purpose. Limiting the seller's financial exposure was precisely the cap's purpose.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Latency alone likewise did not make allocation unconscionable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: "Latency," the fact that the defect was hidden, likewise did not by itself make the risk allocation "unconscionable," meaning shockingly unfair.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: The historical Indiana strict-liability statute covered sudden, major property damage but excluded gradually developing damage and resulting economic loss.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: The historical Indiana "strict-liability" statute, imposing liability for defective products without proof of fault, covered sudden, major property damage. It excluded damage that developed gradually and the resulting "economic loss," meaning purely financial losses.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: It nevertheless rejected an alternative suggestion that a distributor escaped merely because fault concerned the manufacturer; indemnity would follow liability where appropriate.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: The court nevertheless rejected an alternative suggestion that a distributor escapes liability merely because the fault lay with the manufacturer. Where appropriate, "indemnity," reimbursement from the party truly at fault, would follow liability.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.sentence: Warranty rules allocated commercial risk, and negligence could not bypass their negotiated limits.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-090.plain: Businesses divide the risk of disappointing products through warranty terms. Letting a negligence claim recover the same financial loss would let buyers escape the limits they agreed to.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: It designated the National Arbitration Forum and its code, provided a hearing in the federal district containing the billing address, invoked the Federal Arbitration Act, and expressly warned that claims otherwise brought in court or representative litigation would require arbitration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: The new term "designated" (named) the National Arbitration Forum and its code of rules, and provided a hearing in the federal district containing the billing address. It invoked the Federal Arbitration Act and expressly warned that claims otherwise brought in court, or in "representative litigation" such as class actions, would require arbitration.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: On November 22, before service on any defendant, Sky Scanner Satellite voluntarily appeared and removed to the Northern District of Mississippi, invoking federal statutes including the Truth in Lending Act.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: On November 22, before any defendant had been formally served, Sky Scanner Satellite voluntarily appeared and "removed" the case from state court to the Northern District of Mississippi, a federal court. It relied on federal "statutes," including the Truth in Lending Act, a consumer-credit law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Judge Neal Biggers remanded the action on August 23.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Judge Neal Biggers "remanded" the action, sending it back to state court, on August 23.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: On September 7, Bank One brought this separate action against Coates under § 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act and identical actions against the other state plaintiffs.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: On September 7, Bank One brought this separate "action" (lawsuit) against Coates under § 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act, which lets a party ask a federal court to order arbitration. It filed identical actions against the other state-court "plaintiffs."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Coates asked federal Chief Judge Tom S. Lee to abstain, to join additional parties including local agent or employee S. Broadwater and dismiss for lost diversity, or to permit discovery before deciding arbitration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Coates asked federal Chief Judge Tom S. Lee to "abstain," meaning step aside in favor of the state case. Alternatively, Coates sought to join more parties, including local "agent" or employee S. Broadwater, and have the case dismissed for lost diversity (the sides no longer being from different states), or to allow "discovery," meaning fact-gathering, before deciding "arbitration."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: The Federal Arbitration Act authorized enforcement but supplied no independent federal jurisdiction.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: The Federal Arbitration Act authorized courts to enforce arbitration agreements but supplied no independent federal "jurisdiction." A federal court still needed some other basis for its power to hear the case.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: The parties accepted that federal-question jurisdiction was absent in light of the earlier remand, but Bank One’s Ohio citizenship, Coates’s Mississippi citizenship, and more than $75,000 in controversy supplied diversity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: The parties accepted that "federal-question jurisdiction," power based on a claim arising under federal law, was absent given the earlier "remand" to state court. But "diversity" jurisdiction existed: Bank One’s "citizenship" was Ohio, Coates’s was Mississippi, and more than $75,000 was in controversy.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Other alleged joint tortfeasors could remain in state court without becoming indispensable here.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Other alleged joint tortfeasors, others claimed to share responsibility for the same harm, could remain in the state case. They were not "indispensable" here, meaning this federal case could fairly proceed without them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: The exceptional-circumstances abstention principles of Colorado River and Moses H. Cone favored exercising jurisdiction.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: The "abstention" principles of Colorado River and Moses H. Cone let federal courts step aside for parallel state cases only in exceptional circumstances. Those principles favored exercising "jurisdiction," that is, keeping the case.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Piecemeal proceedings did not override the arbitration statute’s willingness to separate arbitrable and nonarbitrable disputes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: "Piecemeal proceedings," splitting the dispute between court and arbitration, did not override the arbitration statute. That law accepts separating "arbitrable" disputes (those that must go to arbitration) from nonarbitrable ones.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Lee applied the inquiry into a valid agreement, coverage, and any external legal obstacle, recognizing generally applicable contract defenses under § 2.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Judge Lee asked whether a valid arbitration agreement existed, whether it covered the dispute, and whether any external legal obstacle barred arbitration. He recognized that "generally applicable" contract defenses, those that apply to any contract, such as fraud or unconscionability, could defeat the agreement under § 2.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: A genuine making-of-agreement dispute could require trial under § 4, but an unsupported denial of assent did not create one.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: A genuine dispute over whether an agreement was ever made could require a trial under § 4. But an unsupported denial of "assent," simply saying one never agreed without evidence, did not create one.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Applying Prima Paint, the Supreme Court’s distinction between fraud concerning an overall contract and fraud specific to arbitration, and the Fifth Circuit’s R. M. Perez decision, Lee sent that overall procurement challenge to arbitration even though Coates called it fraud in the factum.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Lee applied Prima Paint, the Supreme Court’s distinction between fraud concerning the overall "contract" and fraud specific to the arbitration clause, and the Fifth Circuit’s R. M. Perez decision. So he sent Coates's challenge to the "procurement" of the whole agreement, meaning how it was obtained, to arbitration, even though Coates called it "fraud in the factum," deception about the very nature of what was signed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Nor did a valid arbitration agreement require a separate clear and unmistakable Seventh Amendment waiver: moving the covered dispute to arbitration necessarily removed its judicial jury trial.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Nor did a valid arbitration agreement require a separate, clear and unmistakable waiver of the Seventh Amendment jury right. Moving the covered dispute to arbitration necessarily removed its jury trial in court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: Under Green Tree Financial v. Randolph, the Supreme Court’s arbitration-cost decision, Coates needed to establish likely prohibitive expense rather than merely assert it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: Under Green Tree Financial v. Randolph, the Supreme Court’s decision on arbitration costs, Coates had to establish that arbitration would likely be prohibitively expensive. Merely asserting it was not enough.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.sentence: They could not serve as its officers or directors, had duties of neutrality and conflict disclosure, and faced one peremptory strike per party and unlimited cause challenges.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-027.plain: The arbitrators could not serve as the Forum's officers or directors and had duties to stay neutral and disclose conflicts. Each party had one "peremptory strike," the right to reject an arbitrator without giving a reason, and unlimited "cause challenges," objections based on a specific reason such as bias.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The manual disclaimed contractual obligations about salary, salary ranges, movement within those ranges, and benefits.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The personnel manual said its sections on pay and benefits were not binding promises. It did not say that about everything in it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The district court granted defense summary judgment, denied Cabaness’s cross-motion on contract formation, and rejected postjudgment affidavits from two city employees about intent to create a contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The "district court" (the trial court) granted the defense "summary judgment," ending the claims without trial, and denied Cabaness’s "cross-motion" asking it to rule that a contract was formed. It also rejected "postjudgment" affidavits, sworn statements filed after the ruling, from two city "employees" about intent to create a contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The Utah Supreme Court reviewed legal summary-judgment questions for correctness and evidentiary exclusions for abuse of discretion.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The Utah Supreme Court "reviewed" the legal questions in summary judgment for correctness, deciding them fresh. It reviewed the exclusion of evidence only for "abuse of discretion," reversing only if the trial judge's choice was unreasonable.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The employer’s answer had denied a contract, so due diligence required obtaining that evidence before judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The employer’s "answer," its formal written response to the complaint, had denied that a contract existed. So due diligence required Cabaness to obtain that evidence before judgment, not after.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: Safety-committee factual findings qualified under the public-records hearsay exception.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The safety committee's factual findings qualified under the "public-records hearsay exception." Hearsay, an out-of-court statement offered to prove its truth, is usually barred, but official records of factual findings from an investigation can be admitted.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: For an alleged continuing pattern of intentional infliction, the court held limitations ran from the last injury or cessation of conduct, permitting recovery for the whole course.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: For an alleged continuing pattern of "intentional infliction" of emotional distress, the court held that "limitations," the filing deadline, ran from the last injury or the end of the conduct. That permitted "recovery," an award of damages, for the whole course of conduct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: Conduct outside Cabaness’s presence required particularly compelling circumstances, including intent to injure him while absent.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: Conduct outside Cabaness’s presence could count only in particularly compelling circumstances. These included conduct intended to injure him while he was absent.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The court declined to extend intentional-infliction liability to Michaelis merely for failing to curb someone else’s conduct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The court declined to extend "intentional-infliction" liability, for intentionally causing severe emotional distress, to Michaelis merely because he failed to curb someone else’s conduct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: Because reasonable minds could differ, summary judgment could not resolve that element against Cabaness.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: Because "reasonable minds could differ," meaning reasonable jurors could reach different conclusions on it, summary judgment could not resolve that "element," a required part of the claim, against Cabaness.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: Definite communicated manual promises could form a unilateral contract accepted and supported by continued service.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: Definite promises in a manual, communicated to employees, could form a "unilateral contract," one in which the employer's promise is accepted by performance rather than by a return promise. The employee's continued service both accepted the offer and supported it as consideration.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The relevant provisions created a contract as a matter of law with an implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The relevant manual provisions created a contract as a matter of law, meaning the court could decide it without a jury. That contract carried an "implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing," an automatic duty not to undermine the other side's benefit of the deal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: The governing pre-July-2004 immunity statute waived immunity for any contractual obligations.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: The governing pre-July-2004 version of the immunity statute waived immunity, the government's usual protection from being sued, for any contractual obligations.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: An emotional-anguish exception in a separate negligence waiver did not carry over into the unqualified contract waiver.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: An "emotional-anguish" exception, which kept immunity for claims of emotional harm, appeared in a separate waiver covering negligence. It did not carry over into the unqualified waiver for contract claims.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: Drawing on Beck, its insurance-contract decision, and personal-contract authorities, the court allowed the possibility where such harm was foreseeable and explicitly within the parties’ contemplation at formation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: Drawing on Beck, its insurance-contract decision, and cases on personal contracts, the court allowed that emotional-distress damages for breach might be possible. That required the harm to be "foreseeable" and explicitly within the "parties’ contemplation," meaning both sides had it in mind when they formed the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.sentence: Neither side invoked a statutory at-will exception, and Cabaness admitted not pleading a clear, substantial public-policy violation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-018.plain: Neither side invoked a statutory exception to at-will employment, the rule that a job can be ended for any reason. Cabaness also admitted not "pleading," meaning alleging in his complaint, a clear and substantial violation of public policy.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.sentence: The assigned account contrasts this lease with force-majeure clauses expressly preserving the duty to pay rent.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.plain: The assigned account contrasts this lease with force-majeure clauses (provisions excusing performance after disasters and similar events) that expressly preserve the "duty" to pay rent. This lease's clause had no such carve-out.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.sentence: In the March 20, 2023 order, Judge Jennifer S.D. Roberts addressed BP’s objections to proximate causation, reliance on newer cases, interpretation of the lease, and whether rent had only been postponed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.plain: In the March 20, 2023 "order," Judge Jennifer S.D. Roberts addressed BP’s "objections," its arguments against her ruling. These concerned proximate causation (whether the closure directly caused the nonpayment), reliance on newer cases, interpretation of the lease, and whether rent had only been postponed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.sentence: The newer authorities involved either common-law excuses without a force-majeure clause or clauses containing materially different language.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.plain: The newer cases involved either "common-law excuses," judge-made doctrines such as impossibility applied where a lease has no force-majeure clause, or clauses with materially different wording.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.sentence: She read this agreement as excusing rent during the force-majeure event rather than accumulating a debt payable afterward.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.plain: She read this lease to mean Saks owed no rent at all for the mandated-closure period, not that unpaid rent piled up to be paid later.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.sentence: The court also explained that equitable forfeiture reasoning had been an alternative ground in case an appellate court rejected the contract analysis.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.plain: The court also explained that its "equitable forfeiture" reasoning, a fairness-based principle against enforcing an unjust loss of rights, had been an "alternative ground." It was a backup in case an "appellate court" rejected the court's "contract" analysis.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.sentence: It also applied the lease’s provision for reasonable expenses associated with obtaining a favorable final outcome, excluding unsuccessful or unrelated work.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-053.plain: The lease let a party recover reasonable expenses of winning the case, and the court applied it to Saks's legal costs, leaving out work that failed or was unrelated.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-101.sentence: The assigned account calls the claimant a subcontractor while acknowledging it apparently was a sub-subcontractor; it says the court used simplified facts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-101.plain: The assigned account calls the "claimant," the party making the claim, a subcontractor while acknowledging it apparently was a sub-subcontractor, hired by a subcontractor. It says the court used simplified facts.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-101.sentence: Receiving contract rights and undertaking someone else’s debts are distinct steps.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-101.plain: Taking over someone's rights under a contract is a different step from agreeing to pay that person's debts. So the hospital's taking over Walsh's steel contract did not by itself make it pay what Walsh owed; the steel firm had to show the assignment and its acceptance did that.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: Its four counts challenged substantive competition-rulemaking authority, excess of any such authority, retroactivity, and the Commerce Clause.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: Its four "counts," the separate claims in the complaint, challenged the FTC's substantive authority to make competition rules at all and argued the rule exceeded any such authority. They also challenged the rule's "retroactivity" (reaching existing contracts) and its validity under the Commerce Clause.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: Judge Timothy J. Corrigan found federal-question jurisdiction, Ocala venue, and standing because the broker was subject to the rule.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: Judge Timothy J. Corrigan found "federal-question jurisdiction," since the case arose under federal law, and proper venue in Ocala. He also found "standing," the right to sue, because the broker was subject to the rule.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: The broker had to clearly establish substantial likely success, imminent irreparable injury, favorable equities, and public interest; the latter two merged because government opposed relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: The broker had to clearly establish substantial "likely success" on the merits, imminent irreparable injury (harm money cannot fix), favorable equities (the balance of hardships), and the public interest. The last two merged because the government was the party opposing relief.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: Applying Loper Bright, the Supreme Court decision requiring independent statutory judgment while respecting actual delegations, Corrigan treated injunction and stay standards as essentially alike.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: Corrigan applied Loper Bright, the Supreme Court decision requiring judges to exercise independent judgment about what a statute means while respecting actual "delegations," powers Congress truly gave an agency. He treated the standards for an injunction and for a stay (postponement) of the rule as essentially alike.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: He initially rejected likely success on a claim that the FTC possessed no substantive competition-rulemaking authority.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: He initially found no "likely success" on the claim that the FTC had no "substantive competition-rulemaking authority," meaning no power to issue binding rules about unfair methods of competition.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: Standalone commerce, separation-of-powers, and nondelegation theories likewise lacked demonstrated likely success.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: Standalone theories based on the commerce power, "separation-of-powers" (the division of power among the three branches), and nondelegation (limits on Congress handing off lawmaking power) likewise lacked demonstrated "likely success."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: The major-questions doctrine required clear congressional authorization for extraordinary assertions of economic and political power.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: The "major-questions doctrine" required clear authorization from Congress when an agency makes extraordinary claims of economic and political power.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: The broker showed likely success on Count II, excessive statutory authority.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: The broker showed "likely success" on Count II, its claim that the rule exceeded the FTC's "statutory authority," the power Congress gave it by statute.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: The broker had not forfeited irreparable harm by waiting briefly to sue before the effective date.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: The broker had not "forfeited," or lost, its irreparable-harm argument by waiting briefly to sue before the rule's "effective date," the day it would take effect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: They would not readily be recovered from government after invalidation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: Those compliance costs could not readily be "recovered" from the government if the rule were later invalidated, which made the harm irreparable.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: The combined equities and public interest favored preserving the status quo where statutory authorization was likely lacking.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: The combined "equities" (the balance of hardships) and public interest favored preserving the "status quo," keeping things as they were, where the FTC likely lacked statutory authorization for the rule.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.sentence: It neither set aside the rule for everyone nor awarded damages or final merits judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-002.plain: The order protected only this broker: it neither "set aside" the rule for everyone, meaning cancel it nationwide, nor awarded damages. Nor was it a "final merits judgment," a final decision on who wins the case.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: The First Circuit examined the evidence favorably to those asserting supplier liability, without treating product identification as established.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: The First Circuit, the federal appeals court, viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to those asserting the suppliers' "liability," or legal responsibility. It did not treat product identification, meaning whose blanket was used, as established.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: Maine negligence and statutory strict liability required a warning duty, inadequate warning, and proximate causation.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: Under Maine law, both "negligence" (carelessness) and statutory "strict liability" (liability without fault) claims required a "warning duty," an obligation to warn, and an inadequate warning. They also required "proximate causation," meaning the inadequate warning legally caused the harm.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: It predicted that Maine would accept a sophisticated-user doctrine as a corollary of obvious danger, rather than reporting an express state supreme court adoption.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: The court predicted that Maine would accept a "sophisticated-user doctrine," under which a seller need not warn expert users about dangers they already know, as a corollary of the "obvious danger" rule. It did not report that Maine's supreme court had expressly adopted it.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: Excluding that opinion was not an abuse of discretion, and the challenge had not come without notice.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: Excluding that expert opinion was not an "abuse of discretion," meaning the trial judge's choice was within reasonable bounds. And the challenge to the opinion had not come without notice to the claimants.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: The panel reserved whether Maine would adopt a learned-intermediary exception and whether it would apply.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: The panel "reserved," or left undecided, whether Maine would adopt a "learned-intermediary" exception and whether it would apply here. That exception lets a supplier meet its duty by warning a knowledgeable middleman, such as an employer, instead of every end user.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: Prevention of this operation and loss therefore depended on speculation.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: Whether a better warning would have prevented this operation and the loss therefore depended on "speculation," meaning guesswork without supporting evidence.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: Maine’s presumption that a warning would be read and heeded still did not establish that this cutting operation involved the prohibited condition.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: Maine’s "presumption" that a warning would be "read and heeded," meaning people are assumed to read and follow warnings, did not close the gap. It still did not establish that this cutting operation involved the condition the warning prohibited.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: But the suppliers had represented below that they were not asserting Austin used the wrong blanket, apparently waiving that ground.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: But the suppliers had told the trial court ("below") that they were not asserting Austin used the wrong blanket. They were thus apparently "waiving," or knowingly giving up, that ground.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: An earlier ladder decision illustrated why an expert’s disagreement with an industry standard, unsupported by trade customs, literature, or reasonable consumer expectations, did not establish an objective deficiency.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: In an earlier ladder case, an expert's opinion that a product should have been better than the industry standard, with nothing else to back it, did not prove the product was below ordinary quality.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: Maine allowed this warranty theory without contractual privity, so the absence of a direct sale did not defeat it.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: Maine allowed this "warranty" theory without "contractual" privity, a direct buyer-seller relationship between the parties. So the absence of a direct sale did not defeat it.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.sentence: An expert’s belief that the documents would have been found if produced did not establish clear error without evidence of an exhaustive search or comparable support.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0092.plain: An expert’s belief that the documents would have been found if they had been produced did not show "clear error," a definite mistake in the trial judge's fact-finding. That would need evidence of an exhaustive search or comparable support.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.sentence: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s 1996 Generic Environmental Impact Statement classified storage of spent nuclear fuel in pools as a Category I issue with a small environmental impact.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.plain: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s 1996 Generic Environmental Impact Statement, one environmental study covering all nuclear plants, "classified" storage of spent (used) nuclear fuel in pools as a Category I issue with a small environmental impact. A Category I issue is common to all plants, so it need not be studied plant by plant.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.sentence: The Commission’s regulations treated renewal as a major federal action requiring an environmental impact statement.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.plain: The Commission’s "regulations," its own binding rules, treated license renewal as a major federal action. Under federal environmental law, such significant decisions require a full environmental impact statement.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.sentence: The court had jurisdiction over final Commission orders under 28 U.S.C. § 2342(4).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.plain: The court had "jurisdiction," the power to hear the case, over final Commission "orders" under 28 U.S.C. § 2342(4). That statute lets the federal courts of appeals directly review the NRC's final decisions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.sentence: The standard was extremely limited and highly deferential, at the upper end of arbitrary-and-capricious review.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.plain: The standard of review was extremely limited and highly "deferential," meaning the court gave the agency great leeway. It sat at the upper end of "arbitrary-and-capricious" review, the test for whether agency action is unreasonable, so the agency's refusal would be overturned only in rare, compelling cases.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.sentence: The states argued both that scientific evidence made the risk too significant to call small and that mitigation varying among plants could not support a generic classification.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.plain: The states argued that scientific "evidence" made the fire risk too significant to call small. They also argued that because safety measures (mitigation) varied among plants, a "generic classification" covering all plants at once could not stand.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.sentence: One judicial note reserved whether the National Environmental Policy Act required consideration of terrorism in license-renewal statements, an issue dividing the circuits.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-042.plain: One judicial note, a footnote, "reserved" (left undecided) whether the National Environmental Policy Act requires considering terrorism in license-renewal environmental statements. The federal appeals courts, or circuits, were divided on that issue.

cp-jeub.sentence: On that account, B/G asserted a possible right to reimbursement or indemnity if the patrons recovered against it.
cp-jeub.plain: On that basis, B/G asserted a possible right to reimbursement or "indemnity," meaning Swift covering B/G's whole loss, if the patrons "recovered," or won damages, against B/G.

cp-jeub.sentence: Before answering their complaints, it obtained an ex parte order adding Swift as a third-party defendant.
cp-jeub.plain: Before "answering" the patrons' complaints, meaning filing its formal response, B/G obtained an "ex parte" order, one granted without hearing from the other side. The order added Swift as a "third-party defendant," a party the defendant brings into the suit to claim against.

cp-jeub.sentence: Swift argued that Rule 14 created procedure only.
cp-jeub.plain: Swift argued that Rule 14, the federal rule letting defendants bring in third parties, created procedure only. In Swift's view it could not create a right to recover that state law did not give.

cp-jeub.sentence: Minnesota law controlled B/G’s right to contribution or indemnity, and B/G had neither paid a judgment nor otherwise incurred the loss required to enforce such a claim.
cp-jeub.plain: Minnesota law controlled B/G’s right to contribution (a share of the loss) or indemnity (the whole loss). B/G had neither paid a "judgment" nor otherwise suffered the loss required to enforce such a "claim."

cp-jeub.sentence: It could accelerate determination of a contingent obligation without accelerating the substantive right to receive money.
cp-jeub.plain: Rule 14 could speed up deciding a "contingent obligation," a duty to pay that arises only if something else happens first. It did not speed up the "substantive right" to actually receive money, which still depended on B/G's loss.
