cp-jeub.sentence: The court relied on Burris v. American Chicle Company, which allowed judgment against an indemnitor while staying execution until the indemnitee satisfied the plaintiff’s judgment.
cp-jeub.plain: The court relied on Burris v. American Chicle Company, which allowed judgment against an "indemnitor," the party obliged to reimburse. But that court stayed "execution," meaning collection of the judgment, until the indemnitee (the party to be reimbursed) paid the plaintiff's judgment.

cp-jeub.sentence: If B/G proved its account, a food-statute violation might be technical rather than knowing or intentional.
cp-jeub.plain: If B/G's story was true, it broke the food law only technically, not knowingly, so the rule barring contribution for intentional wrongdoing might not apply.

cp-jeub.sentence: One jury could consider the injury and related claim over, while a stay protected Swift from collection before B/G paid or satisfied the patrons’ judgment.
cp-jeub.plain: One jury could consider the injury claims and the related "claim over," B/G's claim passing its liability on to Swift. Meanwhile a "stay," a pause on collection, protected Swift from paying before B/G paid or satisfied the patrons' "judgment."

cp-jeub.sentence: Swift received twenty days after filing of the order to answer, and its exception was reserved.
cp-jeub.plain: Swift received twenty days after the order was filed to "answer," meaning file its response. Its "exception was reserved," meaning its formal objection to the ruling was preserved for appeal.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: A regulation allowed reconsideration when relevant official service-department records had not previously been considered.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: A VA "regulation" allowed a denied claim to be reconsidered when relevant official service-department (military) records had not been considered before. Reconsideration can mean benefits reaching back to the original claim date.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Through one administrative judge, the Board of Veterans’ Appeals read “relevant” to require bearing on the reason for the earlier denial.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Through one administrative judge, the Board of Veterans’ Appeals, the VA's appeals board, read "relevant" to mean records bearing on the reason for the earlier denial.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: The Federal Circuit found both readings plausible and applied Auer deference because the Board’s interpretation was not plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulatory framework.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: The Federal Circuit, the federal appeals court that hears veterans' cases, found both readings plausible. It applied "Auer deference," deferring to an agency's reading of its own rule, because the Board’s interpretation was not "plainly erroneous" (clearly wrong) or inconsistent with the "regulatory" framework.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Justice Kagan’s controlling framework required genuine ambiguity after exhausting text, structure, history, and purpose.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Justice Kagan’s controlling framework allowed deference only for "genuine ambiguity," meaning a regulation that is still truly unclear after a court exhausts its text, structure, history, and purpose.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: The familiar plainly-erroneous formulation did not allow unlimited choice or a more indulgent reasonableness standard than the then-described Chevron regime.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: The familiar "plainly-erroneous" formula did not let an agency choose any reading it liked. Nor did it allow a looser reasonableness test than the "Chevron regime," the deference test then used for agency readings of statutes, as it was described at the time.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Courts had to assess authority, expertise, and fair considered judgment as important, nonexhaustive markers.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Courts had to assess the agency's authority, its expertise, and its "fair considered judgment" (careful, genuine reasoning) as important markers. The list was nonexhaustive, meaning other factors could matter too.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Convenient litigation positions, post hoc rationalizations, and unfair surprise ordinarily defeated deference.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Convenient litigation positions (readings adopted to win a lawsuit), "post hoc rationalizations" (after-the-fact justifications), and unfair surprise to regulated parties ordinarily defeated deference.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: First appearances in briefs generally did not qualify, but Auer’s court-requested amicus position from a nonparty agency illustrated an exception.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Agency views appearing for the first time in briefs generally did not qualify. But Auer’s own facts showed an exception: an "amicus" (friend-of-the-court) position that the Court requested from a "nonparty" agency, one that was not a side in the case.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Without controlling deference, persuasive weight under Skidmore remained possible.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Without controlling deference, an agency view could still get persuasive weight under Skidmore, meaning a court may follow it if its reasoning is convincing.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Roberts, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor joined Kagan’s limits, stare decisis analysis, and disposition.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor "joined" Kagan’s limits, her "stare decisis" analysis (respect for precedent, here keeping Auer), and the disposition. Those parts therefore had five votes and are the Court's binding holding.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: She understood deference as a rebuttable presumption of delegated authority, drawing on agency knowledge of purposes, expertise, accountable policymaking, and uniformity.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Kagan understood deference as a "rebuttable presumption," an assumption that can be overcome, that Congress delegated authority to agencies to resolve unclear points in their rules. It drew on agencies' knowledge of the rules' purposes, their expertise, politically accountable policymaking, and uniformity.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: She read Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706 as not specifying a legal-review standard and § 553 as leaving interpretive explanations distinct from legislative rules: force came from the underlying regulation.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: She read Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706, the judicial-review section, as not specifying a standard for reviewing legal questions. She read § 553 as keeping interpretive explanations separate from "legislative rules" that need public notice and comment, because binding force came from the underlying regulation itself.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Roberts retained Auer on stare decisis grounds and emphasized practical overlap between qualified deference and persuasive, thorough, expert reasoning, while recognizing their conceptual difference.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Roberts kept Auer mainly out of respect for precedent, noting that the limited deference now left looks much like simply being persuaded by good reasoning.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: Gorsuch traced the doctrine to an unexplained wartime dictum and disputed Kagan’s historical account and argued that independent judicial interpretation under § 706, rulemaking procedure under § 553, Article III, and impartial adjudication opposed controlling informal agency readings.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: Gorsuch traced the doctrine to an unexplained wartime "dictum," a passing remark not needed to decide the case, and disputed Kagan’s historical account. He argued that independent judicial interpretation under § 706, rulemaking procedure under § 553, Article III (the Constitution's judicial power), and "impartial" judging all opposed giving controlling weight to informal agency readings.

lrs-i-kisor.sentence: If ambiguity remained, it also needed to ask whether this single Board member’s nonprecedential decision expressed the agency’s considered authoritative view, a concern raised by the Solicitor General.
lrs-i-kisor.plain: If "ambiguity" remained, the lower court also needed to ask whether this single Board member’s "nonprecedential" decision, one not binding in later cases, expressed the "agency’s" considered, authoritative view. The Solicitor General, the federal government's lawyer in the Supreme Court, had raised that concern.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: Its contextual inquiry considered explicitness, repetition or dwelling on the material, and whether a presentation pandered, titillated, or shocked.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The FCC's contextual inquiry considered how explicit the material was, and whether it was repeated or involved "dwelling" on it, meaning lingering over it. It also asked whether the presentation pandered, titillated (aroused), or shocked.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: After the Supreme Court’s earlier broadcast-indecency decision, FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, the Commission generally separated literal descriptions from nonliteral expletives and required repetition before treating expletives as actionable.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: After the Supreme Court’s earlier "broadcast-indecency" decision, FCC v. Pacifica Foundation, the Commission generally separated literal descriptions of sexual or excretory activity from nonliteral expletives used as mere exclamations. It treated expletives as "actionable," meaning punishable, only if they were repeated.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: The Commission rejected the categorical protection that fleeting expletives had received.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The Commission rejected the automatic, categorical protection that "fleeting expletives," single passing curse words, had received.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: The Commission obtained a voluntary remand to hear their objections, then issued a Remand Order retaining both Fox indecency findings without a forfeiture or other sanction.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The Commission obtained a "voluntary remand," asking the court to send the matter back to it, to hear the broadcasters' "objections." It then issued a Remand Order keeping both Fox indecency findings but imposing no "forfeiture" (a fine) or other "sanction," or penalty.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: The Second Circuit majority set aside the orders because the FCC had inadequately explained its departure from its previous policy.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The Second Circuit majority, in the federal appeals court, set aside (threw out) the FCC's orders. It held that the FCC had not adequately explained its departure from its previous policy.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: The Court applied the ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious standard under § 706(2)(A) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The Court applied the ordinary "arbitrary-and-capricious" standard under § 706(2)(A) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Under that test, an agency decision is overturned only if it is unreasoned or arbitrary.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: It need not persuade judges that its new reasons are better than the reasons for its old policy.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: An agency changing policy must give good reasons for the new one, but it does not have to prove the new policy is better than the old one.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: The Court read State Farm’s comparison as addressing rescission versus a failure to act initially, not as imposing heightened review on every policy revision; the distinct functions of § 706(1) and § 706(2) supported that reading.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The Court read State Farm’s comparison as addressing "rescission versus a failure to act" in the first place: repealing a rule needs as much explanation as adopting one. It did not impose "heightened review," stricter scrutiny, on every policy revision, a reading supported by the distinct jobs of § 706(1) (compelling action unlawfully withheld) and § 706(2) (setting aside unlawful action).

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: An agency must confront contrary earlier factual findings and serious reliance interests when they matter.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: An agency must confront earlier "factual findings" that contradict its new policy, and serious "reliance interests," meaning people who built plans around the old policy, when those matter.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: The Court refused to use constitutional avoidance to impose a specially stringent APA explanation standard.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: The Court refused to use "constitutional avoidance," the practice of reading laws to steer clear of constitutional problems, to impose a specially stringent APA standard for explaining the change. Free-speech objections had to be raised directly.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: It distinguished committee oversight wishes from enacted congressional intent, noted Congress’s exclusion from the APA, recognized that oversight cannot expand statutory authority, and resisted importing every notice-and-comment requirement into review of an adjudication.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: This part of Scalia's opinion, joined by only four Justices, distinguished "committee oversight" wishes (pressure from congressional hearings) from congressional intent actually "enacted" into law, and noted Congress's exclusion from the APA. It recognized that "oversight" cannot expand an agency's "statutory authority," and resisted importing every "notice-and-comment" rulemaking requirement into "review" of an adjudication, a decision in a particular case.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: Breyer also objected under Chenery to the Solicitor General’s reliance on the statutory word “any,” a rationale supplied by litigation counsel rather than the agency.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: Breyer also "objected" under Chenery, the rule that courts judge an agency only on its own stated reasons. He rejected the Solicitor General’s reliance on the "statutory" word "any," because that rationale came from litigation "counsel," the government's lawyers, rather than from the agency.

lrs-n-fcc-fox.sentence: Their subsequent-history account describes a 2010 Second Circuit vagueness ruling and the Supreme Court’s 2012 as-applied lack-of-notice decision, while leaving the broader First Amendment issue open.
lrs-n-fcc-fox.plain: Their subsequent-history account describes a 2010 Second Circuit ruling that the policy was unconstitutionally vague. It also describes the Supreme Court’s 2012 "as-applied" decision, limited to these broadcasters' situation, that they lacked fair notice, which left the broader First Amendment free-speech question open.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: Revenue from profitable routes helped support uniform-price service to expensive communities; unrestricted competitors could skim that revenue.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: The monopoly lets the Postal Service use profits from cheap-to-serve routes to deliver everywhere at the same price. Private rivals free to compete could take only the profitable business.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: This was an exercise of statutory suspension authority, not a claim that all private carriage was forbidden.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: This was an exercise of the Postal Service's "statutory" power to suspend its monopoly for this kind of mail. It was not a claim that all private carriage of mail was forbidden.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: Under § 702 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), they challenged record support for the public-interest finding required by 39 U.S.C. § 601(b).
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: Under § 702 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which lets people harmed by agency action sue, the unions challenged whether the record supported the Service's public-interest finding. That finding is required by 39 U.S.C. § 601(b) before the monopoly can be lifted.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: The injury-in-fact finding was not appealed.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: The "injury-in-fact" finding, that postal workers faced a real, concrete harm such as lost work, was not appealed.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: The D.C. Circuit vacated, locating the unions within the statutory zone because the Postal Reorganization Act contained labor protections and the monopoly financed the enterprise.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: The D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court, vacated (wiped out) the lower ruling. It placed the unions within the statutory zone of interests, the group the law protects, because the Postal Reorganization Act contained labor protections and the monopoly financed the whole postal enterprise.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: The remaining standing issue was statutory protection, not whether employees might suffer economically.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: The remaining "standing" question was whether the "statutory" monopoly provisions were meant to protect workers. It was not whether "employees" might suffer economically, which was already accepted.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: The Court explained that APA review concerned a cause of action, and the exemption could operate as a waivable defense rather than an unavoidable jurisdictional defect.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: The Court explained that APA review concerned a "cause of action," the legal right to sue, not the court's basic power to hear the case. So the Postal Service's exemption from the APA could operate as a "waivable" defense, one lost if not properly raised, rather than an unavoidable "jurisdictional defect" the court must notice on its own.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: Even a financial linchpin did not allow beneficiaries of another statutory program to enforce this public-interest restriction.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: Even though the monopoly was the postal system's financial linchpin, that did not let "beneficiaries" of another "statutory" program, the workers covered by separate labor provisions, enforce this public-interest restriction.

lrs-n-standing-air-courier.sentence: That was an alternative reason denying APA review, not a narrower zone-of-interests test.
lrs-n-standing-air-courier.plain: Justice Stevens's alternative reason was that APA review was unavailable for the Postal Service at all. That was a different ground for denying review, not a narrower "zone-of-interests" test, the inquiry into whether a plaintiff's interests are ones the statute protects.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act required consultation, a biological jeopardy assessment, and, where necessary, reasonable and prudent alternatives.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act required the Bureau to consult the Fish and Wildlife Service, which made a biological "jeopardy" assessment of whether the project threatened a species' survival. Where necessary, the Service also had to propose "reasonable and prudent alternatives," workable changes to avoid that harm.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: An incidental-take statement specified conditions for otherwise prohibited taking.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: An "incidental-take statement" specified conditions under which "otherwise prohibited taking," meaning harming or killing a protected species, would be allowed when it happens incidentally to the project.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: A third claimed the minimum levels effectively designated critical habitat without § 1533(b)(2)’s required economic-impact consideration.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: A third claim said the minimum lake levels effectively designated "critical habitat," protected areas essential to the species. That designation required considering economic impact under § 1533(b)(2), which had not been done.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: The Ninth Circuit affirmed, applying that restriction to both APA review and the citizen-suit provision and requiring an interest in species preservation.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: The Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, affirmed. It applied that zone-of-interests limit to both APA review and the "citizen-suit provision," the Endangered Species Act clause letting private persons sue, and required an interest in preserving species.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Economic motives did not disqualify plaintiffs alleging overenforcement rather than underenforcement.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: Economic motives did not disqualify "plaintiffs" alleging overenforcement, too much protection, rather than "underenforcement," too little.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Congress could relax the then-described prudential requirement, though not constitutional standing.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: Congress could relax the then-described "prudential requirement," a court-made limit on who may sue. It could not relax constitutional "standing," the Constitution's minimum requirement of a real injury.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Section 1540(g)(1)(C) allowed suits against the Secretary for nondiscretionary § 1533 duties.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: Section 1540(g)(1)(C), the citizen-suit clause, allowed suits against the Secretary for failing to perform "nondiscretionary" duties under § 1533, meaning mandatory ones. One such duty is weighing economic impact before designating habitat.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Otherwise the narrower subsection (C) and the APA’s finality restriction could be bypassed.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: Reading the clause more broadly would let people sidestep subsection (C)'s specific limits and the APA's rule that only final agency actions can be challenged.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Though nominally advisory, the biological opinion exerted determinative or coercive influence: departure required justification and risked unlawful-taking liability for the Bureau and employees, while compliance with incidental-take terms supplied protection.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: Though officially only advisory, the "biological opinion" had determinative or "coercive" influence, meaning it effectively controlled the Bureau. Departing from it required justification and risked "unlawful-taking liability" for harming the fish, for the Bureau and its employees, while complying with its "incidental-take terms" gave legal protection.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Requiring the best scientific and commercial data also guarded against needless economic disruption through erroneous jeopardy findings, placing these asserted economic injuries within that provision’s zone.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: The requirement to use the best scientific and commercial data also guarded against needless economic disruption from mistaken "jeopardy" findings, findings that a project threatens a species' survival. That placed the ranchers' asserted economic injuries within that provision's zone of interests.

lrs-n-standing-bennett.sentence: Final action ordinarily required consummated decisionmaking and determined rights, obligations, or legal consequences.
lrs-n-standing-bennett.plain: "Final" agency action ordinarily required "consummated decisionmaking," meaning the agency's decision process was complete. It also had to determine rights or obligations, or produce legal consequences.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: The January 1979 complaint accused Havens and Jones of racial steering designed to preserve segregation.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: The January 1979 "complaint," the document starting the lawsuit, accused Havens and its employee Jones of racial steering designed to preserve segregation. Steering means guiding people toward or away from housing because of their race.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: It merely fixed potential damages contingent on the outcome; adverse claims remained, and these plaintiffs could not recover from Coles’s separate fund.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: The side agreement merely fixed potential "damages," the money owed, depending on the outcome. Adverse "claims" remained, and these "plaintiffs" could not "recover" from Coles’s separate fund, so the case was still a live dispute.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: The Court’s Gladstone precedent understood the Fair Housing Act’s private enforcement provision to reach Article III’s limits, without an additional prudential barrier.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: The Court’s Gladstone precedent read the Fair Housing Act’s private enforcement provision as reaching the full limits of Article III, the Constitution's minimum requirements for a case. No additional "prudential" (court-made) barrier applied.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: Section 804(d) prohibited racially discriminatory statements to any person that an available dwelling was unavailable.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: Section 804(d) of the Act prohibited telling any person, because of race, that an available "dwelling" (a house or apartment) was unavailable.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: Her expectation of discrimination and investigative purpose did not erase it.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: That Coleman was a tester who expected to be lied to did not erase the injury of being lied to.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: Those could be personal injuries even when steering directly violated someone else’s statutory rights, provided their own harm was fairly traceable to it.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: Losing the benefits of an integrated community could be a personal injury even when the steering directly violated someone else’s "statutory" rights. That was so as long as the plaintiffs' own harm was "fairly traceable" to the steering, meaning caused by it.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: On remand, the district court had to permit more definite allegations and dismiss if the resulting record still failed to establish standing.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: "On remand," when the case returned to it, the district court had to let the plaintiffs make more definite "allegations" about how they were affected. It had to dismiss if the resulting record still failed to establish standing.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: That was concrete organizational injury beyond frustration of an abstract mission.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: That was a "concrete" injury to the organization itself, a real drain on HOME's own work and resources. It went beyond mere frustration of an abstract mission.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: Because HOME appeared willing to abandon a separate representative claim for injunctions, the Court left associational standing undecided.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: Because HOME appeared willing to "abandon," or drop, a separate claim for injunctions brought on its members' behalf, the Court left "associational standing" undecided. That doctrine concerns when a group may sue for its members.

lrs-n-standing-havens.sentence: Under the Act’s then-existing 180-day period, a continuing unlawful practice extending into the filing window differed from an isolated stale act.
lrs-n-standing-havens.plain: The Act then gave 180 days to file. Under that period, a "continuing unlawful practice," an ongoing pattern of discrimination that extended into the filing window, differed from a single stale act that happened too long ago.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: It did not allege that the organization or any of its members used Mineral King or would suffer diminished activities or enjoyment there.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: The complaint did not "allege," or claim, that the organization or any of its members used Mineral King. Nor did it allege they would suffer diminished activities or enjoyment there.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: The omission was a choice of legal theory, not merely failure to name a person in an otherwise adequate allegation of injury.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: The omission was a deliberate choice of legal theory: the Club relied on its long-standing interest and expertise alone. It was not merely a failure to name a person in an otherwise adequate "allegation" of injury.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: After a two-day hearing, the district court accepted the Club’s standing and granted preliminary relief.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: After a two-day "hearing," the district court accepted that the Club had "standing," the right to sue. It granted "preliminary relief," a temporary order blocking the project.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: Section 702 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) permits review for a person suffering legal wrong or adversely affected or aggrieved within the meaning of a relevant statute.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: Section 702 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) permits "review" of agency action for a person suffering a "legal wrong," a violation of their legal rights. It also permits review for anyone adversely affected or aggrieved within the meaning of a relevant statute, meaning harmed in a way that statute is concerned with.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: Because the Club failed at injury, the Court left the zone question unanswered.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: The Club showed no injury to itself or its members, so the Court never reached the second test, whether its interests were ones the statute protects.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: The missing step was a connection between that harm and the Club or its members.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: A person who hikes or camps in the valley could sue, but the Club had not claimed that it or its members were such people.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: Once standing exists, a litigant can invoke broader statutory and public-interest concerns, including in support of equitable relief.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: Once "standing" exists, a "litigant" (a party to the case) can invoke broader "statutory" and public-interest concerns, not just its own. That includes using them to support "equitable relief," such as an injunction.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: He proposed allowing suit in the name of the threatened natural object: Mineral King itself could seek protection through knowledgeable human representatives.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: Justice Douglas proposed allowing a "suit" in the name of the threatened natural object itself. Mineral King could seek protection through knowledgeable human representatives, people who know and use it.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: His first alternative would reverse the Ninth Circuit and maintain the district court’s standing ruling and injunction on condition that the Club promptly amend to satisfy the majority’s injury requirement.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: Justice Blackmun's first alternative would "reverse" the Ninth Circuit and keep the "district court’s" standing ruling and "injunction" (the order blocking the project) in place. That was on condition that the Club promptly amend its complaint to satisfy the "majority’s" injury requirement, the rule adopted by the Justices in the majority.

lrs-n-standing-sierra.sentence: The Court noted that the Club could seek leave to amend under Rule 15, but did not command acceptance of an amendment or preserve relief while one was sought.
lrs-n-standing-sierra.plain: The Court noted that the Club could seek "leave to amend," meaning permission to change its complaint, under Rule 15. But it did not command that an amendment be accepted, or preserve "relief" (the block on the project) while one was sought.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: Their provider, Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division, was a municipal division managed by commissioners appointed by the City Council and ultimately controlled by the city, which exempted it from state public-service-commission regulation.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: Their provider, Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division, was a city division run by "commissioners" appointed by the City Council and ultimately controlled by the city. That status "exempted" it from state "public-service-commission regulation," the agency oversight that applies to private utilities.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: In February 1974 the Crafts and other customers sued under the federal civil-rights statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, seeking declarations, injunctions and actual and punitive damages against the division and its officials and employees.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: In February 1974 the Crafts and other customers sued under the federal civil-rights statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which allows suits for violations of constitutional rights. They sought declarations, "injunctions" (court orders), and actual and punitive damages against the division and its officials and "employees."

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: It doubted a protected entitlement to continued service during disputed nonpayment and rejected the procedural claim.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: The trial court doubted the Crafts had a legally protected right to keep service while disputing a bill, and rejected their claim that the utility's procedures were unfair.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: The original dismissal of the municipal division under the then-applied § 1983 understanding was unchallenged; references to the utility included individual officials sued personally and officially.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: The original "dismissal" of the city division itself, under the then-applied understanding that city bodies could not be sued under § 1983, was not challenged. So references to "the utility" meant individual officials, sued both personally and in their official roles.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: With no certified class, jurisdiction depended on the Crafts.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: With no "certified class," meaning no group of customers approved by the court to sue together, jurisdiction depended on the Crafts themselves still having a live dispute.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: The Court therefore did not need the capable-of-repetition exception.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: The Court therefore did not need the "capable-of-repetition" exception, which keeps alive disputes that recur but end too quickly for courts to decide them.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: It distinguished just, undisputed bills from bona fide disputes: a utility could cut off proper unpaid charges but acted at its peril if contested charges were wrong.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: Tennessee law distinguished just, undisputed bills from "bona fide" (genuine, good-faith) disputes. A utility could cut off service for proper unpaid charges but acted "at its peril," at its own risk of liability, if contested charges proved wrong.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: An entitlement conditioned on payment of charges actually due remained property even when disputed.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: An "entitlement," a legally protected claim to continued service, conditioned on paying charges actually due remained property protected by due process even while a bill was disputed.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: State law supplied the entitlement; federal law determined constitutional protection and adequate procedure.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: State law created the right to service, but the federal Constitution decides what fair procedure is required before it can be taken away.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: Applying Mathews v. Eldridge’s balance of private interest, error risk and additional safeguards against governmental burden, the Court emphasized that gas, water and electricity were necessities.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: Applying Mathews v. Eldridge’s balancing test, the Court weighed the customer's private interest, the risk of error, and the value of added safeguards against the burden on the government. It emphasized that gas, water, and electricity were necessities.

lrs-o-memphis-light.sentence: A pre-cutoff injunction, later damages or payment followed by a refund suit did not cure this defect.
lrs-o-memphis-light.plain: A pre-cutoff "injunction" (a court order blocking the shutoff), a later suit for damages, or paying first and then bringing a "refund suit" did not "cure," or make up for, this defect: the missing chance to dispute the bill.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: The district court dismissed the covenant and misrepresentation claims as preempted by the Airline Deregulation Act.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: The "district court" (the trial court) dismissed the claims for breach of the "covenant" of good faith and fair dealing and for misrepresentation. It held them preempted, meaning overridden, by the Airline Deregulation Act, a federal law.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: It dismissed the express-contract claim without prejudice for failure to identify a material breach, reasoning that the agreement reserved sole discretion over abuse.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: It dismissed the express (written) contract claim "without prejudice," meaning it could be refiled, for failure to identify a "material breach," a significant violation of the terms. It reasoned that the agreement "reserved" to Northwest sole discretion to decide what counted as abuse.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: Justice Alito’s unanimous opinion explained that the Airline Deregulation Act sought market control of prices, routes, and services and barred state provisions having the force of law related to those subjects.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: Justice Alito’s "unanimous" opinion, joined by every Justice, explained that the Airline Deregulation Act sought to let market forces control prices, routes, and services. It barred state provisions having the "force of law," meaning binding legal rules, related to those subjects.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: Wolens, a later airline-contract decision, distinguished state consumer regulation from enforcement of an airline’s voluntarily accepted promises.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: Wolens, a later airline-contract decision, distinguished state consumer "regulation," rules a state imposes on airlines, from enforcement of promises an airline voluntarily accepted.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: The controlling question was whether the claim enforced private ordering or added a state standard.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: The controlling question was whether the "claim" enforced private ordering, meaning terms the parties set for themselves, or added a standard imposed by the state.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: Nor could an older general aviation saving clause override the later specific preemption provision.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: Nor could an older, general aviation "saving clause," a provision preserving other legal remedies, override the later and more specific "preemption" provision, which displaces state law.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: Minnesota did not allow parties to disclaim its covenant, making it state-imposed.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: Minnesota did not allow parties to disclaim, or contract out of, its "covenant" of good faith and fair dealing. That made the duty state-imposed rather than voluntarily agreed.

northwest-ginsberg.sentence: On April 2, 2014, it reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded because this Minnesota covenant claim enlarged Northwest’s voluntarily assumed obligations and was preempted.
northwest-ginsberg.plain: On April 2, 2014, the Court "reversed" the Ninth Circuit and "remanded," sending the case back. This Minnesota "covenant" claim enlarged the obligations Northwest had voluntarily assumed, so it was "preempted," overridden by the federal airline law.

transatlantic.sentence: The district court dismissed its admiralty libel for the extra costs.
transatlantic.plain: The "district court" (the trial court) dismissed Transatlantic's "admiralty libel," the old name for a lawsuit in maritime court, seeking the extra costs.

transatlantic.sentence: On appeal, Transatlantic argued that usual-route and deviation principles made this specifically a Suez contract; closure made that contract impossible; and completing a different voyage in response to government demands entitled it to quantum meruit, compensation for the value conferred.
transatlantic.plain: On "appeal," Transatlantic argued that "usual-route" and deviation principles, which presume a ship takes the customary route, made this specifically a Suez contract. It argued the canal's closure made that contract impossible, and that completing a different voyage at the government's demand entitled it to "quantum meruit," compensation for the value conferred.

transatlantic.sentence: Judge J. Skelly Wright’s opinion identified three requirements: an unexpected contingency, a risk not allocated by agreement or custom, and resulting commercial impracticability.
transatlantic.plain: Judge J. Skelly Wright’s "opinion" identified three requirements for excuse: an unexpected "contingency," or event; a risk "not allocated by agreement" or by custom; and resulting commercial impracticability, meaning performance became unreasonably costly or difficult.

transatlantic.sentence: Physical possibility alone did not defeat the defense.
transatlantic.plain: Physical possibility alone did not defeat the "defense" of impracticability; performance need not be literally impossible for the excuse to apply.

transatlantic.sentence: Neither express terms, trade usage, circumstances, nor admiralty doctrine made continued access a condition that dissolved the bargain.
transatlantic.plain: Neither "express terms" (the contract's written words), trade usage, the circumstances, nor "admiralty" (maritime) law made the canal's continued availability a condition whose failure dissolved the "bargain."

transatlantic.sentence: Deviation doctrine primarily adjusted insurance consequences of unreasonable departures; its qualified application did not discharge every substituted route.
transatlantic.plain: "Deviation" doctrine, about a ship leaving its customary route, mainly adjusts insurance consequences when the departure is unreasonable. Its qualified, limited application did not discharge a carrier every time a substitute route was used.

transatlantic.sentence: Contracting against that background nevertheless showed acceptance of some abnormal risk and supported stricter scrutiny than a wholly unforeseen event would.
transatlantic.plain: Signing the contract against the background of the crisis nevertheless showed acceptance of some abnormal risk. That supported stricter scrutiny of the excuse than a wholly "unforeseen" event, one no one saw coming, would.

transatlantic.sentence: Transatlantic was at least as able as the government to insure against the contingency and better positioned to evaluate alternate-route expenses and maritime war hazards.
transatlantic.plain: Transatlantic was at least as able as the government to insure against the "contingency," the canal closing. It was also better positioned to evaluate the costs of an alternate route and the hazards of maritime war.

transatlantic.sentence: The inquiry was objective, although limitations known to both parties could inform a complete assessment.
transatlantic.plain: The inquiry was objective, asking what a reasonable carrier could do rather than this company's own situation. But limitations known to both "parties" could inform a complete assessment.

transatlantic.sentence: Even assuming excuse, Transatlantic’s theory treated the charter as a nullity while retaining its payment and profit and transferring only extra expense to the government.
transatlantic.plain: Even assuming excuse, Transatlantic’s theory treated the charter (the shipping contract) as a "nullity," meaning void, while keeping its contract payment and profit. It would shift only the extra expense to the government.

transatlantic.sentence: A restitutionary claim following discharge would address the value of the entire performance, not automatically preserve one party’s bargain and shift the whole loss to the other.
transatlantic.plain: A "restitutionary" claim after discharge, one aimed at paying for value received, would address the value of the entire "performance," the whole voyage. It would not automatically preserve one "party’s" bargain and shift the whole loss to the other.

algernon-blair.sentence: Coastal sued Blair and its payment-bond surety, United States Fidelity and Guaranty, in the United States’ name under the Miller Act for labor and equipment already furnished.
algernon-blair.plain: Coastal sued Blair and its payment-bond surety, United States Fidelity and Guaranty, the company guaranteeing Blair's payments. Under the Miller Act such suits are brought "in the United States’ name," though the claim belongs to Coastal, here for labor and equipment already furnished.

algernon-blair.sentence: Those findings were unchallenged on appeal; wrongful abandonment by Coastal was not the issue.
algernon-blair.plain: Those "findings," the trial court's conclusions about the facts, were unchallenged on appeal. Wrongful abandonment of the job by Coastal was not the issue.

algernon-blair.sentence: Deducting that expected loss in calculating contract damages left no recovery.
algernon-blair.plain: Contract damages aim to give Coastal what finishing the deal would have earned. Deducting the expected loss on the remaining work in calculating those damages left no "recovery," nothing to award.

algernon-blair.sentence: Judge Craven’s opinion held that Coastal could elect quantum meruit, recovery of reasonable value, after Blair’s material breach.
algernon-blair.plain: Judge Craven’s "opinion" held that after Blair’s "material breach," a serious violation of the contract, Coastal "could elect," or choose, quantum meruit. That is "recovery" of the reasonable value of its work and equipment instead of contract damages.

algernon-blair.sentence: Restitution asked what labor and equipment value Coastal had conferred at its expense and Blair retained without full payment.
algernon-blair.plain: Restitution looks backward instead: how much value did Coastal hand over, at its own cost, that Blair kept without paying for it in full?

algernon-blair.sentence: The loss Coastal would have incurred on remaining work did not make its completed performance free.
algernon-blair.plain: The loss Coastal would have suffered on the remaining work did not make its completed "performance," the work already done, free for Blair to keep.

algernon-blair.sentence: Miller Act and construction precedents allowed a promisee to forgo contract damages and seek reasonable value, including against the payment-bond surety under the Act’s protective construction.
algernon-blair.plain: Miller Act and construction "precedents" (earlier decisions) let a "promisee," the party whose contract was broken, forgo contract damages and seek reasonable value. That included claims against the "payment-bond" surety, because courts construe the Act broadly to protect those who supply labor and materials.

algernon-blair.sentence: Imprecision in the complaint’s remedy theory did not bar that recovery, and quantum meruit could be pleaded alongside contract damages.
algernon-blair.plain: Imprecision in the complaint's remedy theory did not "bar," or block, that recovery. And "quantum meruit" (reasonable value) could be "pleaded," meaning asked for in the complaint, alongside contract damages.

algernon-blair.sentence: Federal substantive law controlled a Miller Act action if it differed from state law, although the court thought relevant state law would lead to the same result.
algernon-blair.plain: Federal "substantive law," the rules that decide rights and recovery, controlled a Miller Act case if it differed from state law. The court thought the relevant state law would lead to the same result anyway.

algernon-blair.sentence: The contract price could be evidence of value but neither fixed the measure nor capped recovery under the rule applied to this partial-performance claim.
algernon-blair.plain: Under the rule applied to this partial-performance "claim," the contract price could be evidence of value. But it neither fixed the measure of "recovery" nor capped it.

algernon-blair.sentence: Restitution could thus exceed the promised return under an advantageous bargain.
algernon-blair.plain: So the injured party could recover more in restitution than it would have earned by finishing a deal that was a good bargain for the other side.

algernon-blair.sentence: The district court’s approximate $37,000 figure had served its losing-contract analysis, not a precise reasonable-value finding, so it was not adopted as the final award.
algernon-blair.plain: The "district court’s" approximate $37,000 figure had served its "losing-contract" analysis, deciding whether finishing would have lost money. It was not a precise "reasonable-value" finding, so it was not "adopted" as the final "award."

brief-CP-147.sentence: Parklane Hosiery issued a proxy statement seeking shareholder approval of a merger that would take the company private.
brief-CP-147.plain: Parklane Hosiery issued a "proxy statement," the required disclosure document sent to shareholders before a vote, seeking approval of a merger that would "take the company private." That means buying out the public shareholders so its stock would no longer trade publicly.

brief-CP-147.sentence: After a four-day bench trial, the district court found the statement materially false and misleading and entered a declaratory judgment, although the SEC had sought an injunction.
brief-CP-147.plain: After a four-day "bench trial," a trial before a judge without a jury, the district court found the statement "materially false" and misleading, meaning its falsehoods were important to investors. It "entered," or issued, a declaratory judgment saying so, although the SEC had sought an "injunction," an order forbidding future conduct.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Shore moved for partial summary judgment based on collateral estoppel, now commonly called issue preclusion.
brief-CP-147.plain: Shore moved for "partial summary judgment," a ruling on one issue without trial, based on "collateral estoppel," now commonly called issue preclusion. That doctrine bars a party from relitigating an issue already decided against it in an earlier case.

brief-CP-147.sentence: The district court denied the motion because applying a bench-trial finding would, it thought, deny defendants their constitutional jury right on the damages claim.
brief-CP-147.plain: The "district court" denied the "motion." It thought applying a "bench-trial" finding, one made by a judge, would deny the defendants their constitutional "jury right" on Shore's "damages" claim for money.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Defendants sought Supreme Court review on both nonmutuality—Shore would not have been bound by an SEC loss—and the Seventh Amendment.
brief-CP-147.plain: The defendants sought Supreme Court "review" on two grounds. One was "nonmutuality": Shore would not have been bound by an SEC loss, so he should not benefit from its win; the other was the Seventh Amendment right to a civil jury.

brief-CP-147.sentence: They had no constitutional jury right in the SEC’s equitable action.
brief-CP-147.plain: The SEC's suit asked only for court orders, not money, so the defendants had no right to a jury there in the first place.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Justice Stewart’s eight-Justice opinion distinguished mutuality from a litigant’s own opportunity to be heard.
brief-CP-147.plain: Justice Stewart’s "opinion" for eight Justices distinguished mutuality, the old rule that both sides must be bound by a judgment, from what fairness requires: a "litigant’s" own full opportunity to be heard before being bound.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Offensive nonmutual preclusion nevertheless creates special risks.
brief-CP-147.plain: "Offensive nonmutual preclusion," where a new plaintiff uses an earlier finding against a defendant from a different case, nevertheless creates special risks.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Defensive preclusion can encourage plaintiffs to join available defendants; offensive use can reward waiting plaintiffs who benefit from victory without risking another claimant’s defeat.
brief-CP-147.plain: "Defensive preclusion," a defendant using a plaintiff's earlier loss against it, can encourage plaintiffs to join all available defendants in one suit. Offensive use can reward plaintiffs who wait, since they benefit from another's victory without risking that other "claimant’s" defeat.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Weak incentive to defend a small first case, inconsistent earlier favorable judgments, or a significant new procedural opportunity likely to change the outcome could justify refusal.
brief-CP-147.plain: A court may refuse if the defendant had little reason to fight the first case hard, if other earlier judgments went the defendant's way, or if the new case offers procedures that could well change the result.

brief-CP-147.sentence: A jury’s participation alone did not establish such an advantage.
brief-CP-147.plain: Having a jury in the second case was not, by itself, the kind of new procedural opportunity that would make preclusion unfair.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Stewart answered that the Seventh Amendment preserves the substance of the jury institution without freezing all historical procedure.
brief-CP-147.plain: Stewart answered that the Seventh Amendment preserves the substance of the jury institution, the core of jury trial as it existed in 1791. It does not freeze every historical procedure.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Procedural developments may change which questions remain open, and equitable decrees historically could preclude issues in later legal actions.
brief-CP-147.plain: Procedural developments may change which questions remain open for a jury. And historically, "equitable decrees," judgments of courts of equity, could preclude issues in later legal "actions," meaning suits for damages.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Beacon Theatres protected jury consideration where legal and equitable claims coexist and a court can avoid preclusion by trying legal issues first.
brief-CP-147.plain: Beacon Theatres protected jury consideration where "legal and equitable" claims (jury and non-jury claims) coexist in one case. There, a court can avoid "preclusion" by trying the "legal issues," those for the jury, first.

brief-CP-147.sentence: The recognized force of an equitable judgment was the reason Beacon’s sequence mattered, not a reason to ignore this independent adjudication.
brief-CP-147.plain: The recognized binding force of an "equitable judgment," a judge's ruling in equity, was the very reason Beacon’s order of trial mattered. It was not a reason to ignore this independent, completed adjudication in the SEC case.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Defendants need not have requested a merely advisory SEC jury or accelerated their private case, and they could not require the SEC to postpone enforcement.
brief-CP-147.plain: The defendants had not given up their jury right by failing to ask for a non-binding jury in the SEC case or to rush Shore's case ahead, and they had no power to make the SEC delay its enforcement case.

brief-CP-147.sentence: The result rested on permissible preclusion, not forfeiture of a constitutional demand.
brief-CP-147.plain: They lost a jury on this issue because preclusion lawfully applied, not because they had lost their jury right by failing to claim it.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Historical mutuality meant comparable defendants in 1791 would have received a jury decision, and eliminating a genuinely disputed fact from the jury differed from summary judgment or directed verdict where a legally sufficient controversy was absent.
brief-CP-147.plain: Rehnquist argued that under the 1791 mutuality rule these defendants would have had a jury decide the question. Taking a truly disputed fact from the jury differs from summary judgment or directed verdict, which apply only when there is nothing real for a jury to decide.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Even if constitutionally permitted, he would deny offensive preclusion as a matter of discretion.
brief-CP-147.plain: Even if the Constitution permitted it, he would refuse "offensive preclusion" as a matter of "discretion," the court's own judgment about fairness.

brief-CP-147.sentence: Shore could treat the SEC determination of the proxy statement’s materially false and misleading character as conclusive.
brief-CP-147.plain: Shore could treat the SEC case's determination that the proxy statement was materially false and misleading as conclusive, meaning settled. He still had to prove the rest of his claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Zurich was a foreign corporation authorized to do business in New York.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: Zurich was a "foreign corporation," meaning one incorporated outside New York, authorized to do business in New York.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: The eventual appeal concerned commencing the action, not whether coverage or that sum was owed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: The eventual appeal concerned only commencing the "action," whether the lawsuit was properly started by service of papers. It did not concern whether coverage or that sum was owed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Zurich moved to dismiss later that month because she was only a vice-president’s secretary rather than a statutory service recipient.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: Zurich "moved to dismiss," asking the court to throw out the case, later that month. It argued she was only a vice-president’s secretary, not a "statutory service recipient," one of the people the statute allows to receive legal papers for a company.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Although she denied officer or managing-agent status and express appointment, for at least five years she regularly accepted summonses when Scanlon was absent, taking about half those delivered to his office.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: She denied having officer or "managing-agent" status (a senior employee with broad decision-making power) or any express appointment to accept papers. But for at least five years she regularly accepted "summonses," the papers starting lawsuits, when Scanlon was absent, taking about half of those delivered to his office.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: A Special Referee credited the server despite disputed testimony, found diligence and fair notice, and viewed Robertson’s actual duties as managing or general agency.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: A Special Referee, an official appointed to hear evidence, believed the process server despite disputed "testimony." The referee found diligence and "fair notice," meaning Zurich actually learned of the suit, and viewed Robertson’s actual duties as "managing or general agency," the kind of authority that permits receiving papers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: The Appellate Division affirmed because she was appointed to receive process and certified an appeal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: The Appellate Division, New York's intermediate appeals court, affirmed because she was "appointed to receive process," meaning Zurich had in effect authorized her to accept legal papers. It certified an appeal, formally sending a question to New York's highest court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Zurich argued she lacked managing-agent discretion and that appointment required express authorization plus the formal written filing specified in another statutory provision.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: Zurich argued she lacked the discretion, or decision-making power, of a "managing-agent." It also argued that appointment required express authorization plus the formal written filing specified in another "statutory" provision.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Judge Wachtler’s six-judge majority read the corporate-service statute to fulfill its notice purpose and its history of expanding permissible recipients.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: Judge Wachtler’s six-judge majority read the corporate-service "statute" to fulfill its purpose of giving companies notice of suits. It also relied on the statute's history of expanding who may receive papers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Appointment under the general corporate-service provision differed from optional formal designation under the separate provision, which carried additional legal consequences.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: A company can authorize someone to accept papers informally under the general rule; the formal filing Zurich pointed to is a separate, optional procedure with its own effects, not the only way.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: A corporation could not use that arrangement yet avoid consequences by invoking titles or absent filings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: A "corporation" could not use that arrangement, letting her accept papers, yet avoid its consequences by pointing to job titles or missing formal filings.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Giving papers without inquiry to a building receptionist not employed by the defendant would not become valid merely because she forwarded them.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: Handing papers without inquiry to a building receptionist who was not employed by the "defendant" would not become valid service merely because she forwarded them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: Any mistaken internal direction in those circumstances belonged to Zurich.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: If Zurich's own employees sent the server to the wrong person, Zurich, not the plaintiff, bore the consequences.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: He objected to broader suggestions that a server’s diligence could replace delivery to an eligible person.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: He did not want a rule that a careful process server's good effort is enough even when the papers reach someone not legally authorized to take them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: He allowed that obstruction or misleading conduct by an agent with actual or apparent authority could estop a company from demanding perfect compliance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: He allowed that obstruction or misleading conduct by an "agent" with actual or "apparent authority," authority the company appears to have given, could estop the company. That means it could be barred from demanding perfect compliance with the service rules.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.sentence: All seven judges affirmed the Appellate Division’s order with costs and answered the certified question affirmatively, while six joined the majority reasoning.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085.plain: All seven judges "affirmed," or upheld, the Appellate Division’s "order," with costs charged to Zurich, and answered the "certified question" (the question sent up for decision) yes. But only six "joined," or signed on to, the majority reasoning.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: Judge Harold Baer preliminarily enjoined interference July 16, finding protected art and a statutory exception.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: On July 16, Judge Harold Baer "preliminarily enjoined" the city's interference, issuing a temporary order barring it from stopping the shoot. He found the photograph was protected art and fell within a "statutory" exception in the state nudity laws.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: The Second Circuit stayed relief July 17 and heard expedited argument in September.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: On July 17 the Second Circuit, the federal appeals court, stayed (put on hold) that relief, so the shoot could not proceed. It heard expedited, fast-tracked argument in September.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: The state exposure and promotion statutes exempted persons entertaining or performing in a play, exhibition, show, or entertainment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: The state "statutes" against public exposure and promoting exposure exempted persons entertaining or performing in a play, exhibition, show, or entertainment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: It abandoned licensing and time, place, and manner arguments on appeal; the injunction did not compel a permit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: On appeal the city "abandoned," or dropped, its licensing arguments and its "time, place, and manner" arguments, meaning neutral limits on when, where, and how expression occurs. The injunction did not compel the city to issue a permit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: With conflicting municipal decisions and no controlling state appellate interpretation, the City favored certification and Tunick claimed the exception clearly applied.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: City courts had issued conflicting decisions, and no controlling state "appellate" (higher-court) interpretation existed. So the City favored certification, asking New York's highest court to answer the question, while Tunick claimed the exception clearly applied.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: The panel retained jurisdiction and possible reconsideration of the stay; it decided neither statutory merits nor the final federal constitutional question.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: The panel "retained jurisdiction," keeping the case, and left open possible "reconsideration" of the "stay," its hold on the order. It decided neither the "statutory" merits under state law nor the final federal constitutional question.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: Calabresi drew on abstention and constitutional avoidance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: Judge Calabresi drew on abstention, federal courts stepping back so state courts can decide state questions, and on "constitutional avoidance," avoiding constitutional rulings when another ground can resolve the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: Continued plans for a future shoot and the prospect of guidance justified delay despite serious speech costs and possible mootness if the stay lifted.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: In Calabresi's view, Tunick's continued plans for a future shoot and the prospect of state-court guidance justified delay, despite serious costs to free speech. That held even though lifting the "stay" could bring "mootness," leaving no live dispute to decide.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: Preventing expression under an unclear statute resembled unguided licensing.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: Judge Sack thought preventing expression in advance under an unclear "statute" resembled unguided licensing, letting officials decide without standards who may speak.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: He favored immediate relief against prior restraint, while distinguishing arrest after the photograph; Tunick conceded he sought no immunity from later prosecution.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: Sack favored immediate "relief" against prior restraint, the blocking of expression in advance, while distinguishing an arrest after the photograph was taken. Tunick conceded he sought no "immunity," or protection, from later prosecution.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: Van Graafeiland would dismiss as moot because the complaint and injunction concerned the past July 18 date, leaving a new scheduled shoot for another case.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: Judge Van Graafeiland would "dismiss" as moot, because the "complaint" and injunction concerned the July 18 date that had already passed. A newly scheduled shoot would be a matter for another case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: The New York Court of Appeals unanimously declined the certified questions under its discretionary rule.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: The New York Court of Appeals, the state's highest court, unanimously declined to answer the "certified questions" under its "discretionary" rule, which lets it choose whether to answer.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: The federal court could lift its stay, permit photography, and potentially moot the questions while certification proceeded.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: The federal court could lift its "stay," permit the photography, and potentially "moot" the questions, making any answer pointless, while certification was still pending.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: On May 19 the Second Circuit held the preliminary injunction within discretion because Tunick showed irreparable injury and a clear likelihood of success.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: On May 19 the Second Circuit held that the "preliminary injunction," the temporary order, was within the trial judge's discretion. Tunick showed "irreparable injury" (harm money cannot fix) and a clear "likelihood of success" on the merits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: It dissolved the stay and remanded for a new date and a limited early-morning, nonbusiness-day injunction preventing arrests or interference until photography ended.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: The court "dissolved the stay," lifting its hold on the order, and remanded for the trial judge to set a new date. It directed a limited "injunction," confined to an early-morning shoot on a nonbusiness day, preventing arrests or interference until the photography ended.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: The district court could minimize neighborhood intrusion, and intervening law making the event clearly illegal would qualify relief.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: The "district court" could minimize intrusion on the neighborhood. And intervening law making the event clearly illegal, such as a new statute or ruling, would qualify, or limit, the "relief."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: In his July concurrence, Calabresi predicted state law rather than automatically deciding the federal constitutional issue.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: In his July concurrence, a separate opinion agreeing with the result, Calabresi predicted how state law would be read. He did that rather than automatically deciding the federal constitutional issue.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: That preliminary prediction neither bound New York courts nor foreclosed later prosecution or reasonable regulation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: That preliminary prediction about state law did not bind New York courts. Nor did it foreclose later prosecution or reasonable regulation of the event.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.sentence: His position did not alter the panel’s mandate dissolving the stay and directing limited renewed relief.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-230.plain: Van Graafeiland's position did not alter the panel’s "mandate," the court's official order, which dissolved the stay and directed limited renewed "relief."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: The applicants sued Regents and officials in October 1997 under equal protection, Title VI, and 42 U.S.C. § 1981.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: In October 1997 the applicants sued the Regents, the university's governing board, and university officials. They claimed race discrimination under "equal protection" (the Constitution's guarantee of equal treatment), Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, and 42 U.S.C. § 1981, a federal civil-rights statute.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: The district court certified a Rule 23(b)(2) class represented by Hamacher and separated liability from damages.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: The "district court" certified a Rule 23(b)(2) class, a group seeking court orders on behalf of everyone treated alike, represented by Hamacher. It separated "liability," whether the university broke the law, from damages.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: On cross-motions, it invalidated the 1995–1998 policies but upheld the 1999–2000 approach as pursuing educational diversity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: On "cross-motions," both sides asking for judgment without trial, the court invalidated the 1995–1998 admissions policies. It upheld the 1999–2000 approach as a legitimate pursuit of educational diversity.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Before the Sixth Circuit entered judgment on appeals, the Supreme Court granted certiorari before judgment and considered this case alongside the distinct law-school case Grutter.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Before the Sixth Circuit, the federal appeals court, entered judgment on the appeals, the Supreme Court "granted" certiorari before judgment, agreeing to hear the case early. It considered this case alongside the distinct law-school case, Grutter.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Officials’ qualified immunity and the University’s Eleventh Amendment rulings were outside requested review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Rulings on the officials' "qualified immunity" (protection from personal damages liability unless they broke clearly established law) and on the University’s Eleventh Amendment immunity (a state's protection from certain suits) were outside the review requested.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Chief Justice Rehnquist treated injury as unequal competition, not proof that equal treatment guaranteed admission.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Chief Justice Rehnquist treated the injury as being forced into unequal competition because of race. It did not require proof that equal treatment would have guaranteed admission.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Hamacher’s rejection and stated readiness to transfer supplied a stake at certification, and subsequent graduation did not erase the certified class controversy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: When the class was certified Hamacher had a personal stake, because he had been rejected and said he was ready to transfer. His later graduation did not end the class's dispute.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Though the University had challenged standing at certification, it had not then asserted materially different freshman and transfer concerns.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: The university had questioned Hamacher's standing when the class was certified, but it had not then argued that the freshman and transfer admission policies were importantly different.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Those differences could affect tailoring but not the shared challenge to the justification.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Those differences between the freshman and transfer policies could affect "tailoring," how closely each policy fit its goal. They did not affect the shared challenge to the justification for using race.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: General Telephone v. Falcon, a class-representation precedent, had separated an individual promotion claim based on intentional discrimination from hiring claims resting on different statistical proof.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: General Telephone v. Falcon, a "precedent" on who may represent a class, had separated an individual promotion claim based on "intentional discrimination" from hiring claims. Those hiring claims rested on different, statistical proof.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Here the same express rationale supplied a common legal issue, and class treatment guarded against recurring individual mootness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Here the same express rationale behind both policies supplied a common "legal issue." And class treatment guarded against recurring "mootness," the case dying each time an individual student's own dispute ended.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: The majority acknowledged possible overlap between Article III standing and Rule 23 adequacy without choosing the proper doctrinal category because both were satisfied.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: The "majority" acknowledged that Article III standing (the constitutional right to sue) might overlap with Rule 23 adequacy, whether a class representative is suitable. It did not choose the proper doctrinal category, because both were satisfied.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: The Court rejected that categorical contention for the reasons given in Grutter, while requiring narrow tailoring under strict scrutiny.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: The Court rejected that categorical contention, for the reasons given in Grutter, so diversity can justify considering race. But it required "narrow tailoring" under strict scrutiny, meaning the policy must be closely fitted to that goal under the most demanding test.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Committee review did not cure the general rule: it was exceptional, followed the point award, and was not shown to reach a meaningful share of applicants.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: The individual committee review did not save the system, because it was the exception, came after the automatic points were given, and was not shown to reach a meaningful share of applicants.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: The equal-protection violation also violated Title VI and § 1981 under the principles the Court applied.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: The "equal-protection" violation also violated Title VI and § 1981, under the principles the Court applied, which read those statutes to forbid the same discrimination.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Justice Breyer joined her concurrence except its final sentence joining the Court’s opinion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Justice Breyer joined O'Connor's concurrence except its final sentence, in which she joined the Court’s opinion. He agreed only with the result.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Breyer concurred in the judgment, accepting O’Connor’s assessment, but also joined Part I of Justice Ginsburg’s dissent distinguishing inclusion from exclusion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Breyer "concurred in the judgment," agreeing with the result but not all the reasoning, and accepted O’Connor’s assessment. He also "joined" Part I of Justice Ginsburg's dissent, which distinguished policies meant to include minorities from those meant to exclude them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Souter, would dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Justice Stevens, "joined by" Justice Souter (meaning Souter signed on), would "dismiss" for lack of jurisdiction. He thought no plaintiff had standing to bring the challenge, so the Court should not decide the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Unnamed members could not create a representative’s initial stake.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Other members of the class cannot supply the personal stake the named representative lacks at the start.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Later class mootness rules could preserve a properly begun action, but he found that premise absent.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Special rules can keep a class case alive after the representative's own claim ends, but only if the case was properly brought in the first place, which he thought this one was not.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: On the merits, Souter saw a plus-factor system rather than a quota: all competed for all places, other traits could outweigh race, and explicit numbers resembled implicit holistic weights.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: "On the merits," meaning on the policy's actual legality, Souter saw a "plus-factor" system, with race one plus among many, rather than a "quota" reserving seats. All applicants competed for all places, other traits could outweigh race, and explicit point numbers resembled the implicit weights of "holistic" review, which considers each applicant as a whole.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: He would vacate for want of jurisdiction, but affirm if a proper plaintiff presented the merits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: He would "vacate," or wipe out, the lower ruling for want of jurisdiction. But if a proper plaintiff presented the merits, he would "affirm," upholding the policy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.sentence: Rehnquist’s opinion was joined by O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas; Breyer’s concurrence in the judgment supplied the sixth vote.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345.plain: Rehnquist’s opinion was joined by O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas. Breyer’s "concurrence in the judgment," agreeing only with the result, supplied the sixth vote.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Wilko sued Hayden, Stone & Co. members under Securities Act of 1933 § 12(2).
