brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Wilko sued members of Hayden, Stone & Co., the brokerage firm, under § 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933. That section lets buyers recover when securities are sold to them through misleading statements.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: His signed margin agreements broadly sent future account controversies to arbitration under New York law before designated organizations or exchanges; the reproduced agreement required at least three arbitrators.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: His signed "margin agreements," contracts for buying securities partly on credit from the broker, broadly sent future account disputes to arbitration under New York law before designated organizations or exchanges. The reproduced agreement required at least three arbitrators.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Before answering, the brokers sought a Federal Arbitration Act § 3 stay, expressing willingness to arbitrate and citing his failure to pursue that route.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Before answering the complaint, the brokers sought a stay (pause) of the lawsuit under Federal Arbitration Act § 3. They said they were willing to arbitrate and pointed to Wilko's failure to pursue that route.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: The district court refused the stay because Securities Act § 14 invalidated waiver of compliance through advance arbitration of this statutory claim.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: The "district court" refused the "stay." It held that Securities Act § 14 voids any "waiver," or giving up, of compliance with the Act, and agreeing in advance to arbitrate this "statutory" claim was such a waiver.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: The Second Circuit reversed, reasoning that substantive protections remained and judicial review could correct failure to apply them.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: The Second Circuit reversed, reasoning that the investor's "substantive" protections, his actual legal rights, remained in arbitration. "Judicial review" by courts could correct an arbitrator's failure to apply them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Justice Reed recognized the Federal Arbitration Act’s conceded coverage and Congress’s purpose of overcoming judicial hostility through prompt, economical commercial resolution.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Justice Reed recognized the Federal Arbitration Act’s conceded coverage of the agreement. He also recognized Congress’s purpose of overcoming courts' hostility to arbitration through prompt, economical resolution of commercial disputes.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Section 12(2) supplied special misrepresentation remedies with purchaser-knowledge and seller reasonable-care requirements.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Section 12(2) supplied special remedies for "misrepresentation" in securities sales. A buyer who did not know of the misstatement could recover unless the seller proved it used reasonable care.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Section 22 broadened judicial forums, removed the ordinary federal amount restriction, provided favorable venue and service, and barred removal of covered state actions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Section 22 broadened the judicial "forums," or courts, where investors could sue and removed the usual minimum dollar amount for federal court. It provided favorable "venue" (place of suit) and service of papers, and "barred" removal, meaning covered state-court cases could not be moved to federal court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Reed treated those procedural advantages as part of protected compliance, not dispensable detail.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Those choices of court were themselves protections that the Act forbids investors to give up.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: The majority’s objection was therefore not formal deletion of law or burdens, but practical enforcement before any controversy was known.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: The "majority’s" objection was therefore not that arbitration formally deleted the investor's legal rights or the seller's burdens of proof. It was that agreeing before any dispute was known weakened their practical enforcement.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Securities disputes required legal decisions about materiality, knowledge, reasonable care, and proof, while arbitrators could proceed without judicial instruction, reasons, or a complete record.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Securities disputes required legal decisions about "materiality" (whether a misstatement was important to a buyer), knowledge, reasonable care, and proof. Yet arbitrators could proceed without a judge's instructions, without giving reasons, and without a complete record.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Federal vacatur grounds for corruption, partiality, procedural misconduct, and excess of powers were limited.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Federal grounds for "vacatur," a court setting aside an arbitration award, were limited: corruption, partiality (bias), procedural misconduct, and arbitrators exceeding their powers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: The majority distinguished ordinary legal error from manifest disregard and noted lack of routine merits review of unrestricted submissions, contrasting English legal-question procedures.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: The majority (the Justices who decided the case) separated an arbitrator's ordinary "legal error", a mere mistake about the law that courts do not fix, from "manifest disregard", knowingly ignoring the law. It noted there was no routine court review of the "merits" (who should win on the law) when parties submitted a dispute without restrictions, unlike the English procedure for sending legal questions to a court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Boyd’s protection of statutory venue choice supported treating forum selection as a meaningful statutory benefit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: An earlier case, Boyd, refused to let a contract take away a statutory right to choose where to sue; likewise, investors' choice of court here was a real benefit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Justice Jackson agreed that a precontroversy agreement could not waive the judicial remedy and believed a later agreement could submit an existing dispute to arbitration.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Justice Jackson agreed that a "precontroversy" agreement, signed before any dispute exists, could not "waive" (give up) the investor's court "remedy", meaning the right to sue in court. He believed a later agreement, made once a dispute already existed, could send that dispute to arbitration.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Justice Frankfurter, joined by Minton, accepted that arbitration inherently depriving statutory protections would fail, but found no such showing.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Justice Frankfurter, "joined by" Justice Minton (meaning Minton signed on to his opinion), agreed that arbitration would be invalid if it necessarily stripped investors of their "statutory" protections, those given by the Securities Act. But he found no showing that it did.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: If statutory violations warranted vacatur, adequate scrutiny through a record or explanation should be implied.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: If an award could be set aside for violating the "statutory" rules of the Act, then "vacatur" (a court canceling the award) needed a way to check. So the law should be "implied", read as silently requiring, enough of a record or explanation for courts to review the award properly.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: This record did not establish forced acceptance of an unconscionable clause, and the Securities and Exchange Commission as amicus did not assert that particular theory.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Nothing in this record showed Wilko was forced into "acceptance" of an "unconscionable" clause, one so one-sided and unfairly imposed that courts refuse to enforce it. The Securities and Exchange Commission, filing as amicus (an outside adviser to the Court), did not argue that particular theory.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.sentence: Its historical holding invalidated the predispute clause as applied to this § 12(2) controversy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591.plain: Its historical holding, since overruled, struck down the "predispute" clause (an arbitration agreement signed before any dispute arose) as applied to this claim under § 12(2) of the Securities Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Chesny sued individually and as estate administrator under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and state tort law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Chesny sued both for himself and as "estate administrator", the person legally representing his dead son's estate. He sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the federal civil-rights statute, and under state "tort" law, the ordinary law of injuries.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Before trial, the officers timely offered $100,000 expressly including accrued costs and attorney’s fees.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Before trial, the officers made a "timely" (made within the deadline) formal settlement offer of $100,000, which expressly included all court costs and attorney's fees built up to that point.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The district court invoked Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 68 to refuse amounts incurred after the offer.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) used Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 68 to deny Chesny the costs and fees he ran up after the offer. Rule 68 applied because Chesny ended up with less than the officers had offered.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The Seventh Circuit reversed the denial of Chesny’s own fees, reasoning that mechanically combining Rule 68 with the civil-rights fee statute could pressure plaintiffs and lawyers to accept inadequate offers.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: The Seventh Circuit, the federal appeals court, reversed the denial of Chesny’s own fees. It reasoned that automatically combining Rule 68 with the civil-rights fee statute could pressure plaintiffs and their lawyers into accepting settlement offers that were too low.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The Supreme Court reviewed both the inclusive offer’s validity and whether § 1988 attorney’s fees counted as Rule 68 costs.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: The Supreme Court "reviewed" (took up and decided) two questions. Was an inclusive offer, a lump sum that did not separate out costs, valid? And did attorney's fees under § 1988, the civil-rights fee statute, count as "costs" that Rule 68 cuts off?

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Chief Justice Burger focused on the judgment the offer authorized.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Chief Justice Burger, writing for the Court, focused on what judgment the offer would have produced if Chesny had accepted it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Provided the offer did not exclude costs from judgment, no allocation was required.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: So long as the offer did not leave costs out of the "judgment" (the court's final order of what is owed), it did not need to say how much of the total was for costs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: A total-exposure figure could promote settlement where defendants would not commit while additional fees remained open.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Letting defendants offer one all-inclusive figure encourages settlement, because they may not offer at all if fees could still be added on top.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Claimed postoffer costs were excluded because they compensated the expense of continuing litigation; adding them would undermine the offer’s operation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Costs after the offer are left out of the comparison, because counting the expense of continuing to litigate would defeat the rule's purpose.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Although ordinary American practice excluded fees from costs, statutes existing when the Rules were adopted in 1938 sometimes expressly included them, and committee materials identified many examples.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Although ordinary American practice did not count lawyers' fees as "costs", some statutes in force when the federal Rules were adopted in 1938 expressly included them. The drafting committee's materials identified many such examples.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The majority therefore understood it to incorporate costs properly awardable under applicable substantive statutes or other authority.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: The majority (the Justices who decided the case) therefore read Rule 68 to include whatever costs could properly be awarded under the "substantive" statute behind the claim, meaning the law that creates the right being sued on, or other authority.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Section 1988 expressly authorized fees as part of costs in § 1983 cases.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Section 1988, the civil-rights fee statute, expressly allowed attorney's fees "as part of the costs" in § 1983 cases. So those fees counted as Rule 68 costs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Roadway Express involved a sanctions statute with its own cost definition and thus did not govern this incorporation question.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Roadway Express, an earlier case, involved a "sanctions" statute (a law penalizing lawyers for misconduct) that defined costs itself. So it did not control this "incorporation" question, whether Rule 68 takes in the meaning of costs from the statute behind the claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The cutoff nevertheless operated by the rule once applicable, not by a separate finding that every hour of postoffer work was unreasonable under § 1988.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: The post-offer fees were still cut off automatically once Rule 68 applied. They were not cut off by a separate "finding" (a court's determination of fact) that every hour of post-offer work was unreasonable under § 1988.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Justice Rehnquist expressly withdrew his Delta dissent’s view excluding attorney’s fees from Rule 68 costs after further consideration.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Justice Rehnquist, after further thought, expressly took back the view in his Delta dissent’s opinion (an earlier case where he disagreed with the majority) that attorney’s fees are not Rule 68 costs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Marshall and Blackmun, favored a uniform meaning based on traditional taxable items in § 1920.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Justice Brennan, "joined by" Justices Marshall and Blackmun (meaning they signed his dissent), wanted "costs" to mean the same thing everywhere. He would use the traditional list of court expenses that may be charged to the loser in § 1920, which does not include lawyers' fees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Making Rule 68 depend on small wording variations across fee statutes undermined uniformity, and he found the Roadway Express distinction inadequate.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Brennan objected that making Rule 68 turn on small wording differences between fee statutes destroyed uniformity. He also found the Court's way of distinguishing Roadway Express inadequate.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: He argued that § 1988 called for contextual reasonableness: unproductive work could already be denied, and the district court might reject much of this request on that basis.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: He argued that § 1988 already calls for judging reasonableness case by case, so pay for unproductive work could be denied anyway. The district court (the trial court) might have rejected much of this request on that basis.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The rule’s availability only to defending parties was not neutral; early offers before adequate discovery might coerce uninformed decisions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Only defendants can make Rule 68 offers, so the rule is not neutral between the sides. An early offer, made before adequate "discovery" (the pretrial exchange of evidence), could pressure plaintiffs into uninformed decisions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: Brennan treated statutory fee entitlement as substantive and the majority’s procedural alteration as contrary to the Rules Enabling Act.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Brennan treated the "statutory" right to fees, created by Congress, as substantive: a real legal right, not mere procedure. He said the majority’s change, made through a procedural rule, violated the law that lets the Court write procedural rules only if they leave substantive rights alone, the Rules Enabling Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The officers were not liable for Chesny’s approximately $139,692 postoffer costs-and-fees request.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: The officers were not "liable" (legally responsible to pay) for Chesny's request of approximately $139,692 in post-offer costs and fees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.sentence: The damages verdict remained intact, as did the distinct agreed preoffer amount and the unchallenged refusal to shift the officers’ own expenses.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-604.plain: Chesny kept his jury award of "damages" (money compensation for the harm), and the separately agreed $32,000 for pre-offer costs and fees. The unchallenged ruling that he did not have to pay the officers' own expenses also stood.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: A Purdue affiliate pleaded guilty to felony misbranding in 2007, and thousands of civil suits followed, including against family members.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: A Purdue affiliate (a related company) "pleaded guilty" in 2007 to felony "misbranding", the crime of marketing a drug with misleading labeling or claims. Thousands of "civil suits" (private lawsuits for money, not criminal cases) followed, some naming Sackler family members.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Purdue entered Chapter 11 in 2019; the Sacklers did not.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Purdue filed under Chapter 11 in 2019, the part of the Bankruptcy Code that lets a business reorganize instead of shutting down. The Sacklers themselves did not file for bankruptcy.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: They initially offered $4.325 billion over a decade to settle estate claims and obtain release and permanent injunction of victims’ current and future opioid-related claims.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The Sacklers first offered $4.325 billion over ten years to settle the claims Purdue's bankruptcy estate had against them. In return they wanted a "release" (a legal end to claims) and a permanent court order barring victims' current and future opioid lawsuits against them.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: The protection reached negligence, fraud, and willful misconduct claims against numerous family members and controlled entities without every claimant’s consent.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: That protection covered claims of "negligence" (carelessness), fraud, and "willful misconduct" (intentional wrongdoing) against many family members and companies they controlled. It applied without every claimant’s consent, so it bound victims who never agreed.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: The bankruptcy court confirmed.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The bankruptcy court approved the plan.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: The district court vacated because the Code did not authorize extinguishing claims against nondebtors without consent.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: On appeal the district court threw out that approval, because nothing in the Bankruptcy Code lets a court wipe out victims' claims against people who are not themselves bankrupt without the victims' agreement.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: A divided Second Circuit revived the modified plan, with Judge Wesley separately criticizing statutory authority.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: A divided Second Circuit, the federal appeals court, reinstated the revised plan. Judge Wesley wrote separately, criticizing whether there was "statutory authority", meaning whether the Bankruptcy Code actually allowed such releases.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: The Supreme Court stayed the decision and treated the stay request as a certiorari petition to resolve the circuit division.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The Supreme Court "stayed" the decision, putting it on hold. It treated the stay request as a "certiorari" petition, a request for the Court to take the case, to resolve the "circuit division", the disagreement among federal appeals courts on this question.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Justice Gorsuch’s majority contrasted ordinary debtor submission of virtually all assets for a limited discharge with Sacklers seeking comparable protection without bankruptcy or anything close to all assets.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Justice Gorsuch’s majority opinion contrasted the ordinary bargain, where a debtor hands over virtually all its assets to get a limited "discharge" (debts wiped out), with what the Sacklers wanted. They sought similar protection without filing for bankruptcy or giving up anything close to all their assets.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Section 1123(b)’s first five optional-plan paragraphs addressed debtor claims, property, contracts, and creditor relations.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Section 1123(b) of the Bankruptcy Code lists optional things a reorganization plan may include. Its first five paragraphs deal only with the debtor's own claims, property, contracts, and dealings with creditors.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Applying ejusdem generis, which reads residual language with the preceding category, the majority found other linked the catchall to those provisions.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The majority applied "ejusdem generis", the rule that "residual language" (general words at the end of a list) covers only things like those listed. It read the word "other" as tying the "catchall" ("any other appropriate provision") to the earlier items about the debtor's own affairs.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: It added powers but not the fundamentally different power to extinguish victims’ independent nondebtor claims without consent.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: That catchall added similar powers, but not the fundamentally different power to "extinguish" (permanently wipe out) victims' own claims against "nondebtor" parties, people who are not in bankruptcy, without the victims' consent.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Appropriate did not mean anything not expressly forbidden.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The word 'appropriate' did not let a plan do everything the Code fails to expressly forbid.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Section 105(a)’s authority to carry out Code provisions could not create that missing substantive power.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Section 105(a) lets bankruptcy courts issue orders to carry out the Code's provisions. But it could not create that missing "substantive" power, meaning a real power to change people's rights that the Code itself does not give.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Paragraph three’s authority to settle derivative claims was no answer.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The Code does let a plan settle claims that belong to the bankrupt company, but that did not help the Sacklers.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Such a claim substantively belonged to the corporation or estate even if someone else asserted it.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Such a claim legally belonged to the "corporation" or its bankruptcy estate, even if someone else, such as a creditor, was the one bringing it.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: A victim’s direct Sackler claim did not become estate property because Purdue’s conduct mattered.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: A victim's personal claim against a Sackler stays the victim's, even though Purdue's conduct is part of the story.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Ordinary discharge reserved benefits for debtors surrendering assets and retained protections involving fraud, willful injury, and jury rights for personal-injury and wrongful-death claims.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: An ordinary discharge (debts wiped out) "reserved" its benefits for "debtors" who give up their assets, and kept exceptions for fraud and willful injury. It also preserved jury-trial rights for personal-injury and "wrongful-death" claims (suits over a death caused by someone's wrong).

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Congress expressly authorized certain third-party injunctions for asbestos bankruptcy in section 524(g), demonstrating how to provide such power.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: In section 524(g), Congress expressly allowed certain court orders protecting third parties in asbestos bankruptcies. That showed Congress knows how to give such power when it wants to.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Pre-Code practice likewise generally confined discharge to debtors surrendering property.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Before the 1978 Code, too, only debtors who gave up their property had their debts wiped out.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Competing indemnification arguments, including good-faith conditions and disallowance or subordination, did not result in a universal ruling on indemnity claims.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The parties also argued about "indemnification" (Purdue reimbursing the Sacklers for claims against them), including whether it depended on the Sacklers acting in "good-faith", and whether such claims faced "disallowance" (being refused) or subordination (being paid last). The Court made no general ruling on those indemnity claims.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: The decision left consensual third-party releases undisturbed without defining consent, did not address plans fully satisfying nondebtor claims, and did not decide whether effective, substantially consummated plans must be unwound.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The ruling did not disturb consensual "third-party releases" (releases that claimants agree to), and did not define what counts as consent. It also did not address plans that pay "nondebtor" claims in full, or decide whether plans already in effect and "substantially consummated" (largely carried out) must be undone.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Bankruptcy prevented races to exhaust assets, and nondebtor releases could preserve or enlarge a shared estate where indemnification, insurance, and settlement contributions intertwined interests.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The dissent said bankruptcy exists to stop creditors racing to grab assets first. "Nondebtor releases" (releases protecting people who are not in bankruptcy) can preserve or enlarge the shared pot when "indemnification" duties, insurance, and "settlement" payments tie third parties' interests to the company's.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Here he stressed Sackler indemnification, Purdue’s roughly $1.8 billion estate, a $2 billion government superpriority claim, and contributions enlarging total assets to about $7 billion.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: He stressed the Sacklers' "indemnification" rights (Purdue might have to reimburse them for claims against them) and Purdue's estate of roughly $1.8 billion. He also pointed to a $2 billion government claim with "superpriority", meaning it is paid before others, and to contributions that would enlarge total assets to about $7 billion.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Kavanaugh argued paragraph three already affected derivative creditor claims by settling estate actions against nondebtors, so paragraph six could reach direct claims threatening the estate.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: Justice Kavanaugh argued that paragraph three already affects claims a "creditor" brings on the company's behalf ("derivative" claims), by letting plans settle the estate's suits against "nondebtors", people not in bankruptcy. So, he said, paragraph six, the catchall, could also reach victims' "direct claims" (their own personal claims) when those threaten the estate.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Consensual and full-payment releases, exculpation, and Energy Resources, a precedent recognizing plan-related authority, supported breadth.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: He said several accepted practices supported a broad reading: releases claimants agree to, releases where claims are paid in full, and "exculpation" clauses shielding those who run the bankruptcy from suit. He also relied on Energy Resources, a "precedent" (an earlier decision) recognizing courts' authority over plan-related matters.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: He invoked asbestos savings language and read section 524(e) to say debtor discharge did not automatically release others, not to prohibit an additional negotiated release.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: He relied on the asbestos provision's "savings" language, which says it does not limit other powers. He read section 524(e) to mean only that a "debtor" getting its debts wiped out does not automatically release others, not that a plan may never add a negotiated release of them.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: Modern practice and related-to jurisdiction, including stays of third-party litigation, were more useful than superseded early practice.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: He thought modern practice, and "related-to jurisdiction" (bankruptcy courts' power over suits connected to the case, including pausing suits against third parties), mattered more than early practice that has been "superseded", meaning replaced by later law.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.sentence: It imposed no tort judgment on the Sacklers, fixed no replacement payment, and decided no final lawful reorganization.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-PURDUE.plain: The decision did not impose any "tort" judgment on the Sacklers (it did not find them liable for wrongful injury), did not set any replacement payment, and did not approve any final lawful reorganization plan.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The contract count alleged an undertaking to cure the stomach problem, unskillful performance, inadequate postoperative care, and failure of satisfactory results.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The contract count of the complaint alleged an "undertaking" (a promise) to cure the stomach problem. It also alleged unskillful "performance" of the surgery, inadequate care after the operation, and a failure to produce satisfactory results.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The trial court denied a directed verdict.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The trial court refused to grant a "directed verdict", which would have ended the case in the surgeons' favor without letting the jury decide.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The jury found for the surgeons on malpractice and awarded the plaintiffs $50,000 on contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The jury found for the surgeons on the "malpractice" claim (professional negligence), but awarded the plaintiffs, Guilmet and his wife, $50,000 on the breach-of-contract claim.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The court denied judgment notwithstanding that verdict; the Court of Appeals affirmed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The trial court refused to enter "judgment" notwithstanding the verdict, meaning it would not override the jury's decision. The Court of Appeals "affirmed", agreeing with that ruling.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The Supreme Court reviewed whether the contract verdict had sufficient support, not whether to find negligence anew.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The Michigan Supreme Court "reviewed" only whether enough evidence supported the "contract" verdict. It did not decide afresh whether there had been "negligence" (carelessness).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: Justice T. G. Kavanagh rejected a requirement of a separate special contract with separate consideration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: Justice T. G. Kavanagh, for the majority, rejected any requirement of a "special contract", a separate deal for the guarantee backed by its own "consideration" (something extra given in exchange for the promise).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The plaintiffs said the assurances were offered before accepting the operation agreement and formed terms of that same bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The plaintiffs said the doctor's assurances came before Guilmet accepted the agreement to have the operation. So, they argued, the assurances were terms of that same "bargain".

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: Unlike a later independent promise, those alleged preacceptance warranties raised no past-consideration problem.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: A promise made later, after the deal, raises a "past-consideration" problem: something already given cannot pay for a new promise. These "alleged" warranties, made before acceptance, had no such problem.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The majority declined to make the label “cure” decisive when the parties had not used it; replacing one condition with another need not deliver the described result.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The majority declined to treat the word "cure" as decisive when the parties had not used it. Trading one condition, the ulcer, for another need not deliver the result that was described.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: Recovery required a specific, clear, express promise to cure or achieve an identified result, reasonably contemplated by both sides and relied on by the patient.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: "Recovery" (winning money) required a specific, clear, "express" (stated outright) promise to cure or to achieve an identified result. Both sides must have reasonably "contemplated" (understood and had in mind) that result, and the patient must have relied on it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The evidence permitted that finding here, making judgment notwithstanding the verdict inappropriate.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The "evidence" here allowed a jury "finding" of such a promise. So a "judgment notwithstanding the verdict", overriding the jury's decision, was inappropriate.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: Justice T. E. Brennan concurred in affirmance but disputed that the verdict necessarily meant a guaranteed cure despite nonnegligent conduct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: Justice T. E. Brennan "concurred" in affirmance, meaning he agreed the result should stand. But he disputed that the verdict necessarily meant the doctor guaranteed a cure even though his conduct was "nonnegligent" (not careless).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The contract count also alleged promised care and skill, and the jury returned a general verdict.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The contract count also "alleged" a promise to use proper care and skill. The jury returned a "general verdict", saying only who won without stating which theory it accepted.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: In his view, the trial judge’s oral clarification that there was “no negligence” did not turn it into a special verdict or confine the contractual basis.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: In his view, the trial judge’s spoken clarification that there was "no negligence" did not turn the result into a "special verdict" (a verdict with specific factual findings). Nor did it limit which promise the "contractual" claim rested on.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The judge had removed several allegations from the tort count for insufficient evidence of departure from community standards but had not similarly narrowed the contract count.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The judge had removed several "allegations" from the "tort" (negligence) count for "insufficient evidence" that the doctors fell below "community standards", the accepted level of local medical practice. But he had not narrowed the contract count the same way.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: He read the contract claim as charging negligent performance of the same acts as the tort claim, defeated by the jury’s finding of no negligence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: Justice Black read the contract claim as charging careless performance of the same acts as the "tort" (negligence) claim. So, in his view, the jury's finding of no negligence defeated it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: He distinguished precedents with different pleadings or separately supported arrangements and warned that medical encouragement could create contract exposure beyond malpractice limitation periods.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: He "distinguished" (explained why they did not apply) earlier cases that had different "pleadings" (the written claims filed) or separately supported agreements. He warned that a doctor's encouragement could expose doctors to contract suits even after malpractice deadlines had passed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The addendum continued to contest the contractual theory and broad assignment of oral-agreement questions to juries, concluding with a vote to reverse and remand for defense judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: His "addendum" (an added note) kept rejecting the contract theory and the broad practice of leaving disputes over spoken agreements to juries. He would "reverse" the decision and send the case back for a "defense judgment", one in the surgeons' favor.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.sentence: The six-to-one judgment affirmed the $50,000 recovery and allowed plaintiffs to tax costs.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-001.plain: The six-to-one "judgment" upheld the $50,000 recovery and let the plaintiffs charge their court costs to the surgeons.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: Keller had no money with that banker and intended to place a condition on the check preventing liability, but omitted the condition.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: Keller had no money on deposit with the banker the check was drawn on. He intended to write a condition on the check preventing any "liability" (legal duty to pay) on it, but he left the condition out.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: Although the judge found that neither participant contemplated a serious purchase and sale, he held Keller liable because the check lacked the intended condition and Keller had retained the watch.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: The judge found that neither man intended a serious purchase and sale. Even so, he held Keller "liable" (legally bound to pay) because the check lacked the intended condition and Keller had kept the watch.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: Keller sought review by writ of error, putting the legal consequence of the judge’s own factual findings before the Michigan Supreme Court.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: Keller sought "review" by writ of error, an old procedure for correcting a lower court's legal mistakes. The question was what legal effect followed from the judge's own "factual findings" that the deal was not serious, and he put it before the Michigan Supreme Court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: Holderman therefore had no cause of action on the check.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: So Holderman had no "cause of action", meaning no legal basis to sue, on the check.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: On May 12, 1863, the court reversed and awarded costs in both the Supreme Court and the court below; the other justices concurred without a separate writing.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: On May 12, 1863, the court reversed and awarded Keller his costs both in the Supreme Court and in the court "below" (the trial court). The other justices "concurred", agreeing, without writing separately.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: The court did not order a new trial, award the watch’s reasonable value or decide a separate restitution action.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: The court did not order a new trial or "award" Holderman the watch's "reasonable value" (what it was fairly worth). It also did not decide a separate "restitution" action, a suit to get back the value of what was handed over.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.sentence: Nor did it authorize escape from a reasonably understood serious promise through a secret intention to joke.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-033.plain: The ruling does not let someone escape a promise the other side reasonably took as serious by claiming to have been secretly joking; here both sides knew it was a joke.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: By September 4, the pinspotters stood at the lanes, but the special master later found them inoperative, in poor condition, and not installed as promised.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: By September 4, the pinspotters were at the lanes. But the "special master", a court-appointed official who heard the evidence, later found them inoperative, in poor condition, and not installed as promised.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: As administratrix, Bonebrake sought the unpaid contract price.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Frances Bonebrake, Simek's sister, sued as "administratrix" (the woman managing his estate) for the unpaid "contract price", the money still owed under the agreements.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The Coxes counterclaimed for losses and argued that Simek or the estate breached first.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The Coxes "counterclaimed", suing back for their losses. They argued that Simek or his estate "breached" (broke the contracts) first.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: He also excluded the April mixed goods-and-services agreement from Article 2 and treated the buyers’ takeover as their breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The master also held that the April agreement, a "mixed goods-and-services" deal (equipment plus installation work), fell outside Article 2 of the UCC, which governs sales of goods. He treated the Coxes' taking over the work as their own breach.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Although he did not expressly resolve anticipatory repudiation, that conclusion implicitly rejected it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The master did not expressly decide whether there had been "anticipatory repudiation", the seller's side making clear before performance was due that it would not perform. But calling the Coxes the breaching party implicitly rejected it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The panel examined notice and cure, Article 2 coverage, and that implied rejection of repudiation under commercially practical Code principles.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The appeals panel examined three issues: notice and "cure" (the seller's chance to fix defects), whether Article 2 of the UCC covered the April deal, and the master's "implied" rejection of "repudiation". It applied the Code's practical, business-minded principles.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The master found that installation required making the pinspotters operative, constituting a fitness warranty the equipment did not meet.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The "master" (the court-appointed official who heard the evidence) found that promising installation meant promising to make the pinspotters work. That amounted to a "fitness warranty", a guarantee the goods would be fit for their purpose, which the equipment did not meet.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: But he believed inadequate notice and interference with cure eliminated the buyers’ warranty remedies.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: But he believed the Coxes lost their warranty remedies through "inadequate notice" (not telling the seller enough about the problems) and by interfering with "cure", the seller's chance to fix the defects.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Iowa §554.2607(3)(a), corresponding to Uniform Commercial Code §2-607(3)(a), governed accepted goods.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Iowa §554.2607(3)(a), which matches Uniform Commercial Code §2-607(3)(a), governed here because the Coxes had accepted the goods, meaning they kept them rather than refusing them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: It must convey that the transaction was troublesome and claimed to involve breach, permitting negotiation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: It only has to tell the seller there is a problem the buyer considers a breach, so the two can try to work it out.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The master instead imported the more particularized rule for rejection in §554.2605(1), addressing omitted discoverable defects when cure was possible or in specified merchant dealings.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The master instead borrowed the stricter rule for rejected goods in §554.2605(1). That rule deals with a buyer who fails to list "discoverable" defects (ones a reasonable inspection would reveal), either when "cure" (the seller fixing them) was possible or in certain dealings between merchants.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The cure analysis made the same category error.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The master's "cure" analysis, about the seller's right to fix defects, made the same mistake of applying a rule meant for refused goods.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Section 554.2508 concerned a rejected nonconforming tender.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Section 554.2508 deals with a rejected "nonconforming tender", a delivery of goods that do not match the contract and that the buyer has refused.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: These buyers accepted goods and sought damages; accepting a later cure proposal was not a prerequisite to all recovery.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: These buyers kept the goods ("accepted goods") and sued for damages. Accepting a later "cure" proposal, an offer to fix things, was not a condition of any "recovery" (winning money) at all.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Refusing it could affect mitigation and damages, but did not erase the warranty claim.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Refusing the offer to fix things could affect "mitigation" (the duty to keep one's losses down) and so the amount of damages. But it did not erase the "warranty" claim, the claim for breach of the seller's guarantee.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The master relied on substantial labor, a lump price, and indivisibility to exclude the April contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The master relied on the heavy labor involved, the single lump-sum price, and "indivisibility" (the deal could not be split into parts) to rule that the April "contract" was not a sale of goods.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: But Article 2 covered transactions in goods, defined by movability when identified to the contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: But Article 2 of the UCC covers deals in "goods", defined as things that are movable at the time they are "identified to the contract", meaning set aside or designated as the goods being sold.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Later attachment did not turn the bargain into house construction.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Fastening the equipment into the building later did not turn the "bargain" (the deal) into a house-construction contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The governing predominant-factor inquiry asked whether the transaction primarily supplied services with incidental goods or goods with incidental labor.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The controlling "predominant-factor" test asks what the deal was mainly about: supplying services with some goods thrown in, or supplying goods with some labor thrown in.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The court did not equate every seller’s death with repudiation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The court did not hold that every seller's death counts as "repudiation", a refusal to perform the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Here the sole proprietorship, severe defects, absent equipment, approaching league schedule, fruitless searches, and lack of anybody able to continue performance together indicated rejection of the continuing obligation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Here several facts together showed the seller's side rejected its ongoing duty: Simek ran a "sole proprietorship" (a business owned by one person), the defects were severe, equipment was missing, and league play was near. The searches for help failed, and nobody could continue "performance" of the contracts.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Under §554.2610 and the Code commentary, repudiation did not require literal impossibility or malevolence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Under §554.2610 and the official Code commentary, "repudiation" does not require that performance be literally impossible or that the seller act out of ill will.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Conduct reasonably indicating rejection sufficed even while the performance period remained open.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Conduct that reasonably signaled rejection of the contract was enough, even while the time for "performance" (doing what was promised) had not yet run out.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: The panel found clear error in the implied contrary finding and regarded the buyers’ protective steps as justified rather than a prior breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The panel found "clear error", a plain mistake, in the master's "implied" finding that there was no repudiation. It saw the Coxes' protective steps as justified, not as a "prior breach" (breaking the contract first).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Even if their later completion proposal counted as retraction under §554.2611, the buyers had already materially changed position, making it too late.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: The estate's later offer to finish the work might count as "retraction" under §554.2611, taking back the repudiation. Even so, it came too late, because the Coxes had already "materially changed position", meaning they had significantly relied on the repudiation by making other arrangements.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Both agreements received the proper goods-law analysis, acceptance no longer barred warranty damages through misplaced rejection rules, and the buyers’ response to repudiation was not treated as their breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: Both agreements were now analyzed under the law of goods. The Coxes' "acceptance" of the goods no longer barred "warranty" damages through misapplied "rejection" rules (rules for refused goods), and their response to the "repudiation" was not treated as their own breach.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.sentence: Mitigation and the support for particular losses remained relevant.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-069.plain: "Mitigation", whether the Coxes reasonably kept their losses down, and whether each particular loss was proved, still remained to be considered.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: In 1991, Calvin Klein Inc. (CKI), beneficial owner of the trademarks, gave Piccoli A/S exclusive Scandinavian distribution rights.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: In 1991, Calvin Klein Inc. (CKI), the "beneficial owner" of the "trademarks" (the one who really held the rights to the brand names), gave Piccoli A/S the exclusive right to distribute in Scandinavian markets.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: That apparent sublicense did not make Piccoli a party to Jeanswear’s contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Piccoli later got its rights second-hand through European, an apparent "sublicense" (a license passed on by someone who holds one). That did not make Piccoli a party to Jeanswear's separate contract with CKI.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Jeanswear and Azteca moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim; World Apparel sought judgment on the pleadings.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Jeanswear and Azteca "moved to dismiss", asking the court to throw out the case because it lacked subject-matter "jurisdiction" (power over this kind of case) and the complaint stated no legal claim. World Apparel sought "judgment on the pleadings", a ruling based only on the written claims and answers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Judge Kaplan assumed the complaint’s facts and considered incorporated contracts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Judge Kaplan, at this early stage, assumed the facts in Piccoli's complaint were true and read the contracts the complaint relied on.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Under New York law, intended-beneficiary status could arise if nobody but the third party could recover for breach, or contractual language otherwise clearly authorized third-party enforcement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Under New York law, an outsider has "intended-beneficiary" status, and can enforce someone else's contract, in two ways. Either nobody but that "third party" could recover for the breach, or the contract's words otherwise clearly allow third-party enforcement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Piccoli failed the first route because CKI expressly retained damages and injunction remedies.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Piccoli failed the first route because CKI expressly kept its own "remedies" (legal ways to enforce), namely "damages" (money) and injunctions (court orders), against Jeanswear.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Piccoli’s motion-paper assertion of unique injury could not amend its pleading and, even considered, did not eliminate CKI’s enforcement right.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Piccoli claimed in its motion papers that only it was injured, but legal briefs cannot "amend" (change) the complaint. Even if considered, that claim did not remove CKI’s right to enforce the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Naming Piccoli individually was unnecessary, but protective enforcement intent needed to appear on the face of the agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The contract did not need to name Piccoli. But an intent to let distributors like Piccoli enforce it had to appear "on the face of" the agreement, meaning in its own words.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: The court read cooperation with provisions making the agreement personal, restricting assignment and sublicensing without consent, and limiting binding effect and benefit to parties and permitted successors and assigns.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The court read the cooperation clause together with others: the agreement was personal, it included terms "restricting assignment" (transfer) and sublicensing without consent, and it bound and benefited only the parties and their permitted "successors and assigns" (those who lawfully take over their rights).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: The court expressly rejected treating an anti-assignment clause alone as fatal to third-party rights; those concepts could coexist.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The court expressly refused to treat an "anti-assignment" clause (barring transfer of the contract) as alone fatal to "third-party" rights, because the two ideas can coexist.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Even assuming extrinsic circumstances were admissible, knowledge of the franchise, worldwide territorial cooperation, and investment did not overcome the text.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Even if the court considered "extrinsic circumstances" (facts outside the contract's text), they did not overcome the text. Those facts were knowledge of the "franchise" (Calvin Klein's distribution network), worldwide cooperation on territories, and Piccoli's investment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: The implied covenant also failed because Piccoli had neither its own agreement with Jeanswear nor beneficiary rights under CKI’s agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The "implied covenant" claim, based on the duty of good faith read into every contract, also failed. Piccoli had no agreement of its own with Jeanswear and no "beneficiary" rights under CKI’s agreement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Authorities recognizing tort duties arising from contracts did not establish one merely because firms held analogous distribution roles.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Cases recognizing "tort" duties (legal duties outside contract) that arise from contracts did not create one here just because the companies held similar distribution roles.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: World Apparel proposed Danish law for nonfederal claims, but nobody identified an actual conflict, so the court applied New York law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: World Apparel proposed applying Danish law to the "nonfederal claims" (those based on state law, not federal law). But no one showed the two laws actually differed, so the court applied New York law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Unjust enrichment required more than advantage from somebody else’s activity: Piccoli’s market-building work had to be rendered for defendants.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: For unjust enrichment it is not enough that the defendants benefited from Piccoli's efforts; Piccoli had to have done the work for them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Allegedly exploiting the resulting demand did not establish that quasi-contract obligation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: "Allegedly" cashing in on the demand Piccoli had built did not create that "quasi-contract" obligation, a duty to pay that the law imposes to prevent unfair gain even without a contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Because cancellations were not alleged to breach customer contracts, interference concerned prospective relations.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Because the customers' cancellations were not "alleged" to break any contracts with Piccoli, the interference claim concerned "prospective relations", meaning expected future business.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: That indirect link failed the required direct-interference showing.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: New York requires conduct aimed at the plaintiff's customers; selling discounted goods that drew them away was too indirect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Common-law unfair competition required a colorable property or financial interest, not necessarily trademark ownership.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: "Common-law" (judge-made) unfair competition required only a "colorable" (plausible) property or financial interest, not necessarily ownership of the trademark.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Alleged bad-faith appropriation or passing off was not merely disguised contract enforcement: Piccoli lacked a contract with defendants, while market conduct supplied a potentially separate duty.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The "Alleged" bad-faith taking of Piccoli's market, or "passing off" (selling goods in a way that misleads buyers about their source), was not a contract claim in disguise. Piccoli had no contract with the "defendants", and their market conduct could create a separate duty.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: The Lanham Act false-designation claim against Jeanswear also survived.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The "Lanham Act" claim against Jeanswear, for false designation (misleading buyers about the goods' origin) under this federal trademark statute, also went forward.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Under the then-existing circuit framework for foreign conduct, the court examined substantial effects on United States commerce.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Under the "circuit" (federal appeals court) test then in use for conduct abroad, the court asked whether that conduct had substantial effects on United States commerce.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Alleged organized use of American commerce prevented exclusion of every possible basis on the pleadings; defendants could renew the issue on a fuller record.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Piccoli alleged an organized scheme run through American commerce, so the court could not rule out every possible basis for the claim on the "pleadings" (the written complaint alone). The defendants could raise the issue again once a fuller record of evidence existed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: Piccoli’s pecuniary interest supported its Section 43 theory although it lacked the ownership associated with Section 32 infringement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: Piccoli's "pecuniary interest" (financial stake) supported its claim under Section 43 of the Lanham Act, for misleading buyers about origin. That was so even though it lacked the trademark ownership tied to an infringement claim under Section 32.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: The Paris Convention theory failed because controlling circuit law treated its Section 44 implementation as adding no substantive domestic rights.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The "Paris Convention" claim, based on an international trademark treaty, failed. Under controlling "circuit" law (the federal appeals court's precedent), Section 44, which puts the treaty into effect, added no "substantive" rights beyond existing U.S. law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: The conspiracy allegations identified an agreement, overt acts, intentional participation, and harm sufficiently under New York law and the then-prevailing Rule 8 standard rather than Rule 9(b).
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: The conspiracy claim described an agreement, "overt acts" (steps taken to carry it out), intentional participation, and harm. That was enough under New York law and the then-governing general pleading standard of Rule 8, rather than the stricter Rule 9(b) standard for fraud.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: For the federal claim, mere knowledge was insufficient, but knowing participation in a common scheme adequately alleged concerted conduct and control.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: For the federal "claim", merely knowing about the scheme was not enough. But knowingly taking part in a common scheme adequately "alleged" that the defendants acted together and had control.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: That was pleading sufficiency, not a finding of agreement or involvement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: That ruling concerned only "pleading" sufficiency, whether the claim was properly stated. It was not a "finding" (a determination of fact) that any agreement or involvement actually existed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.sentence: On September 8, 1998, Kaplan granted Jeanswear’s motion except for Lanham Act and common-law unfair-competition claims.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-080.plain: On September 8, 1998, Judge Kaplan "granted" Jeanswear's "motion" (request) to dismiss, except for the "Lanham Act" claim under the federal trademark law and the common-law unfair-competition claim.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: Chief Justice Hill accepted the administrator’s premise that Harrison had not agreed, but rejected its proposed consequence.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: Chief Justice Hill accepted the administrator's starting point, that Harrison never agreed to pay the doctors. But he rejected the conclusion the administrator drew from it, that the doctors got nothing.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: Drawing on Sceva v. True, a precedent distinguishing actual promises from duties imposed by law, the court explained that implied-in-fact contract rests on conduct demonstrating agreement, while quasi-contract can impose an obligation without a meeting of minds.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: The court relied on Sceva v. True, a "precedent" separating real promises from duties the law imposes. A contract implied in fact is a real agreement shown by conduct, while a quasi-contract imposes a duty to pay even without a "meeting of minds", meaning actual agreement.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: Necessary professional services supplied in good faith to a person helpless through injury justified reasonable compensation.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: Needed professional services, provided "in good faith" (honestly) to a person left helpless by injury, justified reasonable payment.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: The court did not pretend that unconsciousness concealed consent; it recognized a settled legal remedy comparable to necessary services for others unable to contract.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: The court did not pretend that Harrison's unconsciousness hid some secret consent. It recognized a settled legal "remedy" (a legal way to get payment), like the one for necessities provided to others who cannot make contracts.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: Urgency and inability to make arrangements distinguished this intervention from imposing an unwanted service on a capable person who could first be asked.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: This rule does not let people force services on someone and then demand payment; it applies because of the emergency and Harrison's inability to be asked.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: A physician ordinarily undertook professional skill and care, not a guaranteed cure unless specially promised.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: A doctor normally promises to use proper skill and care, not to guarantee a cure.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: A fee custom might illuminate an actual agreement through the parties’ shared circumstances and expectations.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: A custom about fees, such as charging richer patients more, might help explain a real agreement by showing the parties’ shared circumstances and expectations.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: A legal obligation for fair time, services, and skill did not import every advantageous price term a physician might have negotiated.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: When the law imposes a duty to pay, it is only for the fair value of the work, not the higher price a doctor might have bargained for.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: The collateral heirs were even less relevant.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: Evidence about the "collateral heirs" (relatives other than a spouse or children who would inherit Harrison's estate) was even less relevant.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: The court could not deem error harmless merely because one estimate supported the amount; improper factors might explain the jury’s choice within the range.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: The court could not call the error "harmless" (too small to have changed the result) just because one witness's estimate supported the amount. Improper factors, such as Harrison's wealth, might explain why the jury picked that figure within the range.

brief-CT-CB-0146.sentence: Justices Battle and Wood agreed with liability and exclusion of the collateral-heir evidence but disagreed that estate value and a related instruction were erroneous.
brief-CT-CB-0146.plain: Justices Battle and Wood agreed on "liability" (that the estate must pay) and that the collateral-heir evidence should be kept out. But they disagreed that admitting the estate's value, and a related jury "instruction" (the judge's directions to the jury), were errors.

cp-american-well.sentence: It accused competitor Layne & Bowler and the other defendants of falsely and maliciously telling customers that the pump and its components infringed their patent, suing users without probable cause, and threatening everyone who used the pump.
cp-american-well.plain: American Well accused its competitor Layne & Bowler and the other "defendants" of "maliciously" (spitefully and knowingly) telling customers falsely that the pump and its parts "infringed" (violated) their patent. It also accused them of suing users without "probable cause" (a reasonable basis) and threatening everyone who used the pump.

cp-american-well.sentence: After removal, it sought remand, but the federal district court dismissed.
cp-american-well.plain: After "removal", when the defendants moved the case from state to federal court, American Well asked for "remand" (sending it back to state court). But the "federal district court" (the federal trial court) dismissed the case instead.

cp-american-well.sentence: The judge treated the suit as arising exclusively under federal patent law and reasoned that the state court lacked jurisdiction, leaving the receiving federal court without jurisdiction over the removed action as well.
cp-american-well.plain: The judge treated the "suit" as arising only under "federal patent" law, which only federal courts can hear, so the state court "lacked jurisdiction" (power) over it. Under the rule then applied, a removed case gets no more power than the state court had, so the federal court lacked jurisdiction too.

cp-american-well.sentence: A proper certificate brought that jurisdictional issue directly to the Supreme Court.
cp-american-well.plain: A "proper certificate", the district court's formal statement of the question about its power, sent that "jurisdictional" issue directly to the Supreme Court.

cp-american-well.sentence: Justice Holmes described the alleged wrong as injury to a business through words tending to stop the public dealing with it.
cp-american-well.plain: Justice Holmes described the "alleged" wrong as harming a business with words that tended to stop the public from dealing with it.

cp-american-well.sentence: Competition, good faith, reasonable grounds, or truth might justify the defendants’ conduct.
cp-american-well.plain: The defendants' conduct might be justified by fair competition, "good faith" (honest belief), reasonable grounds, or the truth of their statements.
Those were "matters of defense": issues for the defendants to raise and prove, not part of what American Well had to prove.

cp-american-well.sentence: American Well Works did not need to establish the validity or infringement of defendants’ patent, or the validity of its own patent, as an element of this business-injury claim.
cp-american-well.plain: American Well Works did not have to prove the validity or "infringement" of the defendants' patent (whether it was valid and whether the pump violated it), or the validity of its own patent, as an "element" (a required part) of this business-injury "claim".

cp-american-well.sentence: Thus the suit arose under the law creating the claim; possible federal content in a defense did not transform its source.
cp-american-well.plain: A case 'arises under' the law that creates the claim, here state law. A federal patent issue appearing only in a defense does not make it a federal case.

cp-american-well.sentence: The claim’s state-law character defeated the exclusive-patent-jurisdiction basis for the dismissal.
cp-american-well.plain: Because the claim came from state law, it was not a patent case that only federal courts could hear, so the dismissal was wrong.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Insurance Company of North America, or INA, covered the first $10 million; twenty-one foreign insurers subscribed to the excess through London.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Insurance Company of North America, or INA, covered the first $10 million of losses. Twenty-one foreign insurers took shares of "the excess", the coverage above that amount, arranged through the London market.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: The foreign insurers initialed placing slips effective February 12, 1974, showing their shares.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: The foreign insurers initialed placing slips (London market documents showing each insurer's share of the risk), effective February 12, 1974.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: In December 1975 CBG sued in the Western District of Pennsylvania under diversity, with separate primary and excess counts.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: In December 1975 CBG sued in the federal court for the Western District of Pennsylvania under "diversity" jurisdiction, which lets federal courts hear cases between parties from different states or countries. It made separate claims against the primary insurer and the excess insurers.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: INA accepted jurisdiction, while the foreign insurers contested it.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: INA did not dispute that the Pennsylvania court had power over it; the foreign insurers argued it did not.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: CBG sought policies showing the foreign insurers’ Pennsylvania contacts.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: In discovery, CBG asked for documents showing how much business the foreign insurers did in Pennsylvania, since that would show whether the court had power over them.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: In December 1978 the court found no conscientious effort, expressly warned that continued failure would establish personal jurisdiction under Rule 37, and invited statistics or other evidence negating jurisdiction.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: In December 1978 the court found the insurers had made no conscientious effort to produce documents. It expressly warned that continued failure would establish "personal jurisdiction" (power over them) as a penalty under Rule 37, and invited statistics or other evidence showing there was no jurisdiction.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: After further nonproduction, the court imposed the sanction in April 1979, treating sufficient business contacts as established for this litigation.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: When the insurers still did not produce documents, the court imposed the "sanction" (penalty) in April 1979. It treated it as established, for this case only, that they had enough business contacts with Pennsylvania.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: It independently found actual contacts sufficient under Pennsylvania law and inferred submission from adopting INA’s contract.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Separately, it found that the insurers really did have enough Pennsylvania connections, and that by adopting INA's policy terms they had agreed to the court's power.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: The Third Circuit affirmed the petitioners solely on sanction grounds, reversed as to three compliant insurers lacking contacts, and reversed an injunction against parallel English proceedings.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: The Third Circuit, the federal appeals court, "affirmed" as to the "petitioners" (the insurers now appealing) only on "sanction" grounds. It "reversed" as to three insurers that had complied and lacked contacts, and also reversed an injunction blocking parallel English proceedings.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: The insurers argued that a court without proven jurisdiction could neither create it nor command their obedience.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: The insurers argued that a court whose "jurisdiction" (power) over them had not been proved could neither create that power nor order them to obey.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Justice White’s eight-Justice opinion distinguished Article III and statutory subject-matter limits from personal jurisdiction’s protection of individual liberty.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Justice White’s opinion for eight Justices contrasted limits on subject-matter power (from Article III of the Constitution and from statutes, called "statutory" limits) with "personal jurisdiction". The latter, power over a particular defendant, protects that individual's liberty.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Parties generally cannot create subject-matter power by consent, waive it by silence, or stop courts examining it, though the opinion recognized preclusion limits after an opportunity to litigate jurisdiction.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Parties generally cannot create "subject-matter power" (power over a type of case) by agreeing, "waive" it by staying silent, or stop courts from examining it. But the "opinion" recognized that once parties had a chance to "litigate" (fight out in court) jurisdiction, the ruling may be final.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Personal jurisdiction can be waived or affected by conduct, including contractual submission, stipulation, participation, and failure to raise a timely Rule 12 objection.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: "Personal jurisdiction" can be "waived" (given up) or affected by conduct. Examples are agreeing in a contract, a stipulation (agreement in court), taking part in the case, or not making a "timely" (early enough) objection under Rule 12.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Its federalism dimension ultimately served individual due-process liberty, rather than an unwaivable independent sovereign restriction.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Its "federalism" dimension (limits on one state's reach over outsiders) ultimately protects the individual's "due-process" liberty, the right to fair treatment. It is not an "unwaivable" (impossible to give up) restriction protecting other states.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Footnote 10 did not abolish minimum contacts; the issue was how facts demonstrating them could be established after obstructed discovery.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Footnote 10 of the opinion did not abolish the "minimum contacts" requirement, that a defendant have enough connection with the state. The issue was how facts showing those contacts could be proved after a defendant blocked discovery.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: By submitting the objection for decision, a defendant accepts lawful procedures for resolving it, including appropriate factual presumptions.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: By asking the court to decide its objection, a defendant accepts the court's lawful procedures for resolving it. Those include appropriate "presumptions", meaning facts the court may assume, such as against a party that withholds evidence.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: A limited appearance did not automatically concede contacts or waive all objections.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: A "limited appearance", coming to court only to contest jurisdiction, did not automatically admit the contacts or "waive" (give up) all objections.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: It differed from refusing participation, risking default, and later challenging jurisdiction collaterally.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: That differed from refusing to take part at all, risking a default judgment, and later attacking "jurisdiction" collaterally, meaning in a separate case.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Once litigated, the determination could have preclusive force.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Once "litigated" (fought out in court), the jurisdiction ruling could have "preclusive" force, meaning it would bind the parties later.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Hammond Packing permitted a presumption against a defense when a party withheld material proof; Hovey rejected striking a defense simply to punish violation of an unrelated deposit order.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Hammond Packing allowed a "presumption" (an assumed fact) against a defense when a party withheld important evidence. Hovey rejected "striking" (throwing out) a defense simply to punish disobeying an unrelated order to deposit money.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Rule 37 implemented the former evidentiary principle, not denial of a hearing merely for disobedience.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Rule 37, the discovery-sanctions rule, carried out the first principle: drawing reasonable conclusions from withheld evidence. It did not allow denying a party a hearing merely to punish disobedience.
