cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: The Rule required a just sanction specifically related to the discovery issue.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: The Rule required a just "sanction" (penalty) that was specifically tied to the "discovery" issue, meaning the evidence the party had refused to hand over.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Review was for abuse of discretion, not whether the Supreme Court would select the same response.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: "Review" was for "abuse of discretion": the Supreme Court asked only whether the trial judge's choice was unreasonable, not whether it would have chosen the same response.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Their legal consequence—personal jurisdiction—did not make the inference unrelated.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: That the facts treated as proved had a legal consequence, establishing "personal jurisdiction" (power over the defendants), did not make the "inference" (the conclusion drawn from withheld evidence) unrelated to the violation.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Justice Powell concurred only in the judgment.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Justice Powell "concurred only in the judgment", meaning he agreed with the result but not with the majority's reasoning.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: In a diversity case, he emphasized, personal jurisdiction must arise under the forum’s long-arm statute and constitutional limits.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: In a "diversity case" (a federal case between parties from different states or countries), he stressed, "personal jurisdiction" must come from the forum’s long-arm statute, the state law on reaching outsiders, and stay within constitutional limits.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Rule 37 was no independent grant, and Rule 82 cautioned against extending jurisdiction through procedural rules.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Rule 37 was not an independent grant of power over defendants. And Rule 82 warns against expanding jurisdiction through the procedural rules.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: He feared the majority’s liberty theory could loosen contacts for an unconsenting defendant or imply a new federal jurisdictional basis.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: He feared the majority’s theory, treating jurisdiction as a matter of personal liberty, could weaken the "contacts" requirement for a "defendant" who had not consented, or suggest a new federal basis for jurisdiction.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Here CBG had made a prima facie contacts showing, and the district court considered the evidence independently sufficient.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: Here CBG had made a "prima facie" showing of contacts, meaning evidence enough to establish them unless rebutted. The district court (the trial court) also considered that evidence sufficient on its own.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: Powell would authorize discovery on that basis and accept the unrebutted showing after refusal.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: That first showing justified ordering discovery, and when the insurers refused, the court could treat CBG's uncontradicted evidence as established.

cp-insurance-ireland.sentence: He warned against speculative foreign fishing expeditions but found this record adequate.
cp-insurance-ireland.plain: He warned against speculative "fishing expeditions", digging through foreign companies' records on a hunch, but found this record adequate.

cp-transunion.sentence: Without comparison of other identifying data, matching names generated false positives.
cp-transunion.plain: Because the system checked only names, many innocent people with common names were flagged as matches.

cp-transunion.sentence: TransUnion first mailed a disclosure and required rights summary omitting the OFAC information, then a separate OFAC letter without another summary.
cp-transunion.plain: When Ramirez asked for his file, TransUnion first mailed it with the legally required summary of his rights, but left out the OFAC information (the alert matching him to the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control list). It then sent the OFAC alert in a separate letter without another rights summary.

cp-transunion.sentence: The Fair Credit Reporting Act required reasonable procedures assuring maximum possible accuracy, requested disclosure of all file information, and a rights summary with written disclosures.
cp-transunion.plain: The Fair Credit Reporting Act required reasonable procedures to assure the maximum possible accuracy of files, disclosure of all file information on request, and a summary of rights along with written disclosures.

cp-transunion.sentence: Willful violations permitted actual damages or $100–$1,000 statutory damages, plus punitive damages and fees.
cp-transunion.plain: For "willful violations", meaning knowing or reckless ones, a consumer could recover actual damages or "statutory damages" (a set amount fixed by law) of $100 to $1,000. Punitive damages (meant to punish) and lawyers' fees were also available.

cp-transunion.sentence: The district court certified over TransUnion’s objection and found all members had standing.
cp-transunion.plain: The district court (the trial court) certified the class over TransUnion’s objection, letting the case proceed as a class action. It found that all members had "standing", meaning a sufficient injury to sue.

cp-transunion.sentence: The parties stipulated to 8,185 members and third-party reports for only 1,853, including Ramirez, during the seven-month period.
cp-transunion.plain: The parties "stipulated" (formally agreed) that the class had 8,185 members. Only 1,853 of them, including Ramirez, had their reports sent to "third-party" businesses during the seven-month period.

cp-transunion.sentence: The Ninth Circuit sustained standing and typicality but reduced punitive damages to $3,936.88 each, producing roughly $40 million.
cp-transunion.plain: The Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, upheld standing and "typicality" (that Ramirez's claims were typical of the class). But it cut "punitive damages" to $3,936.88 per member, producing a total of roughly $40 million.

cp-transunion.sentence: Article III required concrete, particularized, actual or imminent injury, likely causation, and likely redress.
cp-transunion.plain: "Article III" of the Constitution requires an injury that is concrete, "particularized" (personal to the plaintiff), and actual or "imminent" (about to happen). It also requires likely "causation" by the defendant and a likelihood that the court can redress, or fix, the harm.

cp-transunion.sentence: Particularization did not itself establish concreteness.
cp-transunion.plain: An injury being particularized (personal to the plaintiff) did not by itself establish its "concreteness", that it was real.

cp-transunion.sentence: Physical or monetary injury readily qualified; intangible harms could bear a close relationship to traditionally actionable harms such as reputational injury, privacy disclosure, or intrusion.
cp-transunion.plain: Physical or money injuries clearly qualified. "Intangible harms" (non-physical ones) could count if they closely resembled harms traditionally "actionable" (a basis for suit), such as injury to reputation, disclosure of private information, or intrusion on privacy.

cp-transunion.sentence: Congress’s judgment deserved respect and could make previously inadequate concrete harms legally actionable.
cp-transunion.plain: Congress's "judgment" deserved respect, and Congress could make real harms that courts once found inadequate legally "actionable", meaning a basis for suit.

cp-transunion.sentence: A statutory cause of action alone nevertheless did not eliminate concrete injury.
cp-transunion.plain: Even so, a "statutory" cause of action, a law saying you may sue, did not by itself remove the need for a "concrete" (real) injury.

cp-transunion.sentence: The majority connected that limit to separation of powers and courts’ inability to supervise general regulatory compliance through uninjured plaintiffs.
cp-transunion.plain: The majority tied that limit to the "separation of powers", the Constitution's division of government functions. Courts cannot supervise general "regulatory" compliance through uninjured "plaintiffs"; that is the executive branch's job.

cp-transunion.sentence: Each member needed standing to recover individual damages, separately for every claim and form of relief, with proof appropriate to the litigation stage.
cp-transunion.plain: Each class member needed standing to recover individual "damages" (money), separately for every claim and every form of "relief" (remedy sought). The proof required depended on the stage of the case; after trial, that meant actual proof.

cp-transunion.sentence: The Court reserved whether every class member must prove standing before certification and assumed without deciding that the statute reached undistributed alerts.
cp-transunion.plain: The Court "reserved" (left open) whether every "class member" must prove standing before the class is certified. It "assumed without deciding" that the "statute" covered alerts never sent to anyone.

cp-transunion.sentence: The 1,853 reports sent to third-party businesses created harm closely analogous to defamation.
cp-transunion.plain: The 1,853 reports sent to "third-party" businesses caused harm closely similar to "defamation", the traditional wrong of harming someone's reputation with false statements to others.

cp-transunion.sentence: An internal inaccurate file resembled a defamatory letter left in a drawer.
cp-transunion.plain: An inaccurate file kept inside the company was like a "defamatory" (reputation-damaging) letter left in a drawer: no one else saw it, so it did no reputational harm.

cp-transunion.sentence: A newly offered theory of publication to employees or printing vendors was forfeited; the majority also found no traditional publication relationship or proof anyone read rather than processed the information.
cp-transunion.plain: A new theory, that the information was "publication" (communicated to others) to employees or printing vendors, was "forfeited" because it was raised too late. The majority also found no traditional publication relationship, and no proof anyone read the information rather than just processed it.

cp-transunion.sentence: A substantial imminent risk could support prospective relief, but an unrealized risk alone did not support retrospective damages without separate concrete harm from exposure to the risk.
cp-transunion.plain: A substantial, "imminent" risk could support "prospective relief" (a court order preventing future harm). But a risk that never came true did not support "retrospective damages" (money for past harm) without a separate "concrete" harm from being exposed to the risk.

cp-transunion.sentence: It did not invoke or establish emotional harm from knowing the risk, so that theory remained reserved.
cp-transunion.plain: The class did not claim or prove emotional harm from knowing about the risk, so that theory was "reserved", left undecided.

cp-transunion.sentence: Members received the information in the challenged two-mailing arrangement, so public-information precedents invoked by the United States did not control.
cp-transunion.plain: Class members did receive the information, just in the challenged two-letter format. So "precedents" (earlier cases) cited by the United States about being denied public information did not control.

cp-transunion.sentence: No downstream harm from an asserted informational deficit was shown.
cp-transunion.plain: No one showed that getting the information in the wrong format caused them any real-world harm.

cp-transunion.sentence: He distinguished private individual rights from public duties: historically, invasion of a private right could support suit without additional loss, including newly created statutory rights and minimum damages.
cp-transunion.plain: Justice Thomas, dissenting, separated rights owed to an individual from duties owed to the public. Historically, invading a "private right" allowed suit without further loss, including newly created "statutory" rights and minimum "damages" set by law.

cp-transunion.sentence: State courts, which are not governed by Article III, could remain a forum for claims excluded from federal court.
cp-transunion.plain: State courts, which are not bound by Article III, could remain a "forum" (a place to sue) for claims shut out of federal court.

cp-transunion.sentence: Kagan, joined by Breyer and Sotomayor, agreed with the result and generally joined Thomas but retained Spokeo’s concrete-injury requirement for statutory violations.
cp-transunion.plain: Justice Kagan, "joined by" Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, also dissented. She agreed with Thomas's result and generally joined his opinion, but kept Spokeo's rule that even a statutory violation requires a concrete, real injury.

cp-transunion.sentence: She would defer to Congress except in highly unusual cases where it could not reasonably think suit would compensate or prevent real harm.
cp-transunion.plain: She would defer to Congress except in highly unusual cases where Congress could not reasonably think a "suit" would compensate for or prevent real harm.

cp-transunion.sentence: The Court left Rule 23 typicality undecided and required reconsideration of certification in light of these limits.
cp-transunion.plain: The Court left Rule 23 "typicality" (whether Ramirez's claims were typical of the class) undecided. It required "reconsideration" of class certification in light of these standing limits.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: Using that authority, the agency adopted Part 50 regulations through notice and comment.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: Using that authority, the agency adopted its Part 50 "regulations" (binding rules) through notice and comment: it published a proposal and invited public comment first.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The Mine Safety and Health Administration addressed that uncertainty through Program Policy Letters concerning chest x-rays.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The Mine Safety and Health Administration addressed that uncertainty through "Program Policy Letters", informal guidance letters about when a chest x-ray counts as a diagnosis.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: If the initial reader lacked B-reader certification, enforcement would be stayed while a certified reader examined the film.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: If the first doctor reading the x-ray lacked "B-reader" certification (government certification to read such x-rays), enforcement would be "stayed", put on hold, while a certified reader examined the film.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The American Mining Congress and National Industrial Sand Association filed three petitions challenging the successive letters because none underwent Administrative Procedure Act notice and comment.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The American Mining Congress and the National Industrial Sand Association filed three "petitions" (formal requests for court review) challenging the successive letters. They argued none had gone through notice and comment under the Administrative Procedure Act.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The agency defended them solely as interpretive rules.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The agency defended the letters only as "interpretive rules": rules that explain what an existing rule means, which the APA exempts from notice and comment.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The petitioners did not contest Federal Register publication or the interpretation’s substantive validity.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The "petitioners" (the challengers) did not dispute that the letters were published in the Federal Register, the government's official daily publication, or the "substantive" correctness of the agency's interpretation. They challenged only the procedure.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: Drawing on the Attorney General’s Manual and precedent, the court distinguished rules that supply legal duties under delegated legislative authority from interpretations of existing duties.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: Drawing on the Attorney General’s Manual (a 1947 Justice Department guide to the APA) and precedent, the court separated two things. Rules that create legal duties using "delegated legislative authority" (lawmaking power Congress gave the agency) differ from interpretations explaining duties that already exist.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: If a statute prohibits nothing until rules supply a prohibition, legislative action is necessary before enforcement.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: If the statute itself forbids nothing until the agency writes a rule, the agency must make a real (legislative) rule, with notice and comment, before it can enforce.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: Even an incorrect interpretation does not become legislative merely through error.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: An interpretation that turns out to be wrong is still an interpretation; being wrong does not make it a rule requiring notice and comment.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The court’s concluding test asked four questions: did the rule supply a necessary legislative basis for enforcement or benefits that otherwise was absent; was it published in the Code of Federal Regulations; did the agency explicitly invoke general legislative authority; or did it effectively amend a prior legislative rule?
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The court's test asked four questions: would there be no legal basis for enforcement or benefits without the rule; was it published in the Code of Federal Regulations (the official book of binding rules); did the agency expressly invoke its "general legislative authority"; or did it effectively "amend" (change) an existing "legislative rule"? A yes to any makes it a binding rule that needs notice and comment.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: An affirmative answer to any identified legislative action under this formulation.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: A 'yes' to any one of those questions meant the document was a legislative rule.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: A policy statement ordinarily describes future discretionary choices, so evidence that it actually binds the agency can undermine its claimed tentativeness.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: A policy statement ordinarily describes how an agency may use its discretion in the future. So "evidence" that it actually binds the agency can undercut the claim that it is only tentative.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: Consequently, the binding-norm analysis associated with the Pacific Gas policy-statement precedent could not alone decide whether these interpretations exercised legislative power.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: So the "binding-norm" test, which asks whether a document binds the agency and comes from the Pacific Gas "precedent" on policy statements, could not alone decide whether these interpretations used "legislative power". Interpretations naturally use binding language.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The statute’s broad reporting authorization had required legislative implementation, but Part 50 already supplied it.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The statute alone did not require reporting; a binding rule was needed, and Part 50 was that rule.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The letters therefore did not repudiate or contradict Part 50; drawing a sharper line within a general term did not itself amend the rule.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The letters therefore did not "repudiate" (reject) or contradict Part 50. Drawing a sharper line within a general term like "diagnosis" did not by itself "amend" (change) the rule.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The court stressed that genuine interpretations might still exceed statutory authority or otherwise fail on the merits.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The court stressed that a genuine interpretation might still exceed the agency's "statutory authority" (the power the law gives it) or otherwise fail "on the merits", meaning for being substantively wrong. No one raised those challenges here.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: Guidance could improve notice, while eventual judicial review encouraged consideration of opposing evidence and arguments, especially without an earlier formal comment process.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: Written guidance can give regulated companies better notice. And because "judicial review" by a court may come later, the agency has reason to consider opposing "evidence" and arguments, especially when there was no earlier formal comment process.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The agency argued that supersession made the earlier challenges moot.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The agency argued that "supersession", later letters replacing the earlier ones, made the challenges to the earlier letters "moot", meaning there was no longer a live dispute to decide.

lrs-n-american-mining-congress.sentence: The holding concerned the notice-and-comment classification, leaving substantive challenges to the interpretation available.
lrs-n-american-mining-congress.plain: The holding decided only the "notice-and-comment" question: no public-comment process was needed. "Substantive" challenges, arguing that the agency's interpretation was wrong, remained available.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Congress expressly subjected establishment, amendment, and revocation of standards to review under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Congress expressly made the agency's decisions on establishment, "amendment" (change), and revocation of safety standards reviewable by courts under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: After notice, written comments, and public hearings, NHTSA rescinded the passive-restraint requirement in 1981.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: After notice, written "comments" from the public, and public "hearings", NHTSA, the federal highway-safety agency, rescinded the "passive-restraint" requirement in 1981. Passive restraints are automatic belts or airbags that protect occupants without any action by them.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: It grouped continuous, nondetachable belts with other devices that compelled use rather than analyzing their different operation.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: It lumped belts that could not be detached together with devices, like ignition interlocks, that force people to buckle up, without examining how the two actually worked differently.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company and the National Association of Independent Insurers petitioned for review in the D.C. Circuit.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company and the National Association of Independent Insurers "petitioned for review", asking a court to overturn the rescission. They filed in the federal appeals court in Washington, the D.C. Circuit.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: It also inferred from congressional activity a growing commitment to passive restraints requiring increasingly strong reasons to reverse course.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: That court also read Congress's activity as showing a growing commitment to "passive restraints" (automatic belts or airbags). On that view, the agency needed increasingly strong reasons to reverse course.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: That distinction mattered to the eventual vacatur and remand.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The Supreme Court agreed with the appeals court's result but not all of its method. That difference mattered to the final "vacatur" (wiping out the appeals court's judgment) and remand, rather than a simple affirmance.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: The agency urged the exceptionally narrow scrutiny associated with refusing to initiate regulation.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The agency urged the extremely narrow review courts use when an agency refuses to start "regulation", meaning refuses to begin making a rule at all.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: The Court instead applied ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious review under APA § 706(2)(A).
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The Court instead applied ordinary "arbitrary-and-capricious" review under APA § 706(2)(A). That test asks whether the agency's decision was reasoned and adequately explained.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: The Safety Act treated revocation like establishment and amendment, and rescission abandoned an existing regulatory judgment.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The Safety Act treated revoking a standard just like its establishment and "amendment". And rescinding the rule abandoned a "regulatory" judgment the agency had already reasoned out.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: A court asks whether the agency examined relevant material and connected its findings to its choice.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: A court asks whether the agency examined the relevant material and connected its "findings" (its conclusions of fact) to the choice it made.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Unauthorized considerations, failure to consider an important aspect, contradiction of the record, or an explanation too implausible to reflect expertise or reasonable judgment can establish arbitrariness.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: "Arbitrariness" can be shown if the agency relied on factors Congress did not authorize, failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, or contradicted the record. It can also be shown by an explanation too implausible to reflect expertise or reasonable judgment.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Courts may follow an imperfect but discernible explanation; they may neither supply missing reasons nor substitute their preferred policy.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Courts accept a clumsy explanation if its reasoning can be followed, but they may not invent reasons for the agency or impose their own policy views.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: This review of compliance with a statutory mandate differs from the minimal constitutional rationality review applied to economic legislation.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: This review, which checks compliance with a "statutory" command (what the statute requires), differs from the minimal constitutional rationality review courts give to economic laws passed by legislatures.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Congress’s interlock prohibition, failure to veto the 1977 rule, and unenacted proposals did not establish a different APA standard.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Congress's ban on ignition interlocks, its failure to veto the 1977 rule, and proposals it never passed did not create a different APA standard of review.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: A reasonable agency inference can reach beyond conclusive data, provided the explanation addresses the evidence and ordinarily explains why more information was not sought.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: An agency may draw a reasonable inference beyond what the data conclusively prove. But its explanation must address the "evidence", and it should ordinarily explain why it did not seek more information.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: The agency needed to explain why the manufacturers’ preference justified ending the obligation altogether rather than considering an airbags requirement.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Just because carmakers chose a weak kind of seatbelt, the agency could not drop the whole requirement without considering simply requiring airbags.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Under Chenery, post hoc litigation rationales could not repair the decision.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Under Chenery, an earlier precedent, post hoc reasons, invented afterward by lawyers in court, could not save the decision. A court judges the agency only on the reasons it gave at the time.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: The manufacturers invoked Vermont Yankee’s restriction on judicially invented procedures.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The manufacturers relied on Vermont Yankee’s rule that courts may not invent extra procedures for agencies beyond those the law requires.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Requiring analysis of an established compliance option directly implicated by withdrawal was substantive review of the reasons already required.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Requiring the agency to analyze an established way of complying, such as airbags, that the withdrawal directly affected was "substantive" review. It checked the reasons already required, not a new procedure.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: But those limits did not answer inertia: once reconnected, an automatic belt keeps working without another decision on each trip.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: But the agency ignored inertia: once an automatic belt is connected it stays on without the rider doing anything, so more people might end up wearing it.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Costs and consumer resistance depended in turn on the disputed estimate of minimal benefit.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Whether the cost and public resistance were worth it depended on how much safety benefit the belts gave, which the agency had not properly assessed.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Rehnquist added that a new presidential administration could legitimately reassess costs, uncertainty, public resistance, and priorities.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Rehnquist said a newly elected administration may legitimately weigh costs and priorities differently.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: On June 24, 1983, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit’s judgment and directed a remand to NHTSA for further consideration.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: On June 24, 1983, the Supreme Court "vacated" (wiped out) the D.C. Circuit’s judgment. It directed a "remand" (sending the matter back) to NHTSA for further consideration.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: It also reports a distinct 1986 D.C. Circuit decision finding the withdrawal challenge unripe and upholding the remaining alternatives analysis.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The note also reports a separate 1986 D.C. Circuit decision. It found the challenge to the planned withdrawal "unripe" (brought too early to decide) and upheld the agency's analysis of the remaining alternatives.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: The seventh examines remand without vacatur, defect severity, disruption, delay, and disputes over that remedy’s legality.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: The seventh note examines "remand without vacatur": sending a flawed rule back for better reasoning while leaving it in force. It discusses how serious the defect is, disruption, delay, and disputes over whether that "remedy" is lawful.

lrs-n-state-farm.sentence: Neither these notes nor the historic usage figures certify current safety statistics, Standard 208, or present citator treatment.
lrs-n-state-farm.plain: Neither these notes nor the historical seatbelt "usage" figures vouch for current safety statistics or the current Standard 208. They also do not show present "citator" treatment, meaning how later cases have treated the decision.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: As successive reorganization plans for Federal Water Service Corporation came before the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) under the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, its officers, directors, and controlling shareholders bought preferred stock on the open market.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: As successive "reorganization" plans for Federal Water Service Corporation went before the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) under the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, its officers, "directors", and controlling shareholders bought "preferred stock" (shares with priority for dividends) on the open market.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: That qualification matters throughout the dispute: the SEC eventually relied on structural conflicts of interest rather than discovering dishonest purchases.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: That qualification matters throughout: the SEC ultimately relied on "structural" conflicts of interest, built into the managers' position, rather than finding that the purchases were dishonest.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Public holders could obtain new equity, while management would recover acquisition cost with an additional payment instead of the full appreciation and control associated with conversion.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Public "holders" of the shares could get new stock in the reorganized company. Management would "recover" only what it paid plus an extra amount, not the full rise in value and control that converting the shares would bring.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: In Chenery I, 318 U.S. 80, the Supreme Court held that the judicial equity principles the SEC had invoked could not sustain its original order.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: In Chenery I, 318 U.S. 80, the Supreme Court held that the judge-made "equity" principles the SEC had relied on (rules about fiduciaries) could not "sustain", or support, its original order.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The Court directed further agency proceedings without deciding whether a properly exercised statutory administrative judgment could justify the same treatment.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The Court sent the case back for further "agency" proceedings. It did not decide whether the SEC, properly using its own judgment under the statute, could justify the same treatment.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The individual management interests intervened in support.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The individual managers "intervened", formally joining the proceeding, to support the request.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: This time it expressly relied on the Act’s standards governing fairness, investor protection, and allocation of voting power.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: This time the SEC expressly relied on the Act’s own standards on fairness, protection of investors, and how voting power is divided.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The Court of Appeals, 154 F.2d 6, reversed because it understood the first Supreme Court decision to foreclose the renewed refusal.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The Court of Appeals, in its decision at 154 F.2d 6, "reversed" the SEC again. It understood the first Supreme Court decision to rule out the renewed refusal.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Counsel had not merely supplied an alternative argument for an unchanged agency decision: the Commission itself had reconsidered and supplied a new statutory explanation.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: This was not "Counsel" (the SEC's lawyers) offering a new argument for an unchanged "agency" decision. The Commission itself had reconsidered and given a new "statutory" explanation, based on the Act.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Justice Murphy’s opinion reaffirmed Chenery I: a reviewing court must evaluate the grounds the agency actually invoked, stated clearly enough for judicial scrutiny.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Justice Murphy’s "opinion" reaffirmed Chenery I: a reviewing court must judge the grounds the agency actually relied on, and those grounds must be stated clearly enough for courts to examine.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: That conclusion did not resolve the policy judgment the statute committed to the SEC, and it did not create a vested right to management’s requested distribution.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: That conclusion did not decide the policy question the "statute" left to the SEC. And it did not give management a "vested right" (a fixed, guaranteed legal right) to the share distribution it requested.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: On remand it could, and had to, exercise that delegated function afresh.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: "On remand", when the case went back to it, the SEC could, and had to, use afresh the decision-making role Congress had delegated to it.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Here the court had an actual agency explanation to review, preserving rather than abandoning the allocation of decision-making authority underlying Chenery I.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Here the court had the agency's own actual explanation to review. That respected, rather than abandoned, the division of decision-making power that Chenery I rested on.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: An agency cannot knowingly approve a transaction inconsistent with the governing statute simply because it did not anticipate the precise problem in a prospective rule.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: An agency cannot knowingly approve a deal that conflicts with the governing "statute" just because it did not foresee the exact problem in a "prospective rule", a general rule written in advance for the future.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Choosing between rulemaking and case-by-case development therefore lies primarily within the agency’s informed discretion.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: So the choice between "rulemaking" (issuing general rules in advance) and developing policy case by case lies mainly within the agency's informed discretion.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: That principle does not excuse failure to follow rulemaking procedures that Congress separately requires.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: That principle does not "excuse" an agency from following "rulemaking" procedures that Congress separately requires.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Application to already completed purchases did have a retroactive effect.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Applying the standard to purchases already completed did have a "retroactive" effect, meaning it reached back to past conduct.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: It likened a first administrative adjudication to a first-impression judicial decision that applies a newly articulated principle to earlier conduct.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The Court compared a first "administrative adjudication" (an agency deciding a specific case) to a court deciding a question for the first time, which applies a newly stated principle to past conduct.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Retroactivity was a matter requiring evaluation, not automatic invalidation.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: "Retroactivity", applying a standard to past conduct, had to be weighed case by case; it did not automatically make the order invalid.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The holding addressed this adjudicative application; it did not authorize retroactive legislative rules or every conceivable retrospective sanction.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The holding covered only applying the standard in deciding this case. It did not approve "retroactive" legislative rules (general rules reaching back in time) or every possible after-the-fact "sanction" (penalty).

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: A protective standard could therefore address the danger without proof of fraud in each purchase.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: So a protective standard could address the danger of these conflicts without proving "fraud" (deliberate deception) in each purchase.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The Supreme Court accepted that as an administrative judgment under the statute, not a newly discovered common-law breach.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The Supreme Court accepted that as the SEC's administrative judgment under the statute, not as a "newly discovered" "breach" of traditional judge-made (common-law) duties.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The Court found a rational statutory foundation, substantial evidentiary support, and no plain abuse of discretion.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: The Court found a rational basis in the statute, substantial support in the evidence, and no plain "abuse of discretion", meaning no clearly unreasonable use of the SEC's judgment.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Justice Burton concurred only in the result, without explanation; the notation does not establish agreement with every part of Murphy’s rationale.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Justice Burton "concurred" only in the result, without explaining why. That notation does not show he agreed with every part of Murphy’s reasoning.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The conduct, record, statute, and economic deprivation had not changed; in his view the SEC had repackaged the same unsupported result as expertise.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Justice Jackson said the conduct, the record, the "statute", and the financial loss to the managers had not changed. In his view, the SEC had simply repackaged the same unsupported result as expert judgment.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: General reorganization authority, he thought, did not supply an ascertainable rule authorizing that deprivation.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: In his view the SEC's general power over reorganizations gave no clear rule allowing it to take away the managers' gains.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Administrative experience deserved consideration within legal bounds, not as a replacement for law defining the bounds.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Agency expertise matters within the limits the law sets, but cannot replace the law itself.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: Above all, Jackson objected to announcing a prohibition after the transaction and applying it to the same parties whose conduct had previously been lawful.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: Above all, Justice Jackson objected to announcing a prohibition after the transactions and applying it to the same people, whose conduct had been lawful when they acted.

lrs-o-chenery-ii.sentence: The two Chenery proceedings thus end differently because the agency grounds changed.
lrs-o-chenery-ii.plain: So the two Chenery cases came out differently because the "agency" changed the grounds it relied on: the SEC lost the first time and won the second with new, proper reasons.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: The warrant was sealed to protect the continuing investigation, so the notice omitted its number.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: A court kept the warrant confidential so the investigation would not be compromised, which is why the notice did not give its number.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: The original complaint alleged lack of probable cause, a search beyond the warrant’s scope, and a municipal policy permitting unlawful searches.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: The family's original "complaint" alleged that the police lacked "probable cause" (enough grounds) for the warrant, searched beyond the warrant's scope, and acted under a "municipal policy" (a city policy) allowing unlawful searches.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: It also invited briefing on a due-process question the plaintiffs had not raised: whether adequate remedies existed for recovering seized property.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: The trial court also invited "briefing" (written legal arguments) on a "due-process" question the "plaintiffs" had not raised. The question was whether "adequate remedies" existed for "recovering" the seized property, meaning fair legal ways to get it back.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: On the appeal concerning the Fourth Amendment claims, the Ninth Circuit remanded for a due-process decision.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: On the appeal of the "Fourth Amendment" claims about the search, the Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, sent the case back for a decision on the "due-process" (fair procedure) question.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: It accepted that a postdeprivation remedy was sufficient and that California’s statutory and decisional remedies met due process.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: The appeals court accepted that a "postdeprivation remedy", a way to get property back after it is taken, was enough. It also accepted that California's "statutory" and court-made "remedies" satisfied due process.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: Drawing on Memphis Light, a Supreme Court utility-cutoff case, it nevertheless required officials to explain those remedies and supply information needed to invoke them.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: Relying on Memphis Light, a Supreme Court case about cutting off utility service, it still required officials to explain those "remedies" to owners and give them the information needed to use them.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: A meaningful opportunity to be heard generally requires knowing that a matter affecting one’s property is pending.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: A meaningful "opportunity to be heard" (a real chance to contest something) generally requires knowing that a matter affecting one's property is pending.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: Because the family conceded receiving notice and the inventory, the Court did not decide the exact required detail or timing of seizure notice.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: Because the family admitted getting notice and the inventory of what was taken, the Court did not decide exactly how detailed or how timely notice of a "seizure" must be.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: The same rationale did not require individualized instructions about publicly accessible law.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: But police need not explain the legal procedures, since anyone can look up published law.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: California permitted a motion under Penal Code §1536 or §1540, and the family did not independently challenge those mechanisms’ adequacy.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: California law let an owner file a "motion" (a request to a court) for return of property under Penal Code §1536 or §1540. The family did not separately argue that those procedures were inadequate.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: Notice could be required for that otherwise inaccessible procedure without creating a general obligation to advise owners about published legal remedies.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: Notice could be required for a procedure owners otherwise had no way to find out about. That did not create a general duty to explain "remedies" already set out in published law.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41(d) required a warrant copy and receipt, not instructions for obtaining return.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41(d) required officers to leave a copy of the warrant and a receipt, not instructions for getting property back.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: Because the factual premise failed, the Supreme Court did not further decide the narrower constitutional issue.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: The family's narrower claim rested on the factual premise that the warrant number was essential, and that premise had no evidence behind it. So the Supreme Court did not decide the narrower constitutional issue.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: He rejected Kennedy’s suggestion that due process supplied the obligation to notify an owner of property seized under a criminal warrant, regarding it as dictum that improperly extended civil procedural principles into a Fourth Amendment setting.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: Justice Thomas rejected Kennedy’s suggestion that due process required notifying an owner whose property was seized under a criminal "warrant". He saw it as "dictum", a comment not needed to decide the case, that wrongly carried civil-case procedure rules into a Fourth Amendment setting.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: Any constitutional notice duty, in his view, would concern whether execution of the warrant was reasonable.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: In his view, any constitutional duty to give notice would be part of asking whether officers carried out the "warrant" reasonably under the Fourth Amendment.

lrs-o-west-covina.sentence: His notes also acknowledged lower-court decisions declining to treat Rule 41(d)’s requirements as constitutionally mandatory.
lrs-o-west-covina.plain: His notes also acknowledged lower-court decisions refusing to treat the copy-and-receipt requirements of Rule 41(d) as demanded by the Constitution.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act required specified federal contracts to include minimum wages the Labor Secretary determined prevailed for comparable work in the relevant industry and locality.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act required certain federal contracts to include minimum wages. Those were the wages the Labor Secretary found prevailed for similar work in the relevant industry and area.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: After Perkins v. Lukens Steel denied prospective contractors litigable rights under the earlier statute, Congress enacted the 1952 Fulbright Amendment.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: After Perkins v. Lukens Steel held that companies seeking contracts had no "litigable rights" (rights they could sue to enforce) under the earlier "statute", Congress responded. It passed the 1952 Fulbright Amendment.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: It made the Administrative Procedure Act, or APA, applicable, required an on-the-record determination after an opportunity for hearing, and allowed adversely affected or aggrieved persons, including qualifying manufacturers and dealers, to seek review.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: It made the Administrative Procedure Act, or APA, apply and required an "on-the-record" decision, based only on evidence from a formal hearing. It let "adversely affected or aggrieved" persons (those harmed), including qualifying manufacturers and dealers, ask courts for review.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: Then-APA § 7(c) placed the burden on a rule’s proponent, demanded reliable, probative, substantial evidence, and protected rebuttal and cross-examination necessary for full disclosure.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The APA's then § 7(c) put the burden of proof on a rule's "proponent" (the side proposing it) and demanded reliable, "probative" (tending to prove), substantial evidence. It protected "rebuttal" (contradicting evidence) and cross-examination needed for a full disclosure of the facts.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: These safeguards applied because Congress expressly required formal rulemaking, not because every informal rule must receive a trial.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: These safeguards applied because Congress expressly required formal "rulemaking" with a trial-like hearing. They did not mean every informal agency rule needs a trial.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The pledge restricted access to sworn Bureau employees and promised no company-identified disclosure.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The confidentiality pledge limited access to sworn employees of the Bureau of Labor Statistics and promised that no figures identifying a company would be disclosed.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The day before the hearing it sought a subpoena for questionnaires, recipient and respondent lists, and correspondence, offering confidential inspection by counsel.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The day before the hearing, the industry group asked for a "subpoena" (a court-style order to produce documents) for the questionnaires, lists of recipients and of each "respondent" (company that answered), and correspondence. It offered confidential inspection by its "counsel" (lawyers) only.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The examiner denied access because of the pledge and possible harm to future voluntary surveys.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The "examiner" (the official presiding over the hearing) denied access, citing the confidentiality pledge and possible harm to future voluntary surveys.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: At the hearing, the BLS supervisor could not answer some questions without consulting the underlying material, and government counsel successfully opposed that consultation.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: At the "hearing", the BLS (Bureau of Labor Statistics) supervisor could not answer some questions without checking the underlying survey material. Government "counsel" (the government's lawyer) successfully opposed letting him check it.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: NEMA sought to introduce error-identifying affidavits and strike the tables.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: NEMA, the manufacturers' association, offered "affidavits" (sworn written statements) pointing out errors in the tables, and asked that the tables be struck from the evidence.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: Convenient summaries need not place every underlying document into the record if adequate access permits testing and resolves objections.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: Convenient summaries need not put every underlying document into the record, as long as the other side has enough access to test them and resolve its "objections".

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: Here, however, the parties lacked material needed to test authenticity, accuracy, and meaning, even under their offered confidentiality arrangement.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: Here the companies had no way to check whether the figures were genuine and accurate.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The Department’s concern about future collection could be substantial but did not override express rebuttal and cross-examination rights.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The Department’s concern about collecting survey data in the future might be serious. But it could not override the express rights to "rebuttal" (contradicting evidence) and cross-examination that Congress had given.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: Lack of a vested right to a government contract likewise did not answer those statutory protections.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: That no company has a "vested right" (a guaranteed legal right) to a government contract likewise did not cancel those protections in the statute.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The Government could withhold information and risk failure of proof, or disclose enough to permit testing.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The Government could keep the information secret and risk "failure of proof", meaning its evidence would fall short. Or it could disclose enough for the data to be tested.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The Secretary offered no adequate corroboration to rehabilitate the challenged data.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The Secretary of Labor offered no adequate independent support to "rehabilitate" the challenged data, meaning to restore its credibility after it was attacked.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: Standing alone, the tables failed the statutory substantial-evidence requirement.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: Standing alone, the tables did not meet the "statutory" requirement of substantial evidence, the level of support the law demanded.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The court reserved situations without impeachment, with rehabilitation, or with different disclosure, and disclaimed effects on other industries’ determinations.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The court "reserved" (left undecided) cases where the data was not attacked through "impeachment", was shored up afterward, or was disclosed differently. It also said its ruling did not affect wage findings for other industries.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The Fulbright Amendment displaced Perkins’s denial of litigable rights but still demanded actual adversity.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The Fulbright Amendment replaced Perkins’s holding that companies had no "litigable rights" (rights they could sue to enforce). But it still required real "adversity", meaning the company must actually be harmed.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: Firms already paying at or above the minimum could not establish injury through speculation about future labor competition; forcing competitors to raise wages might improve their current position.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: Firms already paying at or above the minimum could not show injury through "speculation" about future competition for workers. Forcing competitors to raise wages might even improve their current position.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The D.C. Circuit returned the record to the district court to identify plaintiffs with standing, retained appellate jurisdiction, and continued the stay.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The D.C. Circuit sent the record back to the "district court" (trial court) to identify which "plaintiffs" had standing, meaning real harm. It "retained appellate jurisdiction" (kept the appeal open) and kept the "stay" holding the wage order in place.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: If even one plaintiff had standing, it contemplated enjoining the whole determination because firm-specific relief would create unfair bidding advantages and undermine an industrywide rule.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: If even one "plaintiff" had standing, the court planned on "enjoining" (blocking by court order) the whole wage determination. "Relief" for only some firms would give them unfair bidding advantages and undermine an industry-wide rule.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: That conclusion rested on this quasi-legislative measure, its review statute, and competitive effects rather than a universal remedial rule.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: That conclusion rested on the nature of this "quasi-legislative" measure (an agency rule that works like a law), its review "statute", and its effects on competition. It was not a general "remedial" rule about how broad relief must always be.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The court accepted direct, immediate injury through wage increases or abandonment of government contracting.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: These companies were harmed because they would have to raise wages or stop bidding on government contracts.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The per curiam June 29, 1964 supplement rejected either as rehabilitation.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: In an unsigned "per curiam" opinion supplementing its decision on June 29, 1964, the court rejected both of the Secretary's proposals as "rehabilitation", meaning as ways to restore the old survey's credibility.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The Department could commence a lawful new determination, not maintain the invalid one until replacement.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The Department of Labor could start a new, lawful wage determination, but could not keep the invalid one in force until a replacement came.

lrs-o-wirtz.sentence: The supplemental decision struck down the determination and stayed the injunction for sixty further days to permit seeking Supreme Court review.
lrs-o-wirtz.plain: The supplemental decision struck down the wage determination. It "stayed" (delayed) the injunction for sixty more days so the government could seek Supreme Court review.

masterson.sentence: Dallas and Rebecca Masterson owned a ranch as tenants in common.
masterson.plain: Dallas and Rebecca Masterson owned a ranch as "tenants in common", meaning each held a share in the whole property.

masterson.sentence: The deed reserved a right for the grantors to repurchase by February 25, 1968.
masterson.plain: The deed reserved for the "grantors" (the Mastersons, who transferred the land) an option to buy the ranch back by February 25, 1968.

masterson.sentence: The price referred to the consideration previously paid, augmented by the depreciation value of improvements the Sines might add beginning two and one-half years after the conveyance.
masterson.plain: The buy-back price was the "consideration" (price) the Sines had paid, increased by the "depreciation" value of improvements they might add starting two and one-half years after the "conveyance" (the transfer of the land).

masterson.sentence: His trustee and Rebecca sought a declaration that they could exercise.
masterson.plain: The bankruptcy trustee managing Dallas's property for his creditors, together with Rebecca, asked the court to declare they could use the option.

masterson.sentence: Transferability determined whether the trustee could realize the option’s value for creditors.
masterson.plain: "Transferability", whether the option could pass to someone else, decided whether Dallas's bankruptcy trustee could capture the option's value for his creditors.

masterson.sentence: The Sines asserted that the parties had separately agreed the option was personal to the grantors and nonassignable to preserve the ranch in the Masterson family.
masterson.plain: The Sines claimed the "parties" had separately agreed that the option was personal to the "grantors" and could not be assigned to anyone else, to keep the ranch in the Masterson family.

masterson.sentence: That asserted agreement was an offer of proof, not an established appellate fact.
masterson.plain: That claimed agreement was only an "offer of proof", what the Sines wanted to prove. It was not a fact established on "appellate" review.

masterson.sentence: At the bench trial, extrinsic evidence explained that both sides meant a $50,000 base plus capital improvement expenditures less depreciation allowable under federal tax rules at exercise.
masterson.plain: At the "bench trial" (a trial before a judge, without a jury), outside evidence explained the price. Both sides meant a $50,000 base plus spending on capital improvements, minus "depreciation" allowed under federal tax rules when the option was used.

masterson.sentence: The judge admitted that explanation but excluded evidence of the alleged personal restriction.
masterson.plain: The judge admitted that explanation but excluded evidence of the "alleged" agreement that the option was personal.

masterson.sentence: Judgment declared the plaintiffs entitled to exercise, prescribed how, and retained jurisdiction over exercise and improvement compensation.
masterson.plain: The "Judgment" declared the "plaintiffs" (the trustee and Rebecca) entitled to exercise the option and said how. The court "retained jurisdiction", keeping the case open to oversee the exercise and payment for improvements.

masterson.sentence: The evident intended option should not fail through an excessively demanding insistence on textual completeness, and the explanatory evidence supplied sufficient certainty for specific enforcement.
masterson.plain: The parties clearly meant to create an option, so it should not fail just because the wording was not perfectly complete. The explanatory evidence made the terms certain enough for "specific enforcement", a court order requiring the sale itself.

masterson.sentence: Reversal therefore would not invalidate the option for indefiniteness; it concerned the excluded assignment restriction.
masterson.plain: So "Reversal" would not strike the option down for "indefiniteness" (vagueness). It turned on the excluded evidence about "assignment", whether the option could be transferred.

masterson.sentence: A writing adopted as the complete final embodiment bars additional or varying terms; a partially integrated writing protects its written portion while allowing proof of matters not recorded.
masterson.plain: A writing the parties adopted as their complete, final agreement bars any added or different terms. A "partially integrated writing", meant to cover only part of the deal, protects its written terms but allows proof of matters it does not record.

masterson.sentence: The key was intended exclusivity.
masterson.plain: The key question was intended "exclusivity": whether the parties meant the writing to be the only statement of their deal.

masterson.sentence: A merger clause could help, but courts also needed the alleged collateral agreement and circumstances to assess whether the writing included, excluded, or otherwise addressed that subject.
masterson.plain: A "merger clause" (a clause saying "this is the entire agreement") could help. But courts also needed to consider the "alleged" side agreement and the circumstances to judge whether the writing included, excluded, or otherwise dealt with that subject.

masterson.sentence: A facially complete instrument could memorialize only part of a transaction, as a promissory note might express one obligation without revealing all others.
masterson.plain: A document that looks "facially" complete (complete on its face) might record only part of a deal. A "promissory note" (a written promise to pay), for example, states one debt without revealing the rest of the bargain.

masterson.sentence: He balanced written reliability and fabricated-memory risks against defeating actual intent, while retaining exclusion of direct contradictions.
masterson.plain: He weighed the risk of made-up oral terms against the risk of ignoring what the parties really agreed, but kept the rule that evidence cannot contradict the writing.

masterson.sentence: For collateral terms he applied the first Restatement’s inquiry whether similarly situated parties might naturally agree separately.
masterson.plain: For "collateral terms" (side terms outside the writing), Traynor used the "first Restatement" test. The Restatement’s question was whether "similarly situated" parties, people in the same position, might naturally have made that agreement separately.

masterson.sentence: He also discussed the Uniform Commercial Code’s more permissive treatment of terms that certainly would appear in the writing, without applying goods law directly to this land option.
masterson.plain: He also discussed the Uniform Commercial Code’s more lenient approach, which excludes only terms that certainly would have been written down. He did not apply that law of goods directly to this land option.

masterson.sentence: The majority thought a deed’s formal structure made exhaustive collateral terms less natural.
masterson.plain: The majority thought a deed's formal, set structure made it less natural for the parties to put all "collateral terms" (side terms) of their deal into it.

masterson.sentence: Recording the reservation could protect the grantors against later purchasers without stating personal character, and the record showed no warning to these family participants about omitting the whole bargain.
masterson.plain: "Recording" the reservation in the public land records could protect the "grantors" against later buyers without stating that the option was personal. And the record showed no warning to these family members that leaving out part of the "bargain" would matter.

masterson.sentence: Options ordinarily are assignable absent prohibition or personal performance.
masterson.plain: Options ordinarily can be assigned (transferred) unless the parties forbid it or the option calls for personal "performance", such as personal services.

masterson.sentence: But that was a legal presumption, not an express term.
masterson.plain: But that was a legal "presumption", a default rule the law supplies, not an "express term" written into the deed.

masterson.sentence: Evidence could rebut what law would supply without contradicting a written provision.
masterson.plain: "Evidence" could disprove what the law would otherwise supply by default without contradicting any written provision of the deed.

masterson.sentence: The majority read several contrary authorities as complete-integration cases rather than rules making implied terms irrebuttable.
masterson.plain: The majority read several contrary cases as "complete-integration" cases, where the writing was meant to be the whole agreement. It did not read them as making "implied" (default) terms impossible to disprove.

masterson.sentence: He viewed the unrestricted option as granting transferability reinforced by Civil Code rules favoring transfer of property and obligation rights.
masterson.plain: Justice Burke, dissenting, saw the unrestricted option as granting "transferability". He said California's Civil Code rules favoring transfer of property rights and contract rights reinforced that.

masterson.sentence: An oral restriction contradicted that substantive incident rather than supplied a missing detail.
masterson.plain: An oral restriction on transfer would contradict that "substantive" feature the deed granted, transferability, rather than fill in a missing detail.

masterson.sentence: For him, the statutory parol-evidence rule embodied an already-made legislative reliability judgment, not a policy balance for judges to redo.
masterson.plain: For Burke, the parol-evidence rule in the statute reflected a "judgment" the legislature had already made about the reliability of writings. It was not a policy balance for judges to redo.

masterson.sentence: Unwritten family limitations could remove assets from creditors and unsettle title reliance.
masterson.plain: Allowing unwritten family side deals could let debtors keep assets from creditors and make land titles unreliable.

masterson.sentence: Rehearing was denied March 6, with modification into the reported form; the dissenters favored rehearing.
masterson.plain: "Rehearing" (reconsideration of the case) was denied on March 6, and the opinion was revised into its published form. The dissenters favored granting rehearing.

pacific-gas.sentence: Thomas promised to work at its own risk and expense and to indemnify PG&E against losses, damages, expenses, and liability arising from injury to property connected with performance.
pacific-gas.plain: Thomas promised to do the work at its own risk and expense. It also promised to "indemnify" PG&E (repay it) for losses, "damages", expenses, and "liability" (legal responsibility) arising from injury to property connected with "performance" of the work.

pacific-gas.sentence: Thomas also promised at least $50,000 in property-liability insurance, naming PG&E as an additional insured and including a cross-liability clause extending coverage to PG&E’s property.
pacific-gas.plain: Thomas also promised to carry at least $50,000 in property-liability insurance naming PG&E as an "additional insured", someone else the policy also protects. The policy had to include a "cross-liability clause" extending coverage to damage to PG&E's own property.

pacific-gas.sentence: PG&E pursued negligence and contractual indemnity, then dismissed negligence during trial.
pacific-gas.plain: PG&E sued on two theories: "negligence" (carelessness) and contractual "indemnity" (the contract duty to repay its losses). It dropped the negligence claim during trial.

pacific-gas.sentence: Thomas offered admissions by PG&E’s agents, conduct under similar contracts between the companies, and other evidence that indemnity was intended only for third-party property, excluding PG&E’s own property.
pacific-gas.plain: Thomas offered "admissions" by PG&E's own agents, how the companies had handled similar contracts, and other "evidence". It aimed to show the indemnity clause covered only "third-party" property (other people's), not PG&E's own.

pacific-gas.sentence: Nevertheless, the judge read its plain language to cover PG&E’s property and excluded outside evidence inconsistent with that reading.
pacific-gas.plain: Even so, the judge read the contract's "plain language" (its words taken at face value) to cover PG&E's own property, and excluded outside evidence that conflicted with that reading.

pacific-gas.sentence: Chief Justice Traynor’s California Supreme Court opinion rejected an admissibility test controlled solely by a judge’s impression of facial clarity.
pacific-gas.plain: Chief Justice Traynor’s "opinion" for the California Supreme Court rejected a test of "admissibility" (whether evidence may be heard) based only on the judge's impression of "facial clarity", whether the words seem clear on their face.

pacific-gas.sentence: The question was whether offered evidence supported a meaning the contractual language could reasonably bear.
pacific-gas.plain: The question was whether the offered evidence supported a meaning the "contractual" language could reasonably bear.

pacific-gas.sentence: The rule against adding to, subtracting from, or varying an integrated writing remained.
pacific-gas.plain: The rule against using outside evidence to add to, subtract from, or vary an "integrated writing" (a written contract meant as the parties' final agreement) still stood.

pacific-gas.sentence: But the court first had to ascertain the writing’s meaning before deciding whether evidence would change it.
pacific-gas.plain: But a court must first work out what the words mean before deciding whether evidence would change them.

pacific-gas.sentence: An asserted private intention outside the language’s reasonable susceptibility still would not suffice.
pacific-gas.plain: A party still cannot prove a secret meaning the words cannot reasonably bear.

pacific-gas.sentence: Courts therefore had to consider credible offered evidence preliminarily, including the agreement’s object, subject matter, nature, and surrounding circumstances.
pacific-gas.plain: So courts must first consider, provisionally, any "credible" (believable) evidence offered. That includes the agreement's purpose, subject matter, nature, and surrounding circumstances.

pacific-gas.sentence: Evidence supporting either meaning became admissible if the words could fairly carry both in that context.
pacific-gas.plain: If the words could fairly carry either meaning in that context, evidence supporting either meaning became "admissible", meaning it could be heard.

pacific-gas.sentence: Calling this ambiguity resolution was acceptable if external evidence could itself expose the ambiguity.
pacific-gas.plain: You may call this resolving ambiguity, so long as outside evidence can be used to show that words that look clear are in fact ambiguous.

pacific-gas.sentence: Although Thomas’s offer might ordinarily have been too general, repeated categorical exclusions excused a more formal offer of proof in this trial.
pacific-gas.plain: Thomas's offer of evidence might ordinarily have been too general. But the judge's repeated "categorical exclusions" (refusing all such evidence) excused a more formal "offer of proof", a specific description of what the evidence would show.

pacific-gas.sentence: The court supplied an alternative ground: exclusion was erroneous even under a facial-ambiguity test.
pacific-gas.plain: The court gave an "alternative ground", a second independent reason: excluding the evidence was wrong even under the old "facial-ambiguity" test, which asks whether the words look ambiguous on their face.

pacific-gas.sentence: “All” could mean every claim within the category covered, and references to loss, damage, and expense could describe settlement of third-party claims rather than direct insurance of PG&E’s property.
pacific-gas.plain: "All" could mean every claim within the covered category. And references to loss, damage, and expense could describe "settlement" of outsiders' claims, rather than direct insurance of PG&E's own property.

pacific-gas.sentence: Doing work at Thomas’s own risk could release PG&E from injuries to Thomas’s property without making Thomas the insurer of PG&E’s property.
pacific-gas.plain: Doing the work "at its own risk" could mean Thomas released PG&E from responsibility for damage to Thomas's own property. It need not make Thomas the "insurer" of PG&E's property.

pacific-gas.sentence: These points established a permissible interpretation; they did not finally select it.
pacific-gas.plain: This showed the narrow reading was possible, not that it was correct.

pacific-gas.sentence: Under the historical indemnity rule applied, PG&E’s active negligence causing the harm would suffice to defeat generally worded indemnity for that harm.
pacific-gas.plain: Under the older indemnity rule applied here, if PG&E's "active negligence" (its own careless acts) caused the harm, that alone would defeat a generally worded indemnity clause for that harm.

pacific-gas.sentence: Invoices alone could not establish incurred liability, payment, or reasonable charges, but could corroborate actual payment testimony; paid charges were evidence of reasonableness.
pacific-gas.plain: Invoices alone could not prove that PG&E incurred "liability" for the charges, paid them, or that they were reasonable. But they could "corroborate" (back up) testimony of actual payment, and charges that were paid were evidence of reasonableness.

pacific-gas.sentence: No qualified witness established them as accurate work records, and no other evidence supplied that missing fact.
pacific-gas.plain: No "qualified witness" (someone able to vouch for how the records were made) established the invoices as accurate records of work done, and no other "evidence" supplied that missing fact.

pacific-gas.sentence: Because the engineer’s reasonableness opinion depended on inadmissible proof that the repairs occurred, Thomas’s objections should have been sustained.
pacific-gas.plain: The engineer's opinion on reasonableness depended on "inadmissible" proof (evidence that should not have been allowed) that the repairs happened. So Thomas's objections should have been "sustained", meaning upheld.

stees.sentence: Their August 18, 1868 agreement was under seal and incorporated detailed plans and specifications prepared by M. Sheire & Bro.
stees.plain: Their August 18, 1868 agreement was a formal sealed contract. It made part of the agreement detailed plans and specifications prepared by M. Sheire & Bro.

stees.sentence: That was the pleaded demand, not a separately reported jury-award amount.
stees.plain: That was the "pleaded" demand, the amount the owners asked for in their complaint, not a separately reported jury award.

stees.sentence: The builders moved for a new trial on a bill of exceptions and appealed the denial.
stees.plain: The builders moved for a new trial on a "bill of exceptions", a formal document listing the trial rulings they objected to, and appealed when it was denied.

stees.sentence: They challenged exclusion of evidence that, in their view, showed compliance with the specifications discharged their duties, the owners selected the site and owed a suitable foundation, the owners orally promised before signing to drain if necessary, and later promises and drainage work excused the builders from doing that work themselves.
stees.plain: They challenged the exclusion of evidence that, they said, showed: following the plans "discharged" (fully satisfied) their duties; the owners chose the site and owed a suitable "foundation"; the owners orally promised before signing to drain if needed; and later promises and drainage work excused the builders from draining.

stees.sentence: The builders analogized soil to materials an owner must supply and called the earlier drainage promise collateral to the writing.
stees.plain: They argued the ground was like materials the owner provides, and that the oral drainage promise was a separate side deal the written contract did not cover.

stees.sentence: For later arrangements, they invoked consideration, modification through performance, estoppel, and liability for negligent performance of even a gratuitous undertaking.
stees.plain: For the later arrangements, they relied on "consideration" (something given in exchange), modification through "performance", and estoppel (barring going back on a relied-on promise). They also invoked "liability" for careless performance of even a "gratuitous undertaking", an unpaid promise.

stees.sentence: The owners answered that the evidence contradicted both the written contract and the defenses actually pleaded.
stees.plain: The owners answered that the evidence contradicted both the written contract and the "defenses" the builders had actually pleaded in their answer.

stees.sentence: Justice Young’s opinion held that latent soil problems did not excuse an absolute promise to erect a building whose completion remained possible.
stees.plain: Justice Young’s "opinion" held that "latent" (hidden) soil problems did not excuse an "absolute promise", one made without conditions, to put up a building that could still be completed.

stees.sentence: The court’s historical formulation required performance of a positive express undertaking despite unforeseen hardship, subject to prevention by an act of God, the law, or the other party; difficulty short of absolute impossibility was insufficient.
stees.plain: Under the court's historical rule, a party must carry out an "express undertaking" (a stated promise) despite unforeseen hardship. "Performance" was excused only by "prevention" through an "act of God" (an uncontrollable natural event), the law, or the other party; difficulty short of absolute impossibility was not enough.

stees.sentence: A contractor could qualify the undertaking in the agreement.
stees.plain: A contractor could protect itself by qualifying the "undertaking" (the promise) in the agreement itself.

stees.sentence: The phrase “act of God” therefore did not automatically excuse every natural destruction: rebuilding might still be possible and within the promise.
