stees.plain: So the phrase "act of God" did not automatically excuse every destruction by natural forces. Rebuilding might still be possible and within what the builders promised.

stees.sentence: The stated footing dimensions described features of the result; they did not eliminate the broader obligation to deliver the building.
stees.plain: The foundation measurements in the plans described what the building must have, not a limit on the duty to deliver a standing building.

stees.sentence: The site-selection theory also failed on the pleadings: although the contract imperfectly described the location, the answer admitted contracting to build on the identified parcel and beginning there.
stees.plain: The site-selection theory also failed on the "pleadings" (the parties' written court filings). Although the "contract" described the location imperfectly, the builders' "answer" admitted they agreed to build on that parcel and began work there.

stees.sentence: Because drainage was integral to completing construction, the alleged earlier oral allocation of that duty was not collateral.
stees.plain: Because drainage was an essential part of completing the building, the "alleged" earlier oral agreement assigning that duty to the owners was not collateral, a separate side matter outside the written contract.

stees.sentence: It could not vary the later written agreement.
stees.plain: So the earlier oral promise could not change the written contract signed afterwards.

stees.sentence: The court recognized an American exception allowing subsequent oral arrangements to modify a sealed contract when executed or acted on so that enforcing the original promise would be inequitable.
stees.plain: The court recognized an American exception: a later oral agreement may "modify" (change) a sealed contract when it has been "executed" (carried out) or acted on, so that enforcing the original promise would be "inequitable", meaning unfair.

stees.sentence: A mismatch between the answer and offered proof made those questions unnecessary.
stees.plain: The court did not need to decide, because the builders' evidence did not match what they had alleged in their answer.

stees.sentence: It alleged no consideration or performance supporting estoppel; a naked promise alone did not release the builders.
stees.plain: The builders' answer alleged no consideration or "performance" supporting estoppel. A "naked promise" (a bare promise with nothing given in exchange) did not by itself "release" the builders from their duty.

stees.sentence: The court expressly declined to hold that theory insufficient if properly pleaded, but it contradicted the pleaded total nonperformance.
stees.plain: The court expressly did not hold that theory would fail if properly "pleaded". But it contradicted the answer's claim of total "nonperformance", that the owners never drained at all.

stees.sentence: Each offer was tendered as a whole, so inadmissible material allowed rejection of the whole offer.
stees.plain: Each offer of evidence was made as a single package, so if any part was "inadmissible" (not allowed), the judge could reject the whole offer.

stees.sentence: The objection that it was incompetent, irrelevant, and immaterial was sufficiently specific because defense counsel knew the answer’s contents.
stees.plain: The owners' objection that the evidence was "incompetent, irrelevant, and immaterial" was specific enough, because "defense counsel" (the builders' lawyer) knew what his own answer said.

swiss-2024.sentence: Paying the penalty would not release the responsible party from continued compliance with the noncompetition undertaking or from liability for consequential damage.
swiss-2024.plain: Paying the penalty would not "release" the responsible party from continuing to obey the "noncompetition undertaking" (the promise not to compete), or from "liability" for consequential damage, further harm caused by the breach.

swiss-2024.sentence: Truth and necessity nevertheless remained distinct questions under this contract.
swiss-2024.plain: Under this contract it was not enough that the letter's statements were true; what they said also had to be necessary.

swiss-2024.sentence: The defendant had not shown an absence of fault.
swiss-2024.plain: The defendant had not proved that he was without fault, so he could not escape the penalty on that ground.

swiss-2024.sentence: The lower court considered his business experience and deliberate adaptation of the earlier client letter and found at least conditional intent in preparing and sending the candidate letter.
swiss-2024.plain: The "lower court" considered his business experience and his deliberate reworking of the earlier client letter. It found at least "conditional intent" in preparing and sending the candidate letter: he knowingly accepted the risk that it broke the contract.

swiss-2024.sentence: The claimant did not substantiate damage or a risk of damage.
swiss-2024.plain: The claimant did not "substantiate" (back up with specific facts) any damage or any risk of damage.

swiss-2024.sentence: It required a substantive answer, at least in broad terms, to the defendant’s account that the letter had caused no adverse consequences.
swiss-2024.plain: The court required a "substantive" answer, one with real facts, at least in broad terms, to the defendant's account that the letter had caused no harm.

swiss-2024.sentence: The underlying transaction was financially significant, however, and a contractual penalty retained a punitive function.
swiss-2024.plain: But the underlying deal was financially significant, and a "contractual penalty" (a sum the contract sets for a breach) keeps a punishing function. So some penalty was still appropriate.

swiss-2024.sentence: The claimant did not allege additional violations beyond those the lower court had found and did not establish arbitrary fact-finding.
swiss-2024.plain: The claimant did not "allege" (formally claim) any violations beyond those the lower court found. It also did not establish "arbitrary fact-finding", meaning clearly untenable findings, the narrow ground for reviewing facts on appeal.

swiss-2024.sentence: The appellate argument therefore failed to meet the required grounding rather than establishing additional injuries for the reviewing court to accept.
swiss-2024.plain: So the "appellate" argument failed because it lacked the required supporting grounds. It did not establish additional injuries for the "reviewing court" (the court hearing the appeal) to accept.

swiss-2024.sentence: Article 163 of the Swiss Code of Obligations allowed parties to choose a contractual penalty while requiring a court to reduce an excessive amount in its discretion.
swiss-2024.plain: Article 163 of the Swiss Code of Obligations, the main Swiss contract statute, let parties choose a "contractual penalty" of any amount. But it required a court to reduce an excessive one, using its "discretion" (judgment).

swiss-2024.sentence: Contractual freedom and good faith called for restraint.
swiss-2024.plain: "Contractual" freedom (parties may set their own terms) and "good faith" (honest dealing) called for courts to show restraint in cutting penalties.

swiss-2024.sentence: Reduction was justified where the stipulated amount was grossly disproportionate to the claimant’s legitimate interest in full enforcement when the breach occurred.
swiss-2024.plain: A court may reduce the penalty when it is wildly out of proportion to what the claimant legitimately needed at the time of the breach.

swiss-2024.sentence: The debtor generally had to raise and establish a basis for reduction.
swiss-2024.plain: The "debtor", here the party owing the penalty, generally had to ask for a reduction and prove a basis for it.

swiss-2024.sentence: Reducing it did not offend the principle that parties define the matters for decision.
swiss-2024.plain: Since the defendant had argued the penalty was excessive, the court did not overstep by deciding an issue the parties had not raised.

swiss-2024.sentence: A penalty could become payable without compensable damage.
swiss-2024.plain: A penalty could become payable even without "compensable" damage, meaning a loss the law would pay for.

swiss-2024.sentence: The Federal Supreme Court rejected the proposed burden-of-proof objection on that basis.
swiss-2024.plain: On that basis, the Federal Supreme Court rejected the proposed objection about the burden of proof: a court may still consider the absence of harm when deciding whether a penalty is excessive.

swiss-2024.sentence: The claimant’s new assertion that the defendant intended to cause harm was unsupported and late, and assertions about several confused candidates relied on facts unavailable for the review as framed.
swiss-2024.plain: The claimant's new assertion that the "defendant" intended to cause harm was unsupported and came too late. Its claims about several confused candidates relied on facts the review, as framed, could not consider.

swiss-2024.sentence: Repeating the absence of operational activity and adverse effects did not identify an abuse of discretion: the lower court had already taken those circumstances into account.
swiss-2024.plain: Repeating that the earlier business had no operations and that no harm resulted did not show an "abuse of discretion", a clearly unreasonable use of judgment. The lower court had already taken those facts into account.

swiss-2024.sentence: The comparison with domestic penalty doctrine concerns the different response shown here: a reduced award can retain a punitive function, whereas the familiar domestic analysis may invalidate a penalty and leave ordinary breach damages.
swiss-2024.plain: The comparison with U.S. (domestic) penalty doctrine shows a different response. Swiss courts cut an excessive penalty down, and the reduced award can still punish; the familiar U.S. analysis may void a penalty clause and award only ordinary "breach" damages.

swiss-2024.sentence: It is necessary to identify the governing jurisdiction before transferring either consequence.
swiss-2024.plain: Before carrying either approach over to a case, one must first identify the governing "jurisdiction", meaning which country's law controls.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.sentence: Paragraph 20 allowed termination through mutual written consent, insolvency, material breach after notice and an opportunity to cure, or a change of ownership subject to specified conditions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.plain: Paragraph 20 allowed ending the contract four ways: by both sides' written consent, by "insolvency" (a party being unable to pay its debts), by material breach after "notice and an opportunity" to cure (a warning and chance to fix it), or by a change of ownership under specified conditions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.sentence: Whittlestone’s damages demand was no defense, repeated no other claim, directly concerned the alleged harm and requested relief, and was not claimed to be scandalous.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.plain: Whittlestone's damages demand was not a defense, did not repeat another "claim", directly concerned the "alleged" harm and the "relief" (remedy) requested, and was not said to be scandalous. So it fit none of the categories Rule 12(f) lets a court strike.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.sentence: The panel also noted that Rule 12(d) protects a reasonable opportunity to present material when outside evidence converts a dismissal motion into summary judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.plain: The panel also noted that Rule 12(d) protects a fair chance to submit evidence. When a judge considers outside evidence, it turns a "dismissal motion" (a request to throw out the complaint) into one for summary judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.sentence: The material-breach route gave the nonbreaching party a right to terminate after notice and failed cure; it did not necessarily let a breacher activate the exclusion through its own withdrawal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.plain: The "material-breach" route let the innocent party end the contract after notice and a failed "cure" (the breaching side not fixing the problem). It did not necessarily let the breaching party trigger the damages exclusion by quitting itself.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.sentence: Judge N. R. Smith, joined by Reinhardt and Fletcher, reversed and remanded on August 17, 2010, directing that lost profits and consequential damages not be dismissed under Rule 12(f).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-284.plain: Judge N. R. Smith, "joined by" Judges Reinhardt and Fletcher, "reversed" and sent the case back on August 17, 2010. The court directed that claims for lost profits and consequential (indirect) damages not be "dismissed" under Rule 12(f).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.sentence: Under Title IV of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act, a member first exhausted internal remedies, then complained for investigation; probable cause required an authorized government suit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.plain: Under Title IV of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act, a union member must first have "exhausted internal remedies" (used the union's own complaint process), then complain to the Secretary of Labor. If the investigation found "probable cause" (good reason to believe the law was broken), the government had to sue.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.sentence: Trbovich sought intervention under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a), offering evidence and argument in support of the Secretary while adding two grounds: pensioner locals allegedly constituted contrary to the union constitution and a pension increase allegedly arranged by the incumbent president to influence pensioners.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.plain: Trbovich sought "intervention" (joining the suit as a party) under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a) to offer "evidence" and argument backing the Secretary. He added two grounds: retiree locals were "allegedly" set up against the union constitution, and the president allegedly arranged a pension increase to sway retirees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.sentence: Legislative debates over competing public- and private-enforcement proposals showed concern for screening frivolous challenges and concentrating disputes over one election in one proceeding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.plain: Congress's debates over public versus private enforcement showed two concerns: screening out "frivolous" (baseless) election challenges, and keeping all disputes over one election in a single case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.sentence: But adding grounds the Secretary presumably considered meritless would bypass his assigned screening role, even if adding them here was less burdensome than a separate action.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.plain: But adding grounds the Secretary presumably found "meritless" would bypass his assigned screening role, even if adding them here was less burdensome than a separate "action" (lawsuit). So Trbovich could support the existing claims but not add new ones.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.sentence: The member who had initiated enforcement therefore did not have to prove official dereliction to justify participating in protection of his own interest.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-335.plain: Because the Secretary also had to serve the broader public interest, his choices might differ from what Trbovich wanted. So Trbovich did not have to prove the Secretary was neglecting his duty; the risk that the Secretary might not fully represent his interests was enough to let him join.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.sentence: On October 8 it sued Mercury and the architect in North Carolina court, disputing liability and arbitrability and seeking indemnity from the architect if liable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.plain: On October 8 the hospital sued Mercury and the architect in North Carolina state court. It disputed "liability" (that it owed anything) and arbitrability, and sought "indemnity" (repayment) from the architect if it was liable.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.sentence: Its separate attempt to remove the state action failed because the hospital and architect were both North Carolina corporations; that remand was not under review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.plain: Mercury's separate attempt to "remove" the state case to federal court failed, because the hospital and architect, on opposite sides, were both North Carolina corporations. That remand to state court was not under "review" here.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.sentence: It alternatively qualified as a collateral order: the refusal to proceed was conclusive, separate from the merits, and unreviewable effectively after preclusion attached.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.plain: Alternatively, the stay was appealable as a "collateral order": it conclusively refused to let the case proceed, was separate from "the merits" (who owed what), and could not be effectively reviewed later once "preclusion" attached, meaning the state ruling would bind the parties.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.sentence: Separate proceedings involving the architect followed from an arbitration agreement that did not bind the architect; that unavoidable division could not defeat Mercury’s agreed arbitration, although related nonarbitrating litigation might be stayed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.plain: Separate proceedings against the architect resulted from an arbitration agreement that did not bind the architect. That unavoidable split could not defeat the arbitration Mercury had agreed to, although the related court case could be "stayed" (paused).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.sentence: Although appellate courts ordinarily should leave such issues for initial district-court decision, full briefing and evidence, no factual dispute requiring a jury, the interest in prompt arbitration, and no apparent prejudice justified the direction here.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-592.plain: "Appellate courts" ordinarily should let the trial court decide such issues first in "district-court" proceedings. Here the direction was justified: there was full "briefing" (written argument) and evidence, no fact dispute needing a jury, an interest in prompt "arbitration", and no apparent "prejudice" (unfair harm) to anyone.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.sentence: At oral argument, the jurors received permission to supplement their answers with a prematurity objection, also operating as cross-motions against the complaints.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.plain: At "oral argument", the jurors were allowed to add to their answers an objection that the suits were premature. That objection also worked as "cross-motions", their own requests to dismiss the complaints.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.sentence: Liability arising from compelled grand-jury service affected the statewide judicial system and did not depend on classifying defendants narrowly as formal state officers.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.plain: "Liability" arising from compelled grand-jury service affected the whole state court system. So it did not depend on narrowly classifying the "defendants" (the jurors) as formal state officers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.sentence: Ackerson struck portions of the first defense containing evasive or unresponsive denials, demands for proof of matters never alleged, and unnecessary legal or evidentiary detail.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.plain: Judge Ackerson "struck" (removed) parts of the jurors' first defense that contained evasive or unresponsive denials, demanded proof of things never alleged, or added unnecessary legal or evidentiary detail.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.sentence: He treated a separately reserved Rule 40 prematurity question differently: reservation of a legal question functioned like a demurrer, so he denied the attack without prejudice to a proper preliminary motion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.plain: He treated the separately reserved Rule 40 prematurity question differently. Reserving a "legal question" worked like a "demurrer" (an old objection that a complaint fails as a matter of law), so he denied the attack "without prejudice", leaving the jurors free to raise it in a proper preliminary motion.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.sentence: A clear absence of all jurisdiction differs from error or excess within actual or colorable jurisdiction; deciding an arguable jurisdictional question is itself judicial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-243.plain: A "clear absence of all jurisdiction" (plainly no authority at all) differs from an error, or overreach, within actual or "colorable" (at least arguable) jurisdiction. Deciding an arguable "jurisdictional" question about one's own authority is itself a protected judicial act.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.sentence: The board accepted and resolved, in consideration of ending the employment agreement, to pay $25,000 and grant a five-year nonqualified option for 50,000 common shares at $2 each.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.plain: The board accepted, and resolved, in exchange for ending his employment agreement, to pay him $25,000. It also granted a five-year nonqualified option (one without special tax treatment) to buy 50,000 "common shares" (ordinary stock) at $2 each.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.sentence: After a diversity bench trial, Judge Glasser rejected Acton’s contention that the plan reference incorporated every cancellation provision.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.plain: After a "bench trial" (a trial before a judge without a jury) held in federal court on "diversity" grounds, meaning the parties were from different states, Judge Glasser rejected Acton's argument that the contract's reference to the plan brought in every one of the plan's cancellation provisions.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.sentence: The judge found it implausible that an experienced executive would surrender approximately $100,000 of remaining salary for $25,000 and an illusory option.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.plain: The judge found it implausible that an experienced executive would give up about $100,000 of remaining salary for $25,000 and an "illusory" option, meaning one the company could cancel at will, so it promised nothing real.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.sentence: On March 7, 1984, Judges Meskill, Pierce and Pratt issued a per curiam Second Circuit decision affirming against Acton but granting a limited remand on Hermanowski’s cross-appeal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.plain: On March 7, 1984, Judges Meskill, Pierce and Pratt of the Second Circuit (the federal appeals court) issued a "per curiam" decision, an unsigned opinion for the whole panel. It was "affirming" (upholding) the judgment against Acton, but granted a "limited remand", sending one narrow issue back to the trial judge, on Hermanowski's "cross-appeal", his own appeal from the same judgment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.sentence: An apparently unanswered Rule 36 admission request, the district finding of proportionate adjustments, and Acton’s failure to dispute $100,000 in trial submissions supported reconsideration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-117.plain: Three things supported "reconsideration" (a second look at whether the total exercise price stayed $100,000). Acton apparently never answered a formal request to admit facts under Rule 36, and an unanswered request counts as an admission; the trial judge had made a "finding" (a ruling on the facts) of proportionate adjustments; and Acton never disputed the $100,000 figure in its trial papers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.sentence: Earlier litigation construed Article 11(a) to relieve the United States from liability for a shortage caused by statutory mandate, while allowing a separate challenge to the merits of statutory compliance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.plain: Earlier litigation "construed" (interpreted) Article 11(a) of the contract to free the United States from "liability" (a legal duty to pay) for a water shortage that a statute required. It still allowed a separate challenge to "the merits", meaning whether the government had actually complied with the statute.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.sentence: On June 5, 1998, the district court dismissed statutory claims for lack of Tucker Act jurisdiction, noting possible proceedings in the Court of Federal Claims, and rejected the theory that reclamation statutes themselves were contracts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.plain: On June 5, 1998, the district court (the federal trial court) dismissed the claims based on statutes for lack of jurisdiction under the Tucker Act, which sends money claims like these against the United States to the Court of Federal Claims; it noted the farmers might sue there. It also rejected the theory that the reclamation statutes, the federal irrigation laws, were themselves contracts.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.sentence: On April 12, 2000, reconsideration under Klamath Water Users Protective Association v. Patterson led it to classify the farmers as incidental beneficiaries and find no waiver.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.plain: On April 12, 2000, on "reconsideration" in light of Klamath Water Users Protective Association v. Patterson, a new appeals-court decision, the court changed its view. It classified the farmers as "incidental beneficiaries", people who benefit from a contract without being meant to enforce it, and found no "waiver", meaning the government had not given up its immunity from their suit.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.sentence: Section 390uu permitted joining the United States as a necessary defendant to adjudicate contractual rights of a contracting entity and the Government under reclamation contracts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.plain: Section 390uu allowed the United States to be joined as a "necessary defendant" in a suit deciding the contract rights of a contracting entity and the Government under reclamation (federal irrigation) contracts. The farmers argued that, as intended beneficiaries, they fit within it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.sentence: Even assuming it, the farmers neither sought judicial compulsion against Westlands nor alleged the Government directly participated in a trust breach, as required by the exception invoked to sue in the trustee’s place.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-096.plain: Even assuming Westlands held rights in trust for the farmers, beneficiaries may sue an outsider in the trustee's place only under a narrow exception. The farmers did not meet it: they neither asked the court to compel Westlands to act nor alleged (formally claimed) that the Government directly took part in a breach of the trust.

brief-CT-CB-0569.sentence: Chief Justice Roberts’s majority applied Federal Arbitration Act § 16(a)(3): although interlocutory orders compelling arbitration generally are unappealable, Randolph treated an order compelling arbitration and dismissing all underlying claims as final.
brief-CT-CB-0569.plain: Chief Justice Roberts's majority opinion applied Federal Arbitration Act § 16(a)(3). Normally "interlocutory orders" (rulings made mid-case) compelling arbitration are "unappealable" right away, but Randolph treated an order that both compels arbitration and dismisses all the underlying claims as final, because it ends the court case, so it can be appealed.

brief-CT-CB-0569.sentence: The Court compared rules refusing to infer delegation of gateway questions from silence or ambiguity, but did not decide whether class availability itself was such a gateway question: everyone agreed a court would decide here.
brief-CT-CB-0569.plain: The Court drew a comparison to rules that refuse to infer, from a contract's silence or "ambiguity" (unclear wording), that parties handed "gateway questions" (basic threshold issues) to the arbitrator. But it did not decide whether the availability of class arbitration is itself such a gateway question, because everyone agreed a court would decide it here.

brief-CT-CB-0569.sentence: The majority viewed contra proferentem, construing unresolved wording against its drafter, as a last-resort allocation of uncertainty based on fairness and policy rather than discovery of actual shared intent.
brief-CT-CB-0569.plain: The majority viewed "contra proferentem", the rule of "construing" (interpreting) unclear wording against the party who drafted it, as a last-resort way of assigning the risk of uncertainty, based on fairness and policy. It is not a way of discovering what the parties actually intended together.

brief-CT-CB-0569.sentence: In her account, a statute originally protecting merchant arbitration had expanded to consumer and employment forms offering little choice, where mandatory individual proceedings could defeat low-value enforcement.
brief-CT-CB-0569.plain: In Ginsburg's account, a statute originally meant to protect arbitration between merchants had grown to cover take-it-or-leave-it consumer and employment contracts. There, requiring individual (one-by-one) proceedings could make small-value claims not worth pursuing at all.

brief-CT-CB-0569.sentence: The FAA permitted early appeal when arbitration was denied and usually delayed review when ordered; he viewed dismissal as an impermissible workaround, read Randolph differently, and relied on Microsoft.
brief-CT-CB-0569.plain: Breyer noted that the FAA (Federal Arbitration Act) allows an early appeal when a court denies arbitration but usually delays review when a court orders it. He saw dismissing the case to allow an appeal as an improper workaround, read Randolph differently from the majority, and relied on Microsoft, an earlier decision.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.sentence: Expecting crude prices to rise, the parties replaced an escalator that passed through only half of increases with one intended to transmit crude-cost changes proportionately.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.plain: Expecting crude oil prices to rise, the parties replaced the contract's "escalator" (a clause that adjusts the price as costs change), which passed through only half of any increase, with one meant to pass changes in crude costs through in full proportion.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.sentence: Under the court’s account, output at a well’s May 1972 level was controlled old oil; added output was new oil, accompanied by release of a matching amount of old oil from controls.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.plain: Under the court's account of the 1973 federal price controls, oil from a well up to its May 1972 output level was price-capped "old oil". Any extra output was uncapped "new oil", and for each such barrel an equal amount of old oil was also released from the cap.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.sentence: Gulf challenged mutuality and definiteness, accused Eastern of manipulating requirements, and asserted commercial impracticability under Florida’s Uniform Commercial Code sections 2-614 and 2-615.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.plain: Gulf challenged the contract's "mutuality" (whether it truly bound both sides) and its definiteness (whether its terms were clear enough to enforce), and accused Eastern of manipulating how much fuel it required. It also claimed "commercial impracticability", an excuse when unforeseen events make performance far more costly, under sections 2-614 and 2-615 of Florida's Uniform Commercial Code, the state's commercial-sales statute.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.sentence: The judge addressed section 2-615 on the merits despite Eastern’s notice objection because Gulf had identified the defense in its summer 1974 opposition memorandum and later answer.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.plain: Eastern objected that Gulf had not given proper notice of an impracticability defense, but the judge decided section 2-615 on the merits anyway, despite that "objection". Gulf had named the defense in its summer 1974 "opposition" memorandum (its written response to Eastern's motion) and later in its answer.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.sentence: Even if serious hardship had been established, the court considered Middle Eastern volatility, supply interruption, host-government control, expected crude increases, and changing domestic controls sufficiently foreseeable business risks for Gulf to address.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0172.plain: Even if Gulf had proved serious hardship, impracticability excuses only unforeseen events. The court found Middle Eastern instability, supply cutoffs, foreign governments' control over oil, expected crude price increases, and changing domestic price controls were foreseeable business risks Gulf could have dealt with in the contract.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.sentence: Three days later, the Government served a notice to appear charging removability and identifying the immigration court, but leaving the hearing date and time to be set.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.plain: Three days later, the Government served a "notice to appear", the document that starts deportation proceedings. It charged him with being removable (deportable) and named the "immigration court", but left the hearing date and time to be set later.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.sentence: Thirteen years later, he sought reopening based on Pereira, the Supreme Court decision concerning a notice lacking time and place, and the deficient initial document.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.plain: Thirteen years later, he asked to reopen his case based on Pereira, the Supreme Court decision about a notice that lacked the hearing's time and place, and on the defects in his own first notice.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.sentence: Rescission was available for exceptional circumstances raised within 180 days, government custody causing absence without the noncitizen’s fault, or nonreceipt of notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.plain: Rescission was available, meaning an order entered in the person's absence could be canceled, on three grounds: "exceptional circumstances" raised within 180 days; government custody that kept the noncitizen from attending through no fault of his own; or failure to receive notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2).

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.sentence: The noncitizens argued that lack of either kind independently allowed rescission and that a paragraph-(2) change required an earlier compliant paragraph-(1) notice.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.plain: The noncitizens argued that missing either kind of notice was enough by itself and allowed rescission (cancellation of the absence order). They also argued that a paragraph (2) notice changing the hearing time works only if an earlier, proper paragraph (1) notice existed to change.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.sentence: Pereira observed that paragraph (2) presupposed an earlier time-and-place notice, but addressed the stop-time rule for cancellation eligibility, not this paragraph’s meaning.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-011.plain: Pereira had remarked that a paragraph (2) change notice assumes an earlier notice giving a time and place. But Pereira was about the "stop-time rule", which stops the clock on the years of residence needed to be eligible for cancellation of removal, not about what this paragraph means.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.sentence: Christiana Western Structures signed a collective-bargaining agreement with United Furniture Workers Local 1010, a union that did not represent the workers covered by the arrangement.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.plain: Christiana Western Structures signed a "collective-bargaining agreement" (a union contract setting wages and work terms) with United Furniture Workers Local 1010, a union that did not represent the workers the contract would cover; in fact, the employer had no such workers yet.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.sentence: On January 2, 1970, the Southern California District Council of Laborers and affiliated Local 1184 filed charges alleging violations of National Labor Relations Act §§ 8(a)(1), (2) and (3).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.plain: On January 2, 1970, the Southern California District Council of Laborers and its affiliated Local 1184 filed charges with the labor board alleging (formally claiming) violations of National Labor Relations Act §§ 8(a)(1), (2) and (3). Those sections forbid interfering with workers' rights, dominating or propping up a union, and pressuring workers over union membership.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.sentence: Ordman invoked Local Lodge No. 1424, a Supreme Court decision rejecting use of continued maintenance to evade a time bar on attacking an agreement’s execution.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.plain: Ordman relied on Local Lodge No. 1424, a Supreme Court decision holding that a challenger cannot get around the "time bar" (the six-month deadline for attacking how an agreement was signed) by arguing that keeping the agreement in force is a new violation.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.sentence: Starting the clock then could insulate a handpicked-union arrangement simply by delaying hiring six months, or shorten the complaint period for workers hired earlier.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.plain: If the six-month deadline ran from signing, an employer could shield a deal with a union it picked just by waiting six months to hire anyone, before any worker existed to complain; workers hired soon after would also get less than the full six months.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.sentence: Correcting that threshold statutory error, in undisputed circumstances the judge called extreme, differed from reviewing an informed discretionary refusal.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-034.plain: Correcting that threshold "statutory" error, a mistake about what the statute allowed, on undisputed facts the judge called extreme, differed from reviewing an informed "discretionary" refusal, a judgment call the General Counsel was entitled to make. A court may do the first.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.sentence: It conceded voter authority over state-legislative districts but argued that the federal Elections Clause specifically assigned congressional districting to the elected assembly.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.plain: The legislature conceded that voters could control districts for state-legislative seats. But it argued that the federal "Elections Clause" specifically gave congressional "districting" (drawing the district maps) to the elected assembly, the state 'Legislature'.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.sentence: Justice Ginsburg’s majority applied injury, traceability, and redressability: the alleged loss of a constitutional mapmaking prerogative was an institutional injury an injunction could redress, even though the Court would reject the asserted exclusive right on the merits.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.plain: Justice Ginsburg's majority applied the three standing tests: injury, "traceability" (the defendant caused it), and redressability (a court can fix it). The legislature's alleged loss of its constitutional mapmaking power was an "institutional injury", a harm to the body itself, that an injunction could redress, even though the Court went on to reject that claimed exclusive right on the merits.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.sentence: Raines v. Byrd involved individual Congressmembers claiming a widely shared institutional harm without authorization from houses that opposed the suit.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.plain: Raines v. Byrd involved individual Congressmembers who claimed a harm shared by all of Congress (an institutional harm) without authorization from their houses, which opposed the suit; they lacked standing.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.sentence: Hawke, by contrast, excluded referendum from constitutional-amendment ratification, a distinct federal function rather than ordinary lawmaking.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.plain: Hawke, by contrast, held that a "referendum" (a popular vote) could not be part of "ratification" (approval) of a federal constitutional amendment. Ratifying is a distinct federal function, not ordinary lawmaking, so 'Legislatures' there meant only the elected body.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.sentence: Later one-person, one-vote decisions had rendered four default rules practically obsolete, but did not erase recognition of state-law processes.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-080.plain: Later "one-person, one-vote" decisions, which require districts of equal population, made four "default rules" (fallback rules in the federal statute) practically obsolete. But they did not erase the statute's recognition of each state's own lawmaking processes.

cp-adickes.sentence: The district court required a state-enforced custom specifically denying service to white patrons accompanied by Black patrons and directed a verdict because she had not shown enough similar Hattiesburg incidents.
cp-adickes.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) required proof of a state-enforced custom specifically denying service to white customers who came with Black customers. Because she had not shown enough similar incidents in Hattiesburg, it "directed a verdict", ending the case without letting the jury decide.

cp-adickes.sentence: Had the officers supplied affidavits denying presence, Adickes would have needed a competent eyewitness affidavit or a former Rule 56(f) affidavit explaining why the evidence was unavailable.
cp-adickes.plain: If the officers had filed "affidavits" (sworn written statements) denying they were present, Adickes would have needed an affidavit from a competent eyewitness. Otherwise she would have needed an affidavit under former Rule 56(f) explaining why she could not yet get that evidence.

cp-adickes.sentence: For the discrimination count, Harlan read statutory custom or usage as requiring a practice with the force of law through persistent official conduct, rather than private prejudice alone.
cp-adickes.plain: On the discrimination "count" (a separate claim in the complaint), Harlan read the "statutory" phrase "custom or usage" to require a practice with the "force of law", created by persistent conduct of officials. Private prejudice alone was not enough.

cp-adickes.sentence: Enforcement need not rely only on trespass law: false vagrancy arrests punishing interracial dining or police tolerance of violence against challengers could show official compulsion.
cp-adickes.plain: Enforcement did not have to come only through "trespass" law (the law against staying on property after being told to leave). False vagrancy arrests punishing people for dining together across races, or police tolerating violence against those who challenged segregation, could also show that officials compelled the custom.

cp-adickes.sentence: He separated state action required by the underlying equal-protection right from the statutory color-of-authority element, joining the conspiracy discussion with a qualification about statutory wording.
cp-adickes.plain: Brennan separated two requirements: "state action", the government involvement the "equal-protection" right itself requires, and the statute's separate "element" (required part of the claim) that the defendant acted under color of state authority. He joined the discussion of the "conspiracy" claim, with a reservation about the statute's wording.

cp-dice.sentence: The judge entered judgment notwithstanding the verdict, reassessed the fraud proof, characterized not reading as negligence, and found the evidence inadequate under a clear-and-convincing formulation.
cp-dice.plain: The judge "entered judgment" notwithstanding the verdict, overriding the jury, and reassessed the fraud proof himself. He called Dice's failure to read the paper "negligence" (carelessness) and found the "evidence" inadequate under a "clear-and-convincing" standard, a higher bar than ordinary proof.

cp-dice.sentence: It applied Ohio law, bound a literate signer despite the alleged deception and assigned the pertinent fraud issues to a judge under state practice.
cp-dice.plain: The Ohio Supreme Court said that under Ohio law, a person who can read is bound by what he signs even if he was allegedly tricked, and that a judge, not a jury, decides this kind of fraud question.

cp-dice.sentence: The federal rule invalidated a release when authorized representatives induced the signature through deliberately false, material statements intended to deceive the employee about its contents.
cp-dice.plain: The "federal rule" made a release invalid when the railroad's authorized agents "induced" (brought about) the worker's signature through deliberate, material lies meant to deceive him about what the paper said.

cp-dice.sentence: The jury had heard conflicting evidence and found for Dice; calling the allocation local procedure did not immunize its effect on the federal remedy.
cp-dice.plain: The jury had heard conflicting "evidence" and found for Dice. Calling Ohio's division of work between judge and jury "local procedure" did not shield it, because it still affected the federal "remedy", the worker's right to recover under federal law.

cp-dice.sentence: The majority did not decide a challenge to the jury’s clear-and-convincing instruction: Dice won and did not object to it as overly demanding.
cp-dice.plain: The majority did not decide a challenge to the jury's "clear-and-convincing" instruction, which told jurors to require especially strong proof of fraud. Dice had won anyway and did not "object to" it as too demanding.

cp-hall.sentence: After a disagreement over Samuel’s management of her real estate, Ethlyn created an inter vivos trust, transferred her property into it, and named her daughter Elsa as successor trustee.
cp-hall.plain: After a disagreement over Samuel's management of her real estate, Ethlyn created an "inter vivos trust" (a trust set up during her lifetime), moved her property into it, and named her daughter Elsa as "successor trustee", the person who would take over managing the trust after her.

cp-hall.sentence: On Samuel’s motion, the district court consolidated them under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 42(a) and directed that filings go on the trust case’s docket.
cp-hall.plain: On Samuel's "motion" (formal request), the district court "consolidated" the two cases, combining them for joint handling under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 42(a). It directed that all filings go on the trust case's "docket", that case's official court record.

cp-hall.sentence: Samuel and his firm argued that consolidation had effectively created one case, so no final decision existed while the individual case remained unresolved.
cp-hall.plain: Samuel argued that combining the cases made them one, so Elsa could not appeal until both were finished.

cp-hall.sentence: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, courts of appeals review final district-court decisions—decisions ending the merits litigation and leaving only execution of judgment.
cp-hall.plain: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, federal courts of appeals review "final" district-court decisions (decisions of the federal trial courts). A final decision is one that ends the litigation on "the merits" (the actual claims) and leaves only "execution" of the judgment, meaning enforcing it.

cp-hall.sentence: It held that, at least when one constituent action is finally resolved, the losing party can appeal that decision immediately even if another consolidated case remains pending.
cp-hall.plain: The Court held that, at least when one of the combined cases is fully resolved, the losing "party" can appeal that decision right away, even if another consolidated case is still pending.

cp-poller.sentence: The district court granted summary judgment because CBS could buy WOKY with regulatory approval and exercise its cancellation right; economic injury from those steps did not establish illegality.
cp-poller.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) granted summary judgment, ending the case without trial, because CBS could lawfully buy WOKY with "regulatory" (government agency) approval and use its right to cancel the affiliation. Economic harm to Poller from those steps did not show "illegality".

cp-poller.sentence: Poller answered that independently lawful acts could implement an unlawful scheme, citing relationships, transaction circumstances, CBS market studies and the destruction of WCAN.
cp-poller.plain: Poller answered that acts lawful on their own can still be steps carrying out an unlawful scheme. He pointed to the parties' relationships, the circumstances of the deals, CBS market studies, and the destruction of WCAN.

cp-poller.sentence: The Supreme Court reviewed whether the record left a genuine material dispute under then-Rule 56(c), rather than trying the antitrust claims or fixing damages and market definition.
cp-poller.plain: The Supreme Court reviewed only whether the record left a "genuine material dispute", a real disagreement over important facts that needs a trial, under the Rule 56(c) then in force. It did not try the "antitrust" (competition-law) claims itself or fix "damages" (money owed) or how to define the market.

cp-poller.sentence: The majority thought independent participation could be found, leaving unnecessary the separate claim that a corporation could not conspire with its own division or subsidiary.
cp-poller.plain: The majority thought a jury could find that Holt took part as an independent player, not just as CBS's agent. That made it unnecessary to decide the separate claim that a "corporation" cannot conspire with its own division or subsidiary.

cp-poller.sentence: That evidentiary setting supported caution with summary judgment in complex antitrust disputes: intent mattered, much proof lay with alleged participants and credibility could be important.
cp-poller.plain: That kind of evidence called for caution with "summary judgment" (ending a case without trial) in complex antitrust disputes. Intent mattered, much of the proof was in the hands of the alleged participants, and whether witnesses were believable could be important.

cp-ragan.sentence: He sought damages from Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Company and, invoking diversity jurisdiction, filed in the federal District Court in Kansas on September 4, 1945.
cp-ragan.plain: He sought "damages" (money compensation) from Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Company, filing in the federal District Court in Kansas on September 4, 1945. He relied on "diversity jurisdiction", which lets federal courts hear state-law claims between citizens of different states.

cp-ragan.sentence: After examining Kansas decisions, it concluded that timely service was integral to the state limitations scheme and that the district court should have granted summary judgment.
cp-ragan.plain: After examining Kansas decisions, the appeals court concluded that "timely" service on the defendant was an essential part of the state's deadline rule for suing. So the district court should have granted summary judgment for the defendant, deciding the case without trial.

cp-ragan.sentence: The Supreme Court heard argument on April 20, 1949, about whether timely filing under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 3 nevertheless preserved this state-created claim.
cp-ragan.plain: The Supreme Court heard argument on April 20, 1949, on whether "timely" filing of the complaint, which starts a federal lawsuit under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 3, still preserved this state-created "claim" even though service came after the state deadline.

cp-ragan.sentence: Erie and Guaranty Trust Co. v. York were the earlier decisions requiring federal diversity courts to respect state-created substantive rights and their limitations.
cp-ragan.plain: Erie and Guaranty Trust Co. v. York were the earlier decisions holding that federal "diversity courts", which hear state-law cases between citizens of different states, must respect "substantive rights" created by state law, including the state's deadlines for suing.

cp-ragan.sentence: He accepted Erie as a sound administrative principle for substantive state law but questioned its constitutional foundation and resisted extending it to every circumstance in which state courts would close their doors.
cp-ragan.plain: Rutledge accepted Erie as a sound working principle for applying "substantive" state law (the law of the rights themselves), but doubted that the Constitution required it. He also resisted extending Erie to every situation in which a state court would refuse to hear a claim.

cp-stewart.sentence: A divided Eleventh Circuit panel reversed and instructed transfer; the en banc court largely adopted its approach, treating venue as federal procedure and borrowing The Bremen’s forum-clause standards from admiralty.
cp-stewart.plain: A divided Eleventh Circuit panel reversed and ordered the case transferred; the "en banc" court (all the circuit's judges) largely adopted that approach. It treated venue, the choice of where a case is heard, as federal procedure and borrowed the strong pro-enforcement standard for forum clauses from The Bremen, an "admiralty" (maritime-law) case.

cp-stewart.sentence: Congress’s constitutional authority was straightforward: transfers among federal district courts concern judicial administration under Article III and the Necessary and Proper Clause, consistent with Hanna’s account of federal practice authority.
cp-stewart.plain: Congress plainly had constitutional power here: moving cases among federal district courts is part of running the courts, which Article III and the Necessary and Proper Clause let Congress regulate. That fit Hanna's account of Congress's power over federal court practice.

cp-stewart.sentence: The complaint’s federal antitrust theory also did not supply the holding; the Court reserved whether mixed federal-question and diversity jurisdiction independently changed the analysis because § 1404(a) sufficed.
cp-stewart.plain: The "complaint" (the initial filing) also raised a federal antitrust claim, but that did not drive the holding. The Court "reserved" (left open) whether having both "federal-question" jurisdiction and diversity jurisdiction changed the analysis, because § 1404(a), the transfer statute, settled the case.

cp-stewart.sentence: Justice Scalia agreed that statutory scope came first but distinguished antecedent contract validity from a valid agreement’s weight.
cp-stewart.plain: Justice Scalia agreed that the statute's scope was the first question, but he separated the "antecedent" question, whether the contract clause was valid at all, from how much weight a valid clause gets. He read the transfer statute as covering only the second.

cp-stewart.sentence: Different state and federal treatment would strongly encourage filing and removal choices and materially change litigation opportunities based on diversity.
cp-stewart.plain: Treating forum clauses differently in state and federal courts would strongly encourage strategic choices about where to file and whether to remove a case to federal court. It would materially change parties' litigation chances based only on "diversity" (the parties being from different states), which Erie tries to prevent.

lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.sentence: The deadline was not an inflexible jurisdictional rule: good cause could excuse delay when a litigant reasonably thought its first evidence sufficient or standing apparent.
lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.plain: The deadline was not an inflexible "jurisdictional" rule that a court can never bend. Good cause could "excuse" a delay, for example when a "litigant" (party to the case) reasonably thought its first evidence was enough or its standing was obvious, but no such reason applied here.

lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.sentence: Lost time posed a closer question, but the organization identified no pertinent statutory protection against making the call or traditional analogue supporting this theory.
lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.plain: Lost time, such as time spent calling to ask for paper copies, was a closer question. But the organization pointed to no relevant "statutory" protection (a law) against having to make the call, and no traditional kind of harm recognized by courts that resembled it.

lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.sentence: Each securities statute allowed review of certain SEC orders, but “order” included rules under the Securities Act and Investment Company Act, not the Exchange Act.
lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.plain: Each securities statute let challengers seek review of certain SEC "orders" directly in an appeals court. But "order" included rules issued under the Securities Act and the Investment Company Act, not rules under the Exchange Act.

lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.sentence: Occasional agreement with a paper-preferring investor did not establish systematic alignment, and the potential conflict could grow with internet use.
lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.plain: Paper companies want more paper whatever investors want. Agreeing now and then with investors who prefer paper did not make their interests line up with the investors the law protects, and the gap could grow as more people go online.

lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.sentence: Consumer Action had not timely established an Article III basis through evidence of member injury; the paper-industry petitioners’ interests were outside those arguably protected or regulated by the securities laws.
lrs-n-standing-twin-rivers.plain: Consumer Action had not "timely" (in time) shown an Article III basis for standing through "evidence" that a member was injured. The paper-industry petitioners' interests (the companies bringing the challenge) were outside those arguably protected or "regulated" by the securities laws, so neither could challenge the rule.

lrs-o-church-christ.sentence: During an earlier renewal cycle, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) deferred action and found Fairness Doctrine failures but ultimately renewed the license because it viewed the failures as isolated.
lrs-o-church-christ.plain: During an earlier renewal round, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) put off acting and found the station had broken the Fairness Doctrine, the rule requiring balanced coverage of controversial issues. But it ultimately renewed the license because it saw the failures as isolated.

lrs-o-church-christ.sentence: After reviewing the station’s responses, it acknowledged serious public-interest concerns and called the hearing issue close, but granted one year beginning June 1, 1965, rather than the customary three.
lrs-o-church-christ.plain: After reviewing the station's responses, the FCC acknowledged serious "public-interest" concerns (doubts about whether the station served the public) and called the need for a hearing a close question. But it renewed the license without a hearing for one year beginning June 1, 1965, rather than the usual three.

lrs-o-church-christ.sentence: A broadcaster received free exclusive access to a limited public resource with enforceable public obligations, whatever differences separated broadcasting from utilities and newspapers.
lrs-o-church-christ.plain: A broadcaster gets free, exclusive use of a limited public resource, the airwaves, and in return takes on public obligations that are "enforceable" (legally binding). That is true whatever differences separate broadcasting from utilities and newspapers.

lrs-o-church-christ.sentence: It could limit numbers, assess usefulness in relation to other participants and issues, consolidate submissions, and screen captious, obstructive, or disguised private-interest protests.
lrs-o-church-christ.plain: The FCC could limit how many people join, combine their filings, and keep out petty, obstructive, or secretly self-interested objectors.

lrs-o-church-christ.sentence: Section 309(e) required a hearing when a substantial and material factual question existed or the Commission was unable for any reason to make the necessary public-interest finding.
lrs-o-church-christ.plain: Section 309(e) required the Commission to hold a full hearing when there was a substantial "material factual question", an important fact in real dispute. It also required one if the Commission could not, for any reason, make the necessary "public-interest finding", a conclusion that renewal would serve the public.

lrs-s-humphrey.sentence: The FTC investigated unfair competition, held notice-and-hearing proceedings, made findings, and issued cease-and-desist orders subject to judicial enforcement and review.
lrs-s-humphrey.plain: The FTC investigated unfair competition and held "notice-and-hearing" proceedings, giving companies warning and a chance to be heard. It made "findings" (conclusions of fact) and issued "cease-and-desist orders", commands to stop a practice, which courts could enforce and review.

lrs-s-humphrey.sentence: The Supreme Court would characterize those statutory responsibilities as predominantly quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial; that characterization belonged to the particular Commission analyzed in 1935.
lrs-s-humphrey.plain: The Supreme Court would describe those "statutory" duties as mostly "quasi-legislative" and quasi-judicial, meaning like lawmaking and judging rather than purely carrying out the law. That description belonged to the particular Commission it examined in 1935.

lrs-s-humphrey.sentence: Treating those grounds as exclusive there could effectively confer life tenure absent specified cause; that unusual consequence required clearer legislative direction.
lrs-s-humphrey.plain: In Shurtleff, the official had no fixed term, so treating the listed firing grounds as the only ones allowed could have given him "life tenure" unless one of the specified grounds ("cause") was shown. Such an unusual result needed clearer direction from Congress.

lrs-s-humphrey.sentence: At-will removal would undermine the practical assurance: an officer dependent on another’s pleasure would tend to follow that person’s wishes even without formal commands.
lrs-s-humphrey.plain: "At-will removal", letting the President fire a commissioner for any reason, would undermine the practical guarantee of independence. An officer who keeps his job only at another's pleasure tends to follow that person's wishes even without formal orders.

lrs-s-humphrey.sentence: Congress could provide an agency exercising independent judgment to implement legislative policy and assist judicial functions, with tenure protection incident to that design.
lrs-s-humphrey.plain: Congress could create an agency that uses independent judgment to carry out legislative policy and to assist judicial functions. "Tenure protection", limiting when its members can be fired, is part of that design.

lrs-s-morrison.sentence: The Division concluded it could not override his final refusal to request separate investigations, but read the original grant to permit investigation of whether Olson conspired with others, including those officials, to obstruct the Committee.
lrs-s-morrison.plain: The Division, the special court of judges, concluded it could not override the Attorney General's final refusal to request separate investigations of the other officials. But it read Morrison's original grant to allow investigating whether Olson "conspired" (agreed and worked) with others, including those officials, to "obstruct" (block) the Committee's inquiry.

lrs-s-morrison.sentence: The divided D.C. Circuit reversed: it considered counsel a principal officer, judicial appointment improper, the Division’s duties incompatible with Article III, and executive control impermissibly impaired.
lrs-s-morrison.plain: The divided D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court in Washington, reversed: it held the counsel was a "principal officer" whom judges could not appoint, the Division's duties were incompatible with Article III (the Constitution's limits on federal courts), and the President's control over law enforcement was impermissibly weakened.

lrs-s-morrison.sentence: The Appointments Clause generally required presidential nomination and Senate consent for principal officers but allowed Congress to vest inferior-officer appointments in the President alone, department heads, or courts of law.
lrs-s-morrison.plain: The Appointments Clause generally requires "principal officers" (top officials) to be nominated by the President and confirmed with Senate consent. But it allows Congress to give the appointment of "inferior-officer" positions (lower-level officials) to the President alone, department heads, or courts of law.

lrs-s-morrison.sentence: The more troubling termination power was construed narrowly: the Division could end an office whose work was truly complete or substantially complete, not remove counsel during an ongoing investigation or proceeding.
lrs-s-morrison.plain: The more troubling termination power was "construed" (interpreted) narrowly. The Division could end an office whose work was truly or substantially complete, but could not use that power to remove counsel during an ongoing investigation or proceeding.

lrs-s-morrison.sentence: He accepted good-cause protection for inferior officers supervised by principal officers enjoying the President’s confidence, at least where the President or a principal executive official appointed them; refusal of supervision would constitute cause.
lrs-s-morrison.plain: Scalia accepted "good-cause protection" (a ban on firing without a good reason) for inferior officers supervised by "principal officers" who have the President's confidence, at least where the President or a top executive official appointed them. In that setting, refusing supervision would itself count as cause to fire.

mattei.sentence: The trial court understood the satisfaction provision as leaving Mattei free to choose whether to buy without a legally enforceable restriction.
mattei.plain: The trial court read the "satisfaction provision", the clause conditioning the deal on Mattei being satisfied with the leases, as leaving Mattei free to decide whether to buy, with no legally "enforceable" limit. On that view he had not really promised anything.

mattei.sentence: The satisfaction clause made Mattei’s duty to complete the purchase conditional and gave him a contractual power to terminate if satisfactory leases could not be obtained.
mattei.plain: The satisfaction clause made Mattei's "duty" to complete the purchase "conditional": he had to buy only if satisfactory leases were obtained. It also gave him a "contractual" power, one created by the contract itself, to end the deal if such leases could not be obtained.

mattei.sentence: Matters such as commercial value, quality, operative fitness, or mechanical utility ordinarily permit an objective reasonable-person standard.
mattei.plain: For things like commercial value or whether a machine works properly, courts ask whether a reasonable person would be satisfied.

mattei.sentence: Matters of taste, fancy, or judgment instead turn on the particular person’s actual satisfaction, constrained by honesty and good faith.
mattei.plain: Matters of taste, fancy, or judgment instead turn on whether this particular person was actually satisfied. That judgment is limited only by honesty and "good faith", meaning a genuine, not pretended, dissatisfaction.

mattei.sentence: The later Restatement (Second) § 79 expresses the related point that, once consideration exists, mutuality adds no separate requirement.
mattei.plain: The later Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 79 states the related point: once a deal has consideration (something given in exchange), "mutuality" adds no separate requirement that both sides be equally bound.

speakers-sport.sentence: Speakers sued ProServ in federal court under diversity jurisdiction, asserting tortious interference and related violations of Illinois law.
speakers-sport.plain: Speakers sued ProServ in federal court under "diversity jurisdiction", which lets federal courts hear state-law claims between parties from different states. It claimed "tortious interference" (wrongfully luring away its client) and related violations of Illinois law.

speakers-sport.sentence: The Seventh Circuit construed the pitch as aspirational puffery: ProServ would try to obtain endorsements and was optimistic about the result.
speakers-sport.plain: The Seventh Circuit read ProServ's pitch as aspirational "puffery", the kind of sales hype no one takes literally. ProServ was saying it would try to get endorsements and was optimistic about the result, not guaranteeing it.

speakers-sport.sentence: Independently, Illinois promissory-fraud doctrine required a fraudulent scheme supported by more than the allegedly false promise itself.
speakers-sport.plain: Separately, Illinois "promissory-fraud" doctrine (fraud based on a broken promise about the future) required a "fraudulent scheme", a larger plan to cheat. Proof of more than the allegedly false promise itself was needed, and Speakers showed none.

speakers-sport.sentence: Even if it supplied an enforceable norm, Speakers was outside the protected interest, and violating it was not itself a violation of law establishing wrongful interference.
speakers-sport.plain: Even if baseball's rule against agents' lies created an "enforceable" standard, it protected players, not rival agents like Speakers. And breaking it was not itself a violation of law that would make the interference wrongful.

speakers-sport.sentence: As a nonconsumer competitor, it had to show by clear and convincing evidence that the conduct implicated consumer-protection concerns, but made no effort to do so.
speakers-sport.plain: As a competitor rather than a consumer, Speakers had to show by "clear and convincing evidence" (proof well beyond more-likely-than-not) that ProServ's conduct raised consumer-protection concerns. It made no effort to do so.

stoll.sentence: The buyers pleaded unconscionability, fraud, merger into a deed omitting the term, statutory impossibility, trespass, and shed damage, requesting reformation or invalidation.
stoll.plain: The buyers "pleaded" (formally raised) many defenses: the clause was unconscionable (grossly unfair), they were defrauded, the term ended by "merger into a deed" because the deed left it out, statutory impossibility (a law made it impossible), trespass, and damage to their shed. They asked for "reformation" (rewriting the clause) or for it to be declared invalid.

stoll.sentence: The trial court held the paragraph unconscionable, granted the buyers’ motion, denied his, and entered judgment against his petition.
stoll.plain: The trial court held the poultry-litter paragraph "unconscionable", so unfair it could not be enforced. It granted the buyers' "motion" for judgment without trial, denied Stoll's, and "entered judgment" against his "petition", the lawsuit he had filed.

stoll.sentence: On de novo review, with reasonable inferences favoring Stoll, Judge Hetherington rejected his contention that only fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake, or illegality could defeat enforcement.
stoll.plain: Reviewing "de novo" (taking a fresh look without deferring to the trial court) and drawing all "reasonable inferences" in Stoll's favor, Judge Hetherington rejected his argument that only fraud, duress (threats), undue influence (improper pressure), mistake, or illegality could block enforcement of a signed contract.

stoll.sentence: Oklahoma unconscionability doctrine examined the commercial setting at formation, meaningful choice, and terms so one-sided as to oppress or unfairly surprise.
stoll.plain: Oklahoma's "unconscionability" doctrine looks at the commercial setting at "formation" (when the contract was made), whether the weaker side had a meaningful choice, and whether the terms are so one-sided as to "oppress or unfairly surprise" that side.

stoll.sentence: The court applied the principle of Uniform Commercial Code § 2-302 by analogy to land, consistently with Restatement § 208.
stoll.plain: Uniform Commercial Code § 2-302, the rule against unconscionable terms, covers sales of goods, but the court applied its principle by analogy to this land sale. That was consistent with Restatement § 208, the matching general contract rule.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Fox sued for a declaration that its clearances were reasonable and lawful and to stop Beacon from bringing antitrust litigation while the declaratory case was pending.
brief-CP-109.plain: Fox sued for a "declaration" that its "clearances" (agreements giving a theater exclusive first-run showing for a set time and area) were reasonable and lawful. It also sought to stop Beacon from bringing an antitrust suit while the "declaratory" case, one asking the court only to declare rights, was pending.

brief-CP-109.sentence: District Judge Harry C. Westover directed that Fox’s supposedly equitable case go first to the court, followed by the counterclaim and cross-claim, invoking Rules 42(b) and 57.
brief-CP-109.plain: District Judge Harry C. Westover ordered that Fox's supposedly "equitable" claims (the kind a judge decides) be tried to the court first, followed by Beacon's "counterclaim" against Fox and cross-claim. He relied on Rules 42(b), which allows separate trials, and 57, on declaratory judgments.

brief-CP-109.sentence: That court denied relief because it viewed the declaratory and injunctive claims as equitable and sequence as discretionary.
brief-CP-109.plain: The Ninth Circuit denied "relief" (refused to order the judge to change course), because it saw the "declaratory" and injunctive claims as equitable and the order of trial as "discretionary", meaning up to the trial judge.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Westover appeared as the writ respondent because his proposed procedure was at issue, not because he participated in the theaters’ commercial dispute.
brief-CP-109.plain: Westover was named as the respondent in the "writ" (mandamus) proceeding, the party answering the request for an order, only because his trial plan was being challenged. He had no part in the theaters' business dispute.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Justice Black, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justices Douglas, Clark, and Brennan, treated antitrust treble damages as a legal claim carrying a jury right.
brief-CP-109.plain: Justice Black, "joined by" (writing with the agreement of) Chief Justice Warren and Justices Douglas, Clark, and Brennan, treated Beacon's claim for antitrust treble (triple) damages as a legal claim, the kind that carries a constitutional right to a jury.

brief-CP-109.sentence: A declaration of nonliability anticipated that legal controversy; the Declaratory Judgment Act did not eliminate the jury merely because the opposing party filed first.
brief-CP-109.plain: Fox's request for a declaration that it was not liable was just the mirror image of that legal dispute over damages. The Declaratory Judgment Act did not take away the jury merely because the "opposing party", Fox, filed first.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Even assuming genuine equitable protection of Fox’s business relationships, the court had to ask whether equity required priority and whether modern legal procedures were adequate.
brief-CP-109.plain: Even assuming Fox had a genuine "equitable" claim, one a judge decides, to protect its business relationships, the court had to ask two things. Did equity truly require deciding it first, and were modern legal (jury-trial) procedures adequate?

brief-CP-109.sentence: A nominal later jury opportunity was insufficient if binding judicial findings had already disposed of common facts.
brief-CP-109.plain: A jury trial offered later was meaningless if the judge's binding "findings" (rulings on the facts) had already decided the facts the two sides' claims shared.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Only the most imperative circumstances could justify losing jury consideration through an earlier equitable adjudication, and the Court anticipated none here.
brief-CP-109.plain: Only extremely compelling circumstances could justify letting a judge's earlier equitable ruling take issues away from the jury, and the Court expected none here.

brief-CP-109.sentence: The All Writs Act permitted mandamus to protect the improperly denied right; this was more than appellate preference about convenient proof order.
brief-CP-109.plain: The All Writs Act allowed mandamus, an order directing the judge to act, to protect the jury right he had wrongly denied. This was more than an "appellate" court (an appeals court) preferring a different, more convenient order of proof.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Fox’s complaint, liberally understood, invoked equitable protection of existing business and contract relations, not merely a reversed damages suit.
brief-CP-109.plain: Read generously, Fox's complaint asked for a court order protecting its existing business and contracts, which is an equitable claim, not just Beacon's damages suit turned backward.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Procedural merger could not enlarge the historical jury right, and Stewart saw no abuse warranting an extraordinary writ.
brief-CP-109.plain: "Procedural merger", combining law and equity into a single court system, could not expand the jury right beyond its historical scope. Stewart saw no abuse of discretion serious enough to justify an extraordinary writ such as mandamus.

brief-CP-109.sentence: Beacon’s common legal issues could not be preempted by the proposed court-first trial, but no damages or clearance-legality judgment followed.
brief-CP-109.plain: The proposed judge-first trial could not decide Beacon's shared legal issues ahead of the jury. But the ruling produced no "judgment" (final decision) on damages or on whether the clearances were legal.

brief-CP-111.sentence: The first grievance proceeding directed McLean to recall affected transferred drivers, lay off certain recalled inactive drivers, and preserve the special rights until the inactive drivers were properly recalled.
brief-CP-111.plain: The first "grievance" proceeding, the union contract's complaint process, ordered McLean to recall the affected transferred drivers and lay off certain recalled inactive drivers. It also ordered McLean to keep the transferred drivers' special seniority rights until the inactive drivers were properly recalled.

brief-CP-111.sentence: In July 1983, they sued McLean for breach of the collective bargaining agreement under §301 of the Labor Management Relations Act and Local 391 for breach of its fair-representation duty.
brief-CP-111.plain: In July 1983, the drivers sued McLean for "breach" (breaking) of the "collective bargaining agreement", the union contract, under §301 of the Labor Management Relations Act. They sued Local 391 for breaching its "fair-representation duty", a union's legal duty to represent its members fairly.

brief-CP-111.sentence: A union’s exclusive authority over bargaining representation carried a duty to act honestly, in good faith, and without hostility, discrimination, or arbitrary conduct.
brief-CP-111.plain: Because a union has exclusive authority to bargain for the workers it represents, it has a "duty" to act honestly and in good faith, without hostility, discrimination, or arbitrary treatment.

brief-CP-111.sentence: Marshall first rejected the union’s analogy to an equitable action setting aside an arbitration award.
brief-CP-111.plain: Marshall first rejected the union's comparison to an "equitable action" (a suit decided by a judge) to set aside an arbitration award.

brief-CP-111.sentence: The trust analogy was more persuasive to the four Justices joining this part.
brief-CP-111.plain: Four Justices found the comparison to a trustee more convincing; a suit against a trustee for breach of duty was historically an equity case, decided without a jury.

brief-CP-111.sentence: Marshall therefore found the historical inquiry inconclusive for this combined representation-and-contract dispute, rather than treating the trust analogy as decisive for everything.
brief-CP-111.plain: So the historical comparison pointed both ways for this mixed claim, and Marshall did not let the trust analogy decide everything.

brief-CP-111.sentence: The request therefore lacked the restitutionary character of recovering money wrongfully held by the defendant.
