brief-CP-111.plain: The drivers' request therefore lacked the "restitutionary" character of a claim for "recovering" money the defendant wrongfully held, which equity could order. They sought compensation for their losses, which is ordinary legal damages.

brief-CP-111.sentence: Calling the relationship trust-like could not automatically make every monetary remedy equitable, because that would collapse the separate remedial inquiry into the historical analogy despite the greater weight given to remedy.
brief-CP-111.plain: Calling the union like a trustee could not automatically make every money award equitable; otherwise the remedy test, which is supposed to count more, would be swallowed by the historical comparison.

brief-CP-111.sentence: Local 391 invoked the equitable treatment of Title VII backpay and its relationship to National Labor Relations Act remedies.
brief-CP-111.plain: Local 391 pointed to how back pay under Title VII, the federal job-discrimination law, is treated as "equitable" (decided by a judge). It also pointed to that remedy's link to remedies under the National Labor Relations Act.

brief-CP-111.sentence: Congress expressly described Title VII relief in equitable terms; no comparable designation governed this fair-representation remedy.
brief-CP-111.plain: Congress expressly described Title VII relief in equitable terms. No similar label applied to this "fair-representation" remedy, the claim against a union for failing to represent its members fairly.

brief-CP-111.sentence: The Court assumed without deciding the absence of a jury right for Title VII backpay in that context.
brief-CP-111.plain: The Court "assumed without deciding" that there is no jury right for Title VII back pay in that setting, meaning it accepted the point for argument's sake without ruling on it.

brief-CP-111.sentence: These damages were legal, supporting a jury on all issues in the remaining suit.
brief-CP-111.plain: The damages sought were "legal" (the jury kind), so the drivers got a jury on every issue left in the case.

brief-CP-111.sentence: The six-Justice remedial holding supported the result without making the four-Justice trust comparison a unanimous or majority characterization of the entire claim.
brief-CP-111.plain: Six Justices agreed on the remedy analysis, which supported the result. Only four agreed on comparing the "claim" to a trust lawsuit, so that comparison was neither a "unanimous" nor a majority description of the whole claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: The district court found years of bad faith by Goodyear and its lawyers aimed at frustrating a merits resolution.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) found years of "bad faith", deliberate dishonest conduct, by Goodyear and its lawyers, aimed at preventing a "merits resolution", a decision of the case on its actual facts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: Settlement prevented the default judgment the trial judge otherwise wanted, so the court used its inherent authority to award litigation fees and costs.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: The case settled, which prevented the "default judgment" (a ruling against Goodyear as punishment) the trial judge otherwise wanted. So the court used its "inherent authority", the built-in power every court has, to award "litigation fees" and costs to the Haegers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: The district court awarded approximately $2.7 million, covering all fees and costs from Goodyear’s first dishonest discovery response forward.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: The district court ordered Goodyear to pay about $2.7 million, covering all the Haegers' "fees and costs" from Goodyear's first dishonest discovery response (its answer to a request for evidence) onward.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: Judge Watford dissented: simultaneous timing was not causation, and Goodyear retained plausible defenses even with full disclosure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: Judge Watford dissented: costs arising at the same time as misconduct did not prove "causation", that the misconduct caused them. Goodyear still had plausible "defenses" even if it had fully disclosed the evidence.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: The Supreme Court considered whether an inherent-power fee sanction imposed through civil procedures could exceed the expenses caused by misconduct.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: The Supreme Court considered whether an "inherent-power" fee sanction, a penalty using a court's built-in power and imposed through ordinary civil procedures, could exceed the expenses the misconduct actually caused.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: Federal courts possess inherent power to manage litigation and sanction bad-faith abuse, including reimbursement of an opponent’s legal expenses.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: Federal courts have "inherent power", built-in authority, to manage their cases and to "sanction" (penalize) bad-faith abuse. That includes ordering a party to repay the opponent's "legal expenses".

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: Through ordinary civil procedures, however, that award must compensate rather than punish.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: But in a civil case such an award may only make up for losses; it may not punish.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: Drawing on Fox v. Vice, an earlier fee-allocation decision, the Court required expenses that the innocent party would not have incurred but for the misconduct.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: Drawing on Fox v. Vice, an earlier fee-allocation decision, the Court allowed only expenses the innocent "party" would not have had "but for" the misconduct, meaning without it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: A judge familiar with the litigation could estimate time, allocate percentages, or attribute an entire expenditure category to misconduct, with substantial appellate deference.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: A judge familiar with the case could estimate time, assign percentages, or attribute a whole category of spending to the misconduct, rather than tallying every hour. "Appellate" courts (appeals courts) give that estimate substantial deference, meaning they rarely second-guess it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: The district court expressly substituted severity for causation, and the Ninth Circuit used the period of bad faith as its boundary.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) openly replaced "causation", what the misconduct actually caused, with how severe the misconduct was. The Ninth Circuit simply counted everything spent during the period of bad faith.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: But the Haegers argued that Goodyear waived further challenge by submitting that only about $700,000 would have been incurred regardless of misconduct.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: But the Haegers argued that Goodyear had "waived" (given up) any further challenge to the backup award by stating that only about $700,000 would have been spent even without its misconduct.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: If waiver existed, the contingent award could end the dispute; otherwise, the district court had to reassess fees under but-for causation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: If there was a "waiver", the "contingent" award (a backup award meant to apply only in certain conditions) could end the dispute. If not, the district court had to recalculate fees using "but-for causation", counting only costs that would not have arisen without the misconduct.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.sentence: Nor did this ruling establish that settlement invariably disables Rule 37 sanctions: the opinion explained settlement’s effect on default judgment and recounted the district court’s view that Rule 11 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927 did not reach all the misconduct.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385.plain: Nor did this "ruling" hold that settling always rules out discovery sanctions under Rule 37. The "opinion" only explained why settlement made a default judgment impossible and reported the district court's view that Rule 11 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927, other sanction rules, did not reach all the misconduct.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: The Federal Advisory Committee Act imposed public-meeting and disclosure obligations on covered groups but excluded committees composed entirely of qualifying federal personnel.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: The Federal Advisory Committee Act required covered advisory groups to hold public meetings and disclose records. But it excluded committees made up entirely of qualifying federal officials, so the case turned on whether outsiders were in effect members.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: The organizations sought discovery of actual participation; the government disputed coverage and argued that investigating presidential consultation itself burdened protected deliberation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: The organizations sought "discovery" (pretrial gathering of evidence) of who actually took part. The government disputed that the law applied and argued that merely investigating whom the President consulted burdened protected confidential policy discussions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: It nevertheless allowed claims against executive officials under the federal mandamus statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1361, and against agencies under the Administrative Procedure Act.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: But the court let "claims" go forward against executive officials under the federal "mandamus statute", 28 U.S.C. § 1361, which lets courts order officials to perform a clear duty. It also let claims go forward against agencies under the Administrative Procedure Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: It deferred whether a clear nondiscretionary duty supported mandamus, whether requisite agency action existed, and constitutional objections, expecting discovery to develop membership facts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: The court put off deciding whether there was a clear "nondiscretionary" duty (one the officials had no choice about) that could support "mandamus", whether there was the required agency action, and the constitutional objections. It expected discovery to bring out the facts about who the members were.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: It then filed an appeal and an All Writs Act § 1651 mandamus petition, seeking vacation of discovery, decision on administrative materials and suitable affidavits, and dismissal of Cheney.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: The government then appealed and also filed a mandamus petition under the All Writs Act, § 1651, asking the appeals court to order the judge to act. It sought "vacation of discovery" (canceling the discovery orders), a decision based on the official records and suitable "affidavits" (sworn statements), and dismissal of Cheney from the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: Appellate Rule 4(a) governed notices of appeal, not All Writs petitions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: Appellate Rule 4(a), the deadline rule for notices of ordinary appeals, did not govern petitions under the All Writs Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: Laches did not apply because the government actively sought less drastic remedies; doing so was consistent with mandamus’s demand for inadequate alternatives.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: "Laches", the doctrine that bars relief after unreasonable delay, did not apply because the government had actively tried milder remedies first. Doing so fit mandamus's own requirement that other remedies be inadequate.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: A petitioner still needed no adequate other remedy, a clear and indisputable entitlement, and a showing that issuance was appropriate even if the first two conditions were met.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: A "petitioner" (the party asking for the writ) still had to show three things: no other adequate "remedy", a clear and indisputable right to relief, and that issuing the writ was appropriate even if the first two were met.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: Nixon did not require privilege invocation before every separation-of-powers objection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: Nixon did not require the executive to formally invoke privilege before raising every "separation-of-powers" objection, the argument that a court is intruding on another branch's role.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: Justice Stevens joined remand because the D.C. Circuit originated de facto membership doctrine and should direct next steps, though he thought the discovery order should be vacated.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: Justice Stevens "joined" the decision to send the case back because the D.C. Circuit had created the "de facto membership" theory (outsiders as members in practice) and should direct the next steps. But he thought the discovery order should be "vacated" (canceled).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: Plaintiffs seeking § 1361 mandamus nevertheless needed sweeping discovery to establish entitlement, undermining the clear-right requirement and risking a freestanding enforcement vehicle for statutes lacking private remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: Plaintiffs seeking § 1361 mandamus still needed sweeping discovery just to prove their right, which undercut the "clear-right requirement" that the right be obvious. It also risked turning mandamus into a stand-alone way to enforce statutes that give private people no "remedies" of their own.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: She agreed discovery was overbroad but thought the government sought wholesale protection rather than meaningful narrowing invited below, leaving an adequate alternative.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: Ginsburg agreed the discovery was overbroad. But she thought the government had sought total protection instead of the meaningful narrowing the court "below" (the trial court) had invited, which left it an adequate alternative remedy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.sentence: The appellate court had ended its inquiry prematurely under a mistaken Nixon reading and now had to consider separation-of-powers and other arguments, including unwarranted impairment of executive duties, before deciding whether to issue mandamus.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-508.plain: The "appellate court" (the D.C. Circuit) had stopped its inquiry too early because it misread Nixon. It now had to consider the separation-of-powers and other arguments, including unwarranted interference with executive duties, before deciding whether to issue "mandamus".

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Ives conceded bioequivalence and equal bioavailability, so lawful copying of the unpatented drug differed from falsely naming its source.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Ives admitted "bioequivalence" and equal bioavailability, meaning the generic capsules worked the same way in the body as its own. So lawfully copying a drug whose patent had expired was different from falsely presenting a copy as coming from Ives.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Pharmacists transferred capsules to dispensing bottles and created the labels consumers saw, providing the opportunity for mislabeled generics.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Pharmacists, not the manufacturers, put the pills into the bottles and wrote the labels patients saw, which is where a generic could be wrongly labeled as the brand.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Ives sued manufacturers and wholesalers under §§32 and 43(a) of the Lanham Act and New York unfair-competition law, seeking damages and an injunction against matching capsules.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Ives sued the manufacturers and wholesalers under §§32 and 43(a) of the Lanham Act, the federal trademark law, and under New York unfair-competition law. It sought "damages" (money) and an "injunction" (court order) stopping sales of look-alike capsules.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Under §43(a), Ives alleged false designation through copied colors and marketing, arguing that the colors were nonfunctional identifiers of origin.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Under §43(a), Ives claimed "false designation" of origin through the copied colors and marketing. It argued the colors were "nonfunctional" identifiers of origin, serving only to show who made the drug and having no useful purpose.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Substitution and mislabeling remained distinct: a pharmacist might both violate a no-substitution instruction and mislabel, or permissibly substitute but still falsely use CYCLOSPASMOL on the label.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Substituting a generic and mislabeling it were separate wrongs. A pharmacist might both ignore a doctor's no-substitution instruction and mislabel, or lawfully substitute but still falsely put CYCLOSPASMOL on the label.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: The instances reflected misunderstanding of state substitution law rather than deliberate passing off.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: The instances of mislabeling came from pharmacists misunderstanding state substitution law, not from deliberate "passing off", which means selling one maker's goods as another's.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Contributory liability extended to a manufacturer or distributor intentionally inducing infringement or continuing supply to someone it knew or had reason to know was infringing.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: "Contributory liability" (responsibility for someone else's infringement) reached a manufacturer or distributor that intentionally induced trademark infringement. It also reached one that kept supplying someone it knew or "had reason to know" (should have realized) was infringing.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a) required acceptance of findings unless the whole record produced a definite and firm conviction of mistake.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a) required appeals courts to accept a trial judge's factual findings unless the whole record left them with a "definite and firm conviction" that a mistake had been made.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Findings based on a mistaken legal principle were different.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: If a finding rests on the wrong legal rule, the appeals court need not defer to it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Emphasis could differ, but the district judge’s conclusion that suppliers had not encouraged infringement was not unreasonable as a matter of law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Someone could weigh the evidence differently, but the district judge's conclusion that the suppliers had not encouraged infringement was not unreasonable "as a matter of law", meaning no legal rule forced a different result.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: Even improperly omitted relevant evidence ordinarily called for remand to the factfinder, not appellate factfinding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Even when relevant evidence was wrongly left out, the usual step was a "remand" (sending the case back) to the "factfinder", the trial judge here, not "factfinding" by the appeals court itself.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: White also considered functionality a complete defense to a contributory claim based solely on reproducing a functional attribute.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: White also considered "functionality" a complete defense to a contributory "claim" based only on copying a "functional attribute", a feature that is useful rather than merely identifying, such as the capsule colors.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.sentence: He agreed that findings could not be rejected without identifying clear error but preferred the court of appeals, with greater routine experience in factual review, to decide whether clear error actually existed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-530.plain: Rehnquist agreed that findings could not be rejected without identifying clear error. But he preferred to let the "court of appeals", which reviews facts more routinely, decide whether clear error actually existed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The Olivers appealed on offer, acceptance, and definiteness and added a general demurrer in the Supreme Court invoking the statute of frauds.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The Olivers appealed on offer, acceptance, and definiteness (whether the terms were clear enough). In the state Supreme Court they also added a "general demurrer", an objection that the complaint stated no claim, relying on the "statute of frauds", which requires certain contracts, like land sales, to be in a signed writing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: A price quotation alone ordinarily invited negotiation, but surrounding circumstances could make it a commitment completed by assent.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: A "price quotation" alone ordinarily just invites negotiation. But the surrounding circumstances could make it a real commitment, which the other side completes by "assent" (agreeing).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: Language, identified rather than indefinite recipients, and definiteness all informed that objective question.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The wording, the fact that it went to specific identified people rather than the public, and its "definiteness" (how precise its terms were) all bore on that "objective question": would a reasonable person read it as an offer?

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: His land-only acceptance matched the offer instead of selecting part of an inseparable bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: Southworth's acceptance of the land alone matched the offer, which he could reasonably read as offering the land by itself. He was not picking one part out of an inseparable "bargain" that had to be bought whole.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The sellers argued that failure to select security made the bargain too indefinite.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The sellers argued that the failure to choose the "security" (collateral backing the unpaid balance) made the "bargain" too indefinite to enforce.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The Court distinguished a prior case lacking agreement about conveyance or an entitlement to compel installments, where the buyer could pay cash instead.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The Court "distinguished" (explained why it did not control) an earlier case where the parties never agreed on the "conveyance", how the land would be transferred. There the seller also had no right to insist on installments, because the buyer could pay cash instead.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: Within reasonable limits, equity could settle subordinate details after sufficient manifested intent to contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: Within reasonable limits, "equity" (a court ordering the sale to go through) could fill in minor details, once the parties had "manifested" (outwardly shown) enough intent to make a contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The appellate demurrer asserted that Joseph had not subscribed the agreement, Arlene had not signed, and the complaint lacked an allegation of Joseph’s written authority to bind her.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The "appellate" demurrer, first raised on appeal, asserted that Joseph had not "subscribed" (signed at the end of) the agreement and Arlene had not signed at all. It also asserted that the "complaint" contained no "allegation" that Joseph had written authority to bind her.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The sellers invoked a precedent permitting a failure-to-state-a-claim objection at any time, but there the demurrer had actually been raised and rejected below.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The sellers relied on a "precedent" (an earlier decision) allowing a failure-to-state-a-claim objection at any time. But in that case the "demurrer" had actually been raised and rejected "below", in the trial court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The statute-of-frauds defense could be waived.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The "statute-of-frauds" defense, that the deal needed a signed writing, could be "waived" (given up) by failing to raise it in time.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: Those circumstances might support ratification, waiver, or estoppel, but the Court expressly did not decide their sufficiency.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: Those facts might support "ratification" (Arlene later approving the deal), waiver (giving up the defense), or "estoppel" (being barred from denying the letter because of their own conduct). But the Court expressly did not decide whether they were enough.
The issue was decided simply because the Olivers had not raised it in time in the trial court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.sentence: The result followed a completed trial and established offer, acceptance, and sufficient certainty, not merely an adequate pleading.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-037.plain: The result came after a completed trial that established offer, acceptance, and sufficiently certain terms. It was not merely a ruling that the "pleading" (the written complaint) was adequate.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: Webb sued McGowin’s executors in assumpsit, the historical action used to enforce this undertaking, for installments accruing after January 27 through commencement of suit.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Webb sued McGowin's "executors", the people managing his estate, in "assumpsit", the historical form of lawsuit for enforcing an "undertaking" (a promise) like this one. He sought the installments that came due after January 27 up to the "commencement" (start) of the suit.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: After amendment, the trial court sustained demurrers asserting no cause of action, no consideration or prior agreement, and the Statute of Frauds.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: After Webb's "amendment" of his complaint, the trial court "sustained demurrers", agreeing with the estate's objections that even if his facts were true he had no "cause of action" (legal claim). The objections were no consideration, no earlier agreement, and the Statute of Frauds, which requires certain promises to be in writing.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: Webb took a nonsuit because of that ruling and appealed.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Webb took a "nonsuit" (voluntarily ended his case in the trial court) because of that ruling, so that he could appeal it.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: A moral obligation linked to an actual material benefit could support a later express promise even without an original legal payment duty.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: A "moral obligation" tied to an actual "material benefit" (a real, substantial benefit received) could support a later "express" promise, one stated outright, even without any original legal duty to pay.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: Years of payment and acceptance supported a compensatory arrangement rather than detached gifts.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Years of payment by McGowin and "acceptance" by Webb supported a deal to compensate Webb, rather than a series of unrelated gifts.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: Bricken acknowledged decisions enforcing later promises only when an earlier legal or equitable duty had become unenforceable, but recognized a qualification for material benefits conferred directly on the promisor.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Judge Bricken acknowledged decisions enforcing later promises only when an earlier "legal or equitable" duty had become unenforceable, for example a debt barred by time. But he recognized an exception for material benefits given directly to the person who made the promise.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: The later express undertaking ratified the completed service and carried a presumption of prior request.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: McGowin's later "express undertaking" (his outright promise) ratified, or approved, Webb's completed service. It also carried a "presumption of prior request", meaning the law treated McGowin as if he had asked for the service beforehand.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: The court distinguished promises by later purchasers for improvements made while land still belonged to the United States: those promisors were not the relevant owners when the services were rendered.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: The court distinguished cases where later buyers promised to pay for improvements made while the land still belonged to the United States. Those "promisors" (the people making the promises) did not own the land when the work was done, so they had not personally benefited.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: Judge Samford concurred, acknowledging uncertainty under strict common-law formulations but emphasizing that doubtful law should not be divorced from justice.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Judge Samford "concurred" (agreed with the result), admitting the outcome was uncertain under strict "common-law" rules, the traditional judge-made rules. But he stressed that doubtful law should not be applied in a way divorced from justice.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: On November 12, 1935, the Court of Appeals reversed the demurrer ruling and remanded for further proceedings.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: On November 12, 1935, the Court of Appeals reversed the ruling on the "demurrer" (the estate's objection) and "remanded" the case, sending it back for further proceedings. It did not itself award the payments.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: On May 14, 1936, Justice Foster’s Alabama Supreme Court opinion denied certiorari.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: On May 14, 1936, in Justice Foster's "opinion" for the Alabama Supreme Court, the court denied certiorari, meaning it declined to review the case.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: He cautioned that denial ordinarily did not endorse every lower-court principle, but expressly agreed here that an actual material and substantial personal benefit could support an executed payment or executory promise, strengthened by the rescuer’s injury.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Justice Foster cautioned that denying review ordinarily does not endorse every principle stated by the lower court. But here he expressly agreed that an actual "material and substantial personal benefit" could support an "executed payment" (one already made) or an executory promise (one still to be performed), especially given the rescuer's injury.

brief-CT-CB-0076.sentence: The rescue preceded the promise, so this was neither an ordinary negotiated exchange nor action taken in reliance on promised payments.
brief-CT-CB-0076.plain: Because Webb saved McGowin before any promise existed, this was not a typical bargain, and Webb did not act relying on a promise.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Congress then enacted the Bevill Amendment, temporarily withholding Subtitle C regulation for extraction, beneficiation, and processing of ores and minerals while requiring a study, report, and regulatory determination.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: Congress then "enacted" the Bevill Amendment, temporarily exempting wastes from mining "extraction", "beneficiation" (concentrating the ore), and processing of ores and minerals from Subtitle C, the strict hazardous-waste rules. Meanwhile it required EPA to study them, report, and make a regulatory determination.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Litigation produced distinct schedules for extraction/beneficiation and processing, and the circuit’s EDF II decision rejected continued overbroad processing coverage.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: Litigation produced separate deadlines for extraction and "beneficiation" wastes and for processing wastes. In EDF II, the "circuit" (the federal appeals court) rejected EPA's continued, overbroad exemption of processing wastes.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Denying Bevill status did not alone put a waste under Subtitle C; it also needed a relevant hazardous characteristic.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: Denying a waste Bevill status (the exemption) did not by itself put it under Subtitle C, the hazardous-waste rules. The waste also needed a relevant hazardous characteristic, such as toxicity or corrosivity.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Under the Chevron framework then governing, imprecise statutory concepts left room for reasonable standards consistent with EDF II, while technical explanations received arbitrary-and-capricious review.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: Under the "Chevron framework" then in force, vague statutory terms left room for any reasonable agency standard consistent with EDF II. EPA's technical explanations received "arbitrary-and-capricious" review, which asks only whether the agency reasoned sensibly.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Meaningful Administrative Procedure Act § 553 notice required access to supporting technical material.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: For notice under Administrative Procedure Act § 553 (the public notice-and-comment process) to be meaningful, the public needed access to the technical material supporting a proposed rule.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Yet supplementary data confirming a method or correcting deficiencies need not always reopen comments absent prejudice.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: But new data that merely confirmed a method or corrected flaws did not always require reopening comments, unless someone showed "prejudice", meaning real harm from not being able to comment.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: EPA could likewise interpret the Simpson Amendment’s relaxed-control authority as concerning the same special-waste category; legislative materials did not compel broader coverage.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: EPA could likewise read the Simpson Amendment's authority to relax controls as covering the same category of special wastes. The legislative materials did not require broader coverage.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: EPA also applied the Subtitle C mixture rule to Bevill/non-Bevill combinations and required treatment permits for mixing.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: EPA also applied the Subtitle C "mixture rule" to mixtures of exempt (Bevill) and non-exempt (non-Bevill) wastes, treating them as regulated hazardous waste. It also required treatment permits for doing such mixing.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: The separate Shell Oil decision had vacated the underlying mixture rule procedurally.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: The separate Shell Oil decision had already "vacated" (struck down) the underlying mixture rule on procedural grounds, because EPA had not followed proper rulemaking steps.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: This court remanded the derivative Bevill rule and permit requirement without deciding their substantive validity.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: This court "remanded" (sent back to EPA) the Bevill rule and permit requirement that depended on the mixture rule, without deciding their "substantive" validity, meaning whether their content was lawful.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: SCM had not presented its comparable argument to the agency, and its process was not obviously identical, so it received no parallel relief.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: SCM had not presented its similar argument to the "agency" (EPA) first, and its process was not obviously identical, so it got no matching relief.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: Unlike the general survey substitution, this changed both methodology and relevant data without meaningful comment.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: Here EPA changed both its method and data for this waste without giving the public a real chance to comment.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.sentence: On February 26, 1992, the court denied EPA rehearing on the last two matters because its proposed Shell Oil distinction had not been briefed originally, while leaving appropriate distinctions open on remand.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-071.plain: On February 26, 1992, the court denied EPA a rehearing on the last two issues, because EPA's proposed distinction of Shell Oil had not been "briefed" (argued in its written filings) originally. But it left EPA free to raise appropriate distinctions on remand.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: It eliminated longshoremen’s unseaworthiness suits against vessels and prohibited employer-indemnity arrangements underlying the Sieracki–Ryan litigation triangle, the sequence of worker claims and vessel recourse against employers.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: The 1972 amendments eliminated longshoremen's "unseaworthiness" suits, which let them recover from ships for unsafe conditions without proving fault. They also banned the employer-indemnity arrangements behind the Sieracki–Ryan "litigation triangle": worker "claims" against the ship, followed by the ship's "recourse" (reimbursement claim) against the employer.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Administrative law judges awarded compensation, and the Benefits Review Board sustained the awards.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: "Administrative law judges" (agency judges) awarded compensation, and the Benefits Review Board, the Labor Department's appeals body, sustained (upheld) the "awards".
The 60-day deadline ran from the date the Board issued its order, even though the agency apparently failed to notify the parties directly.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: The Second Circuit granted Dellaventura’s dismissal motion without deciding the Solicitor of Labor’s authority to make a parallel motion.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: The Second Circuit granted Dellaventura's "dismissal motion" (request to throw out the petition), without deciding whether the Solicitor of Labor, the Labor Department's chief lawyer, had authority to make a parallel "motion".

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Employers urged a first/last-point-of-rest rule: unloading coverage ended at cargo’s first resting place after discharge, and loading coverage began at its last resting place before vessel loading.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: Employers argued coverage should end once unloaded cargo first comes to rest on land, and begin only when outgoing cargo leaves its last resting place before loading.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Judge Friendly, joined by Judge Oakes, accepted substantial-evidence review of facts but rejected sustaining statutory coverage merely because the Board’s interpretation was rational.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: Judge Friendly, "joined by" Judge Oakes, accepted "substantial-evidence" review of the facts, upholding findings that enough evidence supports. But he rejected "sustaining" (upholding) the Board's finding of statutory coverage merely because its reading of the law was rational.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Here, the Board adjudicated rather than made national policy, lacked a comprehensive record of waterfront practices, and had little experience with the amendments.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: Here the Board "adjudicated" (decided individual cases) rather than set national policy. It lacked a full record of waterfront practices and had little experience with the "amendments", so its legal views got less deference.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: The Act’s factually rebuttable coverage presumption did not answer a general construction question.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: The Act's "rebuttable" coverage presumption, which treats a claim as covered unless evidence about the facts shows otherwise, did not answer a general question about what the statute means.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Remedial purpose mattered alongside text, structure, and legislative history.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: "Remedial purpose", the law's aim of helping injured workers, mattered alongside the text, structure, and "legislative history" (records of how Congress wrote the law).

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Text and committee reports treated shore-based container stripping and stuffing as functional parts of vessel unloading and loading.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: The text and committee reports treated "stripping" (emptying) and stuffing (packing) shipping containers on shore as functional parts of unloading and loading ships.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: The majority protected at least eligible-location workers stripping or stuffing containers and cargo handlers through departure from the pier who spent a significant part of their work in typical vessel loading or unloading.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: The majority held that the law covers at least two groups at eligible locations: workers "stripping" (emptying) or stuffing containers, and cargo handlers up to the cargo's departure from the pier. Each must spend a significant part of their work in typical ship loading or unloading.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: Congress had constitutional authority to extend maritime compensation onto adjoining structures; maritime employment contracts supplied an additional basis if necessary.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: Congress could extend maritime compensation onto adjoining docks, and maritime employment contracts were another constitutional basis if needed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.sentence: The court denied the Blundo and Caputo petitions on the merits, leaving those awards intact, while dismissing the Dellaventura and Scaffidi petitions without deciding coverage.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-073.plain: The court denied the Blundo and Caputo petitions on the merits, leaving those awards in place. It was "dismissing" the Dellaventura and Scaffidi petitions without deciding whether those workers were covered.

cp-clearfield.sentence: The bank accepted it for collection, guaranteed prior endorsements, and collected federal payment through the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.
cp-clearfield.plain: Clearfield Trust took the check "for collection", meaning it acted as Penney's agent to get it paid, and stamped a guarantee that all earlier endorsements (signatures) were genuine. It then collected payment from the government through the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Each was a distinct step; knowledge that the check was missing did not occur simultaneously with the later demand.
cp-clearfield.plain: Each event happened at a different time, so knowing the check was missing was not the same as demanding repayment.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Penney intervened, and the district court decided on pleadings and stipulated facts.
cp-clearfield.plain: Penney "intervened" (joined the case as a party), and the district court decided it on the "pleadings" (the written filings) and facts both sides agreed to.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Justice Douglas began with the federal character of paying for work under a federal relief program.
cp-clearfield.plain: Douglas stressed that paying workers on a federal relief program was a federal activity.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Issuance of the check rested on constitutional and statutory powers, not Pennsylvania law, and the related governmental rights and duties arose from those same sources.
cp-clearfield.plain: The government's power to issue the check came from the Constitution and federal statutes, so federal law, not Pennsylvania law, governed the government's rights on it.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Erie’s requirement to follow state law for state-governed matters therefore did not decide this transaction.
cp-clearfield.plain: Erie requires federal courts to follow state law on matters states control, but this was a federal matter, so Erie did not decide it.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Different treatment of identical instruments according to location would create uncertainty, making national uniformity appropriate.
cp-clearfield.plain: Treating identical "instruments" (here, government checks) differently depending on the state would create uncertainty, so "national uniformity", one federal rule for the whole country, was appropriate.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Earlier commercial decisions could inform the choice without reviving Swift’s general federal common law.
cp-clearfield.plain: Earlier commercial-law decisions could guide the choice of rule without reviving Swift's discredited general "federal common law", the idea that federal judges could make their own general law in any case.

cp-clearfield.sentence: A presenter warranted entitlement to payment.
cp-clearfield.plain: A "presenter", whoever presents a check for payment, implicitly promised that it was entitled to be paid on it.

cp-clearfield.sentence: The forged payee endorsement defeated that entitlement, so the government’s recovery claim arose when it paid, without timely notice or demand as a condition to the claim’s existence.
cp-clearfield.plain: The forged endorsement of the payee (the person the check was made out to) meant there was no right to payment. So the government's "recovery" claim, to get its money back, arose the moment it paid; prompt notice or demand was not a condition for the claim to exist.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Forgery of a payee endorsement differed from a forged drawer signature: the drawee was not charged with knowing every payee’s signature.
cp-clearfield.plain: "Forgery" of the "payee" endorsement differed from forgery of the "drawer" signature, that of the person who wrote the check. The "drawee", the party ordered to pay, is expected to know the drawer's signature but not the signature of every payee.

cp-clearfield.sentence: Delay could nevertheless support a defense if Clearfield showed resulting damage after the government learned of forgery.
cp-clearfield.plain: Delay in giving notice could still support a defense if Clearfield showed it suffered a loss because of the delay after the government learned of the "forgery".

cp-clearfield.sentence: The Court left open whether the express guarantee created anything beyond the warranty implied on presentment.
cp-clearfield.plain: The Court left open whether Clearfield's "express guarantee", the stamped promise that endorsements were genuine, created anything beyond the "warranty" (legal promise) the law already implies when a check is presented for payment.

cp-mottley.sentence: Alternatively, they argued that taking away the promised transportation would deprive them of property without due process under the Fifth Amendment.
cp-mottley.plain: Alternatively, they argued that if the law did forbid their passes, taking away the promised free travel would "deprive" them of property without "due process", the fair procedure guaranteed by the Fifth Amendment.

cp-mottley.sentence: The railroad demurred, arguing that the allegations did not justify relief without going to a factual trial.
cp-mottley.plain: The railroad "demurred", arguing that even if all the "allegations" (the facts claimed in the complaint) were true, they did not justify relief, so no trial on the facts was needed.

cp-mottley.sentence: The circuit court overruled that objection and granted the requested decree.
cp-mottley.plain: The "circuit court" (the federal trial court then) overruled that objection and granted the requested "decree", a court order requiring the railroad to honor the passes.

cp-mottley.sentence: Both the Mottleys and the railroad were Kentucky citizens, so diversity supplied no jurisdiction.
cp-mottley.plain: Both the Mottleys and the railroad were Kentucky "citizens", so "diversity" (parties from different states) could supply no "jurisdiction", no power for the federal court to hear the case.

cp-mottley.sentence: The question was whether this contract suit arose under federal law within Congress’s jurisdictional grant.
cp-mottley.plain: The question was whether this contract suit "arose under" federal law, within the jurisdiction Congress's statute grants to federal courts.

cp-mottley.sentence: The plaintiffs’ own cause of action sought enforcement of a promise exchanged for release of injury claims.
cp-mottley.plain: The "plaintiffs'" own cause of action (the Mottleys' claim) sought to enforce a promise given in exchange for their "release" (giving up) of injury claims, an ordinary state contract claim.

cp-mottley.sentence: Federal law entered through the railroad’s expected statutory defense and the Mottleys’ constitutional answer to that defense.
cp-mottley.plain: Federal law came into the case only through the railroad's expected "statutory" defense, that a federal law banned the passes, and the Mottleys' constitutional reply to that defense.

cp-mottley.sentence: Even writing both federal arguments into the complaint could not turn them into elements of the affirmative claim.
cp-mottley.plain: Even writing both federal arguments into the complaint could not make them "elements" (required parts) of the "affirmative claim", the plaintiffs' own case for relief.

cp-mottley.sentence: The likelihood that federal questions would dominate the litigation was insufficient.
cp-mottley.plain: The likelihood that "federal questions" (issues of federal law) would dominate the case was not enough.

cp-mottley.sentence: A complaint had to establish the plaintiff’s claim; it could not manufacture jurisdiction by stating a hypothetical affirmative defense and an advance reply to it.
cp-mottley.plain: A complaint had to set out the plaintiff's own claim. It could not create federal jurisdiction by predicting a hypothetical "affirmative defense" (a defense that defeats the claim even if its facts are true) and answering it in advance.

cp-mottley.sentence: On November 16, 1908, the Supreme Court reversed the decree and sent the case back with instructions to dismiss for want of jurisdiction.
cp-mottley.plain: On November 16, 1908, the Supreme Court "reversed" (overturned) the decree and sent the case back with instructions to dismiss it for "want of jurisdiction", because the federal court never had power to hear it.

cp-mottley.sentence: The parties’ willingness to litigate the federal merits could not confer authority Congress had not granted.
cp-mottley.plain: The parties' willingness to "litigate" (argue in court) the federal "merits", the substance of the dispute, could not give a court authority Congress had not granted.

cp-mottley.sentence: Its well-pleaded-complaint rule addressed statutory original federal-question jurisdiction, rather than defining every possible reach of Article III.
cp-mottley.plain: Its "well-pleaded-complaint rule", which looks only at the plaintiff's own claim, interprets the statute granting original federal-question jurisdiction. It does not define every possible reach of Article III, the Constitution's outer limit on federal court power.

cp-tolan.sentence: For Cotton’s summary-judgment motion, competent evidence and reasonable inferences had to be viewed favorably to Tolan.
cp-tolan.plain: On Cotton's "summary-judgment" motion, a request to win without trial, the court had to view the competent evidence and draw reasonable inferences in Tolan's favor.

cp-tolan.sentence: This review concerned Cotton’s alleged Fourth Amendment excessive force against Tolan.
cp-tolan.plain: This review concerned only Cotton's "alleged" (claimed, not proven) use of "excessive force" against Tolan, in violation of the Fourth Amendment's ban on unreasonable seizures.

cp-tolan.sentence: Cotton had also been indicted and acquitted of aggravated assault by a public servant; criminal-trial testimony entered the civil record, but acquittal did not resolve civil summary judgment.
cp-tolan.plain: Cotton had also been "indicted" (formally charged) and acquitted of "aggravated assault by a public servant". His criminal-trial "testimony" became part of the civil record, but the acquittal did not decide the civil "summary judgment" question, which uses a lower standard of proof.

cp-tolan.sentence: After discovery Cotton sought qualified immunity.
cp-tolan.plain: After "discovery" (the pretrial evidence-gathering stage), Cotton sought "qualified immunity", a shield from suit for officials whose conduct did not violate clearly established law.

cp-tolan.sentence: En banc rehearing failed with three judges favoring it.
cp-tolan.plain: "En banc" rehearing, review by the full appeals court, failed, with three judges voting in favor.

cp-tolan.sentence: Tolan challenged the treatment of disputed facts and separately argued that the appellate court placed analysis of Cotton’s beliefs under the wrong immunity prong.
cp-tolan.plain: Tolan challenged how the court treated disputed facts. He separately argued that the "appellate court" (the appeals court) analyzed Cotton's beliefs under the wrong "prong", or part, of the immunity test.

cp-tolan.sentence: Qualified immunity asks whether plaintiff-favorable facts show a federal-right violation and whether that right was clearly established, giving a reasonable official fair warning.
cp-tolan.plain: "Qualified immunity" asks two questions: whether the facts, taken in the plaintiff's favor, show a violation of a federal right, and whether that right was "clearly established", meaning earlier law gave a reasonable official "fair warning" that the conduct was unlawful.

cp-tolan.sentence: In excessive force, the first inquiry balances Fourth Amendment intrusion against governmental justification.
cp-tolan.plain: In an "excessive force" case, the first question weighs the intrusion on the person's Fourth Amendment rights against the government's justification for the force.

cp-tolan.sentence: Neither prong permits weighing genuinely disputed facts on summary judgment.
cp-tolan.plain: Neither "prong" (part) of the test lets a judge weigh genuinely disputed facts at summary judgment.

cp-tolan.sentence: Rule 56 asks whether a material dispute exists, not whose testimony is true.
cp-tolan.plain: Rule 56 asks only whether a genuine dispute over a "material" (important) fact exists, not whose "testimony" is true.

cp-tolan.sentence: Together the errors showed a clear misapprehension of summary-judgment requirements, not grounds for a new substantive excessive-force rule.
cp-tolan.plain: Together the errors showed a clear misunderstanding of what summary judgment requires. They were not grounds for a new "substantive" rule, a rule changing the law itself, on excessive force.

cp-tolan.sentence: On May 5, 2014, the Court granted certiorari, summarily vacated the Fifth Circuit judgment and remanded.
cp-tolan.plain: On May 5, 2014, the Court "granted" certiorari (agreed to hear the case) and, without full briefing or argument, summarily vacated the Fifth Circuit judgment and "remanded" (sent the case back).

cp-tolan.sentence: Such intervention could change customary certiorari practice under Rule 10’s caution about factual mistakes or misapplication of a correct rule.
cp-tolan.plain: Stepping in like this could change the Court's usual "certiorari" practice, its choice of which cases to review. Its Rule 10 warns that it rarely takes cases just to correct factual mistakes or the misapplication of a correct rule.

cyberchron.sentence: Cyberchron representative Howard Paul understood the clause as assuring reimbursement if the transaction ended; Calldata viewed it as termination for convenience of a valid purchase order, not default.
cyberchron.plain: Cyberchron's representative Howard Paul understood the clause as promising reimbursement if the deal ended. Calldata saw it as covering only "termination for convenience" (cancellation for the buyer's own reasons) of a valid "purchase order", not cancellation for Cyberchron's failure to perform.

cyberchron.sentence: Calldata issued a September 6 show-cause notice, received Cyberchron’s response, and terminated for asserted default on September 25.
cyberchron.plain: Calldata issued a September 6 show-cause notice, demanding that Cyberchron explain why the order should not be cancelled, and received its response. On September 25, Calldata terminated the order for claimed "default", meaning Cyberchron's failure to perform.

cyberchron.sentence: Judge Arthur Spatt in the Eastern District of New York rejected Cyberchron’s contract claim, Calldata’s contract counterclaim, and Cyberchron’s quantum-meruit claim.
cyberchron.plain: Judge Arthur Spatt in the Eastern District of New York rejected Cyberchron's contract claim, Calldata's contract "counterclaim" (its own claim back against Cyberchron), and Cyberchron's quantum-meruit claim for the reasonable value of its work.

cyberchron.sentence: Restitution failed because Cyberchron had not fully performed and Calldata received no unjustly enriching benefit.
cyberchron.plain: "Restitution", recovery to prevent unjust enrichment, failed because Cyberchron had not fully performed and Calldata received no benefit that unfairly enriched it.

cyberchron.sentence: Overhead and lost profits were excluded, and shutdown costs were not addressed.
cyberchron.plain: "Overhead" (general business expenses) and lost profits were excluded from the award, and the court did not address Cyberchron's shutdown costs.

cyberchron.sentence: Cyberchron sought independent termination-clause recovery and fuller damages; Calldata attacked estoppel and its scope.
cyberchron.plain: On appeal, Cyberchron sought "recovery" (payment) under the termination clause on its own and fuller damages. Calldata attacked the estoppel ruling and how far it reached.

cyberchron.sentence: New York law governed; Rule 52(a) clear-error review applied to relevant findings.
cyberchron.plain: New York law governed. Under Rule 52(a), the trial judge's relevant factual findings could be overturned only for clear error, meaning they were clearly wrong.

cyberchron.sentence: Paul’s testimony preserved the independent termination-liability theory despite Calldata’s abandonment objection.
cyberchron.plain: Paul's "testimony" kept alive Cyberchron's separate theory that Calldata owed money under the termination clause, despite Calldata's objection that Cyberchron had made an "abandonment" of (given up) that theory.

cyberchron.sentence: New York estoppel required a clear promise, reasonable foreseeable reliance, and resulting injury.
cyberchron.plain: Under New York promissory estoppel, Cyberchron had to show a clear promise, reasonable and foreseeable reliance on it, and resulting harm.

cyberchron.sentence: The court discussed cases demanding unconscionable injury or emphasizing injustice without resolving every variation, finding the trial findings satisfied both ordinary elements and that added concern.
cyberchron.plain: The court discussed cases that also require "unconscionable" (shockingly unfair) injury or stress injustice, without settling every version of that rule. It found the trial findings met both the ordinary "elements" (required parts) of estoppel and that added concern.

cyberchron.sentence: Calldata’s reliance on Swerdloff’s narrow categories of estoppel was unpersuasive dictum inconsistent with later New York and Second Circuit authority.
cyberchron.plain: Calldata relied on Swerdloff's narrow list of situations where estoppel applies, but that list was unpersuasive "dictum", a side remark not needed to decide the case. It was also inconsistent with later New York and Second Circuit decisions.

cyberchron.sentence: Reliance could include real indirect expenses, not only labor and materials.
cyberchron.plain: Reliance damages can include a fair share of real overhead costs, not just direct labor and materials.

cyberchron.sentence: On February 1, 1995, the Second Circuit affirmed estoppel entitlement, rejected independent termination-clause recovery, and vacated the judgment for damages redetermination on existing or additional evidence.
cyberchron.plain: On February 1, 1995, the Second Circuit affirmed that Cyberchron was entitled to recover on estoppel and rejected separate recovery under the termination clause. It vacated (wiped out) the damages "judgment" and sent the case back to recalculate damages on the existing "evidence" or additional evidence.

dorton.sentence: A buyer affidavit described staff or the salesman agreeing to sell during ordering; the seller’s position and forms suggested written acknowledgment supplied acceptance.
dorton.plain: A buyer's "affidavit" (sworn statement) described the seller's staff or salesman agreeing to sell during the ordering calls. The seller's position and its forms suggested that its later written acknowledgment was what accepted the order.

dorton.sentence: Collins & Aikman removed on diversity and moved under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act to stay litigation.
dorton.plain: Collins & Aikman "removed" the case (moved it from state to federal court) on diversity grounds, since the parties were from different states. It then moved under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act to stay (pause) the lawsuit so the dispute could go to arbitration.

dorton.sentence: The district court found no binding arbitration agreement, treating contracts as formed by conduct under Uniform Commercial Code § 2-207(3) and omitting the added term.
dorton.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) found no binding agreement to arbitrate. It treated the contracts as formed by the parties' conduct under Uniform Commercial Code § 2-207(3), which left out the arbitration term the seller's forms added.

dorton.sentence: The Sixth Circuit accepted interlocutory review under the then-applicable arbitration-stay doctrine and § 1292.
dorton.plain: The Sixth Circuit accepted "interlocutory" review, hearing the appeal before the case was over, under the then-applicable rule for orders refusing to stay a suit for arbitration and § 1292.

dorton.sentence: Section 2-207 responds to mismatched commercial boilerplate, avoiding a mirror-image rule that turns varied responses into counteroffers and lets the final form win through performance.
dorton.plain: Section 2-207 deals with businesses exchanging forms whose "boilerplate" (standard fine print) does not match. It avoids the old "mirror-image" rule, under which any change made a reply a counteroffer and the last form sent won once the parties began "performance" (shipping and accepting goods).

dorton.sentence: The provision applied either way; two written forms were unnecessary, but the sequence identified the bargain against which arbitration must be compared.
dorton.plain: Section 2-207 applied either way, and two written forms were not required. But the order of events identified the "bargain" (the deal already struck) against which the arbitration term had to be compared.

dorton.sentence: An acceptance was expressly conditional under subsection (1) only if it clearly communicated unwillingness to proceed without the offeror’s assent to the different or additional terms.
dorton.plain: Under subsection (1), a reply was an "expressly conditional" acceptance only if it clearly said the seller would not go ahead without the "offeror's" agreement (the buyer's assent) to its "different or additional terms".

dorton.sentence: The forms were therefore effective acceptances or confirmations rather than grounds to bypass subsections (1) and (2) in favor of conduct-only formation.
dorton.plain: The forms were therefore effective acceptances or confirmations. They gave no reason to skip subsections (1) and (2) and jump to "formation" (creation of the contract) by conduct alone under subsection (3).

dorton.sentence: If arbitration was added, the merchant rules of subsection (2) applied.
dorton.plain: If arbitration was an added term, the special rules for merchants in subsection (2) applied. Between merchants, an added term becomes part of the contract unless, among other things, it "materially alters" the deal, in which case it drops out unless the buyer agrees.

dorton.sentence: A substantial change in terms was not, merely because substantial, an expressly conditional acceptance.
dorton.plain: A big change in terms did not, just because it was big, make the seller's form an "expressly conditional" acceptance, one that is really no acceptance at all.

dorton.sentence: Under Prima Paint’s distinction between an arbitration-agreement challenge and fraud in the overall contract, a broad agreed clause would encompass the carpet-composition fraud claims.
dorton.plain: Prima Paint separates a challenge to the arbitration agreement itself from a claim of fraud in the overall "contract". Under it, a broad agreed arbitration clause would cover the fraud claims about what the carpet was made of, sending them to the arbitrator.

dorton.sentence: On January 6, 1972, the court remanded for findings on oral formation, any earlier arbitration agreement, and material alteration if the clause was additional.
dorton.plain: On January 6, 1972, the court "remanded" (sent the case back) for findings on three questions: oral "formation" (whether contracts were made by phone), whether arbitration had been agreed earlier, and, if the clause was an added term, whether it materially altered the deal.

dorton.sentence: The later comparison to C. Itoh concerns language that did satisfy the expressly-conditional proviso, highlighting the distinct inquiries rather than changing this remand.
dorton.plain: The later comparison to C. Itoh involves form language that did meet the "expressly-conditional" proviso, clearly making acceptance conditional. That shows the two questions are separate; it does not change this "remand" (sending the case back).

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: In 1996, Rohan Ingram was convicted in Canada of using a firearm in commission of an indictable offense under Canadian Criminal Code section 85(1)(a).
lrs-k-gayle.plain: In 1996, Rohan Ingram was convicted in Canada of using a firearm while committing an "indictable offense", the Canadian term for a serious crime, under Canadian Criminal Code section 85(1)(a).

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: A superseding indictment charged conspiracy to export defense articles on the United States Munitions List, conspiracy to travel intending illegally to acquire firearms, and firearm possession by someone with a qualifying prior conviction under 18 U.S.C. sections 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2).
lrs-k-gayle.plain: A "superseding indictment" (a revised set of charges) charged him with conspiracy to export defense articles on the United States Munitions List (military-listed weapons) and conspiracy to travel intending to buy firearms illegally. It also charged gun possession by someone with a qualifying prior conviction, under 18 U.S.C. sections 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(2).

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: On January 30, 2002, he received seventy-eight months in prison, three years of supervised release, and a $300 assessment.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: On January 30, 2002, he was sentenced to seventy-eight months in prison, followed by three years of "supervised release" (court-monitored supervision after prison), plus a mandatory $300 assessment.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: A separately filed order affirmed refusal to suppress the firearms; the foreign-predicate opinion did not supply that order’s reasoning.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: A separately filed order "affirmed" (upheld) the refusal to suppress (exclude) the guns as evidence. The "foreign-predicate" opinion, about whether a foreign conviction counts, did not give that order's reasoning.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: Section 922(g)(1), part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, bars specified firearm transactions and possession by a person convicted in any court of a crime punishable by more than one year’s imprisonment.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: Section 922(g)(1), part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, bars certain gun transactions and gun possession by anyone convicted "in any court" of a crime punishable by more than one year in prison.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: The Tenth Circuit’s contrary Concha decision involved a sentencing enhancement but relied on the same predicate language.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: The Tenth Circuit's contrary Concha decision involved a "sentencing enhancement" (a longer sentence because of a prior conviction), but it relied on the same "predicate" language, the wording describing which earlier convictions count.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: Section 921(a)(20) excluded specified federal or state business-regulation offenses, including antitrust crimes, and certain state misdemeanors.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: Section 921(a)(20) expressly did not count certain federal or state business-regulation crimes, including antitrust crimes, and certain state misdemeanors.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: A reading reaching foreign courts would make foreign antitrust convictions disabling when equivalent domestic convictions were excluded.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: If foreign convictions counted, a foreign antitrust conviction would ban gun ownership while the same U.S. conviction would not, which made little sense.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: These considerations, alongside the plausible argument for foreign violent-crime predicates, established ambiguity rather than resolving the question by text alone.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: With good arguments on both sides, the text was ambiguous, so the court had to look beyond the words.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: The Conference Report adopted the House’s punishment-based formulation instead of the Senate’s felony terminology, but did not reject the domestic limitation or discuss foreign convictions.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: The Conference Report, the final House-Senate committee report, adopted the House's punishment-based wording ("punishable by more than one year") instead of the Senate's "felony" term. But it did not reject the domestic-only meaning or discuss foreign convictions.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: After supplemental briefing, both parties agreed that its criminal-statute interpretation did not receive Chevron deference, the administrative-law doctrine then associated with agency readings of ambiguous statutes.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: After "supplemental briefing" (extra written arguments), both sides agreed that the firearms agency's reading of a criminal statute did not get Chevron deference. Chevron was the administrative-law doctrine then telling courts to accept agency readings of "ambiguous" (unclear) statutes.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: Although the panel discussed Concha’s use of lenity, it resolved this ambiguity through context and legislative history rather than automatically favoring the defendant at the first sign of ambiguity.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: The panel discussed Concha's use of "lenity", the rule that unclear criminal laws are read in the defendant's favor. But it resolved this "ambiguity" through context and legislative history, rather than favoring the defendant at the first sign of unclear wording.

lrs-k-gayle.sentence: On August 27, 2003, the Second Circuit reversed Ingram’s felon-in-possession conviction and remanded for resentencing on the remaining conspiracy convictions.
lrs-k-gayle.plain: On August 27, 2003, the Second Circuit reversed Ingram's "felon-in-possession" conviction (having a gun after a qualifying prior conviction). It "remanded" (sent the case back) for resentencing on the remaining conspiracy convictions.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: In 2022, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) adopted a rule applying existing licensing, recordkeeping, serialization, and background-check requirements to certain weapon-parts kits and incomplete components.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: In 2022, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the federal gun agency, adopted a rule applying existing requirements to certain gun-parts kits and unfinished components. Those were dealer licensing, recordkeeping, serial numbers, and background checks.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: The challengers filed a pre-enforcement action under the Administrative Procedure Act seeking to set aside the rule as exceeding statutory authority.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: The challengers filed a "pre-enforcement" suit, before the rule was used against them, under the Administrative Procedure Act. They asked the court to "set aside" (strike down) the rule as "exceeding statutory authority", going beyond what Congress allowed.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: They described their challenge as facial.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: They argued the rule was invalid as written, in its basic terms, not just as applied to particular products.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: The Northern District of Texas granted summary judgment and vacated the rule.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: The Northern District of Texas "granted" summary judgment, ruling for the challengers without trial, and "vacated" (struck down) the rule.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: The majority retained two requirements under subsection (A): an object must be a weapon, and it must have the specified relationship to firing through present ability, design, or ready conversion.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: The majority kept two requirements under subsection (A): the object must be a weapon, and it must have the specified link to firing, by being able to, being designed to, or being readily converted to expel a projectile.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: Gorsuch described “weapon” as an artifact noun: an object people make and identify substantially by its intended function.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: Gorsuch described "weapon" as an "artifact noun", a word for an object people make and identify largely by its intended purpose. So it can cover something unfinished or unassembled, much as a table bought flat-packed is still a table.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: The majority nevertheless retained the judiciary’s independent duty to interpret the statute; historical practice did not restore mandatory deference to any reasonable agency interpretation.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: The majority still kept the courts' independent duty to interpret the statute themselves. The agency's past practice was evidence, but it did not bring back mandatory "deference" (automatic acceptance) of any reasonable agency reading.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: The challengers warned that this reasoning could turn ordinary semiautomatic receivers into machinegun receivers under the National Firearms Act.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: The challengers warned that this reasoning could turn ordinary "semiautomatic receivers" (the main frame part of a semiautomatic gun) into machine-gun receivers under the stricter National Firearms Act.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: Text, context, and structure resolved the categorical dispute, so lenity and constitutional avoidance did not change the result.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: Text, context, and structure settled the dispute about the category, so "lenity" (reading unclear criminal laws for the defendant) and constitutional avoidance (reading laws to avoid constitutional problems) did not change the result.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: He distinguished offenses requiring willfulness from background-check offenses requiring knowledge.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: He separated crimes that require "willfulness" (knowing the conduct is illegal) from background-check crimes that require only "knowledge" (knowing the facts of what one is doing).

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: Under the authority he discussed, willfulness generally required awareness of unlawfulness, while knowledge ordinarily concerned the facts constituting the offense.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: Willfulness usually means knowing your conduct was illegal, while knowledge usually just means knowing the facts.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: Alito would have sought supplemental briefing or vacated and remanded for the Fifth Circuit to consider the appropriate test.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: Alito would have asked for "supplemental briefing" (extra written arguments), or would have vacated the decision and "remanded" it for the Fifth Circuit to consider which test applies.

lrs-k-vanderstok.sentence: Its footnote added a remand constraint: forfeiture and law-of-the-case principles prevented these parties from using remand to inject arguments they had not pursued in the Supreme Court.
lrs-k-vanderstok.plain: A footnote added a limit on the remand: forfeiture (losing an argument by not pressing it) and "law-of-the-case" principles (earlier rulings in the same case bind later stages) kept these parties from using the remand to raise arguments they had not pursued in the Supreme Court.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: In May 1981 the Department’s Office of General Counsel warned that gaps undermined enforcement and Congress’s goal, citing administrative decisions that treated equipment outside the specified prohibitions as allowed even when it caused soreness.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: In May 1981 the Department's Office of General Counsel, its own lawyers, warned that gaps in the rules undermined enforcement and Congress's goal. It cited agency decisions that treated equipment not specifically prohibited as allowed even when it caused soreness in horses.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The Association sought judicial intervention to require rulemaking.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: The Association sought judicial "intervention", asking a court to require the agency to begin "rulemaking" (writing new regulations).

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: No document formally labeled a petition appeared, but neither the Department regulation nor Administrative Procedure Act § 553(e) required specified formalities.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: No document was formally labeled a "petition". But neither the Department regulation nor Administrative Procedure Act § 553(e), which gives people the right to petition for rules, required any particular formalities.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The district court granted the Secretary summary judgment, relying on litigation affidavits from the Deputy Administrator of Veterinary Services.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) granted the Secretary "summary judgment", ruling without trial. It relied on "affidavits" (sworn statements) written for the lawsuit by the Deputy Administrator of Veterinary Services.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The Association appealed, contesting both reviewability and the adequacy of those explanations.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: The Association appealed, contesting both "reviewability" (whether courts could review the refusal at all) and whether those explanations were adequate.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: Heckler v. Chaney’s nonenforcement presumption rested on expertise and priorities, absence of coercive action and prosecutorial discretion.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: Heckler v. Chaney's presumption that courts cannot review an agency's decision not to enforce rested on three things: agency expertise and priorities, the absence of "coercive" action (no one is being forced to do anything), and its likeness to "prosecutorial discretion", a prosecutor's choice not to charge.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The first two considerations could affect rulemaking too, but the prosecutorial analogy was weaker.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: The first two considerations could apply to refusals to begin "rulemaking" too, but the comparison to a prosecutor's choice was weaker there.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: APA § 553(e) gave interested persons a right to petition for rules, and § 555(e) required brief explanations of denials.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: APA § 553(e) gave interested persons a "right to petition" an agency for new rules, and § 555(e) required the agency to briefly explain any denial.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: Review under § 706(2)(A) remained at the especially deferential end of arbitrary-and-capricious scrutiny.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: Review under § 706(2)(A) stayed at the especially "deferential" (lenient) end of "arbitrary-and-capricious" scrutiny, which asks whether the agency acted unreasonably.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The first affidavit was conclusory: saying current rules were best did not explain how studies and policy supported retaining them.
