lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: The first "affidavit" (sworn statement) was conclusory: merely saying the current rules were best did not explain how the studies and policy supported keeping them.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: Properly understood, the general prohibition reached soreness from unlisted devices.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: Read correctly, the general ban covered soreness from unlisted devices too.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The court instead required renewed consideration.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: Instead the court told the agency to reconsider and explain itself.

lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.sentence: The D.C. Circuit vacated the district court judgment and remanded with instructions to remand to the Secretary.
lrs-n-american-horse-lyng.plain: The D.C. Circuit vacated (wiped out) the district court judgment and "remanded" the case, telling the trial court to send the matter back to the Secretary for reconsideration.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Its reconsideration denial invoked available information and expertise while disclaiming a need to link particular records to determinations.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: In denying "reconsideration", the agency relied on the information and expertise available to it, while saying it did not need to tie particular records to its decisions.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: The agency had used informal notice and comment with a technical conference, proposals, and reconsideration.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: The agency had used informal notice and comment, publishing proposals and taking public comments, along with a technical conference and "reconsideration", rather than a trial-like hearing.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: The D.C. Circuit used Automotive Parts’ approach: searching arbitrary-and-capricious examination of legislative materials, not mandatory formal substantial-evidence review.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: The D.C. Circuit followed Automotive Parts' approach: a searching "arbitrary-and-capricious" examination of the rulemaking record, rather than the formal substantial-evidence review used for trial-like hearings.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Section 103 required objective standards meeting safety needs and economic practicability.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: Section 103 required objective safety standards that met safety needs and had "economic practicability", meaning they were affordable and workable for the industry.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Section 201 separately commanded permanent, conspicuous tire information including actual ply number and maximum load.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: Section 201 separately commanded, in the statute itself, that certain tire information be marked permanently and conspicuously, including the actual ply number and maximum load.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Later vehicle transfers, resale, or replacement matching might justify lasting information, but the Secretary supplied no record illustrations showing their frequency and significance.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: Later vehicle transfers, "resale", or matching replacement tires might justify lasting information. But the Secretary gave no examples in the record showing how often that happened or how much it mattered.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Judicial review of discretionary agency choices could not reweigh Congress’s explicit selection.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: "Judicial review" of the agency's own discretionary choices could not reweigh a choice Congress had made explicitly in the statute.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Saying administrative-procedure tests did not govern Congress did not immunize statutes from all constitutional review.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: That the agency-review standard does not apply to Congress does not mean statutes are immune from constitutional challenge.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: But serious, specific burdens required support, persuasive explanation, or an inherently plausible answer.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: But when the industry raised serious, specific cost problems, the agency had to answer with evidence, a convincing explanation, or an obviously sensible response.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: A working method for stable information did not establish economic feasibility for frequent changes.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: A workable method for marking information that rarely changes did not prove the "feasibility" (practical affordability) of marks that change frequently.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Under § 706(2)(A) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the discretionary permanent-label additions were arbitrary on this record.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: Under § 706(2)(A) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the permanent-label requirements the agency added on its own, as "discretionary" choices not ordered by Congress, were arbitrary on this record. A better-supported rule could be adopted later.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: Judge Spottswood W. Robinson III concurred in disposition on economic practicability.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: Judge Spottswood W. Robinson III "concurred" in the disposition (agreed with the result) only on the ground of "economic practicability", whether the requirements were affordable and workable.

lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.sentence: On January 8, 1974, the court vacated permanent labeling of size, maximum inflation, ply rating, tube type, and applicable construction designation.
lrs-n-national-tire-brinegar.plain: On January 8, 1974, the court "vacated" (struck down) the permanent labeling of size, maximum inflation, ply rating, tube type, and the applicable construction designation. The labels Congress itself required stayed in place.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Section 7(a)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) requires federal agencies, consulting the appropriate wildlife Secretary, to ensure that actions they authorize, fund, or undertake are unlikely to jeopardize listed species or adversely alter critical habitat.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Section 7(a)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) requires federal agencies, after consulting the appropriate wildlife Secretary, to ensure that actions they authorize, fund, or carry out are unlikely to jeopardize listed species or harm their "critical habitat" (areas essential to their survival).

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: On remand, Secretary of the Interior Manuel Lujan again challenged standing at summary judgment, but the district court treated the appellate ruling as controlling, granted Defenders judgment on the merits, and ordered a new regulation.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: "On remand", when the case went back, Secretary of the Interior Manuel Lujan again challenged standing at summary judgment. But the district court treated the "appellate" ruling as controlling, "granted" Defenders judgment "on the merits" (on the substance of the claim), and ordered a new "regulation".

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: General allegations might suffice at pleading, but affidavits or other evidence had to supply specific facts at summary judgment.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: General "allegations" (claims in the complaint) might be enough at the "pleading" stage. At summary judgment, though, "affidavits" (sworn statements) or other evidence had to show specific facts.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Justice Scalia’s six-Justice principal analysis required concrete and particularized injury that was actual or imminent, fairly traceable to challenged conduct, and likely redressable by a favorable decision.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Justice Scalia's main opinion, joined by six Justices, required an injury that is "concrete" and particularized (real and personal), actual or "imminent" (about to happen), fairly traceable to the challenged conduct, and likely "redressable", meaning a court win would fix it.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Where plaintiffs are not the objects of challenged government action, causation and relief depend on third parties’ choices.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: When plaintiffs are not the ones the government action targets, "causation" (whether the action caused the harm) and relief depend on the choices of "third parties", people not in the case.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Those four Justices found the record insufficient to show that an injunction against Interior would bind the separate funding agencies or that consultation and changed United States funding would stop the foreign projects.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Those four Justices found the record did not show that an "injunction" (court order) against Interior would bind the separate funding agencies. Nor did it show that consultation and changed United States funding would stop the foreign projects.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: The Court recognized that a procedural right may relax immediacy and redressability for someone whose concrete interest is threatened.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: The Court recognized that a "procedural right", such as a right to required consultation, may relax the timing and redressability requirements. But that applies only to someone whose own "concrete" interest is threatened.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Congress could not provide standing merely by authorizing any citizen to sue for lawful administration.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Congress could not create "standing", the right to sue, merely by authorizing any citizen to sue to make the government follow the law.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: The ESA citizen-suit language did not remove Article III’s concrete-injury minimum.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: The ESA "citizen-suit" language, letting "any person" sue, did not remove Article III's minimum requirement of a "concrete" injury, a real and personal harm.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Applying the presumption against extraterritoriality, he read § 7(a)(2) as excluding foreign-country activities.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Applying the "presumption against extraterritoriality", the rule that federal laws are presumed to apply only within the country, he read § 7(a)(2) as not covering activities in foreign countries.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Rule 56(e)’s need for specific evidence differed from Rule 56(c)’s question whether that evidence raised a genuine issue.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Rule 56(e)'s requirement of specific evidence was different from Rule 56(c)'s question of whether that evidence raised a "genuine issue", a real dispute needing trial.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: On June 12, 1992, the Supreme Court reversed the Eighth Circuit and remanded for lack of Article III standing.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: On June 12, 1992, the Supreme Court "reversed" the Eighth Circuit and "remanded" (sent the case back) because the groups lacked Article III standing, the constitutional right to sue.

lrs-n-standing-lujan.sentence: Six Justices supported the three-part formulation and rejection of indefinite return intentions, four supported the detailed redressability section, and Stevens reached the same judgment through his own statutory merits analysis.
lrs-n-standing-lujan.plain: Six Justices supported the three-part standing test and the rejection of vague plans to return, and four supported the detailed redressability section. Stevens reached the same "judgment" (result) through his own "statutory" analysis of the merits, reading the law itself as not covering foreign projects.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: An administrative law judge found partial rather than total disability.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: An "administrative law judge" (an agency judge) found Harcum partially rather than totally disabled, so he got lower partial-disability benefits.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: The Benefits Review Board affirmed and held that employer payments could stop after 104 weeks, with a statutory special fund assuming responsibility.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: The Benefits Review Board, the Labor Department appeals body, affirmed. It held that the employer's payments could stop after 104 weeks, with a "statutory" special fund, one created by the law, taking over responsibility.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: The Fourth Circuit raised standing itself.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: The Fourth Circuit raised the question of "standing" (the Director's right to appeal) on its own, without either party asking.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: It held that the Director was not a person adversely affected or aggrieved by denial of full-disability benefits under § 21(c) of the Longshore and Harbor Workers’ Compensation Act.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: It held that the Director was not a person "adversely affected or aggrieved" (legally harmed) by the denial of "full-disability" benefits under § 21(c) of the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, so she could not appeal.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: It separately allowed her challenge involving the special fund she administered.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: Separately, the court did allow her challenge involving the "special fund" she administered, the Labor Department fund that takes over some payments from employers.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: The Director argued that an erroneous award frustrated her duties to secure proper compensation, administer the Act uniformly, and support effective informal settlements.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: The Director argued that a wrong award frustrated her duties to secure proper compensation, apply the Act uniformly, and support effective informal settlements.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: Justice Scalia, writing for eight Justices, distinguished a government entity injured in the same capacity as a private participant, such as a shipper contesting an unlawful rate, from an administrator dissatisfied with a decision’s policy effects.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: Justice Scalia, writing for eight Justices, separated two kinds of government interest. A government body injured the same way a private party would be, like a shipper challenging an unlawful rate, differs from an administrator unhappy with a decision's policy effects.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: Treating the latter interest as ordinary aggrievement would repeatedly put courts in intrabranch and intraagency disputes.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: Treating that second kind of interest as ordinary "aggrievement" (legal injury giving a right to appeal) would repeatedly put courts in the middle of disputes within a single branch or agency.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: The Administrative Procedure Act excluded agencies from its definition of person, while other statutes expressly authorized official appeals.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: The Administrative Procedure Act's definition of "person" left out agencies, while other statutes expressly authorized officials to appeal, something this law did not do.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: Under the administrative-law framework then applied, the Director retained rulemaking as a means to address disagreement with a Board rule of law.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: Under the administrative-law framework then applied, the Director could still use rulemaking (issuing regulations) to deal with a legal rule of the Board that she disagreed with.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: Liberal construction could clarify an ambiguous statutory element, but could not add powers Congress had withheld merely to advance a remedial purpose.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: "Liberal construction", reading a law generously, could clarify an "ambiguous" (unclear) part of a statute. But it could not add powers Congress had withheld just to advance the law's "remedial purpose" of helping injured workers.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: She regarded that disparity as apparent oversight, but correction required congressional judgment beyond fixing a scrivener’s error.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: Ginsburg saw that difference as an apparent oversight by Congress. But fixing it required Congress's own judgment, which went beyond correcting a "scrivener's error", a simple drafting typo.

lrs-n-standing-newport.sentence: It did not determine Harcum’s disability, resolve special-fund standing, or decide whether the Director could be a respondent in someone else’s appeal.
lrs-n-standing-newport.plain: The Court did not decide how disabled Harcum was, resolve the Director's standing on the special-fund issue, or decide whether the Director could be a "respondent" (the party defending) in someone else's appeal.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: Two counts sought individual damages, and a third sought declaratory and injunctive relief for a certified class of Dade County students.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: Two counts (separate claims) sought "damages", money for the two boys individually. A third sought "declaratory" relief (a court statement of rights) and an injunction for a "certified class", a group the court approved to sue together, of Dade County students.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: After a week of plaintiffs’ evidence, including testimony from sixteen students, defendants sought Rule 41(b) dismissal of the equitable count and a ruling that the evidence could not support damages.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: After a week of the "plaintiffs'" evidence, including "testimony" from sixteen students, the defendants asked for "dismissal" of the "equitable" count (the claim for a court order) under Rule 41(b). They also asked for a ruling that the evidence could not support damages.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: The district court assumed the testimony credible, made no credibility findings, heard no defense evidence, and dismissed all three counts because it found no available federal constitutional relief.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: The district court assumed the students' "testimony" was believable and made no "credibility findings", and it heard no "defense" evidence. It dismissed all three "counts" because it found no federal constitutional "relief" available.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: Certiorari covered the Eighth Amendment and procedural due process only.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: "Certiorari", the Supreme Court's grant of review, covered only two questions: the Eighth Amendment (whether paddling can be cruel and unusual punishment) and procedural due process (whether a hearing is required first).

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: Justice Powell’s majority traced the Eighth Amendment’s linked limits on bail, fines, and punishment through the English Bill of Rights, Virginia Declaration of Rights, ratification debates, and First Congress.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: Justice Powell's majority traced the Eighth Amendment's linked limits on bail, fines, and punishment through the English Bill of Rights, the Virginia Declaration of Rights, the "ratification" debates, and the First Congress. It concluded the Amendment limits only criminal punishment.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: Evolving standards of decency informed assessment of criminal penalties rather than expanding the Amendment at the threshold to educational discipline.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: "Evolving standards of decency" (society's changing views) help judge criminal penalties. They do not expand the Amendment at the outset to cover school discipline.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: Florida preserved civil damages for excessive force and criminal penalties for malicious punishment.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: Florida kept civil "damages" suits for excessive force and criminal penalties for malicious punishment of students.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: Under the balancing approach of Mathews v. Eldridge, the students’ interest in avoiding wrongful pain was substantial.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: Under the "balancing" test of Mathews v. Eldridge, which weighs the interests at stake to decide what process is due, the students' interest in avoiding wrongful pain was substantial.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: It compared common-law review afterward to review of warrantless public arrests based on probable cause.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: The Court compared after-the-fact "common-law" review (lawsuits under traditional judge-made law) to court review of public arrests made without a warrant but based on "probable cause", a reasonable basis to believe a crime occurred.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: It held that Florida’s preserved limitations and judicial remedies afforded the process constitutionally required here without prior notice and hearing.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: It held that Florida's legal limits on paddling and its court "remedies" (the right to sue or prosecute afterward) gave all the process the Constitution required here, without notice and a hearing beforehand.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: On due process, he would require the informal exchange recognized in Goss: notice of the accusation, explanation of disputed evidence, and a chance to give the student’s version.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: On "due process", White would require the informal exchange recognized in Goss: telling the student the accusation, explaining any disputed evidence, and giving the student a chance to tell his side.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: A brief warrantless arrest began a system of prompt judicial control; punishment without a prior response was already final.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: A brief "warrantless" arrest (one made without a warrant) starts a system of prompt review by a judge. But a paddling given without first hearing the student is already final and cannot be undone.

lrs-o-ingraham.sentence: The decision did not approve the alleged beatings as reasonable, award tort damages, or settle whether extreme arbitrary punishment could violate substantive due process, a question outside the grant of review.
lrs-o-ingraham.plain: The decision did not approve the "alleged" (claimed, not proven) beatings as reasonable, award tort damages, or settle whether extremely arbitrary punishment could violate substantive due process. That question was outside the "grant" of review.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Wisconsin law granted permanent employment after four continuous years, conditioned on efficiency and good behavior, and protected permanent teachers against discharge without cause and specified procedures.
lrs-o-roth.plain: Wisconsin law gave "permanent employment" (tenure) after four continuous years, conditioned on efficiency and good behavior. It protected permanent teachers from discharge without cause and required specified procedures.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Rules gave nontenured faculty some review of dismissal during an existing year but distinguished dismissal from nonretention for the next.
lrs-o-roth.plain: University rules gave untenured faculty some review of a "dismissal" (firing) during a current year. But they distinguished dismissal from "nonretention", simply not being rehired for the next year.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Roth sued in federal district court on both a substantive free-speech theory and procedural due process.
lrs-o-roth.plain: Roth sued in "federal district court" on two theories: a "substantive" free-speech claim (he was punished for his speech) and "procedural due process" (he was owed a fair process before losing the job).

lrs-o-roth.sentence: The Court rejected the old idea that government could escape due process by calling public benefits privileges.
lrs-o-roth.plain: The Court rejected the old idea that government could skip due process by calling benefits mere "privileges".

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Balancing its importance against administrative needs helps design process only after a protected deprivation is identified; need, desire, and unilateral expectation do not alone create entitlement.
lrs-o-roth.plain: "Balancing" an interest's importance against administrative needs helps design the process due, but only after a protected loss of liberty or property is identified. Need, desire, or a one-sided expectation do not by themselves create an entitlement.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: A name-clearing hearing also would not automatically confer tenure.
lrs-o-roth.plain: A "name-clearing hearing", a chance to answer charges that hurt his reputation, also would not automatically give him tenure or a right to keep the job.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Property arises from independent rules or understandings supporting a legitimate claim of entitlement.
lrs-o-roth.plain: A property interest exists only where some law, contract or understanding gives a person a legitimate claim to the benefit.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: A claimant need not win the underlying dispute first: Goldberg’s recipients possessed a statutory entitlement framework even though a hearing was needed to decide eligibility.
lrs-o-roth.plain: A "claimant" (a person seeking a benefit) need not win the underlying dispute first. The welfare recipients in Goldberg had a "statutory" entitlement, one created by law, even though a hearing was needed to decide whether they were eligible.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Roth argued that annual appointees generally returned, but the lower courts had not found that practice created a binding institutional common law.
lrs-o-roth.plain: Roth argued that teachers on one-year appointments were usually rehired. But the "lower courts" had not found that this practice created a binding institutional "common law", an unwritten rule the university had to follow.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: The Court expressly referred to Perry’s recognition that sufficiently established understandings could matter; it did not make formal written tenure indispensable.
lrs-o-roth.plain: The Court noted, per Perry, that established informal understandings could create such an interest, so formal tenure is not always required.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Lack of entitlement did not authorize retaliatory nonrenewal.
lrs-o-roth.plain: Having no entitlement to the job did not allow a "retaliatory" nonrenewal, refusing to rehire him to punish his speech.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: He proposed abstention when uncertain state contract law controlled the antecedent entitlement question; the Court did not order that disposition here.
lrs-o-roth.plain: Burger proposed "abstention", having federal courts hold off, when unclear state contract law controlled the "antecedent" question of whether an entitlement existed. The Court did not "order" that approach here.

lrs-o-roth.sentence: Roth addresses whether an interest receives procedural protection; Mathews addresses design of process after such an interest is accepted.
lrs-o-roth.plain: Roth decides whether an interest is protected at all; Mathews decides what process is required once it is.

luttinger.sentence: The agreement conditioned purchase on a $45,000 first mortgage from a bank or other lending institution for at least twenty years at no more than 8.5 percent annual interest.
luttinger.plain: The buyers only had to go through with the purchase if they got a $45,000 bank mortgage for at least 20 years at no more than 8.5% interest.

luttinger.sentence: If they failed despite that effort and gave notice within the specified time, their deposit would be returned and the contract would end without further obligation.
luttinger.plain: If they failed despite that effort and gave notice within the stated time, their deposit would be returned and the "contract" would end with no further obligation on either side.

luttinger.sentence: The clause thus allocated unavailable-financing risk and its consequences, rather than merely describing a preferred source of money.
luttinger.plain: The clause decided who bears the loss if suitable financing could not be found: the buyers could walk away.

luttinger.sentence: Its commitment instead required the prevailing rate at closing, with a minimum of 8.75 percent.
luttinger.plain: The lender's "commitment" (its promise to lend) instead required the going interest rate at closing, with a minimum of 8.75 percent, above the contract's limit.

luttinger.sentence: Sellers’ counsel then proposed funding the difference between the lender’s rate and 8.5 percent for all twenty-five years, without defining exact terms.
luttinger.plain: The sellers' "counsel" (lawyer) then offered to pay the difference between the lender's rate and 8.5 percent for all twenty-five years of the loan, without spelling out exact terms.

luttinger.sentence: The Rosens appealed, briefing two issues: whether a single mortgage application met due diligence and whether their proposed subsidy meant the financing condition should be treated as fulfilled.
luttinger.plain: The Rosens appealed on two issues: whether a single "mortgage" application showed "due diligence" (reasonable effort), and whether their offer to cover the extra interest meant the "financing condition" should be treated as met.

luttinger.sentence: Further applications would have been futile, and the law did not require them.
luttinger.plain: Applying elsewhere would have been pointless, and the law does not require useless acts.
Making the promised effort and actually getting the loan were two separate questions.

luttinger.sentence: A buyer might violate an effort promise even if financing remained unavailable, but these buyers had satisfied their promised effort.
luttinger.plain: A buyer who did not really try could breach even if no loan was available; but these buyers did try.

luttinger.sentence: A condition precedent is an event intended to occur before a right to performance arises.
luttinger.plain: A condition precedent is an event that must happen before a party's right to "performance" (the other side's duty to do what it promised) arises.

luttinger.sentence: The contract unambiguously required an institutional mortgage on specified terms before the purchase obligation matured.
luttinger.plain: The contract clearly required a mortgage on the stated terms before the buyers had to buy.

luttinger.sentence: The sellers’ subsidy would add a new financing arrangement beside the mortgage; it did not change the lender’s commitment into the one specified.
luttinger.plain: The sellers' subsidy would add a new financing arrangement alongside the "mortgage". It did not turn the lender's "commitment" into the loan the contract specified.

luttinger.sentence: Testimony about it was irrelevant to whether the original condition occurred, so exclusion of that evidence was proper.
luttinger.plain: "Testimony" about the sellers' offer did not bear on whether the original condition occurred, so keeping that evidence out was proper.

mckenna.sentence: Payment required the architect’s certificates, with eighty percent of work in place payable as construction progressed and payment also contemplated after completion.
mckenna.plain: Each payment required "architect's certificates", the architect's written approval of the work. Eighty percent of the value of work in place was payable as construction progressed, with payment also planned after completion.

mckenna.sentence: On appeal, Vernon chiefly argued that no action could proceed without a final architect’s certificate of compliance.
mckenna.plain: On "appeal", Vernon mainly argued that McKenna could not sue at all without the architect's final certificate saying the work complied with the contract.

mckenna.sentence: He challenged the refusals of compulsory nonsuit, binding instructions, and judgment notwithstanding the verdict, as well as evidence and charge rulings.
mckenna.plain: Vernon challenged the trial judge's refusals to grant a "compulsory nonsuit" (ending the case for lack of proof), binding instructions (directing the jury to find for him), and "judgment notwithstanding the verdict" (overriding the jury). He also challenged rulings on evidence and the jury charge.

mckenna.sentence: Justice Stewart found no special contractual distinction between certificates for progress payments and the certificate associated with final payment.
mckenna.plain: Justice Stewart found that the contract drew no special distinction between the certificates for "progress payments" (payments made as work went along) and the certificate tied to final payment.

mckenna.sentence: All payments required certification, yet six of seven were made without even requesting it.
mckenna.plain: Every payment needed a certificate, yet the owner made six of seven without asking for one.

mckenna.sentence: His constant and repeated disregard of it, coupled with the architect’s substantive approval and his own observation without protest, prevented him from using the missing certificate as a complete defense to payment for honestly and substantially performed work.
mckenna.plain: The owner's constant, repeated disregard of the certificate requirement, together with the architect's "substantive" approval of the work itself and his own watching without protest, barred him from using the missing certificate as a "complete defense" to paying for work honestly and substantially performed.

mckenna.sentence: The reasoning depended on that actual course of performance; it did not declare certificates irrelevant in every construction contract or make one isolated exception a waiver of all future conditions.
mckenna.plain: The reasoning depended on these parties' actual "course of performance", how they behaved in carrying out the "contract". It did not declare certificates irrelevant in every construction contract, or make one isolated exception a "waiver" (giving up) of all future "conditions".

mckenna.sentence: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court held that nonsuit and binding instructions had properly been refused.
mckenna.plain: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court held that the trial judge had properly refused a "nonsuit" (ending the case) and binding instructions directing a verdict for Vernon.

mckenna.sentence: It does not decide whether an owner could later reinstate the certification requirement after waiver; that question appears in editorial discussion, not the judgment.
mckenna.plain: The case does not decide whether an owner could later "reinstate" (insist again on) the certificate requirement "after waiver" of it. That question comes up in editorial discussion, not in the court's "judgment".

anderson-binance.sentence: That initial agreement later supplied Binance’s theory of amendment, but assent to it did not itself resolve acceptance or temporal reach of a later document.
anderson-binance.plain: That original agreement later supplied Binance's theory of "amendment": that it could change the terms by posting updates. But users' assent to it did not by itself "resolve acceptance" of the later document, or decide how far back in time that document reached.

anderson-binance.sentence: On March 28, 2025, the district court denied arbitration for earlier claims but left unresolved claims accruing after the amendment and before actual notice and the asserted class waiver.
anderson-binance.plain: On March 28, 2025, the district court denied arbitration for claims that arose earlier. It left unresolved the claims "accruing" (arising) after the "amendment" but before users had "actual notice" of it, and the claimed class waiver.

anderson-binance.sentence: That dismissal mooted the later-claim issue.
anderson-binance.plain: That "dismissal" of the later claims made the question about them moot, meaning there was nothing left to decide.

anderson-binance.sentence: For passive assent through use, the question was whether a reasonably prudent user had actual or constructive notice.
anderson-binance.plain: When a company claims "assent" (agreement) merely from continued use, the question is whether a "reasonably prudent" (ordinarily careful) user had actual notice or "constructive notice", meaning the user should have known of the terms.

anderson-binance.sentence: Even assuming constructive notice of the 2019 terms, the court held that they did not extend to claims accrued before their effective date.
anderson-binance.plain: Even assuming users had "constructive notice" (should have known) of the 2019 terms, the court held that those terms did not reach claims that had arisen before their "effective date".

anderson-binance.sentence: California’s implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing limited a unilateral amendment power silent about known or accrued claims.
anderson-binance.plain: California's "implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing", a duty of fairness read into every contract, limited Binance's "unilateral" (one-sided) power to amend. Because the clause said nothing about known or "accrued" (already existing) claims, it could not be used to take them away.

anderson-binance.sentence: Carter distinguished Peleg’s treatment of express powers to affect accrued claims as illusory from a silent clause constrained by the covenant; he did not declare Binance’s entire contract illusory.
anderson-binance.plain: Carter distinguished Peleg, where a clause that expressly let a company change terms for "accrued" claims made the promise "illusory" (meaningless). Binance's clause was silent, so the "covenant" of good faith simply limited it, and he did not declare Binance's whole contract illusory.

anderson-binance.sentence: The heading and warning said the section involved waiver of certain rights, including class proceedings, but no operative clause defined the surrender or expressly barred federal-court class actions.
anderson-binance.plain: The heading and warning said the section involved "waiver" (giving up) of certain rights, including "class proceedings" (group lawsuits). But no "operative clause", an actual binding sentence, defined what was given up or expressly "barred" class actions in federal court.

anderson-binance.sentence: The standardized, unnegotiated terms were adhesive, and the court construed ambiguity narrowly against Binance as drafter without declaring all adhesion contracts invalid.
anderson-binance.plain: The standardized, unnegotiated terms were "adhesive", a take-it-or-leave-it form contract. So the court "construed" (interpreted) unclear wording narrowly against Binance "as drafter" (the party that wrote it), without declaring all adhesion contracts invalid.

anderson-binance.sentence: Initially agreed releases and indemnities did not govern this later unilateral change; the same temporal limits applicable to arbitration also defeated waiver of the remaining accrued claims.
anderson-binance.plain: "Releases" (giving up claims) and indemnities (promises to cover Binance's losses) in the original agreement did not govern this later "unilateral" change. The same time limits that applied to arbitration also defeated the waiver of the remaining "accrued" claims.

anderson-binance.sentence: Post-effective-date claims were already dismissed by stipulation, so their arbitrability was not decided on the merits.
anderson-binance.plain: Claims arising after the effective date had already been "dismissed" by stipulation (agreement of the parties). So their "arbitrability", whether they had to go to arbitration, was not decided "on the merits".

anderson-binance.sentence: The plaintiffs won a forum ruling, not securities liability, damages, or class certification, and the earlier vacated arbitration opinion does not replace this limited disposition.
anderson-binance.plain: The "plaintiffs" won only a "forum" ruling, about where the case is heard, not securities liability, damages, or "class certification" (approval to sue as a group). The earlier "vacated" (withdrawn) arbitration opinion does not replace this limited "disposition" (ruling).

brief-CP-131.sentence: The district court sustained objections to the interrogatories.
brief-CP-131.plain: The district court (the federal trial court) sustained the plaintiffs' objections to the "interrogatories", the defendants' written questions that must be answered under oath.

brief-CP-131.sentence: The district court certified the order under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), identifying a controlling legal question with substantial ground for disagreement.
brief-CP-131.plain: The district court certified the "order" for immediate appeal under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b). It identified a controlling legal question on which there was substantial ground for disagreement.

brief-CP-131.sentence: The defendants then applied to the Second Circuit for leave to appeal.
brief-CP-131.plain: The defendants then applied to the Second Circuit for leave (permission) to appeal right away, which that court could grant or refuse.

brief-CP-131.sentence: Permitting the discovery could produce numerous full-scale inquiries into electricity rates, dwarfing even the extensive pretrial proceedings already undertaken.
brief-CP-131.plain: Allowing the "discovery" (pretrial evidence-gathering) could produce many full-scale investigations of electricity rates. That would dwarf even the extensive "pretrial proceedings" already carried out.

brief-CP-131.sentence: If the discovery restriction later proved wrong and contributed to an adverse judgment, the defendants could challenge it together with other errors in a final appeal.
brief-CP-131.plain: If the discovery limit later proved wrong and helped produce a "judgment" against them, the defendants could challenge it along with other errors in an appeal at the end of the case.

brief-CP-131.sentence: The court doubted that later discovery or hearings about passed-on damages, if legally appropriate, would impose a greater burden than undertaking them immediately.
brief-CP-131.plain: The court doubted that later "discovery" or hearings about "passed-on damages" (whether the plaintiffs passed the overcharges on to their own customers), if legally appropriate, would be more burdensome than doing them immediately.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.sentence: It argued that the parent’s ownership and practical influence could support a turnover order under New York Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5225(b).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.plain: It argued that the Canadian parent bank's ownership and practical influence over its subsidiary could support a "turnover order", a court order to hand over a debtor's money, under New York Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5225(b).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.sentence: The problem was not only personal jurisdiction over the parent: the statute referred to a third party’s possession or custody of the debtor’s assets, which the parent might lack even though its subsidiary held the money.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.plain: The problem was not only "personal jurisdiction" (the court's power over the parent). The statute refers to a "third party's" possession or custody of the debtor's assets, which the parent might lack even though its subsidiary held the money.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.sentence: It considered the New York Court of Appeals better placed to interpret the provision within the state’s statutory scheme, including legislative intent and the significance of matching language in § 5225(a).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.plain: It considered the New York Court of Appeals, the state's highest court, better placed to interpret the provision within the state's "statutory scheme". That court could weigh the legislature's intent and the significance of matching wording in § 5225(a).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.sentence: Under New York Court of Appeals Rule 500.27 and Second Circuit Local Rule 27.2, the panel certified two questions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.plain: Under New York Court of Appeals Rule 500.27 and Second Circuit Local Rule 27.2, which let federal judges ask the state's highest court about state law, the panel certified (sent) two questions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.sentence: It directed transmission of the opinion, briefs, appendix and record to the New York Court of Appeals, with certification fees and costs shared equally.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.plain: It ordered the "opinion", the briefs, the appendix, and the record sent to the New York Court of Appeals, with the certification fees and costs split equally between the parties.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.sentence: The later prohibition on the requested turnover order belongs to the subsequent state answer and final federal disposition, not this certification order.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-483-CERTIFY.plain: This "certification order" only asked the questions. The later ruling against the requested turnover order came from the New York court's answer and the federal court's final decision afterward.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: On an emergency request, the district court authorized service under Rules 4(h)(2) and 4(f)(3) by mail to Carpenter, mail to IEC, and the company’s email.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: On the casino's emergency request, the district court authorized service (formal delivery of the lawsuit) under Rules 4(h)(2) and 4(f)(3), which let a court approve methods for foreign defendants. It allowed mail to Carpenter (the company's lawyer), mail to IEC (its courier), and the company's email.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: The defendant appeared, challenged service and personal jurisdiction, lost on written submissions, and answered with twenty-two affirmative defenses.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: The "defendant" appeared in court and challenged service and personal jurisdiction (the court's power over it), losing on the written papers. It then answered the complaint with twenty-two "affirmative defenses" (reasons it should win even if the claims were true).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: After an order compelling responses and explicit warning that money was inadequate and preclusive sanctions would follow, it again failed to comply and later supplied only partial answers.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: The court ordered it to respond and explicitly warned that fines were not enough and that "preclusive sanctions" (barring it from defending on issues) would follow. It again failed to comply and later gave only partial answers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: Methods had to be court-directed, not prohibited by international agreement, and reasonably calculated to notify and allow objections.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: The service method had to be ordered by the court, not forbidden by an international agreement, and "reasonably calculated" (likely enough) to tell the defendant about the suit and let it raise "objections".

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: Reviewing jurisdiction de novo under Nevada’s then-coextensive long-arm law, the panel required purposeful contacts, connection to the claim, and reasonableness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: "Reviewing" jurisdiction de novo (fresh, without deferring), under Nevada's long-arm law, then-coextensive with (reaching exactly as far as) constitutional limits, the panel required three things. These were "purposeful contacts" (deliberately reaching into Nevada), a connection between those contacts and the claim, and reasonableness.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: On written submissions the casino needed only a prima facie showing, with uncontroverted allegations accepted and conflicts resolved in its favor.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: Because the court decided on written papers, the casino needed only a "prima facie" showing: evidence that, if believed, would establish jurisdiction. "Uncontroverted" (unchallenged) allegations were accepted, and conflicts in the evidence were resolved in its favor.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: Under then-Rule 37(b)(2)(C), the panel considered timely resolution, docket management, prejudice, merits adjudication, and lesser sanctions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: Under then-Rule 37(b)(2)(C), the panel weighed five factors: "timely" resolution, the court's need to manage its docket, "prejudice" (harm) to the casino, the preference for deciding cases on the merits, and whether lesser "sanctions" would work.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.sentence: Only merits resolution favored the company; repeated disobedience, warnings, and consideration of ineffective alternatives supported default without abuse of discretion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-088.plain: Only the preference for a "merits resolution" (deciding the case on its facts) favored the company. Its repeated disobedience, the warnings, and the court's consideration of milder steps that would not work supported the default judgment, which was no "abuse of discretion".

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: That court denied relief July 12, 1966, reconsidered August 16, and issued the writ October 4 without new briefs, oral argument, or an opinion identifying extraordinary circumstances.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: The appeals court denied "relief" on July 12, 1966, reconsidered on August 16, and issued the writ (mandamus) on October 4. It did so without new briefs, oral argument, or an opinion explaining what extraordinary circumstances justified it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: Exceptional circumstances involving judicial usurpation and a clear, indisputable entitlement were essential.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: Mandamus requires truly exceptional circumstances, such as "judicial usurpation" (a judge grabbing power he lacks), plus a clear and indisputable right to relief that is beyond reasonable argument.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: Mere disagreement with an interlocutory ruling would otherwise displace Congress’s policy against piecemeal appeals.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: Otherwise any party unhappy with an "interlocutory ruling" (a mid-case ruling) could use mandamus to appeal early. That would defeat Congress's policy against "piecemeal appeals," meaning appeals of a case bit by bit instead of once at the end.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: Calling an error beyond a judge’s “power” did not supply those circumstances: courts ordinarily have authority to decide matters incorrectly.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: Labeling a mistake as beyond the judge's "power" does not change that. Judges have power to decide issues even if they decide wrongly; ordinary mistakes are fixed on a regular appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: A Rule 7(f) amendment effective July 1, 1966 removed the former cause requirement, but the challenged order predated its promulgation; the amendment’s meaning and effect were left for remand.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: A July 1, 1966 amendment to Rule 7(f) removed the old requirement to show good cause for a bill of particulars, but the judge's order came before the amendment's "promulgation" (its official issuance). What the amendment means and how it affects this case were left for "remand," meaning the case was sent back to the lower court to decide.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: Schlagenhauf, involving exceptional questions about a novel examination order and Rule 35’s scope, likewise did not make mandamus a general discovery-error remedy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: Schlagenhauf, an earlier case, allowed mandamus because it raised new, important questions about a court-ordered medical exam and the scope of Rule 35, the rule on such exams. That does not make mandamus a general "remedy" (a fix) for ordinary discovery mistakes.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.sentence: Justice Black concurred in the judgment and substantially agreed with Warren, but emphasized that absence of final judgment does not itself bar an extraordinary writ.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505.plain: Justice Black "concurred in the judgment," meaning he agreed with the result, and he mostly agreed with Chief Justice Warren's reasoning. But he stressed that the lack of a "final judgment" (the decision that ends the case) does not by itself "bar" (block) an extraordinary writ like mandamus.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: Conciliation failed, and Anderson received a right-to-sue letter before bringing a Title VII action in the Western District of North Carolina.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: "Conciliation" (the agency's attempt to get the city to settle) failed, and Anderson received a "right-to-sue letter," the agency's official permission to sue. She then brought a Title VII action, a sex-discrimination claim under the federal law against job discrimination, in the federal court for the Western District of North Carolina.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: The city lodged extensive objections, Anderson replied, and the judge entered formal findings differing substantially from her proposal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: The city objected in detail, Anderson responded, and the judge issued his own official findings, which differed a lot from her draft.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: Because Anderson conceded that ordering her appointment would be inappropriate, the court awarded $30,397 in backpay and $16,971.59 in attorney’s fees.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: Since Anderson agreed that ordering the city to appoint her to the job would be inappropriate, the court instead awarded $30,397 in "backpay" (the wages she lost) and $16,971.59 in attorney’s fees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: Pullman-Standard v. Swint, the Court’s precedent treating discriminatory intent under Title VII as factual, made Rule 52(a) applicable rather than unrestricted review of a legal conclusion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: Pullman-Standard v. Swint, an earlier Supreme Court "precedent," held that whether an employer intended to discriminate under Title VII is a question of fact. So Rule 52(a), which protects a trial judge's fact findings, applied. The appeals court could not review the issue from scratch as if it were a "legal conclusion."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: Justice White explained that clear error requires a definite and firm conviction of mistake on the whole evidence.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: Justice White said an appeals court may overturn a finding as "clearly erroneous" only if, after looking at all the evidence, it is firmly convinced a mistake was made.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: If the trial judge’s account is plausible on the complete record, choosing it over another permissible account is not clearly erroneous.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: If the trial judge's version of events is plausible in light of the whole record, choosing it over another reasonable version is not "clearly erroneous," the high bar an appeals court must find before overturning a trial judge's fact findings.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: Trial judges’ factfinding expertise, the cost of duplicating trial, and the trial’s place as the principal factfinding event supported deference.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: Appeals courts show "deference" (respect for the trial judge's view) because trial judges are skilled at "factfinding," redoing the trial would be costly, and the trial is meant to be the main event for deciding what happened.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.sentence: But adopted findings remained judicial findings reviewed for clear error.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-532.plain: Still, once a judge adopts findings they are the judge's own, and they get the same deferential review.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: In 1993, the Marxes sought vacation of the dedication and a declaration quieting title, alleging that neither township nor road commission had accepted it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: In 1993 the Marxes asked the court for "vacation" (cancellation) of the "dedication," the old offer of Birch Lane for public use, and for a declaration "quieting title," meaning a ruling that the strip was theirs. They alleged that neither the township nor the road commission had ever accepted the offer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: The government defendants sought summary disposition under Michigan Court Rule 2.116(C)(10), relying on plat approval, asserted maintenance expenditure, and an alleged assumption of jurisdiction under the McNitt Act.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: The government defendants asked for summary disposition (a ruling without a trial) under Michigan Court Rule 2.116(C)(10). They relied on the township's approval of the plat (the recorded subdivision map), money they asserted was spent maintaining the lane, and an alleged takeover of "jurisdiction" (control) over it under the McNitt Act.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: The road commission relied on the McNitt Act, repealed in 1951, which directed staged incorporation of township highway mileage and then dedicated roads in specified recorded plats.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: The road commission relied on the McNitt Act, an old law repealed in 1951. It directed the staged "incorporation" of township highway mileage into the county road system, and then of roads "dedicated" (offered for public use) in specified recorded plats.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: Kraus, an earlier dedication decision, required identification of the road or plat; even a general resolution claiming all township roads did not manifest knowing acceptance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: Kraus, an earlier "dedication" case, held that acceptance must identify the specific road or plat. Even a general resolution claiming all township roads did not "manifest" (clearly show) that the government knowingly accepted this one.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: A valid dedication required the recorded manifestation of the proprietor’s intent and timely acceptance by the proper authority.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: A valid "dedication" (gift of land for public use) required a recorded "manifestation" of the "proprietor's" intent, meaning the owner's clear, recorded showing that it meant to give the land. It also required "timely" acceptance by the proper government body, meaning acceptance within a reasonable time.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: The commission argued at oral argument that only it could accept, but failed to brief the issue; the court treated it as abandoned and did not decide which body possessed the power.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: At "oral argument" the road commission argued that only it could accept roads, but it had not raised that in its written brief. So the court treated the point as "abandoned" (given up) and did not decide which body had that power.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: The offer had therefore lapsed before the resolution.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: So the offer had "lapsed" (expired) before the township's 1979 resolution trying to accept it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: Withdrawal required conduct inconsistent with public ownership, assessed with its nature and government acquiescence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: "Withdrawal" of the offer required the owners to act in ways inconsistent with public ownership. The court weighed the nature of that conduct and the government's "acquiescence," meaning whether it let the conduct go on without objecting.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.sentence: A general public-policy argument favoring lake access was abandoned because it was omitted from the statement of questions and lacked pertinent authority.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-068.plain: A general argument that public policy favors lake access was "abandoned" (treated as given up). It was left out of the brief's "statement of questions," the list of issues presented for review, and was not supported by relevant legal authority.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: The September 2020 third amended complaint alleged plan breach, ASA breach as a beneficiary, and breach of good faith and fair dealing, seeking punitive damages and attorney fees.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: The September 2020 third amended complaint alleged a "breach" (violation) of the plan; breach of the ASA, Meritain's contract with the hospital, which Peterson said he could enforce as a "beneficiary" it was meant to benefit; and breach of the duty of "good faith and fair dealing." It sought punitive damages, meant to punish, and attorney fees.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: The district court nevertheless treated lack of privity and beneficiary status as dispositive.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: The "district court" (the trial court) still treated two points as "dispositive," meaning enough to decide the case: Peterson had no "privity" (direct contract) with Meritain, and he was not a beneficiary of its contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: Meritain first invoked the ASA’s New York choice-of-law clause on appeal; that nonjurisdictional, nonfundamental issue was waived, so Wyoming law applied.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: Meritain first invoked the ASA’s clause choosing New York law (a "choice-of-law clause") on appeal. Because the issue was "nonjurisdictional" (not about the court's basic power to hear the case) and not fundamental, raising it so late meant it was "waived," or given up, so Wyoming law applied.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: Contractual adoption of lawful ERISA terms was possible, but references to procedures, definitions, and discretion did not incorporate a fiduciary cause of action against this administrator.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: The plan could adopt ERISA-style terms by contract, but borrowing ERISA's procedures, definitions and grants of discretion did not give members ERISA's right to sue this administrator as a fiduciary (a trustee-like manager).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: It adopted a duty for an administrator acting sufficiently like an insurer without making direct privity indispensable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: The court held that a plan administrator acting enough like an insurer owes a duty to handle claims in good faith, even without direct "privity," meaning a direct contract with the member.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: Earlier fee sanctions already existed, and disputed prejudice, explanations, and culpability left the additional request within trial discretion.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: Meritain had already been ordered to pay fee "sanctions" (penalties) earlier. Because "prejudice" (harm to Peterson), Meritain's explanations, and its "culpability" (fault) were all disputed, denying more was within the trial judge's "discretion," the room to make a judgment call.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: Sensitive information and proportionality constrained relevance; training, qualifications, and incentives could be explored by interrogatories or deposition, and exclusive need for files was not shown.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: Employees' files held sensitive information, and "proportionality" (keeping discovery in scale with the case's needs) limited what was relevant. Peterson could learn about training, qualifications, and incentives through "interrogatories" (written questions) or depositions, and he did not show that only the files would do.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.sentence: The district court could reconsider particular documents on remand with protective measures or in camera review, so the ruling created no permanent personnel-file immunity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-083.plain: "On remand" (when the case went back), the district court could reconsider specific documents with protective measures or "in camera" review, meaning the judge looks at them privately first. So the ruling gave personnel files no permanent "immunity" from being produced.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: Lewis claimed a warranty of suitability for his particular system, breach through lack of additives, and resulting repair costs and lost profits.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: Lewis claimed a "warranty," a promise by Mobil that the oil was suitable for his particular system, and a "breach" of it because the oil lacked additives. He sought the resulting repair costs and lost profits.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: Mobil denied the warranty, attributed breakdowns to filtration and air entrainment, and challenged notice, mitigation, causation, and damages.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: Mobil denied making any "warranty" (promise about the oil) and blamed the breakdowns on poor filtering and air getting mixed into the oil ("air entrainment"). It also challenged whether Lewis gave proper notice, whether he reasonably limited his losses ("mitigation"), whether the oil caused the damage, and the damages amount.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: The seller needed reason to know the buyer’s particular purpose and reliance on its skill or judgment.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: For the UCC's implied warranty that goods fit a buyer's particular purpose, the seller must have had reason to know that purpose. It must also have had reason to know the buyer was relying on the seller's skill or "judgment" to pick suitable goods.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: Section 2-712’s cover provision concerned nondelivery or a buyer able to reject known defects, rather than automatically governing continued use under uncertainty, while the general duty to avoid preventable loss still applied.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: Section 2-712's "cover" rule, which lets a buyer buy substitute goods, applies when a seller fails to deliver or when a buyer knows of defects and can reject the goods. It did not automatically govern a buyer who kept using the goods while unsure of the cause, though the general duty to avoid preventable losses still applied.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: Repeated communications also supplied § 2-607 notice that the transaction was troublesome; Lewis need not list every legal objection or prove bad faith.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: Lewis's repeated complaints also gave Mobil the notice § 2-607 requires, warning it that the deal was troublesome. He did not have to list every legal objection or prove "bad faith," meaning dishonesty.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: Arkansas’s older tacit-agreement approach did not control Code consequential damages: § 2-715’s comments rejected requiring a conscious promise to insure losses.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: Arkansas's older "tacit-agreement" test, which asked whether the seller had in effect agreed to cover the buyer's losses, did not control "consequential damages" (indirect losses, like lost profits) under the Code. The comments to § 2-715 reject requiring a conscious promise to insure such losses.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: The January 7, 1971 opinion initially understood the lump verdict to include losses during thirty months of Ambrex use and later losses caused by capital shortages despite successful equipment operation.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: The court's January 7, 1971 "opinion" first read the "lump verdict" (the jury's single, undivided damages figure) as covering two things. It included losses during the thirty months Ambrex was in use, and later losses caused by Lewis's shortage of capital (money) even after the equipment worked properly.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.sentence: Unable to separate permissible and impermissible sums, the court reversed for a new trial on damages only, leaving liability intact.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0093.plain: Because it could not separate the allowable damages from the improper ones, the court "reversed" and ordered a new trial on damages only. The finding of "liability," that Mobil was legally responsible, stood.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: Dow invoked the Securities and Exchange Commission’s then-existing Rule 14a-8 exclusions for proposals primarily promoting general political or social causes and for ordinary business matters.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: Dow relied on two exclusions then in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s Rule 14a-8. They let a company leave out shareholder proposals mainly promoting general political or social causes, or dealing with "ordinary business" matters, meaning routine management decisions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: The agency’s Division of Corporation Finance relied on Dow’s letter and counsel’s opinion in advising that it would recommend no action if Dow omitted the proposal.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: The agency’s Division of Corporation Finance, an SEC staff office, relied on Dow's letter and its "counsel's" (lawyers') opinion. It advised that it would "recommend no action," meaning it would not ask for enforcement, if Dow left the proposal out.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: The Commission’s approved no-action position was reviewable because of its practical finality, impact, and procedural formality.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: The Commission’s approved "no-action position" (its decision not to act against Dow) could be reviewed in court. That was because in practice it was final, it had real effects, and it came out of a formal process.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: The Committee, a beneficiary of statutory corporate-suffrage protections, had expended effort pursuing it, lost possible agency assistance, and faced an adverse agency interpretation in any private suit.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: The Committee was a "beneficiary" of the law's "corporate-suffrage" protections, meaning shareholders' right to a voice and vote in the company. It had spent effort pursuing the proposal, lost possible help from the agency, and would face the agency's unfavorable view if it sued Dow itself.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: Rule 14a-8 required an adversarial exchange in which management supplied the proposal, exclusion reasons, and legal support to both shareholder and agency; management bore the burden of establishing exclusion.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: Rule 14a-8 required an "adversarial" (two-sided) exchange: management had to send the proposal, its reasons for leaving it out, and its legal support to both the shareholder and the agency. Management "bore the burden," meaning it had to prove the exclusion was allowed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: Direct appellate review also matched the requested relief: correction of a legal approach and reconsideration, without a fact trial or injunction requiring a district court.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: "Direct appellate review" (going straight to the appeals court) also fit the "relief" sought: correcting the SEC's legal approach and "reconsideration" of its decision. No fact trial or "injunction" (court order to do or stop something) was sought, which would have needed a district court, the trial-level court.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: Voluntary cessation would not moot likely recurring conduct, but the majority found no reasonable expectation of recurrence here.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: Normally "voluntary cessation" (a defendant simply stopping its conduct) does not make a case "moot," or no longer a live dispute, if the conduct is likely to recur. But the majority found no reasonable expectation that it would happen again here.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.sentence: Article III therefore barred a merits ruling.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-035.plain: So Article III, the part of the Constitution limiting federal courts to real, ongoing disputes, barred a "merits ruling," meaning a decision on who was actually right.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.sentence: As the jury was about to be selected, she challenged the array because its source lists contained no women.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.plain: Just before jury selection, she "challenged the array," meaning she objected to the whole pool of potential jurors, because the lists it was drawn from included no women.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.sentence: The Commonwealth joined an issue of law, and the judge sustained its position.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.plain: The Commonwealth (the state of Massachusetts, as prosecutor) "joined an issue of law": it did not dispute the facts and argued only that leaving women off was legal. The judge "sustained" (agreed with) the state's position.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.sentence: Welosky was convicted and preserved exceptions concerning the jury, evidence, and instructions.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.plain: Welosky was convicted and preserved "exceptions," meaning formal objections recorded so a higher court could review them, to the judge's rulings on the jury, the evidence, and his instructions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.sentence: Chief Justice Rugg’s Supreme Judicial Court opinion stressed that earlier justices’ adverse advisory answers to the legislature were individual constitutional advice, not adjudications entitled to stare decisis.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.plain: Chief Justice Rugg’s opinion for the Supreme Judicial Court, the state's highest court, said earlier justices' "advisory answers" to the legislature, saying women could not serve, were only individual constitutional advice. They were not court decisions, so they did not bind the court under "stare decisis," the rule that courts follow their own past decisions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.sentence: The court had to examine the actual litigants’ questions afresh, including statutory eligibility, federal equal protection, and the state guarantee of judgment by peers.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.plain: So the court had to consider afresh the actual litigants’ questions (those of the parties in this very case): whether the statute made women eligible, whether excluding them violated federal "equal protection," and whether it violated the state's guarantee of judgment by one's peers.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.sentence: The court acknowledged federal supremacy and the Fourteenth Amendment’s broader protection but distinguished the Reconstruction Amendments from the Nineteenth Amendment’s voting command.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-062.plain: The court acknowledged "federal supremacy" (federal law overrides state law) and the Fourteenth Amendment's broader protection. But it distinguished the Reconstruction Amendments, the post-Civil War amendments used to bar racial exclusion from juries, from the Nineteenth Amendment, which only commands that women be allowed to vote.

cp-afa.sentence: Whitchurch moved for summary judgment on whether the information was confidential enough to qualify as trade secrets.
cp-afa.plain: Whitchurch moved for "summary judgment" (a ruling without a trial) on whether the information was confidential enough to count as "trade secrets," business information the law protects.

cp-afa.sentence: At oral argument, the district judge raised the amount in controversy sua sponte.
cp-afa.plain: At "oral argument" (the hearing), the district judge "sua sponte" (on his own, without either side asking) raised the "amount in controversy": whether enough money was at stake for the case to be in federal court.

cp-afa.sentence: At the end of that same hearing, the judge dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, reasoning AFA could not prove more than $50,000 in damages.
cp-afa.plain: At the end of that same hearing, the judge "dismissed" (threw out) the case for lack of subject-matter "jurisdiction," meaning the federal court's power over this kind of case. He reasoned that AFA could not prove more than $50,000 in "damages," the minimum then required.

cp-afa.sentence: Under St. Paul Mercury’s amount-in-controversy standard, a sum apparently claimed in good faith controlled unless it was legally certain that the claim did not exceed the jurisdictional threshold.
cp-afa.plain: Under St. Paul Mercury’s amount-in-controversy standard (from an earlier Supreme Court case), the sum the plaintiff claims "in good faith" (honestly) controls. The only exception is when it is legally certain the claim could not exceed the "jurisdictional threshold," the minimum needed for federal court.

cp-afa.sentence: Before finding the minimum impossible, a court had to give an appropriate, reasonable chance to show a good-faith basis for recovery above it.
cp-afa.plain: Before "finding" (ruling) that recovery above the minimum is impossible, a court must give the plaintiff a fair, reasonable chance to show a "good-faith" (honest) basis for claiming more.

cp-afa.sentence: Controlling New York law apparently permitted punitive damages for sufficiently gross and wanton trade-secret misconduct.
cp-afa.plain: Controlling New York law apparently allowed "punitive damages," extra money meant to punish, for trade-secret misconduct that was gross and "wanton" enough, meaning outrageous and reckless.

cp-afa.sentence: The assigned note describes different circuits’ approaches to whether defendant-side compliance costs may also value nonmonetary relief, so the decision did not settle every jurisdiction’s valuation perspective.
cp-afa.plain: The assigned note explains that federal "circuits" (regional appeals courts) differ on whether "nonmonetary relief," such as a court order, can also be valued by what obeying it would cost the defendant. So this decision did not settle how every "jurisdiction" (court system) values such relief.

cp-afa.sentence: Whitchurch’s original trade-secret argument did not supply an alternative basis for affirmance.
cp-afa.plain: Whitchurch's original argument, that the information was not a trade secret, did not give the appeals court another basis for "affirmance," meaning upholding the dismissal.

cp-afa.sentence: Viewing reasonable inferences for AFA as the summary-judgment opponent, the appellate court found genuine material disputes.
cp-afa.plain: Drawing "reasonable inferences" (sensible conclusions from the evidence) in AFA's favor, as required for the side opposing a summary-judgment motion, the "appellate court" (appeals court) found genuine disputes over material facts. So a trial was needed.

cp-afa.sentence: AFA gained a fair opportunity to substantiate the jurisdictional amount and pursue the claims, not a damages award or injunction.
cp-afa.plain: AFA won only a fair chance to "substantiate" (prove with evidence) that enough money was at stake and to pursue its claims. It did not win a "damages award" (money) or an injunction (a court order).

cp-atlantic-marine.sentence: Atlantic Marine moved to dismiss under § 1406(a) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(3), arguing that the clause made Texas venue improper.
cp-atlantic-marine.plain: Atlantic Marine moved to dismiss under § 1406(a) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(3), the provisions for cases filed in the wrong place. It argued that the forum-selection clause made Texas "venue" improper, meaning Texas was a legally wrong place to sue.

cp-atlantic-marine.sentence: It correctly selected § 1404(a) as the route for the federal forum clause but put the burden on Atlantic Marine and weighed the clause among ordinary private and public factors.
cp-atlantic-marine.plain: The trial court correctly chose § 1404(a), the transfer-for-convenience statute, as the way to enforce a "forum clause" pointing to another federal court. But it made Atlantic Marine bear the burden of justifying transfer and weighed the clause as just one of the usual private-convenience and public-interest factors.

cp-atlantic-marine.sentence: Venue legislation, generally § 1391, determines whether a federal location is wrong or improper under § 1406(a) and Rule 12(b)(3).
cp-atlantic-marine.plain: Venue laws, mainly the general statute § 1391, decide whether a federal court is a "wrong" or improper place under § 1406(a) and Rule 12(b)(3), not private contracts.

cp-atlantic-marine.sentence: Private agreement does not convert a statutorily proper district into an improper one.
cp-atlantic-marine.plain: A private contract cannot turn a court that is "statutorily" proper (proper under the venue statutes) into an improper one.

cp-atlantic-marine.sentence: Third, transfer to enforce the clause would not carry Texas choice-of-law rules.
