brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: The Court read Delaware's Nottingham Partners decision and the later Union Square "arbitration" case to allow settlements releasing related claims that Chancery (Delaware's Court of Chancery) could not itself "adjudicate," or decide. Those claims had to share the settled case's "factual predicate," meaning they rested on the same facts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: Its judgment could nonetheless operate as a collateral bar when the federal court applied § 1738.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: Even so, Delaware's judgment could work as a "collateral bar," blocking the separate federal case, when the federal court applied § 1738's command to respect state judgments.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: Section 27 contained no express exception to § 1738, so respondents needed an implied partial repeal based on irreconcilable conflict.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: Section 27 contained no "express" (stated in words) exception to § 1738. So the shareholders needed an "implied partial repeal," meaning Congress silently overrode § 1738 in part, which requires an "irreconcilable conflict" between the two laws.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: Evaluating potential claim value to determine fairness was not deciding the claims’ merits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: Estimating what the claims might be worth to judge a settlement's fairness was not deciding the claims' "merits" (who would actually win).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: That differed from a court lacking power over the proceeding it actually entertained.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: This was not a case where the state court had no power to hear the very case in front of it, which would make its judgment worthless elsewhere.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: He also stressed its ability to examine whether adequacy of representation had been fully and fairly litigated in Delaware.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: Justice Stevens also stressed that the lower federal court could examine whether "adequacy of representation" (whether the class leaders and lawyers properly represented absent shareholders) had been fully and fairly "litigated" in Delaware.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: She questioned blending an identical-factual-predicate test with a broader same-transaction approach.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: Justice Ginsburg questioned the majority's blending of the narrower "identical-factual-predicate" test (released claims must rest on the very same facts) with a broader same-transaction approach (any claims arising from the same deal).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: Her Part II–B, joined by Stevens and Justice Souter, emphasized that absent class members still required adequate representation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: Her Part II–B, "joined by" (agreed to by) Justice Stevens and Justice Souter, stressed that absent class members, who took no part in the case, still had to be adequately represented before they could be bound.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.sentence: Recognition of a settlement judgment was the holding; approval of the settlement’s due-process sufficiency was not.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-MATSUSHITA-EPSTEIN.plain: The Court held only that the Delaware judgment had to be respected. It did not decide that the settlement treated class members fairly enough to satisfy due process.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: In November 2001 she sued the restaurant’s owner, Y & H Corporation, under Title VII and Louisiana law, invoking federal-question and supplemental jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: In November 2001 she sued the restaurant's owner, Y & H Corporation, under Title VII (the federal job-discrimination law) and Louisiana law. The federal court had "federal-question" jurisdiction over the claim arising under federal law, and supplemental jurisdiction over the closely related state claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: With consent to a magistrate judge’s adjudication, a two-day jury trial found harassment and constructive discharge under federal and state law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: With both sides' consent to a magistrate judge's adjudication (deciding the case), a two-day "jury trial" found sexual harassment and "constructive discharge" under federal and state law. Constructive discharge means conditions were so bad she was effectively forced to quit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: Two weeks later Y & H invoked the rule requiring dismissal whenever subject-matter jurisdiction was lacking.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: After losing, Y & H argued for the first time that the court had no power to hear this kind of case at all, a defect that requires dismissal whenever it is found.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: It vacated the verdict judgment, dismissed the federal claim with prejudice, and dismissed the state claims without prejudice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: It "vacated" (erased) the "judgment" entered on the jury's verdict, dismissed the federal claim with prejudice, meaning for good, and dismissed the state claims "without prejudice," which left her free to refile them in state court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: True jurisdictional defects were nonwaivable and demanded attention even after judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: True "jurisdictional" defects, meaning a real lack of court power, were "nonwaivable": the parties cannot give them up, and courts must address them even after "judgment."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: A failure-to-state-a-claim defense survived through merits trial, but not this far beyond it.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: A "defense" of failure to state a claim, meaning the facts alleged do not add up to a legal claim, could be raised as late as the "merits" trial. It could not be raised this long after trial, as Y & H tried to do.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: Calling workforce coverage jurisdictional would also require independent judicial investigation without congressional instruction, permit judicial resolution of facts that belonged to a jury as claim elements, and compel dismissal of the entire case including tried state claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: Calling the workforce-size requirement "jurisdictional" would force courts to investigate it themselves without any instruction from Congress. It would let judges decide facts that, as elements of the claim, belonged to a jury, and would compel "dismissal" of the whole case, including the state claims already tried.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: A merits defeat instead allowed discretion concerning supplemental claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: A loss on the "merits" instead left the judge "discretion" (a choice) whether to keep deciding the supplemental state claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: The Court adopted a rule requiring Congress clearly to classify a statutory-coverage threshold as jurisdictional before courts treated it that way.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: The Court adopted a rule: a statutory coverage threshold counts as "jurisdictional," a limit on court power, only if Congress clearly says so. Otherwise it is just part of what the plaintiff must prove.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: Rather, the employer could not revive an untimely merits objection as a claim that the completed judgment was jurisdictionally void.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: Rather, the employer could not revive an "untimely" (too late) objection on the merits by claiming the completed judgment was "void," meaning legally nothing, for lack of jurisdiction.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.sentence: The Court also preserved the distinct bar against federal claims manufactured solely to obtain jurisdiction or wholly insubstantial and frivolous; Arbaugh’s claim plainly was not one.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-010.plain: The Court also kept the separate "bar" against federal claims invented solely to get federal "jurisdiction," or so insubstantial they are frivolous (wholly without merit). Arbaugh's claim plainly was not one of those.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: King’s Bench and Chancery disputed whether equity could intervene after a common-law judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: King’s Bench, England's top common-law court, and Chancery, the Chancellor's court of equity (fairness-based relief), disputed whether equity could step in after a common-law judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Opponents invoked the praemunire statute of 27 Edward III, chapter 1, and a prohibition under 4 Henry IV.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: Chancery's opponents cited the "praemunire" statute of 27 Edward III, chapter 1, which punished taking matters belonging to the King's courts to other authorities. They also cited a prohibition, allowing royal-court judgments to be undone only through regular common-law review, in a statute of 4 Henry IV.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: The practice continued from Henry VII through the current Chancellor and covered real and personal actions, multiple common-law courts, verdicts, demurrers, and writs of error.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: The practice ran from Henry VII to the current Chancellor and covered "real and personal actions" (suits over land, and suits over debts or damages) in several common-law courts. It reached cases decided by jury "verdicts," by demurrers (rulings on pure points of law), and after "writs of error" (review by a higher court).

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Equity could follow judgment and even execution, often on grounds existing beforehand rather than a later bargain.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: "Equity" could give relief after judgment and even after "execution" (enforcement of the judgment), often on grounds that existed beforehand rather than on a later "bargain" (new agreement).

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: B accepted that the judgments were correct under strict common-law rules but claimed equitable grounds unavailable through error, attaint, or other common-law remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: B accepted that the "judgments" were correct under strict common-law rules. But he claimed "equitable" (fairness-based) grounds that "error" (common-law appeal), attaint (a challenge to a false jury verdict), or other common-law "remedies" could not provide.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Counsel found orders and decrees releasing judgments, preventing or correcting possession obtained through them, handling mesne profits, and releasing costs.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: "Counsel" (the lawyers) found Chancery orders and "decrees" releasing people from judgments and preventing or undoing takeovers of land obtained through them. Others dealt with "mesne profits" (income from land while it was wrongly held) and released court costs.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Their eight praemunire reasons emphasized that the statute targeted prejudice to royal jurisdiction through another authority, while Chancery was itself the King’s court.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: Their eight reasons on praemunire stressed that the "statute" targeted harm to royal "jurisdiction" (the King's courts' power) by turning to another authority, such as the Pope. Chancery, by contrast, was itself the King's court.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Severe exclusion from royal protection fit adherence to foreign jurisdiction rather than excess within a royal tribunal.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: The statute's severe penalty, putting offenders outside the King's protection, fit loyalty to a foreign "jurisdiction," not a royal "tribunal" (court) going beyond its proper bounds.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Error and attaint reversed judgments, while proper Chancery relief addressed the prevailing party’s conscience.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: Error and attaint "reversed" judgments, undoing them for legal mistakes or false jury verdicts. Proper Chancery relief instead acted on the prevailing party’s conscience: the judgment stood, but the winner was ordered not to use it unfairly.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Requiring anticipatory equity before knowing whether common law would provide relief could also leave a deserving party without an effective remedy.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: Requiring people to seek "equity" in advance, before knowing whether the common law would give "relief," could leave a deserving party with no effective remedy.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: He commanded the Chancellor or Keeper of the Great Seal to continue relief warranted by the merits and justice of complaints despite common-law proceedings, consistently with ancient continuing Chancery practice.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: King James commanded the Chancellor or Keeper of the Great Seal (the head of Chancery) to keep granting relief warranted by "the merits" and justice of complaints, despite common-law proceedings. That matched Chancery's long-standing practice.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: He asserted authority to settle jurisdictional differences among his courts and ordered enrollment to reduce future disputes.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: James claimed authority to settle "jurisdictional" disputes among his courts, meaning which court could decide what. He "ordered" the decision enrolled (officially recorded) to reduce future disputes.

brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.sentence: Its premise was equitable conscience distinct from the legal issue already decided and merit in the specific equitable cause.
brief-CP-COMP-HIST-CHANCERY-1616.plain: Its premise was an "equitable" ground of conscience, separate from the "legal issue" already decided, and real merit in the specific equitable claim.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Alvin and Irene Gustafson owned a 160-acre Fayette County farm as tenants in common, including a five-acre home and building site.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Alvin and Irene Gustafson owned a 160-acre Fayette County farm as "tenants in common," meaning each held a share of the whole. It included a five-acre home and building site.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Annual $28,000 installments included principal and 7.5-percent interest, with a March 1, 1987 balloon.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Annual $28,000 "installments" covered both principal and 7.5-percent interest, with a "balloon" payment, one large final payment of the remaining balance, due March 1, 1987.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Forfeiture carried no deficiency.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: "Forfeiture," meaning the buyers losing the farm and what they had paid if they defaulted, carried no "deficiency": they would not also owe any remaining shortfall.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: An initial appeal, reported separately at 271 N.W.2d 738, was premature because a motion to enlarge findings was unresolved.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: An initial appeal, reported separately at 271 N.W.2d 738, was "premature" (too early). A "motion to enlarge findings," asking the trial judge to expand its findings, was still unresolved, so the judgment was not yet final.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Justice McGiverin’s Iowa Supreme Court opinion reviewed de novo, weighing credibility findings without being bound.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Justice McGiverin’s Iowa Supreme Court "opinion" reviewed the case de novo, deciding the facts afresh. It gave weight to the trial judge's "credibility findings" (whom to believe) without being bound by them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Iowa’s § 622.32 restricted competent oral proof of land transfers rather than intrinsically voiding every oral contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Iowa's § 622.32, its statute of frauds, limited using oral testimony as "competent" (legally admissible) proof of land transfers. It did not work by "voiding" (canceling) every oral contract in itself.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Section 622.33 excepted transactions where vendors received any purchase money.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Section 622.33 made an exception when the "vendors" (sellers) had received any "purchase money," meaning any part of the price.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Buyers still needed a preponderance of clear, satisfactory, and convincing proof.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: The buyers still had to prove the oral deal by a "preponderance" (the greater weight) of clear, satisfactory, and convincing evidence.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: A contemplated writing did not prevent an immediate oral contract unless execution was a condition of obligation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Planning to sign a writing later did not prevent an immediate "oral contract" unless signing was "a condition" of being bound, meaning the parties intended no deal until they signed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Section 561.13 separately required both spouses’ execution of the same instrument to transfer homestead rights.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Section 561.13 separately required both spouses to sign the same "instrument" (legal document) to transfer homestead rights, the special protections for a family home. So an oral deal could not transfer the home site.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Oral-transfer cases after relinquishment depended on abandonment, but the Gustafsons still possessed their home.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Cases enforcing oral sales of a home involved owners who had given it up; the Gustafsons still lived in theirs.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: The buyers could nevertheless elect partial performance for the remaining 155 acres.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: The buyers could still elect "partial performance," meaning force the sale of the remaining 155 acres without the home site.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Although rural homestead law ordinarily allowed up to forty acres, the sellers had identified and marked only the five-acre site; they were estopped against these buyers from expanding it to defeat the remaining sale.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Rural "homestead" law usually allowed a home site of up to forty acres, but the sellers had identified and marked only five acres. They were "estopped" (barred by their own conduct) from expanding it against these buyers to defeat the rest of the sale.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Delivering an unprivileged document to counsel did not make it confidential, so it could identify the tract to subtract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Giving an unprivileged document, one not protected as a lawyer-client secret, to "counsel" (a lawyer) did not make it confidential. So it could be used to identify the tract to subtract from the sale.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Recognizing the existing earnest money also let the September agreement escape the oral-proof bar, but did not furnish consideration for the extra $10,000.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Recognizing the "earnest money" (deposit) already paid also got the September agreement past the oral-proof bar. But it did not furnish "consideration" (something given in exchange) for the extra $10,000, so that promise was not binding.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Actual mutual rescission discharges reciprocal duties and allows a fresh bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: A genuine mutual "rescission," both sides agreeing to cancel the contract, discharges both sides' duties and allows a fresh "bargain."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Modification leaves the original obligations standing except as altered.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: A change to a contract keeps the old deal in place except for the changed terms, and traditionally the change needs something new in exchange to bind.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: The draft Restatement permitted fair and equitable modifications for unanticipated circumstances.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: A draft of the Restatement, an influential summary of contract law, allowed contract changes without new consideration if they were fair in light of unexpected events.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Real estate presumptively justified specific performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Real estate "presumptively" justified specific performance, meaning courts assume, unless shown otherwise, that land is unique enough to order the sale actually completed rather than award money.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Possession would occur sixty days after procedendo issued; buyers then owed the remaining $35,000 down payment, with the original $5,000 credited.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: The buyers would take possession sixty days after "procedendo" issued, the formal order sending the case back to the trial court. They then owed the remaining $35,000 of the down payment, with the original $5,000 credited.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.sentence: Accounting balances bore legal interest only from possession.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-038.plain: Balances owed between the parties in the accounting bore "legal interest," the rate set by statute, only from the date of possession.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: On February 22, 1995, it granted Orion Sales an exclusive, nontransferable three-year license for specified Emerson-brand video and television goods sold to Wal-Mart, historically Emerson’s largest customer.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: On February 22, 1995, Emerson granted Orion Sales an exclusive, "nontransferable" (it could not be passed on) three-year "license" (permission to use the brand) for specified Emerson-brand video and television "goods" sold to Wal-Mart. Wal-Mart had historically been Emerson's largest customer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: In this diversity case, Judge Sloviter’s Third Circuit opinion applied New Jersey law and reviewed summary judgment and legal interpretation plenarily, drawing reasonable inferences for Emerson.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: In this "diversity case," a federal case between parties from different states, Judge Sloviter’s Third Circuit opinion applied New Jersey law. It "reviewed" the summary judgment and questions of legal interpretation "plenarily," meaning completely afresh, drawing reasonable inferences in favor of Emerson, the side that lost without trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: The district court recognized two plausible meanings of exploit—advancing the licensed brand or advancing Orion’s own interests—yet treated uncertainty as a reason to reject an affirmative duty.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: The "district court" saw two plausible meanings of "exploit": advancing the licensed Emerson brand, or advancing Orion's own interests. Yet it treated that uncertainty as a reason to reject any affirmative duty on Orion to promote the brand.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Ambiguity was a legal question informed by wording, proposed meanings, and relevant external evidence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: Whether contract wording is ambiguous is a "legal question" for the judge, informed by the wording, each side's proposed meaning, and relevant outside evidence.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: One reasonable interpretation could permit summary judgment; competing reasonable meanings ordinarily required factfinding.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: If only one interpretation is reasonable, "summary judgment" (a ruling without trial) may be proper. Competing reasonable meanings ordinarily require "factfinding," usually by a jury, about what the parties meant.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Cases linking exploitation of licensed property with diligence largely involved implied duties and did not control this express term.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: Cases linking "exploitation" of licensed property with diligence mostly involved "implied duties" (duties courts read into a contract), so they did not control this "express term," one written into the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Here substantial guaranteed compensation—$4 million each year for three years—protected against nonuse; Emerson’s chief executive acknowledged that purpose.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: Courts imply an efforts duty when the owner would earn nothing if the other side sat idle. Here Emerson was guaranteed $4 million a year no matter what, and its own chief executive admitted that guarantee was meant to protect against Orion doing nothing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Authorities examining consideration and intention, and restraint in revising a counseled, elaborate bargain, supported rejection.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: Cases examining "consideration" (what each side gave in exchange) and the parties' intentions, and courts' reluctance to revise an elaborate "bargain" negotiated with lawyers, supported refusing to imply an efforts duty.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: New Jersey’s implied covenant protected justified expectations and the bargain’s fruits even where express terms were satisfied.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: New Jersey's "implied covenant" of good faith and fair dealing, an unwritten promise in every contract, protects each side's justified expectations and the bargain’s fruits. It can be broken even where all the "express terms" (written terms) are followed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: The court cited the Uniform Commercial Code’s honesty-in-fact concept by analogy while recognizing that this license was not governed by the Code’s sales provisions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: The court borrowed, by analogy, the Uniform Commercial Code's "honesty in fact" idea of good faith, meaning actual honesty. It recognized that the Code's sales rules did not govern this license.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Economic vulnerability was relevant, not an indispensable element; evidence of losses and returns burdens also existed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: Emerson's economic vulnerability to Orion was "relevant" to the bad-faith claim but not an "indispensable" (required) element. There was also evidence of Emerson's losses and of burdens from returned goods.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Tortious interference ordinarily required an outsider, and that limit extended to agents acting within their corporate relationship.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: "Tortious interference," the wrong of meddling with someone else's contract, ordinarily required an outsider to the contract. That limit also covered agents acting within their corporate relationship with a party.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: The district court entered both awards with prejudgment interest and offset them.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: The "district court" added prejudgment interest (interest for the time before judgment) to both awards and then "offset" them, subtracting one from the other.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.sentence: Interest on Orion’s amount from July 15, 1995, reasonably used the midpoint of the improper-charge period and was no abuse of equitable discretion.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-084.plain: Starting interest on Orion's award from July 15, 1995, reasonably used the midpoint of the period of improper charges. It was no abuse of "equitable discretion," the judge's fairness-based judgment call.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: The agreement provided individual allotments and tribal trust lands, then ceded the remaining 549,559 acres to the United States.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: The agreement gave tribal members individual "allotments" (plots) and kept tribal trust lands, held by the U.S. for the tribe. It then "ceded" (transferred) the remaining 549,559 acres to the United States.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Of that, $626,222 was payable per capita as soon as practicable, and $1 million would remain in trust earning 5%.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: Of that, $626,222 was to be paid "per capita" (to each tribal member individually) as soon as "practicable," meaning feasible. Another $1 million would stay in trust, earning 5% interest.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Under Indian Claims Commission Act § 2(3) and (5), the Tribe sought revision for fraud, duress, or unconscionable consideration and relief for unfair and dishonorable dealings outside ordinary legal and equitable rules.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: Under Indian Claims Commission Act § 2(3) and (5), the Tribe sought revision of the deal for fraud, duress, or "unconscionable" (shockingly unfair) consideration. It also sought "relief" for unfair and dishonorable dealings, even outside ordinary "legal and equitable" rules.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: The Commission called one optimistic and the other pessimistic, said evidence might support $4 at most, and found the price gap insufficiently unconscionable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: The Commission called one expert's valuation optimistic and the other pessimistic, said the "evidence" might support $4 an acre at most, and found the price gap not "unconscionable" enough for relief.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Commissioner Scott separately thought the aggregate shortfall unconscionable but believed precedent requiring very gross disparity prevented relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: Commissioner Scott separately thought the total shortfall "unconscionable" (shockingly unfair). But he believed "precedent" (earlier decisions) requiring a very gross gap between price and value prevented "relief."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Nonetheless, substantial evidence supported $4 and the overwhelming weight made it a minimum, not the highest plausible value.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: Even so, "substantial evidence" (enough evidence a reasonable person could accept) supported $4 an acre. And the overwhelming weight of the evidence made $4 the minimum value, not the highest plausible one.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Precedent required very gross inequality when price alone supplied unconscionability, but no fixed percentage.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: "Precedent" required a very gross inequality when price alone was the basis for "unconscionability," but set no fixed percentage.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: The Commission also misused the Miami comparison, whose prior appeal corrected consideration to 38% of value rather than deciding that 63% was adequate.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: The Commission misread the Miami case: on an earlier appeal there, the court had recalculated the price paid as only 38% of the land's value; it never held that a price of 63% of value was fair.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Most importantly, $4 marked the least a reasonable willing seller would accept, and the legitimate valuation range began there and extended upward.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: Most importantly, $4 marked the least a reasonable "willing seller" (an owner free to refuse a bad offer) would accept. The legitimate range of values began there and went upward.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Neither the differential nor illustrative interest became a money judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: Neither the price differential nor the illustrative interest figures became a "money judgment," a court order to pay; they only showed how large the underpayment was.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Interest against the United States ordinarily required express statutory or contractual authority, apart from the identified constitutional-taking exception.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: The United States does not have to pay interest on money it owes unless a law or contract expressly says so, except when it takes property and owes just compensation under the Constitution.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.sentence: Pawnee involved an express sum unpaid; this case involved money beyond the promised amount.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-013.plain: The Pawnee case involved a promised sum the government never paid; here the Tribe sought interest on extra money beyond anything the agreement promised.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: It sued in the federal District of Connecticut for breach, quantum meruit for services anticipating later phases, and detrimental reliance on a promise to pay for preconstruction work.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: Klewin sued in the federal District of Connecticut for "breach" of contract and for quantum meruit, the fair value of services it performed in anticipation of later phases. It also claimed "detrimental reliance," losses from relying on a promise to pay for preconstruction work.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: General Statutes § 52-550(a)(5) required a signed writing for an agreement not to be performed within one year of its making.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: Connecticut General Statutes § 52-550(a)(5), part of its statute of frauds, required a signed writing for an agreement that is not to be performed within one year of being made.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: It certified whether an agreement stating no performance time is indefinite and outside the provision, and whether the provision bars an agreement whose performance contemplates more than a year but whose terms do not expressly exclude earlier completion.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: The federal appeals court certified two questions to Connecticut's top court. Is an agreement stating no time for "performance" "indefinite," and so outside the one-year provision? And does the provision bar an agreement expected to take over a year if its terms do not expressly rule out finishing sooner?

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: The statute descended from the 1677 English law addressing fraud and perjury, but its one-year clause poorly tracked modern evidentiary concerns.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: The statute descends from a 1677 English law aimed at preventing "fraud" and perjury (lying under oath) about agreements. But its "one-year clause" fits poorly with modern "evidentiary" concerns, meaning concerns about reliable proof.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: It measured neither the interval before litigation nor the size of an undertaking: immediate suit could be barred while memories remained fresh, and one day’s work scheduled thirteen months away could fall within the clause while a full year’s work beginning immediately did not.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: The rule's results are arbitrary: it can bar a suit filed right away while memories are fresh, and it covers one day's work set thirteen months out but not a full year's work starting today.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: Russell v. Slade demanded that inability to perform within a year appear from the agreement; Clark v. Pendleton distinguished an expected eighteen-month voyage from a contractual duration.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: Russell v. Slade held that the rule applies only if the agreement itself shows it cannot be performed within a year. Clark v. Pendleton distinguished a voyage merely expected to take eighteen months from a contract that fixed that duration.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: Repeated legislative reenactment of similar wording supported that interpretation.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: The legislature's repeated "reenactment" (re-passing) of similar wording, without changing the courts' narrow reading, supported that interpretation.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: Burkle involved an obligation understood as permanent or perpetual, even though described there as indefinite; perpetual and unspecified durations were different.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: In Burkle the obligation was meant to last forever, which by its nature cannot be completed within a year. That differs from a contract that simply names no end date.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: An oral agreement without an express duration beyond one year was functionally an indefinite-duration agreement for this provision, regardless of actual performance time.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: For this provision, an "oral agreement" that did not expressly last beyond one year was treated as an "indefinite-duration" agreement, one with no fixed end. That was true however long "performance" actually took, so no writing was needed.

brief-CT-CB-0385.sentence: It did not establish that the handshake formed a sufficiently definite contract, that the blank signed form satisfied other writing requirements, or that Flagship owed the contemplated management fee.
brief-CT-CB-0385.plain: The ruling did not establish that the handshake formed a "sufficiently definite" contract (clear enough terms to enforce), or that the blank signed form met other writing requirements. Nor did it establish that Flagship owed the expected management fee.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: The Fund used resources including those funds for independent candidate-support expenditures and direct contributions before November elections.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The Fund used money, including those funds, for "independent candidate-support expenditures," spending on its own to help candidates, and for direct "contributions" to campaigns before the November elections.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: It treated the third as an unlawful corporate contribution.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The FEC said the Institute's sending the money back amounted to an illegal corporate donation to a political committee.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: On cross-motions for summary judgment, defendants disputed statutory coverage, raised the First Amendment, and challenged separation of powers.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: On "cross-motions for summary judgment" (each side asking for a ruling without trial), the defendants argued the law's "statutory" coverage did not reach them and raised the First Amendment. They also challenged the FEC's structure under the "separation of powers."

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: The district court found a violation, regarded structural objections as nonjusticiable, rejected the speech defense, imposed a civil penalty measured by investigation and litigation expense, and enjoined similar transfers.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The "district court" found a violation and held the "structural" objections to the FEC's makeup "nonjusticiable," meaning not proper for a court to decide. It rejected the free-speech defense, imposed a "civil penalty" measured by the costs of investigation and litigation, and "enjoined" (barred) similar transfers.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: The Senate Secretary and House Clerk or designees remained nonvoting ex officio members.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House, or their designees, remained nonvoting "ex officio" members, serving automatically by virtue of their offices.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: Civil sanctions supplied injury, vacatur redress, and direct exposure to government authority sufficed for the independence and congressional-agent challenges.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The civil "sanctions" (penalties) were a real injury, and "vacatur" (cancelling them) would remedy it. That, plus direct exposure to the agency's power, gave the defendants standing to challenge the FEC's independence and its seating of Congress's agents.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: Defendants need not prove an unknowable lawful-agency counterfactual.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: Defendants did not have to prove a "counterfactual," meaning what a lawfully structured agency would have done, which no one could know.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: The court thought an implied good-cause limit likely but assumed only that good-cause removal was available at minimum, without finally deciding its scope.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The court thought commissioners were likely protected by an "implied" limit allowing firing only for good cause. But it assumed only that "good-cause removal" was available at a minimum, without finally deciding how far the President's removal power went.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: Using the anti-encroachment reasoning of Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority and Bowsher, despite their actors’ express decision powers, the court held congressional membership crossed the boundary into execution.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The court used the anti-encroachment reasoning (Congress may not reach into the executive branch) of Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority and Bowsher, even though the officials in those cases had express decision powers. It held that seating congressional members on the Commission crossed into executing the law, which belongs to the executive.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: The de facto officer argument did not justify denying these enforcement defendants relief: Buckley’s prospective posture was different, and declaring composition invalid while preserving their sanctions would be inadequate.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The "de facto officer" doctrine, which can preserve past acts of improperly appointed officials, did not justify denying these enforcement "defendants" relief. Buckley’s "prospective" (forward-looking) posture was different, and declaring the Commission's makeup invalid while keeping their "sanctions" would be inadequate.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: The FEC petitioned in its own name January 18, 1994, two days before the ninety-day deadline, without seeking or obtaining Solicitor General approval.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: The FEC filed its petition for Supreme Court review in its own name on January 18, 1994, two days before the ninety-day deadline. It neither sought nor obtained approval from the Solicitor General, who normally handles the government's Supreme Court cases.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: Chief Justice Rehnquist’s majority held that 28 U.S.C. section 518(a) and implementing regulation ordinarily assigned Supreme Court litigation for the United States to the Solicitor General.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: Chief Justice Rehnquist’s majority opinion held that 28 U.S.C. section 518(a) and its implementing "regulation" ordinarily assign Supreme Court litigation for the United States to the Solicitor General, the government's chief Supreme Court lawyer.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: Under the agency-law principles applied, ratification could not defeat intervening rights after the act’s deadline.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: Under the agency-law principles the Court applied, "ratification" (approving an unauthorized act after the fact) could not defeat "intervening rights," rights others gained in the meantime, once the deadline for the act had passed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: By May 26, the Solicitor General could not himself file timely, so retroactive approval would impermissibly extend the mandatory period.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: By May 26, the Solicitor General himself could no longer file a "timely" (on-time) petition, so his retroactive approval would improperly extend the mandatory filing period.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: It seemed anomalous that the FEC could formerly invoke mandatory Supreme Court jurisdiction but lacked discretionary access.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: Justice Stevens, dissenting, found it odd that the FEC could formerly invoke the Supreme Court's mandatory "jurisdiction" (appeals the Court had to hear) yet lacked "discretionary" access, the right to ask the Court to choose to hear a case.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.sentence: On December 6, 1994, Rehnquist, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-001.plain: On December 6, 1994, Rehnquist, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Breyer "dismissed" the case for want of jurisdiction, meaning the Court lacked power to decide it because no valid petition was filed in time.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: He sought a declaration that the proposed Nineteenth Amendment was void and injunctions against its proclamation and enforcement, including interlocutory relief.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: He sought a declaration that the proposed Nineteenth Amendment, granting women the vote, was void, and "injunctions" (court orders) against its "proclamation" (official announcement) and enforcement. He also sought "interlocutory" relief, a temporary order while the case went on.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: The trial court ordered the defendants to show cause concerning interlocutory relief.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: The "trial court" ordered the "defendants" (the officials) to show cause, meaning explain why it should not grant "interlocutory" relief, a temporary order during the case.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: After their response and dismissal motion, it discharged that order and dismissed the bill on July 14, 1920.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: After the officials' response and "dismissal motion" (a request to throw out the case), the court discharged (cancelled) that order and dismissed Fairchild's bill on July 14, 1920.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: Putting a request in the form of an equity suit did not create an Article III case.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: Framing a request as an "equity suit," one asking for an injunction, did not by itself create an Article III case, the kind of real dispute federal courts may decide.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: Judicial power protected or enforced rights and prevented or redressed wrongs; Fairchild identified no personal right needing the requested intervention.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: "Judicial power" exists to protect or enforce rights and to prevent or remedy wrongs. Fairchild identified no personal right of his own that needed the court's "intervention."

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: His remaining interest was the citizen’s general concern for lawful administration and avoidance of wasted public money.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: All he had was the interest every citizen shares in government obeying the law and not wasting money, which is not enough to sue.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.sentence: The Court affirmed the decree without deciding ratification validity or excluding a later suit by proper parties with an affected right.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-048.plain: The Court "affirmed" (upheld) the decree dismissing the case. It did not decide whether ratification was valid, and it did not rule out a later suit by proper parties whose own rights were affected.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-072-DISTRICT.sentence: The dispute concerned whether executive-branch placement necessarily entailed unrestricted presidential removal authority.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-072-DISTRICT.plain: The dispute was whether placement in the executive branch necessarily meant unrestricted "presidential removal" authority, the power to fire the commissioners for any reason.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-072-DISTRICT.sentence: This was provisional protection, not a recovered final merits judgment setting out every tenure protection.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-072-DISTRICT.plain: This was provisional protection while the case continued. It was not a "recovered" final judgment on the merits, one actually obtained, setting out every "tenure protection" (limit on firing the commissioners).

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-072-DISTRICT.sentence: On November 30, 1983, the D.C. Circuit vacated the district judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the suit as moot.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-072-DISTRICT.plain: On November 30, 1983, the D.C. Circuit "vacated" (erased) the district court's "judgment" and remanded with instructions to dismiss the suit as "moot," meaning no live dispute remained because the Commission as it had existed had expired by law.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: A Senate-confirmed Director served five years and could be removed by the President for cause.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: A Senate-confirmed Director served five years and could be removed by the President only "for cause," meaning for a good reason such as misconduct, not policy disagreement.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: Funded by assessments rather than annual appropriations, the agency could regulate, investigate, subpoena, issue orders and penalties, and appoint itself conservator or receiver.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: Funded by fees assessed on the companies it oversaw rather than annual "appropriations" (money Congress votes each year), the agency could "regulate," investigate, subpoena, and issue "orders" and penalties. It could also appoint itself "conservator" or receiver, taking control of a troubled company.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: Treasury initially promised up to $100 billion to each, receiving senior preferred shares, liquidation preferences, warrants for up to 79.9 percent of common stock, and cash dividends initially calculated at a ten-percent annual rate.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: Treasury first promised up to $100 billion to each company in exchange for "senior preferred" shares (ranking ahead of other shareholders), liquidation preferences (repayment first if the company was wound up), and "warrants for" up to 79.9 percent of the "common stock," meaning rights to buy ordinary shares. It also got cash dividends first set at a ten-percent annual rate.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: An Acting FHFA Director adopted an August 2012 third amendment replacing the fixed formula with quarterly payment of net worth above a specified reserve.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: An Acting FHFA Director, a temporary head of the agency, adopted an August 2012 "third amendment" to the deal. It replaced the fixed dividend formula with quarterly payment to Treasury of the companies' net worth above a specified reserve.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: A fractured en banc Fifth Circuit revived the statutory claim, found removal protection unconstitutional, and severed that protection without undoing the amendment.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: A fractured "en banc" Fifth Circuit (the full appeals court, deeply divided) revived the "statutory" claim that the agency exceeded its legal powers. It found the Director's "removal protection" unconstitutional and "severed" (cut out) that protection without undoing the "amendment."

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: In January 2021, a fourth amendment suspended the challenged variable-dividend formula while specified capital levels were built, changing the prospective-relief question.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: In January 2021, a "fourth amendment" to the deal (not the Constitution's Fourth Amendment) paused the challenged "variable-dividend" formula while the companies built specified capital levels. That changed the question of prospective (forward-looking) relief, leaving mainly money already paid.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: Section 4617(f) barred judicial action restraining or affecting authorized conservator or receiver powers, though not action exceeding them.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: Section 4617(f) barred courts from taking action that would restrain or affect the agency's authorized powers as conservator or receiver, but not action against conduct exceeding those powers.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: The Act permitted action in the interests of the regulated entity or the agency.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: The Act permitted the agency to act in the interests of the "regulated" entity (the company) or of the agency itself.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: Shareholders alleged concrete financial injury traceable to adoption and implementation of the amendment, potentially redressable retrospectively.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: The shareholders alleged a concrete financial injury "traceable" to (caused by) the adoption and carrying out of the "amendment." A court could potentially fix it "retrospectively," by ordering money already taken to be returned.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: Standing did not require already proving that removal protection caused the loss; entitlement to relief was separate.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: "Standing" (the right to sue) did not require already proving that the "removal protection" caused their loss. Whether they were entitled to "relief" was a separate question.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: The succession clause transferred shareholder rights concerning company assets and affairs to the conservator, but did not transfer away a constitutional right to challenge separation-of-powers violations possessed by persons with standing.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: The "succession clause" passed shareholders' rights over the companies' assets and affairs to the "conservator" (the agency). It did not take away the shareholders' own constitutional right, as persons with "standing," to challenge "separation-of-powers" violations.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: The ordinary presumption of presidential removal therefore made the Acting Director removable at will.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: The ordinary "presumption" that the President can remove executive officers therefore made the Acting Director removable at will, since the firing limit covered only Senate-confirmed Directors.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: The defect therefore did not automatically void the amendment or every implementation act.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: So the defect did not automatically "void" (cancel) the amendment or every act carrying it out, because the Directors had been lawfully appointed.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: A removal restriction could nevertheless cause compensable harm—for example, if a President was actually prevented from removing an officer or announced that the law blocked a desired removal.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: A "removal restriction" could still cause "compensable" harm, meaning harm that money can make up for. Examples: if a President was actually prevented from firing an officer, or announced that the law blocked a firing he wanted.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: The Court left those contentions and a disputed, fact-dependent laches defense to the lower courts.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: The Court left those arguments, and a disputed, fact-dependent "laches" defense (that the shareholders waited unreasonably long to sue), to the lower courts.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.sentence: He regarded acts of an unconstitutionally insulated officer as unauthorized and ordinarily subject to being set aside, with traditional equitable defenses such as laches remaining.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COLLINS.plain: Justice Gorsuch regarded acts of an officer unconstitutionally shielded from removal as unauthorized and ordinarily subject to being "set aside" (undone). Traditional "equitable" defenses, such as "laches" (unreasonable delay in suing), would remain.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Under 12 U.S.C. § 242, Governors serve their terms unless sooner removed for cause by the President.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Under 12 U.S.C. § 242, Federal Reserve Governors serve their full terms unless "removed for cause" by the President, meaning fired early for a legally adequate reason.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: She argued separately that the alleged conduct was not statutory cause, that the statute required notice and an opportunity to respond, and that constitutional due process independently required pretermination procedure.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: She argued three separate points: the "alleged" conduct was not "statutory" cause, a reason the law accepts; the statute required "notice and an opportunity to respond"; and constitutional "due process" (fair procedure) independently required "pretermination" procedure, a fair process before firing.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: It found likely success because it read cause as limited to in-office conduct and treated protected tenure as a constitutional property interest.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: The lower court found "likely success" (that she would probably win) because it read "cause" as limited to conduct while in office. It also treated her protected term of office as a constitutional "property interest."

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: This was an interim application pending appeal, not a final merits appeal after factual development.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: This was an interim request while the "appeal" was pending, not a final appeal on the "merits" after the facts were developed.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Section 242 assigned the decision to the President but did not make every asserted reason sufficient or eliminate judicial review.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Section 242 gave the removal decision to the President, but it did not make every reason he asserts sufficient or eliminate "judicial review," meaning courts' power to check it.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: It did not establish blanket nonreviewability.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: It did not establish blanket "nonreviewability," meaning that courts can never review a removal.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Section 242 drew on the common-law concept of substantial, reasonable, and just cause informed by the particular office, not an unidentified external statutory list.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Section 242 drew on the "common-law" (traditional judge-made) idea of substantial, reasonable, and "just cause," judged in light of the particular office. It did not refer to some unidentified "statutory" list taken from other laws.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Review was deferential but need not ignore pretext.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: "Review" was deferential, giving the President leeway, but courts need not ignore "pretext," a stated reason that is really a cover for another motive.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Roberts distinguished that final determination, traditionally associated with mandamus or quo warranto, from interim protection of an incumbent while title was litigated.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Chief Justice Roberts distinguished that final decision about who holds an office, traditionally made through "mandamus" or quo warranto (special court orders), from "interim protection" of the current officeholder while "title was litigated," meaning while the right to the office was being fought out.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: The majority also rejected Thomas’s insistence on an express congressional cause of action, relying on traditional equitable suits preventing unlawful official conduct.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: The "majority" also rejected Thomas’s demand for an express "cause of action" from Congress, a statute specifically authorizing the suit. It relied instead on traditional "equitable" suits to stop unlawful conduct by officials.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: A protected term of years carried a background understanding that removal for cause required notice and an opportunity to defend.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: A protected term of years, with "removal for cause" only, carried a background understanding: before removal, the official had to get notice of the charges and an opportunity to defend.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: The majority treated that interpretation as governing rather than disposable dicta, distinguished precedent-based presumptions from those depending on broad lower-court consensus, and declined to infer the opposite from express procedures in other statutes.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: The majority treated that interpretation as binding, not disposable "dicta" (side remarks a later court may ignore). It distinguished "presumptions" based on Supreme Court precedent from those resting on broad "lower-court" agreement, and refused to infer the opposite from express procedures in other "statutes."

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Because that statutory defect prevented the government from showing likely success, the Court did not decide whether Cook’s office was constitutional property or what the Due Process Clause independently required.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Because that statutory defect, the missing notice and chance to respond, kept the government from showing "likely success" (that it would probably win), the Court did not decide whether Cook's office was constitutional property. Nor did it decide what the Due Process Clause independently required.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: The seventh note rejected constitutional avoidance because the statutory reading was unambiguous and Thomas’s narrower process approach would not eliminate his objection to any removal limit.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: The seventh note rejected "constitutional avoidance," the practice of reading a statute to sidestep a constitutional question, because the statute's meaning was "unambiguous" (clear). And Thomas's narrower process-based approach would not have removed his objection to any limit on removal.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: Justice Jackson also joined but would deny the stay on equitable grounds alone.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Jackson joined the majority, but she would have refused the government's request simply on the fairness-and-harm factors courts weigh for temporary relief, since the government showed no concrete harm from Cook staying in office meanwhile.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: He further argued that Cook lacked an authorized action overcoming sovereign immunity, had not met demanding ultra vires or mandamus standards, and could not obtain equitable reinstatement.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Justice Thomas further argued that Cook lacked an authorized action overcoming "sovereign immunity," the government's protection from suits without its consent. He said she had not met the demanding standards for "ultra vires" (beyond legal power) or mandamus relief, and could not obtain "equitable" reinstatement, a court order restoring her to office.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: That interference supplied irreparable harm, reduced by the government’s concession that policy disagreement alone could not justify removal.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: Justice Barrett read the order as blocking even a properly conducted firing, and thought that interference with the President was "irreparable harm," harm that cannot be undone later. But the government's concession that policy disagreement alone could not justify removal made that harm smaller.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.sentence: On June 29, 2026, the Court denied the stay application 5–4.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-COOK.plain: On June 29, 2026, the Court denied the "stay application" (the government's request to let the firing take effect during the case) by a 5–4 vote.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: Individual members, however, could be removed only on restrictive good-cause grounds: willful violations, willful abuse, or unreasonable failure to enforce compliance, determined on a record after notice and a hearing opportunity.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: Individual Board members, however, could be removed only on restrictive "good-cause" grounds: "willful" (deliberate) violations, willful abuse of authority, or unreasonable failure to enforce compliance. Those grounds had to be found on a formal "record" after notice and a chance for a hearing.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: The second layer was therefore an assumption, not a holding finding express tenure language in the SEC statute.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: So the second layer of protection, for SEC commissioners, was an assumption by the Court, not a "holding" (a binding decision) that the SEC statute contains express tenure language.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: Under Thunder Basin, the precedent governing implied review-channel exclusivity, the Court considered meaningful review, whether the claim was collateral, and agency expertise.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: Under Thunder Basin, the "precedent" on when Congress implicitly makes an agency's review process the only route ("exclusivity"), the Court asked three things. Could the "agency" process give meaningful review, was the claim "collateral" (separate from ordinary agency matters), and did agency expertise matter?

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: No sanction existed to appeal, and petitioners did not have to incur one deliberately to challenge the regulator’s constitutionality.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: No "sanction" (penalty) existed to appeal, and the petitioners did not have to deliberately incur one just to challenge whether the "regulator" (the Board) was constitutional.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: Executive power and faithful execution required presidential supervision and electoral accountability for executive officers.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: Because the Constitution gives the President the executive power and the duty to see the laws carried out, he must be able to oversee executive officials so voters can hold him responsible.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: The President could assess commissioners’ conduct but ordinarily could not override their reasonable judgment that cause was absent.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: The President could not fire commissioners just because he disagreed with their reasonable decision not to fire a Board member, so he had no real control over the Board.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: The Court severed §§7211(e)(6) and 7217(d)(3), the substantive restrictions on removing Board members.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: The Court "severed" (cut out) §§7211(e)(6) and 7217(d)(3), the "substantive" limits on removing Board members, leaving the rest of the law in place.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: With at-will removal and existing supervision, Board members qualified as inferior officers under Edmond, the precedent emphasizing supervision of such officers.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: With "at-will removal" (firing for any reason) by the SEC and its existing supervision, Board members qualified as "inferior officers" under Edmond, the "precedent" stressing that such lower-level officers are supervised by higher officials.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: The SEC was a freestanding, self-contained executive component and thus a department for appointment purposes.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: The SEC counted as a 'department' whose head may appoint lower-level officers under the Constitution.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: The chair’s agreement with previous appointments did not defeat standing because the Court could not assume identical choices if the chair alone held authority.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: The SEC chair's agreement with the earlier appointments did not defeat "standing" (the challengers' right to sue). The Court could not assume the same people would have been chosen if the chair alone held the appointment power.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: It also reserved whether the SEC counted as an executive department for the Opinions Clause or Twenty-Fifth Amendment.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: The Court also "reserved" (left undecided) whether the SEC counts as an "executive department" for the Opinions Clause or the Twenty-Fifth Amendment. Both are constitutional provisions that use that term.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: Because the SEC statute was silent, Breyer also criticized assuming commissioners’ protection and then using that assumption to invalidate another statute.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: Because the SEC statute said nothing about firing commissioners, Justice Breyer also objected to assuming they were protected and then using that assumption to strike down another statute.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.sentence: Petitioners were entitled to declaratory relief ensuring regulation by a constitutionally accountable agency, but not a broad injunction dismantling Board operations.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-FREEENTERPRISE.plain: "Petitioners" (the challengers) were entitled to "declaratory relief," a court statement ensuring they would be regulated by a constitutionally accountable "agency." They were not entitled to a broad "injunction" shutting down the Board's operations.

cp-calder.sentence: South and Calder received process by mail in Florida, appeared specially, and moved to quash service.
cp-calder.plain: South and Calder received "process" (the lawsuit papers) by mail in Florida. They "appeared specially," coming to court only to contest California's power over them, and moved to quash (cancel) the service.

cp-calder.sentence: The California Superior Court thought conduct causing local injury ordinarily supported jurisdiction, but gave extra weight to the chilling effect of requiring reporters and editors to defend far away.
cp-calder.plain: The California Superior Court, the trial court, thought conduct causing injury in California ordinarily supported "jurisdiction" there. But it gave extra weight to the "chilling effect," the discouragement of free speech, of making reporters and editors defend suits far away.

cp-calder.sentence: It relied on intended and actual tortious effects in California and rejected an extra First Amendment barrier.
cp-calder.plain: The appeals court relied on the "tortious" (wrongful, injury-causing) effects that were intended in and actually felt in California. It rejected any extra First Amendment barrier to jurisdiction.

cp-calder.sentence: The U.S. Supreme Court held that route unavailable because the state court had decided whether the Constitution permitted jurisdiction under a statute extending to constitutional limits, not whether that statute itself was constitutional.
cp-calder.plain: The U.S. Supreme Court held the automatic-appeal route unavailable. The state court had decided whether the Constitution permitted "jurisdiction" under a long-arm statute reaching to constitutional limits, not whether that statute itself was constitutional.

cp-calder.sentence: Although no merits trial had occurred, the federal jurisdictional issue was sufficiently final.
cp-calder.plain: Although there had been no trial on the "merits," the state courts' ruling on the federal jurisdiction issue was final enough for Supreme Court review.

cp-calder.sentence: The individuals argued that employees should not inherit their employer’s forum contacts.
cp-calder.plain: The writer and editor argued that "employees" should not inherit their employer's "forum contacts," meaning its connections to the state where the suit was filed.

cp-calder.sentence: California was the focal point of both the allegedly libelous story and harm.
cp-calder.plain: California was the focal point of both the "allegedly" libelous story, claimed to be false and damaging, and the harm it caused.

cp-calder.sentence: This alleged intentional targeting differed from untargeted negligence.
cp-calder.plain: This "alleged" intentional targeting of California differed from untargeted "negligence," such as carelessly making a product that happens to end up there.

cp-calder.sentence: But acting officially for a corporation did not immunize a person whose own conduct established the necessary relationship.
cp-calder.plain: But acting officially for a "corporation" did not shield a person whose own conduct created the necessary connection to the state.

cp-calder.sentence: The Court rejected an additional speech-based adjustment to personal jurisdiction.
cp-calder.plain: The Court rejected any extra speech-based adjustment to "personal jurisdiction," a court's power over a particular defendant.

cp-calder.sentence: Reusing those protections to defeat otherwise proper jurisdiction would complicate the contacts inquiry and count the safeguards twice.
cp-calder.plain: Free-speech protections already apply when the libel claim itself is decided. Reusing them to defeat otherwise proper jurisdiction would complicate the "contacts" inquiry (the defendant's connections to the state) and count those safeguards twice.

graham.sentence: Disputes connected to an engagement went finally to the union executive board or appropriate local board.
graham.plain: The contracts said any dispute about a concert would be decided, with no appeal, by the musicians' union's own board.

graham.sentence: After an initial arbitration order and reconsideration allowing discovery about agreement and revocation, the trial court finally compelled arbitration in March 1976.
graham.plain: The trial court first ordered "arbitration" (deciding the dispute outside court), then on "reconsideration" allowed discovery about whether there was an agreement and about its "revocation." It finally "compelled arbitration" in March 1976.

graham.sentence: It rejected waiver and rescission grounds and found the pleaded disputes arbitrable.
graham.plain: It rejected the "waiver" argument (that the right to arbitrate had been given up) and the rescission argument (that the contracts were cancelled). It found the "pleaded" disputes, those raised in the court papers, subject to arbitration.

graham.sentence: Graham appealed confirmation, through which the otherwise nonappealable compulsion order could be reviewed; Scissor-Tail appealed the fee ruling.
graham.plain: Graham appealed the court's confirmation (approval) of the arbitration award, which let him challenge the otherwise "nonappealable" order compelling arbitration. Scissor-Tail appealed the "ruling" on fees.

graham.sentence: The California Supreme Court separated adhesive formation from invalidity of a particular provision.
graham.plain: The California Supreme Court separated two questions: whether the contract was "adhesive," meaning a take-it-or-leave-it form, and the "invalidity" of a particular provision in it.

graham.sentence: Adhesive provisions could fail either because they fell outside reasonable expectations or because, even if expected, they were oppressive or unconscionable in context.
graham.plain: "Adhesive" provisions, terms in take-it-or-leave-it contracts, could fail if they fell outside the weaker party's "reasonable expectations." Even if expected, they could fail if oppressive or "unconscionable" (grossly unfair) in context.

graham.sentence: The arbitration term was therefore expected.
graham.plain: So the "arbitration" term was expected: Graham knew disputes would go to the union, so it did not surprise him.

graham.sentence: That surrendered adjudicative power to the adverse interest and made the substitute for courts illusory.
graham.plain: Letting one side, or its ally, be the only judge surrendered "adjudicative power" (the power to decide the dispute) to the adverse interest. That made the "arbitration" an illusory substitute for a court, not a real one.

graham.sentence: A procedure essentially preventing fair presentation could supply another ground, but prearbitration refusal on that basis was reserved for the clearest cases; ordinarily actual deprivation could be tested in a later vacation petition.
graham.plain: A procedure that essentially prevents a party from fairly presenting its case could be another reason to refuse arbitration. But refusing before arbitration on that basis was "reserved" (kept) for the clearest cases. Usually, actual unfairness is tested afterward in a "vacation petition," a request asking a court to set aside (vacate) the award.

graham.sentence: As sole adjudicator it lacked the minimum structural integrity required of the contractual substitute.
graham.plain: Because the union was aligned with the musician, as sole "adjudicator" (the only decision-maker) it lacked the minimum "structural" fairness, built into how the forum is set up, that a "contractual" substitute for a court must have. An arbitrator must at least not be aligned with one party.

graham.sentence: Scissor-Tail argued that Form B effectively created a collective bargaining agreement under Labor Management Relations Act § 301, requiring the union forum.
graham.plain: Scissor-Tail argued that Form B, the union form contract, effectively created a "collective bargaining agreement" (a union labor contract) under Labor Management Relations Act § 301, a federal labor law. That, it said, would require using the union's forum.

graham.sentence: On February 5, 1981, the court reversed confirmation and required vacation of the order compelling the union forum.
graham.plain: On February 5, 1981, the court "reversed" (overturned) the lower court's confirmation, or approval, of the award. It also required "vacation of the order" (cancelling the order) that had compelled the parties to use the union "forum," meaning the union's decision-making body.

lrs-i-biden-missouri.sentence: On November 5, 2021, the Secretary issued an interim final rule requiring covered facilities to ensure that staff were vaccinated against COVID-19.
lrs-i-biden-missouri.plain: On November 5, 2021, the Secretary issued an "interim final rule," one that took effect right away, before public comment. It required covered facilities, those receiving Medicare or Medicaid money, to ensure their staff were vaccinated against COVID-19.

lrs-i-biden-missouri.sentence: Citing the Delta variant and approaching winter, he invoked good cause to proceed without advance notice and comment.
lrs-i-biden-missouri.plain: Citing the Delta variant and approaching winter, he invoked "good cause," the legal exception for urgent situations, to skip "advance notice" and comment. That usual step means publishing the proposal and taking public comments first.

lrs-i-biden-missouri.sentence: It sought permission to enforce the vaccination rule while litigation continued, not a stay of the rule itself.
lrs-i-biden-missouri.plain: The government sought permission to enforce the vaccination rule while the lawsuits continued. It asked the Court to pause the lower courts' orders blocking the rule, not for a "stay" (a pause) of the rule itself.

lrs-i-biden-missouri.sentence: The Court emphasized the rule’s express severability provision rather than allowing those categories to determine treatment of all the others.
lrs-i-biden-missouri.plain: The rule had an "express" (written-out) severability provision: if part of it was invalid, the rest should survive. The Court relied on it, so doubts about a few facility types did not decide how all the others were treated.
