brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.sentence: Section 556(d) protected cross-examination necessary for full and true disclosure, not unlimited questioning.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.plain: Section 556(d) protected the "cross-examination" (questioning opposing witnesses) needed for full and true disclosure of the facts. It did not protect unlimited questioning.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.sentence: When the medical association called him, the examiner barred Federation representative Dr. Miles Robinson from cross-examining and denied an interlocutory appeal.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.plain: When the medical association called him as a witness, the "examiner" (hearing officer) barred the Federation's representative, Dr. Miles Robinson, from "cross-examining" him. The examiner also denied an "interlocutory appeal," an immediate review of that ruling before the hearing ended.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.sentence: This was a limited reopening, not an unrestricted new hearing, and exceptions work could continue.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.plain: The hearing would be reopened only for this questioning, not started over, and the separate work on exceptions could carry on meanwhile.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.sentence: On August 15, 1974, the unanimous court granted the petitions in part and denied them in part, ordered the specified stay and injunctions, and remanded without costs.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-014.plain: On August 15, 1974, the "unanimous" court granted the "petitions" in part and denied them in part. It "ordered" the specified "stay" (hold) and injunctions, and "remanded" (sent the matter back to the FDA) without costs, so each side paid its own.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.sentence: Albert Levitt appeared without counsel and asked the Supreme Court for leave to file an original petition concerning Justice Hugo Black.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.plain: Albert Levitt, appearing without "counsel" (a lawyer), asked the Supreme Court for "leave to file," permission to start an original petition directly in that Court, concerning Justice Hugo Black.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.sentence: The proposed petition would require Black to show cause why he should be permitted to serve as an Associate Justice.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.plain: The proposed petition would require Black to "show cause," that is, come forward and justify why he should be permitted to serve as an Associate Justice.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.sentence: He invoked the constitutional ineligibility provision in Article I, § 6, clause 2, and argued that there was no vacancy to which Black could lawfully have been appointed.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.plain: He invoked the Constitution's "ineligibility provision" in Article I, § 6, clause 2, which bars a member of Congress from appointment to certain offices created or improved during his term. He argued there was no "vacancy" (open seat) that Black, a former senator, could lawfully fill.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.sentence: The Court treated those interests as insufficient to invoke judicial power to determine the validity of legislative or executive action.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.plain: The Court held that Levitt's interests as a citizen and a member of its bar were not enough to invoke "judicial power," a court's authority to decide, to rule on whether the President's and Senate's actions were valid.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.sentence: A general interest common to the public did not meet that requirement.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.plain: An interest every member of the public shares, such as wanting officials to follow the Constitution, was not enough to bring the suit.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.sentence: The volume’s participation note excludes Black from consideration and decision of orders announced October 11 or earlier.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-050.plain: The official report notes that Black took no part in deciding any orders issued on or before October 11, including this one.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Howard relied on a Washington law permitting the appointing officer to revoke appointments at pleasure.
cp-aldinger.plain: Howard relied on a Washington law letting the appointing "officer," the official who hired someone, revoke the appointment "at pleasure": at any time, for any reason.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Her state-law claim against the county depended on Washington provisions waiving immunity and imposing vicarious liability for officials’ tortious conduct.
cp-aldinger.plain: Her state-law claim against the county depended on Washington laws "waiving immunity," letting the county be sued, and imposing "vicarious liability," making it answer for its officials' "tortious" (wrongful) conduct.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Everyone was a Washington citizen, so diversity jurisdiction could not bring that claim into federal court.
cp-aldinger.plain: Every party was a Washington "citizen," so diversity jurisdiction, which requires parties from different states, could not bring that claim into federal court.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Under the Supreme Court’s then-controlling interpretation of § 1983, a county was not a covered person.
cp-aldinger.plain: At the time, the Supreme Court read § 1983 as not allowing civil-rights suits against counties at all, so Aldinger had no federal claim against Spokane County.

cp-aldinger.sentence: It entered a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) judgment allowing an immediate appeal.
cp-aldinger.plain: The judge entered a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) judgment, a final judgment on the county claim alone. That allowed an immediate appeal while the rest of the case went on.

cp-aldinger.sentence: The Ninth Circuit affirmed under its approach rejecting pendent-party jurisdiction.
cp-aldinger.plain: The Ninth Circuit "affirmed" under its approach rejecting "pendent-party jurisdiction," meaning bringing in an extra defendant based only on a related state-law claim.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Although the complaint also mentioned § 1331 and its then-required jurisdictional amount, Aldinger had pursued the county through § 1983, § 1343(3), and pendent jurisdiction.
cp-aldinger.plain: The complaint also cited § 1331, the federal-question statute, and its then-required "jurisdictional amount," a minimum sum in dispute. But Aldinger had pursued the county through § 1983, § 1343(3), and "pendent jurisdiction," the court's power to hear related state claims.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Aldinger relied on United Mine Workers v. Gibbs: the same discharge supplied a common nucleus of operative fact for the federal and state claims, and one proceeding would save resources.
cp-aldinger.plain: Aldinger relied on United Mine Workers v. Gibbs. The same firing supplied a "common nucleus of operative fact," a shared set of core facts, for her federal and state claims, and one proceeding would save resources.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Justice Rehnquist, writing for six Justices, distinguished Gibbs’s related claims against a defendant already properly before the court from adding another defendant solely on a state claim.
cp-aldinger.plain: Justice Rehnquist, writing for six Justices, distinguished Gibbs: it allowed related claims against a defendant already properly in court. Adding another defendant, like the county, solely on a state claim was different.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Article III’s permissible reach and trial convenience could not replace Congress’s authorization.
cp-aldinger.plain: Article III’s permissible reach, what the Constitution would allow, and trial convenience could not replace Congress's grant of jurisdiction to the lower federal courts.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Because the latter then excluded counties from federal liability, the Court inferred that Congress had also implicitly withheld this means of adding the county on state law.
cp-aldinger.plain: Since Congress had then chosen not to make counties liable under § 1983, the Court concluded Congress also did not want counties pulled into federal court on related state claims.

cp-aldinger.sentence: The Court observed that exclusive federal jurisdiction over a claim against the United States might strengthen the argument for hearing related claims together, because only the federal forum could accommodate all of them.
cp-aldinger.plain: The Court noted that "exclusive federal jurisdiction," as over a claim against the United States, might strengthen the case for "hearing" related claims together. Only the federal "forum" (court) could take all of them.

cp-aldinger.sentence: Exemption from a federally created municipal obligation did not necessarily bar a federal court from enforcing an obligation state law already imposed.
cp-aldinger.plain: In Brennan's dissenting view, "exemption" from a federally created obligation on municipalities (Congress not making counties liable under federal law) did not necessarily bar a federal court from enforcing an obligation state law already imposed.

cp-aldinger.sentence: In 1978, Monell held that municipalities are § 1983 persons, while rejecting liability based solely on employing a tortfeasor.
cp-aldinger.plain: In 1978, Monell held that cities and counties are "persons" who can be sued under § 1983. It rejected "liability" based solely on employing a "tortfeasor," the person who committed the wrong.

cp-aldinger.sentence: That later development changed Aldinger’s substantive premise; Aldinger’s 1976 analysis cannot simply be restated as current municipal or supplemental-jurisdiction law.
cp-aldinger.plain: That later development changed Aldinger's substantive starting premise. Its 1976 analysis cannot simply be restated as current law on suing local governments or on "supplemental-jurisdiction," hearing related state claims.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Gasperini, a California citizen, sued the New York-incorporated and headquartered Center in the Southern District of New York under diversity jurisdiction.
cp-gasperini.plain: Gasperini, a California "citizen," sued the Center, New York-incorporated and headquartered, in the Southern District of New York, a federal court in Manhattan. He relied on diversity jurisdiction, since the parties were from different states.

cp-gasperini.sentence: The Center conceded liability, leaving value disputed.
cp-gasperini.plain: The Center conceded "liability" (legal responsibility) for losing the slides, leaving only their value in dispute.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5501(c) required asking whether an award materially departed from reasonable compensation, rather than merely shocked the conscience.
cp-gasperini.plain: Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5501(c), New York's law, asked whether an award "materially departed" from reasonable compensation, judged against similar cases. That is stricter than the old test, whether the award "shocked the conscience."
Giving the winner a choice between accepting a smaller award and facing a new trial is called remittitur.

cp-gasperini.sentence: New York’s test had substantive significance under Erie, the doctrine protecting state-created rights in federal diversity litigation.
cp-gasperini.plain: New York's test had substantive significance under Erie, the doctrine protecting "state-created rights" in federal "diversity litigation" (cases there because the parties are from different states). It mattered because it limited how much a plaintiff could recover.

cp-gasperini.sentence: A looser federal test could yield substantially more money for the same state claim, encouraging forum shopping and unequal administration.
cp-gasperini.plain: If federal courts used a looser test, plaintiffs could get much bigger awards for the same claim just by suing in federal court, which would encourage choosing courts for advantage and treat similar cases unequally.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Comparison-based limits functioned like a ceiling even without a fixed sum; diversity supplied another forum, not enlarged compensation.
cp-gasperini.plain: Comparison-based limits worked like a ceiling even without a fixed dollar figure. Diversity jurisdiction gives an out-of-state party another "forum" (court), not larger compensation.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Drawing on Byrd’s recognition of federal interests in allocating judicial responsibilities, it considered the Seventh Amendment’s Reexamination Clause and federal trial-appellate relations.
cp-gasperini.plain: Drawing on Byrd, which recognized federal interests in dividing work between judge and jury, the Court considered the Seventh Amendment's Reexamination Clause. That clause limits re-examining facts a jury found. It also weighed relations between federal trial and appeals courts.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Trial judges historically granted new trials for verdicts against the evidence, including excessiveness, and could condition relief on refusal of remittitur.
cp-gasperini.plain: Historically, trial judges granted new trials for verdicts against the evidence, including excessive damages. They could condition that "relief" on the plaintiff's refusal of "remittitur," an offer to accept a lower amount instead of a new trial.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Earlier Supreme Court cases had reserved whether appellate excessiveness review was constitutional, while federal appeals courts had adopted abuse-of-discretion review.
cp-gasperini.plain: Earlier Supreme Court cases had "reserved" (left undecided) whether appellate "excessiveness review," appeals courts checking whether an award is too high, was constitutional. Meanwhile federal appeals courts had adopted "abuse-of-discretion" review, reversing only unreasonable rulings.

cp-gasperini.sentence: The majority read Rule 59 as authorizing the new-trial mechanism without supplying a conflicting substantive measure of allowable compensation.
cp-gasperini.plain: The majority read Rule 59 as authorizing the new-trial mechanism only. It did not supply a conflicting "substantive" measure of allowable compensation, so that standard came from state law.

cp-gasperini.sentence: The scope question mattered because Hanna’s framework would govern if a valid Federal Rule directly controlled the disputed issue.
cp-gasperini.plain: This mattered because, under Hanna, if a valid Federal Rule directly covers an issue, the federal court follows the Rule, and the ordinary Erie balancing does not apply.

cp-gasperini.sentence: His historical reading prohibited appellate reconsideration of a jury’s damages against the weight of evidence.
cp-gasperini.plain: In his historical reading, the Seventh Amendment bars "appellate" reconsideration, meaning appeals courts second-guessing a jury's damages as against the weight of the evidence.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Westminster new-trial review belonged to the original proceeding rather than a modern appeal; relabeling review abuse of discretion did not remove its factual character.
cp-gasperini.plain: In the old Westminster courts, the central English courts, new-trial review belonged to the "original proceeding," the trial itself, rather than to a modern appeal. Relabeling appellate review "abuse of discretion" review did not remove its character as a re-examination of the jury's facts.

cp-gasperini.sentence: Rules specifying compensable injuries and amounts differed from a review standard regulating how closely judges supervise juries.
cp-gasperini.plain: Scalia said rules specifying "compensable" injuries (those that can be paid for) and amounts are substantive. They differ from a "review standard," which regulates how closely judges supervise juries, a matter of procedure; New York's test was the latter.

cp-kearns.sentence: Ford removed under the Class Action Fairness Act’s diversity provision, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d).
cp-kearns.plain: Ford "removed" the case (moved it from state to federal court) under the Class Action Fairness Act's diversity provision, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d). That provision lets large class actions involving parties from different states be heard in federal court.

cp-kearns.sentence: Kearns unsuccessfully invoked the local-controversy exception to seek remand.
cp-kearns.plain: Kearns invoked the "local-controversy exception," arguing the case was essentially a local California dispute, to seek "remand" (return to state court). He did not succeed.

cp-kearns.sentence: Kearns argued that California pleading precedent did not impose the federal fraud rule on his consumer statutes, that nondisclosure and other portions did not sound in fraud, and that the court should separately consider the Unfair Competition Law’s unfairness branch.
cp-kearns.plain: Kearns argued that California pleading precedent did not impose the federal fraud rule on his consumer "statutes"; that nondisclosure and other parts did not "sound in" fraud, meaning were not really fraud claims; and that the court should separately consider the Unfair Competition Law's unfairness branch.

cp-kearns.sentence: Reviewing dismissal de novo, the Ninth Circuit distinguished Rule 8’s short-and-plain-statement requirement from Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement for circumstances constituting fraud.
cp-kearns.plain: "Reviewing" the dismissal de novo, deciding it afresh, the Ninth Circuit distinguished two rules. Rule 8 requires only a short and plain statement of a claim, but Rule 9(b) requires "particularity," specific detail, about the circumstances constituting fraud.

cp-kearns.sentence: If a complaint mixes fraudulent and nonfraudulent conduct, deficient fraud allegations are stripped away and the remaining allegations are assessed under Rule 8.
cp-kearns.plain: If a complaint alleges both fraud and other wrongs, the court disregards any vague fraud allegations and judges what is left under the simpler Rule 8 standard.

cp-kearns.sentence: California law supplied the substantive elements; federal law governed pleading in federal court, whether jurisdiction rested on diversity or federal questions.
cp-kearns.plain: California law supplied the "substantive" elements, what Kearns had to prove. Federal law governed "pleading," the detail his complaint needed, in federal court, whether jurisdiction rested on "diversity" (parties from different states) or on federal questions.

cp-kearns.sentence: Dismissal of the entire complaint made the challenge to striking its first footnote moot, so the court did not decide that ruling’s merits.
cp-kearns.plain: "Dismissal" of the entire complaint made the challenge to "striking" (removing) its first footnote "moot," meaning it no longer mattered. So the court did not decide that ruling’s merits.

cp-keeton.sentence: Ohio’s limitations period barred libel, and the Ohio court applied New York’s limitation to the privacy claim.
cp-keeton.plain: Ohio's "limitations period," the deadline for suing, barred the libel claim, and the Ohio court applied New York's deadline to the privacy claim.

cp-keeton.sentence: Its six-year period made New Hampshire the only state where the libel action was timely when filed.
cp-keeton.plain: New Hampshire's six-year deadline made it the only state where the libel "action" (lawsuit) was timely when filed.

cp-keeton.sentence: The First Circuit also relied on the single publication rule, under which one action ordinarily addresses damages from a publication across jurisdictions.
cp-keeton.plain: The First Circuit also relied on the "single publication rule": one action ordinarily covers the damages from a publication across all "jurisdictions" (states) where it circulated.

cp-keeton.sentence: Thousands of monthly copies represented purposeful exploitation of a market, not random or isolated contact.
cp-keeton.plain: Selling thousands of copies there every month showed "purposeful" exploitation of a market, deliberately doing business in New Hampshire, not a random or isolated contact.

cp-keeton.sentence: New Hampshire’s long-arm statute covered torts committed wholly or partly within the state and extended to constitutional limits.
cp-keeton.plain: New Hampshire's "long-arm statute," its law for suing out-of-state defendants, covered torts (wrongs) committed wholly or partly within the state. It extended as far as constitutional limits allow.

cp-keeton.sentence: Nor did due process require Keeton herself to have minimum contacts with New Hampshire.
cp-keeton.plain: Nor did "due process," the Constitution's fairness requirement, demand that Keeton herself have "minimum contacts" with New Hampshire. That test concerns the defendant's ties to the state, not the plaintiff's.

cp-keeton.sentence: The Court also rejected a special First Amendment jurisdictional shield; speech protections operated through substantive law.
cp-keeton.plain: The Court also rejected any special First Amendment shield against being sued in distant states. Free-speech protections operate through "substantive law," on whether a publisher is liable, not on where it can be sued.

cp-keeton.sentence: A single action covering the publication, followed by a preclusive merits judgment between the parties, conserved resources and protected the publisher from repeated litigation.
cp-keeton.plain: A single action covering the whole publication, followed by a "preclusive" merits judgment (one barring the parties from suing again), conserved resources. It also protected the publisher from repeated litigation.

lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Public Citizen "intervened," joining the lawsuit as an additional party challenging the Department.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: The district court accepted coverage but dismissed because application would intrude on Article II nomination authority.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: The "district court" (trial court) accepted that the Act covered the ABA committee. But it "dismissed" the case because applying the Act would intrude on the President's Article II authority to nominate judges.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: The ABA intervened and argued that a generalized grievance and possible exemptions defeated standing.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: The ABA intervened and argued the groups lacked "standing" (the right to sue). It said their complaint was a "generalized grievance," shared by the whole public, and that possible exemptions in the Act might leave them nothing even if they won.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: Denial of requested information and advance notice was a particular injury even if many people could make the same request.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Being denied information they requested, and "advance notice" of committee meetings, was a particular injury to these groups. That was so even if many other people could make the same request.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: The majority considered imposing FACA’s intrusive controls on such exchanges sufficiently odd to examine context, not merely when a result became utterly impossible or absurd.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: The majority thought applying FACA’s heavy requirements to such everyday consultations would be odd enough to justify looking beyond the bare words, even though the result was not so absurd that Congress could not possibly have meant it.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: Invoking Holy Trinity, the majority treated words as primary evidence while permitting persuasive evidence of intended meaning.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Relying on Holy Trinity, the majority said a statute’s words come first, but strong evidence of what Congress actually meant can lead a court to a different reading.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: It did not accord it the force of a binding legislative definition.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: The Court did not treat the GSA regulation’s definition as binding law that it had to follow.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: A fairly possible alternative reading supported by statutory history avoided those questions.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Because the statute could fairly be read not to cover the ABA, and its history supported that reading, the Court adopted it so it would not have to decide those constitutional questions.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: A genuine absurdity exception was narrow; occasional casual conversations could differ from this relationship, and constitutional questions or disputed policy outcomes were not absurdity.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Kennedy said courts may ignore plain words only when the result would be truly absurd, and that was not the case here. Casual chats might be different from this long-standing arrangement, and a result that raises constitutional problems or bad policy is not “absurd.”

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: Avoidance still required a fairly possible reading; constitutional doubt could not circularly prove that an application was never covered.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Courts may dodge a constitutional question only if the statute can fairly be read another way. Worry about the Constitution cannot itself be the proof that the statute never applied.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: Unlike implied-function cases where balancing might apply, the Constitution had allocated this function.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: In cases where the Constitution only implies a function, "balancing" (weighing how much a law intrudes) might apply. But here, for Kennedy, the Constitution had expressly given nominations to the President, so Congress could not intrude.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: Brennan wrote for White, Marshall, Blackmun, and Stevens; Kennedy’s three-Justice concurrence agreed only in the judgment.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: Brennan wrote for White, Marshall, Blackmun, and Stevens. Kennedy's three-Justice "concurrence" agreed only in the "judgment," the result, not in Brennan's reasoning.

lrs-k-public-citizen.sentence: The controlling majority resolution was statutory exclusion strengthened by constitutional avoidance.
lrs-k-public-citizen.plain: The controlling "majority" holding was "statutory" exclusion: the Act does not cover the ABA committee. That reading was strengthened by "constitutional avoidance," choosing an interpretation that avoids constitutional problems.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Their proceeding therefore did not present a refusal to initiate rulemaking or a demand to perform one expressly required ministerial act.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: So the case did not present a refusal to begin "rulemaking" (writing new rules), or a demand that the FDA perform one expressly required "ministerial act," a simple duty with no judgment involved. It concerned a refusal to enforce.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Because this second ground did not depend on the first, a reviewing court could address enforcement discretion without resolving the jurisdictional disagreement.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Because the Commissioner's second reason did not depend on the first, a reviewing court could address "enforcement discretion," the choice not to enforce, without resolving the "jurisdictional" disagreement over whether the FDA had power over execution drugs.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Whether those materials required enforcement, as distinct from authorizing it, became the central legal dispute.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: The key question was whether those laws and statements forced the FDA to act, or merely allowed it to.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: The district court granted summary judgment for the government because it treated the enforcement refusal as committed to agency discretion.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: The "district court" (trial court) granted summary judgment, a ruling without trial, for the government. It treated the refusal to enforce as "committed to agency discretion," left entirely to the FDA and so not reviewable by courts.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: The court of appeals concluded that the FDA possessed jurisdiction, that the refusal was reviewable, and that the refusal was arbitrary and capricious.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: The "court of appeals" held that the FDA had "jurisdiction" (power) over the drugs, that the refusal was "reviewable" by courts, and that it was "arbitrary and capricious," meaning unreasonable and inadequately justified.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Section 701(a)(2) instead addresses decisions for which the law supplies no meaningful standard to judge the discretion, even without affirmative evidence that Congress intended preclusion.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Section 701(a)(2) instead covers decisions where the law supplies no meaningful standard for judging the agency's "discretion." Then courts have nothing to apply, even without affirmative "evidence" that Congress intended to bar review.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Section 706 authorizes courts to set aside abuses of discretion when legal criteria identify an abuse; its general words do not create criteria absent from the governing law.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Section 706 lets courts "set aside" (strike down) abuses of discretion when legal criteria identify an abuse. Its general words do not create criteria that the governing law itself lacks.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Refusing enforcement also ordinarily involves no coercive exercise of agency power over an individual’s liberty or property, while affirmative enforcement supplies a concrete exercise of authority to evaluate.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Refusing "enforcement" also ordinarily involves no "coercive" use of agency power, force against someone's liberty or property. Affirmative enforcement, by contrast, supplies a concrete action for a court to evaluate.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: These considerations produced a presumption that nonenforcement decisions fall within § 701(a)(2).
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: These considerations produced a presumption that decisions not to enforce fall within § 701(a)(2): they are "committed to agency discretion by law" and cannot be reviewed by courts.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Dunlop showed that Congress can overcome the presumption with substantive enforcement instructions, not that the APA makes all refusals reviewable.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Dunlop showed that Congress can overcome the "presumption" against review by giving substantive instructions on when the agency must enforce. It did not show that the APA makes every refusal reviewable.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: The Court rejected that negative implication.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: The Court rejected that "negative implication," the inference that because the law let the FDA use mere warnings for minor violations, it must require action against major ones.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Footnote 4 left that situation and an extreme general policy amounting to abdication of statutory responsibilities for another case.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Footnote 4 left two situations for another case: a refusal based only on the agency's belief that it lacked power, and an extreme general policy amounting to "abdication," effectively giving up its statutory responsibilities.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: The Court’s final paragraph reserved a colorable constitutional challenge because none had been presented.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: The Court's final paragraph "reserved" (left open) a "colorable," or plausible, constitutional challenge to a refusal, because none had been presented.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: Justice Marshall concurred only in the judgment.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: Justice Marshall "concurred only in the judgment": he agreed with the result, reversing the appeals court, but not with the majority's reasoning.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: If courts nevertheless had to examine every unlawful reason or binding constraint first, the threshold inquiry might resemble merits review.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: If courts still had to examine every unlawful reason or binding constraint first, the threshold question of whether review is allowed might look just like "merits" review, judging the decision itself.

lrs-n-heckler-chaney.sentence: The majority neither decided FDA jurisdiction nor sustained the agency’s substantive assessment after arbitrary-and-capricious review.
lrs-n-heckler-chaney.plain: The majority neither decided the FDA's "jurisdiction" (power) over execution drugs nor upheld the agency’s substantive assessment after "arbitrary-and-capricious" review, the reasonableness check. It held only that courts could not review the refusal.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: Section 109 of the Federal Credit Union Act restricted membership to groups sharing a common bond of occupation or association, or groups within a defined geographic community.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: Section 109 of the Federal Credit Union Act limited membership to groups sharing a "common bond" of occupation or association, such as the same employer, or to groups within one defined geographic community.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: The banks challenged agency charter amendments under § 702 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: The banks challenged the agency's amendments to the credit union's charter (its founding document) under § 702 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). That section lets people harmed by agency action ask a court to review it.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: The district court initially dismissed for lack of what the case called prudential standing, reasoning that Congress had not enacted § 109 to protect banks.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: The "district court" (trial court) first dismissed for lack of what the case called "prudential standing," a court-made limit on who may sue. It reasoned that Congress had not "enacted" (passed) § 109 to protect banks.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: On remand, the district court found ambiguity at step one of the then-operative Chevron framework, under which the first question was whether Congress had clearly resolved the statutory issue.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: "On remand," back in the trial court, the judge found "ambiguity" (unclear meaning) at step one of the then-operative "Chevron framework." Step one asked whether Congress had clearly resolved the statutory issue; if not, courts accepted the agency's reasonable reading.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: Competitive injury sufficient for Article III was not disputed.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: No one disputed that the banks suffered "competitive injury," losing potential customers to the credit union. That met Article III, the Constitution's basic requirement for being allowed to sue.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: The threshold question was the additional relationship between the banks’ affected interest and the interests arguably protected or regulated by § 109.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: The "threshold question," the preliminary one, was a further relationship: whether the banks' affected interest fit the interests arguably protected or regulated by § 109.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: It was at least arguably within the statutory zone, even if Congress’s purpose was promoting credit unions rather than shielding banks.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: The banks’ interest was at least arguably the kind the statute dealt with, even if Congress meant to help credit unions, not to protect banks.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: That reading would leave “common bond” largely redundant.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: If every employer group had a “common bond” just by working for the same company, the phrase would add almost nothing.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: Avoiding surplusage, reading the two limits consistently, and preserving their practical force supplied the fuller analysis.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: The fuller analysis rested on standard reading rules: avoid "surplusage" (reading words so they do nothing), read the statute's two parallel limits consistently, and preserve their practical force.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: The Court held the statute unambiguous under Chevron step one.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: The Court held the statute unambiguous under "Chevron step" one: its meaning was clear, so the Court did not defer to the agency's interpretation.

lrs-n-standing-ncua.sentence: Emphasizing the limited judicial role underlying the then-described prudential requirement, O’Connor would vacate the appellate judgment and remand for dismissal.
lrs-n-standing-ncua.plain: Stressing the limited judicial role behind the then-described prudential requirement, a court-made limit on who may sue, O'Connor would "vacate" (wipe out) the appeals court's judgment and remand for dismissal.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: On January 30, 1984, arbitrators acting under the collective-bargaining agreement upheld discharge.
lrs-o-brock.plain: On January 30, 1984, "arbitrators," private decision-makers acting under the "collective-bargaining agreement" (the union contract), upheld the driver's discharge, his firing.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Backpay after lengthy proceedings might not remove the deterrent to reporting, so the Act required temporary reinstatement after investigation and a reasonable-cause finding.
lrs-o-brock.plain: "Backpay," lost wages recovered after lengthy proceedings, might not remove the fear that deters drivers from reporting hazards. So the Act required temporary "reinstatement" (rehiring) after an investigation and a "reasonable-cause" finding, good reason to believe the firing was retaliation.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: An employer could seek an expeditious hearing and final decision, but its request did not stay reinstatement.
lrs-o-brock.plain: An employer could seek an expeditious (quick) hearing and final decision, but its request did not "stay," or pause, the reinstatement order.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Roadway obtained a preliminary injunction and then summary judgment from the Northern District of Georgia declaring § 405 unconstitutional insofar as it allowed reinstatement without a prior evidentiary hearing.
lrs-o-brock.plain: Roadway won a "preliminary injunction," a temporary block, and then "summary judgment" (a ruling without trial) from the Northern District of Georgia. The court declared § 405 unconstitutional insofar as it allowed "reinstatement" without a prior "evidentiary hearing," one with witnesses and evidence.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Although the final order now supplied Roadway’s reinstatement obligation, the earlier-order dispute was capable of repetition yet evading review: preliminary orders lasted too briefly for full litigation, and a large carrier could reasonably face another.
lrs-o-brock.plain: The final order now governed Roadway’s reinstatement duty, but the earlier-order dispute was "capable of repetition yet evading review": likely to recur yet always ending too soon for full review. Preliminary orders were short-lived, and a large "carrier" (trucking company) could reasonably face another.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: The Secretary conceded that Roadway’s contractual right to discharge for cause was property protected by the Fifth Amendment.
lrs-o-brock.plain: The Secretary conceded that Roadway's contractual right to discharge "for cause," to fire for good reason, was property protected by the Fifth Amendment, so fair procedures were required before taking it.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Preclusion effects of the arbitration could be raised in the administrative case and reviewed by the court of appeals; arbitration did not constitutionally displace the statute.
lrs-o-brock.plain: "Preclusion" effects of the arbitration, whether its decision should settle the matter, could be raised in the agency case and reviewed by the "court of appeals." But the Constitution did not make the arbitration displace the statute.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Applying Mathews v. Eldridge’s contextual balancing, the plurality considered public and private interests, error risk, and additional safeguards’ value.
lrs-o-brock.plain: Applying Mathews v. Eldridge’s contextual balancing test, the "plurality" (the four-Justice lead opinion) weighed the public and "private interests" at stake, the risk of error, and the value of additional safeguards.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Informal statements sufficed at this stage; confrontation and cross-examination did not.
lrs-o-brock.plain: At this early stage, informal statements were enough. "Confrontation" (facing the witnesses) and cross-examination (questioning them) were not required.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Because Roadway lacked the evidence’s substance, however, its answer could not be meaningful and this preliminary order violated due process.
lrs-o-brock.plain: But because Roadway was never told what the evidence against it said, it could not respond meaningfully, so this temporary order violated due process.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: New rules contemplated a hearing within thirty days of objections, an administrative decision within another thirty days, and a final Secretary’s order within 120 days, subject to qualifications and a characterization of the periods as directory.
lrs-o-brock.plain: New rules contemplated a hearing within thirty days of objections, an administrative decision within another thirty days, and a final Secretary’s "order" within 120 days. These came with qualifications, and the periods were called "directory": targets whose breach does not by itself invalidate the process.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: Six Justices found the disclosure inadequate; seven rejected an automatic prior trial-type hearing.
lrs-o-brock.plain: Six Justices found the disclosure of evidence to Roadway inadequate. Seven rejected an automatic prior "trial-type hearing," a full trial-like hearing before temporary rehiring.

lrs-o-brock.sentence: The Secretary was appellant and Roadway appellee, despite the reversed roles in the assigned summary.
lrs-o-brock.plain: The Secretary was the "appellant" (the party appealing) and Roadway the "appellee" (the party defending the lower ruling), even though the assigned summary reverses their roles.

lrs-o-goldberg.sentence: Eligibility rules made these statutory programs, not discretionary gifts.
lrs-o-goldberg.plain: Eligibility rules made these "statutory" programs, set up by law, so people who met the rules had a right to the payments. They were not "discretionary" gifts officials could grant or withhold at will.

lrs-o-goldberg.sentence: Justice Brennan’s majority rejected excluding statutory benefits from constitutional protection by calling them privileges.
lrs-o-goldberg.plain: Justice Brennan’s "majority" refused to strip "statutory" benefits (those the law entitles people to) of constitutional protection by calling them mere "privileges."

lrs-o-goldberg.sentence: Qualified recipients held entitlements, and state termination adjudicated important interests.
lrs-o-goldberg.plain: Qualified recipients held "entitlements," legal rights to the benefits. When the state cut them off, it "adjudicated," or formally decided, important interests in their lives.

lrs-o-goldberg.sentence: The majority recognized both expense and difficulty recovering interim payments from ineligible, judgment-proof recipients.
lrs-o-goldberg.plain: The "majority" recognized both the expense of hearings and the difficulty of recovering interim payments from ineligible recipients who were "judgment-proof," too poor to pay back.

lrs-o-goldberg.sentence: More broadly, he regarded balancing humane procedure as legislative policymaking untethered to written constitutional allocation.
lrs-o-goldberg.plain: More broadly, Black regarded "balancing" (weighing) what procedure would be humane as legislative policymaking, a choice not grounded in what the written Constitution assigns to judges.

lrs-o-goldberg.sentence: The District Court’s requirement of constitutionally adequate pretermination process stood.
lrs-o-goldberg.plain: The District Court’s requirement stood: the state must give constitutionally adequate "pretermination" process, a fair hearing before cutting off benefits.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: From 1954 to 1968, the Federal Power Commission addressed this through individual certificate and rate proceedings, allocating nongas transport costs away from permissible gas charges.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: From 1954 to 1968, the Federal Power Commission handled this case by case, through individual certificate (licensing) and "rate proceedings" (setting prices). It allocated the costs of carrying nongas products away from permissible gas charges.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: They had not been sponsored as evidence, cross-examined, or met with contrary proof and were not prepared for this nationwide rule.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: No witness had vouched for the figures as evidence, no one had questioned them, no one had offered contrary data, and they were not made for a national rule.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: The court rejected privilege because, under the Commission’s previously sustained interpretation, protection belonged to the offeror and Mobil was not the offeror.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: The court rejected Mobil's settlement-talk privilege claim. Under the Commission's previously "sustained" (upheld) reading, the protection belonged to the "offeror," the party making the settlement offer, and Mobil was not the offeror.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: The court set aside liquid-price provisions for want of jurisdiction.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: The court "set aside" (struck down) the rules setting prices for liquid products "for want of jurisdiction": the Commission lacked legal power over that service.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: Mobil could not demand every incident of formal rulemaking under Administrative Procedure Act §§ 556 and 557.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: Mobil could not demand every feature of "formal rulemaking," the trial-style procedures under Administrative Procedure Act §§ 556 and 557.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: The Natural Gas Act lacked the required on-the-record direction, and its legislative history did not supply that intent.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: Formal procedures apply only when a statute directs "on-the-record" rulemaking after a hearing. The Natural Gas Act lacked that direction, and its "legislative history" (the record of its passage) did not supply that intent.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: In its historical approach, intermediate devices—written questions, screening, and limited cross-examination—could test disputed facts without unrestricted oral examination.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: In the court's approach at the time, intermediate "devices," such as written questions, screening of issues, and limited cross-examination, could test disputed facts without unrestricted oral questioning of witnesses.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: Section 16’s necessary-or-appropriate authority implemented existing substantive powers; it neither created new jurisdiction nor erased safeguards.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: Section 16's "necessary or appropriate" rulemaking power implemented the Commission's existing "substantive" powers. It neither created new "jurisdiction" (subjects it could regulate) nor erased procedural safeguards.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: The Natural Gas Act required substantial evidence on the whole record, including contrary material.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: The Natural Gas Act required "substantial evidence," enough relevant evidence, judged on the whole record, including material pointing the other way.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: Florida East Coast Railway did not answer this separate evidentiary problem because its Interstate Commerce Commission proceeding lacked the same congressional substantial-evidence requirement.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: Florida East Coast Railway did not answer this separate evidence problem. Its Interstate Commerce Commission proceeding lacked the same congressional substantial-evidence requirement.

lrs-o-mobil-oil.sentence: The assigned later discussion of burdens from such intermediate hearing requirements and Vermont Yankee’s response is editorial history.
lrs-o-mobil-oil.plain: The textbook’s later notes explain that in-between hearing requirements like these proved burdensome and that Vermont Yankee stopped courts from adding procedures beyond what statutes require; that is background, not part of this case.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: He also invoked statewide coordinating-board guidelines generally contemplating no more than seven years’ appropriate full-time probationary service, with qualifications, and continued tenure employment absent adequate cause.
lrs-o-perry.plain: He also invoked statewide coordinating-board guidelines generally contemplating no more than seven years of full-time "probationary service" (trial employment), with qualifications. After that, employment would continue with tenure absent "adequate cause," a good reason, for dismissal.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: Government may have discretion to deny a benefit for many reasons but cannot withhold it to penalize protected speech.
lrs-o-perry.plain: Government may have "discretion" (freedom) to deny a benefit for many reasons. But it cannot withhold one to punish speech the First Amendment protects.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: Legislative testimony and criticism of public college policy presented a bona fide constitutional issue under precedents protecting teachers’ public-concern speech.
lrs-o-perry.plain: His testimony to lawmakers and criticism of public college policy raised a "bona fide," or genuine, constitutional issue. Earlier "precedents" protect teachers who speak on matters of public concern.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: Procedural due process required its own showing of liberty or property.
lrs-o-perry.plain: To win a hearing under the Due Process Clause, Sindermann had to show he was losing “liberty” or “property,” a separate question from his speech claim.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: As in Board of Regents v. Roth, the companion public-employment case, the relevant property inquiry concerned independent rules or mutually explicit understandings supporting legitimate entitlement.
lrs-o-perry.plain: As in Board of Regents v. Roth, the companion case on public jobs, property depended on independent rules or "mutually explicit understandings," clear understandings shared by both sides, that support a legitimate right to keep the job.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: An institution using annual contracts even for senior faculty could develop a common law of tenure-like security, but repeated appointments did not create a federal guarantee of perpetual renewal.
lrs-o-perry.plain: A college using annual contracts even for senior faculty could develop a "common law" of tenure-like security, unwritten rules built from its practice. But repeated appointments did not create a federal guarantee of renewal forever.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: He suggested that uncertain state contract law should first be resolved by state courts through federal abstention.
lrs-o-perry.plain: He suggested federal "abstention": federal courts should hold off and let state courts first resolve uncertain questions of state contract law.

lrs-o-perry.sentence: Sindermann could litigate motive and attempt to prove de facto tenure.
lrs-o-perry.plain: Sindermann could now "litigate" (argue in court) the college's motive, trying to show he was let go for his speech. He could also try to prove "de facto" tenure, tenure in practice even without a formal grant.

shoe.sentence: The commissioner assessed International Shoe for 1937–1940, delivered notice to a local solicitor, and sent registered notice to headquarters.
shoe.plain: The state commissioner "assessed" International Shoe, calculating what it owed for 1937–1940. He delivered notice to one of its local solicitors (salesmen) in Washington and sent registered-mail notice to its headquarters.

shoe.sentence: The company appeared specially, contesting authority rather than making a general appearance.
shoe.plain: The company "appeared specially," coming to court only to contest Washington's authority over it, rather than making a "general appearance," which would have accepted the court's power.

shoe.sentence: “Presence” simply restates whether its authorized activity makes defense of this particular suit reasonable within the federal system.
shoe.plain: Calling a company "present" in a state simply restates a conclusion: that its authorized activities there make its "defense" of this particular suit there reasonable within the federal system.

shoe.sentence: Continuous local activity producing the liability ordinarily supported suit; casual activity ordinarily did not support unrelated claims.
shoe.plain: Continuous activity in a state that produces the "liability" (legal responsibility) sued on ordinarily supports suit there. Casual, occasional activity ordinarily does not support claims unrelated to it.

shoe.sentence: The solicitor whose conduct formed relevant contacts could reasonably convey a related proceeding, and registered mail to the home office was reasonably calculated to inform the company.
shoe.plain: The solicitor whose work formed the relevant contacts could reasonably pass on notice of a related lawsuit. Registered mail to the home office was also "reasonably calculated" to inform the company, meaning likely to actually reach it.

shoe.sentence: He would dismiss the appeal as unsubstantial rather than create broad constitutional rules.
shoe.plain: Black would "dismiss" the appeal as "unsubstantial," raising no serious federal question, rather than create broad new constitutional rules.

shoe.sentence: The sustained, claim-connected sales operation drove the result; later labels of specific and general jurisdiction help describe the patterns but do not transform this holding into authority over every unrelated corporate claim.
shoe.plain: The "sustained" (ongoing) sales operation connected to this tax claim drove the result. Later labels, "specific" jurisdiction over related claims and "general jurisdiction" over any claim, describe its patterns, but do not turn this holding into power over every unrelated corporate claim.

vokes.sentence: She sued Arthur Murray and Davenport for cancellation of the contracts, an accounting, and recovery of payments not chargeable to instruction already given.
vokes.plain: She "sued" Arthur Murray and Davenport for "cancellation of the contracts," an accounting (a full reckoning of the money paid), and "recovery" (refund) of payments not chargeable to lessons already given.

vokes.sentence: The trial court dismissed her fourth amended complaint with prejudice for failure to state a cause of action.
vokes.plain: The trial court dismissed her fourth amended complaint "with prejudice," for good, for "failure to state a cause of action": even if everything she alleged were true, it gave her no legal claim.

vokes.sentence: Judge Pierce’s opinion for the Florida Second District Court of Appeal rejected a mechanical fact-opinion distinction.
vokes.plain: Judge Pierce’s opinion for the Florida Second District Court of Appeal, an intermediate appeals court, rejected a mechanical "fact-opinion distinction," the automatic rule that only false facts, not opinions, can be fraud.

vokes.sentence: Superior knowledge, trust, unequal ability to evaluate the subject, and devices making an opinion misleading could support relief even when statements were framed as opinions.
vokes.plain: "Superior knowledge" by the speaker, the listener's trust, unequal ability to judge the subject, and "devices" (tricks) making an opinion misleading could support "relief." That was so even when the statements were framed as opinions.

vokes.sentence: An instructor might have no initial duty to disclose every observation, yet could not necessarily give reassuring evaluations while concealing contrary knowledge essential to their meaning.
vokes.plain: An instructor might have no initial "duty to disclose" every observation. But once he gave reassuring evaluations, he could not necessarily hide contrary knowledge essential to their meaning.

vokes.sentence: The related sports-agency dispute in Speakers of Sport v. ProServ illustrates the difference in context: that court construed an endorsement forecast as aspirational and separately applied Illinois’s fraudulent-scheme requirement.
vokes.plain: The related sports-agency dispute in Speakers of Sport v. ProServ shows how context matters. That court "construed" (interpreted) a forecast of endorsement deals as aspirational sales talk, and separately applied Illinois's special requirement for fraud claims based on a fraudulent scheme.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: Indiana initially gave a tax-sale buyer a certificate and a lien superior to existing liens.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: Indiana first gave a tax-sale buyer a certificate and a "lien," a legal claim on the land, that ranked ahead of all existing liens, including the Board's mortgage.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: Interested owners and lienholders could redeem by paying the price, later taxes and assessments, and a statutory additional amount.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: Interested owners and "lienholders" (those with claims on the land, such as mortgage lenders) could redeem, undoing the sale. They had to repay the price, later "taxes and assessments," and an additional amount the statute set.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: The former owner then received another notice and thirty days to redeem, but mortgagees received no corresponding required notice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: Before the deed issued, the former owner got another notice and thirty days to "redeem" (pay and recover the land). Mortgagees, mortgage lenders like the Board, received no corresponding required notice.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: The deed conveyed title free of existing liens, subject to limited challenges.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: The tax deed conveyed title (ownership) free of existing "liens," the earlier claims on the land, subject only to limited challenges.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: The Board therefore faced immediate subordination and eventual destruction of its security, even though it did not own the land outright.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: So the Board faced immediate "subordination," its mortgage dropping behind the buyer's claim, and the eventual destruction of "its security," the mortgage backing its loan. That mattered even though it did not own the land outright.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: When Adams sued to quiet title in November 1979, the Board opposed summary judgment, challenging notice of both the sale and redemption opportunity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: When Adams sued in November 1979 to quiet title, asking a court to declare him the clear owner, he sought "summary judgment" (a ruling without trial). The Board opposed it, challenging notice of both the sale and its "redemption opportunity," the chance to pay and recover the land.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: Justice Marshall’s six-Justice Supreme Court majority applied the Mullane notice standard: a method reasonably calculated in context to inform interested persons and allow objections.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: Justice Marshall’s six-Justice Supreme Court majority applied the "Mullane notice standard." Notice must use a method "reasonably calculated," in the circumstances, to inform interested persons and allow them to make "objections."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: Calling the proceeding one against property did not excuse indirect notice to identifiable interests.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: Treating the tax sale as a case against the land itself, rather than against any person, did not make indirect notice such as posting and newspaper notice enough for people whose interests could be identified.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: Where identity was reasonably ascertainable from a recorded mortgage, publication required supplementation by mail to the last known available address or personal service.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: If a lender's name could reasonably be found in the recorded mortgage, a newspaper notice alone was not enough; the county also had to mail notice to the lender's last known address or deliver it in person.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: She favored state assessment of burdens and affected parties’ ability to protect themselves, subject to correction of irrational choices.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: O'Connor would have let each state weigh for itself how costly notice is and how well affected people can protect themselves, with courts stepping in only if the state's choice was irrational.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.sentence: Inadequate presale notice made it unnecessary to decide a separate duty to notify mortgagees before the tax deed or the constitutionality of Indiana’s later 1980 paid annual-notice-request procedure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-073.plain: Because inadequate notice before the sale decided the case, the Court did not decide whether "mortgagees" (mortgage lenders) also needed notice before the tax deed. Nor did it decide whether Indiana's later 1980 procedure, where lenders pay to request annual notice, is constitutional.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: The "postsale redemption period," the window after the sale when Jones could pay the back taxes and reclaim the house, expired.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: On cross-motions for summary judgment, the trial court ruled for the defendants.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: On "cross-motions for summary judgment," both sides asking for a ruling without trial, the trial court ruled for the "defendants," Flowers and the state official.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: The Arkansas Supreme Court affirmed, treating statutory mailing as adequate without actual receipt.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: The Arkansas Supreme Court "affirmed" (agreed), treating mailing notice as the statute required as adequate even without actual receipt.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to decide whether known failure of the certified-mail attempt required a practicable follow-up before sale.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to decide one question: when the state knows its "certified-mail" attempt failed, must it take a "practicable" (reasonably doable) follow-up step before the sale?

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: But affirmative information that the letters were unclaimed, received while there was time to respond, changed the circumstances.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: But once the letters came back unclaimed, and there was still time to try again, the state actually knew its notice had failed, and that changed what due process required.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: The question was what someone actually desirous of informing the owner would reasonably do next.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: The test was practical: what would a person who genuinely wanted to reach the owner do after learning the letter had not arrived?

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: The State also could not automatically make occupants the absent owner’s agents for retrieving certified mail.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: The state could not simply assume that whoever lived in the house was responsible for picking up the owner's certified mail on his behalf.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: Those practices informed the burden analysis without creating a universal personal-service requirement.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: Arkansas's own extra steps in some cases showed that follow-up was not too burdensome, but the Court did not require hand delivery in every case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.sentence: In his view, later failure information should not turn that ex ante inquiry into a potentially endless obligation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-077.plain: In Thomas's view, notice is judged "ex ante," as of when it is sent. Learning later that it failed should not turn that inquiry into a potentially endless duty to keep trying.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: A March 2006 show-cause order, delayed when Turner failed to appear, culminated in a January 3, 2008 hearing.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: In March 2006 the court issued a "show-cause order," requiring Turner to explain why he should not be held in contempt for unpaid support. It was delayed when he failed to appear and culminated in a January 3, 2008 hearing.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: After briefly hearing Rogers, the judge found willful contempt, imposed twelve months in jail, allowed release only after reducing arrears to zero, and placed a lien on benefits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: After briefly "hearing" from Rogers, the judge found "willful contempt," deliberate disobedience of the support order. He imposed twelve months in jail, allowed release only after Turner reduced his "arrears" (overdue support) to zero, and placed a "lien," a legal claim, on his benefits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: After he served the sentence, the South Carolina Supreme Court rejected the claim because civil contempt did not require every criminal safeguard.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: After Turner served the "sentence," the South Carolina Supreme Court rejected his "claim." It reasoned that civil contempt, which aims to force payment rather than punish, does not require every criminal-case safeguard, such as a free lawyer.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Respondents asserted mootness because confinement ended without alleged collateral consequences.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: "Respondents," the opposing side, asserted mootness: the case was pointless to decide because Turner's confinement had ended and no lasting "collateral consequences" were "alleged."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: The Court instead applied capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review principles.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: The Court used an exception for problems that are likely to happen again but always end too quickly to be reviewed: a jail term of a year or less would run out before an appeal could finish, and Turner himself was likely to face the same situation again.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Failure to stay a federal contempt order differed from state proceedings not readily subject to immediate Supreme Court review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: The Court said a case about failing to ask for a pause (a stay) of a federal contempt order was different: state proceedings like Turner's cannot readily reach the Supreme Court in time, so his case could still escape review.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Civil confinement coerced compliance and ended when contempt was purged.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: Civil-contempt jail is meant to pressure a person into obeying, not to punish; it ends as soon as the person complies, here by paying.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: A person clearly unable to comply could not properly be imprisoned on that rationale; accuracy preserved liberty and the civil-criminal distinction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: If someone truly cannot pay, jailing them to force payment makes no sense. So deciding accurately whether a person can pay protects their freedom and keeps civil contempt from becoming punishment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Gagnon allowed case-specific counsel decisions in probation revocation, and the controlling Vitek position allowed suitable professional help rather than invariably an attorney.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: Gagnon allowed case-by-case decisions on appointing "counsel" (a lawyer) in "probation revocation" hearings. The controlling position in Vitek allowed suitable professional help rather than always an attorney.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: The Court applied Mathews balancing: private liberty, risk and value of safeguards, and countervailing interests.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: The Court used the Mathews test, weighing the person's interest in freedom, the risk of a mistaken jailing and how much an added safeguard would reduce it, and the opposing interests.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Rogers was also unrepresented; giving only the obligor a lawyer might add imbalance, delay, and formality while children and custodial families needed support.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: Rogers, the parent owed support, was also unrepresented. Giving only the "obligor" (Turner, who owed the support) a lawyer might add imbalance, delay, and formality, while the children and "custodial families" caring for them needed the support.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: It left open collection of government reimbursement, where government would likely have counsel or a competent representative, and unusually complex matters requiring trained advocacy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: The Court left open cases where the government collects reimbursement owed to it, and would likely have "counsel" (a lawyer) or a competent representative. It also left open unusually complex matters requiring trained advocacy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Turner had litigated counsel, while the United States as amicus introduced a different procedural theory unaddressed below, without a developed record or fully tested boundaries.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: The dissent noted that Turner had "litigated" (argued) only for counsel. The United States, as "amicus" (friend of the court), introduced a different procedural theory unaddressed "below," in the lower courts, with no developed record or fully tested limits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.sentence: Adopting an amicus argument on an existing issue differed from vacating on a new constitutional basis.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-109.plain: In their view, adopting an "amicus" argument on an issue already in the case differed from "vacating," or wiping out, a judgment on a new constitutional basis.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: The new federal law imposed safe-workplace duties and authorized the Government to seek abatement orders and civil penalties even before anyone was injured, while leaving state remedies for actual injury available.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: The new federal law imposed duties to keep workplaces safe. It let the Government seek "abatement orders" (orders to fix hazards) and civil penalties (fines) even before anyone was hurt, while state "remedies" for actual injury stayed available.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: Unless a commissioner directed review within thirty days, the judge’s ruling became the Commission’s final order.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: Unless a commissioner directed review within thirty days, the judge's "ruling" became the Commission's "final order," the agency's binding decision.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: A court of appeals could review legal questions but had to accept findings supported by substantial evidence on the whole record.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: A "court of appeals" could review "legal questions" but had to accept findings supported by "substantial evidence," evidence that reasonably supports them, on the whole record.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: A later district-court collection suit did not reopen liability or the penalty.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: A later "district-court" (federal trial court) suit to collect the fine did not "reopen" liability, whether the employer broke the law, or the amount of the penalty.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: The Supreme Court granted review only on whether the Seventh Amendment barred this administrative adjudication, leaving their criminal-jury arguments outside the accepted question.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: The Supreme Court "granted review" only on whether the Seventh Amendment, the civil jury right, barred this "administrative adjudication," an agency deciding the cases. The employers' arguments for a criminal-trial jury fell outside the question it accepted.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: Otherwise control over the forum could become control over the right itself.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: Otherwise, the employers warned, Congress's control over the "forum," where a case is heard, could become control over the jury right itself, erased simply by sending cases to an agency.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: It also invited a broader ruling that Government penalty litigation did not carry a Seventh Amendment jury right even in court.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: The Government also invited a broader "ruling": that its suits for penalties carry no Seventh Amendment jury right even in a regular court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: When Congress created statutory public rights and the Government enforced them in its sovereign capacity, it could assign initial adjudication and factfinding to an administrative forum incompatible with juries.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: When Congress created "statutory" public rights, which the Government enforces in its "sovereign capacity" (acting as government), it could assign initial decision and "factfinding" to an administrative "forum" where juries do not fit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: Statutory creation alone did not defeat a jury right.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: A "jury right" was not lost merely because a statute, rather than old common law, created the claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: Curtis v. Loether, addressing a statutory housing-discrimination damages action, and Pernell v. Southall Realty, addressing a judicial possession action, illustrated the requirement to preserve juries when Congress chose ordinary courts for traditionally legal rights and remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: Curtis v. Loether, a "statutory" damages "action" for housing discrimination, and Pernell v. Southall Realty, a court suit to recover possession of property, show the rule. When Congress sends traditionally legal rights and "remedies" to ordinary courts, juries must be preserved there.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: Equity, admiralty, and some common-law proceedings used other arrangements.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: Juries were never the only factfinders: courts of equity and admiralty, and some common-law proceedings, decided facts without them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: Preserving jury trial therefore did not freeze every future regulatory remedy into an ordinary action at law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: Preserving jury trial therefore did not freeze every future regulatory "remedy" into an ordinary "action at law," an old-style lawsuit for money tried to a jury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: The Court distinguished administrative factfinding about private rights when conducted as an adjunct to an Article III court.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: The Court distinguished agency "factfinding" about private rights done as an "adjunct" to an Article III court, a helper to a real federal court that keeps final control.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: It also retained final authority to decide whether a jury was constitutionally required in a legal action before a forum ordinarily using juries.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: The courts also kept final authority to decide whether the Constitution required a jury in a legal action brought before a "forum" (a court) that ordinarily uses juries.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.sentence: The Court reserved whether Congress could assign public-right adjudication and fines to an agency without judicial intervention at any stage.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-416.plain: The Court "reserved" (left open) whether Congress could assign "public-right" cases, those the government enforces for the public, and fines to an agency with no court involvement at any stage.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: After removal, hundreds of actions were consolidated for pretrial proceedings before Judge Anita Brody.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: After "removal" from state to federal court, hundreds of "actions" (lawsuits) were consolidated before Judge Anita Brody for "pretrial proceedings," the stages before any trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: The league sought dismissal based on federal labor-law preemption, arguing that resolving claims required interpreting collective bargaining agreements and arbitration.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: The league sought "dismissal" based on federal "labor-law preemption," arguing federal labor law displaced the state claims. Resolving them, it said, required interpreting the "collective bargaining agreements" (union contracts) and their arbitration provisions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: An August term sheet proposed a capped settlement, which Brody declined preliminarily to approve in January 2014 because the monetary fund might not cover all eligible claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: An August "term sheet," an outline of deal terms, proposed a "capped settlement" with a maximum total payout. In January 2014 Brody declined to give even preliminary approval, because the fund might not cover all eligible "claims."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: An earlier unsuccessful Rule 23(f) petition concerned preliminary certification and was a separate stage.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: An earlier Rule 23(f) petition, a request for a mid-case appeal, had failed. It concerned preliminary "certification," the decision to treat the players as a class, and was a separate stage.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: A claimant did not have to prove NFL participation caused the diagnosis.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: A "claimant" (a player seeking payment) did not have to prove that playing in the NFL caused the diagnosis; a qualifying diagnosis was enough.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: Concussion-related NFL claims were released while collective-bargaining, retirement, disability, and health-insurance benefits were preserved.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: Concussion-related claims against the NFL were released, given up in the settlement. Players' "collective-bargaining" (union contract), retirement, disability, and health-insurance benefits were preserved.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: Judge Ambro, joined by Judges Hardiman and Nygaard, reviewed certification and approval for abuse of discretion, including erroneous law or clearly erroneous factfinding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: Judge Ambro, "joined by" Judges Hardiman and Nygaard, "reviewed" certification and approval for "abuse of discretion." That means asking whether the trial judge used the wrong law or made "clearly erroneous" (plainly mistaken) findings of fact.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: Settlement still required Rule 23(a) and Rule 23(b)(3) compliance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: Even a class formed just to settle must meet Rule 23's ordinary class requirements: (a)'s basic ones and (b)(3)'s added tests for money claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: These players challenged the same alleged course of conduct with common legal theories, also supporting typicality.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: These players challenged the same "alleged" course of NFL conduct with common legal theories. That also supported "typicality," meaning the named players' claims were typical of the whole class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: Predominance demanded more than one common question, but league-wide conduct and scientific causation supplied cohesion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: "Predominance" (shared issues outweighing individual ones) demanded more than one common question. Here the NFL's league-wide conduct and "scientific causation," the general science of brain injury, supplied that cohesion.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.sentence: Superiority was uncontested because settlement avoided prolonged, duplicative litigation and delayed compensation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2016.plain: "Superiority," whether a class action beats other methods, was uncontested. Settlement avoided prolonged, duplicative lawsuits and delayed compensation.
