brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: Ordinary contract principles, which also apply to the government, allowed "restitution" (getting your money back) after repudiation or "nonperformance" amounting to "total breach." That requires a substantial loss of the deal's value, not just any minor delay.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.sentence: Once justified, restitution could restore an advance even if eventual performance would have been financially disadvantageous.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: Once justified, "restitution" could give back an advance payment even if eventual "performance" of the deal (carrying it out) would have lost the companies money.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.sentence: Although the leases expressly incorporated some future regulations under named laws, their catchall did not make the process infinitely changeable through later legislation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: The leases did say some future regulations would apply. But their general catch-all wording did not mean the companies had agreed that later laws could change the approval process however Congress liked.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.sentence: The United States was the contracting obligor; announcing adherence to inconsistent legislation communicated departure from the bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: The United States was the contracting "obligor," the party that owed the promised performance. By announcing it would follow a new, conflicting law, it signaled it would depart from the "bargain" it had made.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.sentence: It did not reconsider sovereign acts, because the Government did not challenge the trial court’s rejection of that defense.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: The Court did not revisit the government's 'sovereign acts' defense (that it is not liable for general laws passed for the public), because the government had not challenged the trial court's rejection of it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.sentence: They need not prove certain permission or profit to recover the price of an opportunity the Government had substantially altered.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: The companies did not need to prove they would surely have gotten permission to drill, or made a profit, to "recover" what they paid. They had paid for an opportunity, and the government had substantially altered it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.sentence: Stevens favored at most modest delay damages, regarding $156 million as disproportionate relief from known investment risk.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-088.plain: Justice Stevens, dissenting, favored at most modest "delay damages" (compensation only for the holdup). He saw refunding $156 million as disproportionate "relief" from investment risks the companies knew they were taking.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: An asset-freeze temporary restraining order followed May 29 and a stipulated preliminary injunction June 11.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: An "asset-freeze" temporary restraining order, an emergency order locking up the defendants' money, followed on May 29. A "stipulated" preliminary injunction, one the defendants agreed to, followed on June 11, keeping restrictions in place until the case was decided.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: By consent, Magistrate Judge Denlow conducted a seven-day bench trial between June 6 and July 11, 2006, then made Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52 findings.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: "By consent" of both sides, Magistrate Judge Denlow held a seven-day "bench trial" (a trial without a jury) between June 6 and July 11, 2006. He then made written findings of fact and conclusions of law under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Their express or obvious implied character permitted direct evaluation without a consumer survey or psychology expert, although an expert offered for consumer-perception testimony would still need proper qualifications.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: The ads' claims were "express or obvious implied," stated outright or plainly suggested, so the judge could decide their meaning himself without a consumer survey or psychology expert. An expert offering "testimony" on how consumers understand ads would still need proper qualifications.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Deception required a material representation, omission, or practice likely to mislead reasonable consumers.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: An ad is deceptive under the FTC Act if it says or leaves out something important that is likely to mislead ordinary, reasonable consumers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Express and important health claims were presumptively material under the applied precedents.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: Under the "precedents" (earlier cases) the court applied, "express and important health claims" were presumed material, meaning presumed to matter to buyers' decisions without separate proof.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: The bracelet was a statutory device because its advertised intended use mitigated pain and affected bodily function, regardless of actual success.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: The bracelet was a "statutory" device, a medical device under the law, because its advertised "intended use" was to relieve pain and affect how the body works. Whether it actually worked did not matter to that question.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: A simple efficacy claim differed from an establishment claim asserting a particular proof level.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: A simple "efficacy claim" ("this works") differs from an establishment claim, which says a particular level of proof exists, such as "tests prove this works."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: For these strong health claims, competent and reliable evidence required a well-conducted randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: For these strong health claims, competent and reliable evidence required a well-run "randomized" (participants assigned by chance), double-blind (neither they nor researchers know who gets what), "placebo-controlled" study, compared against a fake treatment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Pantron and Acu-Dot, precedents addressing placebo-based defenses, supported rejecting subjective improvement as proof of represented inherent effectiveness.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: Pantron and Acu-Dot, "precedents" on "defenses" based on the placebo effect, supported rejecting people's own feeling of improvement as proof. The ads claimed the product itself worked, which subjective improvement does not show.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Count II independently succeeded because claims that tests proved relief were unsupported by the studies, making falsity and inadequate basis converge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: Count II, the second claim, won on its own: the ads said tests proved pain relief, but the studies did not support that. So falsity and lack of an adequate basis came to the same thing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: A prior Illinois consumer-class-action directed verdict for Park did not preclude federal enforcement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: Park had won a "directed verdict" (a judge's ruling ending the case without a jury decision) in an earlier Illinois consumer class action. That did not bar the federal enforcement suit.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: The FTC was neither party nor privy to private claimants; it vindicated a public statutory interest.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: The FTC was neither a party to that case nor in privity with (closely tied to) the private "claimants," the buyers who sued. It was enforcing a public "statutory" interest, so the earlier judgment did not bind it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Individual responsibility required participation or authority to control plus requisite knowledge, not subjective intent to defraud.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: "Individual responsibility" (personal liability) required that a person took part in, or had authority to control, the practices, plus the "requisite" (required) knowledge. It did not require a personal intent to defraud.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.sentence: Applying § 13(b) equitable precedents then governing, the court rejected an absolute net-profit ceiling and distinguished direct consumer losses from payments retained by nonparty intermediaries.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-010.plain: Applying the "equitable" precedents then governing § 13(b), the FTC's injunction power, the court refused an absolute cap at net profits. It separated direct consumer losses from payments kept by "nonparty" middlemen, companies not in the case.

brief-CT-CB-0131.sentence: Justice Carley’s majority accepted that Wright was neither a biological nor adoptive parent and expressly rejected virtual adoption as the basis for this support obligation.
brief-CT-CB-0131.plain: Justice Carley’s majority accepted that Wright was neither the boy's biological nor adoptive parent. It expressly rejected "virtual adoption," treating someone as having informally adopted a child, as the basis for this support duty.

brief-CT-CB-0131.sentence: Those limits on ordinary parental duties did not exclude an independently enforceable undertaking.
brief-CT-CB-0131.plain: Those limits on ordinary parental duties did not rule out a separate, "enforceable" promise that Wright himself had made to support the boy.

brief-CT-CB-0131.sentence: Georgia’s statutory promissory-estoppel rule, O.C.G.A. § 13-3-44(a), protected a promise reasonably expected to induce action or forbearance that did induce it and required enforcement to prevent injustice.
brief-CT-CB-0131.plain: Georgia's statutory promissory-estoppel rule, O.C.G.A. § 13-3-44(a), enforces a promise the promisor should expect to cause action or "forbearance" (holding back from acting), which does cause it. Enforcement is required when needed to prevent injustice.

brief-CT-CB-0131.sentence: Wright was presumed to understand the consequences associated with acknowledging fatherhood, and his knowledge of nonpaternity made this a voluntary commitment rather than mistake.
brief-CT-CB-0131.plain: Wright was "presumed" (assumed by law) to understand what acknowledging fatherhood meant. Because he knew of his "nonpaternity," that he was not the biological father, this was a voluntary commitment, not a mistake.

brief-CT-CB-0131.sentence: The asserted reliance was an alternative opportunity forgone: Newman refrained from identifying and seeking support from the biological father.
brief-CT-CB-0131.plain: Newman's reliance was what she gave up: relying on Wright, she did not track down the real father or seek support from him.

brief-CT-CB-0131.sentence: An opportunity not pursued was not necessarily an opportunity irretrievably lost.
brief-CT-CB-0131.plain: The dissent said not going after the real father was not the same as losing that chance forever, and Newman had not shown it was too late to pursue him.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.sentence: The city’s bill of exceptions provided that the verdict would stand if unused lumber was compensable; otherwise Young would receive a smaller agreed amount.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.plain: The city's "bill of exceptions" (its formal list of objections for the higher court) set out an agreement. If the unused lumber was "compensable," meaning the city had to pay for it, the "verdict" would stand; otherwise Young would receive a smaller agreed amount.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.sentence: Justice Hammond held that destruction discharged further performance of the entire repair contract while allowing recovery for qualifying partial performance.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.plain: Justice Hammond held that the fire's destruction "discharged" (excused) further performance of the whole repair "contract." But it still allowed "recovery" (payment) for qualifying "partial performance," work already done that counted.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.sentence: The owner’s obligation covered work sufficiently identified with the existing structure that it would have benefited the owner in the contemplated way absent destruction.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.plain: The city had to pay for work that had become part of the bridge and would have benefited the city as planned if the fire had not happened.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.sentence: Young retained title, care and control of the unused stock and could exchange it for other lumber.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.plain: Young "retained title" (kept legal ownership), care and control of the unused lumber, and could exchange it for other lumber.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.sentence: On October 18, 1904, the Supreme Judicial Court sustained the city’s exceptions, set aside the verdict and directed entry of the smaller stipulated judgment for Young.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0178.plain: On October 18, 1904, the Supreme Judicial Court, the state's highest court, upheld the city's objections. It chose to "set aside the verdict" (cancel the jury's award) and ordered the smaller "stipulated judgment," the amount the parties had agreed on, for Young.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: The National Firearms Act defined machinegun by automatic firing of more than one shot, without manual reloading, through a single trigger function, and included certain conversion parts and combinations.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: The National Firearms Act defined a machinegun as a weapon firing more than one shot automatically, without manual reloading, with a single function of the trigger. The definition also covered certain parts and combinations of parts that convert a gun into one.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: The President selected Sessions’s chief of staff, Matthew Whitaker, to exercise the Attorney General’s duties under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: The President chose Matthew Whitaker, Sessions's chief of staff (a job that did not need Senate confirmation), to carry out the Attorney General's duties temporarily. He did this under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA), the general law on filling vacant offices.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: It construed a single trigger function as one pull or analogous motion, and automatic firing as a self-acting or self-regulating mechanism permitting multiple rounds through that function.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: ATF "construed" (interpreted) a "single function of the trigger" as one pull or a similar "motion." It read "automatically" as a self-acting or self-regulating mechanism that fires multiple rounds from that one function.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: The challengers alleged unlawful statutory interpretation and defects in explanation, disclosure, and responses to comments under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: The challengers "alleged" (claimed) that ATF misread the statute. They also claimed it failed to explain itself, disclose information, and respond to public comments, as required by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the law on agency rulemaking.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: By then William Barr had replaced Whitaker after approximately one hundred days of acting service and was automatically substituted under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 25(d).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: By then William Barr had replaced Whitaker after about one hundred days of "acting service" (temporary service in the job). Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 25(d), Barr automatically replaced Whitaker as the official named in the suit.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: Preliminary relief required a clear showing of likely success, likely irreparable harm, favorable equities, and consistency with the public interest.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: "Preliminary relief" (an order blocking the rule before final decision) required a clear showing of four things: "likely success" on the claims, likely harm money could not fix, "favorable equities" (fairness tipping their way), and consistency with the "public interest."

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: Under the then-governing Chevron framework, clear statutory instructions controlled, while a permissible interpretation of ambiguity received deference.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: Under the "Chevron framework" then in force, clear instructions in the statute controlled. Where there was "ambiguity," meaning the statute was unclear, the court deferred to the agency's reading if it was permissible, or reasonable.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: A policy change required acknowledgment and good reasons, not an extra substantive burden solely because the policy differed.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: An agency changing its policy had to acknowledge the change and give good reasons. It did not face an extra "substantive" burden, a tougher standard on the merits, just because the policy differed from before.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: Those old legal opinions were not critical factual support that had to be disclosed for rebuttal: the device’s operation was undisputed, and the opinions contradicted the new position.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: ATF's old legal "opinions" (its earlier letters on these devices) were not critical factual support it had to disclose so the public could offer "rebuttal," a response. How the device worked was undisputed, and the opinions cut against the new position anyway.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: Section 926(b)’s opportunity-for-hearing language did not require an oral hearing.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: Section 926(b)'s promise of an "opportunity for a hearing" did not require an "oral hearing," a live, in-person proceeding; written comments were enough.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: No inadequacy of Tucker Act or Little Tucker Act compensation, or applicable exception, had been shown.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: Owners could seek payment from the United States under the Tucker Act or Little Tucker Act, laws allowing money claims against the government. No one showed that route was inadequate, or that an exception applied.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: The Coalition argued that 28 U.S.C. §508 required exhaustion of the Deputy Attorney General, Associate Attorney General, and further designated successors before resort to the FVRA.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: The Coalition argued that 28 U.S.C. §508, a Justice Department succession law, required going through the Deputy Attorney General, the Associate Attorney General, and further named successors first. Only after that, it said, could the President resort to the FVRA.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: Friedrich read §3347 differently: another applicable succession statute made the FVRA nonexclusive, not unavailable.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: Judge Friedrich read §3347 differently. When another succession statute applies, the FVRA becomes "nonexclusive," meaning the President may use either law, not unavailable.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: Friedrich instead applied Eaton, which held that performing a superior’s duties for a limited time under special temporary conditions did not transform a subordinate into a permanent principal officer.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: Friedrich instead applied Eaton, an 1898 case. It held that doing a superior's duties for a limited time, under special temporary "conditions," did not turn a subordinate into a permanent "principal officer," a top-level officer needing Senate confirmation.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.sentence: The court thus rejected the alternative challenges without simply assuming that his chief-of-staff post already made him an inferior officer.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-006.plain: The court thus rejected the backup challenges without simply assuming that Whitaker's chief-of-staff post already made him an "inferior officer," a lower-level officer under the Constitution.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: The President could remove the Director only for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The President could remove the Director only for "inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance," meaning poor performance, failing to do the job, or misconduct, and not over policy disagreements.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Funding came from the Federal Reserve subject to a statutory ceiling, rather than annual appropriations.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The Bureau's funding came straight from the Federal Reserve, up to a "statutory" ceiling (a cap set by law). It did not depend on annual "appropriations," the yearly money Congress votes.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: The Ninth Circuit affirmed, regarding Humphrey’s Executor, which upheld protection for Federal Trade Commission members, and Morrison, which upheld protection for an independent counsel, as controlling despite institutional differences.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The Ninth Circuit affirmed. It treated Humphrey’s Executor (upholding firing protection for Federal Trade Commission members) and Morrison (upholding it for an independent counsel, a special prosecutor) as controlling despite the CFPB's different setup.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: A court-appointed friend of the Court defended the judgment, while the parties continued to dispute whether Seila Law had to comply.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Because the government no longer defended the law, a court-appointed "friend of the Court" (an outside lawyer) defended the "judgment" below. Meanwhile the "parties" (the two sides) still disputed whether Seila Law had to comply with the demand.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: It also had standing to appeal: compelled disclosure was a concrete injury attributable to the judgment and redressable by rejecting enforcement.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Seila Law also had "standing" to appeal, the right to bring it. Being forced to disclose information was a "concrete" (real) injury, caused by the "judgment," that a ruling refusing enforcement would fix.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Appointed adversarial briefing addressed prudential concerns about the presentation of the issue.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Appointing a lawyer to argue the other side gave the Court "adversarial" briefing, with both sides truly argued. That answered "prudential concerns," the Court's own practical worries, about how the issue was being presented.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Article II vested executive power in the President, who needed authority to supervise subordinate officers carrying out executive responsibilities.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Article II gives the executive power, the power to carry out the laws, to the President. So the President needs authority to supervise, including by firing, the officers who carry out executive duties.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: It identified two recognized categories of protected officers: the expert multimember body described in Humphrey’s Executor and certain inferior officers with limited duties described in Perkins and Morrison.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The Court identified two accepted kinds of protected officers. One is the expert board with several members described in Humphrey’s Executor; the other is certain "inferior officers" (lower-level officers) with limited duties, described in Perkins and Morrison.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: The Bureau lacked the partisan balance and staggered membership of the commission described in Humphrey’s Executor and could impose final relief or seek substantial judicial penalties, not merely recommend action.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The Bureau lacked the "partisan balance" (members from both parties) and staggered terms of the commission in Humphrey’s Executor. It could also impose final "relief" (binding orders) or seek large court penalties, not merely recommend action.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: The President’s singular power carried electoral accountability; an unelected subordinate making major policy without removable supervision did not.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Voters can hold the President responsible. A single unelected director making major policy whom the President cannot fire answers to no one.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: It also rejected an expansive construction of inefficiency, neglect, or malfeasance to avoid the constitutional issue.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The Court refused to stretch 'inefficiency, neglect, or malfeasance' to let the President fire the Director over policy disagreements, a reading that would have sidestepped the constitutional problem.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Agencies could not exercise quasi-legislative or quasi-judicial authority outside the Constitution’s three branches.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Justice Thomas said agencies could not exercise "quasi-legislative" (lawmaking-like) or quasi-judicial (case-deciding-like) power while sitting outside the Constitution's three branches.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Thomas would deny the enforcement petition without deciding severability.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Thomas would simply have refused to enforce the demand, without deciding whether the rest of the law could survive once the unconstitutional part was cut out.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Drawing comparisons to Booker and Free Enterprise Fund, he disputed the plurality’s choice to preserve enforcement powers by severing tenure protection.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Comparing Booker and Free Enterprise Fund, Thomas disputed the "plurality's" (the lead opinion's) choice to keep the Bureau's enforcement powers by "severing," or cutting out, its firing protection.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: The Constitution’s silence on removal, Necessary and Proper Clause, Appointments Clause, and interdependent branch design left Congress broad organizational choices so long as the President retained the ability to perform constitutional duties.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Justice Kagan pointed to the Constitution's silence on removal, the Necessary and Proper Clause (Congress's power to set up the government), the Appointments Clause, and the branches' interlocking design. Together these leave Congress broad choices, so long as the President can still perform the President's own constitutional duties.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: She read Humphrey’s Executor, Wiener, and Morrison as limiting Myers through a functional inquiry into interference with presidential duties.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Kagan read Humphrey’s Executor, Wiener, and Morrison as narrowing Myers, the 1926 broad-removal case. In her view the test is functional: does a firing protection actually interfere with the President's duties?

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: The Government contended that an Acting Director removable at will had ratified the demand.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: The Government argued that an Acting Director, a temporary Director the President could fire at will, had "ratified" (later approved) the demand, curing any problem.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Roberts’s Part IV, joined only by Alito and Kavanaugh, addressed severability because ratification would be futile if the Bureau’s powers fell with its structure.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Roberts's Part IV, "joined" only by Alito and Kavanaugh, addressed severability: whether the rest of the law survives without the invalid part. "Ratification" would be pointless if the Bureau's powers fell along with its unconstitutional structure.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: Seven Justices therefore supported preserving the Bureau by severing removal protection, though only three joined that analysis.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: Seven Justices therefore supported keeping the Bureau by "severing" (cutting out) only its firing protection, though only three joined Roberts's reasoning for it.

brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.sentence: On June 29, 2020, the Court vacated the Ninth Circuit and remanded.
brief-LRS-COMP-SLAUGHTER-SEILA.plain: On June 29, 2020, the Court "vacated" (cancelled) the Ninth Circuit's decision and "remanded," sending the case back for more proceedings.

cp-capron.sentence: The proceedings called Van Noorden formerly of Pitt County but did not allege that Capron was an alien, a citizen of any state, or resident anywhere.
cp-capron.plain: The court papers described Van Noorden as formerly of Pitt County, North Carolina. But they did not "allege" (state) that Capron was an "alien" (a foreign citizen), a citizen of any state, or a resident anywhere, so the record did not show the parties were from different places.

cp-capron.sentence: Capron then obtained a writ of error seeking review of mistakes shown by the record.
cp-capron.plain: Capron, the losing plaintiff, then obtained a "writ of error," the older procedure asking a higher court to review mistakes shown in the court record.

cp-capron.sentence: Harper characterized assurance of subject-matter jurisdiction—the legal authority to hear that category of dispute—as the court’s responsibility.
cp-capron.plain: Harper, Capron's lawyer, said it was the court's own responsibility to make sure it had "subject-matter jurisdiction," the legal authority to hear that category of dispute, whatever the parties did.

cp-capron.sentence: The disposition allowed the losing plaintiff to challenge a judgment whose record failed to establish the federal citizenship basis despite his own choice of forum.
cp-capron.plain: The "disposition" (the Court's ruling) let the losing "plaintiff" attack a judgment whose record never established the citizenship basis for federal power. That was so even though the case was in that court by his own "choice of forum."

cp-capron.sentence: The broader lesson that parties cannot create limited federal jurisdiction by agreement follows from the issue, counsel’s argument, and result, rather than a quoted authored rationale.
cp-capron.plain: The broader lesson is that parties cannot create the limited federal "jurisdiction" (court power) by agreeing to it. That follows from the issue, "counsel's" (the lawyer's) argument, and the result, not from any written explanation by the Court.

cp-lacks.sentence: Almost two years after appellate review ended, Irene moved under Civil Practice Law and Rules 5015(a)(4), permitting relief from a judgment entered without jurisdiction.
cp-lacks.plain: Almost two years after "appellate" review (her appeals) ended, Irene moved under Civil Practice Law and Rules 5015(a)(4), New York's procedure rules. That provision allows relief from a judgment entered without "jurisdiction," meaning by a court lacking power to make it.

cp-lacks.sentence: Her jurisdictional classification was the route around the final judgment.
cp-lacks.plain: Calling the defect "jurisdictional," a lack of court power, was her only route around the "final judgment," because that kind of defect can be raised at any time.

cp-lacks.sentence: Judicial usage sometimes calls failure to state a claim, inability to grant a remedy, and fundamental lack of adjudicative competence “jurisdiction.”
cp-lacks.plain: Courts sometimes use the word "jurisdiction" loosely. They apply it to "failure to state a claim" (a claim the law does not support), to a court's inability to grant a remedy, and to a true lack of power to decide the type of case.

cp-lacks.sentence: Although matrimonial relief was statutory, failure to satisfy a statutory condition did not necessarily remove power over matrimonial suits.
cp-lacks.plain: "Matrimonial" relief, such as divorce, existed only by statute. But failing to meet one of the statute's conditions did not necessarily take away the court's power over matrimonial "suits" (lawsuits).

cp-lacks.sentence: The residence rule remained mandatory, but its violation would make a decision erroneous rather than void under this remedy.
cp-lacks.plain: The "residence" rule (the residency requirement for divorce) still had to be followed. But under this "remedy," a motion to undo a judgment made without power, breaking it made the decision erroneous, a mistake to fix on appeal, not void, a nullity open to attack forever.

cp-lacks.sentence: The extraordinary nonwaivable, void-judgment consequences of genuine jurisdictional defects made that expansion disruptive.
cp-lacks.plain: Genuinely "jurisdictional" defects, true lacks of court power, can never be waived and make a judgment void. Those extraordinary consequences made expanding the category to ordinary mistakes disruptive, since finished cases could be reopened endlessly.

cp-lacks.sentence: This affirmance concerned the collateral postjudgment proceeding, distinct from the earlier appeal of the divorce itself.
cp-lacks.plain: This "affirmance" (the higher court upholding the ruling) concerned Irene's separate "postjudgment" proceeding, her later motion to undo the divorce. It was distinct from the earlier appeal of the divorce itself.

cp-lacks.sentence: The casebook later compares Arbaugh’s treatment of Title VII’s employee threshold as a merits ingredient rather than a late jurisdictional objection.
cp-lacks.plain: The casebook later compares Arbaugh’s treatment of Title VII’s minimum-employee requirement as a "merits" ingredient, part of the claim the plaintiff must prove. It is not a "jurisdictional" limit on the court's power that could be raised late.

cp-shoshone.sentence: Revised Statutes sections 2325–2326 authorized an adverse suit to establish possession before the Land Department issued the patent.
cp-shoshone.plain: Revised Statutes sections 2325–2326, federal mining law, authorized an "adverse suit," in which a rival claimant sues to establish who has the right to possess the claim. That suit came before the Land Department issued the "patent," the government's official deed to the land.

cp-shoshone.sentence: The Supreme Court therefore had to decide whether federal authorization of this type of suit itself made it a federal-question case.
cp-shoshone.plain: The parties were not from different states, so the Supreme Court had to decide whether federal authorization of this type of suit itself made it a "federal-question" case, one arising under federal law.

cp-shoshone.sentence: But these provisions directed claimants to a court of competent jurisdiction, invoking ordinary jurisdictional rules rather than creating an exclusively federal forum or a new allocation of judicial power.
cp-shoshone.plain: But these provisions sent claimants to a "court of competent jurisdiction," one that already had power to hear such cases, using ordinary "jurisdictional" rules. They did not create an "exclusively federal" forum or a new division of "judicial power" between courts.

cp-shoshone.sentence: Recognition of those sources did not convert them into federal law.
cp-shoshone.plain: Federal law's choosing to respect local mining customs and state statutes did not turn them into federal law.

cp-shoshone.sentence: The Court distinguished a statute authorizing a suit to establish a right from one creating the right whose scope must be construed.
cp-shoshone.plain: The Court distinguished a "statute" that merely authorizes a suit to establish a right from one that creates the right itself, whose scope must be "construed" (interpreted). Only the second makes a case arise under federal law.

cp-shoshone.sentence: State courts were expected to enforce federal enactments under the Supremacy Clause.
cp-shoshone.plain: State courts were expected to enforce federal "enactments" (laws passed by Congress), because federal law binds them under the Supremacy Clause.

cp-shoshone.sentence: That court was to reverse its decree, dismiss the action originally filed federally, and remand the removed action to state court.
cp-shoshone.plain: The federal trial court was to "reverse" (undo) its decree and "dismiss" the "action" (lawsuit) originally filed in federal court. It was also to "remand" (send back) the case that had been removed from state court to that state court.

dyer.sentence: Dyer had not reciprocally promised to work for life, and he had surrendered no viable claim because workers’ compensation apparently supplied his exclusive remedy.
dyer.plain: Dyer had not promised in return to work for life. And he "surrendered no viable claim," meaning the injury claim he gave up was worthless, because workers' compensation apparently was his "exclusive remedy," the only way to recover for a job injury.

dyer.sentence: For consideration analysis, the Iowa Supreme Court assumed that tort claims against the employer and coemployees were clearly invalid.
dyer.plain: To test consideration (whether Dyer gave something of value in exchange), the Iowa Supreme Court assumed that his "tort" claims, injury lawsuits against the employer and co-workers, were clearly invalid.

dyer.sentence: Surrender of an invalid claim could supply consideration if the claim was objectively doubtful because law or facts were uncertain, or if the surrendering party honestly believed it might fairly be found valid.
dyer.plain: "Surrender of an invalid claim" can still supply "consideration," something of value given in exchange for a promise. It does so if the claim was objectively doubtful because the law or facts were uncertain, or if the person giving it up honestly believed it might fairly be found valid.

dyer.sentence: Reasonable grounds would generally help persuade a factfinder that the professed belief was honest.
dyer.plain: Reasonable grounds for the belief would generally help persuade a "factfinder," the jury or judge deciding the facts, that Dyer's stated belief was honest.

dyer.sentence: Requiring good faith prevented manufactured nuisance claims from automatically purchasing concessions.
dyer.plain: Requiring "good faith" (honest belief) kept made-up "nuisance claims," bogus claims brought just to pressure the other side, from automatically buying concessions.

dyer.sentence: Invalidity alone therefore did not entitle National By-Products to summary judgment on the appealed consideration ground.
dyer.plain: "Invalidity" of the claim alone therefore did not entitle National By-Products to "summary judgment" (a win without trial) on the consideration ground it had "appealed." Whether Dyer honestly believed in his claim still had to be decided.

greenfield.sentence: Its operative clause made the recordings, reproductions, and embodied performances entirely Philles’ property, free of the artists’ claims.
greenfield.plain: The contract's "operative clause," the part that actually transfers rights, made the recordings, copies of them, and the performances on them entirely Philles' property. The artists kept no "claims" to them.

greenfield.sentence: The Appellate Division affirmed and permitted unjust-enrichment recovery at an industry-standard royalty of 50% for synchronization and third-party licensing.
greenfield.plain: The Appellate Division, New York's intermediate appeals court, affirmed. It allowed "unjust-enrichment" recovery (repaying what Philles unfairly gained) at an industry-standard "royalty" of 50% for "synchronization" (licensing songs for films and TV) and licensing to other companies.

greenfield.sentence: Under New York law a complete, clear writing supplies the best evidence of intent; ambiguity is a legal question, and outside evidence cannot rewrite definite language to produce a fairer bargain.
greenfield.plain: Under New York law, a complete, clear writing is the best evidence of what the parties intended. Whether there is "ambiguity" (unclear wording) is a "legal question" for the judge, and outside evidence cannot rewrite definite terms to make a fairer "bargain."

greenfield.sentence: These masters predated federal statutory copyright protection for sound recordings in 1971, so the court addressed the common-law contract transfer before it.
greenfield.plain: These master recordings were made before federal "statutory" copyright protection for sound recordings began in 1971. So the court addressed what the contract transferred under "common-law," or state judge-made, rules that came before.

greenfield.sentence: Those decisions supported requiring an express reservation when the grant was comprehensive.
greenfield.plain: Those decisions supported requiring an "express reservation" when the grant of rights was comprehensive: the seller keeps a particular right only if the contract clearly says so.

greenfield.sentence: Unlike New York’s four-corners approach to the recording contract, California permitted preliminary consideration of credible evidence supporting a meaning the release could reasonably bear, as explained in Pacific Gas & Electric.
greenfield.plain: New York reads the "recording" contract by a "four-corners" approach, from its text alone. California, which governed the divorce release, lets a court first consider "credible" (believable) outside evidence for a meaning the release could reasonably bear, as explained in Pacific Gas & Electric.

greenfield.sentence: On October 17, 2002, the Court of Appeals modified the order without costs and remitted the case to Supreme Court to calculate royalties consistently with the contract, otherwise affirming.
greenfield.plain: On October 17, 2002, the Court of Appeals, New York's highest court, changed part of the "order" and "remitted the case" (sent it back) to Supreme Court, the trial court, to recompute royalties under the contract. It otherwise affirmed, with neither side paying the other's costs.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: The HEROES Act of 2003 separately allowed the Secretary of Education to waive or modify covered Title IV provisions when necessary in war, military operations, or national emergency to prevent affected recipients being placed in a worse financial position regarding assistance because of the emergency.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: The HEROES Act of 2003 separately let the Education Secretary "waive" (set aside) or modify Title IV student-aid rules when needed in a war, military operation or national emergency. The goal was to keep affected borrowers from being left financially worse off because of the emergency.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: The Eighth Circuit found Missouri likely had standing and substantial merits questions, issuing a nationwide preliminary injunction pending appeal.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: The Eighth Circuit found Missouri likely had "standing" (the right to sue) and raised substantial "merits questions" about who should win. So it issued a "nationwide" preliminary injunction blocking the program everywhere while the appeal went on.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: The government asked the Supreme Court to vacate the injunction or take review before judgment.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: The government asked the Supreme Court to "vacate" (lift) the injunction, or to take "review" of the case right away, before the appeals court reached judgment.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: Chief Justice Roberts’s majority described MOHELA as Missouri’s instrumentality in law and function.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: Chief Justice Roberts’s majority described MOHELA as Missouri's "instrumentality," an arm of the State, both legally and in what it did. So harm to MOHELA was harm to Missouri.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: Kagan distinguished the Arkansas university case and rejected using Missouri students’ interests to evade restrictions on parens patriae suits against the federal government.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: Justice Kagan "distinguished" (explained why it did not apply) the Arkansas university case. She rejected using Missouri students' interests to get around limits on "parens patriae" suits, in which a state sues on behalf of its citizens, against the federal government.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: Drawing on MCI, the majority understood “modify” as modest adjustment rather than fundamental transformation.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: Drawing on MCI, an earlier case, the majority read "modify" to mean a modest adjustment, not a fundamental transformation.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: It did not strike down the Act as an unconstitutional delegation.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: The Court did not strike down the Act as an "unconstitutional delegation," meaning Congress giving away too much of its own lawmaking power. It held only that the Act did not authorize this program.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: The majority regarded unprecedented use of the Act, fiscal magnitude, and political and economic importance as requiring clear congressional authorization.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: The majority said the unprecedented use of the Act, its huge cost, and its political and economic importance called for "clear congressional authorization," an unmistakable grant of power by Congress, which it found lacking.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: Barrett joined fully but separately distinguished contextual interpretation from a strong substantive canon requiring a less natural permissible reading to protect an external value.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: Justice Barrett joined the majority fully but wrote separately. She saw the major questions idea as reading a law in context, not a strong "substantive canon," a rule forcing a less natural but permissible reading to protect an outside value.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: She regarded major questions here as replacing Congress’s broad delegation with judicial demands for particularity.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: Kagan, dissenting, said the major questions approach here replaced the broad "delegation" (grant of power) Congress actually gave with judicial demands for more specific authorization.

lrs-i-biden-nebraska.sentence: It denied as moot the government’s application to vacate the Eighth Circuit injunction.
lrs-i-biden-nebraska.plain: Since the Court decided the case itself, it denied as "moot" (no longer mattering) the government's "application to vacate," its request to lift the Eighth Circuit's "injunction."

lrs-o-little.sentence: The ship was taken to Boston and libeled as American property subject to forfeiture.
lrs-o-little.plain: The ship was taken to Boston, where it was "libeled," meaning an admiralty lawsuit was filed against the ship itself. The claim was that it was American property subject to "forfeiture," meaning the government could take it as a penalty.

lrs-o-little.sentence: Section 5 authorized presidential instructions to public armed ships to stop and examine suspected American vessels on the high seas.
lrs-o-little.plain: Section 5 let the President instruct public armed ships (Navy vessels) to stop and search suspected American ships on the "high seas," the open ocean beyond any country's waters.

lrs-o-little.sentence: The instructions thus pursued the statute’s purpose while extending beyond its specific authorization for high-seas seizure of vessels sailing to a French port.
lrs-o-little.plain: The President's instructions served the statute's goal, but went beyond what the statute (the law Congress passed) specifically allowed. Congress authorized seizing ships on the high seas sailing to a French port, and the instructions also reached ships coming from one.

lrs-o-little.sentence: The Massachusetts District Court restored the ship and cargo because the libellants had not established forfeiture, but denied damages and costs.
lrs-o-little.plain: The Massachusetts District Court, the federal trial court, gave back the ship and cargo because the "libellants" (the side that filed the case seeking forfeiture) had not proved forfeiture. But it refused to award "damages," money to make up the owner's loss, or court costs.

lrs-o-little.sentence: The Circuit Court reversed the denial of damages and costs, and assessors fixed damages at $8,504.
lrs-o-little.plain: The Circuit Court, the next court up, "reversed" (overturned) the refusal to award damages and costs. "Assessors," officials appointed to calculate the loss, then fixed the damages at $8,504.

lrs-o-little.sentence: Congress had prescribed a method of execution excluding this capture.
lrs-o-little.plain: By spelling out which ships could be seized at sea, Congress implicitly ruled out seizing others like this one.

lrs-o-little.sentence: But he expressly abandoned that position and accepted his colleagues’ conclusion: instructions could not transform the transaction or legalize a capture otherwise constituting a trespass.
lrs-o-little.plain: But Marshall expressly "abandoned" that view, meaning he gave it up, and accepted the other Justices' conclusion. The President's instructions could not change the nature of the seizure or make legal a capture that was otherwise a "trespass," a wrongful taking of property for which the captain was personally liable.

lrs-o-little.sentence: It also rejected an objection to the damages account: no defect appeared on its face, and counsel had not excepted before the proper tribunal.
lrs-o-little.plain: The Court also rejected a challenge to the damages account, because nothing was wrong with it on its face. And the captain's counsel (lawyers) had not "excepted," meaning formally objected, before the proper tribunal, the court where that objection belonged.

ng-giap.sentence: Clause 18 expressed the entire understanding, disclaimed outside oral, written, express or implied obligations, and preserved accrued rights under earlier agreements.
ng-giap.plain: Clause 18 said the written contract was the "entire understanding," the whole deal. It disclaimed any other obligations, whether oral, written, "express" (stated outright) or implied (unstated), but kept rights already earned under earlier agreements.

ng-giap.sentence: The High Court bifurcated liability and quantum and dismissed at liability.
ng-giap.plain: The High Court, the trial court, split the case into two stages: "liability" (whether the defendants were legally responsible) and "quantum" (how much they owed). It dismissed the case at the liability stage.

ng-giap.sentence: It partly relied on the entire-agreement clause against implied good faith and rejected a poorly developed quantum-meruit theory.
ng-giap.plain: The court relied partly on the "entire-agreement clause," the term saying the written contract was the whole deal, to rule out an implied duty of good faith. It also rejected a poorly developed "quantum meruit" theory, a claim to be paid the reasonable value of the work done.

ng-giap.sentence: This clause’s own reference to implied terms contemplated their existence and did not bar implication.
ng-giap.plain: Because Clause 18 itself mentioned implied terms, it assumed they could exist, so it did not stop the court from reading terms into the contract.

ng-giap.sentence: A term implied in fact fills a necessary gap in the particular agreement according to presumed intention.
ng-giap.plain: A term 'implied in fact' fills a gap in this specific contract based on what the parties would have intended if they had thought about it.

ng-giap.sentence: Business efficacy and the officious-bystander inquiry complemented each other: would both parties unhesitatingly agree because the term was necessary?
ng-giap.plain: "Business efficacy" (is the term needed to make the deal work?) and the "officious-bystander" test (would both sides have said "of course" if a meddling onlooker suggested it?) work together. The question is whether both parties would unhesitatingly agree because the term was necessary.

ng-giap.sentence: A term implied in law instead applies on broader policy grounds to a class of contracts and carries wider future consequences.
ng-giap.plain: A term 'implied in law' is added by the law to every contract of a certain type for policy reasons, so recognizing one affects many future cases.

ng-giap.sentence: The court used Luxor v. Cooper to examine risk allocation and the exact event earning commission, not to impose a universal commission rule.
ng-giap.plain: The court used Luxor v. Cooper, an English case on agents' commissions, to examine "risk allocation" (who bore the risk that the deal fell through) and the exact event that earned the commission. It did not use the case to impose one universal commission rule.

ng-giap.sentence: On April 29, 2009, it dismissed with costs and the usual consequential orders, with no separate opinion.
ng-giap.plain: On April 29, 2009, the court dismissed the appeal with costs, meaning Ng had to pay the other side's legal costs, along with the usual follow-on orders. It gave no separate written opinion explaining its reasons.

ricketts.sentence: The executor denied those allegations and raised want of consideration.
ricketts.plain: The executor denied those allegations (the claims Katie made) and raised "want of consideration," meaning the note could not be enforced because Katie gave nothing in return for it.

ricketts.sentence: The executor then brought error to the Nebraska Supreme Court, challenging admission of the note, the sufficiency of consideration, and the treatment of the undisputed evidence.
ricketts.plain: The executor "brought error" to the Nebraska Supreme Court, meaning he asked it to review the trial for mistakes. He challenged the admission of the note into evidence, the sufficiency of the consideration (whether anything adequate was given for it), and how the undisputed evidence was handled.

ricketts.sentence: Justice Sullivan’s opinion accepted the difficulty in the executor’s consideration argument.
ricketts.plain: Justice Sullivan’s opinion accepted that the executor's consideration argument had real force: nothing was bargained for in exchange for the grandfather's promise.

ricketts.sentence: Writing the promise in the form of a promissory note established evidence of the promise and its amount; between the original parties and their representatives, it did not prevent the estate from raising want of consideration.
ricketts.plain: Putting the promise in a "promissory note," a signed written promise to pay, proved the promise and its amount. But between the "original parties" (the grandfather and Katie) and those standing in for them, such as his estate, the note did not stop the estate from raising "want of consideration," the lack of anything given in return.

ricketts.sentence: Although some decisions called the resulting expenditure consideration, the Nebraska court identified equitable estoppel as the operative principle: a donor who induces the recipient to assume obligations on the faith of the promise cannot then shift that resulting loss to the recipient by invoking want of consideration.
ricketts.plain: Some courts called a recipient's spending in reliance on a promise "consideration." Nebraska said the real principle is "equitable estoppel," a fairness rule: a donor who induces (leads) someone to take on obligations by relying on the promise cannot then push that loss onto them by raising want of consideration.

ricketts.sentence: The opinion described estoppel in pais as a consequence of acts, admissions, or conduct inducing another person to change position in accordance with the actor’s real or apparent intention.
ricketts.plain: The opinion described "estoppel in pais" (estoppel by conduct) as arising from acts, admissions, or conduct inducing another person to change position, meaning change their situation, in line with what the actor really or apparently intended.

ricketts.sentence: When the other person relies in good faith and changes position for the worse, the actor may be precluded from asserting an otherwise available right against that person.
ricketts.plain: When the other person relies "in good faith" (honestly) and changes position for the worse, the actor may be "precluded," or barred, from asserting a right they would otherwise have against that person.

ricketts.sentence: The supreme court agreed that the undisputed facts required a directed legal result for one party.
ricketts.plain: The supreme court agreed that because the facts were undisputed, the law required a "directed" result for one party, decided by the judge without leaving anything to a jury.

ricketts.sentence: A verdict for the executor would therefore have lacked support, and the asserted intervening trial errors could not have changed the judgment properly due.
ricketts.plain: So a verdict (the jury's decision) for the executor would have had no support. The trial errors he claimed happened along the way could not have changed the judgment (the court's final decision) that was properly due.

ricketts.sentence: Later writers describe this kind of enforcement of reliance on a future promise as promissory estoppel.
ricketts.plain: Today this idea, enforcing a promise because someone reasonably relied on it, is called promissory estoppel.

specht.sentence: That license defined its programs as Communicator and Navigator, contained an integration clause, and required arbitration in Santa Clara County for disputes relating to the agreement.
specht.plain: That license defined its programs as Communicator and Navigator and contained an "integration clause," a term saying the written license was the complete agreement. It also required arbitration (private dispute resolution instead of court) in Santa Clara County for disputes relating to the agreement.

specht.sentence: Netscape sought compelled arbitration and a stay under Federal Arbitration Act § 4.
specht.plain: Netscape asked for "compelled arbitration," a court order sending the cases to arbitration, and a "stay," pausing the lawsuits, under section 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act.

specht.sentence: It invoked both software licenses and, against Specht, direct-benefit estoppel.
specht.plain: Netscape relied on both software licenses. Against Specht, who never downloaded SmartDownload, it also argued "direct-benefit estoppel": that he was bound because he benefited from the contract.

specht.sentence: California formation law became fixed on appeal.
specht.plain: On appeal, everyone accepted that California law decided whether a contract had been formed.

specht.sentence: Legal formation, scope, and estoppel issues received fresh review; subsidiary factual findings were reviewed for clear error.
specht.plain: Legal questions about formation (whether a contract was made), scope, and estoppel received "fresh review," meaning the appeals court decided them anew. The trial court's underlying findings of fact were reviewed only for "clear error," so they stood unless clearly wrong.

specht.sentence: Favorable treatment of disputes within an existing clause could not answer whether these parties ever made the agreement containing it.
specht.plain: The law's favorable treatment of disputes that fall within an existing arbitration clause could not answer the earlier question: whether these parties ever made the agreement containing that clause.

specht.sentence: California law allowed assent by words, writing, or conduct, but conduct carried contractual meaning only where the actor intended the act and knew or reasonably should know that the other side could infer agreement.
specht.plain: California law allowed "assent" (agreement to a contract) by words, writing, or conduct. But conduct counted as agreement only if the person meant to do the act and knew, or reasonably should have known, that the other side could take it as agreement.

specht.sentence: ProCD and Hill concerned product recipients supplied terms and a stated opportunity to review and return before retention or use counted.
specht.plain: ProCD and Hill, earlier cases enforcing terms that came with a product, involved buyers who were given the terms. They were told they could review them and return the product before keeping or using it counted as agreement.

specht.sentence: Section 4 calls for a summary trial if formation is genuinely disputed.
specht.plain: Section 4 of the arbitration law calls for a "summary trial," a quick trial on that question alone, if it is genuinely disputed whether an arbitration agreement was formed.

specht.sentence: The Communicator arbitration clause was broad, making disputes related to that existing agreement presumptively arbitrable.
specht.plain: The Communicator license's arbitration clause was broad. So disputes related to that existing agreement were "presumptively arbitrable," meaning assumed to belong in arbitration unless shown otherwise.

specht.sentence: The claims were collateral to that agreement and outside its clause.
specht.plain: The privacy claims were separate from the browser license, so its arbitration clause did not reach them.

specht.sentence: A nonsignatory knowingly taking a concrete, direct benefit under a contract may not accept that benefit while resisting its arbitration provision.
specht.plain: A "nonsignatory," someone who did not sign the contract, who knowingly takes a concrete, direct benefit under it cannot accept that benefit while refusing its arbitration provision.

watkins.sentence: These facts later prevented the contractor from treating its surprise as a mutual mistake relieving the original duty.
watkins.plain: These facts later stopped the contractor from treating its surprise as a "mutual mistake," an error both sides shared about a basic fact, which might have released it from its original duty.

watkins.sentence: A referee found that the oral agreement superseded the written contract.
watkins.plain: A "referee," an official appointed to hear the evidence and make findings, found that the "oral agreement" (spoken, not written) on the new rock price superseded, meaning replaced, the written contract.

watkins.sentence: Carrig argued that Watkins promised only performance it already owed, so the extra payment lacked consideration.
watkins.plain: Carrig argued that Watkins promised only performance (doing the work) that it already owed. So Carrig's promise of extra payment lacked "consideration," something new given in exchange, and was unenforceable.

watkins.sentence: Thus the court enforced the later arrangement while accepting that the initial obligation already required the rock work at the fixed price.
watkins.plain: So the court enforced the later price arrangement, while accepting that the original contract already required the rock work at the "fixed price," the set amount agreed at the start.

watkins.sentence: A modification incorporated a partial rescission.
watkins.plain: Changing a contract includes cancelling part of the old one, here the old price for rock.

watkins.sentence: If parties could voluntarily discharge an existing duty, combining that release and a new promise in one transaction did not make the release vanish.
watkins.plain: If parties could voluntarily "discharge" (cancel) an existing duty, then combining that "release" (letting the other side off) with a new promise in one transaction did not make the release disappear.

watkins.sentence: Within the transaction, the discharge legally preceded the new duty.
watkins.plain: Within the transaction, the discharge (cancellation of the old duty) legally came first, before the new duty. So Watkins's promise to do the work was new and could support Carrig's promise to pay more.

watkins.sentence: The gift was not the still-executory promise to pay more money.
watkins.plain: The 'gift' was not Carrig's promise to pay more in the future, which was not yet carried out.

watkins.sentence: The court distinguished releasing one’s own debtor from assigning an intangible claim to someone else and regarded the former as capable of completion by a voluntary present release.
watkins.plain: The court said releasing (freeing) your own debtor, the person who owes you, is different from assigning an intangible claim, a legal right, to someone else. The first could be completed at once by a voluntary present release.

watkins.sentence: Later Restatement § 89 comment b criticized simultaneous rescission as a fiction and instead tested a modification’s fairness and justification directly.
watkins.plain: Later, Restatement § 89 comment b, part of an influential summary of contract law, criticized the idea of simultaneous rescission (cancel and remake at the same moment) as a fiction. It instead tests directly whether a modification is fair and justified.

watkins.sentence: Nor does absence of protest universally defeat duress.
watkins.plain: Not protesting at the time does not always defeat a claim of "duress," meaning wrongful pressure that makes an agreement involuntary.

brief-CP-137.sentence: The corporations moved for summary judgment under the then-existing Rule 56(b), invoking the prior judgment.
brief-CP-137.plain: The corporations (the companies) moved for summary judgment, asking the judge to decide the case without a trial, under Rule 56(b) as it then read. They relied on the earlier judgment against Mathews, which had already decided these events.

brief-CP-137.sentence: Judge MacMahon held that the corporations and employees were identified in interest for the derivative liability asserted.
brief-CP-137.plain: Judge MacMahon held that the corporations and their employees were "identified in interest," legally treated as on the same side, for this claim. Mathews asserted "derivative liability": the companies were blamed only for what their employees did.

brief-CP-137.sentence: Because the alleged corporate liability depended on those agents’ actionable wrongdoing, the principals stood or fell with them in this claim.
brief-CP-137.plain: The alleged (claimed, not proven) liability of the companies depended on their agents’ (employees') actually having done something legally wrong. So the principals, the companies the agents worked for, stood or fell with the agents on this claim.

brief-CP-137.sentence: Mathews could not save alternative theories arising from that invasion for serial suits after losing.
brief-CP-137.plain: Mathews had to bring all his legal theories about the incident in one lawsuit. After losing, he could not start a new suit by giving the same events a different legal label.

brief-CP-137.sentence: MacMahon also relied on the earlier actual findings, describing Mathews as directly and collaterally estopped.
brief-CP-137.plain: MacMahon also relied on the findings (facts the first judge actually decided). He described Mathews as "directly and collaterally estopped": barred from suing again on the same claim, and barred from re-arguing facts already decided.

brief-CP-137.sentence: The result applied preclusion to this repeated transaction and alleged derivative liability; it did not announce universal identity between every employer and employee.
brief-CP-137.plain: The ruling applied "preclusion" (the rule barring relitigation) to this repeated transaction, the same set of events, and to the alleged derivative liability, where the companies were blamed only for their employees' acts. It did not say every employer and employee are always treated as one party.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: Rather than transmit process to Germany, he served the American subsidiary as the parent’s domestic agent.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: Instead of sending process (the official lawsuit papers) to Germany, Schlunk served Volkswagen's American subsidiary. He treated it as the German parent's domestic "agent," someone in the U.S. who could legally receive the papers for it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: The parent appeared specially, contending that the Hague Service Convention provided the exclusive permissible method and had not been followed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: The German parent "appeared specially," coming to court only to challenge how it was served without otherwise accepting the case. It argued that the Hague Service Convention, a treaty on serving papers abroad, was the only permitted method and had not been followed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: The Cook County circuit court found an involuntary agency under Illinois law based on complete ownership, overlapping directors, and the subsidiary’s exclusive American importer-distributor role.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: The Cook County circuit court (the state trial court) found an "involuntary agency" under Illinois law, meaning the subsidiary counted as the parent's agent even though never appointed. Reasons: the parent owned it completely, they shared directors, and it was the sole American importer and distributor.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: On certified questions, the Illinois Appellate Court affirmed agency and found no treaty violation; the state Supreme Court denied leave.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: On "certified questions," legal issues the trial court sent up for early answers, the Illinois Appellate Court "affirmed" (agreed with) the agency ruling and found no treaty violation. The Illinois Supreme Court "denied leave," declining to hear a further appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: Because the treaty did not supply a complete sufficiency standard, forum law identified when that act required sending papers abroad.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: The treaty did not supply a complete standard for when service is sufficient. So "forum law," the law of the place where the suit was filed, decided when serving someone required sending papers abroad.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: If service was already complete domestically, an agent’s later communication to its foreign principal was not itself transmission abroad for service.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: If service was already complete inside the country, the agent’s later forwarding of the papers to its "foreign principal" (the overseas company it acts for) was not itself sending papers abroad for service.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: The parent feared states could evade notice protections with domestic labels and invoked notification au parquet, deposit with a local official that could count as service before effective foreign notice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: The parent feared countries could dodge the treaty's notice protections just by calling service "domestic." It pointed to "notification au parquet," a French-style practice of leaving papers with a local official, which could count as service before the foreign defendant actually got notice.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: Due process independently required a method reasonably calculated to inform and allow response.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: Separately from the treaty, due process (the Constitution's fairness guarantee) required a service method "reasonably calculated" to tell the defendant about the suit and allow it to respond, meaning likely to actually reach it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: The Court’s note separately warned that subsidiary activity did not automatically establish jurisdiction over a parent and that constitutional sufficiency of substituted service could demand factual inquiry.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: The Court's footnote separately warned that a subsidiary's activity did not automatically give a court "jurisdiction" (power to decide cases) over its parent. And whether substituted service, serving someone through a stand-in, satisfies the Constitution could require looking at the facts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.sentence: Justice Brennan, joined by Marshall and Blackmun, agreed with affirmance but resisted leaving treaty reach entirely to local classifications.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-087.plain: Justice Brennan, joined by (with the agreement of) Justices Marshall and Blackmun, agreed with the "affirmance," the decision upholding the lower court. But he did not want the treaty's reach left entirely to how each country labels its own procedures.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: The amended bill added former treasurer Currie and successor Samuel Sullivan, seeking discovery, return, and protection against use or further collection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: The "amended bill," the Bank's revised complaint in equity, added former state treasurer Currie and his successor Samuel Sullivan. It sought "discovery" (forced disclosure of facts), return of the money, and protection against its use or any further collection.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: Unlike the earlier charter in Deveaux, which generally supplied capacity to sue in courts of record, this charter expressly allowed suit in any federal Circuit Court as well as competent state courts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: The Bank's earlier charter, considered in the Deveaux case, gave only general "capacity to sue" (the legal ability to bring suits) in courts of record. This charter expressly allowed suit in any "federal Circuit Court" as well as competent state courts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: It extended judicial power to cases arising under federal law, not isolated questions stripped of ordinary facts, payment, release, limitations, and other nonfederal issues.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: Article III extended "judicial power" (the authority of federal courts) to whole cases arising under federal law. Those cases are not isolated federal questions stripped of ordinary facts and nonfederal issues like payment, release, or limitations (filing deadlines).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: A federal question could be an ingredient of the original cause even when the case contained other issues.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: A "federal question," an issue of federal law, could be an ingredient of the original claim, so the case arose under federal law, even when the case also contained other issues.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: If the tax was invalid, Osborn’s procurement and Harper’s execution of collection made them jointly responsible without an official-position justification.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: If the tax was unconstitutional, Osborn (who arranged the collection) and Harper (who carried it out) were both personally liable. Their state offices gave them no legal excuse.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: Equity also was appropriate: repeated annual exactions threatened destruction of the Bank’s Ohio franchise, not merely one compensable trespass.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: Equity, the court's power to order relief like an injunction rather than just money, was also proper. Repeated yearly "exactions" (forced tax collections) threatened to destroy the Bank's Ohio "franchise," its right to do business there, not merely cause one "compensable" trespass, a single wrong money could fix.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: In the historical reasoning of this opinion, the Eleventh Amendment restriction applied to a State named on the record.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: In this opinion's historical reasoning, the Eleventh Amendment's limit on suits against states applied only to a State "named on the record," meaning formally listed as a party in the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: Sovereign exemption did not immunize agents enforcing an invalid law; difficulty protecting Ohio’s interests through them followed from the State’s immunity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: Ohio's "sovereign" exemption (a State’s immunity from suit) did not protect its agents enforcing an invalid law. If it was hard to protect Ohio's interests through those officials, that followed from the State’s own immunity.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: Marshall distinguished taxation of local property from state control of essential operations and held Ohio’s statute repugnant to valid federal law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: Marshall distinguished a state taxing the Bank's local property from a state controlling its essential operations. He held Ohio's statute (the tax law) "repugnant," meaning in conflict with, valid federal law and therefore invalid.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.sentence: On March 19, 1824, the Court affirmed recovery of Sullivan’s segregated $98,000 and the remaining $2,000 from Osborn and Harper, but reversed interest on Sullivan’s specie.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-133.plain: On March 19, 1824, the Court "affirmed" (upheld) recovery of the $98,000 Sullivan kept separate and the remaining $2,000 from Osborn and Harper. But it "reversed" (struck) the interest charged on Sullivan's "specie," the coins he held.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.sentence: A federal district court specially constituted under the then-applicable three-judge-court statute permanently enjoined enforcement as confiscatory.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.plain: A federal district court specially set up with three judges, as a statute (law) then required, permanently blocked enforcement of the rate orders as "confiscatory." That meant the rates were so low they would unconstitutionally take the company's property.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.sentence: The Supreme Court held that having received an unqualified injunction against the rate orders, the company could not prosecute an appeal from its favorable decree merely to revise those valuation and return determinations.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.plain: The Supreme Court held that the company had received an unqualified injunction (a court order) against the rate orders. So it could not appeal its own favorable "decree," the final court order, just to revise the findings on property value and rate of return.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.sentence: The Court expressly stated that the valuation and return portions of this decree would not operate as res judicata concerning later legislative action by the Public Service Commission fixing future rates or judicial proceedings involving those future rates.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.plain: The Court expressly said the value and return findings in this decree would not act as "res judicata," a binding earlier decision. They would not control the Public Service Commission when it later fixed future rates, or court cases over those future rates.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.sentence: The ruling did not erase the decree, reopen the original controversy or declare that all favorable judgments lack preclusive effect.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-523.plain: The ruling did not erase the decree (the court's order), reopen the original dispute, or declare that judgments in a party's favor never have preclusive (binding) effect in later cases.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: Payment was to be by a two-month bill in two months, with weighing by the buyers’ agent within fourteen days.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: Payment was to be by a "two-month bill," a written order to pay due in two months. The buyers' agent would weigh the wool within fourteen days.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: The buyers then sued for nondelivery under the agreement, placing the effect of their posted acceptance in issue.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: The buyers sued because the wool was never delivered. The key question was whether a contract was formed when they mailed their acceptance, before the sellers received it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: At the Worcester Lent assizes, Justice Burrough directed the jury to regard the answer as arriving in due course because the delay resulted from the sellers’ mistake.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: At the Worcester Lent "assizes," the spring trial sessions, Justice Burrough told the jury to treat the reply as arriving in due course (on time). The delay came from the sellers' own mistake in addressing their letter.
