brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: The sellers obtained a conditional rule for a new trial in Easter Term.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: The sellers obtained a "conditional rule" for a new trial: an order granting one unless the buyers could show why not. They got it in Easter Term.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: Relying on the offer decisions Payne v. Cave and Cooke v. Oxley, they argued that no contract bound them until actual receipt on Tuesday and that Monday’s resale had withdrawn the offer.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: Relying on two cases about offers, Payne v. Cave and Cooke v. Oxley, the sellers argued that no contract bound them until they actually received the acceptance on Tuesday. They said their resale of the wool on Monday had already withdrawn the offer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: It treated the offer as continuing throughout the letter’s journey and the buyers’ acceptance as completing the bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: The court treated the offer as continuing, still open, throughout the letter's journey, and the buyers' acceptance as completing the bargain (the contract).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.sentence: On June 5, 1818, the court discharged the rule.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-079.plain: On June 5, 1818, the court "discharged the rule," meaning it cancelled the conditional order, so there would be no new trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: The judgment carried statutory interest at four percent under §17 of 1 & 2 Vict. c.110.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: The judgment earned statutory interest, set by law, at four percent a year under §17 of 1 & 2 Vict. c.110, a statute of Queen Victoria's reign.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: The memorandum expressed Beer’s conditional undertaking, not a new promise by Foakes to make installments.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: The memorandum recorded only Beer's conditional promise, not to sue if paid on schedule. It contained no new promise by Foakes to pay in installments.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: Cave held that the agreement barred execution for any balance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: Justice Cave, the trial judge, held that the agreement barred "execution," meaning using the court to seize Foakes's property, for any remaining balance.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: Watkin Williams and Mathew JJ., sitting in the Queen’s Bench Division, discharged an order for a new trial based on alleged misdirection.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: Justices Watkin Williams and Mathew (JJ.), sitting in the Queen’s Bench Division of the High Court, discharged (cancelled) an order for a new trial. Beer had alleged "misdirection," that the trial judge wrongly instructed the jury.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: Alternatively, forgiveness lacked consideration because Foakes only performed an existing duty.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: Alternatively, any forgiveness of the interest lacked "consideration," something given in exchange. Foakes only performed a duty he already had, paying what he owed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: Settled authorities rejected less money paid in the same way as satisfaction of a greater liquidated obligation, and analogous rules governed demands for additional pay for an existing duty.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: Settled cases rejected paying less money in the same way "as satisfaction" (as full discharge) of a greater "liquidated obligation," a debt fixed in amount. Similar rules applied to demands for extra pay for doing an existing duty.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: Later compliance did not manufacture accord and satisfaction absent at formation: satisfaction was incomplete while installments remained, and Beer gave no new binding acquittance when the final payment arrived.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: Later compliance could not create an "accord and satisfaction" (a binding settlement) that was missing when the deal was made. Satisfaction (full discharge) was incomplete while installments remained, and Beer gave no new binding "acquittance," a release, when the last payment came.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: Selborne retained the principle associated with Pinnel that less money, paid when due in the same manner, could not alone satisfy the larger obligation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: Lord Selborne kept the old rule from Pinnel's Case: paying part of a debt on the due date, in the normal way, cannot by itself discharge the whole debt.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: He acknowledged an apparently arbitrary boundary between an unsealed concession and a deed and thought some written concessions might beneficially be binding without a seal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: He admitted it seemed arbitrary that a promise binds if made in a formal sealed deed but not in an ordinary signed paper, and thought some unsealed written promises should be enforceable.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.sentence: The House did not unanimously construe the memorandum as expressly preserving interest; two Lords read a possible waiver and rejected its enforceability, while two favored an extension-of-time reading and also rejected waiver on the alternative assumption.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-043.plain: The House of Lords did not unanimously construe (interpret) the memorandum as expressly keeping the interest. Two Lords read it as a possible "waiver" (giving up the interest) but held that unenforceable. Two read it as only extending time to pay, and also rejected any waiver if one existed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: The trial court dismissed the university, contract claim, and official-capacity claims under Alabama constitutional immunity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: The trial court dismissed the claims against the university, the contract claim, and the "official-capacity" claims (suits against officials in their official roles). It relied on Alabama's "constitutional immunity," the state constitution's protection of the state from suit.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: The amended complaint alleged ordinary fraud against Lamar and president William Harris, promissory fraud against Lamar and Steptoe, and suppression against Harris and Williams, naming trustees without a substantive claim.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: The amended complaint alleged ordinary fraud (lying about existing facts) against Lamar and president William Harris. It alleged "promissory fraud" (promises made with no intent to keep them) against Lamar and Steptoe, and "suppression" (hiding facts) against Harris and Williams; it named trustees with no substantive (actual) claim.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: After a movant’s prima facie showing, substantial evidence had to permit fair-minded people reasonably to infer a disputed fact, viewed favorably to Byrd.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: Once the "movant" (the side asking for summary judgment) made a "prima facie" showing, an initial case that there was nothing to try, Byrd needed "substantial evidence." That means enough that fair-minded people could reasonably infer the disputed fact, with the evidence read in the light most favorable to Byrd.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: Harris invoked university immunity, but fraudulent individual conduct fell within the relevant exception, allowing merits review without reviving the university claims.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: Harris invoked "university immunity," the university's protection from suit. But an official's own fraudulent conduct fell within an exception to that immunity, so the court reviewed the "merits" (whether the claim actually held up) without reviving the claims against the university.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: Existing-fact fraud required material misrepresentation, reasonable reliance, and resulting injury.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: "Existing-fact fraud," lying about present facts, required a material (important) false statement, reasonable reliance on it, and injury that resulted.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: Promissory fraud required the ordinary elements plus intent when promising not to perform and to deceive.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: "Promissory fraud," fraud based on a promise, required the ordinary elements (the parts that must be proved) plus one more: that when promising, the person intended not to perform and intended to deceive.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: Failure alone was insufficient, and recklessness did not replace intention, but subsequent events could illuminate earlier intent.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: Simply failing to keep a promise is not enough, and recklessness cannot stand in for an actual intent not to perform. But what happened later can be evidence of what the person intended at the time.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: A hearsay objection came too late because defendants themselves submitted Byrd’s deposition without the relevant objection below.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: The "hearsay" objection, that Byrd's account of what others said was secondhand, came too late. The defendants (the officials being sued) had themselves filed Byrd's deposition, his sworn pretrial testimony, in the trial court without raising that objection.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: Suppression against Harris and Williams, however, required duty, actual knowledge and concealment, induced action or inaction, and harm.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: "Suppression," hiding facts, against Harris and Williams required more: a duty to speak, "actual knowledge" (they really knew the facts), concealment, action or inaction by Byrd that the concealment induced (caused), and resulting harm.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.sentence: It reversed only individual-capacity promissory-fraud judgments for Lamar and Steptoe and remanded, without damages, contract enforcement, or a final finding of fraud.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-071.plain: The court "reversed" (overturned) only the judgments for Lamar and Steptoe on the promissory-fraud claims against them individually, and "remanded" (sent them back) for trial. It awarded no damages, enforced no contract, and made no final finding of fraud.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: Yet the judge held the termination clause unconscionable, imposed a good-cause requirement, and found violations of good faith and Massachusetts chapter 93A’s prohibition of unfair or deceptive conduct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: Yet the judge held the termination clause "unconscionable," too unfair to enforce, and imposed a "good-cause" requirement, meaning Dairy Mart needed a real reason to end the deal. The judge also found violations of good faith and of Massachusetts chapter 93A's ban on "unfair or deceptive" business conduct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: Because the couple kept operating during suit, the separate statutory judgment apparently awarded only costs and attorney fees.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: Because the couple kept running the store during the suit (the lawsuit), the separate judgment under the statute apparently awarded them only court costs and attorney fees.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: Justice Wilkins’s Supreme Judicial Court opinion declined to treat the whole business-format franchise as a sale of goods under Uniform Commercial Code Article 2.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: Justice Wilkins’s opinion for the Supreme Judicial Court, Massachusetts' highest court, refused to treat the whole business-format franchise as a "sale of goods." So the sales rules in Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Article 2 did not directly apply.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: The court instead borrowed unconscionability and good-faith policies by common-law analogy.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: Instead, the court borrowed the UCC's policies on "unconscionability" (terms too unfair to enforce) and good faith, applying them by analogy as common-law rules, meaning judge-made law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: Unconscionability concerned formation, commercial context, unfair surprise, and oppression.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: Unconscionability looked at how the contract was formed and its commercial context. It asked about "unfair surprise" (a term that caught the weaker side off guard) and "oppression" (a term that was harshly one-sided).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: A fair term could still be used unfairly, so the court separately examined performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: A fair term could still be used unfairly, so the court separately examined performance, meaning how Dairy Mart actually used the term.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: The court distinguished Fortune, the precedent protecting an employee from termination designed to withhold earned commissions: Dairy Mart appropriated no earned income or money reasonably due.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: In Fortune, firing a salesman to avoid paying commissions he had earned was bad faith. Here Dairy Mart took nothing the couple had earned or were owed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.sentence: No independently developed goodwill, special trade-building efforts, or unrecoverable investment was demonstrated.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-018.plain: The couple showed no "goodwill" they built on their own (customer loyalty tied to them), no special efforts to build the business, and no investment they could not recover.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Agency labor-market research and competitive-harm findings supported its rulemaking, distinct from proof that an ATS employee intended to depart.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: The FTC, the agency, based its rulemaking (writing a binding regulation) on labor-market research and findings that noncompetes harm competition. That was different from proof that any ATS employee actually intended to leave.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: ATS sued two days later, alleging no substantive authority, excess of authority, arbitrary-and-capricious treatment of existing agreements, and unconstitutional delegation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: ATS sued two days later, alleging the FTC had no substantive authority (power to make binding rules on the subject) and exceeded its authority. It also called the treatment of existing agreements "arbitrary-and-capricious" (irrational), and claimed "unconstitutional delegation," that Congress could not hand over this power.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: ATS needed both likely success and likely immediate irreparable injury before balancing equities and public interest.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: To get the rule blocked for now, ATS needed both "likely success" (it would probably win) and likely immediate "irreparable injury," harm money could not fix. Only then would the court balance the "equities," the harms to each side, and the public interest.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Under A.O. Smith, the Third Circuit’s compliance-cost precedent, ordinary required business expense did not become irreparable merely because government reimbursement was unavailable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: Under A.O. Smith, the Third Circuit’s precedent on compliance costs, the ordinary business expense of following a rule did not become "irreparable" harm merely because the government would not pay it back.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Loss of contract rights did not itself satisfy the case-specific imminence requirement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: Losing contract rights (the ability to enforce its noncompetes) did not by itself meet the requirement to show harm about to happen to ATS specifically.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Applying Loper Bright, the Supreme Court’s independent-interpretation rule, Hodge read § 5’s instruction to prevent unfair competition with § 6(g)’s authority for implementing rules.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: Applying Loper Bright, the Supreme Court’s rule that judges interpret statutes themselves without deferring to agencies, Judge Hodge read § 5's instruction to prevent unfair competition together with § 6(g)'s power to make rules carrying out the Act.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Prevention could reach incipient restraints rather than only react after harm.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: The power to "prevent" could reach "incipient restraints," practices that limit competition in their early stages, rather than only react after harm was done.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: The cited du Pont decision did not require a rule-of-reason test for every noncompete.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: The du Pont decision ATS cited did not require a "rule-of-reason" test for every noncompete, meaning a case-by-case weighing of its harms against its benefits.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Finally, preventing unfair competition supplied an intelligible principle.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: Finally, the goal of preventing unfair competition gave an "intelligible principle," a clear enough guiding standard for the agency, so Congress's grant of power was constitutional.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.sentence: Schechter’s invalidation of the much broader National Industrial Recovery Act contrasted it with the FTC Act; it did not show an adequate adjudicatory standard became unconstitutional when used for rules.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-001.plain: Schechter struck down the much broader National Industrial Recovery Act and contrasted it with the FTC Act. It did not show that a standard good enough for "adjudication" (deciding individual cases) became unconstitutional when used to make rules.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: On February 11, she applied to retire effective the next day with the maximum lifetime allowance and no survivor option, revoking the earlier reserve protection.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: On February 11, she applied to retire the next day with the maximum lifetime allowance (the largest monthly pension) and no "survivor" option, meaning nothing would go to her husband after her death. This revoked her earlier choice that protected him.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: As executor, her husband sought to invalidate the February application for mental incompetence.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: As "executor," the person managing her estate, her husband sued to cancel the February application on the ground of "mental incompetence," that she lacked the mental capacity to make it.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: A divided Appellate Division reversed because the evidence failed the prevailing capacity test.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: A divided Appellate Division, New York's intermediate appeals court, "reversed" (overturned) the ruling because the evidence did not meet the prevailing legal test for mental capacity.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: Judge Breitel explained that a contract of a mentally incompetent person not previously adjudicated insane was voidable, and performance need not prevent avoidance if the parties could be restored.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: Judge Breitel explained that a contract by a mentally incompetent person not previously "adjudicated insane" (declared so by a court) was "voidable," able to be cancelled. Performance, carrying out the deal, did not bar "avoidance" (cancelling it) if the parties could be put back where they were.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: Traditional tests examined understanding, rational judgment, and transaction-related delusions, but could miss someone who comprehended a transaction yet could not control conduct because of mental disease.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: Traditional tests looked at whether the person understood the deal, had rational judgment, and had delusions about it. But they could miss someone who understood a transaction yet could not control their conduct because of mental illness.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: The court adopted tentative Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 18C, later numbered § 15: illness or defect making a person unable to act reasonably in the transaction could make duties voidable when the other party had reason to know.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: The court adopted the draft Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 18C, later numbered § 15. If illness or defect made a person unable to act reasonably in the deal, their duties could be "voidable" (able to be cancelled) when the other party had reason to know.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: The accompanying equitable limit also mattered: where terms were fair, the other party lacked knowledge, and performance or changed circumstances made avoidance inequitable, avoidance could terminate to that extent, with relief on equitable terms.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: An equitable (fairness-based) limit also mattered. If the terms were fair, the other party did not know, and performance or changed circumstances made avoidance (cancelling) inequitable, meaning unfair, the right to cancel ended to that extent. The court would grant relief (a remedy) on fair terms.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: The majority regarded the system as aware, or chargeable with awareness, through medical leave and the education board’s psychiatric involvement.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: The majority treated the retirement system as aware, or "chargeable with awareness" (legally treated as knowing), of her illness, because of her medical leave and the education board's involvement in her psychiatric care.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: The board properly worried about retrospective selection: pension finances depend on prospective elections and mortality experience.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: The board was right to worry about families picking the best option after a member dies. Pension funds depend on choices made in advance and on statistics about when people die.

brief-CT-CB-0458.sentence: The challenger bore the burden absent prior adjudication of incompetence.
brief-CT-CB-0458.plain: Since there had been no earlier "adjudication of incompetence," no court ruling that she was incompetent, the challenger (her husband) "bore the burden," meaning he had to prove it.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Clause 5.3 imposed CHF 100,000 per individual violation, payable by A. and/or Sevenedge AG without releasing compliance or further-damage liability.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: Clause 5.3 set a penalty of CHF 100,000 (Swiss francs) for each individual violation, payable by A. and/or Sevenedge AG (a Swiss company). Paying it would not release A. from complying or from liability (legal responsibility) for further damage.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: B. AG’s civil appeal sought CHF 100,000 with the later interest date or remand; it also filed a subsidiary constitutional appeal.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: B. AG's civil appeal sought the full CHF 100,000 with interest from the later date, or a "remand," sending the case back. It also filed a "subsidiary constitutional appeal," a backup appeal claiming its constitutional rights were violated.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Timely civil review of the final cantonal judgment was available and met the CHF 30,000 threshold, so subsidiary constitutional review was unavailable.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: A timely (filed on time) civil appeal from the final "cantonal" judgment, from the court of the Swiss canton (state), was available and met the CHF 30,000 threshold. So "subsidiary constitutional review," the backup route, was not available.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Factual review generally accepted cantonal findings unless a substantiated, outcome-relevant claim showed arbitrariness or another qualifying error.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: On facts, the federal court generally accepted the cantonal court's findings. It changed one only if a "substantiated" claim, backed with specifics, showed it was arbitrary or otherwise legally flawed and mattered to the result.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Contract interpretation first sought actual shared intent; absent proved agreement, the principle of trust supplied objective contextual meaning.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: Interpreting a contract starts with what both sides actually intended. If no shared agreement is proved, the "principle of trust" applies: the contract means what a reasonable person would understand from its words and context.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Business experience and deliberate revision of the earlier letter supported at least conditional intent.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: A.'s business experience and his deliberate rewriting of the earlier letter supported at least "conditional intent," meaning he knowingly accepted that he might be breaching.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Swiss Code of Obligations article 163 allowed freely set penalties but required discretionary reduction of excessive amounts.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: Article 163 of the Swiss Code of Obligations, Switzerland's main contract statute, let parties freely set penalties. But a judge had to use "discretionary" judgment (case-by-case) to reduce excessive ones.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: Article 161(1) allowed a penalty without actual damage, but no damage or demonstrated risk still mattered to reduction.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: Article 161(1) allowed a penalty even without actual damage (loss). But the lack of any damage or shown risk still mattered in deciding how much to reduce it.

brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.sentence: On September 24, 2024, the First Civil Law Division dismissed both civil appeals insofar as admissible and declined the subsidiary constitutional appeal.
brief-CT-COMP-SUP-0130.plain: On September 24, 2024, the First Civil Law Division of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed both civil appeals "insofar as admissible," meaning to the extent it could hear them. It declined to hear the subsidiary constitutional appeal (the backup).

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: Travelers bonded two and later became a codefendant in one of the resulting actions.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: Travelers bonded two of the contracts, guaranteeing Minweld's performance, and later became a "codefendant," sued alongside Minweld, in one of the resulting cases.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: Article V allowed material supply or termination on two days’ written notice for specified defaults.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: Article V let McCloskey, on two days' written notice, supply materials itself or end the contract for specified "defaults," listed failures by Minweld.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: At the close of its case, the district judge granted defense motions for judgment.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: When McCloskey finished presenting its case, the district judge (the federal trial judge) granted the defense "motions for judgment," ruling for the defendants because that evidence was not enough to win.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: Federal jurisdiction rested on diversity, and the appellate court applied Pennsylvania law to the apparently Pennsylvania-executed contracts.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: Federal "jurisdiction" (the court's power to hear the case) rested on "diversity," meaning the parties were from different states. The appellate court applied Pennsylvania law because the contracts were apparently Pennsylvania-executed (signed there).

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: Pennsylvania law required an absolute and unequivocal refusal to perform or a distinct, positive statement of inability.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: Under Pennsylvania law, breaking a contract before performance is due requires a clear, definite refusal to perform or a clear statement that one cannot perform.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: The First Restatement also distinguished inadequate preparation before performance was due from a failure to perform when due; threatening eventual performance did not itself establish anticipatory breach.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: The First Restatement, an early influential summary of contract law, also separated poor preparation before performance was due from failing to perform when due. Merely threatening eventual performance was not itself an "anticipatory breach," a breach before the deadline arrives.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: Even assuming that interpretation, Minweld had not repudiated the date; it had failed to provide the requested assurance about preparatory arrangements.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: Even assuming McCloskey's reading that a delivery date was set, Minweld had not "repudiated" that date, meaning it never said it would not meet it. It had only failed to give the assurance McCloskey asked for about its supply arrangements.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: The Third Circuit affirmed because McCloskey had not made a prima facie case of anticipatory breach.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: The Third Circuit, the federal appeals court, "affirmed" (upheld) the ruling. McCloskey had not made a "prima facie case" of anticipatory breach, meaning its evidence was not enough even to start to show an early breach.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.sentence: The result concerned these contracts and the letter relied on as repudiation; it did not adjudicate a modern statutory right to adequate assurance.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0137.plain: The result was about these contracts and the letter McCloskey called a "repudiation" (a refusal to perform). It did not adjudicate (decide) the modern right, created by statute, to demand adequate assurance of performance.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: Royster insisted on the contract price and, after refusal of delivery, resold the goods for Columbia’s account below that price.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: Royster insisted on the contract price. After Columbia refused delivery, Royster resold the fertilizer "for Columbia's account," meaning on Columbia's behalf, below that price, so it could charge Columbia the difference.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: Columbia contended that trade usage and six years of dealings meant the document did not impose inflexible quantities and prices.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: Columbia argued that "trade usage," the customs of the fertilizer trade, and six years of dealings between the parties meant the document's quantities and prices were not rigid.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: It also alleged unlawful reciprocal purchasing under federal antitrust law as both a defense and a treble-damages counterclaim.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: Columbia also alleged (claimed) unlawful reciprocal purchasing, "I buy from you if you buy from me," under federal antitrust law, which protects competition. It used this both as a defense and as a "treble-damages" counterclaim, its own claim for triple damages.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: The district court excluded Columbia’s commercial-context evidence, submitted only coercive reciprocity to the jury, and rejected the alternative noncoercive theory.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: The district court (the trial court) kept out Columbia's evidence of commercial context. It let the jury decide only "coercive reciprocity," whether Royster forced the reciprocal deal, and rejected the alternative theory that even a voluntary one was illegal.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: Judge Butzner held that Virginia’s Uniform Commercial Code displaced the older ambiguity prerequisite.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: Judge Butzner held that Virginia's Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) replaced the older rule that outside evidence about a contract is allowed only if its words are ambiguous.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: Under § 8.1-205(4), express terms prevailed where reasonable reconciliation was impossible, and prior dealing prevailed over usage.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: Under § 8.1-205(4), the "express terms" (the written words) won where custom or past dealing could not reasonably be fitted with them. And the parties' own prior dealing won over general trade usage.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: The stereotyped merger language did not specifically negate those categories.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: The stock "merger language," the boilerplate saying the writing is the whole agreement, did not specifically exclude trade usage or past dealing.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: Section 8.2-207 did not make that a new acceptance or confirmation of the kind in Columbia’s cited formation cases: the bargain already existed, and the order expressly referred to the May 8 contract.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: Section 8.2-207, the rule on clashing business forms, did not make Columbia's later order a new acceptance or confirmation like those in its cited "formation" cases (about how contracts are made). The bargain already existed, and the order expressly referred to the May 8 contract.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: Recovery of the contract-resale difference under § 8.2-706 required a good-faith, commercially reasonable resale to Mobil.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: To recover the difference between the contract price and the resale price under § 8.2-706, Royster's resale to Mobil had to be in good faith (honest) and commercially reasonable. That is the good-faith requirement.

columbia-nitrogen.sentence: For noncoercive reciprocity, the panel assumed without deciding a Sherman Act § 1 violation but rejected the contract defense under Kelly v. Kosuga.
columbia-nitrogen.plain: For "noncoercive reciprocity," a voluntary reciprocal deal, the panel "assumed without deciding" that it violated Sherman Act § 1. But following Kelly v. Kosuga, it held that this was no defense to paying under the contract.

cp-bremen.sentence: The contract selected the London Court of Justice and included clauses excluding navigation-error responsibility and placing damage to the towed object on its owner.
cp-bremen.plain: The contract chose the London Court of Justice for disputes. It also had clauses excusing the tug company from responsibility for navigation errors and putting the risk of damage to the towed rig on its owner.

cp-bremen.sentence: On January 12 Zapata sued Unterweser personally and Bremen in rem in Tampa admiralty court for $3.5 million in negligent-towage and contract damages.
cp-bremen.plain: On January 12 Zapata sued Unterweser personally and the tug Bremen "in rem," a claim against the ship itself as property. It sued in Tampa's "admiralty court" (federal maritime court) for $3.5 million, alleging "negligent-towage" (careless towing) and breach of contract.

cp-bremen.sentence: With its American motion unresolved and the six-month limitation deadline approaching, Unterweser filed a Tampa limitation-of-liability proceeding in July, expressly reserving the clause.
cp-bremen.plain: Unterweser's American motion to dismiss was still undecided, and the six-month deadline was near. So in July it filed a "limitation-of-liability" proceeding in Tampa, asking to cap its total liability, while expressly keeping its claim to the London clause.

cp-bremen.sentence: The District Court denied dismissal and stay, followed traditional hostility to supposed contractual ouster of jurisdiction, and applied ordinary convenience balancing favoring Zapata’s choice.
cp-bremen.plain: The District Court refused to dismiss or "stay" (pause) the case. It followed the old hostility to contracts that supposedly "oust" a court of jurisdiction (its power to hear a case), and used ordinary convenience balancing, weighing the factors, in favor of Zapata's chosen court.

cp-bremen.sentence: The majority stressed Gulf events, nearby witnesses and repairs, depositions, and concerns about English enforcement of exculpatory terms and materially lower limitation exposure.
cp-bremen.plain: The appeals court majority stressed that events, nearby witnesses and repairs were in the Gulf area, along with depositions (sworn pretrial testimony). It worried England would enforce the "exculpatory terms" excusing the tug owner, and that "limitation exposure," the capped liability, would be much lower there.

cp-bremen.sentence: A freely negotiated clause was prima facie valid in admiralty.
cp-bremen.plain: In admiralty (maritime law), a freely negotiated forum clause was "prima facie" valid, meaning presumed valid unless shown otherwise.

cp-bremen.sentence: Zapata bore the burden to show unreasonable or unjust enforcement, fraud, overreaching, or another adequate ground.
cp-bremen.plain: Zapata "bore the burden," meaning it had to prove that enforcing the clause would be unreasonable or unjust, or that it resulted from fraud, "overreaching" (unfair bargaining power), or another adequate ground.

cp-bremen.sentence: The Court distinguished Bisso’s domestic-towage rule against negligent-towage immunity from this freely negotiated international arrangement involving a foreign party’s international-waters conduct.
cp-bremen.plain: The Court distinguished Bisso’s rule, which bars towing companies in domestic towage from contracting out of negligent-towage liability (careless towing). This was a freely negotiated international deal about a foreign party’s conduct in international waters.

cp-bremen.sentence: Zapata had to show London so gravely difficult as effectively to deny a meaningful day in court, not simply less favorable witness convenience.
cp-bremen.plain: Zapata had to show that London would be so gravely difficult that it would effectively be denied a meaningful "day in court," a real chance to be heard. Merely less convenient witnesses was not enough.

cp-bremen.sentence: The Court also rejected Zapata’s new Supreme Court arguments that this clause was nonexclusive or failed to cover in rem claims: its actual language was mandatory and comprehensive, without making every court-naming clause so.
cp-bremen.plain: The Court also rejected Zapata's arguments raised for the first time at the Supreme Court: that the clause was "nonexclusive" (allowing but not requiring London) or did not cover "in rem" claims against the tug itself. This clause's actual words were mandatory and covered everything, though not every clause naming a court does.

cp-cooper.sentence: Four branch employees—Sylvia Cooper, Constance Russell, Helen Moore, and Elmore Hannah—intervened with individual and class claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and 42 U.S.C. §1981.
cp-cooper.plain: Four branch employees, Sylvia Cooper, Constance Russell, Helen Moore, and Elmore Hannah, "intervened" (joined the suit). They brought individual and "class claims," on behalf of all Black employees, under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and 42 U.S.C. §1981.

cp-cooper.sentence: The district court conditionally certified a class under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(2) and (3).
cp-cooper.plain: The district court "conditionally certified" a class, meaning it provisionally allowed the case to proceed as a class action, under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(2) and (3).

cp-cooper.sentence: The employees later called the Baxter petitioners received notice, did not opt out, and belonged to that class.
cp-cooper.plain: The employees later called the Baxter petitioners (those asking the Supreme Court for review) got notice of the class action. They did not "opt out," or ask to be excluded, and so were class members.

cp-cooper.sentence: The district court initially found a pattern of discrimination in job grades 4 and 5 but insufficient proof of a classwide pattern above those grades.
cp-cooper.plain: The district court first found a pattern of discrimination in job grades 4 and 5. But it found too little proof of a "classwide" pattern, affecting the class as a whole, in higher grades.

cp-cooper.sentence: Justice Stevens explained that a judgment in a properly entertained class action binds members under ordinary claim- and issue-preclusion principles.
cp-cooper.plain: Justice Stevens explained that a judgment in a properly heard class action binds class members under ordinary preclusion rules. "Claim preclusion" bars suing again on the same claim, and "issue-preclusion" bars re-arguing issues already decided.

cp-cooper.sentence: A pattern-or-practice claim requires a regular discriminatory practice rather than isolated or sporadic acts.
cp-cooper.plain: A "pattern-or-practice" claim, that discrimination was the employer's standard way of operating, requires a regular discriminatory practice, not isolated or occasional acts.

cp-cooper.sentence: Establishing a discriminatory pattern could give class members a favorable presumption.
cp-cooper.plain: If a pattern of discrimination is proved, each class member's employment decision is presumed discriminatory, and the employer must prove otherwise.

cp-cooper.sentence: The employer would then articulate a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason, while the employee retained the ultimate burden of proving intentional discrimination.
cp-cooper.plain: The employer would then state a "legitimate nondiscriminatory reason," a lawful reason for its decision. The employee kept the "ultimate burden," the final duty, of proving intentional discrimination.

cp-cooper.sentence: The classwide result could also help the Bank resist a claim that its stated reasons for an individual decision were pretextual.
cp-cooper.plain: The classwide result, finding no pattern across the class, could also help the Bank defend against a claim that its stated reasons for an individual decision were "pretextual," meaning cover stories.

cp-cooper.sentence: The Court reasoned that requiring adjudication of every individual claim whenever the common claim failed could force every member to intervene and overwhelm the device’s common-question function.
cp-cooper.plain: The Court reasoned that if a failed common claim required deciding every individual claim too, every member would have to intervene (join the suit). That would overwhelm the class-action device, whose job is to decide shared questions together.

cp-hadges.sentence: In 1990 the district court granted the company summary judgment because its action was not state action; the judgment was affirmed.
cp-hadges.plain: In 1990 the district court granted Yonkers "summary judgment," deciding without trial, because its conduct was not "state action," meaning action by the government, which the Constitution's due process clause requires. The judgment was "affirmed" (upheld) on appeal.

cp-hadges.sentence: Hadges then sought to reopen the 1990 judgment through an independent fraud-on-the-court action, treating Garland’s affidavit as proof Galterio’s earlier account was fraudulent.
cp-hadges.plain: Hadges then tried to reopen (undo) the 1990 judgment through a separate "fraud-on-the-court" lawsuit, claiming the court itself had been deceived. He treated Garland's affidavit, a sworn written statement, as proof that Galterio's earlier account was fraudulent.

cp-hadges.sentence: Yonkers had requested sanctions within its dismissal papers, without a separate motion served twenty-one days before presentation.
cp-hadges.plain: Yonkers asked for "sanctions" (penalties) inside its dismissal papers. It did not file a separate motion (formal request) served on Hadges twenty-one days before presenting it to the court.

cp-hadges.sentence: More than a year had passed, preventing a timely Rule 60(b)(3) motion, but the historical savings clause allowed an independent action for fraud upon the court.
cp-hadges.plain: More than a year had passed, so a timely (on time) motion under Rule 60(b)(3) to reopen for fraud was not possible. But the rule's "savings clause," which keeps older remedies, allowed an "independent action," a separate lawsuit, for fraud upon the court.

cp-hadges.sentence: The court therefore found no abuse of discretion without reaching disputed res judicata or abstention grounds.
cp-hadges.plain: The court therefore found no "abuse of discretion," meaning the trial judge acted within his allowed range. It did not reach the disputed defenses of "res judicata" (the matter was already decided) or "abstention" (declining to hear the case).

cp-hadges.sentence: Its separate-motion and safe-harbor safeguards allowed correction or withdrawal before sanctions were sought from the court.
cp-hadges.plain: The rule's separate-motion and "safe-harbor" protections, a 21-day grace period, let a party fix or withdraw a challenged filing before sanctions were requested from the court.

cp-hadges.sentence: Amended Rule 11 barred the specified monetary legal-contention sanction against a represented party.
cp-hadges.plain: Amended Rule 11 barred this kind of money sanction (penalty) for weak legal arguments against a party who had a lawyer; those arguments are the lawyer's responsibility.

cp-hadges.sentence: Court-initiated sanctions could not cure the problem: the judge said he acted on Yonkers’ request and issued no required specific show-cause order.
cp-hadges.plain: Court-initiated sanctions, penalties the judge starts on his own, could not fix the problem. The judge said he acted on Yonkers' request, and he never issued the required specific "show-cause order" telling Hadges to explain why he should not be penalized.

cp-hadges.sentence: The panel doubted the conduct approached the contempt-like situation contemplated for that route.
cp-hadges.plain: The appeals judges also doubted the conduct was serious enough, close to defying the court, to justify a judge imposing sanctions on his own.

cp-hadges.sentence: His reliance also had an objective evidentiary basis: sworn client information, the undated sheet, another lawyer’s affidavit, and his experience in the Meadowlands litigation.
cp-hadges.plain: Kunstler's reliance also had an objective evidentiary basis, real evidence: his client's sworn information, the undated sheet, another lawyer's affidavit (sworn statement), and his own experience in the Meadowlands litigation.

cp-livingston.sentence: The counts placed events in New Orleans but appended the traditional fictional venue of Richmond in Henrico County.
cp-livingston.plain: The counts (the separate claims) said the events happened in New Orleans. But they added the traditional "fictional venue," a legal pretense that they occurred in Richmond in Henrico County.

cp-livingston.sentence: Jefferson demurred to some counts and pleaded denials and justifications, including congressional authority and lack of malice.
cp-livingston.plain: Jefferson "demurred" to some counts, arguing they were legally insufficient even if true. To others he pleaded denials and "justifications," legal excuses such as authority from Congress and lack of malice (ill will).

cp-livingston.sentence: Both concluded that trespass to land remained a local action.
cp-livingston.plain: Both judges concluded that trespass to land (wrongful entry onto someone's land) remained a "local action," a suit that can only be brought where the land is.

cp-livingston.sentence: Tyler explained that many once-local claims had become transitory, but land trespass, traditionally quare clausum fregit, had not.
cp-livingston.plain: Tyler explained that many claims once tied to a place had become "transitory," able to be sued on anywhere. But land trespass, traditionally called "quare clausum fregit" (breaking into someone's enclosed land), had not.

cp-livingston.sentence: He cited a Virginia waste action in the wrong district to show that pleadings could not supply missing authority even after verdict.
cp-livingston.plain: He cited a Virginia "waste action," a suit over damage to land, brought in the wrong district. It showed that the pleadings could not give a court power it lacked, even after a verdict (the jury's decision).

cp-livingston.sentence: General or natural law did not identify a competent court or displace established procedure.
cp-livingston.plain: "General or natural law," broad principles of justice, did not identify a court with power to hear the case or override established procedure.

cp-livingston.sentence: A competent court existed where the land lay, and a defendant’s possible evasion did not authorize judicial creation of jurisdiction merely to prevent a remedial gap.
cp-livingston.plain: A court with power existed where the land lay. A defendant’s possible evasion of that court did not let judges create jurisdiction just to avoid a remedial gap, a situation with no way to get relief.

cp-livingston.sentence: Marshall traced locality to juries of the vicinity and the later fictions permitting foreign personal torts and contracts.
cp-livingston.plain: Marshall traced the local rule to "juries of the vicinity," jurors drawn from the neighborhood who knew the facts. Later pleading fictions let courts hear "foreign" (out-of-area) personal torts, meaning civil wrongs like injuries, and contracts.

cp-livingston.sentence: For damages against a reachable defendant, Marshall saw no satisfactory nontechnical reason for treating trespass differently; proceedings against the property itself presented a more obvious control problem.
cp-livingston.plain: For damages (money) against a defendant the court could reach, Marshall saw no good non-technical reason to treat trespass differently. Proceedings against the property itself raised a more obvious problem, since a court cannot control land outside its territory.

cp-livingston.sentence: Marshall recognized the serious problem of combining party-based federal jurisdiction with a requirement to find the defendant in the land’s district.
cp-livingston.plain: Marshall recognized a serious problem. Federal jurisdiction (power to hear the case) depended on who the parties were, yet the rule required finding the defendant in the land's district, where he might never be.

cp-reasor.sentence: He also cross-complained against Reasor-Hill Corporation, an Arkansas manufacturer, alleging negligence in marketing a chemical unsuitable for cotton.
cp-reasor.plain: Barton also "cross-complained," bringing his own claim within the same lawsuit, against Reasor-Hill Corporation, an Arkansas manufacturer. He was alleging negligence (carelessness) in marketing a chemical unsuitable for cotton.

cp-reasor.sentence: After the circuit court refused, the manufacturer sought a writ of prohibition from the Arkansas Supreme Court.
cp-reasor.plain: After the circuit court (the state trial court) refused to dismiss, the manufacturer asked the Arkansas Supreme Court for a "writ of prohibition," an order stopping the trial court from hearing the claim.

cp-reasor.sentence: Most American jurisdictions then treated injury to foreign land as a local action beyond their courts’ authority; Minnesota was the stated exception.
cp-reasor.plain: Most American jurisdictions (court systems) then treated injury to land in another state as a "local action," one their courts had no authority to hear. Minnesota was the stated exception.

cp-reasor.sentence: If Arkansas also refused suit, the manufacturer could remain outside Missouri until limitations expired and escape liability altogether.
cp-reasor.plain: If Arkansas also refused the suit, the manufacturer could stay out of Missouri until "limitations" (the deadline to sue) expired and escape liability, legal responsibility, entirely.

cp-reasor.sentence: As litigation spread across communities, courts distinguished transitory actions, which could arise anywhere, from local claims tied to land.
cp-reasor.plain: As litigation spread across communities, courts separated "transitory actions," which could arise and be sued on anywhere, from "local claims" tied to land, which had to be brought where it lay.

cp-reasor.sentence: Other states’ statutes and decisions were accessible, and courts already decided out-of-state title incidentally in transitory suits.
cp-reasor.plain: Other states' statutes (written laws) and court decisions were easy to look up. And courts already decided title to out-of-state land along the way in "transitory suits," cases that can be brought anywhere.

cp-reasor.sentence: An airplane could finish spraying and return to Arkansas before Barton discovered damage and obtained an attachment.
cp-reasor.plain: An airplane could finish spraying and fly back to Arkansas before Barton discovered the damage and got an "attachment," a court order seizing property to secure his claim.

cp-reasor.sentence: The majority invoked remedial justice and the state constitution’s assurance of a remedy for injuries.
cp-reasor.plain: The majority relied on fairness and on the Arkansas constitution's promise that every injury should have a legal remedy.

cp-reasor.sentence: Western Union v. Bush, the Arkansas precedent classifying growing-crop injury as injury to real estate, required localization in his view.
cp-reasor.plain: In his view, Western Union v. Bush, the Arkansas precedent (earlier binding decision) treating harm to growing crops as harm to real estate, required that the claim be brought where the land was.

cp-reasor.sentence: He warned that broadly asserting power could extend to ejectment or title without obliging the sister state to recognize the judgment.
cp-reasor.plain: He warned that claiming power so broadly could reach "ejectment" (suits to remove someone from land) or title disputes. Yet the "sister state," the other state where the land lay, would not have to recognize such a judgment.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Under 12 U.S.C. § 1843(c)(8), the Federal Reserve Board could approve activity sufficiently closely related to banking.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: Under 12 U.S.C. § 1843(c)(8), the Federal Reserve Board could approve activity that was sufficiently closely related to banking.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: The Board approved the restricted application July 9 and adopted the regulatory amendments by notice-and-comment rulemaking August 23.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: The Board approved Citicorp's restricted application on July 9 in a case-specific proceeding. On August 23 it adopted the regulatory changes through "notice-and-comment" rulemaking, the standard process of publishing a proposal and taking public comments.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Citicorp urged that standard only for adjudication and ordinary arbitrariness review for the rule, but the provision generally covered both kinds of order.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: Citicorp urged that the substantial-evidence standard applied only to the adjudication (the case-specific order), with ordinary review for "arbitrariness" (irrationality) for the rule. But the provision generally covered both kinds of order.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Section 706 grounds were cumulative: supported findings could still be arbitrary, for example because the agency abruptly departed from precedent without explanation.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: The grounds in Section 706 were "cumulative," meaning agency action must pass all of them. Well-supported findings could still be arbitrary, for example if the agency abruptly departed from its own precedent (past decisions) without explaining why.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: The arbitrary-and-capricious provision supplied a catchall, not permission for an insubstantial factual basis where the specific substantial-evidence clause did not apply.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: The arbitrary-and-capricious provision was a "catchall," a general backstop. It did not allow a thin factual basis in cases where the specific substantial-evidence clause did not apply.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Section 706(2)(E) retained a distinctive role by requiring support in the closed formal record.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: Section 706(2)(E) still had its own role: it required a decision to rest on the "closed formal record," only the evidence in the formal hearing record.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Once Regulation Y established relatedness, the Board could not undo that qualification through the separate balancing inquiry without amending the rule.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: Once Regulation Y, the Board's general rule, had established that an activity was related to banking, the Board could not undo that through its separate balancing inquiry (weighing public costs and benefits) without amending (formally changing) the rule.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Petitioners invoked § 557(c), claiming the application order lacked separate explanations for applications software, facilities management, turnkey systems and software-related services.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: Petitioners (the challengers asking for review) invoked § 557(c), the requirement to explain material issues. They claimed the order lacked separate explanations for applications software, facilities management, turnkey systems and software-related services.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: An agency need not adopt a challenger’s segmentation if its analysis actually resolves the material components.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: An agency does not have to break down its reasoning the way a challenger wants, as long as its reasoning actually covers the important issues.

lrs-n-adapso-board.sentence: Equal factual-support requirements did not erase closed-record rules, comment duties, or the obligation to explain policy changes.
lrs-n-adapso-board.plain: Requiring the same factual support under both tests did not erase other duties: "closed-record" rules (deciding only on the hearing record), duties to allow public comment, or the duty to explain policy changes.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: The National Labor Relations Board directed an election on May 20, 1971, relying on its North Arkansas decision: even managerial workers were covered unless union membership created a relevant labor-relations conflict.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: The National Labor Relations Board ordered a union election on May 20, 1971, relying on its North Arkansas decision. That decision said even managerial workers were covered by the labor law unless union membership created a real labor-relations conflict.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: Bell refused to bargain, producing an unfair-labor-practice finding under §§ 8(a)(5) and (1) and an order to bargain.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: Bell "refused to bargain" with the union, a standard way to get court review of the election. That led to an "unfair-labor-practice" finding under §§ 8(a)(5) and (1) of the Act and an order to bargain.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: It saw substantial evidence that these buyers might occupy too low a position to be truly managerial, but could not tell whether the Board had actually found that or instead relied on its legally erroneous theory that managers generally remained covered.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: The appeals court saw "substantial evidence," enough evidence, that these buyers might be too junior to be truly managerial. But it could not tell whether the Board had found that, or had relied on its legally wrong theory that managers generally remained covered.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: The case therefore presented distinct questions: whether all genuine managerial employees were excluded by the Act, and whether determining these buyers’ status under the proper standard required a general rule rather than adjudication.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: So the case raised two separate questions. Did the Act exclude all genuine "managerial employees"? And did deciding these buyers' status under the right standard require a general rule rather than "adjudication," a case-by-case decision?

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: The proper inquiry concerned duties, authority, and relationship to management: did the employee formulate and effectuate employer policy?
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: The right question was what the employee actually did: did they help make and carry out company policy?

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: A conflict could independently justify exclusion from a bargaining unit, but was not the only reason true managers fell outside statutory coverage.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: A conflict of interest could on its own justify "exclusion" from a "bargaining unit," the group of workers a union represents. But it was not the only reason true managers fell outside statutory coverage, meaning outside the labor law.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: Chenery II recognized the usefulness of prospective rules and the need for adjudication where problems are unforeseen, experience incomplete, or circumstances unusually varied.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: Chenery II, an earlier Supreme Court case, recognized that "prospective" rules (rules for the future) are useful. But agencies also need adjudication, case-by-case decisions, when problems are unforeseen, experience is incomplete, or situations vary too much.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: This record showed no substantial adverse reliance, fines, damages, or new liability for past conduct undertaken in good-faith reliance on Board pronouncements.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: This record showed no one who had relied heavily, to their harm, on Board statements with good-faith (honest) reliance. Nor were fines, damages, or new liability (legal responsibility) for past conduct at stake.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: Justice White, joined by Brennan, Stewart, and Marshall, agreed that rulemaking was unnecessary but rejected the majority’s substantive construction.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: Justice White, joined by (with the agreement of) Brennan, Stewart, and Marshall, agreed that rulemaking (making a general rule) was unnecessary. But he rejected the majority’s substantive construction, its reading of what the law excludes.

lrs-o-bell-aerospace.sentence: On April 23, 1974, the Supreme Court affirmed the Second Circuit’s holding that all properly classified managerial employees are excluded, but reversed its mandatory-rulemaking direction.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace.plain: On April 23, 1974, the Supreme Court "affirmed" (upheld) the Second Circuit’s holding that all properly classified (correctly identified) managerial employees are excluded. But it "reversed" (overturned) the Second Circuit’s order that the Board must use rulemaking.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: Although the arrangement contemplated no business, the Senate passed a payroll-tax extension by unanimous consent on December 23.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: Although no business was planned, the Senate passed a payroll-tax extension on December 23 by "unanimous consent," meaning no senator objected.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: On January 4, 2012, President Obama appointed Sharon Block, Richard Griffin, and Terence Flynn under the Recess Appointments Clause.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: On January 4, 2012, President Obama appointed Sharon Block, Richard Griffin, and Terence Flynn without Senate confirmation. He used the power to fill posts during a Senate recess under the Recess Appointments Clause.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: The administration regarded the pro forma meetings as ineffective interruptions of a longer period when the Senate was unavailable.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: The administration treated the "pro forma" meetings, brief sessions held only for form, as not truly interrupting a longer period when the Senate was unavailable.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: Invalidity of the recess appointments therefore deprived the Board itself of the necessary quorum.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: So the invalidity of the recess appointments (their being unlawful) left the Board itself without the necessary "quorum," the minimum number of lawful members needed to act.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: NLRA § 10(e)’s extraordinary-circumstances exception permitted consideration of a fundamental constitutional challenge to the Board’s authority, rather than an ordinary complaint about a hearing examiner’s qualifications.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: NLRA § 10(e), part of the National Labor Relations Act, allows new arguments in "extraordinary circumstances." That exception covered a basic constitutional challenge to the Board's power, not an ordinary complaint about a hearing examiner's (the hearing officer's) qualifications.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: Chief Judge Sentelle, joined by Henderson and Griffith on this ground, construed “the Recess” as only the interval between formal Senate sessions.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: Chief Judge Sentelle, joined by Judges Henderson and Griffith on this point, construed (interpreted) "the Recess" to mean only the break between formal Senate sessions.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: The Senate had not adjourned sine die before January 3, so no intervening recess captured Becker’s expiration; a President also could not save a vacancy for a later recess after an intervening Senate opportunity to act.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: The Senate had not "adjourned sine die," formally ended its session with no set return date, before January 3. So no recess in between covered the end of Becker’s term. And a President could not hold a vacancy for a later recess once the Senate had a chance to act.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: The majority held that sufficiently long intrasession and intersession recesses can qualify.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: The majority held that long enough "intrasession" breaks (within a Senate session) and "intersession" breaks (between sessions) can both count as recesses.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: The January 3 and January 6 sessions left only a three-day interval, making all three appointments invalid and the Board’s order unsupported by a lawful quorum.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: The January 3 and January 6 sessions left only a three-day gap, too short to be a recess. So all three appointments were invalid, and the Board's order lacked a lawful "quorum," the minimum number of members needed to act.

lrs-o-noel-canning.sentence: Later practice could not acquire structural authority by adverse possession.
lrs-o-noel-canning.plain: Later practice could not gain "structural" authority, power under the Constitution's division of government, by "adverse possession," the way someone can gain land by openly occupying it long enough.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: Congress expressly made violation of the Act or authorized rules punishable under a statutory provision.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: Congress expressly made violating the Act, or the rules properly made under it, a crime punishable under a statutory provision (a section of the law Congress passed).

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: Those were allegations admitted for purposes of testing the indictment’s legal sufficiency, not findings after trial.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: Those facts were allegations (charges not yet proven), accepted as true only to test the indictment’s legal sufficiency, meaning whether the formal criminal charge described a crime at all. They were not findings made after a trial.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: The defendants demurred, arguing that no federal offense had been alleged and that Congress unlawfully delegated legislative power by allowing an administrator to prescribe rules carrying criminal consequences.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: The defendants "demurred," asking the court to dismiss even assuming the alleged facts were true. They argued no federal crime was alleged, and that Congress unlawfully delegated (handed off) its lawmaking power by letting an official write rules with criminal penalties.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: The United States obtained Supreme Court review by writ of error under the Criminal Appeals Act’s provision for decisions based on a statute’s invalidity.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: The United States got Supreme Court review by "writ of error," a form of appeal. It used the Criminal Appeals Act’s provision for appeals when a trial court's decision rests on a statute being invalid.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: Congress selected the resource, objectives, regulated subjects, and duty to comply; the Secretary managed details within that field.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: Congress made the key choices: what to protect, the goals, what would be regulated, and that people must obey. The Secretary only filled in the details.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: He relied on Wayman v. Southard’s distinction between matters requiring legislative regulation and details left to administrators implementing a general provision.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: Justice Lamar relied on Wayman v. Southard’s distinction between matters needing regulation by Congress itself and details that officials may fill in while carrying out a general law.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: The prosecution was for an offense against the United States under that law, not an offense resting solely on administrative discretion.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: The prosecution (the criminal case) was for a crime against the United States under that law. It was not a crime resting only on an official's discretion, meaning the official's own choice.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: The Court distinguished United States v. Eaton, where an administrator demanded records beyond the statutory duty and Congress had not distinctly made breach of that additional requirement punishable.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: The Court distinguished (explained why it differed from) United States v. Eaton. There an official demanded records beyond the statutory duty, the duty the law itself set, and Congress had not clearly made breach (violation) of that extra requirement a crime.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: Congress qualified any implied license by requiring compliance with reserve rules.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: Even if ranchers had an "implied license," unstated permission from years of tolerated grazing, Congress made it conditional on obeying the reserve's rules.

lrs-s-grimaud.sentence: Compared with the conditional-legislation models in Aurora and Field, Grimaud illustrates administrative specification of details inside Congress’s established program.
lrs-s-grimaud.plain: In Aurora and Field, "conditional-legislation" cases, a law took effect when an official found certain facts. Grimaud shows a different model: an official specifying details inside a program Congress had already set up.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: In February 2007 the Attorney General issued an interim rule applying SORNA to pre-Act offenders; a December 2010 final rule repeated that coverage.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: In February 2007 the Attorney General issued an "interim rule," a temporary rule, applying SORNA, the sex-offender registration law, to pre-Act offenders (convicted before the Act passed). A "final rule," the permanent version, in December 2010 said the same.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: Whether Congress had already decided on their coverage or had left that policy to the Attorney General became the constitutional dispute.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: The constitutional dispute was whether Congress had already decided their coverage (whether the law applied to them) or had left that policy choice to the Attorney General.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: The United States prosecuted him under 18 U.S.C. § 2250(a), which, on the interstate-travel basis used here, punishes a person required to register who travels interstate and knowingly fails to register or update registration.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: The United States prosecuted (criminally charged) him under 18 U.S.C. § 2250(a). On the interstate-travel basis used here, it punishes a person required to register who travels between states and knowingly fails to register or update the registration.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: The plurality instead read the complete statute to require application to pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: The "plurality," the largest group of Justices but not a majority, instead read the whole statute (law) as requiring that it apply to pre-Act offenders as soon as "feasible," meaning practically possible.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: With the assignment thus limited, the plurality applied the intelligible-principle test: Congress must supply the general policy and boundaries guiding the official.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: With the power read this narrowly, the plurality applied the "intelligible-principle" test: Congress must supply the general policy and limits that guide the official.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: He agreed that Article I prohibits transferring legislative power and said he would support reconsidering the Court’s permissive doctrine if a majority were willing.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: He agreed that Article I forbids Congress from transferring its "legislative power," the power to make law. He said he would support reconsidering the Court’s permissive (lenient) approach if a majority were willing.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: Delegating the governing choice permits legislators to claim credit for an aspiration while shifting blame for its burdens.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: If Congress hands off the hard choice, lawmakers can take credit for the goal while blaming the agency for the costs.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: Gorsuch identified three permissible assignments: filling details after Congress makes governing policy choices; finding specified facts on which Congress makes its rule contingent; and exercising nonlegislative responsibilities, including another branch’s independent constitutional powers.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: Gorsuch named three permissible assignments. Officials may fill in details after Congress makes the key policy choices; make a "finding" of specified facts on which Congress made its rule contingent (dependent); and exercise non-lawmaking duties, including another branch's own constitutional powers.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: He read J. W. Hampton as a constrained implementation case and argued that later decisions had detached “intelligible principle” from that foundation.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: He read J. W. Hampton, the case that coined "intelligible principle," as a narrow case about carrying out Congress's choices. He argued that later decisions had cut the phrase off from that foundation.

lrs-s-gundy.sentence: The judgment therefore did not make Kagan’s entire four-Justice analysis a majority opinion, adopt Gorsuch’s test, or resolve every objection to registration and custodial travel.
lrs-s-gundy.plain: So the judgment (the case's outcome) did not make all of Kagan's four-Justice reasoning a binding majority opinion. Nor did it adopt Gorsuch's test or settle every objection to registration and travel while in custody.

market-street.sentence: It required reasonable consideration and good-faith negotiations and permitted repurchase if negotiations failed.
market-street.plain: The lease required the landlord to consider such a request reasonably and to hold good-faith (honest) negotiations. If negotiations failed, it allowed the tenant to repurchase the property.

market-street.sentence: After removal, cross-motions for summary judgment resulted in judgment for the trust.
market-street.plain: After "removal," moving the case from state court to federal court, both sides filed cross-motions for summary judgment, asking the judge to rule without a trial. The result was judgment for the trust.

market-street.sentence: The district judge concluded that failing to identify paragraph 34 prevented the required negotiations and breached good faith, inferring that Orenstein hoped Erb would overlook the option.
market-street.plain: The district judge (the federal trial judge) concluded that not pointing to paragraph 34, the buyout clause, prevented the required negotiations and breached (violated) good faith. The judge inferred that Orenstein hoped Erb, the trust's representative, would overlook the option.

market-street.sentence: Before reaching the merits, the Seventh Circuit required citizenship affidavits for every general and limited partner and every trustee.
market-street.plain: Before reaching the merits (who should win), the Seventh Circuit required affidavits, sworn statements, giving the citizenship of every general and limited partner and every trustee. That confirmed its power to hear the case.

market-street.sentence: Contractual good faith could prohibit deliberate exploitation of an oversight in performing an existing bargain.
market-street.plain: Contractual good faith could forbid deliberately exploiting the other side's oversight (mistake) while carrying out an existing bargain (contract).

market-street.sentence: That obligation did not make the tenant a fiduciary, require altruism or universal candor, or deprive it of superior market information and deliberately allocated risks.
market-street.plain: That duty did not make the tenant a "fiduciary," someone bound to put the other side's interests first. It did not require selflessness or telling everything, or take away its better market knowledge and the risks the contract deliberately assigned.

market-street.sentence: It instead addressed opportunism that created no productive gain while inducing defensive costs and defeating contemplated cooperation.
market-street.plain: Instead it targeted "opportunism," sneaky tactics that create no real gain. Such tactics end up inducing (causing) the other side to spend on self-protection, and defeat the cooperation the contract expected.

market-street.sentence: Orenstein might have realized the trust forgot the clause, withheld an easy correction, and lulled it with an apparent abandonment of financing to obtain a bargain purchase.
market-street.plain: Orenstein might have realized the trust forgot the buyout clause and withheld an easy correction. He might also have lulled it by seeming to give up on financing, in order to get a bargain (cheap) purchase.

market-street.sentence: The district judge chose the trust’s favorable inference rather than one reasonably favoring Market Street.
market-street.plain: The district judge drew the "favorable inference" (the reading of the facts) that helped the trust. On summary judgment, the judge should have drawn reasonable inferences in Market Street's favor.

market-street.sentence: A bench trial could evaluate live testimony and credibility; a judge’s eventual role as factfinder did not justify resolving that dispute on depositions.
market-street.plain: A "bench trial," a trial before a judge without a jury, could weigh live testimony and credibility (who to believe). The judge's later role as "factfinder" did not justify deciding that dispute early from depositions, written transcripts of pretrial testimony.

structural-polymer.sentence: If another supplier offered large-tow fiber at a lower market price, Zoltek had first refusal: matching compelled SP to buy from Zoltek; declining permitted the competing purchase.
structural-polymer.plain: If another supplier offered large-tow fiber at a lower market price, Zoltek had a "right of first refusal." If Zoltek matched, SP had to buy from Zoltek; if it declined, SP could buy from the competitor.

structural-polymer.sentence: Judge Carol E. Jackson treated it as an affirmative defense omitted from the answer, refused late amendment and independently held that consideration existed as a matter of law.
structural-polymer.plain: Judge Carol E. Jackson treated that argument as an "affirmative defense," one the defendant must raise in its written answer, which Zoltek had not. She refused a late amendment and separately held that consideration (something of value exchanged) existed as a matter of law.

structural-polymer.sentence: Because both counts claimed the same maximum large-tow quantity, the court used Rule 59(e) to remove the latter amount as duplicative and entered $21,138,518.
structural-polymer.plain: Both counts claimed the same maximum amount of large-tow fiber, so awarding both would pay SP twice. The court used Rule 59(e), which allows correcting a judgment, to remove the second amount as "duplicative" and entered $21,138,518.
