brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The plaintiffs admitted that whether each person was addicted would have to be proved person by person, not for the whole class at once.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Plaintiffs proposed a first jury trial of common conduct and core liability, sample cases to estimate compensation and a punitive ratio, individual claim verification and defenses, and final application of the ratio and reasonableness review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: "Plaintiffs" proposed a first "jury trial" on the companies' shared conduct and "core liability," then sample cases to estimate compensation and a ratio for punitive damages. Individual claims and defenses would then be checked, and finally the ratio applied and reviewed for reasonableness.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: The district court found Rule 23(a) satisfied but denied Rule 23(b)(2) equitable certification, including medical monitoring; plaintiffs did not cross-appeal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The "district court" found Rule 23(a)'s basic class requirements met but denied certification under Rule 23(b)(2), for classes seeking court orders, including "medical monitoring" (paid checkups). The plaintiffs did not "cross-appeal" that denial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Under Rule 23(b)(3), it separated core liability, injury/causation/reliance/defenses, compensation, and punitive damages.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Under Rule 23(b)(3), the money-damages class rule, the court split the case into parts: "core liability"; injury, causation, reliance, and defenses; compensation; and "punitive damages," which are meant to punish.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: It conditionally certified only core liability and punitive issues under Rule 23(c)(4), incorporating parts but not all of plaintiffs’ proposal.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Under Rule 23(c)(4), which allows a class for particular issues, the court "conditionally certified" (provisionally approved) a class only on core liability and punitive damages. It adopted part, but not all, of the plaintiffs' plan.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: The judge thought one conduct trial would advance all cases, relying on asbestos precedents, deferred detailed state-law and reliance issues, and read Eisen as preventing inquiry beyond pleadings into merits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Relying on asbestos "precedents" (earlier cases), the judge thought one conduct trial would move all the cases forward. He put off detailed state-law and reliance issues, and read Eisen as barring any look beyond the "pleadings" into the merits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Its punitive analysis also relied on a vacated Watson panel opinion lacking precedential force.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The court's punitive-damages reasoning also relied on a "vacated" (canceled) Watson appeals-panel opinion, which had no force as precedent.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Defendants obtained § 1292(b) interlocutory review, before later Rule 23(f).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: "Defendants" obtained "interlocutory review" (an appeal before the case ended) under § 1292(b), which allows immediate appeals of key legal questions. This was before Rule 23(f), the later rule allowing such class appeals, existed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Plaintiffs bore the burden of rigorous Rule 23 analysis despite broad trial-court discretion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Even though trial courts have broad discretion, the plaintiffs bore the burden of showing compliance with Rule 23, and the court had to analyze it rigorously.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Conditional certification permitted adjustments to unforeseen developments, not approval first and predominance later.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: "Conditional certification" allowed adjustments to "unforeseen" developments. It did not allow approving the class first and deciding "predominance" (whether common issues outweigh individual ones) later.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Limited state surveys, a jury form, and other certification citations did not show manageable treatment of reliance, disclosure, strict liability, assumption of risk, comparative fault, emotional distress, and other differences.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Limited surveys of state law, a sample jury form, and citations to other certifications did not show how reliance, disclosure, "strict liability," assumption of risk, "comparative fault" (dividing fault between parties), emotional distress, and other state-law differences could be handled manageably.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: The missing inquiry, not a complete appellate choice-of-law determination, was the error.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The error was the missing analysis by the trial court. It was not the lack of a complete "appellate" decision on which state's law governs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Jenkins’s 893 asbestos cases under one state’s law in one district did not establish manageability for this nationwide, multitheory, multidefendant, fifty-year dispute.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The Jenkins asbestos class (893 cases, one state's law, one court) did not show that this far bigger case, spanning the nation, many legal theories, many defendants and fifty years, could practically be tried together.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Eisen and Miller prohibited deciding certification based on perceived likelihood of merits victory, not examining facts and law needed to apply Rule 23.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Eisen and Miller barred deciding certification based on who seemed likely to win on the "merits." They did not bar examining the facts and law needed to apply Rule 23.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Under this court’s historical reading of Rule 23(c)(4), isolating a common issue could not manufacture predominance before the cause as a whole met Rule 23(b)(3).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Under this court's historical reading of Rule 23(c)(4), carving out a common issue could not manufacture "predominance" (common issues outweighing individual ones). The case as a whole first had to meet Rule 23(b)(3).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: The untested addiction-as-injury theory lacked useful individual-trial experience.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The claim that addiction itself is the injury was new, and no individual trials had yet shown how such claims play out.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Nationwide aggregation risked extraordinary, industry-threatening settlement pressure without established proof patterns.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Combining claims nationwide risked extraordinary "settlement pressure" that threatened the whole industry, before any established pattern of proof existed for such claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Later juries comparing fault might reexamine the first jury’s findings, creating a substantial Seventh Amendment separability problem, not a ban on all bifurcation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: Later juries comparing fault might reexamine the first jury's "findings," creating a substantial Seventh Amendment separability problem, since one jury's facts cannot be reexamined by another. That was not a ban on all "bifurcation," meaning splitting a trial into parts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: Because immaturity independently defeated superiority then, another immediate certification attempt could not cure the identified errors.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: "Immaturity" (the claims being new and untested) on its own defeated "superiority," the requirement that a class action be the best method, at that time. So another immediate certification attempt could not "cure" (fix) the errors identified.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.sentence: It expressly left other attacks undecided, including due process concerning the punitive ratio, categorical Erie and Article III objections, and defendants’ alternative predominance theory.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-347.plain: The court expressly left other challenges undecided: "due process" objections to the punitive ratio, categorical Erie (state law in federal court) and Article III (federal court power) objections, and the "defendants'" alternative theory that common issues did not predominate.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Dismissal motions removed foreign entities, repeatedly narrowed fraud theories with amendment allowed, and eliminated an automatic-renewal statutory count with prejudice in 2013.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: Motions to dismiss removed eBay's foreign companies and repeatedly narrowed the fraud theories, with "amendment" (rewriting the complaint) allowed. In 2013 they eliminated an automatic-renewal "statutory" count with prejudice, meaning for good.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Common agreements, schedules, and listing machinery presented central shared questions; representatives suffered the same alleged harm and faced typical defenses, including continued purchases after awareness.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: Common agreements, fee schedules, and listing systems raised central shared questions. The representatives suffered the same "alleged" harm and faced typical defenses, including that they kept buying after learning of the fees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Uniform allocation, period coverage, experienced counsel, and investigation supported adequacy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: A uniform payment formula, coverage of the whole class period, experienced "counsel" (lawyers), and their investigation supported adequacy, meaning the class was fairly represented.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Contract questions predominated, and small claims made separate litigation uneconomical.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: Shared questions about the contract mattered more than individual issues, and each seller's claim was too small to be worth suing over alone, so a class action was the better way.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: The court approved the combined best-practicable plan, not email alone.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: The court approved the combined notice program as the "best-practicable plan," the best notice practical in the circumstances. It did not approve email notice alone.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Dismissed claims and disputed contractual understanding supported compromise.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: "Dismissed" claims and disputes over what the contract meant supported "compromise," meaning settling was reasonable given the risk of losing.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: The fund exceeded seventy-one percent of first-renewal fees but represented about nine percent of all disputed renewal fees; neither denominator alone described the whole recovery.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: The fund exceeded seventy-one percent of the disputed first-renewal fees but was about nine percent of all disputed renewal fees. Neither comparison alone described the whole "recovery."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Ninety-seven exclusions, three objections, and no state attorney-general response to statutory notice favored approval without proving unanimous endorsement.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: Ninety-seven "exclusions" (members opting out), three objections, and no state attorney-general response to the "statutory notice" of the deal favored approval. They did not prove unanimous support.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Because settlement preceded certification, the court separately checked collusion indicators.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: Because the settlement came before class certification, the court separately checked for signs of "collusion," meaning the lawyers secretly trading away the class's interests.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: It awarded $1.6 million fees, twenty-five percent of the fund, checked against an hours-and-rates calculation over $1.035 million for about 2,600 hours and an approximately 1.6 multiplier.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: The court "awarded" $1.6 million in fees, twenty-five percent of the fund. It checked that against an hours-times-rates calculation of over $1.035 million for about 2,600 hours, an approximately 1.6 "multiplier."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.sentence: Liability on remaining underlying claims was not established by compromise.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-238.plain: "Liability" (legal responsibility) on the remaining underlying claims was not established by the "compromise"; settling was not an admission or finding of wrongdoing.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Plaintiffs alleged manufacturers widened the difference between those figures and physicians’ lower acquisition costs, then marketed that spread to encourage prescriptions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: The plaintiffs claimed drug makers pushed the published prices far above what doctors actually paid, then promoted that gap, which doctors could keep through reimbursement, to get doctors to prescribe their drugs.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Medicare generally paid eighty percent, leaving a twenty-percent co-payment, but most members’ supplemental Medigap policies paid eighty percent of that co-payment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Medicare usually paid 80 percent of the inflated price and patients owed a 20 percent co-payment. But most class members had supplemental "Medigap" policies (private insurance that fills gaps in Medicare coverage) that paid 80 percent of that co-payment, so they personally lost only a small part.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: AstraZeneca promised $24 million, including claims for deceased members, and the class expanded to the nine previously excluded states in return for comprehensive peace.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: AstraZeneca agreed to pay $24 million, including claims for members who had died. In exchange the class was widened to the nine states left out before, giving the company "comprehensive peace," meaning an end to all such claims at once.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Administration and initially negotiated $8.7 million fees and costs were separate obligations, not deductions from that compensation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: The cost of running the settlement and the $8.7 million in "fees and costs" first negotiated for the lawyers (their pay plus expenses) were separate obligations. They were not taken out of the $24 million for patients.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Unclaimed money would go to mutually acceptable cancer-research or patient-care charities, subject to later judicial recipient approval and an initial $10 million charitable cap.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Money no one claimed would go to cancer-research or patient-care charities both sides agreed on, with the court approving the recipients later; at first, charities could receive at most $10 million.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: After considering even her tardy reply at the May 2008 fairness hearing, the judge required treble recovery first for the strongest December 1997–2003 claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: At the May 2008 "fairness hearing" (where a judge decides whether to approve a class settlement), the judge considered even Howe's late reply. The judge then required "treble recovery," payment of three times their losses, first for the strongest claims, from December 1997 to 2003.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Chief Judge Lynch’s unanimous First Circuit panel distinguished charitable substitution when individual distribution is infeasible from disposition of a remainder after compensation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Chief Judge Lynch’s "unanimous" First Circuit "panel" (three appeals judges, all agreeing) separated two things. One is giving money to charity instead of class members when paying members individually is "infeasible" (not practical); the other is giving charity what is left over after members have been paid.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Planning it before claims closed did not change its substance: members could receive treble damages before charity received money, while some patients would never claim.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Even though the charity gift was planned before the claims deadline, it was still leftover money. Members could get "treble damages" (three times their losses) before any charity got anything, and some patients were never going to file claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Treble recovery satisfied their compensation concern, and the total also represented losses of nonclaiming patients while preventing AstraZeneca from escaping its agreed payment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: "Treble recovery," paying claimants three times their losses, met the concern that members be compensated first. The leftover total also stood for the losses of patients who never claimed, and sending it to charity kept AstraZeneca from escaping the payment it had agreed to.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Arm’s-length negotiations after adequate discovery supported reasonableness, with judicial examination of benefits, costs, risks, and alternatives still required.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: "Arm’s-length" negotiations (hard bargaining between independent sides) after adequate "discovery" (the pretrial exchange of evidence) suggested the deal was reasonable. But the judge still had to examine its benefits, costs, risks and alternatives.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Counsel’s continuing fiduciary duties required scrutiny, but advocating this residue after substantial recovery did not itself establish disloyalty.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Counsel (the class lawyers) owe the class continuing "fiduciary duties," meaning duties of loyalty and care, so their conduct deserves scrutiny. But pushing for leftover money to go to charity after a substantial recovery for members did not by itself show disloyalty.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: The insurance objection was underdeveloped and waived, and also failed substantively.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Howe's "objection" about insurance was underdeveloped, so it was "waived," meaning she lost the right to press it. It also would have failed on its merits anyway.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: A new appellate objection to the amended class definition was also waived, but the panel explained that incorporation of detailed earlier orders could satisfy the rule without repeating everything.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Her new appellate objection (raised for the first time on appeal) to the amended, or revised, class definition was also "waived" because it came too late. But the panel explained that a certification order can satisfy the rule by "incorporation," meaning referring to detailed earlier orders instead of repeating everything.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.sentence: Counsel had in fact been appointed; a further adequacy attack was waived.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-256.plain: Counsel for the class had in fact been formally appointed. Her further attack on their adequacy, meaning whether they represented the class well, was "waived" because she had not properly raised it in time.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: On March 17, it obtained a writ from the municipal court clerk and attached their checking account.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: On March 17 the agency got a "writ" (a court order) from the clerk of the "municipal court" (a local trial court), not from a judge. It used the writ to attach, or freeze, the Randones' checking account to secure its claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: The bank withheld $176.20 pending release, without a prior judicial determination of the debt.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: The bank "withheld," or held back, $176.20 until the freeze was released, even though no judge had first decided whether the debt was really owed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: On March 31, the Randones moved to dissolve for denial of due process.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: On March 31 the Randones "moved to dissolve," meaning they asked the court to lift the freeze. They argued it denied them "due process," the fair notice and hearing the Constitution requires before property is taken.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: The superior court’s appellate department affirmed without opinion October 29 and refused Court of Appeal certification November 5.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: On October 29 the superior court's appellate department (its appeals panel) "affirmed," or upheld, that ruling without an opinion explaining why. On November 5 it refused "Court of Appeal certification," meaning it would not send the case on to the next-higher appeals court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: The court issued an alternative writ because the constitutional issue was important, lower courts disagreed, and municipal proceedings could otherwise evade its review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: The California Supreme Court issued an "alternative writ," an order telling the lower court to act or explain why not, which let it take up the case directly. It did so because the constitutional issue was important, lower courts disagreed, and municipal court cases might otherwise never reach it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Exercising original jurisdiction entailed finding no adequate ordinary remedy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: Exercising "original jurisdiction" (hearing a case directly instead of on ordinary appeal) required the court to find that no adequate ordinary "remedy," such as a regular appeal, could protect the Randones.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Code of Civil Procedure § 537(1) generally permitted attachment in qualifying unsecured express or implied contract actions for direct money payment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: Code of Civil Procedure § 537(1) generally let a creditor get an "attachment," freezing a debtor's property, in qualifying suits for direct payment of money under an express or "implied contract" (one shown by conduct rather than stated words). It applied when the claim was "unsecured," meaning not backed by collateral.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: A declaration and undertaking let the clerk issue a writ without judicial scrutiny, notice, or a debtor’s opportunity to contest.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: The creditor only had to file a declaration (a sworn statement) and an "undertaking," a bond to cover harm if the seizure proved wrongful. The clerk then issued the "writ" without a judge reviewing it, without notice to the debtor, and without giving the debtor a chance to contest it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Posting security, winning the suit, or seeking exemptions placed initiative and burden on the debtor.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: To free the money, the debtor had to post a bond, win the whole lawsuit, or prove the property was legally protected from seizure; all the effort and burden fell on the debtor.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: The Randones invoked the more general right to prior process before significant deprivation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: The Randones relied on a broader principle: the government must give notice and a hearing before taking away something important, not just wages.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: California’s recent Blair v. Pitchess applied the same reasoning to prejudgment claim and delivery, and federal welfare and access-to-court cases and state notice precedents reflected a wider principle.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: California's recent Blair v. Pitchess applied the same reasoning to "prejudgment claim and delivery," meaning seizing personal property before any judgment. Federal cases on welfare benefits and access to courts, and state "precedents" (earlier decisions) on notice, reflected a wider principle not limited to wages.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Temporary deprivation still mattered; a potentially lengthy denial of use was not negligible because title had not finally changed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: Temporary "deprivation," or taking away, of property still mattered. Being kept from using your money for a possibly long time is a real loss, even though ownership has not finally changed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Historical nonresident attachment also served a jurisdictional function under the framework then prevailing and might less directly affect necessities.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: Historically, attaching the property of a "nonresident" (an out-of-state defendant) also served a "jurisdictional" function: under the rules then in force, it gave the court power to hear the case at all. Such attachments also might affect the necessities of life less directly.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Actual flight or concealment might justify safeguarded immediate relief, but neither particular facts nor proof of such danger was required or shown here.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: If a debtor was actually about to flee or engage in "concealment" of assets (hiding them), immediate "relief," such as a freeze, with safeguards might be justified. But the statute required no particular facts or proof of such danger, and none was shown here.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: A debtor unable to maintain the family or ordinary affairs might abandon even a meritorious defense, undermining the later hearing itself.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: A debtor who cannot support the family or handle ordinary affairs while money is frozen might "abandon" (give up) even a "meritorious" defense, one that could have won. That would undermine the later hearing itself.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: Post-levy exemptions could fail because of ignorance, expense, and delay.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: "Post-levy" exemptions, which let debtors claim protected property only after the seizure (the "levy"), could fail in practice. Debtors often do not know their rights, cannot afford to fight, or face too much delay.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: It also reserved definitive bankruptcy-priority questions for federal proceedings, seeing no inherent constitutional obstacle to using an attachment date for priority.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: The court also "reserved," or left undecided, final questions about how attachments affect bankruptcy priority (who gets paid first), leaving them for federal bankruptcy proceedings. It saw no built-in constitutional barrier to using an attachment date to set priority.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: The court held § 537(1) facially unconstitutional under state and federal due process because it broadly allowed seizure without notice and hearing, lacked extraordinary-need limits, and exposed necessities.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: The court held § 537(1) "facially unconstitutional," meaning invalid in all its applications, under state and federal "due process." The statute broadly allowed seizure without notice and a hearing, was not limited to cases of extraordinary need, and reached the necessities of life.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: A legislature could protect essentials, ordinarily require notice and a probable-validity hearing, and allow carefully limited pre-hearing relief on an actual flight or concealment showing to a magistrate.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: A legislature could protect essentials and ordinarily require notice and a "probable-validity hearing," where the creditor shows its claim is probably valid. It could also allow carefully limited "relief" before a hearing if a "magistrate" (a judicial officer) is shown actual flight or "concealment" of assets.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.sentence: On August 26, 1971, the unanimous court directed a peremptory writ of mandamus ordering the appellate department to require the trial court to dissolve this attachment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE.plain: On August 26, 1971, the unanimous court directed a "peremptory writ" of mandamus, a final order commanding a lower court to act. It ordered the appellate department to require the trial court to dissolve, or lift, this "attachment" on the Randones' account.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The New York FBI maintained a list that included people encountered through leads generating no individualized terrorism suspicion.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The FBI's New York office kept a list of detainees that included people picked up by chance while agents followed leads, with no specific reason to suspect them of terrorism.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Official restrictions and unofficial abuse presented different questions of responsibility.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Who could be blamed differed: conditions set by official policy might trace to the officials who made it, while guards' unauthorized abuse raised separate questions about who knew of it and allowed it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: These remained allegations accepted for dismissal review, not trial findings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: These were still "allegations," claims not yet proved, which the court accepted as true only to review the motion to dismiss. They were not "findings," facts decided after a trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Following Ashcroft v. Iqbal, the Supreme Court pleading decision requiring plausible allegations of each official’s own misconduct, plaintiffs filed a fourth amended complaint informed by two Justice Department Inspector General reports unavailable at the outset.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Ashcroft v. Iqbal is the Supreme Court "pleading" decision requiring complaints to give "plausible" (believable) facts about each official's own misconduct. After it, the plaintiffs filed a fourth amended complaint using two Justice Department "Inspector General" (internal watchdog) reports that had not existed when the suit began.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Those officials appealed; plaintiffs cross-appealed under a Rule 54(b) judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The jail officials appealed the claims that survived against them, and the plaintiffs appealed the dismissals; a Rule 54(b) judgment made those dismissals final so they could be appealed right away.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Judges Pooler and Wesley distinguished whether Bivens, the precedent recognizing some implied constitutional damages actions against federal officers, supplied a remedy; whether each official’s own misconduct was plausibly alleged; and whether qualified immunity nevertheless barred suit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Judges Pooler and Wesley distinguished, or separated, three questions. Does Bivens, the precedent recognizing some "implied" (not written in any statute) constitutional damages actions against federal officers, supply a remedy; is each official's own misconduct "plausibly" alleged; and does "qualified immunity," which shields officials unless the law was clearly established, still bar suit?

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: But deliberate indifference or supervisory conduct could satisfy a particular constitutional wrong without becoming forbidden vicarious liability.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: But a supervisor can still be liable for his or her own role, such as "deliberate indifference" (knowingly ignoring a serious risk) or other supervisory conduct that itself violates a particular right. That is not forbidden "vicarious liability," which blames a boss merely for what employees did.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The court could consider their language and context but could not resolve conflicting accounts as though after an evidentiary hearing.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The court could consider the reports' language and context. But at this early stage it could not resolve conflicting accounts as if it had held an "evidentiary hearing," where witnesses testify and the judge decides the facts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The majority treated Fifth Amendment punitive-confinement and discrimination claims and Fourth Amendment strip searches as existing Bivens contexts because both the rights and injury mechanisms had previously appeared.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The majority treated these as existing Bivens contexts, kinds of damages suits courts had already allowed: Fifth Amendment claims of punitive confinement (punishment through harsh conditions) and discrimination, and Fourth Amendment claims over strip searches. Both the rights and the way they were violated had appeared in earlier cases.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: It therefore expressly did not reach alternative-remedy or special-factors analysis.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: It therefore expressly did not reach whether other remedies existed, or the "special-factors" analysis, which asks whether special reasons, such as national security, weigh against allowing a damages suit. Those questions arise only for new kinds of Bivens claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Under Bell v. Wolfish, the precedent governing punishment of pretrial detainees, restrictions lacking a reasonable relationship to legitimate objectives could support inferred punitive intent.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Under Bell v. Wolfish, the precedent on punishment of "pretrial detainees" (people held without a conviction), such detainees may not be punished. Restrictions not reasonably related to a legitimate goal, such as security, could support an inference that they were meant as punishment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The parties used that standard; the court reserved whether civil immigration detainees deserved greater protection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Both parties (the two sides) used that standard. So the court "reserved," or left open, whether civil immigration detainees, held for civil rather than criminal reasons, deserve greater protection.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: High-level officials could initially expect lawful implementation of a lawful detention policy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Top officials could at first assume that a lawful policy of detaining people would be carried out lawfully by those below them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The majority nonetheless found a plausible inference that the Department of Justice defendants endorsed continued extreme conditions after learning that detainees lacked suspected terrorism connections.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Even so, the majority found a plausible "inference" (a reasonable conclusion drawn from the facts alleged) that the Justice Department defendants, the top officials being sued, approved continuing the extreme conditions after learning that the detainees had no suspected terrorism ties.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The security explanation did not compel dismissal, although discovery might negate personal responsibility.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The government's security explanation did not compel "dismissal," meaning the case did not have to be thrown out at this stage. Still, discovery (evidence gathered later) might show the officials were not personally responsible.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The circuit’s prior Iqbal v. Hasty reasoning also supported denial of qualified immunity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The Second Circuit's own earlier reasoning in Iqbal v. Hasty also supported denying "qualified immunity," the shield that protects officials from suit unless they violated clearly established law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: General allegations against Zenk, who became warden April 22, 2002, when only two plaintiffs remained, did not.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The general "allegations" against Zenk were not enough. He became warden only on April 22, 2002, when only two plaintiffs remained, and the claims did not tie him personally to the conditions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: That pleaded his own indifference rather than liability merely from office.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Those allegations "pleaded," or stated in the complaint, Hasty's own deliberate indifference to the abuse, not liability merely because he held the office of warden.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Equal protection required purposeful discrimination, not knowledge of consequences alone.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: "Equal protection," the constitutional guarantee against unjustified government discrimination, required purposeful discrimination. The plaintiffs had to show officials acted because of race, religion or national origin, not merely that they knew their actions would fall hardest on those groups.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: That many Arab or Muslim detainees went to less restrictive Passaic confinement did not compel dismissal because officials allegedly deferred to discriminatory designations and placement choices.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Many Arab or Muslim detainees were held in less restrictive conditions at the Passaic jail, but that did not compel "dismissal" (throwing out the claim). Officials allegedly went along with designations and placement choices that were themselves discriminatory.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Using the parties’ rational-relationship standard, the majority found no legitimate prison purpose sufficiently established to dismiss or grant immunity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Applying the parties' "rational-relationship standard" (whether a restriction is reasonably related to a legitimate goal), the majority found no legitimate prison purpose clear enough at this stage. So it would not dismiss the claim or grant "immunity" shielding the officials from suit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The separate 42 U.S.C. section 1985(3) claim required an agreement to deny equal protection, an act furthering it, injury or deprivation, and discriminatory animus.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The separate claim under 42 U.S.C. section 1985(3), a federal civil-rights conspiracy statute in the United States Code, had four elements. Officials must have agreed to deny equal protection, done something to carry it out, and caused injury or deprivation of rights, all with "discriminatory animus," meaning hostility toward a group.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: The intracorporate-conspiracy doctrine can treat one entity’s agents as unable to conspire, but varied responsibilities and separate policymaking prevented finding a single policymaking entity on these pleadings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: The "intracorporate-conspiracy doctrine" can treat agents of one organization as a single actor that cannot conspire with itself. But these officials had varied responsibilities and made policy separately, so on these "pleadings" (the complaint's allegations) the court could not treat them as one policymaking entity.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: For policy challenges, she defined the Bivens context through the full setting: immigration, national security, senior officers, and an unprecedented emergency.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: For the policy challenges, Judge Raggi defined the Bivens context (whether a claim resembles damages suits courts have already allowed) by its full setting: immigration, national security, senior officers, and an unprecedented emergency. She found that setting unlike the earlier cases.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Combining a familiar right with a broadly described mechanism did not reproduce the cases Bivens, Davis, or Carlson.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Pairing a familiar right with a loosely described kind of harm did not make this case like the only three cases (Bivens, Davis and Carlson) in which the Supreme Court had allowed such damages suits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Separation of powers, executive responsibilities, congressional action and inaction, and possible prospective relief counseled against creating damages remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: "Separation of powers" (respect for the separate roles of Congress, the President and courts), the executive's security responsibilities, Congress's choices to act or not act, and possible "prospective relief" (orders stopping future violations) all weighed against judges creating "damages" remedies, meaning money awards.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: An alternative could matter without equivalent monetary compensation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Another remedy could count against allowing a Bivens suit even if it did not provide equal money damages.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Her proposed dismissal rested on remedy limits and independently immunity, not findings validating alleged acts after trial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: She would have dismissed because of limits on the Bivens remedy and, independently, because of "immunity" shielding the officials. That was not a finding, after trial, that the alleged acts were lawful.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: Later, in Ziglar v. Abbasi, the Supreme Court reversed the appellate judgment except Hasty’s prisoner-abuse claim, vacated that portion, and remanded.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: Later, in Ziglar v. Abbasi (2017), the Supreme Court reversed this appellate "judgment" (the court's decision) except for the prisoner-abuse claim against Hasty. It vacated, or set aside, that part and "remanded" it, sending it back for further proceedings.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.sentence: It rejected the broad Bivens-context analysis rather than resolving everything simply as implausible pleading.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-TURKMEN-2015.plain: It rejected the Second Circuit's broad Bivens-context analysis, which treated these claims as fitting earlier damages cases, rather than deciding everything simply on the ground that the "pleading" (the complaint) was implausible.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Each district court found the order likely contrary to the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause and §201 of the Nationality Act of 1940, codified at 8 U.S.C. §1401.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Each district court (federal trial court) found the order likely violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Citizenship Clause, which grants citizenship to people born here, and §201 of the Nationality Act of 1940, a statute granting birth citizenship. That statute is now codified at 8 U.S.C. §1401, in the U.S. Code of federal laws.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Each entered a preliminary injunction protecting everyone subject to the policy.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Each court entered a "preliminary injunction," a temporary order issued before a final ruling, blocking the policy for everyone subject to it, not just the people who sued.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The Government sought Supreme Court relief only from the injunctions’ breadth.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The Government asked the Supreme Court for "relief" only from the breadth of the "injunctions" (the court orders). It did not ask the Court to decide whether the citizenship policy was lawful.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The majority distinguished universal injunctions, which protect nonparties, from nationwide injunctions, which describe geographic reach.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The majority separated "universal" injunctions, which protect "nonparties" (people not in the lawsuit), from "nationwide" injunctions, a term that only describes how far an order reaches on the map. An order can apply everywhere while protecting only the parties.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The question was whether the Judiciary Act of 1789’s general grant of equitable authority allowed relief beyond what was necessary to afford complete relief to each plaintiff with standing.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The question was whether the Judiciary Act of 1789’s general grant of equitable authority (federal courts' power to give non-money remedies like injunctions) allowed relief beyond "complete relief," what fully protects each "plaintiff with standing," meaning each plaintiff legally entitled to sue.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Under Grupo Mexicano, the precedent defining that grant by historical equitable remedies, the relevant forms of relief were those traditionally administered by England’s Court of Chancery at the founding.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Under Grupo Mexicano, the precedent defining that grant by historical "equitable" remedies (non-money court orders), the allowed forms of relief were those England's Court of Chancery, its equity court, traditionally gave at the "founding" of the United States, around 1789.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The Government was likely to succeed in showing that the challenged universal relief exceeded that authority.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The Government was "likely to succeed," meaning it would probably win, in showing that the challenged "universal relief" (orders protecting everyone, not just the plaintiffs) went beyond that authority.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Chancery ordinarily resolved the rights of parties before it.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The Court of Chancery, England's old equity court, ordinarily decided only the rights of the parties actually before it.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The historical absence mattered even though a court’s failure to reject universal relief was not itself a holding denying power.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The lack of historical examples mattered, even though the mere fact that earlier courts never rejected universal relief was not itself a ruling about whether courts had that power.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Ex parte Young’s officer relief followed historical antisuit principles rather than a free-ranging authority to invent remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Ex parte Young's "relief" against officers, orders stopping officials from enforcing unconstitutional laws, followed historical "antisuit principles," meaning traditional equity orders blocking someone from bringing enforcement suits. It did not show a free-ranging power to invent remedies.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Bills of peace, the historic representative proceedings invoked by the plaintiffs, concerned cohesive groups whose members could be bound even by an adverse outcome.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: "Bills of peace," the historic English group proceedings the plaintiffs pointed to, involved close-knit groups whose members could be bound by the result even if they lost.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Universal injunctions could benefit nonparties who would not be bound when the plaintiff lost.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Universal injunctions, by contrast, could help "nonparties" (people outside the lawsuit) when the plaintiffs win, while those nonparties would not be bound if the plaintiffs lost.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Universal relief could not serve as a substitute for satisfying them; properly certified classes remained a route to nationwide protection.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: "Universal relief" could not substitute for meeting the class-action requirements. But properly "certified classes," class actions a court has formally approved, remained a route to "nationwide" protection.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The majority treated complete relief as a ceiling: enough to remedy the plaintiffs’ injuries, not the maximum they requested.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The majority treated "complete relief" as a ceiling, the most a court can give. It means enough to "remedy," or fix, the plaintiffs' own injuries, not the maximum they asked for.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Nonparties could receive incidental benefits, and an indivisible injury could require an order with broad practical effects, as some nuisance or districting examples illustrated.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: "Nonparties" could still get incidental side benefits. And an "indivisible" injury, one that cannot be split up, such as a nuisance like pollution or an unlawful districting map, could require an "order" whose practical effects reach many others.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: The Supreme Court did not resolve every State’s standing or rule out nationwide effects from plaintiff-specific relief.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The Supreme Court did not decide whether each State had "standing" (the legal right to sue). Nor did it rule out that relief tailored to the plaintiffs might still have nationwide effects.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: For the majority, competing practical considerations could not create statutory authority.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: For the majority, competing practical considerations (good reasons for or against broad orders) could not create "statutory authority," meaning a power that Congress's statute does not give the courts.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Universal injunctions also allowed one district judge to provide widespread benefits without making all beneficiaries bear the consequences of an adverse judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Universal injunctions also let one "district judge" (a single federal trial judge) give widespread benefits if the plaintiffs win. Yet the "beneficiaries" would not bear the consequences of an adverse "judgment," because outsiders are not bound if the plaintiffs lose.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Applying Nken, the precedent governing stays, the Court found irreparable harm from enforcement of orders exceeding judicial power and held the balance favored a partial stay.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Applying Nken, the precedent governing "stays" (orders pausing a lower-court ruling), the Court found "irreparable harm," injury that cannot be undone, when the government must obey orders beyond judicial power. It held the balance favored a "partial stay," pausing the orders in part.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Likelihood of success concerned remedial scope, so the Court did not first resolve the citizenship merits.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: "Likelihood of success," whether the government would probably win, concerned only the remedy's scope, meaning how broad the orders could be. So the Court did not first decide the citizenship "merits," whether the policy itself is lawful.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: His discussion of Frothingham connected standing and equitable limits, and he raised serious Article III concerns even if Congress authorized broader remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Justice Thomas's discussion of Frothingham, a case on taxpayer suits, linked "standing" (who may sue) to the limits of "equitable" remedies. He raised serious Article III concerns, under the part of the Constitution defining federal judicial power, even if Congress authorized broader remedies.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Justice Alito, joined by Thomas, warned against avoiding the ruling through expansive third-party standing or casual class certification.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Justice Alito, "joined by" Thomas (meaning Thomas signed on to his opinion), warned against getting around the ruling through expansive "third-party standing" (letting parties sue for other people's rights) or casual "class certification," approving class actions too loosely.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Injury to a State itself differed from asserting residents’ rights, and Rule 23 requirements had to be established, not merely alleged.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: A State suing over injury to itself is different from asserting its residents' rights. And Rule 23 requirements, the federal rule governing class actions, had to be proved, not merely "alleged" (claimed).

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Justice Kavanaugh joined the majority in full and described how nationwide interim rules could emerge through certified classes, Administrative Procedure Act (APA) litigation where available, and Supreme Court emergency review.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Justice Kavanaugh "joined" (signed on to) the majority in full. He described how nationwide "interim rules," temporary rules that apply while a case proceeds, could still emerge through "certified classes" (court-approved class actions), Administrative Procedure Act (APA) suits against agency action where available, and Supreme Court emergency review.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: He distinguished incidental benefits, recognized statutory direct-review routes, and explained that Supreme Court stays included likely review and a fair prospect of reversal alongside harm and equitable considerations.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: He noted that incidental side benefits to others are allowed and that some statutes send challenges straight to appeals courts for direct review. He also explained that Supreme Court "stays" (pauses of lower-court orders) depend on likely "review" by the Court and a fair prospect of reversal, along with harm and "equitable" (fairness) considerations.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: His discussion of APA vacatur remained separate from the Court’s reservation of that issue.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: His discussion of APA vacatur (a court canceling an agency action for everyone) was separate from the Court's "reservation" of that issue, meaning the Court itself left the question open.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Preventing likely unlawful action did not, in her view, establish governmental irreparable harm; the longstanding legal regime was the proper status quo.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: In Justice Sotomayor's view, being stopped from likely unlawful action is not "irreparable harm" (injury that cannot be undone) to the government. The proper "status quo," the situation to preserve, was the long-standing legal rule of birthright citizenship.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Prudential restraint differed from a categorical lack of power, and she disputed the majority’s uses of Frothingham and Grupo Mexicano.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Courts choosing to hold back as a matter of judgment is different from having no power at all, she said, and she disagreed with how the majority read Frothingham and Grupo Mexicano.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: She argued that the Government had forfeited particular narrowing proposals and had not demonstrated workable alternatives or abuse of discretion below.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: She argued that the Government had "forfeited," or lost by not raising in time, particular proposals for narrower orders. It also had not shown workable alternatives or an "abuse of discretion" below, meaning that the lower judges had unreasonably misused their judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Rule 23(b)(2) remained available, but certification and interlocutory proceedings could produce delay and expense.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: Rule 23(b)(2), which allows class actions seeking a court order rather than money, remained available. But certifying a class and interlocutory proceedings (appeals taken in the middle of a case) could produce delay and expense.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: A lawsuit invoked tools to enforce an existing universal duty; it did not create the duty.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The government's duty to obey the Constitution is owed to everyone; a lawsuit is only a tool to enforce it, so Jackson thought relief need not be limited to the people who sued.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: She also disputed the majority’s distinction between nonparty benefits and formal relief under Rule 71.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: She also disputed the majority's line between nonparties who merely benefit from an order and formal "relief" for them under Rule 71, the rule that lets nonparties enforce orders made in their favor.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: On June 27, 2025, the Court granted all three applications only insofar as the injunctions exceeded what was necessary to afford complete relief to each plaintiff with standing.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: On June 27, 2025, the Court granted all three emergency applications only insofar as the "injunctions" went beyond "complete relief" to each "plaintiff with standing." That is, it narrowed them only where they did more than fully protect each plaintiff entitled to sue.

brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.sentence: Several questions remained expressly open: whether Article III independently prohibited statutorily authorized universal injunctions, the organizations’ standing for unidentified members, the States’ third-party standing, and whether APA §706(2) authorized vacatur with universal effect.
brief-CP-COMP-SUP-CASA.plain: The Court left several questions expressly open. They include whether Article III, the Constitution's judicial-power article, bars universal injunctions even when statutorily authorized (allowed by Congress); organizations' "standing" to sue for unidentified members; States' "third-party standing" to sue for residents; and whether APA §706(2) permits "vacatur," canceling agency action, with universal effect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The agreement required her to arrange satisfactorily to assume two notes and to apply to the Federal Communications Commission for transfer of the operating license.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The agreement required Foster to make satisfactory arrangements to "assume two notes," meaning take over two debts. She also had to apply to the Federal Communications Commission, the agency that licenses broadcasters, to transfer the station's "operating license" to her.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: A provision could release them if transfer permission was not obtained within nine months of filing, absent specified outstanding protest or litigation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: If the agency did not approve the transfer within nine months after the application was filed, both sides could walk away, unless a listed protest or lawsuit was still pending.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: About two weeks after the telegram, Colorado Radio sued in diversity for breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: About two weeks after the telegram, Colorado Radio sued in diversity (in federal court, allowed because the parties were from different states) for "breach," meaning breaking the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Foster argued that satisfactory arrangements for the notes were a condition precedent that had never occurred, so her purchase obligation never arose.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Foster argued that making satisfactory arrangements for the notes was "a condition precedent," an event that had to happen before her duty to buy arose. Since it never happened, she said, her obligation to purchase never arose.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The Tenth Circuit held that she could not rely on a condition’s failure when her own inaction caused it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The Tenth Circuit, the federal appeals court, held that she could not rely on a condition's failure when her own inaction caused it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: She also invoked a New Mexico statute requiring a performance demand before certain contracts without a fixed performance time could become money demands.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: She also relied on a New Mexico "statute" (a law passed by the legislature) for certain contracts with no fixed time for performance. It required a "performance demand," asking the other side to perform, before such a contract could become a claim for money.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Demanding that necessary first step satisfied the statute here.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Demanding that she take the necessary first step, filing the license application, satisfied that "statute" here.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Neither the unfinished transfer nor the nine-month transfer provision excused her affirmative application duty.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Neither the unfinished transfer nor the nine-month walk-away clause on the transfer "excused" her, meaning released her from, her affirmative duty to file the application.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: At trial the parties stipulated that, apart from incidental damages, recovery would equal the contract price minus the resale price.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: At trial the parties (both sides) stipulated, or formally agreed, that apart from "incidental damages" (minor extra costs caused by the breach), recovery would equal the contract price minus the resale price.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Foster invoked New Mexico’s Uniform Commercial Code §§ 2-706(1) and (3), which allowed the price-difference remedy for a qualifying resale but required reasonable notification of a private sale.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Foster invoked New Mexico's Uniform Commercial Code §§ 2-706(1) and (3), the sales-of-goods law. It allowed the seller the price-difference "remedy" after a qualifying resale, but required reasonable notice to the buyer before a private resale.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The appellate court therefore understood the stipulation as selecting the measure if the resale was legally proper, without dispensing with the statutory prerequisite.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: So the appellate court read the "stipulation" (the parties' agreement at trial) as choosing the damages formula only if the resale was legally proper. It did not excuse the notice the statute required first.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The Tenth Circuit agreed that this record supported treating the license, goodwill, real estate, studios, and transmission equipment as nonmovables and therefore non-goods.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The Tenth Circuit agreed that this record supported treating the license, "goodwill" (the value of the station's reputation and customer base), real estate, studios, and transmission equipment as nonmovables. As things that are not movable, they were not "goods" under the sales law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Colorado Radio conceded that the office equipment and furnishings were movable goods, but argued that their incidental role in transferring a going concern removed them from Article 2.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Colorado Radio conceded that the office equipment and furnishings were movable goods. But it argued that their minor role in transferring a "going concern," a running business, removed them from Article 2, the sales-of-goods part of the Code.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Article 2’s language governing transactions in goods did not permit disregarding a conceded goods sale because non-goods dominated the larger bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Article 2’s language governs transactions in goods. So the court could not ignore a conceded sale of goods just because non-goods dominated the larger "bargain," the overall deal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The seller relied on Epstein, a beauty-service decision treating a product applied during a service as part of the service for warranty purposes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The seller cited Epstein, where a product used during a beauty treatment was treated as part of the service, not a sale of goods, for warranty purposes.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: For the goods portion, missing notice foreclosed the Code’s resale-price remedy.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: For the goods portion, the missing notice foreclosed, or ruled out, the Code’s resale-price "remedy."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Because the parties had stipulated to that specific measure, this breach component was unremediable in this case.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Because the parties had stipulated to that "specific measure" of damages, the resale-price formula only, this part of the breach was unremediable here, meaning the seller recovered nothing for it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Using the uncontradicted valuation testimony most favorably to Foster, the court assigned ten percent to the goods and reasonably attributed ten percent of the damages to refusal to buy them.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Reading the "uncontradicted" (undisputed) valuation testimony most favorably to Foster, the court assigned ten percent of the value to the goods. It reasonably attributed ten percent of the damages to her refusal to buy them and cut that amount.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: An in-court stipulation entered with open eyes controlled.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: An in-court "stipulation," a formal agreement made in court, entered with open eyes (knowingly) controlled the outcome and bound the party who made it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The evidence also supported the calculation: although Walton’s writing contained a lease provision, uncontroverted extrinsic evidence showed that was a mistake and the real estate had been sold.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The evidence also supported the calculation. Although Walton’s writing (the resale document) contained a lease provision, "uncontroverted" (undisputed) extrinsic evidence, meaning evidence from outside the document, showed that was a mistake and the real estate had been sold.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The trial judge found the purchase-contract provision ambiguous and consulted the separate escrow agreement, which expressly preserved damages and other remedies beyond payment of the fund.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The trial judge found the purchase-contract provision "ambiguous," meaning open to more than one reading. So the judge consulted the separate "escrow agreement" (governing the deposit held by a third party), which expressly preserved damages and other remedies beyond keeping the $5,000 fund.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: But this damages action was founded on the purchase contract, not the escrow agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: But this "damages" action, a suit for money compensation, was founded on the purchase contract, not the "escrow agreement" governing the deposit. So the rule about attaching the founding document did not apply to the escrow agreement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: The latter was admissible to explain whether the parties intended an exclusive remedy, and the finding that they did not was correct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: The escrow agreement was "admissible," meaning allowed as evidence, to show whether the parties intended the $5,000 as an "exclusive remedy," the only remedy. The "finding" (the judge's factual conclusion) that they did not was correct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.sentence: Chief Judge Murrah, writing with Judge Hickey and District Judge Christensen on July 6, 1967, affirmed as modified.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-070.plain: Chief Judge Murrah, writing with Judge Hickey and District Judge Christensen (a trial judge sitting on the appeals panel) on July 6, 1967, "affirmed" as modified. That means the court upheld the judgment but changed part of it, reducing the damages.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: Fraud had not been pleaded as a defense and was treated as unavailable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: Fraud had not been "pleaded" (raised in the buyers' written answer) as a "defense," so the court treated it as unavailable.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: Unconscionability remained independently available under UCC § 2-302.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: But "unconscionability," the doctrine that a court may refuse to enforce a grossly unfair contract, remained available on its own under UCC § 2-302, the Uniform Commercial Code's sales-law section on unfair terms.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: When that issue emerged, Judge Francis Donovan adjourned the trial to let both sides present evidence of the bargain’s commercial setting, purpose and effect.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: When that issue came up, Judge Francis Donovan "adjourned," or paused, the trial. He let both sides present evidence of the bargain’s commercial setting, purpose and effect, as the Code requires.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: He found the price and terms oppressive in combination with the buyers’ limited understanding and the unexplained form, invoking the Code’s protection against oppression and unfair surprise.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: He found the price and terms oppressive in combination with the buyers' limited understanding and the unexplained English form. He relied on the Code’s protection against "oppression" (grossly one-sided terms) and unfair surprise (hidden traps).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: Because the buyers kept the appliance, Donovan required payment of Frostifresh’s $348 cost, allowing nothing for commissions, attorney fees, service charges or overhead.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: Because the buyers kept the appliance, Judge Donovan required payment of Frostifresh’s $348 cost for it. He allowed nothing for commissions, "attorney fees" (lawyers' charges), service charges or "overhead," meaning general business expenses.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: The per curiam opinion reversed without costs and ordered a new trial limited to assessing damages and entering judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: The "per curiam" opinion (an unsigned opinion by the court as a whole) reversed without costs, meaning neither side paid the other's court costs. It ordered a new trial limited to assessing "damages," the amount owed, and entering judgment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.sentence: The buyers were not entitled to the appliance free, but reasonable compensation did not revive the original terms.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-011.plain: The buyers could not keep the refrigerator for free, but paying a fair amount did not mean the original unfair price would be enforced.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-026.sentence: In the supplied passage, publicity was an anticipated product of the engagement known to both sides, not simply a personal hope developed later by the employee.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-026.plain: In the passage, both sides knew when they contracted that the performer would gain publicity from the job; it was not just something he hoped for later. That matters because contract damages cover losses both sides could foresee.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-026.sentence: The Oliver quotation itself identifies valuable billing and advertising; it does not establish compensation for injured feelings or all later reputational consequences.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-026.plain: The Oliver quotation itself recognizes that billing and advertising (a performer's credited, publicized place on the program) have real value. It does not establish compensation for hurt feelings or for all later harm to reputation.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Payment would come ten days after arrival at Liverpool, provided Cutter proceeded, continued, and performed his duty as second mate throughout the passage.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Cutter would be paid only if he served as second mate for the entire voyage to Liverpool; the money was due ten days after the ship arrived.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Cutter's administratrix, acting for his estate, sued Powell in assumpsit for the work and labor Cutter had performed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Cutter's "administratrix," the woman appointed to manage his estate, sued Powell in "assumpsit," an old form of action for breach of a promise. She sought payment for the work and labor Cutter had performed.
Powell simply denied the whole claim, as the old pleading rules allowed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: A Lancaster jury found for the administratrix for £31 10s., but made its verdict subject to the King's Bench's legal decision on the stated case.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: A Lancaster jury returned a "verdict" (decision) for the administratrix, the estate's manager, for £31 10s., the full thirty guineas. But it was conditional on the King's Bench's ruling on the "stated case," the agreed facts sent to that high court in London to decide the legal question.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: The ship had completed its voyage and earned freight, so a rule tying wages to freight did not defeat payment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Under an old rule, sailors were paid only if the ship earned its carrying charges; this ship did finish the voyage and earn them, so that rule was no obstacle.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: The administratrix characterized the note as security for the promised sum, with a condition encouraging good conduct, rather than a complete exclusion of all other compensation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: The administratrix (the estate's manager) characterized the note "as security" for the promised sum, meaning a guarantee of it, with a condition encouraging good conduct. She said it was not a complete exclusion of all other pay.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Alternatively, even if failure to complete barred the thirty guineas, she argued that the express promise addressed only completed service; an implied undertaking could still pay for work actually supplied.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Alternatively, she argued that even if failing to complete the voyage barred the thirty guineas, the "express" (stated) promise covered only completed service. An "implied undertaking," a promise the law infers, could still pay for work actually supplied.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Powell answered that the agreement was entire and indivisible.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Powell answered that the agreement was "entire and indivisible": all-or-nothing, so the whole voyage had to be served before anything was earned.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: His estate could not substitute a different implied arrangement when the express condition failed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: When the "express condition" (the stated requirement of finishing the voyage) failed, his estate could not substitute a different "implied arrangement," an unwritten deal the law would infer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Ordinary yearly hiring, in which an executor might recover a proportion after the worker's death, was different from this unusually large and expressly conditional payment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Ordinary yearly hiring was different: there, an "executor" (the person handling a dead person's estate) might recover a proportion of the wages after the worker's death. This payment was unusually large and expressly conditional on completing the voyage.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Chief Justice Lord Kenyon qualified the rent illustration by referring to equitable relief where a tenant surrendered the lease.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Chief Justice Lord Kenyon qualified the rent example by noting "equitable relief," help from a court of equity based on fairness, where a tenant surrendered (gave up) the lease after the fire.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Where parties expressly fixed compensation, the law would not imply an inconsistent obligation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: When the parties had spelled out the pay in their agreement, the law would not create a contrary unwritten promise.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: His comparison to insurance described the allocation of compensation risk: Cutter would receive the larger amount for completing the duty, but nothing under this bargain if he did not.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Kenyon's comparison to insurance described how the deal allocated the risk over pay. Cutter would get the larger amount for completing his duty, but nothing under this "bargain" (the agreed deal) if he did not.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Kenyon remained open to evidence of usage.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Kenyon was willing to change his view if evidence showed an established merchant custom about such notes.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Justice Ashhurst likewise treated complete performance as a condition precedent to payment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Justice Ashhurst likewise treated complete "performance," serving the whole voyage, as a condition precedent: something that had to happen before any payment was owed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Justice Lawrence compared an entire-service agreement reported in Salkeld: a promise of £100 for a year did not support a £75 claim for three quarters.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Justice Lawrence compared an "entire-service agreement" (an all-or-nothing deal for a whole period of work) reported in Salkeld, an old book of case reports. There, a promise of £100 for a year's service did not support a £75 claim for three quarters of a year.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: Lawrence also suggested that impressed-seaman cases might be exceptional because the king's officers commonly supplied a replacement, preserving service for the owner; he did not announce a universal rule for interruptions by public authority.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: Lawrence also suggested that "impressed-seaman" cases, where sailors were forced into the navy, might be exceptions because the king's officers usually supplied a replacement, so the shipowner still got the service. He did not announce a universal rule for interruptions by public authority.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.sentence: The report directed the postea to the defendant unless additional information about usage was supplied before the term ended.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-063.plain: The report directed the "postea" (the record of the trial result, which governs entry of judgment) to the "defendant," Powell, meaning judgment for him. That held unless more information about "usage," a merchant custom, was supplied before the court's term ended.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Judge Loretta Preska accepted material allegations and favorable reasonable inferences but could consider incorporated agreements known to plaintiffs and relied on in suit without converting dismissal into a trial.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: On the motion to dismiss, Judge Loretta Preska accepted the plaintiffs' important factual "allegations" as true and drew "reasonable inferences" (sensible conclusions) in their favor. She could still read the incorporated agreements, which plaintiffs knew of and relied on in their "suit," without turning the motion into a trial.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Waivers identified publicity and likeness claims, intrusion, prima facie tort, and fraud involving deception or surprise about the film or agreement.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: The "waivers," signed releases giving up claims, listed publicity and likeness claims (misuse of name or image), intrusion (invasion of privacy), prima facie tort (deliberately causing harm without justification), and fraud involving deception or surprise about the film or the agreement.
