brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Paragraph 5 specifically denied reliance on statements about the nature of the film and identities of participants or others involved.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: In Paragraph 5, each signer stated they were not relying on anything they had been told about what the film was or who was involved in it.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: This was more targeted than a general merger provision excluding outside contractual terms.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: That clause was more targeted than a general "merger provision," a standard clause saying the written contract is the whole deal and excluding outside terms.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Under the undisputed New York choice-of-law clause, ambiguity was a legal threshold determined in contractual context and relevant usage.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: The contracts' undisputed "choice-of-law clause" picked New York law. Under it, whether a term is ambiguous (unclear) is a legal question the judge decides first, reading the term in its contractual context and in light of how such words are normally used.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Disagreement or strained alternatives did not create it.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: A term is not unclear just because the parties disagree or one side offers a far-fetched reading.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: The dispute concerned what fit the category, not competing reasonable definitions.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: The parties agreed on what a documentary is; they disagreed only on whether Borat fit, so the word was not ambiguous.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: The consents therefore applied unambiguously and could be enforced on the pleadings.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: So the consents (the signed releases) applied "unambiguously," meaning clearly, and could be enforced on the "pleadings" (the court papers alone), without a trial.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Fraudulent inducement under the applied New York rule required knowing material misrepresentation or omission, intent, reasonable reliance, and resulting harm.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: "Fraudulent inducement," being tricked into signing, required under the New York rule applied here a knowing "material misrepresentation" (a lie about something important) or omission, intent to deceive, and "reasonable reliance" on it. It also required resulting harm.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: The court applied Danann, a precedent allowing sufficiently specific disclaimers to defeat reliance on the disclaimed subject.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: The court applied Danann, a New York precedent holding that sufficiently specific "disclaimers" (contract statements that a party is not relying on statements about a subject) defeat any claim of reliance on that subject.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Plaintiffs could not plead reasonable reliance on those subjects after expressly disclaiming it.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: Plaintiffs could not "plead," or claim in their complaint, reasonable reliance on those subjects after expressly "disclaiming" it, meaning signing papers saying they were not relying on what they were told.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: The waiver released substantive claim categories; nonreliance defeated the attempted fraud-based escape.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: The "waiver" (the release) gave up the listed kinds of claims. The nonreliance clause, in which plaintiffs said they were not relying on any statements, defeated their attempt to escape the release by claiming fraud.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Plaintiffs also invoked a disclosure duty and an exception for facts peculiarly within defendants’ knowledge.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: Plaintiffs also invoked a "disclosure duty," a duty to reveal the truth, and an exception for facts "peculiarly within" the defendants' knowledge, meaning facts only the filmmakers could know. That exception can sometimes override a nonreliance clause.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: Recasting the same film and identity representations as omissions did not supply reliance negated by these terms.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: Calling the same statements about the film and the people 'omissions' instead of lies did not get around the clause in which the plaintiffs disclaimed reliance.

brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.sentence: On September 3, 2008, Preska granted dismissal in Psenicska, Streit, and Martin, directed closure of each action, and denied all pending motions as moot.
brief-CT-SUP-0022-PSENICSKA-DISTRICT.plain: On September 3, 2008, Preska "granted" dismissal in Psenicska, Streit, and Martin and directed that each case be closed. She "denied all pending motions as moot," meaning she did not decide the other requests because the dismissals made them pointless.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Public utility districts formed Clark-Cowlitz Joint Operating Agency, which applied in 1977 and invoked the Federal Power Act’s preference for state and municipal applicants whose plans were equally well adapted.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: "Public utility districts" (local government-owned power agencies) formed the Clark-Cowlitz Joint Operating Agency, which applied for the license in 1977. It invoked the Federal Power Act’s preference, a tie-breaker favoring state and city applicants whose plans were equally well adapted (as good as a competitor's).

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: As many licenses neared expiration, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, convened a declaratory proceeding on whether that preference applied against incumbents seeking renewal.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: With many licenses near expiration, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, held a "declaratory proceeding," one to decide a general legal question. The question was whether that preference applied against "incumbents," current license holders seeking renewal.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The Eleventh Circuit upheld that interpretation in Alabama Power in 1982 as reasonable under a deferential standard; it did not hold it the only permissible reading.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: In 1982, in Alabama Power, the Eleventh Circuit (a federal appeals court) upheld that interpretation as reasonable under a "deferential standard," giving the agency the benefit of the doubt. It did not hold it was the only permissible reading.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: A Supreme Court brief by the Solicitor General disclosed its changed view and requested further consideration below, but certiorari was denied.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: In a Supreme Court brief, the Solicitor General, the government's top lawyer before that Court, disclosed the agency's changed view and asked for further consideration "below," in the lower court. But certiorari was denied, meaning the Supreme Court declined to hear the case.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: An administrative law judge found the plans equally well adapted and favored Clark-Cowlitz, subject to Commission review.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: An "administrative law judge," the agency's in-house judge, found the plans equally well adapted and so favored Clark-Cowlitz, subject to review by the full Commission.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Alternatively, it found the proposals unequal because Pacific Power’s customers would incur greater replacement-power costs if it lost than Clark-Cowlitz’s customers would if that applicant lost.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: As a backup reason, it found the plans were not equal: Pacific Power's customers would pay more for replacement electricity if it lost the dam than Clark-Cowlitz's customers would if Clark-Cowlitz lost.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: During judicial review, the 1986 Electric Consumers Protection Act eliminated municipal preference in relicensing but expressly excluded Merwin.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: During "judicial review" (a court's review of the agency decision), the 1986 Electric Consumers Protection Act eliminated the municipal tie-breaker in relicensing. But it expressly excluded Merwin, so the old law still governed this dispute.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Clark-Cowlitz argued that the declaratory order and judicial affirmance bound the participants.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Clark-Cowlitz argued that the "declaratory order" (the agency's earlier ruling on the general legal question) and its judicial "affirmance," a court upholding it, bound everyone who took part. So, it said, the agency could not abandon that ruling in this case.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The majority distinguished the earlier question—whether the Bountiful reading was reasonable—from whether the later contrary construction was also reasonable.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The majority separated two questions about "construction," meaning interpretation of the statute. The earlier court decided only whether the Bountiful reading was reasonable, not whether the later contrary reading was also reasonable.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The Eleventh Circuit’s criticism of the alternative was unnecessary dicta, and Clark-Cowlitz and FERC had supported the same position there rather than litigating this issue adversely.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The Eleventh Circuit’s criticism of the alternative reading was unnecessary "dicta," side remarks that are not binding. And there Clark-Cowlitz and FERC had supported the same position, rather than "litigating" (fighting out in court) this issue against each other.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Even if party preclusion were the focus, pure legal rulings could be reconsidered to avoid inequitable administration, with flexibility for administrative adjudication.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Even if "party preclusion" (whether these particular parties were bound) were the focus, pure legal rulings could be reconsidered to avoid "inequitable administration," meaning treating similar parties unequally. "Administrative adjudication," agencies deciding cases, also gets extra flexibility.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: This was not a rule that agency declaratory orders never carry preclusive force.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: This did not mean that agency declaratory orders never carry "preclusive" force, the power to bind the parties in later disputes.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The majority began with the general ability of an agency adjudication to apply its new interpretation in the case announcing it, subject to preventing manifest injustice.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The majority began with the general rule that in "agency adjudication" (an agency deciding a case) the agency may apply a new interpretation to the very case announcing it. That is subject to preventing "manifest injustice," meaning obvious unfairness.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Retail, Wholesale, the circuit precedent on retroactive agency change, supplied five nonexclusive considerations.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Retail, Wholesale, the D.C. Circuit "precedent" (earlier binding decision) on applying changed agency rules retroactively, to earlier events, supplied five nonexclusive considerations, meaning factors that are not necessarily the only ones.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: In this test, first impression could mean the case first announcing a new rule, even if the underlying issue had been addressed.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Under that test, a 'first impression' case can be the one that first announces a new rule, even if the question had come up before.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Allowing a successful challenger to benefit encouraged reconsideration, though other factors could outweigh it.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Allowing a successful challenger to benefit encouraged "reconsideration," meaning parties asking agencies to rethink old rules. Other factors could outweigh it, though.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The majority recognized at most six months of reasonable optimism after appellate approval before the Solicitor General disclosed the impending change; hope afterward was not justified reliance.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The majority recognized at most six months of reasonable optimism after the appellate approval, until the Solicitor General (the government's Supreme Court lawyer) disclosed the coming change. Hoping after that was not "justified reliance," meaning reasonably counting on the old rule.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Clark-Cowlitz retained a merits opportunity and never held a final license, because the administrative judge’s ruling remained reviewable.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Clark-Cowlitz could still compete on the merits and never actually got a final license, because the in-house judge's ruling could still be reviewed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Fifth, retaining Bountiful could confer a thirty-year advantage contrary to the agency’s understanding of Congress’s best-qualified-applicant aim.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Fifth, retaining Bountiful, the old tie-breaker reading, could confer a thirty-year advantage, the length of a license, won only through the tie-breaker. That would go against the agency's understanding of Congress's aim of choosing the best-qualified applicant.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Under the then-governing Chevron framework, ordinary interpretive tools left ambiguity about preference when an incumbent sought renewal.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Under the "Chevron framework" used then, a court asked first whether the statute was clear. Here ordinary tools for reading statutes left "ambiguity" (unclearness) about whether the preference applied when an "incumbent," the current license holder, sought renewal, so a reasonable agency reading would be upheld.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Section 7(a) referred to new licensees under § 15, which distinguished new from original licensees.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Section 7(a), the preference provision, referred to "new licensees" under § 15. Section 15 treated new licensees differently from original licensees, the existing license holders.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: FERC reasonably treated the incumbent as original and applied municipal preference only when no incumbent competed.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: So FERC reasonably treated the "incumbent" (the current holder) as the original licensee. It applied the "municipal preference," the tie-breaker for state and city applicants, only when no incumbent was competing.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: But another natural reading did not displace a reasonable agency construction.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Under the deference rule then in force, the fact that the statute could naturally be read another way did not override the agency's reasonable reading.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The statute’s permissive “may,” its omission of a plan-equalization command in that setting, and § 10(a)’s comprehensive public-interest standard supported discretion.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The statute's permissive "may," its omission of any command to equalize plans in that setting, and § 10(a)’s comprehensive public-interest standard supported agency "discretion," meaning room for judgment, including to consider costs.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Considering only those customers risked an effective incumbent preference.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Looking only at the two applicants' own customers would tend to favor the current holder every time, in effect creating a preference for incumbents.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: It ignored whether a Clark-Cowlitz award would release subsidized Bonneville power for others and how total regional energy needs and sources remained unchanged despite changed project control.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The agency ignored whether giving Clark-Cowlitz the license would release subsidized Bonneville power (cheap federal power it had been using) for others. It also ignored that total regional energy needs and sources stayed the same, even though control of the project changed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: The court remanded for fuller explanation of the alternative-cost rationale while affirming all other aspects.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: The court "remanded," sending the case back for a fuller explanation of the agency's alternative-cost reasoning, while "affirming," or upholding, all other parts of the decision.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Mikva rejected a presumption favoring retroactivity.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Judge Mikva rejected a "presumption," a starting assumption, in favor of retroactivity, meaning applying a new agency rule to a pending case.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Chenery and Retail, Wholesale required independent balancing without a tilted scale, and agencies could use prospective rulemaking.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Mikva read Chenery and Retail, Wholesale as requiring independent "balancing," a neutral weighing of fairness without a tilted scale. He noted that agencies could instead use "prospective" rulemaking, new rules that apply only going forward.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Merwin was a second-impression reversal of an established rule; a rule could be established without being old or repeatedly applied.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: In his view Merwin was a "second-impression" decision, one reversing an established rule rather than deciding a new question. A rule could be established without being old or repeatedly applied.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: On preclusion, Mikva stressed the competitors’ final adjudication of a ripe dispute rather than FERC’s prior advocacy.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: On "preclusion" (whether the earlier ruling bound the parties), Mikva stressed that the competitors had a final decision on a "ripe" dispute, a real, concrete one ready for decision. What mattered was that, not FERC’s earlier arguments.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: Pacific Power should not escape merely because the decisionmaker changed its mind, turning declaratory proceedings into expensive rehearsals.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: Pacific Power should not escape just because the decisionmaker, the agency, changed its mind. Otherwise "declaratory proceedings" (advance rulings on general legal questions) would become expensive rehearsals that bind no one.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.sentence: On interpretation, municipal preference guided selection of the winner, not just issuance afterward; the “other applicants” language belonged within the three identified situations rather than a catch-all.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-012.plain: On the statute's meaning, he read "municipal preference" (the tie-breaker for state and city applicants) as guiding who wins, not just how the license is issued afterward. The "other applicants" language belonged within the three listed situations rather than being a "catch-all," a sweeping category.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act authorized the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, to regulate drugs and devices, including nonfood articles intended to affect bodily structure or function.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act let the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, regulate drugs and medical devices. Those include nonfood products intended to affect the structure or function of the body, meaning how it is built or works.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: For many years, the FDA disclaimed authority over tobacco products sold without therapeutic claims.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: For many years, the FDA disclaimed (denied) authority over tobacco products sold without "therapeutic claims," meaning claims that they treat or prevent disease.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The FDA found manufacturer intent from foreseeable effects, consumers’ reasons for use, and industry research and product design showing deliberate delivery of active doses.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The FDA concluded that makers intended nicotine's effects on the body, based on those foreseeable effects, why people use tobacco, and company research and product design showing they deliberately delivered effective doses.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The agency used the Act’s restricted-device provision, § 360j(e), claiming that access and promotion controls could reasonably assure safety.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The agency relied on the Act’s restricted-device provision, § 360j(e), which allows limits on selling and using medical devices. It claimed that controls on access and promotion could reasonably assure safety.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: It stayed the upheld provisions except the prohibition on sales to minors and certified an interlocutory appeal.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: It "stayed," or put on hold, the upheld provisions except the ban on sales to minors. It also certified an "interlocutory appeal," allowing an immediate appeal before the case was finished.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The Supreme Court agreed to review authority over tobacco as customarily marketed, without therapeutic claims.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The Supreme Court agreed to "review" (decide) whether the FDA had authority over tobacco as customarily marketed, without "therapeutic claims" that it treats or prevents disease.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Justice O’Connor’s five-Justice majority applied Chevron, the then-governing framework asking first whether Congress had answered the precise statutory question.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: Justice O’Connor wrote for a five-Justice majority applying Chevron, the framework that governed then. Its first question is whether Congress itself answered the precise "statutory" question, meaning the exact question about the law's meaning; if so, the agency must follow that answer.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Although respondents argued that manufacturer intent required an express therapeutic claim, the majority assumed that the intended-effects definition could be satisfied without one.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The "respondents," the tobacco companies, argued that manufacturer intent required an express "therapeutic claim" (a health claim). But the majority assumed, for argument's sake, that the "intended-effects definition," covering products meant to affect the body, could be met without one.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: On the FDA’s own findings, tobacco was dangerous as used, could not bear directions making its intended use safe, and could not satisfy the device-classification safety requirements.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: On the FDA’s own "findings" (its factual conclusions), tobacco was dangerous as used and could not carry directions making its "intended use" safe. So it could not meet the safety requirements for classifying devices.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Jurisdiction under that scheme would therefore require removal from the market.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: So "jurisdiction," meaning FDA power, over tobacco under that scheme would require removing tobacco from the market.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The Act’s safety inquiry concerned therapeutic benefits outweighing risks to the consumer.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The Act’s safety inquiry asked whether a product's therapeutic (health) benefits to the consumer outweighed its risks.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Together, they established a specific scheme reserving central tobacco-policy decisions to Congress.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: Taken together, those laws showed Congress had kept the major tobacco-policy decisions for itself.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The majority did not rely simply on failed bills or congressional silence, nor did it prohibit agencies from changing interpretations.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The majority did not rest simply on Congress's failure to pass bills or its silence, and did not say agencies may never change their reading of a statute.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The earlier agency position mattered because Congress had legislated against that understood allocation of authority.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The earlier "agency" position mattered because Congress had passed its tobacco laws against that understood division of authority, believing the FDA lacked power over tobacco.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The breadth of the claimed power reinforced the conclusion: regulation of a major economic sector, potentially including a complete tobacco ban, was an extraordinary delegation to infer from general definitions and safety provisions.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The breadth of the claimed power confirmed the conclusion. "Regulation" of a major economic sector, possibly including a complete tobacco ban, was an extraordinary "delegation," or handing over of power by Congress, to infer from general definitions and safety provisions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: The Court affirmed the Fourth Circuit on March 21, 2000, concluding at Chevron’s first step that Congress had withheld the asserted authority.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: On March 21, 2000, the Court "affirmed," or upheld, the Fourth Circuit. It concluded at "Chevron’s first step" that Congress had clearly withheld the power the FDA claimed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg, read the broad text, public-health purpose, and 1938 legislative history to encompass nontherapeutic products affecting bodily functions.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: Justice Breyer, "joined by" Justices Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg, read the broad text, the public-health purpose, and the 1938 "legislative history" (records of how Congress passed the law). He found they covered nontherapeutic products, ones sold without health claims, that affect bodily functions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Device provisions allowed remedial discretion and consideration of available alternatives; a regulated market could be safer than driving addicted consumers to dangerous substitutes.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: The device rules let the FDA choose among remedies, and keeping tobacco on a regulated market could be safer than a ban that pushes addicted smokers to dangerous black-market products.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.sentence: Breyer understood prior disclaimers chiefly as reflecting insufficient evidence of manufacturer intent, a problem later evidence and scientific developments could overcome.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-030.plain: Breyer saw the FDA's earlier disclaimers of power mainly as reflecting "insufficient evidence" of what manufacturers intended. Later evidence and scientific developments could cure that problem.

cp-berk.sentence: Berk sued Choy and Beebe for malpractice under Delaware law in federal court, relying on diversity of citizenship.
cp-berk.plain: Berk sued Choy, the doctor, and Beebe, the hospital, for "malpractice" (medical negligence) under Delaware law. He sued in federal court, relying on "diversity of citizenship," which lets federal courts hear cases between people from different states.

cp-berk.sentence: Delaware Code title 18, § 6853 ordinarily required a medical professional’s affidavit of merit with a malpractice complaint, identifying reasonable grounds to believe each defendant committed health-care negligence.
cp-berk.plain: Delaware Code title 18, § 6853 ordinarily required an "affidavit of merit" with a malpractice complaint: a sworn statement from a medical professional. It had to state reasonable grounds to believe each defendant committed health-care negligence.

cp-berk.sentence: Good cause could support one sixty-day extension, but the motion had to precede or accompany the complaint.
cp-berk.plain: "Good cause," a sufficient reason, could support one sixty-day extension. But the "motion," the request for it, had to be filed before or with the complaint.

cp-berk.sentence: Defendants need not respond until twenty days after filing of the affidavit and could request in camera review of its statutory sufficiency.
cp-berk.plain: Defendants did not have to respond until twenty days after the "affidavit" was filed. They could request "in camera" review, meaning the judge privately checks whether it meets the statute's requirements.

cp-berk.sentence: Defendants requested an in camera examination; Berk argued that the Federal Rules displaced the affidavit requirement.
cp-berk.plain: Berk had instead filed medical records under seal, and defendants requested an "in camera" examination, a private review by the judge. Berk argued that the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure displaced, or overrode, the "affidavit" requirement.

cp-berk.sentence: The Third Circuit affirmed, reasoning that no Federal Rule answered whether an affidavit had to accompany the complaint.
cp-berk.plain: The Third Circuit affirmed, agreeing with the trial court. It reasoned that no Federal Rule answered whether an "affidavit" had to come with the complaint.

cp-berk.sentence: It applied ordinary Erie principles and treated the state rule as substantive because omission would affect outcomes, encourage forum shopping and create inequitable administration.
cp-berk.plain: It applied ordinary "Erie principles," the test for when federal courts must follow state law, and treated the Delaware rule as substantive. Ignoring it would change outcomes, encourage "forum shopping" (picking federal court to avoid it), and create "inequitable administration," treating similar cases unequally.

cp-berk.sentence: Justice Barrett explained that the Rules of Decision Act requires state substantive law unless federal law otherwise provides, while the Rules Enabling Act authorizes federal procedural rules.
cp-berk.plain: Justice Barrett explained that the "Rules of Decision Act" requires federal courts to apply state "substantive law" (rules on rights and duties) unless federal law provides otherwise. The "Rules Enabling Act" authorizes federal "procedural rules," the rules for how lawsuits are run.

cp-berk.sentence: When a valid Federal Rule answers the disputed question, it governs despite contrary state law that might otherwise count as substantive.
cp-berk.plain: When a valid Federal Rule answers the disputed question, it governs, even over a contrary state law that might otherwise count as "substantive" and have to be followed.

cp-berk.sentence: A court therefore identifies a conflict and then tests the Federal Rule’s validity under the Enabling Act and Congress’s rulemaking power.
cp-berk.plain: So a court first identifies a conflict between a Federal Rule and state law. It then tests the rule's validity under the Enabling Act and Congress’s "rulemaking" power, its authority to have procedural rules written.

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 8(a)(2), requiring a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief, answered it.
cp-berk.plain: Rule 8(a)(2), requiring a "short and plain statement" of the claim showing the plaintiff deserves relief, answered that question.

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 8 prescribed initial merits information, not evidentiary proof.
cp-berk.plain: Rule 8 sets out the information about the claim's "merits" (its substance) a plaintiff must give at the start, not evidentiary proof.

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 12 reinforced the distinction: a motion under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the stated claim, while consideration of outside material invokes Rule 12(d)’s conversion procedure.
cp-berk.plain: Rule 12 reinforced the distinction. A Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss tests only the stated "claim," while considering "outside material" (evidence beyond the complaint) triggers Rule 12(d)’s "conversion procedure," treating the motion as one for summary judgment.

cp-berk.sentence: Adequate allegations can proceed even when proof seems improbable.
cp-berk.plain: Adequate "allegations" (properly stated claims of fact) can go forward even when proof seems unlikely.

cp-berk.sentence: The majority inferred from Rule 8’s specified requirements that courts could not add claim-specific pleading burdens, while recognizing that the Federal Rules themselves, such as Rule 9, can prescribe special treatment.
cp-berk.plain: Because Rule 8 lists specific requirements, the majority inferred that courts could not add extra "pleading" burdens (complaint requirements) for particular kinds of claims. It recognized that the Federal Rules themselves, such as Rule 9 for fraud, can prescribe special treatment.

cp-berk.sentence: Defendants invoked Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan, which permitted security for expenses in a shareholder derivative suit.
cp-berk.plain: Defendants relied on Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan, which allowed a state requirement of "security for expenses" (money posted to cover the defendants' costs) in a "shareholder derivative suit," where shareholders sue on the company's behalf.

cp-berk.sentence: The majority distinguished it: that state statute created potential expense liability and secured it, while the Federal Rule addressed notice and disclosure.
cp-berk.plain: The majority distinguished Cohen. That state "statute" created possible "liability" (a legal duty to pay) for the defendant's expenses and secured it, while the "Federal Rule" here addressed notice and disclosure, what a complaint must tell the other side.

cp-berk.sentence: It also lacked an authorized dismissal route.
cp-berk.plain: And there was no proper rule under which the court could dismiss the case for lack of the statement.

cp-berk.sentence: Defendants conceded an absent affidavit did not support Rule 12(b)(6); Berk actively litigated, so failure to prosecute did not apply; inherent authority could not bypass the Rules’ proof-testing mechanisms.
cp-berk.plain: Defendants conceded a missing "affidavit" did not support dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim. Berk had actively "litigated" (pursued) the case, so failure to prosecute did not apply, and a court's "inherent authority," its general powers, could not bypass the Rules' own ways of testing proof.

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 56 provided summary judgment with adequate discovery time.
cp-berk.plain: Rule 56 provided the proper tool: summary judgment, which ends a case without trial when the evidence shows no real dispute, after adequate "discovery" (time to gather evidence).

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 11(a) ordinarily dispenses with verification or accompanying affidavits unless a rule or statute specifies otherwise.
cp-berk.plain: Rule 11(a) ordinarily dispenses with "verification" (swearing that a filing is true) or accompanying "affidavits," sworn statements, unless a rule or statute specifies otherwise.

cp-berk.sentence: The majority reserved whether that proviso ever incorporates state affidavit statutes, but held it did not incorporate this one.
cp-berk.plain: The majority reserved, or left undecided, whether that "proviso" (the unless-a-statute-says-otherwise exception) ever brings in state "affidavit" statutes. But it held that the proviso did not bring in this Delaware one.

cp-berk.sentence: The Rules Enabling Act forbids Federal Rules from abridging, enlarging or modifying substantive rights.
cp-berk.plain: The Rules Enabling Act forbids Federal Rules from abridging (shrinking), enlarging or modifying "substantive rights," the underlying legal rights people have.

cp-berk.sentence: Applying Sibbach’s test, the majority asked whether Rule 8 really regulated procedure—the manner and means of enforcing rights.
cp-berk.plain: Applying "Sibbach’s test," from the Sibbach case, the majority asked whether Rule 8 really regulates procedure. Procedure here means the manner and means of enforcing rights in court, not what the rights are.

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 8 controlled what a plaintiff must present at the outset, rather than the substantive right, remedy or rule of decision.
cp-berk.plain: Rule 8 controls what a plaintiff must present at the start of a case. It does not control the "substantive right," the remedy, or the "rule of decision," meaning the law that decides who wins.

cp-berk.sentence: The Court rejected a second validity inquiry into whether Delaware’s displaced rule was substantive.
cp-berk.plain: The Court refused to add a second validity test asking whether Delaware’s displaced rule, the state rule being pushed aside, was substantive.

cp-berk.sentence: Accordingly, the Third Circuit’s ordinary Erie classification could not save the conflicting affidavit requirement.
cp-berk.plain: So the Third Circuit’s ordinary Erie classification of the Delaware rule as substantive could not save the conflicting "affidavit" requirement; the valid federal rule controlled.

cp-berk.sentence: Justice Jackson concurred only in the judgment.
cp-berk.plain: Justice Jackson "concurred only in the judgment," meaning she agreed with the result but not with the majority's reasoning.

cp-berk.sentence: Rule 3, in her view, directly resolved commencement: filing a complaint starts a civil action, while Delaware demanded an additional affidavit or extension motion before filing and docketing.
cp-berk.plain: In her view, Rule 3 directly resolved "commencement," when a suit begins: filing a complaint starts a "civil action." Delaware instead demanded an extra "affidavit" or extension "motion" before filing and "docketing," entering the case on the court's list.

cp-berk.sentence: Walker v. Armco concerned commencement for a state limitations period, a question Rule 3 did not answer; Woods v. Interstate Realty concerned substantive restrictions on a foreign corporation’s access to state court.
cp-berk.plain: She distinguished two cases. Walker v. Armco was about when a suit counts as started for a state "limitations period" (filing deadline), a question Rule 3 did not answer; Woods v. Interstate Realty concerned substantive state limits on a "foreign corporation," one formed in another state, using state courts.

cp-berk.sentence: Jackson advocated interpreting Federal Rules with sensitivity to state policy, citing Gasperini and the five-Justice alignment in Shady Grove.
cp-berk.plain: Jackson urged interpreting Federal Rules with sensitivity to state policy. She cited Gasperini and the five-Justice alignment, the five Justices who took that approach, in Shady Grove.

cp-berk.sentence: Her objection was to the breadth of the majority’s implication, not to negative implications as an interpretive method.
cp-berk.plain: She did not object to reading a rule's list as excluding other requirements in general, only to how far the majority took that idea.

cp-berk.sentence: A merits dismissal relying on such material could not evade conversion.
cp-berk.plain: A court could not dismiss on the merits based on such outside material without treating the motion as one for summary judgment.

cp-berk.sentence: The decision granted no malpractice finding or damages and required analysis of the particular conflict, rather than automatic displacement of every state condition.
cp-berk.plain: The decision made no "malpractice" finding and awarded no "damages"; it did not decide whether anyone was negligent. It required analysis of each particular conflict rather than automatically displacing every state condition in federal court.

cp-doehr.sentence: Connecticut law allowed a judge to authorize attachment of real property without an advance hearing upon a sworn showing of probable cause to sustain the claim.
cp-doehr.plain: Connecticut law let a judge authorize "attachment" of real property, a legal hold on real estate, without an advance hearing. The plaintiff only had to make a sworn showing of "probable cause," good reason to think the claim would succeed.

cp-doehr.sentence: It required no plaintiff’s bond to cover harm from a wrongful attachment.
cp-doehr.plain: It required no bond from the plaintiff to cover harm from a "wrongful attachment," a hold that turned out to be unjustified.

cp-doehr.sentence: The notice explained that he could request a hearing to dispute probable cause, seek modification or vacation, substitute a bond, or assert an exemption.
cp-doehr.plain: The notice told him he could request a hearing to dispute "probable cause" (the basis for the hold), ask to modify or vacate (cancel) it, substitute a bond, or claim an "exemption," meaning the property was legally protected.

cp-doehr.sentence: He instead sued DiGiovanni in federal district court, seeking a declaration that the statute violated Fourteenth Amendment due process.
cp-doehr.plain: Instead, he sued DiGiovanni in "federal district court" (a federal trial court). He sought a declaration that the statute violated Fourteenth Amendment "due process," the guarantee of fair procedure before property is taken.

cp-doehr.sentence: It understood Sniadach and the later prejudgment-remedy cases to permit postponing a hearing only for exceptional circumstances supported by additional safeguards.
cp-doehr.plain: The court read Sniadach and the later prejudgment-remedy cases (on seizing property before trial) as allowing a hearing to be postponed only in exceptional circumstances. Even then, additional safeguards were required.

cp-doehr.sentence: Unlike Mitchell’s documentary payment dispute, this assault claim depended on disputed events in a fight that a judge could not reliably assess from the plaintiff alone.
cp-doehr.plain: Mitchell involved a payment dispute provable by documents. This assault claim, by contrast, turned on disputed events in a fight that a judge could not reliably assess from the "plaintiff" (the person suing) alone.

cp-doehr.sentence: At the appellate court’s invitation, Connecticut intervened after oral argument under 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b) to defend its statute’s constitutionality.
cp-doehr.plain: At the appellate court’s invitation, Connecticut "intervened," or joined the case, after oral argument under 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b), a federal statute letting states defend their laws. It did so to defend its statute's constitutionality.

cp-doehr.sentence: Justice White placed the case in the line of Sniadach, Fuentes, Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing and adapted the Mathews v. Eldridge framework to a private party’s use of state power.
cp-doehr.plain: Justice White placed the case in the line of Sniadach, Fuentes, Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing, the cases on seizing property before trial. He adapted the Mathews v. Eldridge framework, the usual due process balancing test, to a private party’s use of state power.

cp-doehr.sentence: The first factor was the affected private interest; the second was the risk of error and value of further safeguards; the third focused principally on the claimant’s interest in obtaining the remedy, with attention to ancillary governmental interests and administrative burdens.
cp-doehr.plain: The first factor was the private interest affected; the second, the risk of error and the value of more safeguards. The third focused mainly on the claimant’s interest in getting the "remedy" (the hold), with attention to "ancillary," or secondary, government interests and administrative burdens.

cp-doehr.sentence: It nevertheless clouded title, impaired sale or transfer, affected credit, reduced access to a home-equity loan or additional mortgage, and could trigger an insecurity clause in an existing mortgage.
cp-doehr.plain: Even so, it "clouded title" (made ownership uncertain), hampered sale or transfer, hurt credit, and limited access to a "home-equity loan" or additional mortgage. It could also trigger an "insecurity clause" in an "existing mortgage," letting the lender demand full repayment.

cp-doehr.sentence: Due process protects temporary and partial property impairments as well as complete physical losses.
cp-doehr.plain: "Due process," the right to fair procedure, protects against temporary and partial interference with property, not only complete physical losses.

cp-doehr.sentence: Connecticut’s probable-cause standard was obscure: the State initially described an objective likelihood of success, Doehr understood a subjective good-faith belief, and the State’s oral argument likened it to a complaint surviving dismissal.
cp-doehr.plain: Connecticut's probable-cause standard was unclear. The State first described an objective likelihood of success, Doehr understood a subjective "good-faith" (honest) belief, and at "oral argument" the State compared it to a complaint good enough to survive dismissal.

cp-doehr.sentence: A facially valid allegation or sincere belief could support attachment despite defenses, jury rejection, or even failure to state a claim under the weakest understanding.
cp-doehr.plain: Under the weakest reading, a "facially" valid allegation (one that looks fine on paper) or sincere belief could support attachment. That would hold despite good defenses, rejection by a jury, or even "failure to state a claim," meaning no valid legal claim at all.

cp-doehr.sentence: Even an objective-success standard could not make the skeletal, one-sided affidavit reliable.
cp-doehr.plain: Even a standard requiring an objective chance of success could not make the skeletal, one-sided "affidavit" (sworn statement) reliable.

cp-doehr.sentence: An expeditious later hearing, notice, review of an adverse decision and a double-damages action for a suit lacking probable cause did not adequately correct that initial risk.
cp-doehr.plain: A quick hearing afterward, notice, the right to appeal, and the right to sue for double damages if the claim lacked probable cause did not cure the risk of a wrongful hold in the first place.

cp-doehr.sentence: Mitchell had similar protections but also a vendor’s lien, documentary issues and a bond.
cp-doehr.plain: Mitchell had similar protections but also a "vendor’s lien," the seller's existing claim on the goods sold. It also involved issues provable by documents, and a bond was posted.

cp-doehr.sentence: A properly supported allegation of that kind could supply exigent circumstances for postponing the hearing, but it was absent here.
cp-doehr.plain: A properly supported "allegation" that the owner was about to sell or hide the property could supply "exigent circumstances," an emergency, for postponing the hearing. But none was made here.

cp-doehr.sentence: Connecticut could not justify delay through administrative burden when its procedure already offered an immediate post-deprivation hearing.
cp-doehr.plain: Connecticut could not argue an advance hearing was too burdensome when it already offered a prompt hearing right after the hold was placed.

cp-doehr.sentence: All nine Justices agreed that this attachment procedure, as applied to the unrelated tort claim without a property interest or supported urgency, violated due process.
cp-doehr.plain: All nine Justices agreed this "attachment" procedure violated "due process" as applied here. The claim was an unrelated "tort" (an injury claim, here assault), with no "property interest" (existing claim on the house) and no supported urgency.

cp-doehr.sentence: The holding left room for a different balance where a plaintiff had a pre-existing interest, reliable documentary proof, or evidence of imminent dissipation.
cp-doehr.plain: The holding left room for a different balance where a plaintiff had a pre-existing interest in the property, reliable "documentary proof" (evidence in records), or evidence that the owner was about to dissipate, or get rid of, the property.

cp-doehr.sentence: In Part IV, White, Marshall, Stevens and O’Connor would additionally require a bond or other security even when a hearing or exigency justified attachment.
cp-doehr.plain: In Part IV, Justices White, Marshall, Stevens and O’Connor would also require a bond or other security. That would apply even when a hearing or an emergency justified the "attachment."

cp-doehr.sentence: If probable cause meant good faith or facial adequacy, recovery could require something approaching fraud, malice or a complaint that failed to state a claim.
cp-doehr.plain: If "probable cause" meant only good faith or facial adequacy (a valid-looking complaint), the owner's "recovery" of damages could require something close to fraud or malice, or a complaint that failed to state a legal claim.

cp-doehr.sentence: Even assuming ultimate defeat permitted recovery, the plurality identified delay, loss of the remedy following settlement, an advice-of-counsel defense and uncertainty about the original plaintiff’s ability to pay.
cp-doehr.plain: Even assuming the plaintiff's ultimate defeat allowed recovery, the plurality (the four Justices) saw problems. They named delay, loss of the remedy after a settlement, the plaintiff's "advice-of-counsel defense" (that a lawyer advised the suit), and doubt about the original plaintiff's ability to pay.

cp-doehr.sentence: Parts IV and V lacked a majority even though all nine Justices agreed on the disposition stated in Part V: affirmance of the Court of Appeals and remand.
cp-doehr.plain: Parts IV and V lacked a majority, five votes, even though all nine Justices agreed on the "disposition" stated in Part V. That result was "affirmance" (upholding) of the Court of Appeals and a remand, sending the case back.

cp-doehr.sentence: He emphasized that earlier cases involved personal property physically seized from its owner, while Connecticut created an incipient lien and left Doehr in possession.
cp-doehr.plain: Chief Justice Rehnquist stressed that earlier cases involved "personal property" (movable belongings) physically seized from its owner. Connecticut instead created an "incipient lien," a budding claim on the house, and left Doehr in possession.

cp-doehr.sentence: Mechanics’ liens for incorporated labor or materials and lis pendens asserting an interest in the property being litigated involved different property connections.
cp-doehr.plain: "Mechanics’ liens," claims by those whose labor or materials were built into the property, and "lis pendens," a recorded notice claiming an interest in property being "litigated" (fought over in court), are different. Those claimants have a real connection to the property.

cp-doehr.sentence: Because this attachment was not a procedure recognized at common law, he agreed it should be tested under Mathews and failed that test.
cp-doehr.plain: Justice Scalia said that because this attachment was not a procedure recognized at "common law" (traditional judge-made law), it should be tested under Mathews, the modern balancing test. He agreed it failed that test.

cp-doehr.sentence: Later assigned comparisons remain separate: Shaumyan upheld the same statute in a contractor’s documentary payment dispute involving incorporated labor and materials, and Diaz rejected as-applied and consequently facial challenges to New York lis pendens under the Doehr framework.
cp-doehr.plain: Two later cases the casebook assigns are separate. Shaumyan upheld the same statute for a contractor's payment dispute provable by documents, involving labor and materials built into the property; Diaz rejected "as-applied" (to these facts) and therefore "facial challenges" (to the law in all cases) to New York "lis pendens" (notice-of-lawsuit) rules under the Doehr test.

cp-mussat.sentence: IQVIA, incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Pennsylvania, was not subject to Illinois general jurisdiction.
cp-mussat.plain: IQVIA was incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in Pennsylvania, so it was not subject to "general jurisdiction" in Illinois. That means courts there could not hear just any claim against it, only claims connected to Illinois.

cp-mussat.sentence: It argued that Bristol-Myers Squibb required specific jurisdiction for each absent member injured outside Illinois.
cp-mussat.plain: IQVIA argued that Bristol-Myers Squibb, a Supreme Court decision, required "specific jurisdiction" (a claim connected to the state) for each absent, unnamed class member injured outside Illinois.

cp-mussat.sentence: The district court agreed and struck the non-Illinois class allegations, leaving an Illinois-only class possible.
cp-mussat.plain: The "district court" (federal trial court) agreed and "struck," or deleted, the class "allegations" covering people outside Illinois. That left an Illinois-only class possible.

cp-mussat.sentence: Mussat obtained discretionary review under Rule 23(f), which IQVIA contested along with the merits.
cp-mussat.plain: Mussat obtained "discretionary review" under Rule 23(f), meaning the appeals court chose to allow an early appeal of a class-certification ruling. IQVIA contested whether that review was available, as well as the merits.

cp-mussat.sentence: IQVIA emphasized that the ruling granted a Rule 12 motion to strike rather than a motion labeled certification and left a narrower class available.
cp-mussat.plain: IQVIA stressed that the ruling granted a Rule 12 "motion" to strike, a request to delete parts of the complaint, rather than one labeled as a certification decision. It also noted that a narrower class was still available.

cp-mussat.sentence: The panel examined effect, reviewing the jurisdictional issue anew.
cp-mussat.plain: The panel looked at the order's actual effect rather than its label, "reviewing" the jurisdictional issue "anew," meaning freshly, without deferring to the trial court.

cp-mussat.sentence: This ruling foreclosed the national class actually requested; a remaining local possibility did not remove that denial.
cp-mussat.plain: The order effectively denied the nationwide class Mussat asked for, even though a local class was still possible.

cp-mussat.sentence: They were named parties asserting their own cases, not unnamed members of a certified representative class.
cp-mussat.plain: They were "named parties," plaintiffs listed in the case and asserting their own claims. They were not unnamed members of a certified class represented by someone else.

cp-mussat.sentence: Longstanding nationwide-class practice, illustrated by Wal-Mart, Shutts, and Yamasaki, supplied context rather than holdings on this precise later dispute.
cp-mussat.plain: Long-standing practice of nationwide class actions, illustrated by Wal-Mart, Shutts, and Yamasaki, supplied background. But those cases did not decide this exact later dispute.

cp-mussat.sentence: Rule 23 requires all four subdivision (a) safeguards and an applicable (b) category before representation binds absentees.
cp-mussat.plain: Rule 23 requires all four safeguards in subdivision (a), such as adequate representation, and a fit with one (b) category of class action. Only then can representation bind absentees, the members not in court.

cp-mussat.sentence: Taylor v. Sturgell’s rejection of informal virtual representation underscored why a certified class differs from free-form aggregation.
cp-mussat.plain: Taylor v. Sturgell’s rejection of informal "virtual representation" (binding someone because a person with similar interests sued) showed why a certified class is different. A loose, free-form "aggregation," or grouping, of claims lacks a class's safeguards.

cp-mussat.sentence: Devlin also showed that unnamed members can be parties for some purposes and not others.
cp-mussat.plain: Devlin, an earlier Supreme Court case, also showed that unnamed class members can count as parties for some purposes, such as appealing a settlement, and not for others.

cp-mussat.sentence: Absent members’ citizenship ordinarily does not destroy complete diversity; supplemental jurisdiction can cover them where the representative meets the amount requirement; and venue does not require separate proof for each.
cp-mussat.plain: "Absent members" (unnamed class members) ordinarily do not count for complete diversity, and supplemental jurisdiction can cover their claims if the representative meets the amount requirement. And "venue," the proper court location, needs no separate proof for each.

cp-mussat.sentence: The panel reasoned that personal jurisdiction likewise focuses on named representatives, each of whom must establish general or specific jurisdiction over the defendant.
cp-mussat.plain: The panel reasoned that "personal jurisdiction," a court's power over the defendant, likewise focuses on the named representatives. Each must establish general or "specific jurisdiction" (power based on claims tied to the state) over the defendant.

cp-mussat.sentence: IQVIA separately invoked Rule 4(k), generally linking district-court personal jurisdiction to the forum state’s courts.
cp-mussat.plain: IQVIA separately relied on Rule 4(k), which generally gives "district-court" personal jurisdiction (a federal trial court's power over a defendant) the same reach as the courts of the "forum state," the state where it sits.

cp-mussat.sentence: The panel distinguished service and jurisdictional reach from whose claims a representative may assert.
cp-mussat.plain: The panel separated two things: service and "jurisdictional" reach, meaning how far a court's power over a defendant extends, and whose claims a class representative may assert.

cp-mussat.sentence: Rule 17’s executors, guardians, administrators, and trustees illustrated representative litigation more broadly, while Rule 82 cautioned against treating procedural rules as extending or limiting jurisdiction or venue.
cp-mussat.plain: Rule 17’s executors, guardians, administrators, and "trustees" (people managing property for others) showed representative suits more broadly. Rule 82 warns against treating "procedural rules" as extending or limiting "jurisdiction" (court power) or venue.

cp-mussat.sentence: Rule 23(b)(3)’s forum-concentration factor and its Committee Note also contemplate bringing claims together instead of leaving them in individual ordinary forums.
cp-mussat.plain: Rule 23(b)(3)’s forum-concentration factor and its Committee Note, the drafters' official explanation, also contemplate gathering claims in one court. That replaces leaving them in each person's own ordinary "forums," or courts.

cp-mussat.sentence: This permits interstate reach even without general jurisdiction, subject to certification safeguards.
cp-mussat.plain: This allows a class to reach members from other states even without "general jurisdiction" (the defendant being "at home" in the state), as long as the certification safeguards are met.

cp-mussat.sentence: Bristol-Myers had reserved whether Fifth Amendment federal-court restrictions mirror Fourteenth Amendment state restrictions, and Sotomayor separately noted the unaddressed class question.
cp-mussat.plain: Bristol-Myers had "reserved," or left open, whether the Fifth Amendment's limits on federal courts mirror the Fourteenth Amendment restrictions on state courts. Justice Sotomayor separately noted that it did not address class actions.

cp-mussat.sentence: The district court’s use of the Fourteenth rather than Fifth Amendment label was not dispositive.
cp-mussat.plain: The district court’s use of the Fourteenth Amendment label (for state courts) rather than the Fifth Amendment (for federal courts) was not "dispositive," meaning it did not decide the outcome.

frigaliment.sentence: The description specified fresh-frozen, Grade A, government-inspected, eviscerated U.S. chicken, individually Cryovac-wrapped and export-packed, for May 10 shipment free alongside ship in New York.
frigaliment.plain: The contract specified fresh-frozen, Grade A, government-inspected, eviscerated (cleaned) U.S. chicken, individually Cryovac-wrapped and packed for export. It was to be shipped May 10 "free alongside ship" in New York, meaning the seller delivers to the dock beside the ship.

frigaliment.sentence: Frigaliment sued for breach of the statutory warranty that goods correspond to their description.
frigaliment.plain: Frigaliment sued for breach of the "statutory warranty," a promise imposed by statute, that goods will match their contract description.

frigaliment.sentence: He applied New York law because the parties apparently agreed it governed despite acceptance in Switzerland.
frigaliment.plain: Judge Friendly applied New York law because the parties apparently agreed it governed, despite "acceptance" of the deal (the final agreement to its terms) in Switzerland.

frigaliment.sentence: Their failure to invoke a Produce Exchange arbitration clause was treated as agreement to eliminate that remedy.
frigaliment.plain: Neither side invoked the contract's "arbitration clause" sending disputes to a Produce Exchange (trade exchange) arbitrator. The court treated that as their agreement to drop that "remedy" and go to court.

frigaliment.sentence: Nor could Frigaliment rely on its cable as a definition while rejecting the explanatory response of the intermediary entrusted with it.
frigaliment.plain: Frigaliment could not use its own message as proof of what it meant while ignoring what its own go-between said when explaining that message.

frigaliment.sentence: A blank intermediary line on the forms concerned the commission recipient and did not erase his participation.
frigaliment.plain: A blank 'intermediary' space on the forms related only to who earned a commission; it did not show Stovicek played no role.

frigaliment.sentence: To bind a newcomer to a trade usage, Frigaliment needed to show actual knowledge or a sufficiently longstanding, notorious, universal, and reasonable practice to charge the seller with knowledge.
frigaliment.plain: To bind a newcomer to the trade to a "trade usage" (a special meaning used in the industry), Frigaliment needed to show "actual knowledge" of it. Or it had to show a practice so long-standing, "notorious" (widely known), universal, and reasonable that the seller is treated as knowing it.

frigaliment.sentence: The conflict prevented Frigaliment from proving the binding usage it alleged.
frigaliment.plain: The conflicting evidence prevented Frigaliment from proving the binding trade usage it "alleged," or claimed.

frigaliment.sentence: Friendly used the regulations as a contextual dictionary, particularly because government grading appeared in Frigaliment’s original cable.
frigaliment.plain: Friendly used the government "regulations" on chicken categories as a contextual dictionary, a guide to the word's meaning. That was especially fitting because Frigaliment's original cable referred to government grading.

frigaliment.sentence: His conclusion rested on at least an indirect contractual reference, without requiring wholesale incorporation of every regulatory detail.
frigaliment.plain: His conclusion rested on at least an indirect reference in the contract to those rules. It did not require "incorporation" of every "regulatory" detail, meaning treating all the rules as part of the contract.

frigaliment.sentence: Saying that 33 cents lay closer to the broiler price did not explain why the seller would intentionally accept a loss.
frigaliment.plain: Even if 33 cents was closer to the young-chicken price, it made no sense for the seller to agree to sell young chickens at a loss.

frigaliment.sentence: Friendly gave that conduct no interpretive weight because Frigaliment continued to demand contractual performance and reserve responsibility for costs.
frigaliment.plain: Friendly gave that conduct no weight in interpreting the contract, because Frigaliment kept demanding "contractual" performance, meaning what the contract promised. It also kept insisting the seller was responsible for the costs.

frigaliment.sentence: It might affect a disputed New York-versus-European damages measure if liability existed.
frigaliment.plain: That conduct might affect a disputed New York-versus-European "damages measure" (the method of calculating damages), but only if the seller were liable.

frigaliment.sentence: Friendly did not have to decide whether Frigaliment actually intended only young birds: the buyer bore the burden of proving that the contracts used the narrower meaning, and the whole record did not establish it.
frigaliment.plain: Friendly did not have to decide whether Frigaliment really meant only young birds. As the buyer suing, it "bore the burden" of proving the contracts used the narrower meaning, and "the whole record," all the evidence, did not establish it.

frigaliment.sentence: On December 27, 1960, Friendly directed judgment dismissing the complaint with costs.
frigaliment.plain: On December 27, 1960, Friendly "directed judgment" for the seller, dismissing the "complaint" (Frigaliment's lawsuit) and ordering Frigaliment to pay the court costs.

jacob-youngs.sentence: The builder declined, sought its final-payment certificate, and sued when the certificate was refused.
jacob-youngs.plain: The builder declined, asked for its "final-payment certificate" (the architect's approval needed to get the final payment), and sued when the certificate was refused.

jacob-youngs.sentence: The trial court excluded it and directed a verdict for Kent.
jacob-youngs.plain: The trial court excluded that evidence and "directed a verdict" for Kent, meaning the judge decided the case for him without letting the jury decide.

jacob-youngs.sentence: It regarded the evidence as supporting innocent subcontractor oversight rather than fraud or willful substitution and held that a trivial, innocent omission could be compensated without forfeiting the entire unpaid price.
jacob-youngs.plain: It saw the evidence as showing an innocent oversight by the subcontractor, not "fraud" or willful substitution. It held that a trivial, innocent omission could be paid for with money instead of "forfeiting," or losing, the entire unpaid price.

jacob-youngs.sentence: A contractual duty remained distinct from whether every departure defeated the owner’s counterperformance obligation.
jacob-youngs.plain: The builder's "contractual" duty to use Reading pipe still existed. The separate question was whether every departure defeated the owner's "counterperformance" obligation, his own duty in return, to pay.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Some promises were independent, others necessarily dependent, and others could condition payment when a departure was substantial but remain collateral when it was insignificant.
jacob-youngs.plain: Some promises were independent, owed regardless of the other side's performance; others were necessarily dependent. Others could be a "condition" of payment when a departure was substantial, but remain collateral, giving only a right to damages, when it was insignificant.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Presumed intention and justice in the particular transaction governed.
jacob-youngs.plain: Which kind a promise is depends on what the parties presumably intended and what is fair in the particular deal.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Construction becomes inseparable from land, making forfeiture more severe than rejection of a returnable chattel.
jacob-youngs.plain: Construction becomes inseparable from land, so "forfeiture" (losing all payment) is harsher than rejecting a returnable "chattel," a movable item that can be sent back.

jacob-youngs.sentence: The law hesitated to infer an intention that an innocent minor default cause vastly disproportionate loss.
jacob-youngs.plain: Courts are slow to assume the parties meant a small, innocent slip to cause a huge loss.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Doubtful factual inferences belonged to the factfinder; certain ones could be resolved judicially.
jacob-youngs.plain: Doubtful factual "inferences" (conclusions drawn from evidence) belonged to the "factfinder," usually the jury. Certain, clear ones could be resolved by the judge.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Apt and certain language could expressly make every term a condition of recovery, but that allocation was not the question here.
jacob-youngs.plain: Apt and certain language could expressly make every term a "condition of recovery," something that must be met before payment. But that kind of allocation was not at issue here.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Because the offered equivalence evidence could show an unintentional and insignificant deviation within the whole project, excluding it and directing a verdict were errors.
jacob-youngs.plain: The offered equivalence evidence, that the substitute pipe was just as good, could show an unintentional and insignificant deviation within the whole project. So excluding it and "directing a verdict" for Kent were errors.

jacob-youngs.sentence: But where that cost is grossly and unfairly disproportionate to its benefit, diminution in value supplies the allowance.
jacob-youngs.plain: But where the cost of fixing the work is grossly and unfairly out of proportion to its benefit, the owner gets the "diminution in value": the difference in value between the house as promised and as built.

jacob-youngs.sentence: The builder had not reached proof of a precise allowance because exclusion of substantial-performance evidence stopped that progression.
jacob-youngs.plain: The builder never reached proof of a precise allowance, the exact amount to deduct, because the trial court's exclusion of its "substantial-performance" evidence (that it had done essentially what was promised) stopped the case short.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Judge McLaughlin, joined by Judges Pound and Andrews, viewed the conduct as intentional or grossly negligent to equivalent effect.
jacob-youngs.plain: Judge McLaughlin, "joined by" Judges Pound and Andrews in dissent, viewed the builder's conduct as intentional. Or it was "grossly negligent" (extremely careless) to equivalent effect, meaning it should be treated the same as intentional.

jacob-youngs.sentence: Kent could choose a manufacturer even for personal preference, and equivalent utility could not replace the bargain.
jacob-youngs.plain: Kent was entitled to insist on Reading pipe even just because he preferred it; pipe that worked as well was not what he bargained for.

jacob-youngs.sentence: On January 25, 1921, the four-judge majority affirmed the Appellate Division’s order and directed judgment absolute for the builder under the appeal stipulation, with costs in all courts.
jacob-youngs.plain: On January 25, 1921, the four-judge majority affirmed the Appellate Division’s order (the lower appeals court's ruling). Under the "appeal stipulation," Kent's agreement that losing the appeal meant final judgment against him, it "directed judgment" absolute (final) for the builder, with costs in all courts.

jacob-youngs.sentence: For trivial innocent defects, that covenant, like the installation covenant, remained an independent, collateral obligation rather than a condition; the duty survived while the remedy was damages.
jacob-youngs.plain: For trivial innocent defects, the "covenant" (promise) to replace bad work, like the promise to install Reading pipe, was an independent, "collateral obligation" rather than a condition of payment. The duty survived, but the "remedy" for breaking it was damages.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Janas transmitted it by telex March 31 to PepsiCo’s broker, Welsch, referring to satisfactory factory inspection and a definitive contract.
klein-pepsico.plain: On March 31 Janas sent it by "telex" (a printed wire message) to Welsch, PepsiCo's "broker" or sales agent. The message referred to a satisfactory factory inspection and a "definitive contract," a final written agreement.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Kendall’s desire to retain the aircraft explained the withdrawal but did not decide whether the earlier conduct had already bound PepsiCo.
klein-pepsico.plain: Kendall wanting to keep the plane explains why PepsiCo backed out, but the legal question was whether PepsiCo was already bound by a contract before then.

klein-pepsico.sentence: After extensive findings, the district court concluded that UJS and PepsiCo had contracted for the $4.6 million sale and ordered specific performance.
klein-pepsico.plain: After extensive "findings" (factual conclusions), the district court concluded that UJS and PepsiCo had made a contract for the $4.6 million sale. It ordered specific performance, meaning PepsiCo had to actually deliver the jet.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Judge Ervin’s Fourth Circuit opinion reviewed findings for clear error, giving particular weight to credibility determinations supported by corroborating evidence.
klein-pepsico.plain: Judge Ervin’s Fourth Circuit opinion reviewed the findings only for clear error, overturning them only if clearly wrong. It gave special weight to "credibility determinations" (which witnesses to believe) backed by "corroborating evidence," evidence that confirms them.

klein-pepsico.sentence: The later writing could be a memorial rather than a condition of formation.
klein-pepsico.plain: The later writing could be a memorial, simply recording a deal already made, "rather than a condition" of formation that had to exist before any deal did.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Mere disagreement with that reading did not produce a firm conviction of mistake.
klein-pepsico.plain: PepsiCo's mere disagreement with the trial court's reading did not produce a "firm conviction of mistake," the appeals court's standard for overturning a factual finding.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Parties can condition formation on a signed document or withdraw while negotiations remain incomplete; PepsiCo failed to show clear error in finding these negotiations had already produced an agreement.
klein-pepsico.plain: Parties can make contract "formation" depend on a signed document, or withdraw while negotiations are incomplete. But PepsiCo failed to show "clear error" in the trial court's finding that these negotiations had already produced an agreement.

klein-pepsico.sentence: The district court found that PepsiCo’s agreement to repair satisfied the condition and alternatively that refusal to tender excused it.
klein-pepsico.plain: The district court found that PepsiCo's agreement to repair the engine satisfied the inspection condition. Alternatively, PepsiCo's refusal to "tender," or offer delivery of, the jet excused that condition.

klein-pepsico.sentence: A footnote also affirmed rejection of PepsiCo’s arguments about the statute of frauds, Klein’s intended-beneficiary status, and alleged rescission of the Klein–UJS agreement on the district court’s reasoning.
klein-pepsico.plain: A footnote also "affirmed" the rejection, on the district court’s reasoning, of three PepsiCo arguments. They concerned the "statute of frauds" (requiring a signed writing), Klein's "intended-beneficiary" status (as the person the deal was meant to benefit), and "alleged" cancellation, or rescission, of the Klein–UJS agreement.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Virginia’s Uniform Commercial Code § 2-716 permitted specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances, but retained the principle that an adequate damages remedy ordinarily made compelled performance inappropriate.
klein-pepsico.plain: Virginia’s Uniform Commercial Code § 2-716 allowed "specific performance," a court order to deliver, for unique goods or in other proper circumstances. But it kept the principle that adequate money damages ordinarily make compelled "performance" inappropriate.

klein-pepsico.sentence: The district court called the jet unique and relied on supposed inability to cover.
klein-pepsico.plain: The district court called the jet "unique," one of a kind, and relied on Klein's supposed inability to cover, meaning buy a substitute.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Reviewing the remedy for abuse of discretion, the Fourth Circuit found neither ground supported.
klein-pepsico.plain: "Reviewing" the remedy for "abuse of discretion," whether the trial court's choice was unreasonable, the Fourth Circuit found neither ground supported by the evidence.

klein-pepsico.sentence: Greater replacement expense could be compensated in damages.
klein-pepsico.plain: If a substitute plane cost more, money damages could cover the difference.

klein-pepsico.sentence: It separates formation from remedy: losing a no-contract argument does not automatically make forced delivery appropriate, and distinctiveness or higher replacement cost does not alone establish inadequacy of damages.
klein-pepsico.plain: The case separates contract "formation" from remedy. Losing a no-contract argument does not automatically make forced delivery appropriate, and an item's distinctiveness or higher "replacement cost" does not alone make money "damages" inadequate.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Congress assigned the Department of Justice (DOJ) standards and rulemaking.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: Congress gave the Department of Justice (DOJ) the job of issuing the accessibility standards and "rulemaking," the formal process of writing binding rules.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Standard 4.33.3 required integrated wheelchair areas, admission-price choice, comparable sightlines, companion seats, and multiple wheelchair locations for facilities above 300 seats.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: Standard 4.33.3 required "integrated wheelchair areas" (placed among other seats), a choice of admission prices, and "comparable sightlines," views as good as others'. It also required companion seats and, in facilities above 300 seats, multiple wheelchair locations.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: DOJ proposed adopting the Board’s standards and directed comments there.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The Justice Department proposed to adopt the Board's standards as its own and told the public to send comments to the Board.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: DOJ issued identical language the same day but did not adopt that explanation.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The Justice Department issued the same wording that day but did not adopt the Board's statement that standing spectators would be dealt with later.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: In December 1994 it published a technical-manual supplement without notice and comment expressly requiring views over spectators expected to stand.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: In December 1994 DOJ published a "technical-manual supplement," a guidance document, without notice and comment (first inviting public input). It expressly required that wheelchair users be able to see over spectators expected to stand.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: DOJ declined repeated invitations to intervene, appeared as amicus, and was denied a second amicus submission.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: DOJ declined repeated invitations to "intervene," or join the case as a party. It appeared as an "amicus" (a friend of the court filing an outside brief) and was denied permission to file a second amicus brief.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: The judge accepted DOJ’s interpretation but permitted substantial compliance given uneven agency enforcement, competing practical requirements, and owners’ good faith.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The judge accepted DOJ’s interpretation but permitted "substantial compliance," meeting the requirement in most but not all respects. The reasons were uneven "agency" enforcement, competing practical requirements, and the owners' good faith.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: The owners argued that comparable sightlines addressed distribution alone, alternatively sought independent judicial interpretation, and claimed an unauthorized new or changed substantive rule.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The owners argued that "comparable sightlines" concerned only spreading wheelchair spaces around, or else that the court should interpret the standard itself.
