They also claimed the guidance was an unauthorized new or changed "substantive rule," a binding rule needing public comment.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: An unobstructed view naturally supplied additional content.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: Read naturally, 'comparable sightlines' adds a requirement of a view that is not blocked.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Applying 1997 deference precedents, the panel sustained a permissible agency interpretation unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: Applying the 1997 "deference" precedents (rules on accepting agency views), the panel "sustained," or upheld, the agency's permissible reading of its own regulation. It would do so unless the reading was "plainly erroneous" or inconsistent with the regulation.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: It acknowledged incentives for vague rules but treated Administrative Procedure Act (APA) procedure as a constraint against publishing empty generalities and adding the actual law later.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The court admitted deference could tempt agencies to write vague rules. But it treated Administrative Procedure Act (APA) procedure as barring an agency from publishing empty generalities and adding the actual law later without public comment.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: The panel distinguished procedural limits from constitutional nondelegation and considered beneficiaries’ interests as well as regulated parties’ reliance.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The panel separated procedural limits from constitutional "nondelegation," the rule against Congress handing away lawmaking power. It weighed the "beneficiaries’" interests, here disabled spectators, as well as the reliance of "regulated" parties, the owners.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: DOJ’s statutory administrative responsibility, not special insight into drafting, supported deference after adopting the Board’s language.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: DOJ’s "statutory" responsibility for administering the law, given by Congress, supported deference, not special insight into drafting. It had adopted the Board's language rather than writing the words itself.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: It had rulemaking duties and a congressional mandate for technical manuals despite lacking administrative adjudication and enforcing through courts.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: DOJ had "rulemaking" duties and a congressional mandate to issue "technical manuals," even though it lacked "administrative adjudication" (deciding cases itself) and enforced the law by suing in court.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: The panel stated that fundamentally changing a definitive regulatory interpretation required notice and comment, unlike then-recognized flexibility to revise statutory interpretations under Chevron.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The panel said fundamentally changing a definitive reading of an agency's own regulation required notice and comment. That differed from the then-recognized freedom to revise "statutory interpretations" (readings of statutes) under Chevron.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Owners also knew the manual before choosing plans, defeating their claimed detrimental reliance.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The owners also knew of the manual before choosing their plans, which defeated their claim of "detrimental reliance," being harmed by relying on an earlier view.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Guidance explaining a duty fairly included in an existing regulation differed from a requirement with independent force of law.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: Guidance explaining a duty fairly included in an existing regulation differed from a requirement with its own independent "force of law," meaning binding effect.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Close textual connection supported interpretive status, whereas supplying real substance to an empty norm pointed the other way.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: A close tie to the regulation's text supported "interpretive status," being treated as an interpretation rather than a new rule. Supplying real content to an empty standard pointed the other way.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: Comparable sightlines already supplied an arguable enforcement basis.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The standard's 'comparable sightlines' wording already arguably required views over standing fans.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: This classification rationale remained separate from the panel’s interpretation-change doctrine, later rejected by the Supreme Court.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: This reasoning on classifying the guidance as interpretive stayed separate from the panel’s interpretation-change doctrine, its rule about changing interpretations. The Supreme Court later rejected that doctrine.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: The panel questioned deference to that litigation refinement but independently upheld discretion to reject the additional brief.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The panel doubted that the refined position DOJ took in litigation deserved deference. But it independently upheld the trial judge's "discretion," or judgment, to reject the additional brief.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: This was private equitable litigation, not direct review of an agency order.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: This was private "equitable" litigation, a private suit seeking a court order rather than money. It was not direct "review" of an agency order.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: The district judge could shape relief within the regulation’s and manual’s latitude, and an appellate amicus filing did not enlarge the plaintiffs’ entitlement.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: The "district judge" (trial judge) could shape "relief," the remedy, within the room the regulation and manual allowed. An "appellate" amicus brief, filed on appeal, did not enlarge what the plaintiffs were entitled to.

lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.sentence: In 2015, Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association rejected requiring notice and comment merely because an agency significantly changes a genuinely interpretive rule, while leaving the interpretive-versus-legislative distinction intact.
lrs-n-paralyzed-veterans.plain: In 2015, in Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association, the Supreme Court rejected requiring notice and comment merely because an agency significantly changes a genuinely interpretive rule. It left intact the line between interpretive rules and legislative ones, which bind like statutes.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: A five-member commission would select and survey land: three civilians appointed by the President with Senate consent, plus the already presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed Army Chief of Engineers and District Engineer Commissioner.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: A five-member commission would select and survey the land. It had three civilians appointed by the President with "Senate consent" (approval), plus two officers already appointed by the President and Senate-confirmed: the Army Chief of Engineers and the District Engineer Commissioner.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: If agreement failed, the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia appointed three competent, disinterested appraisers.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: If no agreement was reached, the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia (then the District's trial court) appointed three competent, "disinterested" appraisers, meaning neutral experts with no stake, to value the land.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Payment, or judicial deposit if an owner refused payment, completed transfer.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Paying the owner, or depositing the money with the court if the owner refused it, transferred the land to the government.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Separate provisions permitted assessments on specially benefited nearby property, with notice and review.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Separate provisions allowed "assessments," special charges, on nearby property that specially benefited from the park, with notice and a chance for review.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Pierce Shoemaker died afterward; heirs and devisees were substituted, and his executors challenged the process.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Pierce Shoemaker died afterward. His "heirs" and devisees (those inheriting his land by law or by will) were "substituted," replacing him in the case, and his "executors," the managers of his estate, challenged the process.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Immediate review attempts failed because the ruling was interlocutory.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Efforts to appeal right away failed because the ruling did not end the case.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Appraisers heard evidence and reported in December 1891; the court overruled exceptions and confirmed values.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The "appraisers" (the court-appointed valuation experts) heard evidence and reported in December 1891. The court "overruled exceptions," meaning it rejected the owners' formal objections, and confirmed the values.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Its July 16, 1892 final decree vested fee-simple title in the United States and directed possession.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Its July 16, 1892 "final decree" (the court's last order) vested fee-simple "title," meaning full ownership, in the United States and directed that possession be handed over.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: The owners then obtained a writ of error bringing both the final taking and preserved earlier objections before the U.S. Supreme Court.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The owners then obtained a "writ of error," the old way of bringing a case to a higher court for review. It brought both the final taking and their "preserved" earlier objections, ones properly raised below, before the U.S. Supreme Court.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: The owners argued that because the three civilians were officers requiring nomination and confirmation, the two engineer commissioners likewise required new appointments; Congress could create but not fill offices.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The owners argued that since the civilian commissioners were federal officers needing presidential appointment and Senate approval, so were the two engineers; Congress may create offices but may not fill them by naming who serves.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Congress could enlarge those offices with germane responsibilities without repeating nomination, confirmation and appointment.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Congress may add related duties to an existing office without the officer having to be appointed and confirmed all over again.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: These park functions were not dissimilar to or outside the sphere of the officers’ existing duties, even though the military/civil line might sometimes be difficult.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The park work fit within the kind of work the engineers already did, even if the line between military and civilian duties could sometimes be hard to draw.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Courts could test that classification; the land quantity then fell to legislative discretion subject to compensation.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Courts could test whether a use is truly public. Once it is, how much land to take is left to legislative "discretion," Congress's judgment, as long as owners are paid compensation.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Congress’s exclusive District legislation combined national and municipal authority.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Under the Constitution's grant of "exclusive District legislation," Congress had full lawmaking power over the District of Columbia. It acted there both as the national government and as the city government.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Maryland’s cession proviso preserving private property prevented treating cession itself as a transfer of all private land.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: In its "cession," or handover, of land for the District, Maryland included a proviso preserving private property. So the cession itself could not be treated as transferring all private land to the United States.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Read with the grant of full jurisdiction, it did not surrender the power of later compensated public acquisition.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: But read together with the grant of full "jurisdiction," or governing power, that proviso did not give up the power to acquire private land later for public use with compensation.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Presidential approval did not adjudicate an owner’s entitlement.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The President's approval did not "adjudicate," or legally decide, what an owner was entitled to.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Likewise, the appropriation capped total expenditure rather than depressing individual valuation.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Likewise, the "appropriation," the money Congress set aside, capped total spending rather than lowering any individual owner's valuation.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Reducing the acquisition when the full map exceeded funds was permissible; the initial map facilitated negotiation without irrevocably committing every tract.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Taking less land when the original plan cost too much was allowed; the first map was a basis for negotiating, not a binding commitment to take every parcel.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: The Court recognized power to charge proportionate costs to specially benefited property, but declined extended review because no specific error was assigned, no special request had been made below and no appellant was shown actually assessed.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The Court recognized power to charge "proportionate" costs (a fair share) to "specially benefited" property, land that gained value from the park. But it declined extended review because no "specific error was assigned" (pointed out), no special request had been made below, and no "appellant" (owner appealing) was shown to have actually been assessed.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Their oath required faithful, just and impartial valuation by their best skill and judgment, not disregard of evidence.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The appraisers' oath required faithful, just and "impartial" (unbiased) valuation using their best skill and judgment. It did not permit ignoring the evidence.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: The Court approved present cash-market-value instructions excluding speculative enhancement from the park project.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The Court approved instructions to use present cash market value, what the land would sell for now. They excluded "speculative enhancement," any guessed-at rise in value caused by the park project itself.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Disagreement among witnesses or dissatisfaction with the amount did not transfer the appraisers’ function to judges; gross error indicating prejudice, corruption or plain mistake remained reviewable.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Disagreement among witnesses or an owner's dissatisfaction with the amount did not shift the appraisers' job to judges. But gross error showing prejudice, corruption or plain mistake remained "reviewable," meaning a court could correct it.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Proprietary patents expressly reserved royal mines; Maryland’s Revolutionary confiscation and cession then carried public property to the United States.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The proprietary "patents," the original colonial land grants, expressly reserved "royal mines" (gold and silver mines) for the grantors. Maryland's Revolutionary "confiscation" (seizure) of those rights and its later cession then carried that public property to the United States.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: This specific chain differed from the ordinary rule that land ownership includes unreserved minerals.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Normally, owning land includes the minerals under it unless they were held back; here they had been.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: A 1760 patent without a reservation did not supersede the accepted, inconsistent 1772 resurvey grant containing one.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: A 1760 "patent" (land grant) without a mine reservation did not override the later, inconsistent 1772 "resurvey grant," a replacement grant after remeasuring the land. The owner had accepted that grant, and it contained the reservation.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Acceptance surrendered the earlier title between grantor and grantee, though older papers could matter to third-party priorities.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: "Acceptance" of the new grant gave up the earlier "title" (ownership) as between the grantor, the colony's proprietor, and the "grantee," the landowner. But older papers could still matter to "third-party priorities," meaning which outside claimant ranks first.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: A later deed of a confiscated cotenant’s interest transferred that interest, not separately reserved mines.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: A later "deed" (a transfer document) of a "confiscated" cotenant's (co-owner's) share passed only that share. It did not pass the separately "reserved" mine rights.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Maryland could not convey former public property after its 1791 cession; an 1800 warrant and 1803 patent supplied no alternative mineral title.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: After its 1791 "cession" (handover) of the land, Maryland could not "convey," or transfer, former public property. So an 1800 warrant and an 1803 "patent" (land grant) gave no one an alternative "title" to the minerals.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Preservation of private-right law and judgments did not preserve Maryland’s power over ceded public land.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Keeping Maryland's private-rights law and existing "judgments" (court decisions) in force did not keep Maryland's power over the public land it had "ceded," or handed over.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Filing had not deprived the owners of possession; they continued receiving rents, issues and profits while compensation was fixed.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Filing the map had not taken possession from the owners. They kept receiving the "rents, issues and profits," all the land's income, while compensation was being fixed, so no interest was owed for that period.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: Delay inconvenience was presumed reflected in the award.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: Any inconvenience from the delay was assumed to be included in the price awarded.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: There was no interest agreement or failure to pay an already due assessment, and deposit equaled payment when owners declined it.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: There was no agreement to pay interest and no failure to pay an "assessment" (an amount already fixed and due). Depositing the money with the court counted as payment when owners refused to take it.

lrs-s-shoemaker.sentence: The lengthy adopted mineral-title decisions remain lower-court reasoning expressly accepted by the Court, not additional Supreme Court opinions.
lrs-s-shoemaker.plain: The long lower-court rulings on who owned the mines remain lower-court reasoning that the Supreme Court adopted, not separate Supreme Court opinions.

trident.sentence: Sophisticated parties negotiated detailed documents at arm’s length from approximately equal bargaining positions.
trident.plain: Sophisticated parties, experienced businesses with roughly equal bargaining power, negotiated the detailed loan documents at "arm’s length," meaning each side bargained independently for itself.

trident.sentence: A default during the first twelve years gave Connecticut General the option to accelerate and charge a ten-percent prepayment fee.
trident.plain: A default (breaking the loan terms) during the first twelve years gave Connecticut General the option to accelerate, or demand the whole loan at once. It could also charge a ten-percent "prepayment fee" for the early payoff.

trident.sentence: The district court dismissed the complaint and, on its own initiative, sanctioned Trident for a supposedly frivolous action.
trident.plain: The "district court" (trial court) dismissed the "complaint," Trident's suit. On its own initiative, it also "sanctioned," or penalized, Trident for supposedly bringing a "frivolous" (legally baseless) action.

trident.sentence: Judge Kozinski, writing for a Ninth Circuit panel with Judges Hug and Alarcon, rejected Trident’s argument that the default fee offered an alternative form of performance.
trident.plain: Judge Kozinski, writing for a Ninth Circuit panel with Judges Hug and Alarcon, rejected Trident's argument that the default fee offered an alternative form of "performance," simply another permitted way of paying off the loan.

trident.sentence: That construction would let the default provision swallow the express twelve-year prepayment prohibition.
trident.plain: That reading would let the "default provision" (the clause on what happens if Trident breaks the terms) swallow the express twelve-year ban on "prepayment," or paying early.

trident.sentence: The documents instead gave the lender alone the acceleration election.
trident.plain: The documents instead gave the lender alone the "acceleration" election, the choice to demand full early repayment.

trident.sentence: Trident could stop paying but could not force acceleration and its preferred payoff.
trident.plain: Trident could stop paying, but it could not force "acceleration" (the lender calling in the whole loan) so that it could pay off the loan on its preferred terms.

trident.sentence: Whether a ten-percent fee might be an unenforceable penalty for a particular default was unsettled under California law.
trident.plain: California law was unclear whether a 10 percent fee for some defaults might be an unenforceable penalty.

trident.sentence: Possible invalidity did not create a borrower’s option.
trident.plain: The fee's possible "invalidity," meaning it might be unenforceable, did not create an option for the borrower to pay early.

trident.sentence: Nor did California’s one-form-of-action rule force the lender to accelerate and foreclose: it could decline a remedy, and some nonjudicial steps, including enforcing an absolute rent assignment by notice to tenants, were available.
trident.plain: Nor did California's "one-form-of-action rule," limiting a lender to one lawsuit to collect a secured debt, force the lender to accelerate and "foreclose" (take the property). It could decline a remedy, and "nonjudicial steps" were available, such as enforcing an "absolute rent assignment" by telling tenants to pay rent directly to it.

trident.sentence: Those consequences helped enforce the agreed term and could not be judicially removed to make refinancing cost-free apart from the chosen fee.
trident.plain: Those harsh consequences of defaulting help enforce the no-early-payment promise, and a court would not remove them so that Trident could refinance for just the fee.

trident.sentence: The interest-rate risk was reciprocal: rising rates could have made this long loan disadvantageous to Connecticut General.
trident.plain: The interest-rate risk was reciprocal, running both ways. Had rates risen, this long loan could have become a bad deal for Connecticut General.

trident.sentence: The panel found no facial ambiguity supplying the claimed prepayment right.
trident.plain: The panel found no facial "ambiguity," no unclearness on the documents' face, that would supply the claimed right of "prepayment," paying early.

trident.sentence: Under the traditional rule it described, an unambiguous integrated agreement would exclude evidence offered to change that result.
trident.plain: Under the traditional rule it described, an "unambiguous" (clear) integrated agreement, a final written contract, would exclude outside evidence offered to change that result.

trident.sentence: But Pacific Gas & Electric, the governing California interpretation precedent, required preliminary consideration of evidence relevant to the parties’ meaning instead of treating facial clarity as conclusive.
trident.plain: But Pacific Gas & Electric, the governing California "precedent" on interpretation, required judges first to consider evidence relevant to what the parties meant. It rejected treating "facial clarity," words that seem clear on their face, as conclusive.

trident.sentence: The Ninth Circuit understood it to require an opportunity to develop evidence capable of exposing ambiguity even in these extensively negotiated documents.
trident.plain: The Ninth Circuit read it as requiring a chance to develop evidence that could expose "ambiguity" (unclearness) even in these extensively negotiated documents.

trident.sentence: Under Erie, the principle requiring federal courts to follow applicable state substantive law, the panel had to apply California’s approach rather than its preferred traditional one.
trident.plain: Under Erie, the principle requiring federal courts to follow applicable state "substantive law" (the rules on rights and duties), the panel had to apply California's approach. It did so even though it preferred the traditional one.

trident.sentence: After discovery, Connecticut General could seek summary judgment and would prevail unless Trident produced sufficient outside evidence to make its proposed meaning reasonably susceptible and create a genuine factual dispute.
trident.plain: After "discovery" (gathering evidence), Connecticut General could seek "summary judgment," a ruling without trial. It would win unless Trident found enough outside evidence to make the words "reasonably susceptible" to its meaning, creating a "genuine factual dispute."

trident.sentence: Trident also sought rescission for an alleged unilateral mistake of law that Connecticut General supposedly knew about and failed to correct.
trident.plain: Trident also sought "rescission," undoing the contract, for an "alleged" unilateral mistake of law: its own misunderstanding of the terms' legal effect. It claimed Connecticut General knew about the mistake and failed to correct it.

trident.sentence: The panel regarded that allegation as implausible but sufficient to state a California claim under the cited statutes.
trident.plain: The panel saw that "allegation" (claim) as implausible but enough to state a California claim under the cited "statutes," the state laws Trident relied on.

trident.sentence: The district court’s Rule 11 rationale was that no reasonable person, especially capable lawyers, could misunderstand the documents, so the suit must have been brought in bad faith.
trident.plain: The district court’s Rule 11 reasoning (the rule allowing penalties for improper filings) was that no reasonable person, especially capable lawyers, could misunderstand the documents. So, it concluded, the suit must have been brought in "bad faith," meaning dishonestly.

trident.sentence: Yet an interpretation without an objectively reasonable factual basis could still support sanctions under Pacific Gas.
trident.plain: Yet an interpretation with no objectively reasonable factual basis could still support "sanctions," court-imposed penalties, even under Pacific Gas.

trident.sentence: The court also reserved the scope of the note’s attorney-fee provision, under which fees apparently had been awarded.
trident.plain: The court also "reserved," or left undecided, how far the note's "attorney-fee" provision (its clause on paying lawyers' fees) reached. Fees apparently had been "awarded" under it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: The merchants asserted Sherman Act tying and sought Clayton Act treble damages; no violation had been adjudicated.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The merchants claimed illegal tying under the Sherman Act, the main antitrust law: American Express allegedly forced them to take its credit cards as a condition of taking its charge cards. They sought treble (triple) damages under the Clayton Act, but no violation had been "adjudicated," or found by a court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: The merchants said that disparity made individual pursuit irrational and defeated effective vindication of federal rights.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The merchants said that cost gap made it irrational for any one merchant to sue alone, since proving the claim would cost far more than it could win. They argued this defeated "effective vindication" of federal rights, meaning the practical ability to enforce them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: After the Supreme Court vacated in light of Stolt-Nielsen’s prohibition on unagreed class arbitration, the circuit adhered to its result, saying it had not ordered a class proceeding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The Supreme Court "vacated" (set aside) the ruling for reconsideration under Stolt-Nielsen, which bars class arbitration the parties never agreed to. The Second Circuit "adhered" to, or kept, its result, saying it had not "ordered" a class proceeding.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: It reconsidered again after Concepcion but distinguished that state-preemption decision from effective vindication of federal rights.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The Second Circuit reconsidered again after Concepcion, which held the arbitration statute overrides state rules refusing to enforce class waivers. But it said that decision was about state-law preemption, unlike "effective vindication" of federal rights, the practical ability to enforce them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: Justice Scalia, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, emphasized Federal Arbitration Act enforcement of agreed parties and procedures, including federal statutory claims absent a contrary congressional command.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: Justice Scalia, "joined by" Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, stressed that the Federal Arbitration Act requires enforcing arbitration agreements as written, including the agreed "parties" and procedures. That covers federal "statutory" claims too, unless Congress has commanded otherwise.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: The statutes predated Rule 23, and congressional approval of that rule did not guarantee aggregation whenever financially necessary; Eisen had not excused notice expenses simply because they frustrated an antitrust plaintiff.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The antitrust "statutes" predated Rule 23, the class-action rule, and Congress's approval of that rule did not guarantee group suits whenever going alone is too expensive. In Eisen, the Court had not "excused" class-notice costs simply because they frustrated an antitrust plaintiff.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: The Court described Mitsubishi’s effective-vindication discussion as dictum while recognizing its concern with prospective waiver of statutory remedies.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The Court called Mitsubishi's effective-vindication discussion "dictum," a side remark that is not binding. But it recognized that case's concern with "prospective waiver," giving up federal statutory remedies in advance.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: Expressly barring a statutory right, or perhaps filing and administrative fees making forum access impracticable, presented different questions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: A clause expressly barring a "statutory" right, or perhaps filing and administrative fees so high that reaching the "forum" (the arbitration itself) is impractical, would present different questions. Those were not before the Court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: It distinguished potential impossibility of individual proof from loss of aggregation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: The Court said not being allowed to join with others is different from being unable to bring a claim at all. Losing the cost-sharing of a group case did not mean the merchants could not pursue their own claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: Thomas joined fully but separately read the FAA contract-revocation exception as limited to formation defects such as fraud or duress.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: Justice Thomas "joined" the majority fully but wrote separately. He read the FAA (Federal Arbitration Act) exception for grounds to revoke a contract as limited to "formation defects," problems in how the agreement was made, such as fraud or duress (coercion).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: Justice Kagan, joined by Ginsburg and Breyer, treated indirect foreclosure like express waiver.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: Justice Kagan, "joined by" Ginsburg and Breyer in dissent, treated "indirect foreclosure," making a federal claim impossible to bring in practice, the same as an express "waiver" that openly bans it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.sentence: Five Justices joined, three dissented, and Sotomayor did not participate; the mandate did not expressly add a remand.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-365.plain: Five Justices joined the majority, three dissented, and Justice Sotomayor "did not participate" (sat out). The mandate, the Court's official order, did not expressly add a "remand" sending the case back for more proceedings.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: The Illinois Appellate Court ordered Treister’s complaint dismissed because membership was not an economic necessity; the state supreme court denied review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: The Illinois Appellate Court ordered Treister’s "complaint" (his state lawsuit) dismissed because Academy membership was not an economic necessity for him, which Illinois required before courts would review such decisions. The state supreme court "denied review," declining to hear his appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: The district court denied claim-preclusion dismissal and initially refused interlocutory certification.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: The "district court" (federal trial court) refused to dismiss the suit based on claim preclusion, the rule that earlier judgments already settled the matter. It also at first refused "interlocutory certification," permission to appeal that ruling before the case ended.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: The Academy refused even after a confidentiality-protected production order, and the district court imposed criminal contempt and a $10,000 fine.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: The Academy refused to hand over its files even after a "production order" with confidentiality protections. So the "district court" held it in criminal contempt, a punishment for disobeying a court, and fined it $10,000.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Before the second en banc hearing, a newly assigned district judge certified the denial of dismissal under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(b).
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Before the second "en banc" hearing (by the full appeals court), a newly assigned "district judge" certified the refusal to dismiss under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(b). That statute allows early appeals of key legal questions.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: The pending collateral contempt appeal had not stripped the district court of authority over the underlying suit; criminal contempt itself was a final appealable judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: The pending appeal of the collateral (side) contempt ruling had not taken the main suit away from the "district court." Criminal contempt itself was a final "appealable" judgment, one that could be appealed on its own.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Here contempt supplied a route to review, with sanctions remaining if the order proved valid.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Ordinary discovery orders usually cannot be appealed right away. Here contempt supplied a route to review, but the "sanctions" (penalties) would remain if the order proved valid.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Posner treated the order as falling with the precluded action but did not use contempt to reach the entire lawsuit’s merits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Judge Posner reasoned that because the whole lawsuit was barred by the earlier state cases, the discovery order fell with it. But the lawsuit itself was reviewed through the separate early appeal, not through the contempt appeal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Production authority under Rule 37 operated alongside then-existing Rule 26 protection and sequencing powers.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: "Production" authority under Rule 37, the power to order and enforce discovery, operated alongside then-existing Rule 26 powers. Those let judges protect sensitive material and set the order in which things are produced.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: The Academy’s First Amendment claim did not create categorical immunity, but candid membership evaluations and professional exchanges implicated association.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: The Academy’s First Amendment claim did not create categorical "immunity," a complete shield from discovery. But candid membership evaluations and professional exchanges implicated freedom of "association," the right to join with others, so they deserved careful handling.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Accepting exclusive federal Sherman Act jurisdiction while questioning its rationale, he viewed differences in treble damages as practically immaterial.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Judge Posner accepted exclusive federal Sherman Act jurisdiction, meaning only federal courts hear those claims, while questioning its rationale. He viewed differences in "treble damages" (triple damages) as practically "immaterial," not mattering here.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: His reading of section 1738 permitted greater preclusion than the rendering state might give without first resolving Illinois law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: His reading of section 1738, which tells federal courts to give state judgments the effect they have in that state, allowed greater "preclusion" (barring of later suits). It allowed more than the "rendering state," Illinois, whose courts issued the judgment, might give, without first resolving Illinois law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Cudahy characterized it as a plurality, and Flaum supported dismissal through a different rule calling for substantially contemporaneous litigation of related state and exclusively federal theories.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Judge Cudahy characterized Posner's opinion as a "plurality," one speaking for less than a majority. Judge Flaum supported dismissal under a different rule: related state claims and "exclusively federal" theories, ones only federal courts can hear, must be litigated at substantially the same time.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: He would sustain contempt despite reversal of the underlying order because the court had jurisdiction and preclusion was a defense.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Judge Wood would "sustain," or uphold, the contempt despite "reversal" of the underlying discovery order. In his view the court had "jurisdiction" (power over the case) when it issued the order, and preclusion was only a defense to raise, not a reason to disobey.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: Section 1738 required the rendering state’s rules, not an invented stronger federal bar.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: Judge Cudahy said Section 1738 required applying the preclusion rules of the "rendering state," the state whose court issued the judgment, here Illinois. It did not allow an invented, stronger federal bar.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: In No. 83-2683 it reversed denial of the Academy’s motion and directed dismissal of the complaint with prejudice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: In No. 83-2683, the second appeal, the court "reversed" the denial of the Academy’s "motion" to dismiss. It directed dismissal of the "complaint" with prejudice, meaning permanently, so it could not be refiled.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.sentence: The Supreme Court later reversed at 470 U.S. 373 (1985) on other grounds.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-368.plain: The Supreme Court later "reversed" this decision, reported at 470 U.S. 373 (1985), "on other grounds," meaning for reasons different from the ones this court relied on. So this court's approach should not be treated as current law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Merck withdrew the application and used changes-being-effected procedures for the adverse-reaction addition, without the disputed precautions text.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: Merck withdrew its application and used "changes-being-effected" procedures, which let a drug maker make certain label changes right away, before FDA approval. It added the adverse-reaction (side-effect) mention without the disputed precautions text FDA had questioned.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: More than 500 users with atypical fractures between 1999 and 2010 filed separate diversity actions under state warning law.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: More than 500 users who suffered atypical (unusual) thigh fractures between 1999 and 2010 filed separate "diversity actions" under state warning law. These were federal suits allowed because the parties were from different states.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Merck conceded that changes-being-effected rules permitted an attempted warning before 2010 but argued FDA would reject it, relying particularly on the 2008 proposal’s rejection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: Merck conceded that "changes-being-effected" rules let it try to add a warning on its own before 2010. But it argued FDA would have rejected it, relying especially on FDA's rejection of its 2008 proposal.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: The district court granted summary judgment for impossibility preemption.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: The "district court" granted summary judgment, ruling for Merck without trial, based on "impossibility preemption." That doctrine says federal law overrides state claims when a company cannot obey both the state duty and federal requirements.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: The Third Circuit vacated, reading Wyeth v. Levine’s clear-evidence language as an elevated probability burden requiring a factfinder to find rejection highly probable, and assigned that question to a jury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: The Third Circuit "vacated" (threw out) that ruling. It read Wyeth v. Levine’s "clear-evidence" language as a heightened burden requiring a "factfinder" to find FDA rejection highly probable, and it assigned that question to a jury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Justice Breyer’s six-Justice opinion explained that, in a Wyeth-type case, the manufacturer must show it fully informed FDA of the justification for the state-required warning and FDA said that adequate warning would not be approved.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: Justice Breyer’s "opinion" for six Justices explained what a manufacturer must show in a Wyeth-type case. It must prove it fully informed FDA of the reasons for the state-required warning, and that FDA said it would not approve that adequate warning.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: The Court assumed, without deciding, adequate evidence of a state violation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: For argument's sake, the Court assumed there was enough "evidence" that Merck broke state warning law, without actually deciding that question.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Clear evidence was not recast as preponderance, clear-and-convincing proof, or another factual likelihood threshold.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: The Court refused to turn "clear evidence" into a test of how likely a fact is, such as a "preponderance" (more likely than not), "clear-and-convincing proof," or any similar factual threshold. It is a legal question instead.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: The question was irreconcilable legal requirements, not predicted possible rejection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: What matters is whether federal and state law actually conflicted, so Merck could not obey both, not guesses about whether FDA might have said no.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Agency action had to operate within delegated authority and carry legal force, such as rulemaking or formal label rejection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: Only "agency action" with real legal force counts, and the FDA must act within its "delegated authority" (the power Congress gave it). Examples are "rulemaking" (issuing formal rules) or formally rejecting a label change; informal remarks do not count.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: The Court compared Markman and confession-voluntariness analysis rather than sending isolated brute facts to a jury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: The Court compared this to other mixed questions judges decide, like interpreting a patent's words under Markman v. Westview or judging whether a confession was voluntary. Judges, not juries, decide this, rather than handing a jury isolated "brute facts" (raw historical facts).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Justice Thomas joined Breyer and separately preferred logical contradiction over a physical-impossibility formulation.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: Justice Thomas "joined" Justice Breyer's majority opinion, meaning he signed on to it. He also wrote separately that preemption should turn on whether federal and state law logically contradict each other, not on whether obeying both is physically impossible.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: Justice Alito, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh, concurred in judgment and judicial allocation but questioned parts of the account.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: Justice Alito, "joined by" Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh, "concurred in judgment," meaning they agreed with the result but not all the reasoning. They agreed judges should decide this question but questioned parts of the majority's account.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.sentence: The Court neither reinstated Merck’s summary judgment nor decided warning liability.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-421.plain: The Court neither "reinstated" (restored) Merck's "summary judgment," its pretrial win without a trial, nor decided "warning liability," whether Merck is legally responsible for an inadequate warning. The lower courts must apply the clarified rule.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Eramo alleged ignored warning signs; the magazine, Erdely, and Wenner Media denied negligence, actual malice, and advance knowledge that Jackie was unreliable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: Eramo "alleged" (claimed, not yet proven) that the magazine ignored warning signs. The magazine, Erdely, and Wenner Media denied "negligence" (carelessness), denied "actual malice" (knowing or reckless falsity), and denied knowing in advance that Jackie was unreliable.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Eramo sued the publishing defendants and reporter in state court May 12, 2015; they removed May 29.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: Eramo sued the publishing defendants and the reporter in state court on May 12, 2015. On May 29 they "removed" the case, meaning they used their right to move it to federal court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: She served Jackie with a Rule 45 subpoena July 27.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: On July 27, Eramo served Jackie, who was not a party to the lawsuit, with a "Rule 45 subpoena." Rule 45 is the federal rule that lets a party formally demand documents from a nonparty.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: After unsuccessful negotiations, Eramo moved to compel in the Eastern District of Virginia, and the motion transferred December 9 to the Western District.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: When negotiations failed, Eramo "moved to compel" in the Eastern District of Virginia, asking that court to order Jackie to comply. On December 9 the "motion" was transferred to the Western District of Virginia, which was handling the main lawsuit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Jackie invoked Federal Rule of Evidence 412, relevance, burden, and a patient-counselor privilege.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: Jackie invoked "Federal Rule of Evidence 412," the rape-shield rule that protects alleged victims' sexual history. She also argued the material was irrelevant, too burdensome to produce, and covered by a "patient-counselor privilege" keeping her counseling talks confidential.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Chief Judge Glen Conrad applied amended Rule 26(b)(1), requiring relevant, nonprivileged, proportionate discovery without demanding trial admissibility.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: Chief Judge Glen Conrad, the court's senior judge, applied "amended" (recently revised) Rule 26(b)(1). It allows discovery that is "relevant" to the case, not privileged, and proportionate to its needs, without requiring "admissibility," meaning usable as evidence at trial.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: A prima facie discovery showing required a supported answer from the resisting person about relevance or harm; the requesting party did not have to address every proportionality factor automatically.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: Once Eramo made a "prima facie" showing (a basic, on-its-face case) that her requests were relevant, Jackie had to give a supported answer about irrelevance or harm. Eramo did not have to address every proportionality factor automatically.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Rule 26 still limited cumulative, duplicative, excessive, or otherwise out-of-scope requests, and Rule 45 protected a nonparty against significant compliance expense.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: "Rule 26" still limits requests that are "cumulative" (piling on the same material), duplicative, excessive, or otherwise out of scope. "Rule 45" protects a "nonparty," someone outside the lawsuit like Jackie, from significant costs of complying.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Rule 412 generally restricts evidence of an alleged victim’s other sexual behavior or predisposition, using a demanding civil admissibility balance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: "Rule 412," the rape-shield rule, generally keeps out evidence of an alleged victim's other sexual behavior or predisposition. In civil cases it sets a demanding test for "admissibility": the evidence's value must substantially outweigh harm to the victim and unfair prejudice to any party.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Thus rejecting a categorical Rule 412 bar preserved privacy scrutiny rather than making all sexual detail discoverable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: So the court rejected a categorical Rule 412 bar, meaning a total ban on discovery of such material, but still scrutinized privacy closely. Rejecting the ban did not make all sexual detail "discoverable" (obtainable in pretrial discovery).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: It added only conditionally that voluntary disclosure to defendants might waive such a privilege if it existed; it did not declare every possible privilege waived.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: The court added only conditionally that if a counselor privilege existed, Jackie might have "waived" (given up) it by voluntarily sharing the information with the defendants. It did not declare every possible privilege waived.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: On January 25, 2016, the court granted Demands 1, 2, 6, 12, and 18, granted and denied portions of 15 and 16 within the stated limits, and denied withdrawn Demand 17 as moot.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: On January 25, 2016, the court granted Demands 1, 2, 6, 12, and 18 in full and granted parts of Demands 15 and 16 within stated limits. It denied withdrawn Demand 17 as "moot," meaning there was nothing left to decide.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.sentence: Every produced document had to be marked confidential and handled under the existing protective order.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-ERAMO.plain: Every document produced had to be marked confidential and handled under the existing "protective order," a court order limiting who may see and use sensitive discovery material.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: More than 4,500 former players filed similar cases, consolidated for pretrial proceedings before District Judge Anita Brody in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: More than 4,500 former players filed similar cases. They were "consolidated" (grouped together) for pretrial work before District Judge Anita Brody, a federal trial judge, in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: In December Brody appointed Perry Golkin as Special Master to examine financial arrangements.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: In December, Judge Brody appointed Perry Golkin as "Special Master," an outside expert appointed by the court, to examine the settlement's financial arrangements, such as whether the money would be enough.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: The proposed class included retired players, representatives of deceased or incapacitated players, and derivative family-related claimants.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: The "proposed class" (the group the settlement would cover) included retired players, representatives of players who had died or could not act for themselves, and derivative "claimants," such as family members whose claims depend on a player's injury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: This was a proposed definition, not certification.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: This was only the group the parties proposed. The court had not officially approved it as a class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: Members would release claims, dismiss actions, and promise not to sue specified parties.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: Class members would "release" (give up) their claims, dismiss their pending "actions" (lawsuits), and promise not to sue the specified parties.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: Brody explained that preliminary approval was less demanding than final approval but still asked whether obvious defects existed and whether the bargain fell within a potentially fair range.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: Brody explained that preliminary approval is less demanding than final approval. Still, the judge must ask whether there are obvious defects and whether the "bargain" (the deal) falls within a range that could be fair.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: Once counsel and defendants agreed, ordinary adversarial testing could weaken while absent members remained bound by releases.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: Once the players' "counsel" (lawyers) and the defendants agree, the usual "adversarial" testing, where each side attacks the other's position, can weaken. Yet "absent members," class members not in court, would still be bound by the "releases" giving up their claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: Settlement before certification therefore required particular care, and finding obvious defects before notice avoided futile expense.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: Because the "settlement" came before the class was certified (formally approved), the court had to take particular care. "Finding" obvious defects before notice went out to class members avoided wasted expense.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: A settlement class also had to satisfy certification requirements independently.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: A "settlement class," a class formed only to settle, still had to meet the normal "certification" requirements for a class action on their own.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: Because another deficiency was sufficient, Brody did not decide conditional certification.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: Because another problem (missing proof that the money would be enough) was sufficient by itself, Brody did not decide whether to grant conditional certification, meaning provisional approval of the class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: Brody saw no indication of bad faith or bargaining other than at arm’s length.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: Brody saw no sign of "bad faith" (dishonest dealing). Nor did she see any sign that the bargaining was other than at "arm’s length," meaning real negotiation between independent sides rather than secret cooperation.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: On January 14, 2014 Brody denied preliminary approval and class certification without prejudice and directed submission of financial documentation through the Special Master as the first step toward possible approval.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: On January 14, 2014, Brody denied preliminary approval and "class certification" "without prejudice," so the parties could try again. She told them to submit financial documentation through the Special Master, as a first step toward possible approval.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.sentence: She neither required an uncapped settlement as the only lawful design nor found collusion or league liability.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-NFL-2014.plain: She did not require an "uncapped" (unlimited) settlement fund as the only lawful design. She also did not find "collusion" (secret cooperation against the class) or league "liability," meaning legal responsibility for the injuries.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.sentence: The assigned textbook account describes New York’s Chief Administrative Judge beginning a special proceeding against debt-collection attorneys over default judgments allegedly supported by false affidavits of service.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.plain: The textbook says New York's "Chief Administrative Judge," the top court administrator, began a "special proceeding" (a streamlined court action) against debt-collection lawyers. The claim was that they won "default judgments" against people who never responded, using allegedly false "affidavits of service" (sworn proof of notice).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.sentence: The editors then describe settlement through a consent order, with a procedure for vacating illegally obtained defaults, and cite the 2011 Erie County index number 2166/11 for that procedure.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.plain: The editors say the case ended in "settlement" through a "consent order," a court order the parties agreed to. It set up a "procedure" for cancelling illegally won defaults, and the editors cite the 2011 Erie County court file, index number 2166/11.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.sentence: The form linked requested vacatur with renewed service, time to answer, limitations concessions and release of certain claims.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.plain: The form tied the requested "vacatur" (cancelling the default judgment) to other terms: new service of the papers and "time to answer" (to respond to the suit). It also included concessions on filing deadlines (limitations) and a release of certain claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.sentence: Hirsh refused the proposed consent-based order and separately evaluated defective service and insufficient support for the default judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.plain: In one debtor's case, Judge Hirsh would not sign the agreed form. Instead he examined for himself whether the papers had been properly served and whether the default judgment was adequately supported.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.sentence: Effective service and a valid default procedure are distinct from the substantive merits of the debts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.plain: Whether there was effective "service" (proper delivery of the lawsuit papers) and a valid default procedure is separate from the "substantive" merits, meaning whether people actually owed the debts.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.sentence: The eight requests in the separate July 2009 order to show cause cannot be counted as relief granted by the later consent disposition.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-PFAU-2011.plain: The separate July 2009 "order to show cause," a court order requiring the other side to explain why requested orders should not be issued, listed eight requests. They cannot be counted as "relief" (remedies) granted by the later consent settlement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: It offered between 2,000 and 5,000 tons of fifty-pound iron rails at $54 per gross ton, for cash, free on board cars at its mill.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: The mill offered 2,000 to 5,000 tons of iron rails weighing fifty pounds per yard at $54 per "gross ton" (a long ton of 2,240 pounds), for cash. The price was "free on board" cars at its mill, meaning the mill would load the rails and the buyer would bear shipping from there.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: A jury returned a verdict for the mill, and the railway took exceptions and sought a writ of error.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: A jury returned a "verdict" (decision) for the mill. The railway "took exceptions," formally objecting to the trial rulings, and sought a "writ of error," a request for the Supreme Court to review the case for legal mistakes.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: The Supreme Court therefore examined the legal effect of the writings: whether the first response had left the original offer available for acceptance, and whether the later order within the quantity range could complete a bargain.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: So the Supreme Court examined the writings' legal effect. Did the railway's first reply (ordering only 1,200 tons) leave the offer open for "acceptance," and could its later order within the 2,000 to 5,000 ton range complete a "bargain" (a contract)?

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: A response proposing different terms rejects the original offer unless the offeror renews it or accepts the change.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: A reply proposing different terms is a counteroffer, and it rejects the original offer. The offer is gone unless the "offeror" (the person who made it) renews it or "accepts" the change.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: An acceptance deadline does not by itself make such an offer irrevocable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: A deadline for "acceptance," such as "reply by December 20," does not by itself make the offer irrevocable, meaning impossible to end before then. A rejection still ends it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: Because both its telegram and letter referred to the original offer, the Court treated them as a qualified response rejecting that offer, not as an unrelated proposal leaving it untouched.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: The railway's 1,200-ton order expressly answered the mill's offer, so the Court treated it as a counteroffer that rejected the offer, not as a separate inquiry that left the offer open.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: The railway’s December 19 request could not restore the rejected offer merely because the original deadline had not passed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: The railway's December 19 request could not bring back the offer it had already rejected, just because the original deadline had not yet passed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.sentence: Submitting a legal question to a jury supplied no ground for reversal when the jury reached the correct result.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-077.plain: Even if the judge wrongly let the jury decide a question of law, that did not matter, because the jury reached the legally correct answer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: Other suppliers furnished hay at increased expense, and accounting officers proposed deducting the extra cost from the money due for Peck’s wood.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: The government bought hay elsewhere at a higher price and wanted to take that extra cost out of what it owed Peck for the wood he had delivered.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: The Court of Claims considered the agreement with those circumstances, and both sides appealed its judgment to the Supreme Court.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: The "Court of Claims," the court that hears money claims against the federal government, read the agreement in light of those circumstances. Both Peck and the government appealed its judgment to the Supreme Court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: Justice Bradley identified two proper uses of parol evidence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: Justice Bradley identified two proper uses of "parol evidence," meaning evidence from outside the written contract, such as oral statements. It could be used for those purposes, not to change the contract's terms.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: It clarified the subject matter—hay to be cut in the region of delivery—and established the Government’s later interference.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: The outside evidence showed what the contract was about (hay to be cut in the area where it was to be delivered) and proved the government later got in Peck's way.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: A contracting party could not invoke the nonperformance its interference caused.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: A contracting party could not rely on the other side's "nonperformance" (failure to do what was promised) when its own interference caused that failure.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: Bradley compared a mortgage-cancellation bond: the obligee’s direction to place the mortgage with a third person excused incomplete literal compliance that the obligor otherwise might have completed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: Bradley compared a case on a "bond" (a formal written promise) to get a mortgage cancelled. The "obligee," the person owed the promise, told the "obligor," who made it, to give the mortgage to a third person, and that excused incomplete literal compliance the obligor might otherwise have completed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: Another precedent concerned a land-conveyance bond orally rescinded and followed by a sale to someone else, with conduct discharging the obligation despite unsurrendered papers.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: Another "precedent" (earlier decided case) involved a bond promising to convey land that was "rescinded" (cancelled) by spoken agreement, after which the land was sold to someone else. That conduct ended the obligation, "discharging" it, even though the papers were never returned.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.sentence: The published reasoning rejected charging the extra hay cost against the wood account but stated no quantified recovery.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-082.plain: The published reasoning rejected charging the extra hay cost against Peck's wood account. But it did not state a dollar amount for his "recovery," meaning what he was entitled to collect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Sherwood tendered eighty dollars, which the sellers refused, then obtained possession under a replevin writ; a constable weighed her elsewhere at 1,420 pounds.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: Sherwood "tendered" (formally offered) $80, which the sellers refused. He then got possession under a "replevin" writ, a court order to recover specific property, and a "constable" (a local law officer) weighed the cow elsewhere at 1,420 pounds.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Sherwood won in a justice’s court and after an appealed jury trial in Wayne County Circuit Court.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: Sherwood won in a "justice’s court," a small local court. After the case was "appealed," he won again in a jury trial in the Wayne County Circuit Court, the county trial court.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Sellers argued the sale was still executory because weighing and payment had not occurred and alternatively could be avoided for mistake.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: The sellers argued the sale was still "executory," meaning not yet completed, because the cow had not been weighed or paid for. Alternatively, they said it could be undone for "mistake," because both sides were wrong about the cow.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Requested condition-precedent and barren-cow instructions were refused.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: The judge refused the sellers' requested jury "instructions." One said weighing was a "condition-precedent" (something that must happen before the sale takes effect); the other said a shared belief that the cow was barren mattered.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Signed correspondence met the statute for sales over fifty dollars.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: The law required sales over $50 to be backed by a signed writing (the statute of frauds); the letters the parties exchanged satisfied it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Neither payment nor weighing necessarily preceded transfer of title, and physical delivery was not invariably required.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: Ownership could pass to Sherwood before payment or weighing, and even before he took the cow, if that was what the parties intended.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Apparent assent could be avoided before or after completion when both parties misunderstood a material fact going to the substance of the bargain, rather than mere quality or an incidental attribute—even a motivating quality mistake might leave a sale binding.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: Apparent "assent" (agreement) can be undone, before or after the deal is completed, when both "parties" misunderstood a "material" fact going to the substance of the "bargain." A "mistake" about mere quality or a side feature is not enough, even one that motivated the purchase.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: The required instruction was conditional: if both believed her barren and useless for breeding when contracting, but she was capable, sellers could rescind and the verdict should favor them.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: The required jury "instruction" was conditional. If both sides believed the cow barren and useless for breeding when contracting, but she could breed, the sellers could "rescind" (cancel) the sale and the "verdict" should go to them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Justice Sherwood—the judge, not plaintiff Theodore Sherwood—agreed title could pass without advance weighing or payment but rejected mutuality of mistake.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: Justice Sherwood, the dissenting judge and not "plaintiff" Theodore Sherwood (the buyer who sued), agreed that "title" (ownership) could pass before weighing or payment. But he rejected the idea that both sides made the same mistake.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: Both intended the same existing animal without warranty of that uncertain quality.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: Both sides meant to trade this very cow, and the sellers gave no "warranty" (a guarantee) about her uncertain ability to breed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: He used a horse later discovered exceptionally fast to illustrate converting valuation errors into rescission.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: He gave the example of selling a horse that later proves unusually fast: letting the seller undo that sale would turn a bad guess about value into a reason to cancel.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.sentence: On July 7, 1887, the three-to-one court reversed and ordered a new trial, with Supreme Court costs to defendants.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-039.plain: On July 7, 1887, the court, voting three to one, "reversed" (overturned) Sherwood's win and ordered a new trial. It awarded the defendants their Supreme Court costs for the appeal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: The indices, ceiling, favored-customer term, force-majeure provision, and extensive bargaining reflected efforts to limit risk.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: The price indexes, the price ceiling, the "favored-customer term" (a promise of the best price given any customer), the force-majeure clause excusing performance for events beyond control, and the long bargaining all showed efforts to limit risk.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Pennsylvania conflicts rules required honoring the contractual Indiana choice of law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Pennsylvania's "conflicts rules," which decide which state's law governs, required the court to honor the contract's choice of Indiana law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Where Indiana authority did not resolve an issue, the district court predicted how Indiana courts would rule.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Where Indiana cases did not settle an issue, the "district court" (the federal trial court) predicted how Indiana courts would rule.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: On count one, Essex argued that ALCOA had merely forecast future economics incorrectly, that any mistake was ALCOA’s alone, and that the formula’s drafter had accepted the risk by omitting a floor.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: On "count" one (ALCOA's first claim), Essex argued that ALCOA merely predicted future economics wrongly, which is not a legal mistake, and that any error was ALCOA's alone. As the formula's "drafter" (writer), ALCOA took the risk by leaving out a minimum price.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Teitelbaum instead characterized the mistake as a present actuarial error about an elaborate risk-limiting device’s capacity to track costs within tolerable bounds.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Judge Teitelbaum instead called it a present "actuarial" error, a mistake in calculating risk. When signing, both sides wrongly believed the elaborate risk-limiting "device," the price index, could keep ALCOA's costs within tolerable bounds.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: The court considered express allocation, trade usage and common understandings, reasoned allocation where neither controlled, and conscious ignorance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: The court asked whether the contract expressly assigned the risk, whether "trade usage" (industry custom) or common understanding did, and what was reasonable if neither did. It also asked about "conscious ignorance," knowingly going ahead without knowing the facts.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Acceptance of a calculated range differed from an unlimited gamble.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: "Acceptance" of a calculated range of cost changes is different from agreeing to an unlimited gamble on any loss, however huge.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Like mistake, those doctrines concerned basic assumptions and allocation of risk, but focused on severe hardship.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Impracticability and frustration also ask whether a shared basic assumption failed and who bore that risk, but they focus on extreme hardship arising after signing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Higher costs ordinarily belonged to contract risk; relief required expense far beyond ordinary variation and loss not fairly undertaken.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Higher costs are normally a risk each side takes on by making a "contract." Relief requires costs far beyond ordinary variation and a loss the party never fairly agreed to bear.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Frustration concerned ALCOA’s principal purpose of earning money instead of suffering serious losses.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: For frustration, the court said ALCOA's main purpose was to make money, and that purpose was defeated by huge losses.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Essex correctly observed that traditional reformation corrected a writing that failed to record an antecedent agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Essex correctly pointed out that traditional "reformation" meant rewriting a document only when it failed to record an "antecedent" (earlier) agreement the parties had actually reached.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: It used equitable restitution and modification to preserve the exchange and avoid unjust enrichment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: The court instead used "equitable" (fairness-based) powers of restitution and modification to keep the exchange going. This avoided "unjust enrichment," meaning Essex profiting unfairly at ALCOA's expense.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Rescission would give ALCOA a market-price windfall and deprive Essex of secure supply; unchanged enforcement would assign the extraordinary losses to ALCOA.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Rescission, cancelling the contract, would give ALCOA a "windfall" (an unearned gain) by selling at market prices and leave Essex without secure supply. Enforcing it unchanged would put the "extraordinary losses" on ALCOA, so the court took a middle path.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: The court found both credible but held that ALCOA failed to prove agreement by a preponderance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: The judge found both witnesses believable, but held ALCOA failed to prove the claimed agreement by a "preponderance" of the evidence, meaning more likely than not.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: It therefore did not decide the statute-of-frauds issue and granted neither discharge nor requested damages on that theory.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: So the court did not decide the "statute-of-frauds" issue, the rule that some agreements must be in writing. It granted ALCOA neither a discharge from the contract nor the "damages" (money) it asked for on that theory.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Count three invoked a side letter permitting termination if a final court determination classified the transaction as a sale of goods.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: "Count" three, ALCOA's third claim, relied on a "side letter" (a separate letter agreement). It allowed ending the deal if a final court ruling "classified" the transaction as a "sale of goods," a sale of aluminum, rather than a service converting Essex's alumina.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: Independently, estoppel by contract prevented ALCOA from contradicting the side letter’s settled service characterization to obtain cancellation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: Separately, "estoppel by contract" applied: having agreed in the side letter that the deal was a service, ALCOA could not contradict that to get "cancellation" of the contract.

Section 24, the contract's clause for events beyond a party's control, excused the performance those events affected. That covered ALCOA's reduced deliveries when extreme cold, generator failures, and coal-supply problems interrupted its plant.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.sentence: That subsequent-history account does not establish appellate approval of the district court’s prediction of Indiana law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-066.plain: That account of later history does not show "appellate" approval, meaning a higher court's approval, of the district court’s prediction of Indiana law. The case settled during the appeal.

brief-CT-CB-0162.sentence: Mooers sued for himself and a proposed class, seeking disgorgement and prorated tuition and mandatory-fee refunds for the period without in-person services.
brief-CT-CB-0162.plain: Mooers sued for himself and a "proposed class" of other students. He sought disgorgement (giving up money unfairly kept) and "prorated" refunds of tuition and mandatory fees, meaning the share covering the period without in-person services.

brief-CT-CB-0162.sentence: After a stipulation permitting amendment, Mooers amended on March 12, and the college filed a new Rule 12(b)(6) motion on April 12.
brief-CT-CB-0162.plain: After a "stipulation" (the parties' agreement) allowed it, Mooers "amended" his complaint on March 12. On April 12 the college filed a new motion under Rule 12(b)(6), arguing that even if everything alleged were true, it stated no legal claim.

brief-CT-CB-0162.sentence: The new pleading and motion made the first motion moot.
brief-CT-CB-0162.plain: The new "pleading" (the amended complaint) and the new motion made the first motion to dismiss moot, meaning it had nothing left to decide.
