brief-CP-116.sentence: The same distinction between review and belief fit the parallel summary-judgment standard.
brief-CP-116.plain: The same rule, that judges check whether the evidence is enough but do not decide whom to believe, applies to summary judgment before trial.

brief-CP-116.sentence: It resolved sufficiency itself: the district court properly sent the case to the jury, and this verdict stood.
brief-CP-116.plain: The Court decided "sufficiency," whether the evidence was enough, itself. The "district court" (the trial court) properly sent the case to the jury, and the verdict for Reeves stood.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Her complaint asserted Missouri Merchandising Practices Act and state antitrust claims supported by alleged violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA).
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Her "complaint" (the document starting the lawsuit) asserted claims under the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act and state "antitrust" (competition) law. To support them she alleged violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA).

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: In an earlier appeal, the Eighth Circuit held that those embedded federal questions were sufficiently substantial and integral to support federal-question jurisdiction.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: In an earlier appeal, the Eighth Circuit held that those "embedded federal questions," federal issues built into her state claims, were substantial and central enough to support "federal-question jurisdiction," a federal court's power over cases arising under federal law.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: The federal issues supplied original jurisdiction, and factually related state claims fell within supplemental jurisdiction.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: The federal issues supplied "original jurisdiction," the federal court's own power to hear the case. The factually related state claims came in under "supplemental jurisdiction," power over claims tied to ones the court can already hear.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Wullschleger then properly amended the complaint to delete every FDCA reference and requested remand of the exclusively state-law action.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Wullschleger then properly "amended" (rewrote) the complaint to delete every FDCA reference. She asked for "remand," sending the now purely state-law case back to state court.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: It measured jurisdiction at removal and concluded that the later deletion did not extinguish supplemental power.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: The district court measured its "jurisdiction" (power over the case) as of removal to federal court. It concluded the later deletion did not "extinguish" (end) its supplemental power.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: The remand denial itself was not immediately appealable; the jurisdictional issue reached the Eighth Circuit through appeal after the merits dismissal.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: The denial of "remand" was not immediately "appealable." The jurisdiction issue reached the Eighth Circuit only through her appeal after the court dismissed her claims on "the merits," their substance.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Section 1331 covered claims arising under federal law, usually because federal law created them and exceptionally through a substantial, disputed federal issue necessarily embedded in a state claim.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Section 1331 covers claims "arising under" federal law. Usually that is because federal law created the claim; in rare cases, a state claim qualifies because a substantial, disputed federal issue is necessarily built into it.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Section 1441 permitted removal within original jurisdiction, while §1447(c) required remand when subject-matter jurisdiction was absent before final judgment.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Section 1441 lets a defendant move ("remove") a case to federal court only if it falls within "original jurisdiction." And §1447(c) requires "remand" to state court whenever the federal court turns out to lack subject-matter jurisdiction before final judgment.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: This derivative power still depended on something in the action supplying original jurisdiction.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: This borrowed ("derivative") power over related claims still depended on something in the case supplying "original jurisdiction" on its own.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Section 1367(c) addressed discretion to decline power that otherwise existed, including novel or complex state issues, substantial predominance, or judicial dismissal of all original-jurisdiction claims.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Section 1367(c) gives "discretion" to decline power the court otherwise has, for example over new or complex state issues. Other grounds are "substantial predominance" of state claims over the rest of the case, or the court's "dismissal" of all claims within its original jurisdiction.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: With no remaining original-jurisdiction claim, the state claims were supplemental to nothing.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Once no federal claim was left, the state claims had nothing to be attached to, so the federal court had no basis to keep them.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: If jurisdiction survived that withdrawal under subsection (a), subsection (c) would have addressed this especially strong reason for discretionary remand.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: If "jurisdiction" survived a plaintiff's withdrawal of her federal claims under subsection (a), subsection (c) would have listed that especially strong reason for "discretionary" remand, one the court may choose. Its silence suggested no such power survives.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Adding a nondiverse party ordinarily defeated complete diversity, and eliminating such a party could cure it.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: In diversity cases, no plaintiff may share a state with any defendant. Adding a same-state party usually destroys that jurisdiction, and dropping such a party can restore it.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: The time-of-filing rule ordinarily fixed actual citizenship facts rather than the claims and parties selected in superseding pleadings.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: The "time-of-filing rule" ordinarily freezes actual facts like the parties' citizenship as of filing. It does not freeze the claims and parties the plaintiff chooses in "superseding pleadings," later versions of the complaint that replace earlier ones.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Reducing the amount in controversy generally did not remove jurisdiction, reflecting fluctuating, difficult-to-measure case value and the waste of continual remeasurement.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Reducing the "amount in controversy" (the money at stake) generally did not remove "jurisdiction." Case values fluctuate and are hard to measure, and constantly remeasuring them would be wasteful.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: The assumed power to retain had not been analyzed and supported neither the result nor the remand-versus-dismissal reasoning.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Cohill simply assumed the court could have kept the case; it never examined that question, and its decision did not depend on it.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: Kagan nevertheless identified it as dictum.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: Justice Kagan nevertheless identified the footnote as "dictum," a side remark not needed to decide the case, and so not binding.

brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.sentence: The proper amendment removed every federal question, leaving no original-jurisdiction anchor and therefore no supplemental jurisdiction.
brief-CP-SUP-ROYALCANIN.plain: The proper "amendment" removed every "federal question," leaving no claim the federal court could hear on its own, no original-jurisdiction anchor. Without that anchor, there was no "supplemental jurisdiction" over the related state claims either.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.sentence: The assignment makes that receipt deadline the starting point for the later formation questions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.plain: The textbook problem starts from that deadline: the band's offer required a signed agreement to be in its hands by 5 p.m., and whether a contract was formed depends on what happened measured against it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.sentence: The chronology therefore does not simply show timely receipt of the signed agreement the defendants had requested.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.plain: Because the text arrived before the 5 p.m. deadline but the signature only after, the chronology does not simply show "timely" (on-time) receipt of the signed agreement the "defendants" had requested.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.sentence: On May 24, Ellefson’s lawyer purported to withdraw from negotiations.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.plain: On May 24, Ellefson's lawyer tried to back out of the deal; whether that worked depended on whether a binding contract already existed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.sentence: Their later execution and mailing, and the timing of the attempted withdrawal, raised questions beyond whether the first deadline had been missed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.plain: The band later signed and mailed copies, and Ellefson tried to withdraw before he received them. So the question was not only whether the deadline was missed, but whether the band's later signing accepted his late signature before he backed out.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.sentence: The sequence requires attention to the receipt deadline, the late signature, possible acceptance through later conduct, and whether withdrawal preceded a legally effective agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-081.plain: The sequence requires attention to the receipt deadline, the late signature, and possible "acceptance" through later conduct, such as signing and mailing copies. It also requires asking whether Ellefson's "withdrawal" came before a legally binding agreement formed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Subcontractor DRC, Inc. and its managing director Robert Isakson sued on the United States’ behalf as private relators under the False Claims Act.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: Subcontractor DRC, Inc. and its managing director Robert Isakson sued on the United States’ behalf as "relators," private whistleblowers suing in the government's name under the False Claims Act. A successful relator gets a share of what the government recovers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: The government declined to intervene but participated as amicus.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: The government declined to "intervene," meaning take over the case, but participated as amicus, a "friend of the court" filing briefs with its views.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: The district court dismissed a conspiracy count under an intracorporate-conspiracy rationale, confined the currency fraud claims to the $3 million Treasury advance, and severed a claim concerning airport security.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: The district court dismissed a conspiracy count on an "intracorporate-conspiracy" rationale: people within one company cannot conspire with each other. It limited the currency fraud claims to the $3 million Treasury advance and "severed" (split off) the airport security claim to be handled separately.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Before entering judgment on fraud, the judge granted a previously reserved Rule 50(a) motion for judgment as a matter of law, reasoning that presentment to the Authority did not satisfy the statute.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: Before "entering judgment" on fraud, the judge granted a Rule 50(a) "motion" for judgment as a matter of law that he had "reserved," or put off deciding. He reasoned that presenting bills to the occupation Authority did not satisfy the "statute," because that was not presentment to the United States.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: The applicable § 3729(c) covered demands to a grantee or other recipient if the United States provided any portion of the requested money or would reimburse any portion.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: The applicable § 3729(c) defined "claim" to include demands made to a "grantee" (a grant recipient) or other recipient, if the United States provided or would reimburse any portion of the requested money.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Coverage of grantees also refuted any requirement that the government retain title or control after transfer.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: Covering "grantees," who own grant money once they receive it, also showed the government need not "retain title" (keep ownership) or control of the money after transfer.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Nor was contractual privity required: statutory coverage of indirect recipients and subcontractors contradicted that restriction.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: Nor was contractual privity, a direct contract between the government and Custer Battles, required. The "statutory" coverage of indirect recipients and subcontractors contradicted that restriction.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: The appellate court could not determine the loss, so it allowed the relators to elect a new trial; it did not award all approximately $15 million paid under the contract.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: The "appellate court" could not work out the government's loss, so it let the "relators" choose a "new trial." It did not "award" them all of the roughly $15 million paid under the "contract."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Reviewing the Rule 50 ruling de novo without weighing credibility, the court found sufficient evidence of presentment to American officials acting officially under § 3729(a)(1).
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: "Reviewing" the Rule 50 "ruling" de novo, meaning fresh, without weighing "credibility" (whom to believe), the court found enough evidence of presentment. The invoices went to American officials acting in their official roles, which satisfies § 3729(a)(1).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Section (a)(1) identified who received a claim; the court could not import the distinct language about government payment or approval from (a)(2).
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: Part (a)(1) asks only to whom the claim was presented. The court refused to read into it the different 'paid or approved by the Government' wording found only in part (a)(2).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: Reversal still left other Rule 50 arguments unresolved, including material falsity, federal loss, and the individual defendants’ sufficient knowledge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: The reversal still left other Rule 50 arguments undecided. These included "material falsity" (whether the lies mattered to payment), federal loss, and whether the individual defendants’ knowledge was sufficient.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.sentence: If they declined, the district court had to decide the remaining Rule 50 grounds; only if it rejected those grounds was it to enter judgment on the existing verdict.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-094.plain: If the relators declined a new trial, the "district court" had to decide the remaining Rule 50 grounds. Only if it rejected them could it enter judgment on the existing verdict.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: McConnell disputed the allegations, but his motion to strike required their acceptance solely to test legal sufficiency.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: McConnell disputed the bribery "allegations." But his motion to strike the defenses required their "acceptance" as true for now, solely to test whether they would be a legally sufficient defense.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: It distinguished an inherently illegal bargain from lawful services performed through later misconduct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: The court distinguished an "inherently illegal" bargain, one that itself calls for something illegal, from lawful services carried out through later misconduct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: The issue was whether central bribery during performance could defend against compensation on a facially lawful promise, even when Commonwealth had not directed it and McConnell could prove his basic contract elements without revealing it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: The issue was whether bribery central to performance could defeat payment on a "facially lawful" promise, one lawful as written. That was so even though Commonwealth had not directed the bribe and McConnell could prove his basic contract without revealing it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: Restricting that policy to contracts illegal on their face would let a plaintiff draft a lawful promise and fulfill it through dominant corruption.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: Limiting that policy to contracts illegal on their face would let a "plaintiff" write a lawful promise, carry it out mainly through corruption, and still get paid.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: Nor could a plaintiff avoid the policy merely by presenting a prima facie claim without mentioning wrongdoing.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: Nor could a plaintiff escape the policy just by presenting a "prima facie" claim, the basic elements of a contract case, without mentioning the wrongdoing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: It required at least a direct connection between the illegality and obligation, with wrongdoing central or dominant in performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: The rule required at least a direct link between the "illegality" and the obligation sued on. The wrongdoing also had to be central or dominant in "performance," not a minor side issue.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: Its exception prevented a mere depository or escrow holder outside the underlying transaction from keeping another’s property by invoking illegality.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: That precedent's exception only stopped a mere "depository" or escrow holder (someone just holding another's property, outside the underlying deal) from keeping it by pointing to "illegality."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: The court awarded costs in all courts, remitted to the Appellate Division for consistent proceedings, and answered the certified question negatively.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: The court awarded costs in all courts and "remitted to" the Appellate Division, meaning it sent the case back for consistent proceedings. It answered "no" to the "certified question," the formal question sent up for decision.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.sentence: The ruling neither finally established bribery nor adjudicated recovery of the already-paid $10,000.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-040.plain: The ruling neither finally established that bribery happened nor decided "recovery" (getting back) of the $10,000 already paid.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Paragraph 8, called a contingent note payable, applied if Miller left or was terminated for cause and established a consulting or accounting business within fifty miles of a current or former client during the next five years.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Paragraph 8, called a "contingent note payable," was a promise to pay that applied only if Miller left or was "terminated for cause" (fired for a reason the contract allowed). He also had to set up a consulting or accounting business within fifty miles of a current or former client within the next five years.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Miller sought to exclude continuation evidence because paragraph 5 of the complaint said the agreement was not renewed or extended after May 31, 1990.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Miller sought to exclude evidence that the agreement continued, because paragraph 5 of DeMuth's complaint said it was not renewed or extended after May 31, 1990.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: The court entered a compulsory nonsuit on wrongful discharge.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: The court entered a "compulsory nonsuit" on wrongful discharge, throwing out Miller's wrongful-firing claim itself without sending it to the jury.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Through special interrogatories, the jury found the parties remained contractually bound by their conduct and awarded damages later molded to $110,000.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Through "special interrogatories," specific written questions to the jury, it found the parties remained contractually bound by their conduct. It "awarded" damages, which the judge later "molded" (adjusted) to $110,000.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Under the doctrine applied, a binding admission was an express factual concession for the party’s advantage.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Under the doctrine applied, a "binding admission" in a pleading was a clear statement conceding a fact, made for the party's own advantage. A sentence that would wreck the party's own claim did not qualify.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Continued work after a fixed term, without objection or a new arrangement, could imply continuation on prior conditions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: When people keep working together after a contract's term ends, without objecting or making a new deal, the law may treat them as having continued on the old contract's terms.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Miller’s argument that the payment was an unlawful penalty or unreasonable restrictive covenant had not appeared in pretrial, trial, or post-trial motions, and the trial court had not decided it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Miller's argument that the payment was an unlawful penalty or an unreasonable "restrictive covenant" (a promise limiting competition) never appeared in pretrial, trial, or "post-trial motions." The trial court had never decided it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: The appellate court treated that challenge as waived.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: The "appellate court" treated that challenge as "waived," meaning lost because it was raised too late, and refused to consider it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Under the preservation approach then applied, Popovich reviewed them because the lower court had actually decided them.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Under the preservation approach then used, an issue stayed alive for appeal if the "lower court" actually decided it. So Judge Popovich reviewed these arguments.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: He found no governmental action in enforcement of this particular competition promise.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: He found no "governmental action" in a court's enforcement of this particular promise about competing, so the constitutional equal-protection rule did not apply.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: Under Shelley and Barrows, consent to a private agreement did not prevent its judicial enforcement from being state action.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Under Shelley and Barrows, the Supreme Court's racial-covenant cases, a court enforcing a private agreement is "state action" (government conduct), even though the parties consented to the agreement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: He considered enforcement irrational even under rational-basis review: the record showed capable work and partnership prospects, no work-related sexual conduct, and dismissal based on status.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: He thought enforcement irrational even under "rational-basis review," the most lenient test, which asks only for some sensible reason. The record showed capable work, "partnership" prospects, no work-related sexual conduct, and a "dismissal" based on Miller's status as gay.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.sentence: The common conclusions on continuation and preservation did not make Popovich’s entire constitutional discussion a panel-majority rationale.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-044.plain: Two judges agreed on the result and on the contract and preservation issues, but only Judge Popovich adopted his constitutional reasoning, so it is not the court's binding view.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: The lease allowed assignment and waived defenses, counterclaims and setoffs against an assignee that B.C.B.U. might have against the lessor.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: The "lease allowed assignment," meaning Crocker could transfer it to someone else. B.C.B.U. also waived, against any assignee, the "defenses," counterclaims and "setoffs" (amounts deducted for money owed) it might have against the "lessor," Crocker.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, National Association, acting as trustee, reviewed the pool December 8, found nothing amiss, and took assignment December 11.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, National Association, acting as "trustee" holding the pool of leases for investors, reviewed the pool December 8 and found nothing amiss. It "took assignment," becoming the lease's new owner, on December 11.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: After trial on stipulated facts and declarations, the judge enforced the waiver under California Uniform Commercial Code § 9403, awarding $107,656.24 plus interest against the company and declaring Bangerter’s guaranty enforceable.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: After trial on "stipulated facts" (facts both sides agreed to) and declarations, the judge enforced the "waiver" of defenses under California Uniform Commercial Code § 9403. He awarded $107,656.24 plus interest against the company and declared Bangerter's "guaranty," his personal promise to pay, enforceable.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: On appeal, B.C.B.U. relied on § 10407, which makes promises in a nonconsumer finance lease irrevocable and independent upon acceptance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: On "appeal," B.C.B.U. relied on § 10407, which makes the lessee's promises in a "nonconsumer finance lease" (a business lease financed through a third party) irrevocable and independent. That happens only upon "acceptance" of the equipment, and it said it never received any.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: That section allowed enforcement of a debtor’s agreement not to assert defenses when the assignee took for value, in good faith, without notice of a property or possessory claim to the assigned property, and without notice of specified defenses or recoupment claims.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: That section enforced a debtor's agreement not to raise defenses if the "assignee" paid value and took "in good faith." It also had to take without notice of anyone's property or "possessory claim" to the "assigned" property, or of specified defenses or "recoupment" claims (offsetting claims from the same deal).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: It preserved defenses available against a holder in due course.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: It preserved the defenses that work even against a "holder in due course," a good-faith buyer of a check or note who gets special protection. Those are the few serious defenses, such as illegality or being tricked about what the document even was.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: A qualifying assignee thus received analogous protection; the lease did not itself become a negotiable instrument.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: A qualifying "assignee" like Wells Fargo thus got protection similar to a holder in due course. The lease did not itself become a negotiable instrument, such as a check or note.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: The official comments contemplated enforcement even where other law would prevent enforcement by the assignor.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: The "official comments," the drafters' explanatory notes, contemplated enforcing such a waiver even where other law would prevent enforcement by the "assignor," the original party who transferred the contract, here Crocker.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: Failure of consideration was not a defense effective against a protected holder in due course.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: "Failure of consideration," the complaint that B.C.B.U. got nothing for its promise because no equipment came, was not a "defense" that works against a protected "holder in due course."

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: Calling an altered agreement void did not make its object or consideration illegal, and neither form of illegality was asserted here.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: Calling the altered agreement "void" (of no legal effect) did not make its purpose or its consideration, what each side gave, illegal. And no one claimed either kind of illegality here.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: Rescission left no replacement rights and therefore did not fit that protection.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: Cancelling the deal outright created no new contract rights for Wells Fargo to step into, so the rule protecting good-faith changes to an assigned contract did not apply.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: B.C.B.U.’s claim that January 2001 cancellation worked because notice arrived only in January 2003 substituted cancellation for the required payment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: B.C.B.U. claimed its January 2001 cancellation counted because notice of the assignment arrived only in January 2003. But the rule protects a debtor who pays the original creditor before notice, and B.C.B.U. substituted cancellation for that required payment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.sentence: The rehearing petition was seven days late and the point had not previously been raised; additionally, former § 9206 provided the same relevant waiver and holder-in-due-course rule.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-104.plain: B.C.B.U.'s "rehearing" petition, asking the court to reconsider, was seven days late and raised a point never made before. Besides, "former § 9206," the older version of the law, had the same relevant "waiver" and holder-in-due-course rule.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.sentence: On September 13, 2000, the Pau Court of Appeal instead awarded 20,000 francs, reasoning that neither party intended to perform the reciprocal commitments and that the seller’s compensable harm was only delay in transferring the practice.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.plain: On September 13, 2000, the Pau Court of Appeal instead awarded 20,000 francs. It reasoned that neither "party" meant to carry out their reciprocal commitments, so the seller's only "compensable" harm (harm the law will pay for) was delay in transferring the practice.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.sentence: The Court of Cassation rejected the objection because written consent could be granted in advance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.plain: The Court of Cassation, France's highest court, rejected the "objection" because the landlord's written consent could validly be given in advance.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.sentence: Rejection of this incidental appeal was distinct from the seller’s successful challenge to the reduced recovery.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.plain: Rejecting this "incidental appeal," the buyer's own cross-challenge, was separate from the seller's successful challenge to the reduced "recovery" (award).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.sentence: An unpaid contractual creditor could prefer payment of the price to damages or dissolution.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.plain: A seller who has not been paid may choose to demand the agreed price itself, rather than accept damages or undo the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.sentence: Substituting damages failed to give those findings their legal consequence: it refused application of article 1134 and wrongly applied the other provisions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.plain: Awarding damages instead failed to give those "findings" (a valid contract and a seller seeking the price) their legal effect. It refused to apply article 1134, under which contracts bind the parties like law, and wrongly applied the other provisions.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.sentence: On July 9, 2003, the First Civil Chamber quashed the Pau judgment only insofar as it had dismissed M. X’s claim, restored the parties’ prior position on that part and remanded to the Agen Court of Appeal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-004.plain: On July 9, 2003, the First Civil Chamber "quashed" (cancelled) the Pau "judgment" only insofar as it had "dismissed" M. X’s "claim" for the price. It restored the parties' prior position on that part and "remanded" the case to the Agen Court of Appeal to decide again.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: The form became binding upon written acceptance by a principal or authorized officer, or commencement of performance.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: The form became binding upon written "acceptance" by a principal or authorized officer of the company, or upon "commencement of performance," meaning the company starting the work.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: No authorized written acceptance followed, so any formation depended on the permitted performance route.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: No authorized written "acceptance" ever came, so any "formation" of a contract depended on the other permitted route: Ever-Tite starting performance before the Greens backed out.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: The trial court agreed, treating the refusal at arrival as preceding the start of actual roofing, and dismissed at Ever-Tite’s cost.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: The trial court agreed, treating the Greens' refusal when the crew arrived as coming before any actual roofing began. It "dismissed" the suit and made Ever-Tite pay the costs.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: The no-cancellation phrase did not replace that formation inquiry or by itself establish an immediately binding contract from the homeowners’ signatures.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: The form's no-cancellation phrase did not replace that "formation" question. It did not by itself create a binding contract the moment the homeowners signed.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: It discussed a Restatement lapse rule and Louisiana Civil Code provisions then in force.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: The court discussed a Restatement rule on "lapse," that an offer with no deadline expires after a reasonable time, and the Louisiana Civil Code provisions then in force.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: The holding therefore did not depend on an unqualified nationwide rule of instantaneous revocability.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: So the decision did not rest on any general idea that an offer can always be withdrawn at any instant before acceptance.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: Once they refused the already accepted performance, they breached.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: Because loading and sending the crew had already accepted the offer, the Greens' refusal of that "performance" was a breach of the contract.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: Civil Code articles 1930 and 1934 supplied compensation for loss sustained and profit foregone.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: Civil Code articles 1930 and 1934 allowed recovery for both the loss Ever-Tite actually suffered and the profit it gave up.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: That language concerned collecting under the agreement, not damages for being prevented from performing.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: The fee clause covered lawyers hired to collect money owed under the contract, not lawyers suing for damages because the customer blocked the work.

brief-CT-CB-0225.sentence: On November 2, 1955, the Second Circuit Court of Appeal set aside dismissal and rendered judgment against both Greens for $311.37, with five-percent annual interest from judicial demand until payment and all costs.
brief-CT-CB-0225.plain: On November 2, 1955, the Second Circuit Court of Appeal "set aside" (reversed) the dismissal and "rendered judgment" itself against both Greens for $311.37. It added five-percent annual interest from "judicial demand," the date of suit, until payment, plus all costs.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: Richard Whitehead agreed to relinquish any rights and rebut presumed paternity.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: Richard Whitehead agreed to give up any parental rights and to "rebut" (disprove) the legal presumption that he, as Mary Beth's husband, was the child's father.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: A fetal-abnormality clause required abortion on his demand, with refusal ending his contractual duties apart from statutory paternity obligations; undetected abnormalities remained his responsibility.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: A fetal-abnormality clause required an abortion if William demanded it; if Mary Beth refused, his duties under the contract ended, apart from his "statutory" duties as father under the law. Abnormalities not detected before birth remained his responsibility.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: William sued and obtained an ex parte transfer order.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: William sued and obtained an "ex parte" transfer order, one issued without Mary Beth present or heard, handing the baby to him.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: It treated best interests as a prerequisite to specifically enforcing a valid bargain.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: The trial court treated the child's best interests as a required first step before specifically enforcing, or ordering performance of, what it saw as a valid "bargain."

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: The Supreme Court granted direct certification.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: The New Jersey Supreme Court "granted" direct certification, agreeing to hear the appeal right away and skipping the intermediate appeals court.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: First, adoption law prohibited payment connected with placement apart from approved-agency fees and specified medical expenses.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: First, New Jersey law banned paying money in connection with handing a child over for adoption, except fees to approved agencies and certain medical costs.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: Calling $10,000 service compensation and leaving Elizabeth off the agreement did not change payment conditioned on surrender and termination; fetal death yielded markedly less or none despite services.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: Calling the $10,000 pay for services, and leaving Elizabeth (William's wife) off the agreement, did not change that payment depended on surrendering the baby and ending Mary Beth's parental rights. If the fetus died, she would get far less or nothing, despite her services.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: Second, outside qualifying formal agency surrender, termination required stringent abandonment, serious-neglect, or comparable grounds, not a better alternative home.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: Second, apart from a qualifying formal surrender through an approved agency, ending parental rights required strict grounds like abandonment, "serious-neglect," or something comparable. A better alternative home was not enough.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: Third, the contract made surrender irrevocable before conception, bypassing prescribed post-birth agency procedures, acknowledgment, and counseling.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: Third, the contract made surrender "irrevocable" (impossible to take back) even before conception. That bypassed the "agency" procedures the law requires after birth, including formal acknowledgment and counseling.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: These central promises rendered the whole bargain unenforceable despite severability language.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: These central promises made the whole "bargain" unenforceable, even though the contract had "severability" language letting invalid parts be cut out and the rest kept.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: State-law restoration made it unnecessary to decide Mary Beth’s separate constitutional companionship, state-action, or Thirteenth Amendment arguments.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: Because state law restored Mary Beth's rights, the court did not need to decide her separate constitutional arguments: a right to companionship with her child, "state-action," and the Thirteenth Amendment's ban on slavery.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: Between the natural parents, best interests controlled without an automatic sex preference.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: Between the "natural parents," the two biological parents, the child's best interests controlled custody, with no automatic preference for mother or father.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: In future temporary disputes, an invalid contract alone would not justify removing a baby from the mother; highly persuasive evidence of danger, unfitness, or similar circumstances would be needed, with flight threats ordinarily addressed by an injunction.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: In future temporary disputes, an invalid contract alone would not justify taking a baby from the mother. Highly persuasive evidence of danger, unfitness, or similar circumstances would be needed, and threats to flee would ordinarily be handled by an "injunction," a court order forbidding it.

brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.sentence: This was a visitation remand, not a new custody determination or immediate unrestricted access order.
brief-CT-NEXT-CM-0117.plain: The case went back only to set "visitation," meaning visiting arrangements. It was not a new custody decision or an "order" giving Mary Beth immediate unrestricted access.

citoh.sentence: Jordan’s August 19 acknowledgment expressly conditioned acceptance on Itoh’s assent to additional or different terms on the form and reverse side and requested immediate notice of unacceptable terms.
citoh.plain: Jordan's August 19 "acknowledgment" (its reply form) expressly made its acceptance depend on Itoh's "assent" (agreement) to the extra or different terms on the form and its back. It asked Itoh to say at once if any terms were unacceptable.

citoh.sentence: Jordan requested a stay under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act, or FAA.
citoh.plain: So the dispute could go to arbitration, Jordan asked for a "stay," a pause of Itoh's lawsuit, under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act, or FAA.

citoh.sentence: Under the historical interlocutory doctrine, denial was reviewable under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1) because the underlying suit was at law.
citoh.plain: Under the historical "interlocutory" doctrine (rules for appeals before a case ends), denying the stay was "reviewable" at once under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1). That was because the underlying "suit was at law," a damages case, so refusing the stay was treated like refusing an injunction.

citoh.sentence: Itoh’s objection that no written agreement had yet been determined concerned the stay’s merits, not appealability.
citoh.plain: Itoh's "objection" that no one had yet found a written arbitration agreement went to whether the stay should be granted. It did not affect "appealability," whether the appeals court could hear the appeal.

citoh.sentence: Section 3 mandated a stay where a written agreement referred the dispute to arbitration and the applicant was not in default.
citoh.plain: Section 3 required a "stay" where a written agreement sent the dispute to arbitration and the party asking was "not in default," meaning it had not lost its right to arbitrate.

citoh.sentence: The court separated removal of a Statute of Frauds defense from proof of agreement.
citoh.plain: The court separated two things: getting past a Statute of Frauds defense, the requirement of a signed writing, and proving the parties actually agreed to the terms.

citoh.sentence: Jordan’s acknowledgment expressly made acceptance dependent on assent to the extra terms, satisfying § 2-207(1)’s conditional proviso.
citoh.plain: Jordan's "acknowledgment" expressly made acceptance depend on Itoh's "assent" to the extra terms. That met the "conditional proviso" of UCC § 2-207(1), the exception for acceptances made conditional on agreement to new terms.

citoh.sentence: Jordan could not simultaneously deny acceptance pending assent and invoke the ordinary rule converting its response into acceptance.
citoh.plain: Jordan could not have it both ways: it could not say 'I am not accepting unless you agree' and also claim its form was an ordinary acceptance that formed a contract including its terms.

citoh.sentence: Section 2-207(3) recognized a contract through both parties’ conduct.
citoh.plain: Section 2-207(3) recognized a contract formed through both parties’ conduct, here by shipping and paying, even when their exchanged forms did not create one.

citoh.sentence: The same subsection limited terms to those agreed in the writings plus applicable supplementary Code provisions.
citoh.plain: The same subsection limited the contract's terms to those the writings agreed on, plus any applicable supplementary Code provisions, the UCC's standard default terms.

citoh.sentence: Supplementary terms meant Article 2’s standardized gap fillers, not a route to reinsert disputed boilerplate just excluded.
citoh.plain: "Supplementary terms" meant Article 2's standardized gap fillers, the Code's built-in rules for missing terms. They were not a way to slip back in disputed "boilerplate" (fine print) just excluded.

citoh.sentence: Even assuming custom or usage could introduce an unagreed term into a subsection (3) contract in ordinary diversity litigation, the FAA independently required a written arbitration agreement.
citoh.plain: Even assuming custom or usage could add an unagreed term to a subsection (3) contract in ordinary "diversity litigation" (a federal case between citizens of different states), the FAA separately required a written arbitration agreement.

cohen-cowles.sentence: The jury awarded $200,000 in compensatory damages jointly and severally, plus $250,000 in punitive damages against each publisher.
cohen-cowles.plain: The jury "awarded" Cohen $200,000 in "compensatory damages" (payment for his actual losses), owed jointly and severally, meaning collectible in full from either newspaper. It added $250,000 in "punitive damages," meant as punishment, against each publisher.

cohen-cowles.sentence: A broken promise did not itself establish an initially false representation of intent.
cohen-cowles.plain: Breaking a promise later does not prove the promise was a lie when made, which fraud requires.

cohen-cowles.sentence: Simonett acknowledged that offer, acceptance, consideration, and breach seemingly appeared.
cohen-cowles.plain: Justice Simonett acknowledged that the elements of a contract seemed present: an "offer," acceptance, consideration (something given in exchange), and "breach," a broken promise.

cohen-cowles.sentence: This was a disputed, context-specific conclusion about intended legal obligation, not a rule against oral agreements or a requirement that every contracting party expressly announce legal intent.
cohen-cowles.plain: The court's point was only that, in the news business, these parties did not mean to make a legally binding deal. It did not say spoken agreements are unenforceable or that parties must announce they intend a binding contract.

cohen-cowles.sentence: It concluded that enforcing the promise here would burden publication of truthful political information and improperly second-guess editorial judgments under the First Amendment.
cohen-cowles.plain: The state court concluded that enforcing the promise here would burden publishing truthful political information and improperly second-guess editors' judgments. That, it said, violated the free-press guarantee of the First Amendment.

cohen-cowles.sentence: The Court first concluded that the federal question was reviewable because Minnesota had actually decided and relied upon it.
cohen-cowles.plain: The Court first concluded that the "federal question," the First Amendment issue, was reviewable because Minnesota's court had actually decided it and relied on it.

cohen-cowles.sentence: Judicial enforcement through state promissory-estoppel law would constitute state action even though Minnesota had found no conventional contract.
cohen-cowles.plain: A court's enforcement of Minnesota's "promissory-estoppel" law (enforcing a promise someone relied on) would be "state action," government conduct subject to the Constitution. That was true even though Minnesota had found no conventional "contract."

cohen-cowles.sentence: He instead held that the Amendment permitted this application of a generally applicable legal doctrine.
cohen-cowles.plain: White instead held that the First Amendment allowed this use of a "generally applicable" legal rule, one that applies to everyone and is not aimed at the press.

cohen-cowles.sentence: White also rejected the contention that Cohen was evading constitutional limits on defamation suits.
cohen-cowles.plain: White also rejected the argument that Cohen was evading the constitutional limits on "defamation" suits, claims for harm to reputation. Cohen sought compensation for a broken promise, such as losing his job, not damages for harm to his reputation.

cohen-cowles.sentence: That directly burdened protected expression rather than incidentally regulating unrelated conduct.
cohen-cowles.plain: The dissenters said that directly burdened protected speech, rather than "regulating" unrelated conduct in a way that only incidentally affected speech.

cohen-cowles.sentence: Simonett’s January 24, 1992 opinion invoked Minnesota’s appellate authority to consider an issue in the interests of justice.
cohen-cowles.plain: Simonett's January 24, 1992 "opinion" relied on the Minnesota court's "appellate" power to consider an issue "in the interests of justice," even though it had not been properly raised below.

cohen-cowles.sentence: The Minnesota court found a clear promise, intended and actual detrimental reliance, and circumstances requiring enforcement to avoid injustice.
cohen-cowles.plain: The Minnesota court found a clear promise, reliance that was both intended and actual and that harmed Cohen ("detrimental reliance"), and circumstances where enforcement was needed to avoid injustice.

cohen-cowles.sentence: The existing $200,000 verdict was therefore adequate under promissory estoppel and did not require retrial.
cohen-cowles.plain: So the existing $200,000 "verdict" was adequate under "promissory estoppel," the rule enforcing promises people rely on, and no "retrial" was needed.

cp-finley.sentence: Almost a year later Finley requested amendment to add the city and utility federally, lacking any independent federal jurisdictional basis for their claims.
cp-finley.plain: Almost a year later, Finley asked to amend her federal complaint to add the city and the power company as defendants. Her claims against them lacked any independent federal "jurisdictional" basis, meaning a separate ground for federal court power.

cp-finley.sentence: The district court relied on United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, shared operative facts and trial efficiency, allowed amendment and certified under § 1292(b).
cp-finley.plain: The district court relied on United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, the shared operative facts, and the efficiency of one trial to allow the "amendment." It then certified the question for immediate appeal under § 1292(b).

cp-finley.sentence: The Ninth Circuit summarily reversed under precedent rejecting pendent-party jurisdiction in FTCA cases.
cp-finley.plain: The Ninth Circuit summarily reversed, following its "precedent" rejecting "pendent-party" jurisdiction in FTCA cases. That means a federal court hearing a suit against the United States cannot add new state-law defendants who lack their own federal basis.

cp-finley.sentence: The Court assumed without deciding that related claims could constitute one constitutional case, but refused to extend Gibbs’s treatment of additional claims between existing parties automatically to new defendants.
cp-finley.plain: The Court "assumed without deciding" that related claims could form one "constitutional case" a federal court may hear. But it refused to automatically extend Gibbs, which allows added claims between existing parties, to new defendants.

cp-finley.sentence: The majority read that as specifying defendants rather than authorizing every lawsuit containing at least one such claim.
cp-finley.plain: The majority read the FTCA's grant as naming the "defendants" it covers, the United States, rather than authorizing every lawsuit containing at least one such claim.

cp-finley.sentence: Rules 14 and 20 permitted procedural impleader and joinder but did not enlarge subject-matter power; Rule 82 expressly preserved the distinction.
cp-finley.plain: Rules 14 and 20 allowed "impleader" (bringing in a third party) and joinder of parties as matters of procedure, but did not enlarge the courts' "subject-matter power" over claims. Rule 82 expressly preserved that distinction.

cp-finley.sentence: The Court regarded it as stylistic conformity with unified civil-action terminology, without a clearly expressed substantive change.
cp-finley.plain: The Court saw the 1948 wording change as stylistic, matching the new unified "civil action" terminology, with no clearly stated "substantive" change in meaning.

cp-finley.sentence: Federal exclusivity strengthened rather than weakened combined jurisdiction because only the federal court could hear the whole constitutional controversy.
cp-finley.plain: Blackmun argued that "Federal exclusivity" (FTCA claims can be heard only in federal court) strengthened the case for combined "jurisdiction." Only the federal court could hear the whole "constitutional controversy" together.

cp-finley.sentence: He also used Yellow Cab and contribution practice to question the majority’s restrictive sovereign-immunity analogy.
cp-finley.plain: Stevens also pointed to Yellow Cab, which lets private defendants bring the United States in to share liability ("contribution"). He used it to question the majority's restrictive comparison to sovereign immunity, the government's protection from suit.

cp-finley.sentence: That later grant supplied what Finley would not infer; it did not retroactively change the judgment or remove every jurisdictional limit.
cp-finley.plain: That later statute supplied the power Finley would not infer, but it did not "retroactively" (backward in time) change the "judgment." Nor did it remove every "jurisdictional" limit.

cp-hess.sentence: Hess was not personally served and had no property attached in the action.
cp-hess.plain: Hess was not "personally served," meaning handed the court papers in Massachusetts, and none of his property was seized ("attached") for the case.

cp-hess.sentence: Massachusetts treated a nonresident’s driving on its public ways as appointing the registrar to receive process for suits arising from an accident during that operation.
cp-hess.plain: Massachusetts treated a nonresident’s driving on its public roads as appointing the state registrar of motor vehicles to receive "process," the lawsuit papers, for suits arising from an accident during that driving.

cp-hess.sentence: Hess appeared specially, without consenting to jurisdiction, and filed an answer in abatement and a dismissal motion.
cp-hess.plain: Hess "appeared specially," coming to court only to challenge its "jurisdiction" without consenting to it. He filed an "answer in abatement" (a plea that the suit should not go forward) and a "dismissal motion."

cp-hess.sentence: The trial court rejected the objection; the Supreme Judicial Court upheld the statute under the State’s public-safety regulatory power.
cp-hess.plain: The trial court rejected his "objection," and the Supreme Judicial Court, Massachusetts' highest court, upheld the statute under the State's power to regulate for public safety.

cp-hess.sentence: Hess renewed his objection at trial and preserved an exception.
cp-hess.plain: Hess renewed his objection at trial and preserved an "exception," a formal record of his objection so he could raise it on appeal.

cp-hess.sentence: Justice Butler began with the rule that one state’s process could not simply summon an absent nonresident into an ordinary personal money action.
cp-hess.plain: Justice Butler began with the rule that one state's "process" (court papers) could not simply summon an absent "nonresident" to defend an ordinary suit seeking money from him personally.

cp-hess.sentence: Ordinary business by a nonresident individual did not itself imply consent to jurisdiction.
cp-hess.plain: Ordinary business by a "nonresident" individual did not by itself "imply consent" to the state's jurisdiction, meaning treat him as having agreed to be sued there.

cp-hess.sentence: Butler found no substantial constitutional difference between that preliminary formality and treating the act of driving as the appointment, with these safeguards and this limited scope.
cp-hess.plain: Since a state could require drivers to sign up an agent before driving, it made no real constitutional difference to treat the driving itself as naming one, given the mailing and delay safeguards and the limit to accident suits.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: Perry orally moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction just before their last witness testified.
cp-mas-perry.plain: Just before the Mases' last witness "testified," Perry orally "moved to dismiss" for lack of subject-matter "jurisdiction," arguing the federal court had no power to hear the case.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: He argued that complete diversity was missing and that Jean Paul’s claim failed the then-applicable requirement that more than $10,000 be in controversy.
cp-mas-perry.plain: Perry argued that "complete diversity," the rule that no plaintiff may share a state of citizenship with any defendant, was missing. He also argued Jean Paul's claim failed the then-required minimum of more than $10,000 in controversy.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: Federal law controlled, and the party invoking jurisdiction bore the burden of pleading citizenship and proving it when properly challenged.
cp-mas-perry.plain: Federal law controlled, and the party invoking federal "jurisdiction" had the burden of "pleading" (stating in its court papers) the parties' citizenship and proving it when properly challenged.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: Jean Paul’s French citizenship supplied an alienage basis for his claim against Perry under § 1332(a)(2).
cp-mas-perry.plain: Jean Paul's French citizenship gave an "alienage" basis for his "claim" against Perry under § 1332(a)(2), which lets federal courts hear cases between a state citizen and a foreign citizen.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: Her longstanding Louisiana residence and work established residence, but the educational character of the stay and absence of intent to remain did not establish replacement of Mississippi domicile.
cp-mas-perry.plain: Judy's long Louisiana stay and work there established "residence," where she lived. But because she was there as a student with no "intent to remain," she had not replaced her Mississippi domicile, her legal home.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: Citizenship was measured when the complaint was filed.
cp-mas-perry.plain: Citizenship was measured on the day the "complaint," the document starting the suit, was filed.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: The opinion acknowledged the then-used generalization that a wife’s domicile followed her husband’s but refused to extend that fiction mechanically here.
cp-mas-perry.plain: The "opinion" noted the generalization then used that a wife's "domicile" (legal home) followed her husband's. But it refused to apply that legal fiction mechanically here.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: The amount claimed in good faith controlled unless it was legally certain that the claim fell below the jurisdictional threshold.
cp-mas-perry.plain: The amount claimed "in good faith" (honestly) controlled unless it was legally certain the claim fell below the "jurisdictional threshold," the minimum amount for federal court.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: Judy’s larger verdict was not simply added to Jean Paul’s award to cure a deficient claim.
cp-mas-perry.plain: Judy's larger "verdict" was not simply added to Jean Paul’s award to fix a claim that fell short of the minimum. Each spouse's claim had to qualify on its own.

cp-mas-perry.sentence: They also distinguish an American truly domiciled abroad, who is neither an alien nor ordinarily a citizen of a U.S. State for diversity, from someone temporarily abroad retaining a state domicile.
cp-mas-perry.plain: They also distinguish an American truly "domiciled" abroad (with a permanent legal home there), who is neither an "alien" (foreign citizen) nor usually a citizen of any U.S. State for diversity purposes. That person differs from someone only temporarily abroad who keeps a home state.

cp-nicastro.sentence: Correspondence suggested that some inventory remained the manufacturer’s property until sale, functioning as consigned stock.
cp-nicastro.plain: Letters suggested that some machines held by the U.S. distributor stayed the manufacturer's property until sold, functioning as "consigned stock," goods left with a seller to sell on the owner's behalf.

cp-nicastro.sentence: McIntyre UK moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction.
cp-nicastro.plain: McIntyre UK, the English maker, moved to dismiss for lack of "personal jurisdiction," arguing New Jersey's courts had no power over it because of its thin ties to the state.

cp-nicastro.sentence: In an unpublished May 26, 2005 decision, the Appellate Division reversed to permit jurisdictional discovery under traditional contacts doctrine, New Jersey’s Charles Gendler rule and O’Connor’s Asahi approach.
cp-nicastro.plain: In an unpublished May 26, 2005 decision, the Appellate Division reversed so Nicastro could take "jurisdictional discovery," gathering evidence about McIntyre's ties to New Jersey. Those ties would be tested under traditional "contacts" doctrine, New Jersey's Charles Gendler rule, and O’Connor’s Asahi approach.

cp-nicastro.sentence: The court found O’Connor’s stream-of-commerce-plus approach satisfied by the exclusive national distributorship, United States conventions, design for American standards and the sale produced through that arrangement.
cp-nicastro.plain: The court found O’Connor’s "stream-of-commerce-plus" test, which requires more than putting products into the national market, satisfied. It pointed to the "exclusive national distributorship" (a single U.S. distributor), United States trade conventions, design for American standards, and the sale made through that arrangement.

cp-nicastro.sentence: A foreign manufacturer could be sued, the court reasoned, when it knew or reasonably should have known that its nationwide distribution system might produce sales in any state and took no reasonable step to exclude New Jersey.
cp-nicastro.plain: New Jersey's highest court said a foreign maker could be sued in any state its nationwide sales system might reach, unless it took reasonable steps to keep its products out of New Jersey.

cp-nicastro.sentence: In an ordinary products case, purposeful availment of that sovereign’s benefits and protections provided the necessary affiliation.
cp-nicastro.plain: In an ordinary products case, "purposeful availment," deliberately taking advantage of that sovereign’s (that state's) benefits and legal protections, provided the needed connection.

cp-nicastro.sentence: The plurality reserved whether Congress could authorize federal jurisdiction under the Fifth Amendment based on aggregate national contacts.
cp-nicastro.plain: The plurality left open whether Congress could authorize federal "jurisdiction" under the Fifth Amendment based on "aggregate national contacts," a company's ties to the United States as a whole.

cp-nicastro.sentence: The concurrence’s narrower factual reasoning cannot be recast as an expressly declared generally controlling Marks holding: the opinion did not decide that question.
cp-nicastro.plain: Under the Marks rule, the narrowest opinion supporting the result in a split decision can count as the Court's holding. But Breyer's concurrence turned on these particular facts and did not declare a general rule, so it cannot simply be treated as the controlling holding.

cp-nicastro.sentence: Asahi concerned a component supplier with limited control and, after settlement, a foreign indemnity dispute.
cp-nicastro.plain: Asahi involved a parts supplier with limited control over where its parts went. After the injured plaintiff settled, all that remained was a foreign "indemnity" dispute over which company should reimburse the other.

cp-smuck.sentence: The district court permitted intervention to let the appellate court determine its propriety.
cp-smuck.plain: The "district court" let the parents intervene, joining the case, so the "appellate court" could decide whether intervention was proper.

cp-smuck.sentence: Damage to his reputation or suggestions about his former tenure did not establish a continuing appealable interest.
cp-smuck.plain: Damage to Hansen's reputation, or suggestions about his former tenure, did not give him a continuing "appealable" interest, a stake that entitles someone to appeal.

cp-smuck.sentence: Being a named trial defendant did not give him a separate right to overturn the institutional decision.
cp-smuck.plain: Being a named trial "defendant" did not give Smuck a separate right to overturn the board's decision as an institution.

cp-smuck.sentence: Under the 1966 version of Rule 24(a)(2), intervention required a related interest, practical impairment of its protection, and inadequate representation by existing parties.
cp-smuck.plain: Under the 1966 version of Rule 24(a)(2), joining a suit as of right ("intervention") required an interest related to the case and a risk the case could practically impair its protection. It also required "inadequate representation" of that interest by the existing parties.

cp-smuck.sentence: A final decree could practically impair these parents’ interest.
cp-smuck.plain: A "final decree" (the court's final order) could in practice impair these parents' interest, because the board would be bound by it.

cp-smuck.sentence: Still, postjudgment timing required attention to the unusual circumstances; an institution’s refusal to appeal did not automatically entitle every dissatisfied citizen to intervene.
cp-smuck.plain: Still, intervening "postjudgment," after the judgment, required attention to the unusual circumstances. A public institution's refusal to appeal did not automatically let every dissatisfied citizen intervene.

cp-smuck.sentence: Bazelon, Leventhal, and Robinson joined Part I, making this intervention explanation a three-judge plurality, not a majority rationale.
cp-smuck.plain: Bazelon, Leventhal, and Robinson "joined" Part I, so this explanation of intervention was a three-judge "plurality," not a majority's reasoning. That means it is not binding as the court's own rule.

cp-smuck.sentence: No modification was necessary to answer challenges the parents had standing to present.
cp-smuck.plain: No change to the order was needed to answer the challenges the parents had "standing" to raise, meaning the objections they were entitled to bring.

cp-smuck.sentence: Burger, joined by Tamm, separately emphasized judicial limits in contested educational policy and regarded the principal opinion’s narrowed construction as essentially advisory.
cp-smuck.plain: Burger, "joined by" Tamm, separately stressed the limits on courts in disputed educational policy. He saw the main opinion's narrowed reading of the order as "essentially advisory," mere advice rather than a binding ruling.

hawkins.sentence: The judge allowed the jury to decide formation and instructed it to consider operative pain and suffering and injury beyond the hand’s prior condition.
hawkins.plain: The judge let the jury decide "formation," whether a binding promise was made. He told it to consider "pain and suffering" from the operation and injury beyond the hand's earlier condition.

hawkins.sentence: The judge later set the verdict aside and regarded an award above $500 as excessive.
hawkins.plain: The judge later set the verdict aside, regarding any "award" above $500 as "excessive," meaning too much.

hawkins.sentence: The judge initially decides whether words can reasonably bear the asserted contractual meaning; the jury then decides whether they were spoken and what the circumstances establish.
hawkins.plain: The judge first decides whether the words can reasonably carry the claimed "contractual" meaning, a binding promise. The jury then decides whether they were said and what the circumstances show.

hawkins.sentence: If McGee objectively promised the result and Hawkins relied on that manifestation, a private reservation did not undo it.
hawkins.plain: If McGee objectively promised the result and Hawkins relied on that "manifestation," the outward expression of a promise as a reasonable listener would understand it, McGee's private reservations did not undo it.

hawkins.sentence: If McGee promised a good or perfect hand, damages measured the value to Hawkins of that hand against the actual hand, with incidental consequences fairly within the parties’ contemplation.
hawkins.plain: If McGee promised a good or perfect hand, "damages" were the value to Hawkins of that hand minus the value of the hand he actually got. He could also recover incidental losses fairly within the "parties’ contemplation," meaning ones both sides could have foreseen.

hawkins.sentence: Conversely, if the hand became worse, the promised-versus-actual difference already included that worsening; adding it separately duplicated recovery.
hawkins.plain: If the hand became worse, the promised-versus-actual difference already counted that harm. Adding it separately would be "duplicated recovery," paying Hawkins twice.

hawkins.sentence: The court used an analogy to a machine warranted to perform a specified function: the bargain protects the promised performance, rather than merely returning the recipient’s contribution.
hawkins.plain: The court compared a machine guaranteed to do a specified job. The "bargain" protects the promised "performance," what was promised, rather than merely returning what the recipient gave.

hawkins.sentence: On June 4, 1929, the Supreme Court ordered a new trial, sustaining the possibility of a contract while requiring a different damages assessment.
hawkins.plain: On June 4, 1929, the Supreme Court ordered a new trial, "sustaining" (upholding) the possibility that a contract existed while requiring damages to be calculated differently.

kenford.sentence: Kenford and DSI sued in June for specific performance or $90 million, later increasing their damages demand to $495 million.
kenford.plain: Kenford and DSI "sued" in June for "specific performance," a court order forcing the County to go through with the deal, or $90 million. They later raised their "damages" demand to $495 million.

kenford.sentence: Liability was established on summary judgment.
kenford.plain: "Liability," the County's legal responsibility for breaking the contract, was established on "summary judgment," without a trial, leaving only the amount of damages.

kenford.sentence: In 1985, the Appellate Division sustained much of Kenford’s reliance and mitigation recovery, rejected some expenses and DSI’s lost profits, and ordered a new trial on the amount of land appreciation.
kenford.plain: In 1985, the Appellate Division upheld much of Kenford's recovery for money spent relying on the deal and for "mitigation" (efforts to limit its losses). It rejected some expenses and DSI's lost profits, and ordered a new trial on the amount of land appreciation.

kenford.sentence: The Appellate Division affirmed in 1988; two justices concurred only because its 1985 recoverability ruling was law of the case.
kenford.plain: The Appellate Division affirmed in 1988. Two justices "concurred" (agreed with the result) only because the court's 1985 ruling that appreciation was recoverable was "law of the case," binding later stages of the same case.

kenford.sentence: The County’s appeal from the final order brought up the necessarily affecting 1985 nonfinal order under Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5601(d).
kenford.plain: The County's appeal from the "final order" also brought up the 1985 nonfinal order, because that earlier ruling necessarily affected the final one, under Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5601(d).

kenford.sentence: Designated Judge Mollen explained that ordinary damages compensate natural and probable consequences, while extraordinary losses require contemplation at or before formation as a probable result of breach.
kenford.plain: Designated Judge Mollen, a judge assigned to sit on the court, explained that ordinary "damages" pay for the natural and probable results of a breach. "Extraordinary losses" are recoverable only if, at or before the contract was formed, both sides contemplated them as a probable result of breach.

kenford.sentence: The court agreed that appreciation was foreseen, but distinguished anticipating a benefit from promising compensation if it failed to materialize.
kenford.plain: Everyone expected the land to rise in value, but expecting a gain is different from the County promising to pay Kenford if the gain never came.

kenford.sentence: The Court of Appeals held peripheral-land appreciation unrecoverable as a matter of law because the County had not reasonably contemplated liability for it.
kenford.plain: The Court of Appeals, New York's highest court, held the rise in value of the surrounding ("peripheral") land unrecoverable as a matter of law. The County had not reasonably "contemplated" (foreseen and accepted) liability for it.

kenford.sentence: This ruling rested on assumed liability, without separately deciding that the retrial appraisal failed reasonable certainty.
kenford.plain: This ruling rested on what "liability" the County had assumed. It did not separately decide that the retrial's land appraisal failed the "reasonable certainty" standard for proving damages.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: Seaboard obtained coal while avoiding much of the investment and operational profit-or-loss exposure of running a mine.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Seaboard got its coal without putting money into mining equipment or bearing the risk of profit or loss from running a mine.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: It exempted coal consumed by its producer or transported by the producer to itself for consumption.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: The law "exempted" coal (left it outside the law's coverage) when the company that produced it used it itself, or shipped it to itself to use.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: The Supreme Court initially affirmed by an equally divided vote, then granted rehearing.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: The Supreme Court at first "affirmed" (left the lower court's ruling in place) by an "equally divided" vote, meaning the Justices split evenly and wrote no opinion. It then "granted" rehearing, agreeing to hear the case again.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: The statute made supported agency findings of fact conclusive.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Under the statute, courts had to accept the agency's conclusions about the facts if evidence supported them.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: But the absence of factual disputes did not mean judges should independently redo every application of the word producer.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Even though the facts were undisputed, judges should not decide afresh whether Seaboard counted as a 'producer'; Congress left that judgment to the agency.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: A classification would stand unless it was so unrelated to the assigned statutory task that it denied a sensible exercise of that judgment.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Courts would uphold the agency's classification unless it was so far from what the statute asked the agency to do that it could not be a sensible judgment.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: The scheme placed covered coal under the code or subjected relevant non-code dispositions to a 19½-percent excise.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Under the scheme, covered coal was either sold under the price code or, if disposed of outside the code in a relevant way, hit with a 19½-percent "excise," a tax on the transaction.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: On an undisputed record, he regarded producer status as statutory construction that courts were authorized and obliged to review.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Justice Roberts thought that, since the facts were undisputed, whether Seaboard was a "producer" was a matter of "statutory construction," meaning what the statute's words mean. He believed courts were both allowed and required to decide that question for themselves.

lrs-i-gray-powell.sentence: Justice Kagan’s dissent emphasized the agency’s interpretive responsibility and the significance of pre-Administrative Procedure Act practice.
lrs-i-gray-powell.plain: Justice Kagan, dissenting in Loper Bright, stressed the agency's responsibility for interpreting the statute it administers. She also stressed how courts acted before the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946, the general federal law on agency procedure, reading Gray as showing courts already left some interpretation to agencies.

lrs-k-mcboyle.sentence: The government’s necessary reading put a self-propelled airplane within the residual phrase: it transports people or things and does not run on rails.
lrs-k-mcboyle.plain: For the conviction to stand, the government had to argue that an airplane fits the catchall words 'any other self-propelled vehicle not designed to run on rails'.

lrs-k-mcboyle.sentence: The catchall enlarged membership in that category without necessarily abandoning it.
lrs-k-mcboyle.plain: The catchall phrase added more land vehicles to the list, but did not stretch it to things outside land transport.

lrs-k-mcboyle.sentence: This was the operation commonly called ejusdem generis: interpreting general residual language in light of the kind specifically listed.
lrs-k-mcboyle.plain: This was the method called "ejusdem generis," Latin for "of the same kind." It reads "residual language," the general catch-all words at the end of a list, as covering only things like the specific items listed.

lrs-k-mcboyle.sentence: Actual reliance by McBoyle therefore was unnecessary: fair warning constrained judicial enlargement of the prohibition itself.
lrs-k-mcboyle.plain: It therefore did not matter whether McBoyle actually relied on, or even read, the law. The "fair warning" principle limits courts themselves: they may not enlarge a criminal prohibition beyond what its words clearly say.

lrs-k-mcboyle.sentence: Neither shared policy nor speculation about an unmade legislative choice could replace the warning given by the enacted words.
lrs-k-mcboyle.plain: Sharing the same policy goal was not enough, and neither was "speculation" (guessing) that Congress would have covered planes had it thought of them. Only the words actually "enacted" (passed into law) give the required warning.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: Using notice and comment, USDA adopted a structural-strength regulation requiring appropriately constructed, structurally sound, and maintained housing facilities that protected and contained the animals.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: Using "notice and comment" (publishing a draft and inviting public comments), USDA adopted a "regulation," a binding rule, on structural strength.
