It required animal housing to be appropriately built, structurally sound and maintained, so it protected the animals and kept them contained.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: Hoctor limited his judicial challenge to the fence requirement, and both parties agreed that this part of the sanction depended on the memorandum’s validity as an interpretive rule.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: Hoctor challenged in court only the fence requirement, one part of his "sanction" (penalty). Both "parties" (the two sides) agreed that this part depended on whether the memo was a valid "interpretive rule," one that merely explains an existing rule and so can skip public comment.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) generally required notice and comment for legislative rules while exempting interpretative rules and general policy statements.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA), the federal law on agency procedure, generally required notice and comment before an agency issued "legislative rules," meaning new binding rules. It exempted "interpretative rules," which merely explain existing law, and general policy statements, which announce agency plans.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: But selecting a new binding standard under delegated legislative authority required participation and a statement of basis and purpose.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: But choosing a new binding standard using "delegated legislative authority" (lawmaking power Congress handed to the agency) required public participation. It also required a statement of the rule's basis and purpose.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: USDA invoked deference to its interpretation of its own regulation.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: USDA invoked "deference," asking the court to accept the agency's own reading of its own "regulation" (binding rule).

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: More fundamentally, consistency with the regulation was insufficient: the new requirement had to be derivable through a process reasonably described as interpretation.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: More fundamentally, it was not enough that eight feet was consistent with the "regulation." The new requirement had to be derivable from the rule through a process fairly called interpretation, not simply newly chosen.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: Assuming authority to require eight feet therefore established possible power to legislate, not an exemption from the method of legislating.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: So even assuming USDA had authority to require eight-foot fences, that showed only a possible power to make such a rule. It did not give an "exemption" (a release) from the proper procedure for making rules.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: A rebuttable rule of thumb might also remain connected to the underlying standard.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: A "rebuttable" rule of thumb, one a dealer could overcome by showing its fence was secure enough, might still stay tied to the underlying standard and so count as interpretation.

lrs-n-hoctor.sentence: The Seventh Circuit vacated the Department’s order insofar as it rested on the eight-foot perimeter-fence requirement.
lrs-n-hoctor.plain: The Seventh Circuit, the federal appeals court, "vacated" (cancelled) the Department’s "order," its decision imposing the penalty, to the extent the order rested on the eight-foot perimeter-fence requirement.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: Officers, directors, and controlling shareholders associated with the Chenery group controlled Federal through Utility Operators Company, which held all its controlling Class B common stock.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: Officers, "directors" (board members) and controlling shareholders linked to the Chenery group controlled Federal through Utility Operators Company. That company held all of Federal's Class B "common stock," the class of shares that carried voting control.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: It reasoned that those directing a reorganization were fiduciaries subject to equitable restrictions against such trading.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: The SEC reasoned that those directing a reorganization were fiduciaries, owing trustee-like duties of loyalty. It said "equitable" restrictions, traditional court-made fairness rules, barred them from such trading in the company's shares.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: The plan was amended to require surrender of their shares at cost plus four-percent interest instead of conversion into new equity.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: The plan was "amended" (changed) so the managers had to surrender their preferred shares for what they paid plus four-percent interest, instead of converting them into new stock like other holders.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: But identifying a fiduciary relationship did not specify its beneficiary, the particular obligation, its breach, or the consequence of breach.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: But saying a "fiduciary relationship" (a duty of trust) exists did not identify its "beneficiary," the person owed the duty. Nor did it say what the duty required, whether there was a "breach" (violation), or what the consequence of a breach should be.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: The majority read the SEC’s explanation as invoking existing judicial equity rules, particularly an analogy to trustees dealing with trust property, rather than announcing an independent administrative policy under the Act.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: The "majority" (the Justices deciding the case) read the SEC as relying on existing "equity rules," old court-made fairness rules, especially an analogy to trustees dealing with trust property. It did not read the SEC as announcing its own independent policy under the 1935 Act.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: The defect was that the agency had not exercised that administrative judgment as the basis of the order under review.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: The defect was that the "agency," the SEC, had not actually used that kind of policy judgment as the basis for the order under review, even if it might have had the power to.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: An appellate court may sometimes affirm a judicial judgment on another legal ground within its own authority, but cannot supply an unmade jury finding.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: An "appellate court" (a court hearing an appeal) may sometimes "affirm," or uphold, a lower court's "judgment" (final ruling) on a different legal ground within its own authority. But it cannot make a factual finding that a jury never made.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: Agency counsel’s alternative defense could not replace responsible agency action.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: The SEC's lawyers offered an alternative "defense," a different justification for the order. It could not replace responsible "agency action," meaning reasons the agency itself actually adopted.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: Review had to proceed on grounds the record showed the agency actually relied upon, sufficiently disclosed and supported to permit judicial examination.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: Judicial "Review" of the order had to rest on grounds the record showed the agency actually relied on. Those grounds had to be disclosed and supported clearly enough for a court to examine them.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: Nor did the opinion impose an unconditional rule that new policy must always originate through prospective rulemaking.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: Nor did the "opinion" (the Court's written decision) set an absolute rule that new policy must always come through "prospective" rulemaking, meaning general rules that apply only going forward. Policy could also come case by case.

lrs-o-chenery-i.sentence: The first decision’s allocation of responsibility applies beyond notice-and-comment rulemaking even though the casebook places it in a rulemaking chapter: the action here was adjudicatory.
lrs-o-chenery-i.plain: The first Chenery decision's rule on who must supply the reasons applies beyond "notice-and-comment" rulemaking (rules made after public comment), even though the casebook puts it in a rulemaking chapter. The SEC's action here was "adjudicatory": a decision about one company's specific plan.

tolosa.sentence: A promissory note evidenced the debt and a deed of trust secured it.
tolosa.plain: A "promissory note," a signed written promise to repay, showed the debt. A "deed of trust" secured it, letting the lender sell the house if the borrowers did not pay.

tolosa.sentence: For the issue reproduced in the assigned opinion, they alleged that HSBC had promised not to foreclose while reviewing a loan modification.
tolosa.plain: On the issue covered in the assigned "opinion," the borrowers alleged that HSBC had promised not to "foreclose" (sell the house to collect the debt) while it reviewed a loan "modification," a change to the loan's terms. This was alleged, not proven.

tolosa.sentence: HSBC removed on diversity grounds and moved to dismiss, arguing among other things that the statute of frauds barred all the claims.
tolosa.plain: HSBC "removed" the case to federal court on diversity grounds, because the parties were from different states, and "moved to dismiss" (asked the court to end the case). It argued, among other things, that the "statute of frauds," the rule that certain promises must be in a signed writing, barred all the claims.

tolosa.sentence: The statutory definition of a loan agreement included a financial institution’s promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation.
tolosa.plain: The "statutory" definition of a "loan agreement," the one in the Texas law, included a financial institution's promise to delay repayment. It also included a promise to make a "financial accommodation," some other financial break for the borrower.

tolosa.sentence: Relying on Burnette v. Wells Fargo Bank and Ford v. City State Bank of Palacios as authorities for the exception, it required a promise to sign a written document that would satisfy the statute of frauds.
tolosa.plain: Relying on Burnette v. Wells Fargo Bank and Ford v. City State Bank of Palacios, the court held that promissory estoppel gets around the "statute of frauds" (the signed-writing requirement) in only one situation: the lender must have promised to sign a written document that would itself satisfy the statute.

tolosa.sentence: It applied that requirement whether estoppel was an affirmative claim or an answer to the statutory defense.
tolosa.plain: The court applied that requirement whether promissory estoppel was used as an "affirmative claim" (the borrowers' own claim for relief) or as an answer to HSBC's "statutory" defense, the statute of frauds.

tolosa.sentence: It does not specify dismissal with or without prejudice, award damages, describe an appeal, or separately dispose of costs.
tolosa.plain: The order does not say whether the "dismissal" is with or "without prejudice," that is, whether the borrowers may refile. It awards no damages, says nothing about an appeal, and does not separately deal with costs.

austin.sentence: The Court of Appeals had to decide whether the established circumstances amounted to economic duress, whether Loral had to pursue additional sources or a Navy extension, and whether waiting until final delivery ratified the coerced modification.
austin.plain: New York's Court of Appeals, its highest court, had to decide whether the facts amounted to "economic duress," a wrongful threat leaving no real choice. It also asked whether Loral first had to seek other suppliers or a Navy extension, and whether waiting until final delivery "ratified" (accepted) the forced price change.

austin.sentence: A contract was voidable when a wrongful threat deprived the threatened party of meaningful voluntary choice.
austin.plain: A pressured party may undo a contract if it agreed only because the other side made a wrongful threat that left it no real free choice.

austin.sentence: In this setting, threatening to withhold goods already owed was not enough by itself; the buyer also needed to show that suitable replacements were unavailable in the relevant time and an ordinary breach action was inadequate.
austin.plain: Here, threatening to withhold "goods" (the parts) already owed was not enough by itself. The buyer, Loral, also had to show it could not get suitable replacements in time, and that an ordinary lawsuit for breach would not have been an adequate remedy.

austin.sentence: The majority treated that threatened breach as wrongful, then examined Loral’s alternatives.
austin.plain: The majority treated Austin's threatened "breach" (failing to deliver as the contract required) as wrongful, because Austin used owed deliveries as leverage. It then examined whether Loral had realistic alternatives.

austin.sentence: Accepting the demanded prices to secure delivery and then seeking repayment of the excess was therefore a permissible response to duress, not conclusive proof of free agreement.
austin.plain: So Loral could accept the demanded prices to keep the parts coming and later sue to recover the excess. That was a permitted response to "duress" (wrongful pressure), not conclusive proof that Loral freely agreed.

austin.sentence: Prompt disaffirmance ordinarily mattered, but the pressure continued while Austin retained critical obligations under the second subcontract.
austin.plain: Normally a pressured party must "disaffirm," or reject, the forced deal promptly. But the pressure continued while Austin still owed critical deliveries under the second "subcontract," so objecting three days after the last delivery was soon enough.

austin.sentence: Whether the conduct actually produced economic duress was, in their view, a factual issue resolved against Loral at trial and affirmed below.
austin.plain: The three dissenters saw whether the conduct actually caused "economic duress" as a "factual issue," a question about what happened rather than about the law. The trial court had decided it against Loral and the Appellate Division "affirmed" (upheld) that, so in their view the high court should have left it alone.

austin.sentence: The four-to-three division therefore concerned application of duress and the limits of appellate review, not whether economic duress existed as a doctrine.
austin.plain: So the four-to-three split was about how duress applied to these facts and the limits of "appellate" review (how far an appeals court may second-guess lower courts). It was not about whether economic duress exists as a doctrine; all seven judges accepted that it does.

austin.sentence: On July 6, 1971, after argument on May 12, the Court modified the order with costs: it reversed the part affirming dismissal of Loral’s claim and otherwise affirmed.
austin.plain: On July 6, 1971, after argument on May 12, the Court "modified" the lower court's "order" and awarded costs. It "reversed" (overturned) the part "affirming" dismissal of Loral's claim to recover the price increases, sending it back to fix damages, and otherwise affirmed, so Austin kept its recovery on the second subcontract.

austin.sentence: UCC § 2-209 removes the need for new consideration, but duress remains available through § 1-103(b), and Comment 2 to § 2-209 requires good faith.
austin.plain: UCC § 2-209, the sales-code rule on contract changes, removes the need for "new consideration" (something new given in exchange). But the general duress defense still applies through § 1-103(b), and Comment 2 to § 2-209 requires that changes be sought in good faith, so a coerced change can still be attacked.

austin.sentence: The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework maps coerced assent and absence of reasonable alternatives to § 175, and wrongful threatened breach to § 176(1)(d).
austin.plain: The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework fits this case. Section 175 covers coerced "assent" (agreement forced by a threat) where there is no reasonable alternative, and § 176(1)(d) treats a wrongful threatened "breach" of contract as an improper threat.

brief-CP-115.sentence: A separate suit against her grandmother’s estate had already ended in an affirmed directed defense verdict; that was background, not the judgment now under review.
brief-CP-115.plain: A separate suit against her grandmother's estate had already ended in a directed verdict for the defense, where the judge decided without the jury, and that was "affirmed" (upheld) on appeal. That case is background, not the "judgment" now under "review."

brief-CP-115.sentence: The jury awarded Betty $5,000, but the trial court granted judgment notwithstanding the verdict.
brief-CP-115.plain: The jury awarded Betty $5,000, but the "trial court" granted judgment notwithstanding the verdict. That means the judge overrode the jury and ruled for the defense, finding the evidence could not legally support a win for her.

brief-CP-115.sentence: Buckley’s continuous observation over the shorter interval was competent; his inconsistency went to credibility.
brief-CP-115.plain: Buckley watched the car right up until the crash, so his testimony was usable evidence. That he had earlier said he could not estimate its speed only affected how far the jury should believe him, not whether it could hear him.

brief-CP-115.sentence: His testimony could establish excessive and negligent speed, but Betty also had to prove by a preponderance that negligence proximately contributed to her injury.
brief-CP-115.plain: His "testimony" (sworn account) could show Ross drove excessively and negligently fast. But Betty also had to prove by a "preponderance," meaning more likely than not, that this negligence was a proximate (legally close enough) cause contributing to her injury.

brief-CP-115.sentence: Excessive speed might have contributed under some imagined sequences, but the proof gave no sound basis to select one over competing possibilities.
brief-CP-115.plain: One could imagine ways in which speeding caused the collision, but nothing in the evidence made those versions more likely than other explanations, so a verdict for Betty would rest on guesswork.

brief-CP-115.sentence: The absence of defense evidence did not relieve Betty of proving causation.
brief-CP-115.plain: The defense offered no evidence, but that did not relieve Betty, the plaintiff, of proving "causation": that the speeding actually caused her injury.

brief-CP-115.sentence: The court did not find her grandmother responsible or prohibit causal proof by circumstantial evidence generally; it found this record insufficient.
brief-CP-115.plain: The court did not find her grandmother responsible. Nor did it bar "causal" proof (proof of what caused the crash) by "circumstantial evidence," meaning indirect evidence, in general; it held only that this record was not enough.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: The then-applicable procedure allowed forfeiture of covered property worth no more than $100,000 without a judicial case if nobody timely claimed it after publication, with written notice to apparent interested persons.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: Under the procedure then in force, the government could take covered property worth no more than $100,000 by "forfeiture" (loss of ownership to the government) without a court case. It had to publish notice and send written notice to people who appeared to have an interest, and no one could have filed a "timely" claim, one within the deadline.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: The district court rejected the motion as inappropriate in a closed prosecution.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: The "district court" (the federal trial court) rejected Dusenbery's "motion," his formal request under the criminal-procedure rule, as inappropriate because his "prosecution" (criminal case) was already closed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: The Sixth Circuit required construing it as a civil complaint for equitable relief concerning notice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: The Sixth Circuit, the federal appeals court, required the trial court to treat the filing as a civil complaint seeking "equitable relief" (a court order to fix a wrong, rather than money) about the government's notice.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: The district court nevertheless granted the government summary judgment on cash notice, and the Sixth Circuit affirmed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: The "district court" nevertheless granted the government "summary judgment," a ruling without trial, holding its notice about the cash adequate even without proof he personally got the letter. The Sixth Circuit affirmed (upheld) that ruling.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas, applied the notice standard from Mullane: a method reasonably calculated under the circumstances to inform the interested person.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: Chief Justice Rehnquist, "joined by" O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas (they signed his opinion), applied the notice test from Mullane. Notice must use a method "reasonably calculated," under the circumstances, to inform the interested person; it must be reasonable, not perfect.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: He rejected Dusenbery’s proposed use of Mathews v. Eldridge’s broader procedural balancing framework as an all-purpose formula.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: He rejected Dusenbery's request to use Mathews v. Eldridge’s broader "balancing" test as an all-purpose formula. That test weighs the person's interest, the risk of error, and the cost of extra safeguards; the Court said it is not the tool for judging notice.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: The majority regarded that chiefly as proving receipt, which was not constitutionally indispensable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: The majority saw Dusenbery's proposed procedure as mainly a way to prove the prisoner actually received the letter. Proof of actual receipt is not constitutionally "indispensable," meaning the Constitution does not require it.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: Later government improvements did not prove the earlier system unconstitutional, much as later remedial measures did not automatically establish prior fault.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: That the prisons later tightened their mail procedures did not show the old system was unconstitutional, just as fixing a hazard after an accident does not by itself prove you were careless before.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.sentence: She distinguished the common-trust proceeding in Mullane, where another beneficiary might raise a shared objection and a court reviewed the accounting.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-076.plain: Justice Ginsburg distinguished Mullane's "common-trust proceeding," a court case settling a pooled trust fund. There, another beneficiary might raise the same "objection" for someone who missed notice, and a court reviewed the trust's "accounting" (its financial records) anyway.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Smoking Everywhere disputed authorization, assent, formality, consideration, authority, and various performance defenses.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Smoking Everywhere disputed whether the changes were authorized, whether there was "assent" (true agreement), whether they had the required signed form, and whether there was consideration (something new given in exchange). It also disputed Touris's authority to agree and raised various defenses about CX's performance.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: His private understanding could not negate implemented conduct, and agreement did not require identification of one precise formation instant.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Contract law looks at outward conduct, so Touris's private understanding could not cancel the fact that the changes were put into effect. And proving agreement did not require pinpointing one exact instant of "formation," the moment the contract was made.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: It was a counteroffer accepted by reply and immediate performance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Touris's reply was a "counteroffer," a new offer with different terms (unlimited volume but no exclusivity). CX accepted it by replying and by immediate "performance," promptly sending more customers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Intermittent office responses within the day-long conversation did not cause lapse, and no persuasive alternative topic explained Touris’s response.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Pauses in the day-long chat did not mean the proposal had expired before Touris answered it, and there was no convincing claim that his 'no limit' referred to something else.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Because the contract concerned services, Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209’s goods rule did not apply.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Because the contract was for services, not goods, Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209, which governs changes to contracts for goods, did not apply. Ordinary common-law contract rules applied instead.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Under the Delaware common-law rule applied, parties could waive a signed-modification requirement by subsequent agreement or conduct, as implementation showed here.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Under the Delaware "common-law" rule the court applied (judge-made law, not a statute), parties could waive a "signed-modification requirement," a clause saying changes need a signed writing. They can do so by later agreement or conduct, as putting the changes into effect showed here.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: No statute of frauds independently required signed changes; such an affirmative defense also had not been pleaded.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: No "statute of frauds" (a law requiring certain deals to be in a signed writing) separately required signed changes. And that "affirmative defense," one the defendant must raise and prove itself, had not been pleaded anyway.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Alternatively, Smoking Everywhere’s participation and accepted performance supported estoppel after CX Digital materially changed position by directing and paying affiliates.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Alternatively, Smoking Everywhere’s participation and its acceptance of the extra "performance" supported estoppel, barring it from denying the changes. CX Digital had "materially changed position," meaning it significantly relied to its detriment, by directing and paying affiliates.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Increased Sales exchanged for existing-rate payments supplied volume consideration.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: The volume change had consideration: CX provided something new, many more sales, in exchange for the client's continued payment of $45 for each.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Changed URLs supplied none independently, but material reliance supported enforcement under Restatement § 89.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: The changed URLs (web addresses) gave the client nothing new in exchange, so they supplied no consideration on their own. But under Restatement § 89, a change to an ongoing contract can still be enforced when the other side relied on it materially, as CX did.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: Touris had apparent authority: the company presented him as its advertising vice-president, let him sign the original order, and had him implement changes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: Touris had "apparent authority": the company's own conduct made it reasonable to believe he could agree to changes. It presented him as its advertising vice-president, let him sign the original "order," and had him put the changes into effect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: The court rejected frustration and an implied-duty theory aimed at conduct the modified bargain authorized.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: The court rejected the client's frustration defense (that the deal's purpose had been defeated) and an implied-duty theory. Both targeted conduct that the "modified" (changed) bargain itself authorized, such as the higher volume.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.sentence: That second printed base exceeds remaining principal after the August balance by $5,000; the opinion’s stated figure is preserved rather than silently recalculated.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-053.plain: The opinion's second figure for the amount earning interest is $5,000 more than the principal actually left after the August amount; this account repeats the court's printed number rather than quietly correcting it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: These allegations were accepted for dismissal analysis, not found true.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: These "allegations" (claims not yet proven) were treated as true only to test, on the motion to dismiss, whether they state a legal claim. They were not found true.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Although the complaint named negligence, intentional and malicious conduct, and unjust enrichment, Hakimoglu consolidated the theories into a common-law dram-shop claim.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: The "complaint" (the papers starting the suit) named negligence, intentional and "malicious" (spiteful) conduct, and "unjust enrichment," keeping a benefit unfairly. But Hakimoglu combined these theories into one "common-law dram-shop claim": that the casino, like a bar, was liable for harm from serving alcohol to someone visibly drunk.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Hakimoglu defended the credit obligation on intoxication-based incapacity, distinct from an affirmative tort right to recover money already lost.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Against the casino's claim on his credit, Hakimoglu argued "incapacity": that he was too drunk to make a binding deal. That defense to paying differs from an affirmative "tort" claim (a suit for a civil wrong) to "recover" money he had already lost.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: The Third Circuit’s September 6 decision in Greate Bay Hotel & Casino v. Tose then held that the Casino Control Commission lacked exclusive primary jurisdiction over such disputes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: The Third Circuit’s September 6 decision in Greate Bay Hotel & Casino v. Tose then held that the Casino Control Commission, New Jersey's casino regulator, lacked exclusive "primary jurisdiction" over such disputes. So these disputes need not go to the Commission first; courts can hear them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Rule 12(b)(1)’s jurisdictional question differed from Rule 12(b)(6)’s sufficiency inquiry.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Rule 12(b)(1) asks a jurisdictional question: does the court have power to hear the case? Rule 12(b)(6) asks a different sufficiency question: does the complaint describe a claim the law recognizes? Greate Bay answered only the first.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Sitting in diversity, the court had to predict New Jersey law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Sitting "in diversity," hearing the case only because the parties were from different states, the federal court had to "predict New Jersey law." That means forecasting how New Jersey's highest court would decide this new question.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Miller v. Zoby had rejected an implied damages remedy for casino-credit regulation violations without legislative intent.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Miller v. Zoby, an earlier New Jersey case, had rejected an "implied" damages remedy (a right to sue that the rules do not state) for violations of casino-credit regulations. It did so because there was no "legislative intent," no sign the legislature meant to create one.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Taj Mahal argued that equitable estoppel barred incapacity because Hakimoglu had consulted counsel and threatened alcohol-related gambling litigation against Caesars shortly before returning to Taj Mahal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Taj Mahal argued that "equitable estoppel," a fairness rule barring a party from a position that unfairly misled another, blocked the incapacity defense. Hakimoglu had consulted "counsel" (a lawyer) and threatened alcohol-related gambling litigation against Caesars shortly before returning to Taj Mahal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Yet it required justified, reasonable detrimental reliance by an innocent party, not simply substantial reliance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Yet estoppel required "detrimental reliance," meaning reliance that harmed an innocent party, and that reliance had to be justified and reasonable. Simply showing substantial reliance was not enough.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: The surrounding circumstances and the casino’s knowledge presented genuine issues, without establishing either that the warning occurred at a relevant time or that estoppel could never succeed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: What the casino knew, and when, were real factual disputes, so the court could not decide the estoppel question without a trial either way.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: If incapacity failed, Taj Mahal could recover that sum; if it succeeded, the casino could recover neither the money nor compensation for consumed atmosphere.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: If the incapacity defense failed, Taj Mahal could "recover" (collect) the $700,000. If it succeeded, the casino could recover neither the money nor any compensation for the gambling atmosphere he had enjoyed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Under Rule 54(b), the court found no just reason to delay final judgment on the separate claims.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Normally only a "final judgment" ending the whole case can be appealed. Under Rule 54(b), the court found no just reason to delay final judgment on Hakimoglu's separate dismissed claims, letting him appeal while the casino's claim continued.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Visible, obvious intoxication under the proposed tort theory did not alone prove contractual incapacity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: Visible, obvious "intoxication" (drunkenness) might count under the proposed bar-style "tort" theory, but it did not alone prove "contractual incapacity." That requires being so drunk one could not understand the deal.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.sentence: Novel recurring state-law questions and lack of cognizable prejudice supported certification.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-032.plain: The judge certified the early appeal (allowed it to go forward now) because the state-law questions were new and likely to recur. There was also no "cognizable" prejudice, meaning no harm the law recognizes, from letting it proceed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: The Ballards alleged a $93,840 loss, of which the district had paid $20,000, and sought equitable reformation of the writings.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: The Ballards "alleged" (claimed, not yet proven) a $93,840 loss, of which the district had paid $20,000. They sought "equitable" reformation, a fairness-based remedy in which the court corrects the written documents to match what both sides actually agreed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: The district court dismissed for failure to state a claim, relying on Procurement Code § 13-1-106’s restriction on changing bids after opening.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: The "district court" (the trial court) dismissed for "failure to state a claim," meaning that even if true the facts gave no legal right to relief. It relied on Procurement Code § 13-1-106, the public-purchasing rule restricting changes to bids after they are opened.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: On appeal, the Supreme Court accepted well-pleaded facts under the historical Rule 1-012(B)(6) standard and asked whether any provable facts within the claim could permit relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: On "appeal," the Supreme Court accepted the "well-pleaded facts" (facts properly alleged in the complaint) as true under the then-applicable Rule 1-012(B)(6) standard. It asked whether any facts provable under the "claim" could entitle the Ballards to "relief," a legal remedy.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: The Ballards therefore sought correction of existing writings rather than permission to alter the price of an open bid.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: Once the bid was accepted and a contract signed, the Ballards were not trying to change their bid; they were asking to fix a signed contract that recorded the deal wrongly.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: The district’s immunity argument under § 37-1-23 also failed: the contract and change order were both written.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: The district's immunity argument under § 37-1-23 also failed. That law shields public bodies from contract suits only when there is no valid written contract, and here both the contract and the change order were written.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: Section 157 makes failure to discover facts disqualifying only if it falls below good faith and reasonable fair-dealing standards.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: Section 157 of the Restatement makes a party's failure to discover the facts disqualifying only if it falls below standards of "good faith" (honesty) and reasonable fair dealing. Mere carelessness in missing the mistake is not enough.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: An ordinary duty to read therefore did not categorically bar the alleged double-subtraction claim.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: So an ordinary "duty to read," the rule that you are bound by what you sign whether you read it or not, did not automatically "bar" (block) the Ballards' claim about the alleged double subtraction.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.sentence: On January 12, 1994, Justice Frost, joined by Chief Justice Ransom and Justice Montgomery, reversed and set aside dismissal without deciding the merits.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-074.plain: On January 12, 1994, Justice Frost, "joined by" Chief Justice Ransom and Justice Montgomery (they agreed with his opinion), "reversed" and set aside the "dismissal." The court did so without deciding "the merits," meaning whether the Ballards should ultimately win.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.sentence: The chapter reports that the Court of Cassation treated the minimal nature of the difference between promised and actual work as irrelevant to that refusal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.plain: The chapter reports that France's Court of Cassation, its highest court for such cases, treated as irrelevant how small the difference was between the promised and the actual work. The lower court could not refuse to order the work corrected for that reason.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.sentence: That citation remains an unverified identity lead because the full actual judgment has not been recovered.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.plain: That citation is still only an unverified lead to which case this is, because the full "judgment" (the court's actual decision) has not been "recovered," meaning found and read.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.sentence: Nearby scholarly debate about later proportionality reform is not a separate opinion in this case and does not show that the 1977 court applied the later rule.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-013.plain: French law later added a proportionality rule letting courts refuse a fix whose cost is clearly out of proportion to its benefit. Nearby scholarly debate about that reform is not a separate "opinion" (a judge's written view) in this case, and it does not show the 1977 court applied the later rule.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: The Dodd-Frank Act provided that the Deputy Director would serve as acting Director during the Director’s absence or unavailability.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: The Dodd-Frank Act, the law that created the CFPB, provided that the Deputy Director would serve as acting Director when the Director was absent or unavailable.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: President Trump instead invoked the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA) to designate Mick Mulvaney, the Senate-confirmed Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: President Trump instead invoked the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA), a general law on filling vacancies temporarily, to designate Mick Mulvaney. Mulvaney was the Senate-confirmed Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the White House budget office.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: A first assistant ordinarily acted, but §3345(a)(2) allowed presidential selection of another Senate-confirmed officer.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Under the FVRA, a "first assistant" (the office's top deputy) ordinarily acted as head. But §3345(a)(2) let the President instead choose another Senate-confirmed officer, someone the Senate had already approved for a different post.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Section 3347 made this mechanism exclusive unless another statute expressly provided an alternative.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Section 3347 made the vacancies law the exclusive way to fill a vacancy temporarily, unless another "statute" (law passed by Congress) expressly provided an alternative.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Section 3349c excluded certain offices, including appointed members of governing multimember independent bodies.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Section 3349c excluded certain offices from the vacancies law. These included appointed members of independent bodies governed by several members, such as boards and commissions.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: At this time the statute provided a five-year term and for-cause removal protection, whose constitutionality was separately before the D.C. Circuit en banc.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: At this time the "statute" gave the CFPB Director a five-year term and "for-cause removal" protection, meaning the Director could be fired only for good cause. Whether that protection was constitutional was separately before the full D.C. Circuit sitting en banc.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Section 5491(a) applied federal-officer laws unless expressly otherwise provided.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Section 5491(a) of Dodd-Frank applied the general laws about federal officers to the CFPB, unless Dodd-Frank expressly provided otherwise.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: English said the later, specific, mandatory deputy provision displaced the general permissive FVRA.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: English argued that Dodd-Frank's deputy provision (the Deputy "shall" serve) was "later, specific," and mandatory. So, she said, it displaced the older, general, permissive FVRA, which only lets the President pick someone.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Her Appointments Clause theory likewise depended on absence of statutory designation authority.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Her "Appointments Clause" argument, based on the Constitution's rules for appointing officers, likewise worked only if no statute gave the President authority to designate Mulvaney.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Section 3347 made the FVRA nonexclusive when another succession law applied, not unavailable.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Section 3347 made the FVRA nonexclusive when another succession law applied, meaning it was no longer the only option. It did not make the FVRA unavailable; the President could still use it.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: This was not an earlier Congress trying to bind a later one; the later Congress specified how existing officer laws applied to the Bureau it was creating.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: This was not an earlier Congress trying to bind a later one. The later Congress that passed Dodd-Frank itself specified how existing officer laws, including the vacancies law, applied to the Bureau it was creating.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Kelly questioned whether absence or unavailability included permanent resignation but assumed it did without deciding, because that still did not expressly displace presidential authority.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: The judge doubted that a Director who resigns counts as 'absent or unavailable', but even assuming so, nothing in Dodd-Frank expressly took away the President's power under the vacancies law.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Read in context, the direction that the Deputy shall serve was a default qualified by presidential FVRA selection.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Read in context, the direction that the Deputy "shall" serve was a "default," the rule that applies automatically. It gave way when the President made a selection under the FVRA.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Harmonious construction and the presumption against implied repeal favored both statutes; later-specific-over-general canons did not settle a conflict that could be reconciled.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: "Harmonious construction" (reading two laws so both work) and the "presumption against implied repeal" (assuming Congress does not silently cancel a law) favored keeping both "statutes." The "canons," or interpretive rules, that later and specific laws beat general ones resolve only real conflicts, and this one could be reconciled.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Constitutional avoidance supplied additional support: English’s approach could let an outgoing protected Director choose a successor insulated from presidential control, raising serious Take Care Clause concerns.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: "Constitutional avoidance," choosing a reading that avoids serious constitutional doubts, also supported the result. English's approach could let a departing Director protected from firing pick a successor shielded from presidential control, raising serious concerns under the "Take Care Clause," the President's duty to see the laws faithfully executed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: With English unlikely to succeed on the substantive theory, Kelly reserved the defendants’ separate objections based on the de facto officer doctrine and quo warranto.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Because English was unlikely to win on her "substantive" theory (the core legal argument), Judge Kelly "reserved," or left undecided, the defendants' other objections. These rested on the "de facto officer doctrine," which can make an official's acts valid despite a defect in his appointment, and on quo warranto, the traditional action to challenge someone's right to hold office.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: A preliminary injunction required likely success, likely irreparable injury, favorable equities, and public interest; the latter two merged when the Government opposed relief.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: A "preliminary injunction," an early court order, required likely success, likely "irreparable injury" (harm money cannot fix), a balance of hardships favoring her, and service of the "public interest." The last two merged when the Government was the side opposing "relief."

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Kelly did not resolve whether Winter had eliminated the circuit’s earlier sliding scale or whether a mandatory-injunction standard applied.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Judge Kelly did not decide whether the Supreme Court's Winter decision had eliminated the circuit's earlier "sliding scale," under which a strong showing on one factor could make up for a weak one. Nor did he decide whether the tougher standard for a mandatory injunction, an order forcing a change, applied.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: Even assuming her legal theory, she remained employed, faced no identified imminent termination, and submitted no declaration facts establishing personal harm.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Even assuming her legal theory was right, she still had her job, faced no identified threat of being fired soon, and submitted no "declaration facts," facts in sworn written statements, showing she personally would be harmed.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: The last uncontested position was Deputy, so elevating her by injunction would not merely preserve that status quo.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: Her last undisputed position was Deputy. Early injunctions usually preserve the "status quo," the last undisputed state of things, so elevating her to acting Director by "injunction" would change things rather than preserve them.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.sentence: The assigned account’s later July 13, 2018 appeal dismissal was subsequent procedural history, not a new merits ruling made here.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-005.plain: The later dismissal of her appeal on July 13, 2018, described in the assigned account, is subsequent "procedural history," what happened to the case afterward. It is not a new "merits ruling," a decision on who was right, made here.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: In Rasul in 2004, the Supreme Court held statutory habeas jurisdiction extended to the base, leaving the constitutional question open.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: In Rasul in 2004, the Supreme Court held that the federal habeas statute gave courts "statutory" jurisdiction over detainees at the Guantanamo base. It left open whether the Constitution itself guarantees them habeas.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: During those appeals, Congress enacted the Detainee Treatment Act in 2005, withdrawing habeas jurisdiction for Guantanamo aliens and giving the D.C. Circuit exclusive review of final tribunal determinations.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: During those appeals, Congress passed the Detainee Treatment Act in 2005, removing courts' habeas power for "aliens" (non-citizens) held at Guantanamo. In its place it gave the D.C. Circuit exclusive power to review the military tribunals' final determinations.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: The D.C. Circuit held jurisdiction removed and the Suspension Clause inapplicable, making the substitute’s adequacy unnecessary to decide.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: The D.C. Circuit held that Congress had removed habeas jurisdiction and that the Suspension Clause, the Constitution's guarantee of habeas except in rebellion or invasion, did not apply. So it never needed to decide whether the substitute review was adequate.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Congress had supplied the required clarity; statutory avoidance could not preserve jurisdiction by contradicting that choice.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Congress had clearly stated its intent, so "statutory" avoidance, reading a law to dodge a constitutional question, could not keep "jurisdiction" (the courts' power to hear the cases) by contradicting that choice.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Its development through common-law struggles, the Petition of Right, and the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 explained the Constitution’s restricted suspension power.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Habeas developed through "common-law" struggles in English courts, the Petition of Right, and the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679. That history explains the Constitution's restricted "suspension power," which allows habeas to be suspended only in rebellion or invasion.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: The political branches could not retain total control while arranging formal sovereignty to switch constitutional constraints off.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: The "political branches," Congress and the President, could not keep total control of Guantanamo while arranging for formal "sovereignty" (legal ownership) to stay with Cuba just to switch off constitutional limits.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Kennedy read Eisentrager’s postwar Germany setting and military obstacles as integral rather than treating its territorial language as exclusively controlling.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Kennedy read Eisentrager's denial of habeas as depending on its special facts, occupied postwar Germany and real military difficulties, rather than as a rule that habeas never reaches non-citizens held outside U.S. territory.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Tribunal personal representatives were expressly neither lawyers nor advocates, government evidence enjoyed a presumption of validity, and detainees could present only reasonably available evidence.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: "Tribunal personal representatives," the officers assigned to help detainees, were expressly neither lawyers nor advocates. The government's evidence was presumed valid, and detainees could present only evidence that was reasonably available.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: The Military Commissions Act neither purported to suspend formally nor was defended as a formal suspension.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: The Military Commissions Act did not claim to formally suspend habeas, and the government did not defend it as a formal suspension. So it could stand only if it gave detainees an adequate substitute.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Hayman and Swain, precedents approving relocated collateral review, preserved broad powers and savings clauses for ineffective substitutes.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Hayman and Swain, "precedents" (earlier decisions) approving "collateral review" (a later challenge to detention outside the normal appeal) moved to another court, preserved equally broad court powers. They also kept "savings clauses," which leave ordinary habeas available if the substitute proves ineffective.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Here Congress deliberately narrowed review, omitted a savings clause, and assigned exclusive appellate review without district-court factfinding transfer.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Here Congress deliberately narrowed review and left out a "savings clause," a backup route to ordinary habeas. It gave exclusive "appellate" review to one appeals court, with no way to transfer cases to a district-court judge to find facts.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Adequate review had to give a meaningful chance to show detention rested on mistaken law and permit conditional release when necessary.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: A genuine substitute for habeas must let a detainee show he is being held because of a legal error, and must let the court order him released if so.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Kennedy analogized that relationship to procedural rigor in Mathews v. Eldridge without making a due-process holding.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Kennedy compared that relationship to the procedural rigor analysis in Mathews v. Eldridge: the weaker the earlier procedure, the more searching the later review must be. He did this without making any due-process holding.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Asking the Deputy Secretary to convene another tribunal was insufficient because it was discretionary and a refusal was not a reviewable final tribunal determination.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: A detainee could ask the Deputy Secretary of Defense to convene another tribunal, but that was not enough. The decision was "discretionary" (the official was free to say no), and a refusal was not a final tribunal determination that was "reviewable" by a court.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Taken together, the restrictions were facially inadequate, making Military Commissions Act section 7 unconstitutional.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Taken together, the restrictions were "facially inadequate," meaning inadequate on the law's own terms, without looking at how they worked in a particular case. That made section 7 of the Military Commissions Act, which removed habeas, unconstitutional.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: They need not exhaust that route before district-court habeas.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: The detainees need not "exhaust" (first complete) that appeals-court review route before seeking district-court habeas, meaning filing habeas cases in the trial court.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.sentence: Justice Scalia, joined by the same three Justices and also joining Roberts, independently would affirm because the Clause did not protect aliens abroad.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-009.plain: Justice Scalia, "joined by" the same three Justices and himself also joining Roberts' dissent, wrote separately. He would "affirm" (uphold the lower court) on the independent ground that the Suspension Clause did not protect "aliens," non-citizens, held abroad.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: The challenged provision allowed expenditures to be accounted for solely on the agency Director’s certificate.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: The CIA law let the agency's spending be accounted for by the Director's signed certificate alone, so the public statement showed no details.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: The district court dismissed under the taxpayer-standing decision Flast v. Cohen and also considered the dispute a political question.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: The "district court" (trial court) dismissed under Flast v. Cohen, the leading "taxpayer-standing" decision on when being a taxpayer gives a right to sue. It also considered the dispute a "political question," one for Congress and the President rather than the courts.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: It reasoned that accounting was integrally linked to appropriations because Richardson could not challenge expenditures he could not see.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: The appeals court reasoned that a demand for accounts was integrally linked to "appropriations," the laws by which Congress spends money, because Richardson could not challenge expenditures he could not see.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: Flast created a narrow exception requiring a connection both to a challenged congressional exercise of taxing and spending and to a specific constitutional restriction on that power.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: Flast created a narrow exception. The taxpayer had to connect his suit both to a challenged use of Congress's "taxing and spending" power and to a specific constitutional limit on that power.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: It did not license every taxpayer objection to government, and Article III still required a personal stake producing concrete adversity.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: Flast did not allow every taxpayer objection to government. Article III, the Constitution's limit on federal courts, still required a personal stake creating concrete "adversity," a genuine contest between opposing sides.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: The majority considered the nature of the claim to determine standing while expressly reserving its constitutional merits.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: The "majority" considered the nature of the claim only to decide "standing," whether Richardson had the right to sue. It expressly left open the constitutional "merits," whether the CIA secrecy law was valid.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: That concern was common to the public and thus a generalized grievance.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: That concern was shared by the whole public, so it was a "generalized grievance": a complaint so widely shared that it belongs to politics, not courts.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: Levitt’s rejection of a citizen’s challenge to an allegedly unconstitutional judicial appointment showed that an express constitutional prohibition did not eliminate the injury requirement.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: In Levitt, the Court rejected a citizen's challenge to an "allegedly" (claimed but not established) unconstitutional judicial appointment. That showed even an "express" constitutional prohibition, one clearly stated in the text, does not eliminate the requirement of personal injury.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: The Court discussed historical secrecy and congressional reporting authority but reserved the accounting clause’s precise meaning; even an express statutory standing grant would remain subject to Article III.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: The Court discussed the history of secrecy and Congress's power over reporting but "reserved" (left undecided) exactly what the accounting clause means. Even an "express" statutory grant of standing, a law plainly letting people sue, would still be subject to Article III's injury requirement.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: He thought the formula neither measured concrete adversity nor clearly separated constitutional and prudential restrictions.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: Powell thought the Flast formula neither measured concrete "adversity" (a real stake creating a genuine contest) nor clearly separated limits the Constitution imposes from "prudential" ones, limits courts choose for themselves.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.sentence: Justice Brennan’s dissent, printed in the companion Schlesinger case and expressly applying here, likewise separated injury in fact from reviewability and merits.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-045.plain: Justice Brennan's "dissent," printed in the companion Schlesinger case and expressly applying here, likewise treated "injury in fact" (actual harm to the plaintiff) as separate from reviewability and from the "merits," who should win. He thought Richardson's alleged injuries were enough to sue.

cp-bates.sentence: It later moved to dismiss for improper venue.
cp-bates.plain: The agency later "moved to dismiss" (asked the court to end the case) for improper "venue," meaning the case was filed in the wrong district.

cp-bates.sentence: Bates relied on § 1391(b)(2), amended in 1990 to allow suit where a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred.
cp-bates.plain: Bates relied on § 1391(b)(2), the federal venue law as amended in 1990. It allows suit in any district where a substantial part of the events or omissions (failures to act) giving rise to the claim occurred.

cp-bates.sentence: Before 1966, federal-question venue rules could leave no district available when defendants resided in different states.
cp-bates.plain: Before 1966, venue rules for "federal-question" cases (suits under federal law) could leave no proper district at all when defendants lived in different states.

cp-bates.sentence: The 1990 amendment altered the demand to select a single best district by referring to substantial parts of events, with legislative explanation acknowledging events in multiple districts.
cp-bates.plain: The 1990 "amendment" (change to the statute) dropped the demand to pick a single best district by referring to substantial parts of the events. Congress's explanation acknowledged that events may happen in several districts, so more than one can be proper.

cp-bates.sentence: Purposeful forum contacts belonged to the separate personal-jurisdiction inquiry.
cp-bates.plain: "Purposeful" contacts with the forum, meaning deliberate dealings with the place where suit was filed, belonged to the separate "personal-jurisdiction" question: whether the court has power over the defendant at all.

cp-bates.sentence: C & S had waived that defense by omitting it from its answer and dismissal motion; the court did not decide whether involuntary forwarding alone would supply constitutional contacts.
cp-bates.plain: C & S had "waived" (given up) that defense by leaving it out of its "answer," its formal response to the complaint, and its motion to dismiss. So the court did not decide whether an involuntarily forwarded letter alone could supply the contacts the Constitution requires.

cp-bates.sentence: Although a bona fide-error defense could matter, the alleged violations largely concerned its contents rather than the agency’s intention.
cp-bates.plain: A "bona fide-error" defense, a claim of honest mistake, could matter. But the "alleged" (claimed, not proven) violations concerned mostly the letter's contents rather than the agency's intention.

cp-bates.sentence: The court also expressly reserved when a statutory claim accrued for limitations purposes.
cp-bates.plain: The court also expressly "reserved" (left undecided) when the "statutory" claim, the claim under the federal statute, began to run for "limitations" purposes, that is, for the filing deadline.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: It treated the statutory basis for that custody as presumptive, not an established customs violation by Dioguardi.
cp-dioguardi.plain: The court presumed a "statutory" basis (legal authority under a statute) for customs' "custody" of the goods. It did not treat Dioguardi as having been shown to violate customs law.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: Representing himself with limited English, Dioguardi sued Durning individually and as collector for $5,000 plus interest and costs.
cp-dioguardi.plain: Representing himself with limited English, Dioguardi sued Durning both personally and as customs collector, seeking $5,000 "plus interest" (extra money for the delay) and costs.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: On the United States Attorney’s motion, the district court dismissed the original complaint for failure to state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action, allowing amendment.
cp-dioguardi.plain: On the United States Attorney’s motion, the "district court" dismissed the original complaint for failing to state facts sufficient to constitute a "cause of action," meaning a legal claim. It allowed him to amend (rewrite) the complaint.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: Judge Clark, writing for a Second Circuit panel with Judges Swan and Augustus N. Hand, concluded that the allegations could survive a motion directed only at the complaint’s face.
cp-dioguardi.plain: Judge Clark, writing for a Second Circuit panel with Judges Swan and Augustus N. Hand, held that the allegations could survive a "motion" (request to dismiss) aimed only at the complaint's face, meaning what the complaint itself says.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: The former formulation requiring facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action no longer controlled.
cp-dioguardi.plain: The old test, requiring facts sufficient to constitute a "cause of action," no longer controlled. Under the new federal rules, a complaint need only give fair notice of a claim showing the plaintiff is entitled to relief.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: The complaint could reasonably allege that Durning converted or otherwise disposed of the two missing cases.
cp-dioguardi.plain: Read generously, the complaint could reasonably "allege" (claim) that Durning converted the two missing cases, meaning wrongfully took them, or otherwise disposed of them.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: Clark cited authorities recognizing a collector’s personal responsibility for default or negligence in performing official duties, supplying legal substance to the claim against Durning individually.
cp-dioguardi.plain: Clark cited "authorities" (earlier cases) holding a collector personally responsible for default or "negligence" (carelessness) in doing official duties. That gave legal substance to the "claim" against Durning personally.

cp-dioguardi.sentence: He could develop factual defenses at a pretrial hearing or through summary judgment supported by affidavits.
cp-dioguardi.plain: Durning could develop factual "defenses" at a pretrial "hearing," or through "summary judgment," a ruling without trial, supported by "affidavits" (sworn written statements). Attacking the complaint's wording was not the right step.

cp-eisen.sentence: Special dealers handled those trades as principals rather than ordinary round-lot arrangements.
cp-eisen.plain: Special dealers handled these small odd-lot trades as principals, buying and selling for their own account. That differed from ordinary "round-lot" trading in standard blocks, where brokers simply match buyers and sellers.

cp-eisen.sentence: In Eisen I the Second Circuit allowed immediate appeal under its death-knell rationale; Eisen II reversed for renewed consideration of representation, manageability, notice, and other issues, rejected subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(2), and purported to retain appellate jurisdiction.
cp-eisen.plain: In Eisen I the Second Circuit allowed immediate appeal on its "death-knell" theory: denying class status would effectively end a case built on a tiny $70 claim. Eisen II "reversed" for renewed consideration of representation, manageability, notice and other issues, rejected subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(2) as class types, and claimed to keep "appellate jurisdiction" (power over the case).

cp-eisen.sentence: After hearings and submissions, the district court found the action maintainable and proposed fluid recovery: unclaimed money would lower future traders’ differentials.
cp-eisen.plain: After "hearings" and written submissions, the "district court" found the class action could proceed and proposed "fluid recovery." Under it, unclaimed money would lower the "differentials," the extra charges on odd-lot trades, for future traders.

cp-eisen.sentence: After a preliminary hearing predicting more-likely-than-not success, the judge charged defendants ninety percent, or $19,548.
cp-eisen.plain: After a "preliminary hearing" (an early, limited look) predicting Eisen would more likely than not succeed, the judge charged defendants ninety percent of the notice cost, or $19,548.

cp-eisen.sentence: Justice Powell’s majority applied § 1291 and Cohen’s collateral-order reasoning.
cp-eisen.plain: Justice Powell’s majority found appellate jurisdiction under § 1291, the statute allowing appeals from final decisions, using Cohen’s "collateral order" reasoning. That exception lets some orders on separate issues be appealed before the case ends.

cp-eisen.sentence: Defendants’ claimed right not to finance their opponent’s class notice had been conclusively rejected on an issue separate from substantive liability, like Cohen’s security-for-expenses issue.
cp-eisen.plain: Defendants’ claimed right not to pay for their opponent's class notice had been conclusively rejected. That issue was separate from "substantive liability" (who wins on the merits), like the security-for-expenses issue in Cohen.

cp-eisen.sentence: The historical Rule 23(c)(2) required best-practicable notice in (b)(3) actions, including individual notice to everyone identifiable through reasonable effort.
cp-eisen.plain: The then-applicable Rule 23(c)(2) required the best notice practicable in (b)(3) class actions. That included individual notice to every member who could be identified through reasonable effort.

cp-eisen.sentence: Expense and an expectation that tiny claims would produce few opt-outs did not eliminate members’ choices to litigate separately or participate.
cp-eisen.plain: Expense, and the expectation that tiny "claims" would produce few "opt-outs" (members choosing to leave the class), did not remove members' choices. Each must be told so he can decide whether to "litigate" (sue) separately or participate.

cp-eisen.sentence: The Court also answered Eisen’s limitations concern by referring to American Pipe’s class tolling rule.
cp-eisen.plain: Eisen worried that members' claims would expire under the filing deadline once the class was dismissed. The Court answered with American Pipe’s class "tolling" rule: the deadline is paused while a class action is pending.

cp-eisen.sentence: Rule 23 likewise supplied no preliminary merits hearing as a device for establishing class treatment or shifting notice costs.
cp-eisen.plain: Rule 23 likewise provides no preliminary hearing on the "merits" (who will probably win) as a "device," or tool, for deciding class status or shifting notice costs to the defendant.

cp-eisen.sentence: Initial notice ordinarily belonged to the representative financing a genuinely adversarial suit.
cp-eisen.plain: Initial notice costs ordinarily fall on the class representative, who must finance a genuinely "adversarial" suit, one truly contested between opposing sides.

cp-eisen.sentence: The order was without prejudice to redefinition under Rule 23(c)(4) or Rule 15.
cp-eisen.plain: The order was "without prejudice" (it left Eisen free to try again) to redefining the class under Rule 23(c)(4) or amending the complaint under Rule 15.

cp-eisen.sentence: The assigned account’s $20,000-plus number describes the reduced plan, and its reversal shorthand compresses the actual vacatur.
cp-eisen.plain: The assigned account's "$20,000-plus" figure describes the judge's reduced notice plan. And its word "reversal" is shorthand: the Court actually ordered a vacatur, wiping out the appeals-court judgment, and sent the case back.

cp-gillispie.sentence: The defendants filed four separate demurrers challenging the factual allegations and the joinder of parties and causes of action.
cp-gillispie.plain: The defendants filed four separate "demurrers," objections saying that even if the "allegations" were true they stated no legal claim. They also challenged the "joinder" (combining in one suit) of the parties and of the "causes of action," meaning the separate legal claims.

cp-gillispie.sentence: Judge Mintz entered a separate judgment sustaining each, without specifying the ground, and allowed Gillispie thirty days to amend.
cp-gillispie.plain: Judge Mintz "entered" (formally issued) a separate "judgment" upholding each objection, without saying on what ground. He allowed Gillispie thirty days to "amend," or rewrite, her complaint.

cp-gillispie.sentence: A judgment sustaining a demurrer for misjoinder would require dismissal, so leave to amend suggested reliance on failure to state a cause of action.
cp-gillispie.plain: A "judgment" sustaining a "demurrer" for misjoinder (improperly combining parties or claims) would require dismissal. So giving "leave to amend" (permission to rewrite) suggested the judge relied on "failure to state a cause of action," that is, no legal claim stated.

cp-gillispie.sentence: The Court understood that to mean material, essential, ultimate facts establishing a right to relief, rather than the pleader’s conclusions.
cp-gillispie.plain: The Court read that requirement to mean the "ultimate facts": the material, essential facts that establish a right to "relief" (a legal remedy). The pleader's own conclusions, like labeling something "assault," were not enough.

cp-gillispie.sentence: A demurrer admitted pleaded facts for purposes of the challenge, but did not admit legal conclusions.
cp-gillispie.plain: A demurrer treated the pleaded facts as true for purposes of the challenge. It did not accept "legal conclusions," the complaint's labels for what those facts mean legally.

cp-gillispie.sentence: The Court regarded the single sentence alleging trespass, assault, and confinement as conclusions lacking an adequate factual foundation.
cp-gillispie.plain: The Court saw her single sentence "alleging" (claiming) trespass, assault, and confinement as "conclusions": legal labels without an adequate factual foundation describing what anyone actually did.

cp-hanson.sentence: Donner retained lifetime income, amendment and revocation powers, power to appoint remainders, and substantial investment control through an adviser whose consent was required for specified decisions.
cp-hanson.plain: Donner kept the trust's income for life, powers of "amendment" (changing the trust) and revocation (cancelling it), and the "power to appoint" remainders, deciding who gets what is left after her death. She also kept substantial investment control through an adviser whose consent was required for certain decisions.

cp-hanson.sentence: The residuary clause captured property not effectively appointed.
cp-hanson.plain: The will's "residuary clause," its catch-all for property not otherwise given away, captured anything not effectively appointed. That would benefit Katherine and Dorothy.

cp-hanson.sentence: Elizabeth and some children were personally served, but Wilmington Trust and other nonresidents received mailed notice and publication; the trust companies did not appear.
cp-hanson.plain: Elizabeth and some children were "personally served," handed the court papers, in Florida. But Wilmington Trust and other "nonresidents" (parties outside Florida) got only mailed notice and newspaper publication, and the trust companies never appeared in the case.

cp-hanson.sentence: Nevertheless, on January 14, 1955, it invalidated the appointment as testamentary and ineffective against the parties before it.
cp-hanson.plain: Nevertheless, on January 14, 1955, the Florida court held the 1949 appointment invalid as "testamentary," meaning it worked like a will without a will's formalities. It ruled the appointment ineffective as to the parties before it.

cp-hanson.sentence: The Court dismissed the appeal but treated the papers as a certiorari petition and granted it.
cp-hanson.plain: The Supreme Court "dismissed" the appeal, because the case could not come up as an automatic appeal. But it treated the papers as a petition for "certiorari," a request for discretionary review, and "granted" it, agreeing to hear the case.

cp-hanson.sentence: Appearing beneficiaries had a direct interest in jurisdiction over an absent indispensable trustee.
cp-hanson.plain: "Appearing beneficiaries," those who took part in the Florida case, had a direct interest in whether Florida had "jurisdiction" (legal power) over the absent trustee. The trustee was indispensable, a required party, so the judgment depended on that power.

cp-hanson.sentence: Chief Justice Warren’s majority found the trust securities held in Delaware with no established Florida situs.
cp-hanson.plain: Chief Justice Warren’s "majority" found the trust securities were held in Delaware, with no established Florida "situs," the legal location of property. So Florida could not claim power based on where the property was.

cp-hanson.sentence: The defendant needed purposeful availment of forum activities and legal protection.
cp-hanson.plain: The "defendant" itself needed "purposeful availment": deliberately conducting activities in the "forum," the state where suit was brought, and so enjoying the protection of its laws.

cp-hanson.sentence: Another person’s unilateral conduct could not supply that connection.
cp-hanson.plain: Another person's "unilateral conduct," action taken by someone else alone, such as Donner moving to Florida, could not supply that connection to the trustee.

cp-hanson.sentence: Calling a Florida appointment republication might affect choice of law in a competent court, but could not itself create power over the Delaware trustee.
cp-hanson.plain: Calling the Florida "appointment" a republication (re-making) of the trust might affect "choice of law," which state's law applies, in a court that had power. But it could not itself create power over the Delaware trustee.

cp-hanson.sentence: Under § 1738, a judgment lacking constitutionally required jurisdiction did not acquire binding force elsewhere.
cp-hanson.plain: Under § 1738, the full-faith-and-credit statute, other states must honor a judgment only if the court had the "jurisdiction" the Constitution requires. Florida's judgment lacked it, so it gained no binding force elsewhere.

cp-hanson.sentence: The trustee was a stakeholder or agent in privity with Donner and obligated to distribute as directed.
cp-hanson.plain: Douglas, dissenting, saw the trustee as a mere stakeholder or agent in "privity" with Donner, meaning closely tied to her legal interests. It was obligated to distribute the property as she directed.

cp-shutts.sentence: It withheld the corresponding royalty increases unless owners supplied indemnity against possible refunds.
cp-shutts.plain: Phillips withheld the matching "royalty" increases, the landowners' share of the higher gas prices. It did so unless owners provided "indemnity," a promise to repay if the price increase later had to be refunded.

cp-shutts.sentence: It regarded notice, participation, exclusion, and adequate representation as sufficient jurisdictional safeguards, and applied forum law absent compelling reasons for another state’s law.
