cp-shutts.plain: Kansas regarded notice, a chance to participate or opt out, and "adequate representation" as enough "jurisdictional" safeguards to bind out-of-state owners. It applied "forum law," the law of Kansas as the state where suit was brought, unless compelling reasons favored another state's law.

cp-shutts.sentence: Justice Rehnquist’s opinion first held that Phillips could raise the absent owners’ jurisdictional protection because its own interest was at stake.
cp-shutts.plain: Justice Rehnquist’s "opinion" for the Court first held that Phillips could raise the absent owners' jurisdictional protection, even though such rights usually belong to the person protected. Its own interest was at stake, because it needed the judgment to bind them.

cp-shutts.sentence: Its objection sought reciprocal finality, not simply enforcement of an opponent’s rights.
cp-shutts.plain: Phillips wanted to be sure that if it paid, the case would be over for everyone, so owners could not sue it again elsewhere.

cp-shutts.sentence: Those differences justified different jurisdictional safeguards from those protecting an unwilling defendant.
cp-shutts.plain: Absent class members face far fewer burdens than defendants. Those differences justified different "jurisdictional" safeguards from those protecting an unwilling defendant.

cp-shutts.sentence: Affirmative opt-in and defendant-style minimum contacts were unnecessary when those safeguards existed.
cp-shutts.plain: Requiring members to opt in (sign up) and requiring defendant-style "minimum contacts" (ties between Kansas and each member) were unnecessary. That held as long as notice, a chance to be heard or leave, and adequate representation existed.

cp-shutts.sentence: Where applicable laws materially conflicted, Kansas needed sufficient contacts with each claim to create state interests making its choice neither arbitrary nor fundamentally unfair.
cp-shutts.plain: Where the possibly applicable laws "materially conflicted" (would give meaningfully different results), Kansas needed sufficient "contacts" with each claim. Those contacts had to create state interests making its choice of its own law neither arbitrary nor fundamentally unfair.

cp-shutts.sentence: He distinguished full-faith-and-credit concerns about other states’ interests from due-process concerns about unfair surprise, and objected to turning debatable interpretations of state law into constitutional error.
cp-shutts.plain: Stevens separated "full-faith-and-credit" concerns, about respecting other states' interests, from "due-process" concerns about "unfair surprise" to a party. He objected to turning debatable readings of state law into constitutional error.

cp-swift.sentence: Nathaniel Norton and Jairus Keith drew a bill of exchange at Portland, Maine, dated May 1, 1836, payable six months later with the additional grace period described in the opinion.
cp-swift.plain: Nathaniel Norton and Jairus Keith drew a "bill of exchange," a written order directing Tyson to pay, at Portland, Maine, dated May 1, 1836. It was payable six months later plus the "grace period" (customary extra days) described in the opinion.

cp-swift.sentence: Norton endorsed it to Swift to pay an existing promissory-note debt Norton and Keith owed him.
cp-swift.plain: Norton "endorsed" the bill to Swift, signing it over, to pay an existing promissory-note debt that Norton and Keith owed him.

cp-swift.sentence: Swift took the accepted bill before maturity, without notice of any defect in the land transaction underlying Tyson’s acceptance, and believed it properly payable.
cp-swift.plain: Swift took the "accepted bill," one Tyson had already agreed to pay, before it was due. He had no notice of any defect in the land deal behind Tyson's acceptance, and believed it "properly payable," that is, validly owed.

cp-swift.sentence: Those admitted circumstances made the legal significance of the existing debt, rather than Swift’s dishonest knowledge, the central issue.
cp-swift.plain: Since Swift's honesty was not in question, the real issue was whether taking the bill to settle an old debt counted as paying for it.

cp-swift.sentence: Swift objected that defenses between the original parties could not be asserted against him.
cp-swift.plain: Swift objected that "defenses" between the "original parties," such as Tyson's fraud claim against Norton and Keith, could not be asserted against him.

cp-swift.sentence: Tyson urged New York law because acceptance occurred there, treating the Rules of Decision Act’s reference to state laws as including judicial decisions about whether old debt counted as value.
cp-swift.plain: Tyson urged New York law because the "acceptance occurred" there, meaning he agreed to pay in New York. He read the Rules of Decision Act’s reference to state "laws" as including New York court decisions on whether an old debt counted as value.

cp-swift.sentence: Swift argued for independent determination of commercial principle and for the sufficiency of taking paper in payment of an existing obligation.
cp-swift.plain: Swift argued that the federal court could decide the commercial-law question for itself, and that taking a bill to pay an existing debt was enough.

cp-swift.sentence: Story interpreted state laws to include positive enactments, their state-court construction, fixed local usages, and local matters such as land rights and title.
cp-swift.plain: Story read "state laws" to include "enactments" (statutes), state-court interpretations of them, fixed "local usages" (settled local customs), and local matters such as land rights and "title," meaning legal ownership. It did not include judge-made general rules.

cp-swift.sentence: He treated judicial opinions on general commercial law as evidence of law, capable of reconsideration, rather than conclusively binding law.
cp-swift.plain: He treated judicial "opinions" on general commercial law as only evidence of what the law is, open to "reconsideration" by a federal court. They were not law that conclusively bound it.

cp-swift.sentence: This general-law approach is the doctrine later repudiated by Erie, not a rule presented as current federal authority.
cp-swift.plain: This "general-law" approach is the doctrine Erie later "repudiated" (rejected and overruled) in 1938. It is not presented as current federal law.

cp-swift.sentence: Story began with protection for a good-faith holder taking negotiable paper for value before maturity and without notice of earlier defects.
cp-swift.plain: Story began with protection for a "good-faith" (honest) holder who takes "negotiable paper," a transferable written promise or order to pay, for value, "before maturity" (before it is due), and without notice of earlier defects.

cp-swift.sentence: Using negotiable securities to pay or secure debts allowed creditors to realize obligations, extend credit, or forbear collection.
cp-swift.plain: Using "negotiable securities," transferable bills and notes, to pay or secure debts helped commerce. Creditors could collect on obligations, extend more credit, or "forbear," agreeing to wait before collecting.

cp-swift.sentence: Swift’s payment transaction therefore insulated him from the antecedent equities Tyson sought to prove.
cp-swift.plain: Swift took the bill in payment of an existing debt, which counted as giving value. That transaction shielded him from the "antecedent equities" Tyson wanted to prove: earlier defenses, like fraud in the land deal, arising from the prior dealings.

cp-swift.sentence: He did not endorse the further proposition that taking paper merely as collateral for an existing debt produced identical protection.
cp-swift.plain: Catron agreed where the bill paid off the debt, but would not say the same protection applies when a bill is merely pledged as security for a debt that remains unpaid.

cp-swift.sentence: During January Term 1842, the Supreme Court directed certification that Tyson could not assert against Swift the same defense available against the original parties and that the offered proof was inadmissible against Swift on the stated facts.
cp-swift.plain: During its January Term 1842, the Supreme Court directed the lower court to be told that Tyson could not use against Swift the defense available against the "original parties." On the stated facts, his offered proof of fraud was "inadmissible," meaning not allowed as evidence, against Swift.

cp-swift.sentence: The later Erie discussion criticizes the general-law system’s failure to achieve hoped-for uniformity and the forum-dependent differences it produced.
cp-swift.plain: Erie later criticized this "general-law" system for failing to bring the hoped-for uniformity. Instead, results differed depending on the forum, whether a case was in state or federal court, inviting forum shopping.

dalton.sentence: Dalton’s father began an article 78 proceeding, later converted to an action at law, to prevent cancellation and compel release.
dalton.plain: Dalton's father began an "article 78" proceeding, New York's special procedure for challenging an organization's decisions, to stop ETS from canceling the score and force its release. It was later converted to an "action at law," an ordinary lawsuit.

dalton.sentence: Chief Judge Kaye’s majority accepted the supported finding, affirmed below, that relevant information had not been evaluated.
dalton.plain: Chief Judge Kaye’s "majority" accepted the lower courts' finding, supported by evidence and affirmed below, that ETS never actually evaluated Dalton's relevant information.

dalton.sentence: The Court of Appeals could not reweigh conflicting testimony.
dalton.plain: New York's Court of Appeals, its highest court, generally decides questions of law. It could not reweigh conflicting "testimony" (witness accounts) to decide whom to believe.

dalton.sentence: The lower courts’ additional, erroneous investigation theory did not require another trial when the material factual question had already been resolved.
dalton.plain: The lower courts also wrongly held that ETS had to investigate. But that error did not require another trial, because the "material factual question" (the key fact: that ETS ignored his evidence) had already been resolved.

dalton.sentence: That covenant could not contradict the actual agreement.
dalton.plain: That "covenant," the implied promise of good faith in every contract, could not contradict what the actual agreement said.

dalton.sentence: Refusing to exercise that discretion at all instead breached an express or implied contractual duty.
dalton.plain: ETS had "discretion" (the right to judge his evidence). But refusing to exercise that discretion at all "breached" (broke) an express or "implied" contractual duty, one written in the contract or understood as part of it.

dalton.sentence: Specific performance should provide what the contract promised: good-faith reconsideration.
dalton.plain: "Specific performance," a court order to do what was promised, should give what the "contract" actually promised: good-faith "reconsideration" of Dalton's evidence, not release of the score.

dalton.sentence: The court modified the Appellate Division order to require good-faith consideration rather than immediate release, and affirmed as modified without costs.
dalton.plain: The court "modified" the Appellate Division order to require good-faith consideration instead of immediate release of the score. It "affirmed" (upheld) the ruling as modified, with each side paying its own costs.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: IDEA, 20 U.S.C. § 1415(i)(3)(B), allowed discretionary awards of reasonable attorney’s fees as part of costs to prevailing parents.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: IDEA, the disability-education law at 20 U.S.C. § 1415(i)(3)(B), allowed "discretionary" awards, which a court may choose to make, of reasonable attorney's fees to prevailing parents. The statute counts those fees as part of "costs."

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: The Second Circuit reviewed statutory interpretation anew and reviewed the amount for abuse of discretion.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: The Second Circuit reviewed the statute's meaning "anew," deciding it fresh without deferring to the trial judge. It reviewed the fee amount only for "abuse of discretion," changing it only if the judge acted unreasonably.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Crawford Fitting required statutory witness-fee limits under 28 U.S.C. § 1821 absent explicit authorization or contract; West Virginia University Hospitals v. Casey construed the then-existing § 1988 attorney-fee wording to exclude expert fees.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: Crawford Fitting held that, absent explicit authorization by statute or contract, a loser pays only the limited witness fees in 28 U.S.C. § 1821. West Virginia University Hospitals v. Casey read the then-existing § 1988 attorney-fee wording to exclude "expert fees," experts' full charges.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Casey’s footnote 5 had discussed that report as an apparent attempt to depart from ordinary meaning and define a term of art.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: Footnote 5 in Casey had described that report as an apparent attempt to depart from the "ordinary meaning" of "costs." It seemed to make the word a "term of art," a word with a special legal meaning, covering expert expenses.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: The panel inferred that Congress viewed IDEA’s existing formulation, illuminated by its conference report, as already covering experts.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: The panel inferred that Congress saw IDEA's existing wording, explained by its "conference report" (the joint House-Senate committee's explanation), as already covering expert fees.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Justice Alito’s opinion treated IDEA as Spending Clause legislation: a state accepting federal money must knowingly and voluntarily accept the conditions.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: Justice Alito’s "opinion" treated IDEA as "Spending Clause" legislation, a law offering states federal money in exchange for following conditions. A state accepting the money must knowingly and voluntarily accept those conditions, so they must be clear.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Costs was an established term for a restricted category of taxable items.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: In law, 'costs' has long meant a short list of court-related expenses a winner can bill to the loser, not every expense of litigating.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Avoiding surplusage was not an absolute command that converted the study into fee authority.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: Avoiding "surplusage," meaning reading a statute so no words are wasted, is a preference, not an absolute command. It did not turn the GAO study provision into authority for expert fees.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Although the conference report plainly supported the parents, legislative history could not overcome the text, structure, and precedent.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: The "conference report" plainly supported the parents. But "legislative history," what committees and members said, could not overcome the enacted text, the statute's structure, and "precedent" (earlier decisions).

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Pennhurst’s concern about an unexpected substantive condition differed from identifying remedies for breach of an accepted obligation, a distinction reflected in Bell v. New Jersey.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: Ginsburg said Pennhurst’s concern was about states facing an unexpected "substantive" condition, a surprise duty. Identifying the remedies for breaking an obligation a state already accepted is different, a distinction reflected in Bell v. New Jersey.

lrs-k-arlington-murphy.sentence: Souter joined Breyer and separately stressed that the GAO provision had the same statutory dignity as the fee clause.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy.plain: Souter joined Breyer's dissent and separately stressed that the GAO study provision had the same "statutory" dignity as the fee clause: both were enacted law. So it gave a legitimate textual reason to look at the history.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: Texas and seventeen other States sued federal officials, arguing that the provision could no longer rest on the taxing power, exceeded other enumerated powers, and could not be severed from the rest of the Act.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: Texas and seventeen other States "sued" federal officials. They argued the insurance requirement could no longer rest on the "taxing power" once the penalty was $0, exceeded Congress's other "enumerated powers" (those listed in the Constitution), and could not be "severed" (cut out alone) from the rest of the Act.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: The district court found the individuals had standing, declared the coverage requirement unconstitutional and inseverable from the entire Act, and stayed judgment pending appeal.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: The "district court" found the individuals had "standing" (the right to sue). It declared the "coverage requirement" unconstitutional and "inseverable," meaning it could not be cut out alone, so the entire Act fell, but "stayed" (paused) its judgment pending appeal.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: The Fifth Circuit agreed on standing and unconstitutionality but found insufficient justification for invalidating the whole statute and remanded severability analysis.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: The Fifth Circuit agreed on "standing" and that the requirement was unconstitutional. But it found too little justification to strike down the whole "statute" and sent back the "severability" question: how much of the rest should fall with it.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: Even if statutory language influenced their choices, that influence was not traceable to challenged official conduct.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: Even if the "statutory" language influenced the individuals to buy insurance, that influence could not be traced to anything the defendant officials did. Standing requires harm caused by the defendants' own challenged conduct.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: The Declaratory Judgment Act did not create otherwise missing Article III jurisdiction.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: The Declaratory Judgment Act, which lets courts declare parties' rights, did not create Article III jurisdiction that was otherwise missing. Article III limits federal courts to real cases and controversies.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: Merely declaring unenforceable language unconstitutional would provide an advisory legal pronouncement rather than relief against these officials redressing the alleged harm.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: Merely declaring "unenforceable" language (a provision with no penalty to enforce) unconstitutional would be an advisory legal pronouncement, just the Court's opinion. It would not give "relief" against these officials that fixes the "alleged" harm.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: This was a preservation ruling, not a conclusion that all conceivable inseverability theories necessarily failed.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: The Court refused to consider those arguments because they had not been raised properly or in time, without deciding whether they would succeed.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: Independent third-party choices could support causation if evidence showed predictable responses.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: Independent "third-party" choices, here residents signing up for programs, could support "causation" (the link between the law and the harm). But that requires evidence showing people would predictably respond that way.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: Some used § 5000A(f)’s definition of coverage, but incorporating that definition differed from depending on subsection (a)’s command.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: Some of the cost-causing provisions used § 5000A(f)'s definition of "coverage." But borrowing that definition differed from depending on subsection (a)'s command to buy insurance, so they did not stand or fall with the mandate.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: The required link, in his view, ran to the government conduct challenged as unlawful, not necessarily directly to the constitutional defect; otherwise standing and merits would blur.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: In Alito's view, the States only had to trace their costs to the government action they called unlawful (enforcing the other ACA provisions), not to the defective mandate itself; demanding more would mix up the standing question with the question of who should win.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: He disputed forfeiture by pointing to the complaint and briefing.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: He "disputed forfeiture," denying that the States had lost this argument by failing to raise it. He pointed to their complaint and briefs, where he said they had made it.

lrs-n-standing-california-texas.sentence: On June 17, 2021, the Court reversed the Fifth Circuit in respect to standing, vacated the judgment, and remanded with instructions to dismiss.
lrs-n-standing-california-texas.plain: On June 17, 2021, the Court "reversed" the Fifth Circuit on standing, vacated (wiped out) the judgment, and sent the case back with instructions to dismiss. It did not decide whether the mandate was constitutional.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: Civil Service Commission rules made reinstatement conditional for eighteen months: an investigation revealing disqualification could lead the Commission to require removal.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: Civil Service Commission rules made her reinstatement conditional for eighteen months. If an investigation revealed a disqualifying problem, the Commission could require her removal.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: The deficiency alleged was inability effectively to confront the sources, not complete denial of a chance to offer a defense.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: The "alleged" deficiency was that she could not effectively confront the sources, the unnamed informants accusing her. It was not that she was completely denied any chance to offer a "defense."

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: He deferred to the administrative interpretation of that administrative direction and treated security-sensitive specificity as discretionary.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: He deferred to the executive branch's own reading of the President's order. He treated how specifically to reveal security-sensitive accusations as "discretionary," left to the officials' judgment.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: Retained reinstatement preference or civil-service status after the reduction in force was not actual service in a position.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: Keeping a "reinstatement" preference (a right to be rehired first) or "civil-service status" after the "reduction in force," the layoff, was not actually serving in a position. So the 1912 removal-protection law did not cover her.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: He read United States v. Lovett as treating permanent federal-employment proscription as punishment demanding criminal-adjudication safeguards.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: He read United States v. Lovett as treating a permanent "proscription" (ban) from federal employment as punishment. Punishment of that kind requires the safeguards of a criminal trial.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: Instead, the board appeared to punish Bailey individually through adjudication.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: The three-year ban was aimed at Bailey personally, as a penalty, rather than coming from a general rule, so it was invalid without a trial's protections.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: Ordinary removal, unlike individualized proscription, was not punishment requiring Sixth Amendment procedures; Congress and the President historically managed executive personnel subject to statutes without judicial criminal trials for every dismissal.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: Ordinary removal, unlike individualized "proscription" (singling a person out for a ban), was not punishment requiring Sixth Amendment criminal-trial procedures, such as confronting witnesses. Congress and the President have historically managed executive employees, subject to "statutes," without criminal trials for every dismissal.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: The majority then treated officeholding as outside the Fifth Amendment categories of life, liberty, and property.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: The majority then treated holding a government job as outside the Fifth Amendment's protected categories of life, liberty, and property. So due-process protections did not apply to her firing.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: On the First Amendment, it distinguished political expression from entitlement to continued federal employment.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: On the First Amendment, the majority distinguished political expression, which she remained free to engage in, from any entitlement to keep federal employment.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: Third, he rejected the right/privilege response to protected thought, association, and expression.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: Third, Edgerton rejected the "right/privilege" response: the argument that because a government job is a privilege, not a right, it may be taken away for protected thought, association, and expression.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: On March 22, 1950, the D.C. Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded with instructions to preserve removal from office and the rolls while invalidating the orders’ three-year bar.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: On March 22, 1950, the D.C. Circuit affirmed in part and "reversed in part," upholding some rulings and overturning others, and sent the case back. Its instructions kept her removal from office and from the rolls but struck down the three-year ban on future federal jobs in the "orders" against her.

lrs-o-bailey.sentence: On April 30, 1951, the Supreme Court affirmed by an equally divided Court.
lrs-o-bailey.plain: On April 30, 1951, the Supreme Court "affirmed" by an "equally divided" Court: the Justices split 4-4. That leaves the lower-court decision in place but sets no national precedent.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: The Atomic Energy Organization of Iran terminated the contract for convenience on June 30, 1979.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: The Atomic Energy Organization of Iran terminated the contract "for convenience" on June 30, 1979, under a clause allowing cancellation without any fault by the other side.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: Treasury regulations made judicial processes against blocked property void unless licensed and expressly allowed licenses to be amended or revoked.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: "Treasury regulations" on the asset freeze made any court process against "blocked" (frozen) Iranian property void unless "licensed," meaning permitted by Treasury. They expressly said such licenses could be "amended" (changed) or revoked.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: A November 26 license permitted specified litigation without judgment; a December 19 clarification permitted prejudgment attachment.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: A November 26 license permitted certain suits against Iran but not final judgments. A December 19 clarification permitted "prejudgment attachment," seizing a defendant's property as security before winning the case.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: Those interests arose after the freeze under expressly conditional licenses, a sequence crucial to the later compensation analysis.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: Because Dames & Moore got its hold on the property only after the freeze and under revocable permission, it had a weak claim that cancelling that hold took its property.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: On February 24 Reagan ratified those measures and suspended claims presentable to the tribunal, depriving them of legal effect in pending domestic cases.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: On February 24 President Reagan "ratified" (formally approved) Carter's measures. He also suspended all claims that could be presented to the international tribunal, giving them no legal effect in pending U.S. court cases.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: The Supreme Court granted certiorari before Ninth Circuit judgment, heard argument June 24, and decided July 2.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: The Supreme Court "granted" certiorari before the Ninth Circuit ruled, because an international deadline was approaching. It heard argument June 24 and decided the case July 2.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: Justice Rehnquist used Jackson’s Youngstown framework while warning that its categories simplified a spectrum of authorization, silence, and opposition.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: Justice Rehnquist used Jackson’s Youngstown framework, which asks whether Congress approved, was silent about, or opposed the President's actions. He warned that its three categories simplify what is really a spectrum.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: Dames & Moore argued that omission of the Trading With the Enemy Act’s vesting power limited IEEPA to starting or ending a freeze.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: Dames & Moore argued that IEEPA, the 1977 emergency-powers law, left out the Trading With the Enemy Act’s "vesting" power to take ownership of foreign property. So, it said, IEEPA only let the President start or end a freeze.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: The property measures fell within Youngstown’s strongest category of specific congressional authorization.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: The property measures fell within the strongest of Youngstown’s categories: action Congress had specifically authorized, where the President's power is at its height.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: The Court rejected the argument that only future licenses, not completed liens, were revocable and concluded that the contingent interests were not compensable property of the asserted sort.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: The Court rejected the argument that only future "licenses" could be revoked, not "liens" (legal claims on property) already obtained. The attachments were "contingent interests," always subject to the President's later decisions, so they were not "compensable" property requiring payment when cancelled.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: An in personam claim for liability existed apart from particular attached property.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: An "in personam" claim, one against Iran itself for "liability" (owing money), existed apart from any particular "attached property" seized as security. So the freeze law did not by itself authorize suspending it.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: That context combined with a long practice of executive agreements settling nationals’ claims, sometimes without consent in exchange for lump sums or arbitration.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: That context combined with a long practice of "executive agreements," deals the President makes with foreign nations without Senate approval, settling Americans' claims. Some settled claims without the claimants' consent in exchange for lump sums or arbitration.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: The suspension changed the substantive law courts applied rather than stripping them of Article III jurisdiction over unchanged claims.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: The suspension changed the "substantive law," the rules deciding who wins, that courts applied. It did not strip courts of their Article III jurisdiction (power to hear cases) over unchanged claims.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: The Court confined its claims holding to settlement necessary to resolve a major foreign-policy dispute where Congress had acquiesced.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: The Court limited its claims holding to settlements necessary to resolve a major foreign-policy dispute, where Congress had "acquiesced," meaning long gone along with the practice.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: Both sides agreed that whether suspension of the underlying claim caused a compensable taking was unripe.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: Both sides agreed it was unripe, too early to decide, whether suspending the underlying claim was a "compensable taking," a taking of property that requires the government to pay.

lrs-o-dames-moore.sentence: Part V held an appropriate Tucker Act claim could proceed in the Court of Claims despite the treaty exception.
lrs-o-dames-moore.plain: Part V held that a proper Tucker Act claim, a suit against the United States for compensation, could proceed in the Court of Claims. That was so despite the Act's exception for claims arising from treaties.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: If either foreign country changed restrictions so they no longer violated American neutral commerce, the President would proclaim that fact.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: If Britain or France stopped interfering with American ships trading as a neutral nation, the President was to announce that fact publicly.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: Congress supplied the event and domestic consequence; the President’s role operated within that legislative instruction.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: Congress decided what would happen and when; the President only announced whether the triggering event had occurred.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: The District Court for the District of Orleans condemned the goods on the government’s forfeiture libel, the pleading commencing an action against cargo.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: The District Court for the District of Orleans "condemned" (ordered forfeited) the goods on the government's "forfeiture libel." That is the pleading starting an "action" against the cargo itself to have it forfeited.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: Burnside’s counsel characterized revival through proclamation as a transfer of legislative power.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: Burnside's "counsel" (lawyer) argued that reviving the law through a "proclamation," a formal presidential announcement, was a transfer of "legislative power," the lawmaking power belonging to Congress.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: The government answered that Congress merely prescribed evidence of a fact on which its own law operated.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: The government answered that Congress itself made the law and merely set what would count as "evidence" of a fact on which its law operated, here the President's proclamation.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: The 1810 Act supplied fresh authorization, so the proclamation did not rest on independent presidential power to revive a dead law.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: The 1810 Act gave fresh authorization, so the "proclamation" did not rest on any independent presidential power to "revive" (bring back) an expired law.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: It did not use the later “intelligible principle” formulation or confer a general presidential authority over expired statutes.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: The Court did not use the later "intelligible principle" test, which requires Congress to give a clear guiding standard when it delegates power. Nor did it give the President general authority over expired "statutes."

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: An unnamed American in the bill of lading, a consignment to Burnside, and the Liverpool shipper’s identity did not establish beneficial ownership.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: The "bill of lading" (the shipping document) referred to an unnamed American, the goods were consigned (sent) to Burnside, and the Liverpool shipper was identified. None of that established "beneficial ownership," meaning who really owned the goods.

lrs-s-brig-aurora.sentence: The government’s libel needed to plead prohibited importation, not negate the fact establishing a defense or statutory exception.
lrs-s-brig-aurora.plain: The government's "libel," its complaint against the cargo, only had to "plead" (allege) prohibited importation. It did not have to disprove facts supporting a "defense" or statutory exception, such as American ownership, which Burnside had to prove.

sun-printing.sentence: For the remaining year, the parties promised to set both the price and how long it would govern fifteen days before each established period expired.
sun-printing.plain: For the remaining year, 1920, the "parties" promised to agree on both the price and how long it would apply. They were to do so fifteen days before each pricing period expired.

sun-printing.sentence: A price ceiling used Canadian Export Paper Company’s contract rate to large customers, adjusted to give Remington the freight differential.
sun-printing.plain: A "price ceiling," a maximum, used the rate Canadian Export Paper Company charged large customers under its "contract," adjusted so Remington got the freight differential, the difference in shipping costs.

sun-printing.sentence: Remington answered that both price and duration required further assent and that it had granted no series of exclusive monthly options.
sun-printing.plain: Remington answered that both price and duration needed further "assent" (agreement) for 1920. It said it had never granted Sun a series of exclusive monthly options to buy at the capped price.

sun-printing.sentence: Special Term denied Sun’s motion for judgment on the pleadings.
sun-printing.plain: Special Term, the New York trial-level court, denied Sun's "motion for judgment on the pleadings," a request to win based on the written filings alone.

sun-printing.sentence: Remington took a permitted appeal to the Court of Appeals, with the certified question whether the complaint stated sufficient facts for a cause of action.
sun-printing.plain: Remington took a permitted appeal to the Court of Appeals, New York's highest court, on a "certified question." The question was whether the complaint stated enough facts for a "cause of action," a legally enforceable claim.

sun-printing.sentence: If only price were missing, the stated maximum might support a buyer’s option to require delivery at that figure.
sun-printing.plain: If only the price had been left open, Sun might have been able to insist on delivery by agreeing to pay the maximum.

sun-printing.sentence: Duration therefore allocated risk and stability, rather than merely providing administrative convenience.
sun-printing.plain: So the duration term "allocated risk" (decided who bears the risk of market changes) and provided stability. It was not merely an administrative convenience.

sun-printing.sentence: That construction put Remington at the buyer’s successive disposal without agreement to do so.
sun-printing.plain: Sun's reading would let it decide each month whether to buy while Remington was bound to sell, something Remington never agreed to.

sun-printing.sentence: In Cardozo’s view, adding one would alter the bargain, leaving the presented arrangement an agreement to agree for the remaining deliveries.
sun-printing.plain: In Cardozo’s view, a court adding a duration term would change the "bargain." That left the arrangement for the remaining deliveries an "agreement to agree," a promise to agree later, which is not enforceable.

sun-printing.sentence: Cardozo also reserved whether arbitrary refusal to agree about duration might breach a duty if Sun offered to let Remington choose the periods.
sun-printing.plain: Cardozo also "reserved" (left undecided) whether an arbitrary refusal to agree on duration might "breach" a duty if Sun had offered to let Remington choose the periods. Sun never made that offer.

sun-printing.sentence: Crane favored preserving documented commercial intent through gap filling; Cardozo insisted on assent to the particular risk allocation that selecting duration would create.
sun-printing.plain: Crane, dissenting, favored honoring the businesses' documented intent through "gap filling," a court supplying the missing term. Cardozo insisted on "assent" (actual agreement) to the particular "risk allocation" that choosing a duration would create.

sun-printing.sentence: The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division, affirmed Special Term’s denial of Sun’s motion, awarded the stated appellate costs, and answered the certified sufficiency question no.
sun-printing.plain: The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division and affirmed Special Term’s denial of Sun's "motion" for judgment. It awarded the stated "appellate costs" and answered the "certified sufficiency question" (whether the complaint stated a claim) no.

teevee-toons.sentence: Attached terms limited the warranty to six months’ replacement for defective materials and workmanship, excluded other warranties including merchantability and fitness, and stated that the quotation and incorporated writings exhausted the agreement.
teevee-toons.plain: Attached fine print limited the "warranty" (quality promise) to six months' replacement for defective materials and workmanship. It excluded all other warranties, including "merchantability" (fit for ordinary use) and fitness, and said the quotation and incorporated papers were the whole agreement.

teevee-toons.sentence: No listed exclusion fit; manufacturing predominated over design and installation services under Article 3, and neither party expressly opted out.
teevee-toons.plain: No listed exclusion from the treaty applied. Under Article 3, manufacturing "predominated" (was the main part) over design and installation services, and neither party expressly opted out of the treaty.

teevee-toons.sentence: Article 11 permitted contract proof without a writing, while Article 8 looked to intent known or necessarily apparent to the other party, or otherwise a comparable reasonable person’s understanding.
teevee-toons.plain: Article 11 allows a contract to be proven without a writing. Article 8 looks to a party's intent if the other side knew it or could not have been unaware of it; otherwise, to how a comparable reasonable person would understand it.

teevee-toons.sentence: A domestic parol-evidence exclusion therefore could not foreclose evidence contradicting fine print.
teevee-toons.plain: So the American "parol-evidence" rule, which bars outside evidence contradicting a final written contract, could not block evidence contradicting the fine print. TVT could offer evidence of the oral assurance.

teevee-toons.sentence: The specific interaction with a merger clause appeared novel in American CISG decisions.
teevee-toons.plain: How the treaty works with a "merger clause," a clause saying the writing is the whole agreement, appeared to be a new question in American decisions applying the CISG, the U.N. treaty on international sales.

teevee-toons.sentence: TVT had not conclusively proved exclusion of the terms, but its evidence created a genuine question whether Neuber could not have been unaware of Gottlieb’s interpretation at acceptance.
teevee-toons.plain: TVT had not conclusively proven the fine print was excluded. But its evidence raised a genuine question whether Neuber, who acted for Schubert's U.S. agent, could not have been unaware of Gottlieb's understanding at "acceptance," when the deal was accepted.

teevee-toons.sentence: If both intended the writing and merger clause to govern, Article 6 permitted variation and the disclaimers would undermine the pleaded Convention warranties.
teevee-toons.plain: If both sides intended the writing and its "merger clause" (saying the writing is the whole deal) to govern, Article 6 lets parties vary the treaty's default rules. The "disclaimers" (warranty exclusions) would then defeat the Convention warranties TVT "pleaded," meaning claimed in its complaint.

teevee-toons.sentence: October notice after late-August delivery was reasonable under Article 39 in these manufacturing circumstances; shorter-notice foreign cases did not control the particular facts.
teevee-toons.plain: Under Article 39, a buyer must give notice of defects within a reasonable time. Notice in October after late-August delivery was reasonable given these manufacturing circumstances, and foreign cases requiring shorter notice did not control these facts.

teevee-toons.sentence: It was neither a contracting party nor an intended beneficiary known or contemplated by Schubert and could not rely on statements made before it existed.
teevee-toons.plain: SGI was neither a contracting "party" nor an "intended beneficiary," someone the contract was meant to benefit, known or contemplated by Schubert. It also could not rely on statements made before it existed.

teevee-toons.sentence: CISG Articles 45 and 74 permitted breach loss, including lost profits, limited by foreseeability at formation and sufficiently certain computation.
teevee-toons.plain: CISG Articles 45 and 74 let a buyer recover loss from a breach, including lost profits. But the loss is limited by "foreseeability" (what was predictable when the contract was formed) and must be "sufficiently certain," calculable with reasonable reliability.

teevee-toons.sentence: Fraud was not automatically duplicative because TVT alleged misrepresentations of existing capabilities before contracting.
teevee-toons.plain: The fraud claim was not just a repeat of the contract claim, because it alleged lies about the machine's existing abilities that induced TVT to sign.

teevee-toons.sentence: It nevertheless lacked justifiable reliance under New York law.
teevee-toons.plain: TVT nevertheless lacked "justifiable reliance" under New York law, meaning it could not reasonably rely on the alleged lies. Its own hired packaging expert had access to the technical facts.

teevee-toons.sentence: Negligence also failed because the complaint sought economic loss from defective goods and contractual failures without adequately alleging an independent duty.
teevee-toons.plain: The negligence claim also failed. The "complaint" sought only money losses from defective "goods" and broken contract promises, without adequately "alleging" (claiming) a separate duty owed outside the contract.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Its seniority system ordinarily measured service within a department, so a transfer generally sacrificed accumulated seniority.
brief-CP-135.plain: Its "seniority system" (ranking workers by length of service) ordinarily counted service within one department. So a worker who transferred generally gave up the seniority he had built up.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Black employees argued that the resulting deterrent preserved disadvantages from earlier assignment to less desirable jobs.
brief-CP-135.plain: Black workers had earlier been put in the worse departments. They argued that the fear of losing seniority kept them from transferring out, so the old discrimination lived on.

brief-CP-135.sentence: It found no discriminatory intent and held the system protected by Title VII § 703(h).
brief-CP-135.plain: The trial judge found no "discriminatory intent": the system was not created or kept in order to discriminate. He held it protected by Title VII § 703(h), which shields genuine seniority systems even if their effects are unequal.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Although it expressed a firm conviction that a mistake occurred, it also relied on circuit precedent permitting independent review of discrimination as an ultimate fact.
brief-CP-135.plain: The appeals court said it was firmly convinced a mistake occurred, the usual test for overturning a factual finding. But it also relied on "circuit" precedent, its own earlier rule, allowing "independent review" of discrimination as an "ultimate fact," deciding it afresh without deferring to the trial judge.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Justice White explained that under the substantive seniority rule the Court applied, disparate consequences did not by themselves establish illegality; discriminatory purpose mattered.
brief-CP-135.plain: Justice White explained that under the "substantive" seniority rule the Court applied (the rule deciding legality), unequal effects did not by themselves prove "illegality." What mattered was discriminatory purpose.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a) protected factual findings unless clearly erroneous, with no general exception for ultimate facts.
brief-CP-135.plain: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 52(a) required appeals courts to accept factual findings unless "clearly erroneous," meaning clearly wrong. It had no general exception for "ultimate facts," the key facts that decide a case.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Courts of appeals could correct legal standards and legal relevance errors, but could not relabel this motive inquiry to make new facts freely.
brief-CP-135.plain: "Courts of appeals" could correct errors about the legal standard or about which evidence legally matters. But they could not relabel this question of motive as a legal one just to find new facts freely.

brief-CP-135.sentence: An appellate court could set aside a finding for that legal error, but ordinarily had to remand unless the record permitted only one factual resolution.
brief-CP-135.plain: An "appellate court" could set aside a finding for that "legal error," such as treating relevant evidence as legally irrelevant. But it ordinarily had to "remand" (send back) for new findings unless the "record," the trial evidence, allowed only one factual answer.

brief-CP-135.sentence: Even discriminatory purpose by the Machinists could not automatically be imputed to the Steelworkers.
brief-CP-135.plain: Even if the Machinists union had a "discriminatory purpose," it could not automatically be "imputed" to (treated as belonging to) the Steelworkers union. Each union's purpose had to be found separately.

brief-CP-143.sentence: The tax dispute concerned whether his remaining powers nevertheless made the royalties his income.
brief-CP-143.plain: The question was whether Sunnen, because he kept so much control over the patents and the company, should still be taxed on royalties that were paid to his wife.

brief-CP-143.sentence: The Tax Court taxed the later royalties to Sunnen based on retained control, except the $4,881.35 it treated as conclusively governed by the earlier judgment.
brief-CP-143.plain: The Tax Court taxed the later royalties to Sunnen because he kept control. The exception was the $4,881.35 paid under the 1928 contract, which it treated as conclusively governed by the earlier "judgment" holding such payments were not his income.

brief-CP-143.sentence: Because it ruled for Sunnen on those merits, it did not decide his additional preclusion argument about the other contracts.
brief-CP-143.plain: Because the appeals court "ruled" for Sunnen on the "merits" (the main tax question), it did not decide his backup "preclusion" argument: that the earlier case also settled the other contracts.

brief-CP-143.sentence: The Court began with Cromwell, the precedent distinguishing a final judgment on the same cause of action from its narrower effect on a different cause.
brief-CP-143.plain: The Court began with Cromwell, the "precedent" distinguishing two effects of a final judgment. On the same "cause of action" (claim), it bars a second suit entirely; on a different cause, it settles only the issues actually decided.

brief-CP-143.sentence: For the same tax year and claim, a merits judgment generally barred matters raised or that could have been raised.
brief-CP-143.plain: For the same tax year and "claim," a judgment on the merits generally "barred" (blocked) every matter that was raised or could have been raised.

brief-CP-143.sentence: Each new income-tax year, however, created a distinct liability, so collateral estoppel reached only issues actually determined with relevant facts and governing rules unchanged.
brief-CP-143.plain: But each new income-tax year created a separate "liability," a separate tax debt. So collateral estoppel (issue preclusion) reached only issues actually decided, and only if the relevant facts and governing rules were unchanged.

brief-CP-143.sentence: That rule preserved finality without giving one taxpayer a perpetual exemption under superseded law while comparable taxpayers paid.
brief-CP-143.plain: That rule kept decided cases final without giving one taxpayer a permanent "exemption" (freedom from tax) under outdated law while comparable taxpayers paid.

brief-CP-143.sentence: Precedent might support consistency, but stare decisis was different from barring litigation.
brief-CP-143.plain: Precedent might support reaching the same answer, but "stare decisis," following earlier decisions, differs from "barring" a party from litigating the issue at all.

brief-CP-143.sentence: Together with payments staying in the family economic unit and no substantial change in his economic position, these concrete powers supported the Tax Court’s conclusion that he reallocated receipts without shifting their tax incidence.
brief-CP-143.plain: The payments stayed within the family as an economic unit, and Sunnen's economic position barely changed. Together with his concrete powers of control, this supported the Tax Court’s conclusion that he redirected the payments without shifting their "tax incidence," meaning who is taxed on them.

brief-CP-143.sentence: Justices Frankfurter and Jackson stated that substantial evidence and law supported affirming the Tax Court, invoking the review principles associated with Dobson and Scottish American.
brief-CP-143.plain: Justices Frankfurter and Jackson said that "substantial evidence" (enough reasonable evidence) and the law supported "affirming" (upholding) the Tax Court. They invoked the deferential "review" principles associated with Dobson and Scottish American.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Nixon specially appeared to challenge jurisdiction and formally claimed executive privilege.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Nixon "specially appeared," coming to court only to challenge its "jurisdiction" (power over him) without accepting its authority. He also formally claimed "executive privilege," the protection of a President's confidential communications from disclosure.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: On August 29, Sirica ordered Nixon to submit the material for in camera inspection so the judge could decide what, if anything, the grand jury should receive.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: On August 29, Judge Sirica ordered Nixon to submit the material for "in camera" inspection, a private review by the judge alone. The judge would then decide what, if anything, the grand jury should receive.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Nixon petitioned for mandamus to vacate the order.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Nixon "petitioned" (formally asked) the appeals court for mandamus, an order directing a lower judge, to "vacate" (cancel) Sirica's order.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Their substance remained confidential; there was no settlement mooting judicial review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: The content of the talks stayed confidential. There was no "settlement" (agreement ending the dispute) that would make the case moot, so the court still had a live dispute to review.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Ordinary subpoena recipients generally obtain review by refusing compliance and appealing contempt, not immediately appealing enforcement.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Someone served with a "subpoena," an order to produce evidence, generally cannot appeal right away. They must refuse to comply, be held in contempt, and then appeal the contempt ruling.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Requiring presidential disobedience and contempt could be clearly inadequate, and prompt resolution had unusual public importance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Forcing a President to disobey a court and be held in contempt just to get an appeal would be a poor route, and the country needed a quick answer.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: The All Writs Act permitted consideration of his petition.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: The All Writs Act, a federal law letting courts issue special orders, allowed the appeals court to consider Nixon's petition.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Sirica had not finally withheld evidence, and preliminary inspection was not yet suppression or exclusion under the Criminal Appeals Act.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Sirica had not finally withheld any evidence, and his preliminary private inspection was not yet suppression or exclusion of evidence. So prosecutor Cox could not yet appeal under the Criminal Appeals Act.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: It rejected both a complete immunity from judicial process and Nixon’s exclusive power to decide privilege.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: The court rejected Nixon's claim to complete "immunity from judicial process," total protection from court orders. It also rejected Nixon’s claim to the exclusive power to decide whether privilege applies; courts decide that.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: The Burr proceedings showed presidential evidence was not categorically beyond process; Youngstown’s limits on executive action did not depend on formally naming a subordinate.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: In Aaron Burr's trial, a court subpoenaed evidence from President Jefferson, so presidential evidence is not automatically off-limits. And Youngstown's limits on presidential power did not depend on the technicality that the suit there named a cabinet officer rather than the President.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Confidential advice and tentative positions concerning official duties deserved a strong presumption of protection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Private advice to the President and early, unsettled views on official business are presumed to be protected. But that presumption can be overcome by a strong enough need.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Permission for officials to testify affected the confidentiality balance without automatically waiving all privilege over fuller recordings.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Letting officials testify about the meetings weakened the case for secrecy in the balance. But it did not mean "waiving" (giving up) all privilege over the fuller recordings.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Unlike initial inspection, later particular disclosure rulings were treated as appealable by Nixon under § 1291 and Cox under § 3731, with sealed records preserving confidentiality.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Unlike the initial private inspection, later rulings on disclosing particular material were treated as "appealable": by Nixon under § 1291 and by Cox under § 3731. "Sealed records," kept secret by the court, would preserve confidentiality meanwhile.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: Courts could balance ordinary statutory or common-law confidentiality; a constitutional interbranch privilege instead left the President final authority, comparable to other branches’ control of their own protected deliberations.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: Judge Wilkey said courts could balance ordinary "statutory" or common-law confidentiality, protections created by statute or judge-made law. A constitutional privilege between branches instead gave the President final authority, like the other branches' control over their own protected deliberations.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: The mandate was stayed five days to allow an application for Supreme Court review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: The "mandate was stayed" (the ruling's taking effect was delayed) for five days, so Nixon could apply for Supreme Court "review."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.sentence: It illustrates that an extraordinary means of review can be appropriate even when the applicant does not obtain the requested merits relief.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-507.plain: The case shows that an extraordinary means of review, like mandamus, can be appropriate even when the applicant loses on the "merits," the substance of his claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: Its taxable gains depended on proceeds minus basis, here the property’s value on March 1, 1913.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: The company's taxable profit was its sale price minus the property's tax 'basis'. For property owned before the income tax began, the basis was its value on March 1, 1913.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: It argued the earlier valuation supplied an indisputable starting point for subtraction and that the Board must already have determined partially improved value as a necessary step toward fully improved value.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: The company argued the earlier "valuation" (appraisal) of finished lots was an indisputable starting point, from which improvement costs could simply be subtracted. It also said the Board must already have valued the partially improved land as a necessary step toward valuing fully improved lots.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: The improvement-cost finding itself was unnecessary to the earlier judgment and created no estoppel.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: The improvement-cost finding itself was not necessary to the earlier "judgment," so it created no "estoppel," meaning it did not bind the parties in later cases.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: Hand called a fact ultimate when, with other facts, it triggered a legal right, duty, or sanction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: Judge Hand called a fact "ultimate" when, together with other facts, it triggered a legal right, "duty," or sanction. A mere piece of evidence from which such a fact is inferred is different.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: Courts disagreed whether a necessary evidentiary finding in the first action could ever be preclusive.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: Courts disagreed whether a necessary finding about evidence in the first case could ever be "preclusive," meaning binding on the parties in a later case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: Even assuming a first suit’s mediate finding could conclusively establish a second suit’s ultimate fact, an earlier finding could not conclusively supply a mediate datum in the second suit.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: Assume a finding about evidence in a first "suit" could conclusively establish an "ultimate fact," one that directly decides a second suit. Even so, an earlier finding could not conclusively supply a mere piece of evidence from which a different fact is inferred in the second suit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: Turning every earlier determination into indisputable evidence for every rational future inference would multiply exposure beyond what they could calculate.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: Treating every earlier finding as indisputable evidence for every logical "inference" (conclusion drawn from evidence) in future cases would expose parties to consequences far beyond what they could calculate.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.sentence: The thirty-five-cent basis and resulting deficiency determination stood; the company obtained neither mandatory subtraction nor a new valuation proceeding.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-554.plain: The Tax Court's thirty-five-cent basis (value per square foot of the partly improved land) and the "resulting deficiency" determination, the extra tax found owed, stayed in place. The company got neither the mandatory subtraction it wanted nor a new valuation proceeding.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: The theory relied on Kansas’s implied duty of marketability.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The theory relied on Kansas's "implied duty of marketability": an unwritten duty read into gas leases requiring the producer to make the gas sellable at its own expense.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: Unless a lease provided otherwise, a producer bore gathering, compression, dehydration, treatment, and processing costs needed to make gas marketable.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: Unless the lease said otherwise, the producer had to pay the costs of getting gas into sellable condition and could not take them out of owners' royalties.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: The district court certified a class under Rule 23(b)(3), relying on whether the uniform payment methodology breached the marketability duty.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The "district court" certified a class under Rule 23(b)(3), letting the case proceed as a class action. It relied on one common question: whether XTO's uniform payment method "breached" (broke) the marketability duty for everyone.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: The Tenth Circuit allowed a Rule 23(f) appeal in which XTO contested commonality, typicality, adequacy, and predominance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The Tenth Circuit allowed a Rule 23(f) appeal, an immediate appeal of the class ruling. XTO contested "commonality" (shared questions), typicality (claims typical of the class), adequacy of representation, and "predominance," whether common issues outweigh individual ones.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: Judge Kelly, joined by Judges McKay and Matheson, explained that Rule 23 requires proof of compliance, not allegations or a presumption favoring certification.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: Judge Kelly, "joined by" Judges McKay and Matheson, explained that Rule 23 requires actual proof that its requirements are met. "Allegations" (unproven claims) or a "presumption" (an assumption) favoring certification are not enough.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: A common question must yield an answer central to every claim.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The shared question must be one whose answer matters to every class member's claim.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: A deduction was wrongful only if an owner possessed the claimed contractual right and the gas had not already become marketable when the expense arose.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: A deduction was wrongful only if that owner actually had the claimed "contractual" right under its lease, and the gas had not already become marketable when the expense arose. Both points could differ from owner to owner.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: The district court assumed every lease contained the duty because XTO had not identified language unambiguously negating it.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The "district court" assumed every lease contained the duty because XTO had not pointed to language "unambiguously" (clearly) negating it. That wrongly put the burden on XTO rather than on the Trust, which sought the class.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: Rule 23(b)(3) predominance required still more demanding analysis of how the litigation would proceed, including lease rights, marketability, and defenses.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: Rule 23(b)(3) "predominance," requiring common issues to outweigh individual ones, demanded even closer analysis of how the litigation would actually proceed. That included differing lease rights, "marketability" of the gas, and defenses.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: Subclasses or liability-only proceedings followed by individual damages determinations could preserve appropriate class treatment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: "Subclasses" (smaller groups within the class), or proceedings deciding liability for everyone followed by individual damages determinations, could preserve appropriate class treatment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: The Trust argued that collateral or judicial estoppel should bar XTO’s objections because it had settled the Fankhouser royalty class action.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The Trust argued that collateral estoppel (issues already decided) or "judicial estoppel" (barring a party from contradicting a position it took in earlier litigation) should block XTO's objections. XTO had settled the earlier Fankhouser royalty class action.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.sentence: The district court deserved an opportunity to apply those later certification decisions here, and the panel declined equitable foreclosure of XTO’s objection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-REF-348.plain: The "district court" deserved a chance to apply the later, stricter certification decisions here. The "panel" (the three appeals judges) declined to use fairness doctrines to foreclose XTO's objection.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: A special .017 percent sales-and-use tax was credited against the existing statewide rate rather than added to it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: A special .017 percent sales-and-use tax was credited against the existing statewide rate, not added to it. So shoppers paid no more; a slice of the existing state tax went to the stadium.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: Initiative 16 would require voter approval for county facility debt over $50 million and operate from January 1, 1997, potentially reaching the stadium bonds retroactively.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: Initiative 16, a citizen-proposed measure, would require voter approval for county facility debt over $50 million, operating from January 1, 1997. Applied "retroactively" (to actions already taken), it might reach the stadium bonds.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: King County brought an action under Revised Code of Washington 7.25 against representative taxpayers.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: King County brought an "action" (a lawsuit) under Revised Code of Washington 7.25, a procedure for having a court confirm bonds are valid. It sued representative taxpayers who stood in for all county taxpayers.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: On cross-motions the trial court granted county summary judgment, denied the taxpayers’ motion, and entered declaratory judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: On "cross-motions," with both sides asking to win without trial, the trial court "granted" the county summary judgment and denied the taxpayers' motion. It then "entered" (formally issued) a declaratory judgment declaring the bonds valid.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: Because validation conclusively settled matters within its scope, the court addressed the lease, tax collection, delegation, and voting measures.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: A validation ruling settles questions about the bonds for good, so the court decided every challenge that could affect them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: The taxpayers argued that the return was grossly inadequate and violated article VIII, sections 5 and 7 by transferring public value to a private team.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: The taxpayers argued the team gave a grossly inadequate return. They said this violated article VIII, sections 5 and 7 of Washington's constitution, which forbid gifts of public money to private businesses, by transferring public value to a private team.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: Ordinarily courts assess legal sufficiency rather than compare market values; routine judicial appraisal would intrude on governmental contracting.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: Ordinarily courts check only legal sufficiency, that the government got something of real value, rather than comparing market values. Routine judicial "appraisal" (pricing the deal) would intrude on the government's own contracting.
The team's obligations were not "illusory," meaning empty promises it could ignore; they were real, enforceable commitments.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: State law preempted the field, leaving the authorized decision outside the proposed initiative and referendum.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: State law "preempted" the field, fully covering this kind of decision so local measures could not interfere. That left the authorized financing decision outside the reach of the proposed initiative and referendum.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: The initiative’s prospective effect was ripe for resolution in comprehensive validation even though it had not passed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: Even though Initiative 16 had not passed, its "prospective" effect (how it would apply going forward) was "ripe for resolution," ready to decide now, because validation is meant to settle everything comprehensively.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: A peppercorn could support a private promise despite a profound public loss.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: In contract law a "peppercorn," a token payment, can support a private promise. So some return could exist even alongside a profound loss to the public.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: Constitutional text, history, and precedent required scrutiny of adequacy when evidence showed donative intent or grossly inadequate return.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: Justice Sanders said constitutional text, history, and "precedent" (earlier decisions) required courts to examine whether the return was adequate when evidence showed an intent to give a gift or a grossly inadequate return.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: Viewed favorably to the taxpayers at summary judgment, Sanders found evidence warranting trial.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: On summary judgment, the evidence must be read in the light most favorable to the side opposing it. Read that way, Sanders thought there was enough to require a trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: He argued that the county had blocked a timely referendum, had neither pleaded nor proved laches in its proper defensive role, and could not benefit from its own conduct.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: Sanders argued the county itself had blocked a "timely" referendum, one within the deadline. It had neither "pleaded" (raised in its filings) nor proven laches, the defense against unreasonable delay, in its proper defensive role, and could not benefit from its own conduct.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.sentence: Litigation by particular taxpayers did not necessarily extinguish the whole defendant class’s rights.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-009.plain: Lawsuits by particular taxpayers did not necessarily "extinguish" (wipe out) the rights of the whole "defendant class," all the taxpayers the case was brought against.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Stirling invoked its status as a disclosed agent, while Trade-Winds argued that knowingly hiring an unlicensed contractor exceeded the agent’s authority.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Stirling relied on its status as a "disclosed agent," an openly identified representative signing for the owner, which is not personally bound. Trade-Winds argued that knowingly hiring an unlicensed contractor exceeded the agent’s authority, which would make Stirling liable itself.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Trade-Winds responded with allegations of an insurance-payment scheme and a possible third-party benefit in an indemnification agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Trade-Winds responded with "allegations" (unproven claims) of a scheme involving insurance payments. It also claimed a possible "third-party" benefit, a right as an outsider to collect, in an indemnification agreement (a promise to cover losses).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Louisiana decisions treated such contracts as null and void, while permitting unjust enrichment for actual materials, services, and labor costs.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Louisiana decisions treated contracts by unlicensed contractors as null and void. But they allowed recovery for "unjust enrichment," so the contractor could get its actual costs for materials, services, and labor.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Here the parties agreed on the policy’s existence and disputed its legal effect, leaving a question the court could resolve on summary judgment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Here the "parties" agreed the policy existed and disputed only its legal effect. That left a question of law the court could decide on "summary judgment," without a trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Judge Ivan L. R. Lemelle distinguished administrative enforcement discretion from statutory suspension.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Judge Ivan L. R. Lemelle distinguished the licensing board's "enforcement discretion," its choice not to crack down hard, from suspension of the statute itself. Lax enforcement did not cancel the licensing requirement.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Stirling’s alleged knowledge could not estop defendants from invoking those laws.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Stirling's "alleged" (claimed) knowledge that Trade-Winds was unlicensed could not "estop" the defendants, meaning bar them, from relying on those licensing laws.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: Louisiana Civil Code article 3016 generally protected an agent contracting in its principal’s name within its authority; article 3019 could impose personal liability for exceeding authority, subject to exceptions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Under Louisiana Civil Code article 3016, an agent signing in its principal's name within its authority is generally not personally bound. Article 3019 can make an agent personally liable for exceeding its authority, subject to exceptions.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: The court reasoned that those provisions concerned execution of a contract, whereas no valid contract existed here.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: Those agent rules apply to valid contracts. Because this contract was void, there was nothing to hold Stirling liable on.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: A stipulation pour autrui—a contract benefit enforceable by a third party—required a manifestly clear benefit and could not be presumed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: A "stipulation pour autrui," a contract benefit "enforceable" by a "third party" (an outsider to the contract), required a manifestly clear benefit. It could not be presumed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.sentence: The mere existence of an indemnification agreement did not establish that benefit or a genuine issue for trial.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-041.plain: The mere existence of an "indemnification" agreement, a promise to cover losses, did not prove that benefit. Nor did it create a "genuine issue" for trial, a real factual dispute needing a trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: The court ultimately found these supplies unique and irreplaceable because of the shortage and dependent obligations, not merely more expensive to replace.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: The court found the buyer could not get this cotton anywhere else. That matters because courts order a seller to deliver only when money damages cannot fix the problem.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: Mitchell-Huntley filed this federal action September 25 for a declaration, specific performance, and restraints against abnormal harvesting delays, concealment, or other sales.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: On September 25 Mitchell-Huntley filed this federal case seeking a declaration that the contracts were valid and "specific performance," an order to deliver the cotton. It also sought orders forbidding abnormal harvesting delays, "concealment" (hiding) of the cotton, or sales to others.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: Diversity existed between the Delaware corporation with its Tennessee principal place of business and Alabama defendants, with the then-required amount satisfied.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: There was "diversity": the parties were citizens of different states. The buyer was a Delaware "corporation" with its "principal place of business" (headquarters) in Tennessee, the "defendants" were in Alabama, and the "then-required amount" of money at stake was met.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: Related transactions and common questions allowed joinder despite separate contracts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: The transactions were related and raised common questions, so "joinder" (combining the claims in one suit) was allowed despite separate contracts.
