brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: Later evidence at a contempt show-cause hearing supported its necessity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: Later evidence at a "contempt" show-cause hearing, where farmers had to explain why they should not be punished for disobeying the order, confirmed the order had been needed.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: The court found no sufficient detrimental reliance or actionable identity misinformation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: The court found no sufficient "detrimental reliance," meaning the farmers relied on false statements to their harm. Nor was any misinformation about the buyer's identity serious enough to be actionable.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: No demand for assurances was shown, although the court described that possible remedy for insecurity.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: No "demand for assurances" was shown: the farmers never asked the buyer for assurance that it would perform. The court only described that possible remedy for a party feeling insecure about the other side's performance.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: A mutuality objection failed because the promise to buy eligible cotton ginned by the deadline supplied consideration even if the later cotton were optional.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: A "mutuality" objection, that the buyer was not really bound, failed. The buyer's promise to buy all eligible cotton ginned by the deadline "supplied consideration," the binding commitment a contract needs, even if buying later cotton was optional.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: It imposed good-faith performance consistent with promptly harvesting and ginning as cotton matured.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: The court imposed a duty of "good-faith" (honest) performance, meaning harvesting and ginning promptly as the cotton matured, not stalling to slip past the December 15 deadline.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: A personal-service prohibition therefore did not bar relief.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: Courts will not order someone to perform personal services, but this farming work could be done by others. So that prohibition did not "bar" (block) relief here.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: The contracts were genuine intended sales and deliveries, not wagers prohibited by Alabama’s commodity-futures statutes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: The "contracts" were genuine sales meant to end in delivery. They were not "wagers" (bets on future prices) prohibited by Alabama’s "commodity-futures" statutes.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: Under the Alabama law applied, tenants held title and possession of the entire crop subject to landlords’ liens.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: Under the Alabama law applied, tenant farmers held title to (owned) and possessed the entire crop. It was subject to landlords' "liens," legal claims on the crop to secure rent.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.sentence: The preliminary injunction was to become permanent, with specific performance and retained jurisdiction for supplementary relief and costs.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-098.plain: The "preliminary injunction," a temporary order, was to become permanent, along with "specific performance" requiring delivery. The court kept jurisdiction to grant further "relief" and award costs.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: Herzog sued the attorneys to enforce the assignment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: Herzog sued the attorneys to "enforce the assignment," meaning to make them honor Jones's transfer to him of a right to part of the settlement money.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: On stipulated facts, the District Court found a valid transfer; the Superior Court affirmed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: On "stipulated facts," facts both sides agreed to, the District Court found a valid transfer. The Superior Court, the next court up, affirmed (upheld) that ruling.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: The Supreme Judicial Court directly reviewed the District Court, applying clear-error review to factual findings even though the evidence was stipulated and documentary.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: The Supreme Judicial Court, Maine's highest court, reviewed the District Court directly. It applied clear-error review, deferring to the "factual findings" unless clearly wrong, even though the "evidence" was agreed and all on paper.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: An assignment required intent to transfer the right and surrender control and revocation power, but did not require the obligor’s acceptance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: An assignment required intent to transfer the right and to give up control and the power of "revocation" (taking it back). It did not require acceptance by the "obligor," the party who owes the payment.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: Maine recognized equitable assignments of future litigation proceeds, including partial transfers, separately from assignment of the injury claim itself.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: Maine recognized "equitable assignments," transfers enforced on fairness principles, of future lawsuit proceeds, including partial ones. That is separate from assigning the injury claim itself.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: A bankruptcy-preference precedent did not displace that supported finding, and Jones’s later instruction could not revoke the completed transfer.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: A "bankruptcy-preference" precedent, about payments favoring one creditor before bankruptcy, did not override that supported "finding." And Jones's later instruction to his lawyers could not revoke a transfer already complete.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.sentence: Neither required ignoring Jones’s own assignment: he no longer owned the assigned portion, and he, not the lawyers, had created the encumbrance.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-122.plain: Neither ethics rule required the lawyers to ignore Jones's own assignment. He no longer owned the assigned portion, and he, not the lawyers, had created the "encumbrance," the claim on that money.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.sentence: The Court of Cassation’s Third Civil Chamber applied former Civil Code article 1134, governing the binding force of agreements.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.plain: The Court of Cassation’s Third Civil Chamber, part of France's highest court, applied former Civil Code article 1134. That article governs the binding force of agreements: a valid contract binds the parties like a law.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.sentence: It examined another part of the lower court’s own findings: through reasons that court had adopted, it had recognized a commitment to construct a chalet for an identified price under a document corresponding to an individual-house construction agreement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.plain: It looked at another part of the "lower court's" own "findings." Through reasons that court had "adopted" (taken on as its own), it had recognized a promise to build a chalet for a set price under a document matching an "individual-house construction agreement," a regulated contract to build a single home.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.sentence: It could not use subordinate documents to defeat the promise after making those findings.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.plain: After making those "findings," the court could not use lesser, subordinate documents to defeat the promise to build, since the contract made its own terms control.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.sentence: On May 3, 2001, the Court quashed the Nancy judgment in all its provisions, restored the parties to their position before it, and remanded to the Colmar Court of Appeal.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-006.plain: On May 3, 2001, the Court "quashed" (wiped out) the Nancy "judgment" in all its provisions and restored the "parties" to where they stood before it. It "remanded" (sent) the case to the Colmar Court of Appeal to decide again.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-STUDENT-COURSE.sentence: It presents the case as an illustration of a creditor seeking the agreed contract price, as distinct from substitute damages or termination.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-FA26-STUDENT-COURSE.plain: It presents the case as an example of a "creditor," the party owed performance, seeking the agreed "contract price." That differs from "substitute damages," money replacing the lost performance, or from termination of the contract.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: BMS moved to quash service on the nonresidents’ claims.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: BMS "moved to quash" service, asking the court to cancel the formal delivery of the suit, as to the "nonresidents'" claims. It argued California courts had no power over it for those out-of-state plaintiffs' claims.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: The superior court denied relief through general jurisdiction based on extensive local operations, and the court of appeal denied mandamus.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: The "superior court," California's trial court, denied relief, finding "general jurisdiction" (power to hear any claim) because of BMS's extensive California operations. The "court of appeal" denied mandamus, refusing to order that ruling undone.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: After Daimler narrowed the corporate general-jurisdiction analysis around where a corporation is at home, the California Supreme Court ordered reconsideration.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: After Daimler narrowed general jurisdiction over corporations to places where a corporation is "at home," usually its state of incorporation and headquarters, the California Supreme Court "ordered" the case reconsidered.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: Its majority used a sliding scale: broader unrelated forum contacts allowed a less direct link between the forum and individual claims.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: California's "majority" used a "sliding scale." The broader BMS's unrelated "forum contacts" (its business in California), the weaker the link needed between California and each individual claim.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: California’s jurisdictional statute reached the constitutional limit.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: California's "jurisdictional" statute, setting how far its courts' power reaches, went to the constitutional limit. So the only question was what due process allows.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: General jurisdiction ordinarily allowed any claim against a corporation at home in the forum; specific jurisdiction required claims arising out of or relating to forum contacts.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: "General jurisdiction" ordinarily allowed any claim against a "corporation" that is at home in the "forum," the state where suit is filed. Specific jurisdiction required claims "arising out of or relating to" the defendant's contacts with that state.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: Relaxing the latter connection because unrelated business was extensive would collapse the distinction into a substitute general jurisdiction.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: Letting lots of unrelated business replace the needed connection would turn case-specific jurisdiction into all-purpose jurisdiction by another name.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: Relationships with third parties did not by themselves create the required defendant–forum–controversy affiliation.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: Relationships with "third parties," such as the California resident plaintiffs, did not by themselves create the required connection among the "defendant," the forum, and this controversy.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: Due process protected against a State’s coercive authority as well as travel burdens.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: Due process protected not only against the burdens of litigating far away but also against a State's "coercive" authority, its power to force outsiders to answer in its courts.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: Its notes distinguished the defendant’s ability to assert absent plaintiffs’ rights because of preclusion effects from the defendant’s own unasserted rights.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: Its notes distinguished Shutts, where a defendant could assert absent plaintiffs’ rights because of "preclusion," the judgment's binding effect on them. That differs from the defendant's own rights, which were not asserted there.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: Plaintiffs alleged neither relevant joint California acts nor derivative BMS liability for McKesson’s California conduct, and supplied no evidence identifying how their own pills reached pharmacies.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: Plaintiffs alleged no "relevant" joint acts in California by BMS and McKesson, nor that BMS bore derivative "liability" (legal responsibility) for McKesson’s California conduct. They supplied no "evidence" showing how their own pills reached pharmacies.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: She separated purposeful availment, relatedness, and reasonableness.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, separated three steps: "purposeful availment" (did BMS deliberately do business in California), relatedness of the claims to that business, and "reasonableness," whether suit there is fair.

cp-bristol-myers.sentence: The Court expressly reserved whether the Fifth Amendment imposed the same limits in federal court.
cp-bristol-myers.plain: The Court expressly "reserved" (left undecided) whether the Fifth Amendment, which governs federal courts, imposes the same limits in federal court as the Fourteenth does in state court.

cp-conley.sentence: The defendants argued that the National Railroad Adjustment Board had exclusive jurisdiction, that the railroad was an indispensable but absent defendant, and that the complaint failed to state a claim.
cp-conley.plain: The "defendants" (the union side) argued that the National Railroad Adjustment Board, a special federal labor board, had exclusive jurisdiction, and that the railroad was an "indispensable" (required) but absent defendant. They also argued the "complaint" failed to state a claim, giving no remedy even if true.

cp-conley.sentence: Section 3 First (i) addressed grievances and interpretation or application of bargaining agreements between employees and carriers.
cp-conley.plain: Section 3 First (i) of the Railway Labor Act covered "grievances" (workplace complaints) and the interpretation or application of "bargaining agreements" (labor contracts) between employees and "carriers," the railroads.

cp-conley.sentence: These workers instead alleged breach of their bargaining representative’s statutory duty to act without racial discrimination.
cp-conley.plain: These workers instead "alleged" (claimed) that their "bargaining representative," the union, breached its statutory "duty" to represent them without racial discrimination.

cp-conley.sentence: The railroad was not indispensable to this action as framed.
cp-conley.plain: The railroad was not "indispensable" to the case, meaning the case could go ahead without it as a party. As the workers framed the case, they asked nothing of the railroad, and a ruling would not affect its rights.

cp-conley.sentence: A fair agreement on its face could still be administered discriminatorily with a union’s active or tacit consent.
cp-conley.plain: A contract that looks fair "on its face" can still be applied in a discriminatory way. A union that goes along with that, actively or by "tacit consent" (quiet, unspoken approval), breaks its duty to the workers.

cp-conley.sentence: The Court applied its then-stated standard that dismissal was improper unless it appeared beyond doubt that no set of supporting facts could entitle the claimant to relief.
cp-conley.plain: Under the Court's standard at the time, "dismissal" (throwing out the complaint) was improper unless it was beyond doubt that the "claimant," the person suing, could prove no set of facts that would entitle them to relief.

cp-conley.sentence: Rule 8(a)(2) required a short and plain statement giving fair notice of the claim and its grounds, not detailed factual allegations.
cp-conley.plain: "Rule 8(a)(2)" of the federal rules required only a "short and plain statement" of the claim. It had to give the defendant fair notice of the claim and what it rests on, not detailed factual "allegations" (the facts the plaintiff says are true).

cp-conley.sentence: Other procedural tools could clarify the dispute: illustrative forms, more definite statements, motions to strike or for judgment on the pleadings, pretrial proceedings, discovery, summary judgment, and amendment.
cp-conley.plain: If a complaint is vague, other procedural tools can clarify the dispute later. These include model forms, motions for "more definite statements" (asking the plaintiff to be clearer), motions to strike or for "judgment on the pleadings" (a ruling on the filed papers alone), pretrial proceedings, "discovery" (exchanging evidence), summary judgment, and "amendment" (fixing the complaint).

cp-conley.sentence: The no-set-of-facts language belongs to this historical decision; the Court later reexamined it in Twombly.
cp-conley.plain: The "no-set-of-facts" test belongs to this older decision and is no longer the law. In Twombly (2007) the Court reexamined it and replaced it with a requirement of factual allegations that make the claim plausible.

cp-perkins.sentence: The trial court quashed service on Benguet, and Ohio’s intermediate appellate court and supreme court affirmed.
cp-perkins.plain: The "trial court" quashed service on Benguet, ruling that serving papers on its president did not bring the company into the case. Ohio's "intermediate appellate court" (its middle-level appeals court) and its supreme court "affirmed," or upheld, that ruling.

cp-perkins.sentence: Benguet had not obtained a foreign-corporation license or named a statutory service agent, but those omissions did not themselves prevent it from doing business or being sued under Ohio law.
cp-perkins.plain: Benguet had not obtained a license to operate in Ohio as an out-of-state ("foreign") corporation or named a "statutory service agent," a person the law requires to receive lawsuit papers. Under Ohio law, those omissions did not by themselves stop it from "doing business" in Ohio or being sued there.

cp-perkins.sentence: Its syllabus represented the court’s approved law; an accompanying opinion could express only its author’s view on matters outside the syllabus.
cp-perkins.plain: In Ohio then, the "syllabus," a short summary at the top of a decision, stated the court's official, approved ruling. On anything outside the syllabus, the full opinion below it spoke only for the judge who wrote it.

cp-perkins.sentence: The U.S. Supreme Court therefore faced the possibility that Ohio had declined jurisdiction because it mistakenly thought the Constitution left no choice.
cp-perkins.plain: So the U.S. Supreme Court had to consider that Ohio may have refused "jurisdiction" (its power to hear the case) only because it wrongly believed the federal Constitution left it no choice.

cp-perkins.sentence: Together, the Ohio activities amounted to continuous, systematic supervision of Benguet’s necessarily limited wartime business.
cp-perkins.plain: During the war, Ohio was where Benguet's business was actually run, day to day.

cp-perkins.sentence: That concentration made jurisdiction fair and reasonable even for claims entirely distinct from Ohio activities.
cp-perkins.plain: Because Benguet's activities were concentrated in Ohio, where it was effectively based, it was fair and reasonable for Ohio to exercise "jurisdiction" (power over the company) even for claims having nothing to do with its Ohio activities.

cp-perkins.sentence: Due process did not require Ohio to provide this forum.
cp-perkins.plain: "Due process," the Constitution's fairness guarantee, allowed Ohio to hear the case but did not require Ohio to provide this "forum," or court. Ohio could still decline under its own law.

cp-perkins.sentence: He agreed that the federal premise of the accompanying Ohio opinion was wrong, but read the syllabus as a clear, adequate, independent state ground.
cp-perkins.plain: Justice Minton agreed that the accompanying Ohio "opinion" wrongly rested on a federal premise. But he read the "syllabus," Ohio's official ruling, as an "adequate, independent state ground": a basis in Ohio law alone, which the U.S. Supreme Court has no power to review.

cp-perkins.sentence: He viewed the majority’s clarification as advisory and would have dismissed the writ as improvidently granted.
cp-perkins.plain: He saw the majority's clarification as "advisory," giving advice that might not change the outcome. He would have dismissed the "writ" (the Court's order agreeing to hear the case) as "improvidently granted," meaning the Court should not have taken it.

cp-piper.sentence: She sued Piper and Hartzell in California state court for negligence and strict liability, acknowledging selection of an American forum for more favorable liability, damages, and capacity-to-sue rules.
cp-piper.plain: Reyno sued Piper and Hartzell, the American makers, in California state court for "negligence" (carelessness) and strict liability (responsibility for a defect even without carelessness). She admitted she chose an American "forum," or court, because its rules on "liability," damages, and who may sue were more favorable.

cp-piper.sentence: Piper and Hartzell agreed to Scottish jurisdiction and waiver of available limitations defenses.
cp-piper.plain: Piper and Hartzell agreed to accept Scottish "jurisdiction," meaning a Scottish court's power over them. They also agreed to waive any available "limitations defenses," so they would not argue there that the suit was filed too late.

cp-piper.sentence: The manufacturers removed to the Central District of California.
cp-piper.plain: The manufacturers "removed" the case, moving it from California state court to the federal trial court for the "Central District of California."

cp-piper.sentence: Piper requested transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a); Hartzell challenged personal jurisdiction and alternatively requested transfer.
cp-piper.plain: Piper asked to "transfer" the case to a more convenient federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), a federal statute. Hartzell argued the court lacked "personal jurisdiction," the power to hear claims against it at all, or alternatively asked for transfer.

cp-piper.sentence: The Pennsylvania district court found Scotland available and adequate, balanced private and public interests, and dismissed for forum non conveniens.
cp-piper.plain: The Pennsylvania "district court" (federal trial court) found Scotland available and adequate as a place to sue. It weighed the "private and public interests" (the parties' convenience and the public's concerns) and dismissed for "forum non conveniens," the doctrine letting a court send a case to a far more convenient place.

cp-piper.sentence: Because the real parties in interest were foreign, it gave their American choice less deference than a home-forum choice.
cp-piper.plain: Because the "real parties in interest," the people actually suing, were Scottish, the court gave their choice of an American court less "deference," or respect, than it would give a plaintiff's choice of a home court.

cp-piper.sentence: It criticized the balancing and held that an unfavorable substantive-law change itself prevented dismissal.
cp-piper.plain: The appeals court criticized the trial court's "balancing" of the factors. It held that a less favorable "substantive-law" change, meaning worse rules on the rights at issue, by itself prevented "dismissal."

cp-piper.sentence: If less favorable foreign law always defeated dismissal, a legal advantage would defeat the doctrine in the very cases where plaintiffs chose an inconvenient forum for that advantage.
cp-piper.plain: Plaintiffs often pick an inconvenient American "forum," or court, precisely because its law favors them. If less favorable foreign law always blocked dismissal, that legal advantage would defeat the doctrine in exactly those cases.

cp-piper.sentence: Van Dusen’s law-preservation rule concerns statutory transfer within the unified federal system.
cp-piper.plain: Van Dusen’s rule, that the original law travels with a case, applies to "statutory" transfer, meaning a move under a statute between courts in the unified federal system. It does not apply when a court dismisses a case so it can be brought in another country.

cp-piper.sentence: An alternative so clearly inadequate that it effectively supplied no remedy could defeat adequacy or weigh heavily against dismissal.
cp-piper.plain: If the foreign court offered essentially no remedy at all, that could block dismissal. A merely smaller or different remedy is not enough.

cp-piper.sentence: The inability to implead the owner, operator, and pilot’s estate in the American action was particularly significant.
cp-piper.plain: In the American case, the manufacturers could not "implead" the owner, operator, and pilot's estate, meaning bring them into the suit to share the blame. The Court found this especially significant; in Scotland all could be sued together.

cp-piper.sentence: Separate later contribution or indemnity litigation would impose substantial burdens and risk inconsistent findings.
cp-piper.plain: Otherwise the makers would have to bring separate later suits for "contribution" or indemnity, to make the others pay their share or all of it. That would be costly and risk inconsistent "findings," meaning conflicting conclusions about the facts.

cp-piper.sentence: A reasonable district-court balance warranted review for clear abuse of discretion.
cp-piper.plain: When the "district-court" (trial court) judge reasonably weighed the factors, appellate "review" should overturn the decision only for a clear "abuse of discretion," meaning a clearly unreasonable choice.

cp-piper.sentence: The Court also expressly reserved whether federal or state forum non conveniens law governs a diversity action because the relevant standards produced the same result here.
cp-piper.plain: The Court expressly "reserved" (left undecided) whether federal or state forum non conveniens law governs a "diversity action," a case in federal court only because the parties are from different states. Here both standards gave the same result.

cp-sibbach.sentence: Sibbach refused, challenged the order as void, and was directed to show cause on contempt.
cp-sibbach.plain: Sibbach refused, arguing the order was void because the court had no power to order the exam. The court directed her to "show cause," meaning explain why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying.

cp-sibbach.sentence: The district court held Sibbach in contempt and ordered commitment until compliance or other lawful discharge.
cp-sibbach.plain: The district court, the federal trial court, held Sibbach in contempt and ordered "commitment," meaning jail, until she complied with the exam order or was otherwise lawfully released.

cp-sibbach.sentence: The 1934 statute authorized federal civil pleading, practice, and procedure rules without abridging, enlarging, or modifying substantive rights.
cp-sibbach.plain: The 1934 "statute," the Rules Enabling Act, let the Supreme Court write rules of federal civil "pleading" (the papers that start a case), practice, and procedure. Those rules could not shrink, expand, or change "substantive rights," meaning people's actual legal rights.

cp-sibbach.sentence: It also protected jury rights during law-equity merger and required submission to Congress before effect.
cp-sibbach.plain: The Act also protected the right to a jury when the rules merged the old separate systems of law and equity. And it required "submission" of the rules to Congress, which saw them before they took effect.

cp-sibbach.sentence: Rule 37 supplied litigation consequences for refusal: established facts, evidence restrictions, struck pleadings, stay, dismissal, or default.
cp-sibbach.plain: Rule 37 set penalties inside the lawsuit for a refusal: treating facts as established, limiting evidence, striking pleadings, a "stay" (pausing the case), dismissal, or a default judgment against the refusing party.

cp-sibbach.sentence: Justice Roberts’s majority asked whether the rules genuinely regulated procedure—the process for enforcing substantive rights and administering remedies.
cp-sibbach.plain: Justice Roberts’s "majority" opinion asked whether the rules really "regulated" procedure: the process for enforcing "substantive rights" (people's actual legal rights) and giving "remedies," as opposed to changing what those rights are.

cp-sibbach.sentence: If examination was procedural, a valid federal rule displaced old conformity to Illinois practice.
cp-sibbach.plain: If ordering an exam is a matter of procedure, a valid federal rule controls. It replaces the old practice of federal courts following the procedure of the state where they sit, here Illinois.

cp-sibbach.sentence: If a substantive exemption governed, the majority said the Rules of Decision Act pointed to Indiana, which allowed examination.
cp-sibbach.plain: The "majority" added that if a substantive exemption from examination applied, the "Rules of Decision Act," which tells federal courts when to apply state law, pointed to Indiana law, where the injury happened. Indiana allowed such examinations.

cp-sibbach.sentence: Failure to prevent effectiveness suggested at least no perceived legislative-policy violation, supporting rather than replacing the majority’s authority analysis.
cp-sibbach.plain: Congress saw the rules and did not block them, which suggests it saw no problem, though that was only extra support for the majority's reasoning.

cp-sibbach.sentence: It was not constitutionally immutable, but changing it needed clear legislation rather than a broad procedural delegation.
cp-sibbach.plain: Frankfurter thought the old protection against forced exams could be changed, but only by Congress saying so clearly, not by a general grant of power to make procedure rules.

cp-sibbach.sentence: Sibbach had not separately assigned contempt punishment as error on either appeal, but the Court treated it as fundamental plain error.
cp-sibbach.plain: Sibbach had not separately challenged her "contempt" punishment as an error on either appeal. The Court corrected it anyway as fundamental "plain error," an obvious, serious mistake a court may fix even when no one raised it.

cp-sibbach.sentence: Rule 37’s exception was explicit: litigation consequences were available, contempt imprisonment for this refusal was not.
cp-sibbach.plain: Rule 37's exception was explicit. Penalties inside the case were available, but jail for "contempt" (disobeying a court order) was not allowed for refusing this exam.

international-filter.sentence: The proposal said it would become a contract when accepted by the purchaser and approved by an International Filter executive officer at the Chicago office.
international-filter.plain: The proposal form said it would become a "contract," a binding deal, once the purchaser accepted it and an International Filter executive officer approved it at the Chicago office.

international-filter.sentence: It also argued that notice of approval was essential and had not been given, relying both on its reading of the form and Thompson’s testimony about his oral demand for prompt notification.
international-filter.plain: Conroe Gin also argued that notice of approval was required and was never given. It relied on its reading of the form and on Thompson’s "testimony" (sworn statement in court) that he had orally demanded prompt notice.

international-filter.sentence: The Commission of Appeals treated the signed document sent to Chicago as Conroe Gin’s offer to purchase.
international-filter.plain: The Commission of Appeals, a Texas body that helped the state's supreme court decide cases, treated the signed form sent to Chicago as Conroe Gin's offer to buy. International Filter accepted that offer by approving it.

international-filter.sentence: Although notice ordinarily protects an offeror seeking a return promise, an offeror can dispense with notice by selecting another sufficient method.
international-filter.plain: Notice of acceptance usually protects an offeror (the person making the offer) who wants a "return promise," a promise back from the other side. But an offeror can dispense with notice by choosing another sufficient method, here approval in Chicago.

international-filter.sentence: Requiring notice to arrive in Conroe would add a condition and change the specified time and place of formation.
international-filter.plain: Insisting that notice reach Conroe would add a requirement the parties never agreed to and change when and where the contract was formed.

international-filter.sentence: The writing was unambiguous, so the court applied its terms despite Thompson’s claimed oral instruction.
international-filter.plain: The writing was "unambiguous," meaning its terms were clear and open to only one reading. So the court applied those terms and would not let Thompson's claimed spoken instruction change them.

international-filter.sentence: The court further observed that reliance on such a letter might prevent the company from later denying approval.
international-filter.plain: If the buyer had acted on the letter, the company might be barred from later saying it never approved; but this was only a side comment.

international-filter.sentence: The distinction matters when comparing White, where a builder’s general preparations did not express acceptance of the proposed job: the offer and circumstances must make the offeree’s actual conduct sufficient assent.
international-filter.plain: This matters when comparing the White case, where a builder's general preparations did not express acceptance of the proposed job. The offer and circumstances must make the "offeree’s" actual conduct (the person receiving the offer) enough to show "assent," or agreement.

international-filter.sentence: The Commission of Appeals recommended reversing the Court of Civil Appeals and returning the case to that court for questions properly presented but not previously decided.
international-filter.plain: The Commission of Appeals recommended reversing the Court of Civil Appeals, Texas's intermediate appeals court. It would send the case back to that court to decide questions properly raised there but not yet decided.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: He gave small legacies to his daughters, Mrs. Riggs and Mrs. Preston, and left the residue of his real and personal property to his grandson, Elmer E. Palmer.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: His will gave small "legacies" (fixed gifts) to his daughters, Mrs. Riggs and Mrs. Preston. It left the "residue," meaning everything else, of his land and "personal property" (property other than land) to his grandson, Elmer E. Palmer.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: The daughters also held a conditional gift over if Elmer survived Francis but died while under age, unmarried, and without issue.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The daughters also held a conditional "gift over": if Elmer outlived Francis but then died under age, unmarried, and "without issue" (with no children), the property would pass to them instead.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: An antenuptial agreement promised her lifetime support on his farm instead of dower and other claims against the estate.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: Before Francis married Mrs. Bresee, they signed an "antenuptial agreement" (a prenuptial contract). It promised her support for life on his farm in place of "dower," a widow's legal share of her husband's land, and her other claims against the estate.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: Her support was charged on the farm.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: "Her support was charged" on the farm, meaning it was a legal burden attached to the land. Whoever got the farm would have to provide it.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: The civil case was tried before a referee, whose findings established the relevant facts.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The "civil case" (the daughters' private lawsuit, separate from the murder prosecution) was tried before a referee. That court-appointed official heard the evidence, and the referee's findings established the facts.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: The General Term of the Supreme Court in the Third Judicial Department affirmed through an order made February 5, 1887.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The General Term, the appeals branch of New York's Supreme Court (a trial-level court) for the Third Judicial Department, "affirmed," or upheld, the dismissal of the daughters' case. It did so in an "order" made February 5, 1887.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: The dispute was legal: did the statutory rules for wills and descent require Elmer to take because the will was properly executed and never revoked by a prescribed statutory act?
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The dispute was over the law, not the facts. Did the "statutory" rules (rules set by statute) for wills and descent (inheritance without a will) require Elmer to take the property, because the will was properly signed and never revoked by an act the statute prescribes?

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: It instead considered why the legislature protected testamentary disposition: owners should be able to direct property at death and have their lawful final wishes carried out.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The court instead asked why the legislature protects "testamentary disposition," the power to leave property by will. The reason is so owners can direct who gets their property at death and have their lawful final wishes carried out; letting a killer cut that off would defeat it.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: Statutes operate within that legal background unless the legislature displaces it.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: "Statutes" (laws passed by the legislature) are read against long-standing legal principles, such as "no one may profit from his own wrong." Those principles still apply unless the legislature sets them aside.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: The inheritance statutes did not expressly abrogate the principle, so silence about murder did not affirmatively authorize a murderer’s gain.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The inheritance "statutes" did not expressly "abrogate" (cancel) that principle. So their silence about murder was not permission for a murderer to gain.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: It also expressly rejected Owens v. Owens, which had allowed dower to a wife convicted as an accessory before the fact to her husband’s murder.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The court also expressly rejected Owens v. Owens. That case had let a wife claim "dower," a widow's share of her husband's land, though she was convicted as an "accessory before the fact" (someone who helped bring about the crime beforehand) to his murder.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: Denying its acquisition by murder therefore did not, in Earl’s view, confiscate vested property or add imprisonment to the criminal judgment.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: In Judge Earl’s view, Elmer did not yet own the property, so blocking him from getting it by murder did not "confiscate" (take away) property already his. Nor did it add imprisonment or other punishment to the criminal "judgment."

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: Elmer could not avoid the principle by claiming as an intestate heir rather than a devisee, because the causal connection between the killing and the desired property remained the same.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: Elmer could not avoid the rule by claiming as an "intestate heir" (a relative who inherits when there is no will) rather than as a "devisee" (someone given land in a will). Either way, the "causal" link between the killing and the property he wanted stayed the same.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: For Gray, intention to revoke did not complete revocation.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: Judge Gray said wanting to cancel a will is not enough; the law requires a specific act, such as destroying it or signing a new one.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: Its Roman-law comparison described escheat as punishment and treated a possible slayer rule as a legislative choice.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The dissent's Roman-law comparison described "escheat," taking a killer's inheritance and giving it to the state, as a punishment. It treated a possible "slayer rule," barring killers from inheriting, as a choice for the legislature, not the courts.

lrs-k-riggs.sentence: It directed that Elmer and the administrator be restrained from using estate property for Elmer’s benefit, that the devise and bequest to Elmer be ineffective to pass title, and that he have no interest in the estate.
lrs-k-riggs.plain: The court ordered that Elmer and the "administrator" (the person managing the estate) not use estate property for Elmer's benefit. The "devise" (gift of land) and bequest to Elmer could not "pass title," meaning make him the owner, and he had no interest in the estate.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: North Carolina’s 2016 congressional plan followed a judicial finding that two districts in the earlier plan were racial gerrymanders.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: North Carolina's 2016 map of congressional districts came after a court "finding" that two districts in the earlier map were "racial gerrymanders," meaning districts drawn mainly by race.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Success against the earlier racial gerrymander did not itself establish that the later partisan challenge was judicially resolvable.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: Winning the earlier "racial gerrymander" case (districts drawn mainly by race) did not by itself show that courts could decide the later challenge to districts drawn for party advantage.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: The Democratic Party, Common Cause, and voters, later joined by the League of Women Voters and additional voters, alleged equal-protection vote dilution, First Amendment retaliation and associational injuries, interference with Article I § 2’s popular choice of representatives, and misuse of Elections Clause power.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: The Democratic Party, Common Cause, and voters, later joined by the League of Women Voters and more voters, "alleged": equal-protection "vote dilution" (weakening their votes), First Amendment "retaliation" and harm to political association, interference with Article I § 2's popular choice of representatives, and misuse of "Elections Clause" power.
The "Defendants," the side defending the map, appealed straight to the Supreme Court under 28 U.S.C. § 1253. That statute allows a direct appeal from a special three-judge trial court.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: While that appeal was pending, Gill v. Whitford required a vote-dilution plaintiff to identify a particular injury from being packed into or cracked among districts.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: While that "appeal" was pending, Gill v. Whitford held that a voter claiming vote dilution must show a particular injury. He must show his own district was "packed" (his party's voters crowded together) or "cracked" (his party's voters spread thin across districts).

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: The district court again found standing and justiciability, invalidated twelve of thirteen districts under equal protection, reaffirmed its other constitutional conclusions, and prohibited use of the plan after the November 2018 election.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: The "district court" again found "standing" (the voters' right to sue) and that courts could decide the issue. It struck down twelve of the thirteen districts under "equal protection," reaffirmed its other constitutional rulings, and barred use of the map after the November 2018 election.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Chief Justice Roberts’s majority began with Article III and Baker v. Carr’s recognition that a lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards can create a political question.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: Chief Justice Roberts’s "majority" opinion began with Article III, which limits federal courts to real legal cases, and with Baker v. Carr. Baker held that a lack of "judicially discoverable and manageable standards" (clear, workable legal tests) can make an issue a "political question" for the elected branches.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Gaffney permitted attention to party balance; the divided Bandemer Court found justiciability without agreeing on a test; Vieth’s plurality favored nonjusticiability while Kennedy left open a future precise and neutral rule; LULAC produced none; and Gill decided standing.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: In Gaffney the Court let mapmakers consider "party" balance. A divided Bandemer Court found "justiciability" (that courts could decide) without agreeing on a test; Vieth’s "plurality" (the largest group, short of a majority) said courts could not, while Kennedy left open a future precise, neutral rule; LULAC produced none; and Gill decided only standing.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Equal-population cases supply mathematical equality for individual vote weight; racial claims target a suspect classification.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: Equal-population cases have a mathematical measure: equal weight for each person's vote. Racial "claims" target a "suspect classification," a use of race courts presume is improper. Party politics in districting, by contrast, is partly allowed, so there is no clear line.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: The majority reasoned that partisan intent, unlike a suspect racial classification, was not unconstitutional merely because it predominated.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: The "majority" reasoned that partisan intent, unlike a suspect racial classification, was not unconstitutional merely because it "predominated," meaning it was the main reason behind the map.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Treating all partisan classification as viewpoint discrimination would prohibit considerations precedent allowed.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: Treating every use of party data as "viewpoint discrimination," punishing voters for their political views, would ban considerations that "precedent" (past court decisions) had allowed.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: The argument that voters should choose representatives rather than the reverse resembled a Guarantee Clause republican-government objection previously treated as nonjusticiable.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: The argument that voters should choose representatives, not the reverse, looked like an objection under the "Guarantee Clause," which promises each state a republican government. Courts had long treated such claims as "nonjusticiable," meaning not for courts to decide.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Her proposed framework required predominant entrenchment intent, substantial vote dilution, and no legitimate nonpartisan explanation.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: Justice Kagan's proposed test, in dissent, required three things: the mapmakers' main aim was "entrenchment," locking in their party's power; the map caused substantial "vote dilution," weakening the other side's votes; and the state had no legitimate nonpartisan explanation.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: On June 27, 2019, the Supreme Court vacated both district-court judgments and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: On June 27, 2019, the Supreme Court "vacated" (erased) both district-court "judgments." It sent the cases back with instructions to "dismiss" them for lack of jurisdiction, because federal courts have no power to decide such claims.

lrs-k-rucho.sentence: Standing, the issue requiring the earlier Gill remand, remained distinct from this threshold of justiciability.
lrs-k-rucho.plain: Standing, whether a particular voter may sue, was the issue that required sending the case back after Gill. It is a separate question from this threshold one of justiciability: whether courts can decide this kind of dispute at all.

lrs-k-small.sentence: Federal prosecutors invoked 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), restricting specified firearm possession after a qualifying conviction in “any court” for a crime punishable by more than a year.
lrs-k-small.plain: Federal prosecutors relied on 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), which bans possessing certain firearms after a conviction in "any court" for a crime punishable by more than a year in prison. They said Small's Japanese conviction counted.

lrs-k-small.sentence: Small pleaded guilty while reserving whether a foreign judgment qualified.
lrs-k-small.plain: Small "pleaded guilty," formally admitting the crime, but kept the right to appeal one question: whether a foreign "judgment" (a conviction by a court abroad) counts under the law.

lrs-k-small.sentence: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, and Ginsburg, accepted that “any” is broad but considered its domain contextual.
lrs-k-small.plain: Justice Breyer, "joined by" Justices Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, and Ginsburg (who signed his opinion), agreed that "any" is a broad word. But what it covers depends on context, so "any court" could mean any court in the United States.

lrs-k-small.sentence: The presumption against extraterritorial application did not directly apply: the charged possession occurred in the United States.
lrs-k-small.plain: The "presumption against extraterritorial application," the usual rule that U.S. laws do not reach conduct abroad, did not directly apply. The possession Small was charged with happened in the United States.

lrs-k-small.sentence: The majority instead used a related domestic assumption to interpret which earlier judgments the domestic restriction incorporated.
lrs-k-small.plain: The "majority" instead used a related assumption that Congress usually has domestic matters in mind. It used that to decide which earlier "judgments" (convictions) the gun ban covers: American ones.

lrs-k-small.sentence: As a group they might be less reliable proxies for dangerousness under American law.
lrs-k-small.plain: Foreign convictions might not reliably show that someone is dangerous by American standards.

lrs-k-small.sentence: The majority described its default as an aid when Congress likely had not considered the problem and the remaining evidence was approximately balanced.
lrs-k-small.plain: The "majority" described its assumption as only a tiebreaker. It helps when Congress likely never considered the problem and the rest of the "evidence" of meaning points about equally both ways.

lrs-k-small.sentence: A Canadian antitrust judgment could disable possession while its New York equivalent fell within a business-offense exception.
lrs-k-small.plain: Counting foreign courts gives odd results. A Canadian antitrust conviction could bar gun possession, while the same conviction in New York would fall within the "business-offense exception," which exempts such domestic business crimes.

lrs-k-small.sentence: A Senate version used federal-and-state felony language; Conference substituted punishment-based “any court” wording to simplify matters and avoid varying state felony labels.
lrs-k-small.plain: The Senate's version of the bill used federal-and-state felony language. The House–Senate Conference committee, which settles the final text, swapped in the "any court" wording based on the possible punishment, to simplify matters and avoid states' differing felony labels.

lrs-k-small.sentence: He viewed the majority’s domestic assumption as a newly invented clear-statement rule.
lrs-k-small.plain: Justice Thomas saw the majority's domestic assumption as a newly invented "clear-statement rule," meaning a rule that Congress must say expressly that foreign convictions count.

lrs-k-small.sentence: Failure to foresee an application demonstrated breadth rather than ambiguity.
lrs-k-small.plain: That Congress did not foresee this use of the law shows the words are broad, not that they suffer from "ambiguity," meaning they could reasonably be read more than one way.

lrs-k-small.sentence: On April 26, 2005, the Supreme Court reversed the Third Circuit and remanded: § 922(g)(1)’s disputed predicate covered domestic convictions only.
lrs-k-small.plain: On April 26, 2005, the Supreme Court "reversed" the Third Circuit (overturned its ruling) and "remanded," sending the case back. It held that the disputed "predicate" in § 922(g)(1), the earlier conviction that triggers the gun ban, covers only domestic convictions.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: The National Council for Adoption, whose members help prospective parents adopt, challenged lack of notice and comment and substantive legality.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: The National Council for Adoption, whose members help would-be parents adopt, challenged the Guidance for "lack of notice" and comment: the agency never published it and invited public comment first. It also challenged the Guidance's "substantive" legality, arguing its content was unlawful anyway.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: State moved to dismiss because the Council had not identified a member harmed by either precise prohibition.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: The State Department "moved to dismiss," formally asking the court to end the case. It argued the Council had not identified any member harmed by either of the Guidance's specific prohibitions, which an organization suing for its members must do.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: State sought to strike them as late and alternatively challenged sufficiency.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: The Department "sought to strike" the Council's two supplemental member statements, asking the court to disregard them as filed too late. Alternatively, it argued they did not prove harm anyway.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: The district judge struck them, dismissed for lack of standing, and treated both merits motions as moot.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: The "district judge" struck the statements and "dismissed" the case for lack of "standing," the right to sue. That made both sides' "merits" motions (on whether the Guidance was lawful) "moot," meaning there was nothing left to decide.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: Judge Walker, writing with Judge Pillard and Senior Judge Randolph, reviewed standing independently and striking for abuse of discretion.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: Judge Walker, writing with Judge Pillard and Senior Judge Randolph (a semi-retired judge who still hears cases), decided standing fresh for the court. It reviewed the "striking for abuse of discretion," overturning the decision to disregard the statements only if it was unreasonable.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: Existing precedent permitted late evidence reinforcing a reasonably substantial earlier showing and making standing patently apparent without prejudice.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: Existing "precedent" (earlier decisions) let courts accept late evidence that backed up a reasonably substantial earlier showing and made standing obvious. It had to come "without prejudice," meaning without unfair harm to the other side.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: Procedural redressability did not demand proof that comments would change policy.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: "Procedural redressability," the requirement that a court order could fix the harm when an agency skipped a required procedure, did not demand proof that public comments would have changed the policy.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: Adoption completion was germane to the Council’s purpose, and neither claims nor requested relief required individual-member participation.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: Getting adoptions completed was "germane" to (closely related to) the Council's purpose. Neither its "claims" nor the "relief" it asked for required individual members to take part, which completed the test for an organization suing on its members' behalf.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: A legislative rule has legal effect or exercises delegated power with legal force; an interpretive rule explains a proposition compelled or logically justified by existing law.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: A "legislative rule" has legal effect, or uses "delegated power" (authority Congress handed the agency) with the force of law, creating new binding duties. An "interpretive rule" only explains what existing law already requires or logically supports.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 553 exempts genuinely interpretive rules from notice and comment.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 553 "exempts" truly interpretive rules from notice and comment. So agencies need not invite public comment before rules that only interpret existing law, but must for rules that create new duties.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: Even if a practice often harmed children, an individualized standard did not logically command prohibition in every case.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: A rule to act in each child's best interests calls for case-by-case judgment; it does not by itself require a flat ban on a practice.

lrs-n-national-council-adoption.sentence: On July 9, 2021, the unanimous panel reversed and remanded for an order vacating the Guidance and other consistent action.
lrs-n-national-council-adoption.plain: On July 9, 2021, the "unanimous" panel (all three judges agreeing) reversed and "remanded," sending the case back. It directed the trial court to enter an "order" vacating, or cancelling, the Guidance and to take other action consistent with the ruling.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: The Federal Trade Commission adopted a rule treating failure to display octane ratings as an unfair method of competition and an unfair or deceptive act or practice.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: The Federal Trade Commission made a rule that failing to post octane ratings on gas pumps was an "unfair method of competition" and an "unfair or deceptive act or practice." Both are kinds of conduct the FTC Act bans.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: The district court decided only that the Commission lacked power to make substantive rules.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: The "district court" (trial court) ruled only that the Commission lacked power to make "substantive rules," meaning binding rules of conduct. It did not reach the other objections.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act directed prevention of unfair practices through complaints, hearings, findings, and cease-and-desist orders.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: "Section 5" of the Federal Trade Commission Act told the FTC to prevent unfair practices case by case. It brings complaints against particular companies, holds "hearings," makes findings, and issues "cease-and-desist orders," which order a company to stop the practice.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: The companies read that context as restricting § 6(g) to procedural and investigatory rules and treated § 5’s express adjudicatory process as exclusive.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: The companies read that context as limiting § 6(g), the FTC's rulemaking power, to rules about its own procedures and investigations. They treated § 5's express "adjudicatory" process, deciding individual cases, as the only way to set standards.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: A rule did not bypass complaint, hearing, findings, a cease-and-desist order, or judicial review against a respondent.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: A rule did not let the FTC skip the steps against a "respondent," the company charged. It still needed a complaint, a hearing, findings, a "cease-and-desist order" (an order to stop), and court review.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: That binding narrowing distinguished a substantive rule from merely advisory guidance, even though both could induce compliance.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: That binding narrowing of the legal question is what separated a "substantive rule," which has legal force, from merely advisory "guidance," even though both could lead companies to comply.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: Nonuse did not forfeit granted power.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: Not using a power does not "forfeit" it, meaning lose it. The FTC kept its rulemaking power even though it had not used it for decades.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: Respondents also needed some opportunity to show unusual circumstances warranting waiver, such as a case outside the rule’s rationale or compelling hardship.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: "Respondents," the companies charged under the rule, also needed some chance to show unusual circumstances that justified a "waiver" (an exemption). Examples were a case outside the rule's reasoning, or compelling hardship.

lrs-o-national-petroleum.sentence: On June 27, 1973, the D.C. Circuit reversed the categorical denial of substantive rulemaking and remanded for the remaining challenges to this rule’s adoption.
lrs-o-national-petroleum.plain: On June 27, 1973, the D.C. Circuit, the federal appeals court in Washington, reversed the flat ruling that the FTC could never make "substantive" rules. It "remanded," sending the case back to decide the remaining challenges to how this rule was adopted.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Sharon had died between hearing and decision, so the decree was entered nunc pro tunc as of the hearing.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: Sharon died between the hearing and the decision, so the "decree" (the court's final order) was entered "nunc pro tunc," Latin for "now for then." That dated it back to the hearing, when he was still alive.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: In March 1888 Sharon’s son and executor Frederick sought revival against Hill and her new husband, David Terry.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: In March 1888, Sharon's son Frederick, the "executor" managing his estate, asked the court to revive the case so it could continue against Hill and her new husband, David Terry.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: On August 16 fellow deputy A. L. Farrish applied for habeas corpus for Neagle.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: On August 16 a fellow deputy, A. L. Farrish, applied for "habeas corpus" for Neagle. That is a court order requiring the jailer to justify holding someone, and releasing him if the custody is unlawful.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: His lawyers disputed fatal intent, argued that ordinary California self-defense belonged in state court, and read “law of the United States” in Revised Statutes § 753 as enacted law and necessary statutory incidents.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: The sheriff's lawyers disputed that Neagle meant to kill and argued that ordinary California self-defense belonged in state court. They read "law of the United States" in Revised Statutes § 753, the habeas statute, to mean only enacted laws and what those laws necessarily imply.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: They also objected to Farrish’s signing and verification and amendment of the traverse after evidence; the Supreme Court developed its substantive decision without separately resolving those pleading points.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: They also objected to Farrish’s signing and "verification" (sworn confirmation) of the petition, and to amending the "traverse," the reply to the sheriff's answer, after evidence was heard. The Supreme Court decided the "substantive" case without separately ruling on those "pleading" points.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Section 753 extended habeas to custody for acts pursuant to federal law and custody contrary to the Constitution or federal law.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: "Section 753" let federal courts grant habeas to anyone in "custody" (held by authorities) for acts done under federal law, or held contrary to the Constitution or federal law.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Because this was an appeal, not a law-only writ of error, Miller reexamined facts as well as law.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: This was an appeal, not a "writ of error," an older form of review limited to legal questions. So Justice Miller, writing for the Court, reexamined the facts as well as the law.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Miller rejected limiting federal “law” to an enactment naming this precise protective task.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: Justice Miller rejected limiting federal "law" to an "enactment," a statute passed by Congress, that names this exact task of protecting a judge.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Section 788 also gave marshals and deputies corresponding sheriff powers when executing federal law.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: Section 788 also gave federal marshals and deputies the same powers a state's sheriffs had while executing federal law. In California those powers included keeping the peace.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: An assault on Field in federal duty breached the peace of the United States.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: An "assault" (attack) on Justice Field while he was on federal "duty" breached the peace of the United States. A marshal could act to prevent that.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Once the federal court properly established an authorized duty and conduct no more than necessary and proper, the lawful act could not become a state crime.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: If a federal officer was doing an authorized federal job and used no more force than needed, a state cannot prosecute him for it.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: The Necessary and Proper Clause assigned Congress the means of carrying federal powers into effect.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: Justice Lamar, dissenting, said the "Necessary and Proper Clause" gives Congress the job of choosing the means of carrying federal powers into effect. So it is Congress, by law, not the President, that decides this.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Congress’s control of inferior courts and the absence of federal common-law criminal jurisdiction resisted a self-executing executive or judicial power.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: Congress controls the lower federal courts, and there is no "federal common-law criminal jurisdiction," meaning federal courts cannot punish crimes Congress has not defined. Both points, Lamar said, cut against a "self-executing" executive or "judicial power" that works without any law from Congress.

lrs-o-neagle.sentence: Section 788 measured powers for an existing duty; importing state police powers could not create that duty.
lrs-o-neagle.plain: Section 788 only set the powers marshals had for a duty that already existed. Bringing in state "police powers," a sheriff's general peacekeeping authority, could not create a new duty to guard judges.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Existing industry guidance was advisory, not enforceable substantive law.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: Existing industry guidance was only advisory. It was not "enforceable" substantive law, meaning no one could be legally compelled to follow it.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Using informal notice and comment, the Commissioner proposed rules in October 1969.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: In October 1969 the Commissioner, the head of the FDA, proposed rules using informal notice and comment: publishing the proposed rules and inviting public comment, the ordinary way agencies make rules.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: In November 1970 it adopted the final rule, including the Institute’s interim alternative as a permanent option, without meaningfully answering the alternative-preservative or commercial-feasibility objections.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: In November 1970 the FDA adopted the final rule, making the National Fisheries Institute’s interim alternative a permanent option. It did not meaningfully answer two objections: that another preservative method, using salt and nitrite, could be used, and that the required heating was not commercially workable for every kind of fish.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Nova Scotia, two officers, and the intervening National Fisheries Institute appealed on statutory authority, undisclosed science, an inadequate record, and deficient explanation.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: Nova Scotia, two of its officers, and the National Fisheries Institute, an industry group that had intervened (joined the case), "appealed." They argued FDA lacked legal power under the statute, hid its scientific data, built an inadequate record, and did not adequately explain its choices.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Judge Gurfein, writing for a panel also including Judge Waterman and District Judge Blumenfeld, sitting by designation, first addressed 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(4), which treats food prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions that may make it harmful as adulterated, together with § 371(a)’s rulemaking authority.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: Judge Gurfein wrote for a "panel" with Judge Waterman and District Judge Blumenfeld, a trial judge temporarily assigned to the appeals court. It first took up 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(4), which treats food "prepared, packed, or held" under "insanitary" (unclean) conditions that may make it harmful as "adulterated" (illegally tainted), together with § 371(a)'s "rulemaking authority."

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Authority was fairly inferable from statutory purpose and language, not simply from an official’s desire to take initiative.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: FDA's power was fairly inferable from the "statutory" purpose and language, meaning the law's words and public-health goals. It did not rest simply on an official's desire to take the initiative.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: The court required adherence to informal rulemaking’s minimum safeguards instead of converting the process into formal proceedings.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: The court required FDA to follow the minimum safeguards of "informal rulemaking," the ordinary publish-and-comment process. It did not turn that process into formal, trial-like proceedings.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706 required review of the whole record even under arbitrary-and-capricious review.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 706 required a court to review the whole record, everything the agency had before it. That held even under "arbitrary-and-capricious" review, the lenient test asking only whether the agency acted unreasonably.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Nondisclosure impaired relevant comment and risked omission of important factors.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: "Nondisclosure," FDA's failure to reveal the studies it relied on, kept the public from commenting meaningfully on them. It also risked the agency overlooking important factors.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: APA § 553(c)’s concise general statement had to explain major policy questions and agency responses.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: APA § 553(c) requires a "concise general statement" of a rule's basis and purpose. That statement had to explain the major policy questions raised and how the agency responded to them.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: FDA needed to reveal whether it regarded the controls as feasible or deliberately chose stronger protection despite infeasibility.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: FDA needed to say whether it regarded the controls as "feasible," meaning industry could actually comply. Or it had to say it deliberately chose stronger protection despite "infeasibility," even if some products could no longer be made.

lrs-o-nova-scotia.sentence: Because the appeal arose from enforcement, the court said it could not directly remand a review petition for further agency comments.
lrs-o-nova-scotia.plain: Because the "appeal" came from FDA's suit to enforce the rule, not from a "petition" for review of it, the court said it could not directly "remand" (send back) the rule to the "agency" for further comments. It simply refused to enforce the rule here.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: If it declined review and issued a finality order, the initial decision became final as Commission action.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: If the Commission "declined review," choosing not to review the judge's initial decision, it issued a "finality order." That order made the initial decision final as the Commission's own action.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: Before the Commission, Lucia argued that ALJs were officers of the United States requiring appointment under the Appointments Clause.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: Before the Commission, Lucia argued that ALJs, the SEC's administrative law judges, were "officers of the United States" requiring appointment under the Appointments Clause. That clause requires such officers to be appointed by the President, a court, or a department head, not hired by staff.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: The Commission qualified as a department head able to appoint inferior officers but had not appointed Elliot.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: The Commission counted as a "department head," which may appoint "inferior officers" (officers below the top level). But it had not itself appointed the judge in Lucia's case, Elliot.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: On rehearing, ten judges split evenly, leaving a per curiam judgment rejecting the claim, in conflict with the Tenth Circuit’s Bandimere decision.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: On rehearing by the full appeals court, ten judges split evenly, 5–5, leaving a "per curiam" judgment (an unsigned decision of the court) rejecting Lucia's "claim." That conflicted with the Tenth Circuit's Bandimere decision, which had ruled the other way.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: At certiorari the federal government changed position and supported officer status, so the Supreme Court appointed an amicus to defend the judgment.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: When the Supreme Court granted "certiorari" (agreed to hear the case), the federal government switched sides and supported "officer status" for ALJs. So the Court appointed an "amicus," an outside lawyer, to defend the lower court's "judgment."

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: Germaine required a continuing legal position, and Buckley required significant authority under federal law.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: Two earlier cases set the marks of an officer. Germaine required a continuing position created by law, and Buckley required significant authority under federal law.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: In a major Tax Court case a special trial judge’s proposal needed a regular judge’s adoption; an SEC initial decision could itself become final after nonreview and a finality order.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: In a major Tax Court case, a "special trial judge" was held to be an officer even though his proposed decision needed a regular judge's adoption. An SEC initial decision could itself become final after the Commission declined review and issued a "finality order."

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: Under Ryder, a timely challenger to an adjudicator’s appointment receives a hearing before a properly appointed official.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: Under Ryder, a challenger who promptly objects to an "adjudicator's" appointment (the official deciding the case) gets a new hearing before a properly appointed official.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: The Court also reserved validity of the SEC’s November 2017 ratification of past appointments.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: The Court also "reserved," or left undecided, whether the SEC's November 2017 "ratification" of past appointments, its formal re-approval of them, was valid.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: Justice Breyer would hold the selection unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act’s instruction that each agency appoint its ALJs.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: Justice Breyer would hold the selection unlawful under a statute instead: the Administrative Procedure Act’s instruction that each agency itself appoint its ALJs. The SEC had let staff do it.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: No published order delegated this power to staff, and constitutional avoidance favored construing general delegation authority to exclude it.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: No published order had handed this appointment power to staff. And "constitutional avoidance," the practice of reading a law to avoid a constitutional question when possible, favored reading the SEC's general power to delegate as not covering appointments.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: ALJs had good-cause protection administered by the Merit Systems Protection Board, whose members had their own protections.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: ALJs could be removed only for good cause, a protection decided by the Merit Systems Protection Board. That board's members had their own protection from removal, a double layer.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: Applying Free Enterprise Fund’s limits after calling ALJs officers might undermine adjudicative independence Congress intended.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: Free Enterprise Fund limited two layers of removal protection for officers. Applying those limits after calling ALJs officers might undermine the independence in deciding cases that Congress intended ALJs to have.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: SEC ALJs merely recommended under plenary de novo Commission review; even an unreviewed decision required a finality order and became the Commission’s action.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: Justice Sotomayor said SEC ALJs merely make recommendations, because the Commission has "plenary" (complete) power of de novo "review," redoing everything from scratch. Even an unreviewed decision needed a "finality order" and became the Commission's own action.

lrs-s-lucia.sentence: Thus six Justices joined the constitutional officer holding, while Breyer concurred in the judgment in part and dissented in part, agreeing that the challenged appointment was unlawful on another ground and disagreeing with part of the remedy.
lrs-s-lucia.plain: So six Justices "joined" the holding that ALJs are constitutional officers. Breyer "concurred in the judgment in part" and dissented in part: he agreed the appointment was unlawful on another ground, but disagreed with part of the "remedy," the requirement that a new judge hear the case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.sentence: A 2001 appellate ruling found them inadequately represented in the settlement.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.plain: A 2001 "appellate" ruling, by an appeals court, found these later-injured veterans inadequately represented in the earlier class settlement. So that settlement could not simply block their suits.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.sentence: The 2008 panel did not revisit whether it was bound by that decision because the contractor defense independently resolved the appeals.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.plain: The 2008 "panel" of appeals judges did not revisit whether it was bound by that 2001 decision. It did not need to, because the government-contractor defense independently decided the "appeals."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.sentence: Plaintiffs briefed design defect but abandoned failure-to-warn and manufacturing-defect claims and did not appeal refusal to strike defense affidavits and exhibits.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.plain: "Plaintiffs" (the veterans) argued design defect on appeal but "abandoned," or dropped, their failure-to-warn and "manufacturing-defect" (badly made batches) claims. They also did not appeal the refusal to "strike" (throw out) the companies' sworn affidavits and "exhibits," their supporting documents.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.sentence: Boyle, the Supreme Court government-contractor decision, required approved reasonably precise specifications, conformity, and warnings about dangers known to the contractor but not the Government.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.plain: Boyle, the Supreme Court's government-contractor decision, set three requirements. The government approved "reasonably precise specifications," the product conformed to them, and the contractor warned about dangers it knew of that the government did not.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.sentence: The defense protected discretionary procurement decisions against conflicting state duties; it was not automatic immunity for anything sold to government or a direct Federal Tort Claims Act case.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-AGENT-ORANGE-2008.plain: The defense protects the government's discretionary "procurement" decisions (its judgment calls about what to buy) from conflicting state-law duties.
