lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: The court kept that pause because the legal question was serious and the other "stay factors" (such as harm to each side and the public interest) favored it, even though the government was not substantially likely to win.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: But it considered the D.C. Circuit’s prior ruling binding as law of the case.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: Though it now doubted the stay, the district court considered the D.C. Circuit’s earlier ruling in this same case binding as "law of the case," the rule that courts follow earlier decisions made in the same lawsuit.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: In an unsigned opinion, the Supreme Court considered the landlords virtually certain to show that the statute did not authorize this expansive intervention in rental property.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: In an "unsigned opinion," one issued without naming an author, the Supreme Court found the landlords virtually certain to show that the "statute" did not authorize this sweeping intervention in rental property.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: Even assuming ambiguity, the claim’s magnitude required clear congressional authorization.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: Even assuming "ambiguity" (that the statute could be read more than one way), a claimed power this large required "clear congressional authorization," meaning plain permission from Congress.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: The government supplied no limiting principle beyond the agency’s necessity judgment.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: The government offered no "limiting principle," no point where its reading of the power would stop, beyond the agency’s own judgment of what was necessary.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: The majority found landlords exposed to irreparable financial loss without assured recovery, including owners of modest means.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: The "majority" found landlords, including owners of modest means, exposed to "irreparable financial loss": money lost with no assured "recovery," or way to get it back.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: On August 26, 2021, it granted the application to vacate the stay, allowing the district court’s judgment setting aside the moratorium to operate while the appeal remained pending.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: On August 26, 2021, the Court "granted" the landlords' application to vacate (cancel) the "stay." That let the district court’s judgment setting aside the moratorium take effect while the appeal remained pending.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: The six-to-three order was not a final merits affirmance after ordinary appellate review.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: The six-to-three order was an emergency ruling. It was not a final decision on the "merits" (who is legally right) reached after ordinary "appellate" review.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, argued that vacating a lower-court stay required clear and demonstrable error under accepted standards.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: Justice Breyer, "joined by" Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented. He argued that "vacating" (cancelling) a lower court's "stay" required clear and demonstrable error under accepted standards.

lrs-i-alabama-realtors.sentence: He urged respect for expert judgment and full briefing and argument on disputed statutory issues instead of summary resolution.
lrs-i-alabama-realtors.plain: He urged respect for expert judgment and full "briefing" (written arguments) and oral argument on the disputed "statutory" questions, instead of a quick summary ruling.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: They contended that premium tax credits allowed by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) on Virginia’s federal insurance exchange changed their legal obligations.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: The challengers argued that "premium tax credits," subsidies the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) allowed on Virginia's federally run "insurance exchange" (marketplace), changed their legal obligations. The credits made insurance cheap enough that the law required them to buy it or pay a penalty.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: The majority later described these as interdependent responses to adverse selection: if healthy people could wait until illness, rising average costs could drive others out.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: The "majority" later described these as linked responses to "adverse selection": if healthy people could wait until they got sick to buy insurance, rising average costs could drive others out. The mandate and subsidies keep healthy people in.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: Section 36B’s credit calculation referred to coverage through an exchange established by the state under the designated provision.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: "Section 36B" set the tax-credit formula by reference to coverage bought through an exchange "established by the State" under a specified provision. The challengers said that excluded federally run exchanges.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: The Fourth Circuit affirmed after finding ambiguity and deferring under Chevron, which then required acceptance of certain reasonable agency constructions.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: The "Fourth Circuit" affirmed after finding "ambiguity" (unclear wording) and deferring under Chevron. That doctrine then required courts to accept certain reasonable "agency" readings of unclear statutes.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: Even under the 2015 Chevron regime, ambiguity did not always imply delegation.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: Even under the "Chevron regime" as it stood in 2015, ambiguity, or unclear wording, did not always mean Congress had delegated the decision to the agency.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: The judicial interpretation could agree with the agency while rejecting its entitlement to binding deference.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: The Court's own interpretation could agree with the "agency" (the IRS) while rejecting the claim that its view was entitled to binding "deference," meaning it had to be followed.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: The majority found contextual ambiguity, not a universal redefinition of the federal government as a state.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: The "majority" found "ambiguity" in this context only. It did not redefine the federal government as a "state" everywhere.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: The surplusage canon was not absolute.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: The "surplusage" canon, the rule that every word in a statute should be given some meaning, was not absolute. It can give way when it clashes with the law's overall design.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: Because the Court supplied the statutory meaning, it did not leave the IRS free simply to choose the opposite answer as another reasonable construction.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: Because the Court itself supplied the "statutory" meaning, the IRS was not free to choose the opposite answer later as another reasonable "construction," or interpretation.

lrs-i-king-burwell.sentence: Calculators could display zero credits, outreach could explain their absence, and instructions with unsatisfied predicates could be inapplicable.
lrs-i-king-burwell.plain: Scalia replied that the provisions the majority relied on still made sense on his reading: a calculator can show zero credits, and an instruction can simply not apply when its conditions are not met.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: The employees sued under the Fair Labor Standards Act for approximately $77,000 in overtime compensation, liquidated damages, and attorneys’ fees.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: The employees sued under the Fair Labor Standards Act for about $77,000: overtime pay for their on-call nights, "liquidated damages" (an equal extra amount the law adds to unpaid wages), and attorneys' fees.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: It instead concluded as a matter of law that pleasurable activities and personal chores were not work, and denied the entire claim.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: Instead, the trial court ruled "as a matter of law," without weighing the facts, that leisure activities and personal chores were not work. It denied the entire claim.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: The Administrator proposed excluding sleeping and eating time while including other on-call hours.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: The Administrator, the federal wage-and-hour official, proposed excluding sleeping and eating time while counting the other "on-call" hours as work.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: A worker could be hired to wait or could instead wait for employment to begin.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: Some people are hired to wait, so waiting is the job and must be paid; others are just waiting for their work to begin, which is not paid.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: Congress had assigned courts responsibility for coverage decisions in individual suits, rather than creating an administrative tribunal to make the initial factual determinations.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: Congress gave courts the job of deciding coverage in each lawsuit. It did not create an administrative "tribunal," an agency body acting like a court, to make the first factual decisions.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: The interpretations did not result from adversarial administrative factfinding, and they did not bind trial courts as a superior court’s ruling would.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: The Administrator's interpretations did not come from "adversarial" factfinding, with both sides presenting evidence. And they did not bind "trial courts" the way a "superior court" (a higher court) ruling would.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: Their weight depended on the thoroughness of consideration, validity of reasoning, consistency with earlier and later positions, and other qualities making them persuasive.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: How much courts should rely on agency guidance depends on how carefully it was thought through, how sound its reasoning is, and whether the agency has been consistent. It can persuade, but it does not bind.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: Substantial respect could follow from those qualities without giving the official authoritative control of the judicial decision.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: Good agency guidance can earn real respect, but the court still makes the final call.

lrs-i-skidmore.sentence: Although the district court had mentioned the Bulletin, its legal assumption that waiting could not be work apparently restricted the inquiry.
lrs-i-skidmore.plain: The "district court" had mentioned the Administrator's Bulletin, its published guidance. But its legal assumption that waiting could never be work apparently cut its inquiry short, so it never properly examined the facts.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: Sellers represented that the financial statements fairly presented the company’s condition and that no material adverse change had occurred.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The sellers promised that the financial statements fairly showed the company's condition, and that no "material adverse change," no significant bad development, had occurred.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: Buyers nevertheless sought a different remedy: rescission under § 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, which would undo the transaction.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The buyers nevertheless sought a different "remedy": rescission, undoing the purchase, under § 12(2) of the Securities Act of 1933.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: They alleged material inaccuracies in contractual representations and claimed the agreement itself was a prospectus triggering the federal remedy.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: They "alleged" important errors in the sellers' promises in the contract. They also claimed the agreement itself was a "prospectus," the kind of offering document that triggers the federal remedy.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: For the statutory question, the Supreme Court assumed material misstatements and assumed the sellers could not establish due care.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: To decide the "statutory" question, the Supreme Court assumed there were "material misstatements" (important false statements) and that the sellers could not show "due care," meaning reasonable carefulness. It did not find those things true.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: Sellers argued that the term of art meant a document soliciting the public to buy from an issuer or controlling shareholder.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The sellers argued that "prospectus" is a "term of art," a word with a special legal meaning: a document inviting the public to buy from an "issuer" (the company selling its own securities) or its controlling shareholders.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: He did not reason that omitting legally required information magically makes a covered document cease being a prospectus; he distinguished a breached duty from a duty that never attached.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: Justice Kennedy did not say that leaving out legally required information makes a covered document stop being a prospectus. He distinguished a "breached" "duty," one that applied and was broken, from a duty that never applied to this private contract.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: The presumption that identical words in an Act carry the same meaning then linked § 10 to § 12.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The presumption that identical words in one Act carry the same meaning then linked § 10 to § 12. So "prospectus" in § 12 should mean what it means in § 10: a public-offering document.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: Under noscitur a sociis, a word’s companions inform its meaning.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: Under "noscitur a sociis," Latin for "a word is known by its companions," the words around a term help define it. Here the other listed items (notices, circulars, ads, radio, TV) suggested "communication" meant one aimed at the public.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: The list prevented evasion by using another label for a public solicitation; its catchall broadened form without encompassing every private transaction.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The long list exists so sellers cannot dodge the law by calling a public sales pitch something else; the general catchall word covers other formats but not every private deal.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: The Court also worried that rescission for casual secondary-market communications, without fraud or reliance, would give disappointed buyers an option to undo deals even when a negligent omission did not cause their losses.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The Court also worried about "rescission" (undoing the deal) for casual "secondary-market" communications, in resales rather than sales by the company. Without proof of fraud or reliance, disappointed buyers could undo deals even when a "negligent" (careless) omission did not cause their losses.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: An enacted definition displaced ordinary technical usage.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: Justice Thomas said an "enacted" definition, one Congress wrote into the statute itself, displaced the word's ordinary technical usage in the industry.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: A catchall can deliberately overlap listed items as a safety net; associated words should resolve genuine ambiguity, not create it in broad express language.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: A catchall word can deliberately overlap the listed items as a safety net. Associated words should help resolve "genuine ambiguity," truly unclear wording, not create it in broad "express" (explicit) language.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: Ginsburg acknowledged that the broader reading lacked a loss-causation requirement and could anomalously expose private sellers while protecting some public sellers: § 2(10)(a) exempted certain communications following a formal § 10 prospectus, an option private sellers might lack.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: Justice Ginsburg admitted the broader reading had no loss-causation requirement (proof the error caused the loss) and could oddly expose private sellers more than some public sellers. Section 2(10)(a) "exempted" certain communications that follow a formal § 10 "prospectus," an option private sellers might lack.

lrs-k-gustafson.sentence: The controlling formulation encompassed public offerings by issuers or controlling shareholders, not merely the first-ever issuance of a company’s stock; the opinion also recognized registration exemptions in its analysis.
lrs-k-gustafson.plain: The controlling definition covered "public offerings" by issuers or "controlling shareholders" (owners who control the company), not just a company's very first sale of stock. The "opinion" also took registration exemptions into account in its analysis.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: They believed AIPAC was a political committee under the Federal Election Campaign Act, or FECA, and therefore owed public disclosure.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The voters believed AIPAC was a "political committee" under the Federal Election Campaign Act, or FECA. That status would require it to publicly disclose its donors and spending.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: But it still dismissed the complaint under a major-purpose test: AIPAC chiefly engaged in issue-oriented lobbying, rather than candidate nomination or election.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: But the FEC still dismissed the complaint under a "major-purpose test": a group is a political committee only if its main purpose is nominating or electing candidates. AIPAC chiefly engaged in issue-oriented "lobbying," pressing officials on policy.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The agency also separately declined to pursue a corporate-expenditure allegation as an exercise of enforcement discretion.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The FEC also separately declined to pursue an "allegation" that AIPAC illegally spent corporate money. It did so as an exercise of "enforcement discretion," an agency's choice of which cases to pursue.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: FECA allowed any person to submit an administrative complaint and an aggrieved party to seek review of dismissal.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: FECA let any person file an "administrative complaint" with the FEC. It also let an "aggrieved party," someone harmed by a dismissal, ask a court to review it.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The FEC sought Supreme Court review, putting both the voters’ standing and the proper order of statutory decision before the Court.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The FEC sought Supreme Court "review." That put before the Court both the voters' "standing" (their right to sue) and the proper order for deciding the "statutory" questions.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The voters claimed more than a generalized wish for the FEC to obey law: on their legal theory, the statute required information that they were denied and that would aid voting judgments about campaign influence.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The voters claimed more than a general wish for the FEC to obey the law. On their legal theory, the "statute" required disclosure of information they were denied, and it would help them judge campaign influence when voting.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The broad distribution of the alleged loss therefore did not turn it into a nonjusticiable generalized grievance.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: So the wide sharing of the "alleged" harm among many voters did not make it a "nonjusticiable" generalized grievance, a shared complaint too abstract for courts to decide.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The voters identified a concrete interest protected by a disclosure requirement, and still had to establish causation and redressability.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The voters identified a "concrete" (real and specific) interest protected by a disclosure requirement. They still had to show "causation," that the FEC's decision caused their harm, and redressability, that a court ruling could fix it.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The voters did not need certainty that every requested record would ultimately be produced; uncertainty about lawful agency action after remand did not break traceability or redressability.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The voters did not need certainty that every record they wanted would eventually be produced. Uncertainty about what lawful "agency action" would follow on remand did not break "traceability" (the link from the FEC's decision to the harm) or redressability.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The majority distinguished Heckler v. Chaney’s treatment of nonenforcement because FECA expressly authorized review of this category of dismissal.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The "majority" distinguished Heckler v. Chaney, which treats an agency's "nonenforcement," its choice not to act, as usually unreviewable. Here FECA expressly authorized court review of this kind of dismissal.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: The Supreme Court therefore declined to determine whether the major-purpose limitation associated with Buckley applied only to independent expenditures or more broadly.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: So the Supreme Court declined to decide whether the major-purpose limit associated with the Buckley case applies only to "independent expenditures," election spending not coordinated with a campaign, or more broadly.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: These voters sought enforcement against a third party, which might later generate disclosure, rather than release of information an agency already held under a direct statutory disclosure duty.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: Justice Scalia stressed that these voters sought enforcement against a "third party," AIPAC, which might later produce disclosure. They were not seeking information an "agency" already held under a direct "statutory" duty to disclose it.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: Constitutional avoidance favored the narrower interpretation.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: "Constitutional avoidance," the practice of choosing a reading that avoids constitutional problems, favored the narrower interpretation, Scalia said.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: For Scalia, allowing any voter to obtain judicial direction of executive enforcement also transferred the President’s Take Care responsibility to courts.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: For Scalia, letting any voter get courts to direct executive enforcement also shifted to judges the President's Take Care duty: his constitutional job to "take Care" that the laws are faithfully executed.

lrs-n-standing-akins.sentence: It held that the voters had standing, vacated the D.C. Circuit judgment, and remanded for the antecedent expenditure question.
lrs-n-standing-akins.plain: The Court held the voters had "standing" (the right to sue) and vacated (cancelled) the D.C. Circuit judgment. It "remanded," sending the case back, for the "antecedent" question, the one to be decided first, of whether AIPAC's spending counted as expenditures.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: The Supreme Court granted ordinary certiorari there and certiorari before judgment in UNC, where no Fourth Circuit merits judgment existed.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: The Supreme Court "granted" ordinary certiorari (agreed to hear) in Harvard's case. In UNC's case it granted "certiorari before judgment," taking it before the Fourth Circuit had issued any merits judgment.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: The schools defended individualized review and diversity’s educational benefits, arguing that available race-neutral alternatives would not adequately preserve their missions; SFFA sought abandonment of permissive precedent and alternatively disputed narrow tailoring.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: The schools defended individualized review of applicants and diversity's educational benefits, arguing race-neutral alternatives would not adequately serve their missions. SFFA asked the Court to abandon the "precedent" allowing race-conscious admissions, or alternatively disputed "narrow tailoring," whether the programs were closely fitted to their goals.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: Under Hunt, an association can represent members who could sue individually, on interests germane to its purpose, when neither claim nor relief requires individual participation.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: Under Hunt, an association can sue for members who could sue themselves, on interests "germane" (closely related) to its purpose. Neither the "claim" nor the relief may require individual members to take part.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: Those features substituted for formal membership; they were not further requirements for every voluntary association.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: In Hunt, the apple commission's special features, the growers' and dealers' control and funding, stood in for formal membership. They were not extra requirements for every voluntary "association" that has real members.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: Racial classifications require a compelling interest and narrow tailoring.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: Racial classifications by government require a "compelling interest," an extremely important reason. They also require narrow tailoring, meaning the policy is closely fitted to that reason.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: Harvard was evaluated through precedent linking Title VI violations to equal-protection standards; no party sought reconsideration of that linkage.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: Harvard, a private school, was judged through "precedent" (earlier cases) linking violations of Title VI, the civil-rights law for federally funded schools, to equal-protection standards. No party sought "reconsideration" of that link.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: Reviewing Bakke and Grutter, Roberts identified strict scrutiny, absence of racial negatives or stereotypes, and a meaningful endpoint as indispensable conditions.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: Reviewing Bakke and Grutter, earlier affirmative-action cases, Chief Justice Roberts named three "indispensable" (absolutely required) conditions. Race-conscious admissions must survive "strict scrutiny," the toughest review; must never use race as a negative or a stereotype; and must have a meaningful end point.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: The Court viewed finite admissions as zero-sum: racial advantages could reduce others’ opportunities even when described as positive factors.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: The Court saw admissions as zero-sum because seats are limited. A racial advantage for some applicants could reduce others' chances, even when described as a positive factor.

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: His textual and but-for analysis associated with Bostock rejected benign motives, other contributing causes, or group-wide benefit as defenses.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: Justice Gorsuch's text-based, "but-for" analysis, linked to Bostock, asked whether race made the difference for a person. It rejected good motives, other contributing causes, or benefit to a group as "defenses."

lrs-n-standing-sffa.sentence: She accused the majority of displacing precedent without necessary stare decisis and reliance analysis.
lrs-n-standing-sffa.plain: Justice Sotomayor accused the majority of displacing "precedent" without the required "stare decisis" analysis, the doctrine of standing by past decisions, including how much schools had relied on those decisions.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: The applications were actually mutually exclusive; the record suggested no feasible adjustment allowing both, disqualifying deadline, or bad-faith filing by Ashbacker.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: The applications were truly "mutually exclusive": granting one meant denying the other. The record suggested no "feasible" (workable) adjustment allowing both, no missed deadline disqualifying Ashbacker, and no "bad-faith" filing by it.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: In June the FCC granted Fetzer without hearing and on the same day designated Ashbacker for a hearing.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: In June the FCC granted Fetzer's application without a hearing. The same day it "designated," or formally set, Ashbacker's application for a hearing.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: Yet the hearing notice made Ashbacker establish, among other things, the extent of interference with the already-authorized station and resolve specified issues favorably on a formal record.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: But the hearing notice required Ashbacker to prove, among other things, how much its station would interfere with Fetzer's already-approved one, and to win on listed issues on a formal record. Since the two stations could not both operate, that hearing was stacked against Ashbacker from the start.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: Ashbacker appealed the Fetzer construction permit under § 402(b)(2) as an adversely affected person.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: Ashbacker challenged Fetzer's "construction permit" (FCC permission to build a station) in court under § 402(b)(2) of the Communications Act. That provision lets an "adversely affected" person, meaning one harmed by an FCC decision, appeal it.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: Then-§ 309(a) of the Communications Act allowed grants on examination when public interest, convenience, or necessity supported approval; otherwise it required notice and opportunity for hearing.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: Then-§ 309(a) of the Communications Act let the FCC approve an application "on examination" (on the papers) if the public interest, convenience, or necessity supported it. Otherwise the FCC had to give the applicant "notice and opportunity" for a hearing before deciding.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: Granting one mutually exclusive application could not render the other’s hearing empty merely because summary-grant power existed in isolation.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: Granting one of two "mutually exclusive" applications (ones that cannot both be granted) could not make the other applicant's hearing meaningless. That the FCC had "summary-grant" power (power to approve without a hearing) when an application stood alone did not change this.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: No licensee acquired a vested frequency property right, but modification, suspension, and revocation themselves required procedures protecting the incumbent.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: No licensee (holder of an FCC license) got a "vested frequency property right," meaning it did not own its frequency. But changing, suspending, or revoking a license itself required procedures protecting the incumbent (the station already licensed), so Ashbacker would be fighting uphill against it.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: The construction permit differed from the operating license issued after compliance under § 319(b).
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: The "construction permit" (permission to build the station) was a separate, earlier step from the operating license (permission to broadcast), which the FCC issued under § 319(b) only after the builder complied with the permit's terms.

lrs-o-ashbacker.sentence: He assumed both applications had been examined and thought the agency could grant Fetzer conditionally, then modify the authorization if Ashbacker proved superior.
lrs-o-ashbacker.plain: Frankfurter assumed the FCC had examined both applications. He thought the agency could grant Fetzer's application conditionally, then change that approval if Ashbacker later proved the better choice.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: Its basis was an aggregate claim of constitutional and statutory power, not compliance with a particular seizure statute.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Truman's order rested on a general claim of constitutional and statutory power (power from the Constitution and from laws passed by Congress) taken together. It did not rely on following any particular law authorizing seizures.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: Congress had not acted on those reports when the case was decided, but earlier procurement and labor-emergency legislation already occupied the field.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Congress had not acted on Truman's reports when the case was decided. But earlier laws on government procurement (buying supplies) and labor emergencies already "occupied the field," meaning Congress had already covered this subject.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: They argued that seizure made law entrusted to Congress.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: The companies argued that by seizing the mills the President was making law, a power the Constitution gives to Congress.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: It separately argued that compensation was available and irreparable harm absent.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: The government also argued that the companies could be paid later for any loss and that there was no "irreparable harm" (harm money cannot fix), so no emergency court order was needed.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: The legality issue was ripe at that preliminary stage: precedent left uncertain whether the Court of Claims could compensate an unlawful official taking, and operating ongoing businesses caused present and future injuries difficult or impossible to reduce to money.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: The legality question was "ripe" (ready for decision) even at that early stage. Precedent (earlier rulings) left it unclear whether the Court of Claims could pay for an illegal seizure by an official, and the government running the businesses caused present and future harm hard or impossible to measure in money.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: No statute expressly or fairly impliedly authorized this taking.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: No statute (law passed by Congress) authorized this taking of the mills, either in express words or by fair implication.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: The Take Care duty presupposed law to execute; it did not supply legislative power.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: The "Take Care" duty (the President's constitutional duty to see that the laws are faithfully executed) assumes there is already a law to enforce. It does not give the President legislative power, the power to make new law.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: For Frankfurter, systematic, unbroken, previously unquestioned practice known to Congress might supply constitutional gloss.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: For Frankfurter, a systematic, unbroken presidential practice, long known to Congress and never questioned, might add "constitutional gloss," meaning it can help show what power the Constitution gives the President.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: Even temporary industry seizure was a taking requiring compensation, and Congress’s control of revenue and payment meant Congress must authorize or ratify condemnation.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Douglas said even a temporary seizure of an industry is a "taking" that the government must pay for. Because Congress controls revenue and payment, Congress must authorize or "ratify" (approve after the fact) the condemnation.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: When Congress expressly or impliedly authorizes action, presidential authority includes his own powers plus what Congress may delegate and receives the strongest presumption.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Jackson's first category: when Congress expressly or impliedly authorizes the President's action, his authority includes his own powers plus whatever Congress can delegate (hand over) to him. Courts give such action the strongest presumption of validity.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: With neither grant nor denial, independent and possibly concurrent authority forms a zone of uncertain allocation: inertia may enable action in practice, but silence is not invariably permission.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Second category: when Congress has neither granted nor denied power, the President and Congress may have "concurrent authority" (shared power), creating a "zone of uncertain allocation" where the line is unclear. Congressional inertia may let him act in practice, but silence is not always permission.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: Against Congress’s expressed or implied will, presidential power is lowest; sustaining exclusive executive control requires excluding Congress from the subject.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Third category: when the President acts against Congress's expressed or implied will (stated or understood from what it did), his power is at its lowest. He can win only if the Constitution gives the subject to him alone, shutting Congress out.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: Upholding seizure would make strike-bound industry an exclusive presidential domain beyond Congress, which Jackson rejected.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Approving the seizure would mean Congress had no say over industries hit by strikes, which Jackson would not accept.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: Clark affirmatively accepted extensive independent emergency authority where Congress had supplied no controlling procedure, but Little v. Barreme showed that statutory directions displace a different executive method.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: Clark accepted broad independent emergency power for the President where Congress had set no controlling procedure. But Little v. Barreme, an 1804 ship-seizure case, showed that statutory directions (procedures Congress sets by law) override a different method the executive chooses.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: On June 2, 1952, the Court affirmed the district court’s judgment, sustaining its preliminary injunction by six votes to three.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: On June 2, 1952, the Supreme Court "affirmed" (upheld) the district court's judgment by six votes to three. It thereby kept in place the "preliminary injunction," an early court order blocking the seizure.

lrs-o-youngstown.sentence: It did not affirm the appellate stay.
lrs-o-youngstown.plain: It did not "affirm" (uphold) the appeals court's "stay," which had paused that injunction.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: The statute did not expressly address removal.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: The statute (the law creating the commission) did not expressly say whether, or for what reasons, the President could remove the commissioners.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: He made recess appointments the next day, including a replacement for Wiener, and sent nominations to the Senate February 15, 1954.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: The next day, he made "recess appointments," filling posts temporarily without Senate approval while the Senate was on break, including a replacement for Wiener. He sent the nominations to the Senate for confirmation on February 15, 1954.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: An earlier quo warranto proceeding had been dismissed and its appeal dismissed as moot by agreement.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: An earlier "quo warranto" case (a challenge to someone's right to hold an office) had been dismissed. Its appeal was then dismissed by agreement as "moot," meaning no live dispute was left to decide.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: In the Supreme Court, the Government argued that the earlier judgment foreclosed certain issues.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: In the Supreme Court, the Government argued that the earlier judgment (the final ruling in that case) had already settled certain issues, so Wiener could not reargue them.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: The Court did not reach that contention’s merits: in these circumstances the Government should have offered it under the Court’s rules as a reason to deny review.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: The Court did not reach the merits of that argument (whether it was right). In these circumstances, the Government should have raised it under the Court's rules as a reason to deny review, when urging the Court not to take the case.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: In the historical framework the Court applied, Myers concerned an executive postmaster, while Humphrey’s Executor confined its removal principle to purely executive officers and rejected broader language about quasi-judicial officials.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: In the history the Court relied on, Myers involved a postmaster, a purely executive officer the President could fire. Humphrey’s Executor limited Myers's removal rule to purely executive officers and rejected broader language reaching "quasi-judicial" officials, who decide cases like judges.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: Assigned duties therefore best revealed congressional intent.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: So the duties assigned to the job best revealed "congressional intent," meaning what Congress meant about whether the official could be fired.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: If the President could not influence a particular decision, Congress could not plausibly intend a threat of removal merely to obtain his preferred membership.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: If the President cannot interfere with the commission's rulings, Congress could not have meant for him to fire members just to install his own picks.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: The adjudicatory design supplied the protection even without an express for-cause clause or permanent agency tenure.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: Because the commission was designed to decide cases like a court, its members were protected from firing anyway. That held even though the law had no express "for-cause clause" (a rule allowing removal only for good reason) and the agency was temporary.

lrs-s-wiener.sentence: It decided removal solely for presidential personnel preference, not removal for cause concerning a member’s rectitude or temporary suspension while the Senate considered a successor.
lrs-s-wiener.plain: The ruling covered only removal because the President preferred his own people. It did not decide "removal for cause" based on a member's misconduct (lack of rectitude), or a temporary suspension while the Senate considered a successor.

balfour.sentence: She obtained a decree nisi on July 30 and an alimony order on December 16.
balfour.plain: She won a "decree nisi" (a provisional divorce decree that becomes final later unless cause is shown) on July 30, and an alimony (spousal support) order on December 16. Those family-court steps were separate from the contract lawsuit here.

balfour.sentence: Because the husband already owed a duty of support, the judge understood the parties to have contracted to fix its amount.
balfour.plain: Husbands then had a legal duty to support their wives. So the trial judge understood the parties (the husband and wife) to have made a contract fixing how much that support would be: £30 a month.

balfour.sentence: The wife’s consent supplied consideration for the promise.
balfour.plain: A promise is enforceable as a contract only if the other side gives something in return ('consideration'). The trial judge held that the wife's agreement to accept the arrangement was enough.

balfour.sentence: The wife answered that spouses could contract and argued that she had surrendered her power to pledge his credit for necessaries in exchange for the allowance.
balfour.plain: The wife answered that spouses can make contracts. She argued she gave up her power to "pledge his credit" for necessaries, meaning to buy household essentials on her husband's account and make him pay, in exchange for the allowance.

balfour.sentence: The appellate judges questioned both their relevance to spouses still living amicably and whether the asserted independent right to charge his credit existed.
balfour.plain: The appellate judges (judges of the appeals court) doubted that her cases, which involved separated couples, applied to spouses still living amicably. They also doubted she had any free-standing right to "charge his credit" (run up bills on his account) that she could trade away.

balfour.sentence: But the wife needed to show express contractual terms or circumstances necessarily implying them.
balfour.plain: But the wife had to show "express contractual terms" (terms the two actually stated) or circumstances that necessarily implied such terms.

balfour.sentence: She had made no express promise to accept £30 in full satisfaction of her husband’s maintenance obligation regardless of changing needs.
balfour.plain: She made no express (actually stated) promise to accept £30 in "full satisfaction" of his "maintenance obligation," meaning as complete payment of his duty to support her, no matter how her needs changed. Without such a promise, she gave nothing in return.

balfour.sentence: Warrington regarded the husband’s undertaking as an expression of intention and obligation of honour without a corresponding bargain by the wife.
balfour.plain: Warrington saw the husband's undertaking (his promise) as a statement of intention and an "obligation of honour," a moral rather than legal duty. The wife made no corresponding bargain, meaning she gave no promise in exchange.

balfour.sentence: The cited authorities treated her power to charge him as an agency, not the independent and irrevocable right assumed by her lawyer.
balfour.plain: The authorities (earlier cases) her lawyer cited treated a wife's power to charge her husband as "agency": she acted as his agent, a power he could control or end. It was not the independent, irrevocable right of her own that her lawyer assumed.

balfour.sentence: Surrendering something that was not such a right supplied no consideration.
balfour.plain: Giving up something she did not really have the right to could not count as her side of a bargain, so it was not consideration.

balfour.sentence: Her assent to an arrangement within her husband’s discretion did not convert his domestic promise into the alleged contract.
balfour.plain: Her assent (agreement) to an allowance that was within her husband's discretion (his to decide anyway) did not turn his domestic promise into the alleged contract she claimed.

balfour.sentence: Domestic allowances could likewise involve reciprocal promises and something that would count as consideration between other parties, yet lack contractual force because legal consequences were not intended.
balfour.plain: Atkin's point: domestic allowances can involve promises on both sides, and something that would count as "consideration" (what each side gives in exchange) between other parties. Yet they are not contracts when neither side intended legal consequences.

balfour.sentence: Atkin’s description of the home as outside the King’s writ addressed this class of promise, not a general lack of judicial authority over marriage.
balfour.plain: When Atkin said the home lies outside the King’s writ (court orders do not reach there), he meant only this kind of everyday promise between spouses. He was not saying courts lack all authority over marriage.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Her complaint requested injunction and punitive relief; compensatory damages later entered the trial issues without formal amendment.
brief-CP-110.plain: Her complaint asked for an injunction (a court order) and "punitive relief" (damages to punish the landlords). Compensatory damages, money to repay her actual losses, later became a trial issue even without a formal amendment (rewrite) of her complaint.

brief-CP-110.sentence: It excluded Curtis’s actual-loss proof for failure to obey a pretrial discovery order, found discrimination without proved actual damages, and awarded $250 punitive damages.
brief-CP-110.plain: Because Curtis had not obeyed a "pretrial discovery" order (an order to share evidence before trial), the judge excluded her proof of actual loss. The judge found discrimination without proved "actual damages" (real losses) and awarded $250 in "punitive damages," money meant to punish.

brief-CP-110.sentence: The Seventh Circuit reversed, finding a constitutional jury right and construing the statute consistently.
brief-CP-110.plain: The Seventh Circuit (the federal appeals court) reversed. It held the Constitution gave the landlords a right to a jury, and read the housing statute in a way consistent with that right.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Curtis sought Supreme Court review to preserve the judge’s disposition.
brief-CP-110.plain: Curtis asked for Supreme Court review to keep the judge's disposition (his final handling of the case) rather than send the case to a jury.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Justice Marshall’s unanimous opinion rejected confinement of the Seventh Amendment to causes bearing names recognized in 1791.
brief-CP-110.plain: Justice Marshall’s unanimous opinion (all Justices agreeing) rejected limiting the Seventh Amendment jury right to kinds of lawsuits with names recognized in 1791. New claims created by statute can qualify too.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Legislation creating a duty did not categorically remove an ordinary court action enforcing it from the jury guarantee.
brief-CP-110.plain: A law creating a new duty did not automatically take an ordinary court action enforcing it outside the "jury guarantee" (the Seventh Amendment right to a jury).

brief-CP-110.sentence: Curtis sought compensation for discrimination rather than recovery of a particular fund or disgorgement of money belonging to her.
brief-CP-110.plain: Curtis wanted compensation for discrimination, the classic "legal" remedy tried to juries. She did not seek recovery of a particular fund or "disgorgement" (handing back) of money belonging to her, which are equity remedies decided by a judge.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Those involved administrative enforcement or specialized equitable proceedings where jury participation could conflict with statutory structure.
brief-CP-110.plain: Those earlier no-jury examples involved agency enforcement or specialized "equitable" proceedings (judge-run proceedings like bankruptcy), where a jury could clash with the statutory structure Congress designed. This case was an ordinary lawsuit.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Appellate courts had treated it as part of equitable reinstatement or restitution under different language.
brief-CP-110.plain: Appellate courts (courts of appeals) had treated back pay in job-discrimination cases as part of an "equitable" remedy, like reinstatement (getting the job back) or "restitution" (returning what is owed), decided without a jury, because that statute was worded differently.

brief-CP-110.sentence: The Court need not choose whether to assess the case at filing or trial: damages alone were legal, and Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen, precedents protecting jury issues in mixed legal-equitable actions, preserved the right on legal claims and shared facts even if both forms remained.
brief-CP-110.plain: The Court did not need to choose whether to judge the case as first filed or as it stood at trial: a damages claim alone was "legal" and gets a jury. Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen, precedents (earlier rulings) on cases mixing legal and equitable claims, keep the jury right for the legal claims and shared facts even when both remain.

brief-CP-110.sentence: Calling damages incidental could not defeat it.
brief-CP-110.plain: Labeling the damages a minor add-on to the injunction claim did not erase the jury right.

brief-CP-110.sentence: It used the constitutional ground despite ordinary avoidance because existing decisions settled the requirement and no statute was invalidated.
brief-CP-110.plain: Courts usually avoid constitutional rulings when a statute can decide a case. Here the Court ruled on the Constitution anyway, because prior cases made the answer clear and the ruling struck down no law.

brief-CP-110.sentence: That route also limited the decision to federal-court procedure, leaving statutory effects on state-court jury practice undecided.
brief-CP-110.plain: Deciding on Seventh Amendment grounds also limited the ruling to federal-court procedure (how federal courts run trials). It left undecided whether the statute affects jury practice in state courts.

brief-CP-129.sentence: The court dismissed without deciding tort merits because the detention-of-goods exception preserved sovereign immunity.
brief-CP-129.plain: The court dismissed (threw out) the suit against the United States without deciding the tort merits, meaning whether the government wrongfully caused harm. The "detention-of-goods exception" (for goods held by customs officers) kept the government's sovereign immunity from suit in place.

brief-CP-129.sentence: After the FTCA dismissal, the agents invoked 28 U.S.C. § 2676, which makes a judgment in the specified FTCA action a bar to a claimant’s same-subject action against the employee.
brief-CP-129.plain: After the FTCA suit was dismissed, the agents relied on 28 U.S.C. § 2676. It makes a judgment in that kind of FTCA action (lawsuit against the government) a bar to the claimant’s later action against the employee over the same subject.

brief-CP-129.sentence: The district court considered this dismissal procedural and insufficient to activate the bar.
brief-CP-129.plain: The district court (the trial court) saw this dismissal as procedural, a technical immunity ruling rather than a decision on the merits, and so not enough to trigger the bar.

brief-CP-129.sentence: The Second Circuit accepted collateral-order jurisdiction and affirmed rejection of the defense.
brief-CP-129.plain: Normally a party cannot appeal until the case ends. The Second Circuit nonetheless took "collateral-order" jurisdiction (power to hear certain early appeals under a narrow exception) and affirmed rejection of the agents' defense.

brief-CP-129.sentence: An order must conclusively settle the question, decide an important matter entirely separate from merits, and be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.
brief-CP-129.plain: To be appealable early, an order (ruling) must conclusively settle its question, decide an important issue entirely separate from the merits (who should win the case), and be effectively "unreviewable" on appeal after final judgment.

brief-CP-129.sentence: The agents compared absolute and qualified immunity, state sovereign immunity, and double jeopardy, all sometimes protecting against the proceeding itself.
brief-CP-129.plain: The agents compared absolute and "qualified immunity" (officials' protections from suit), state sovereign immunity, and double jeopardy. Each of these sometimes protects against going through the proceeding at all, so can be appealed right away.

brief-CP-129.sentence: If irreversible expenditure alone sufficed, nearly every denied pretrial motion would qualify.
brief-CP-129.plain: If the cost of going through a case that cannot be recovered were enough, almost every denied "pretrial motion" (request before trial, such as to end the case) could be appealed immediately, swallowing the rule.

brief-CP-129.sentence: Those interests explained immediate review more precisely than the phrase right not to be tried.
brief-CP-129.plain: What justifies an immediate appeal is a weighty public value, such as separation of powers or protecting officials, not just a defendant's wish to avoid a trial.

brief-CP-129.sentence: Qualified immunity could be invoked upon service.
brief-CP-129.plain: An official can claim qualified immunity as soon as he is sued, while the FTCA bar arises only after a separate judgment. They are different.

brief-CP-129.sentence: The Court acknowledged that the statutory bar might extend beyond ordinary res judicata without treating their scope as identical.
brief-CP-129.plain: The Court acknowledged that the statutory bar in § 2676 might reach further than ordinary "res judicata" (the rule against relitigating decided claims), without treating the two as identical in scope.

brief-CP-129.sentence: On January 18, 2006, the Supreme Court vacated the Second Circuit’s judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.
brief-CP-129.plain: On January 18, 2006, the Supreme Court "vacated" (erased) the Second Circuit’s judgment. It sent the case back with instructions to dismiss the agents' appeal for "lack of jurisdiction," meaning the appeals court had no power to hear it at that stage.

brief-CP-129.sentence: A potentially dispositive defense and possible district-court error did not establish an immediate appeal of right.
brief-CP-129.plain: A defense that might be "dispositive" (able to end the case) and a possible district-court error did not give the agents an immediate "appeal of right," an appeal they are entitled to bring now.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: Oppenheimer Fund was an open-end investment fund that sold shares at net asset value plus a sales charge.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: Oppenheimer Fund was an "open-end investment fund" (a mutual fund). It sold shares at "net asset value" (the per-share value of its investments) plus a "sales charge" (a commission), so overvaluing the investments raised the price buyers paid.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: The proposed purchaser class sought the difference between purchase prices and actual share value; a separate derivative count sought excessive management fees on the Fund’s behalf.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The proposed class of buyers sought the difference between what they paid and the shares' actual value. A separate "derivative count," a claim brought on the Fund’s behalf rather than the buyers', sought excessive management fees.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: Defendants denied liability and asserted setoff and contingent-liability positions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The defendants denied wrongdoing and raised other technical defenses, such as 'setoff', reducing anything they might owe by amounts owed back to them.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: The en banc court, by seven votes to three, restored it, treating identification as discovery ordinarily performed at the responding party’s expense unless unduly burdensome.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The en banc court (the full appeals court), by seven votes to three, restored the cost order. It treated identifying class members as discovery, normally done at the responding party’s expense (the side producing the information) unless "unduly burdensome," meaning unreasonably costly.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: The Supreme Court accepted the cost order’s collateral-order appealability; certification itself was outside its review.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The Supreme Court accepted the cost order's "collateral-order" appealability, meaning it could be appealed early under a narrow exception. The certification decision (allowing the class action itself) was outside its review.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: Rule 23 required the best practicable notice, including individual notice to reasonably identifiable members of this kind of class.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: Rule 23 required the "best practicable notice" (best notice reasonably possible). For this kind of class, that included individual notice to every member who could reasonably be identified, so they could decide whether to opt out.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: The then-existing Rule 26(b)(1) permitted discovery beyond admissible trial evidence and narrowly pleaded merits issues: information bearing on jurisdiction, venue, certification, or clarification of claims could qualify.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The then-existing Rule 26(b)(1) allowed discovery beyond admissible trial evidence (evidence usable at trial) and narrowly pleaded merits issues (those stated in the papers). Information bearing on jurisdiction (the court's power), venue, certification, or clarifying the claims could qualify.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: A possible future dispute over whether notice had been sent could not make the information discoverable before it was obtained and used.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The names were wanted only to mail notices. A possible future dispute over whether notice was sent could not make the information "discoverable" (obtainable through discovery) before it was obtained and used.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: The Court compared the historical interrogatory rule allowing access to business records when either side could derive an answer with substantially equal effort: greater efficiency could instead justify having the responding party derive it.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: The Court compared the old "interrogatory" rule (on written questions): a company could open its business records when either side could find the answer with substantially equal effort. Greater efficiency could instead justify making the responding party find it, the idea used here.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: Defendants also did not have to purchase the right to make successful objections.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: A defendant that makes a valid objection, for example to an improperly defined class, should win it without having to pay anything in exchange.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: Nor could an unwilling defendant be charged for supposed preclusion advantages from a larger class.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: A bigger class means more people bound by the outcome ("preclusion" benefits for defendants). But an unwilling defendant could not be charged for those supposed advantages.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.sentence: Alleging a fiduciary breach likewise did not establish liability or entitle claimants to litigation financed by the fiduciary and indirectly other beneficiaries.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-350.plain: Alleging (merely claiming) a fiduciary breach, a breach of the managers' duty of loyalty to investors, did not establish liability. It did not entitle the claimants to make the fiduciary, and so indirectly the other beneficiaries (the Fund's shareholders), pay for the lawsuit.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Its approved plan vested fraudulent-conveyance claims in trustee Nordberg, who sued Granfinanciera and Medex in federal district court in 1985.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: The company's approved bankruptcy plan "vested" (placed) its "fraudulent-conveyance" claims, claims to undo improper transfers of its money, in a trustee, Nordberg. In 1985 he sued Granfinanciera and Medex in federal district court.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: He alleged about $1.7 million transferred by the debtor’s predecessor within the preceding year without adequate consideration and sought transfer recovery, damages, expenses, costs, and interest on actual- and constructive-fraud theories.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: He alleged about $1.7 million was transferred by the debtor’s predecessor within the prior year without adequate "consideration" (fair value in return). He sought recovery of the transfers, damages, expenses, costs, and interest, on theories of actual fraud (intent to cheat creditors) and constructive fraud (terms the law treats as fraudulent anyway).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Neither had submitted a claim against the bankruptcy estate, so the trustee was pursuing outsiders to augment assets rather than deciding their shares.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: Neither defendant had filed a claim against the "bankruptcy estate" (the bankrupt company's assets). So the trustee was suing outsiders to add to the assets, not deciding their shares of what already existed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: The bankruptcy judge denied the demand on the view that this core proceeding was historically nonjury.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: The bankruptcy judge denied their jury demand, reasoning that this "core proceeding" (a central bankruptcy matter) was historically "nonjury," meaning traditionally decided without a jury.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: The Court declined the unpreserved, inadequately briefed issue, also noting an unrebutted plausible concern that it would enlarge enforcement rights beyond the judgment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: The Court refused to consider the argument that the Colombian government-owned defendant had no jury right, because it was "unpreserved" (not raised in the lower courts) and barely briefed. It also noted an unanswered, plausible concern that it would widen enforcement rights beyond the judgment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Equity also heard some conveyance disputes, but the trustee’s examples concerned future receivables or trust land, not a definite sum without accounting.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: Equity courts (judges sitting without juries) did hear some conveyance (transfer) disputes. But the trustee's examples involved future receivables (money owed later) or land held in trust, not a demand for a definite sum that needed no accounting.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Fungible dollars fully compensable at law did not become equitable merely through the words avoidance or restitution.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: "Fungible" dollars (interchangeable money), fully "compensable" at law (in jury courts), did not become an "equitable" (judge-only) claim just because bankruptcy law calls it "avoidance" or "restitution."

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Congress could assign some legal public-rights matters to nonjury administrative tribunals, but could not remove traditional private-right jury protection by calling a case core.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: Congress could assign some "public-rights" matters (disputes tied to government programs) to "nonjury" agency tribunals. But it could not strip the traditional jury protection from a "private-right" case, an ordinary dispute between private parties, by calling it a core bankruptcy matter.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Five Justices joined Part IV’s view that closely integrated federal regulatory rights between private parties could qualify as public rights.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: Five Justices joined Part IV of the opinion, which said that even rights between private parties can count as "public rights" (decidable without juries) when they are closely bound up with a federal regulatory program.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: Katchen differed because a creditor filed estate claims and the preference issue had to be decided in allowance or disallowance.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: Katchen was different because there the creditor had filed claims against the estate, so the "preference issue" (whether it got an improper preferential payment) had to be decided as part of the "allowance or disallowance" of its claim, meaning whether it could share in the assets. Here the defendants filed no claims.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: He required the United States as a party for public rights, grounding the exception in sovereign immunity and revenue collection and rejecting flexible balancing.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: Scalia would require the United States to be a party before the no-jury "public rights" exception applies. He grounded it in "sovereign immunity" (the government's protection from suit) and revenue collection, and rejected flexible "balancing" (case-by-case weighing).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.sentence: The Court did not decide whether bankruptcy judges had statutory or constitutional authority to conduct the jury trial, or how district review would respect the bar on reexamining jury-found facts.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-417.plain: The Court left open whether bankruptcy judges may run jury trials, and how a district judge reviewing their work could do so given the Constitution's limits on second-guessing facts a jury found.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Congress approved the Republican River Compact in 1943, making it federal law.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: Congress approved the Republican River Compact, the three states' agreement dividing the river's water, in 1943. That approval made the compact federal law as well as a contract between states.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Kansas’s 1998 original Supreme Court action challenged increased Nebraska groundwater pumping.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: Disputes between states start directly in the Supreme Court. In 1998 Kansas brought this "original" action (lawsuit) there, challenging Nebraska's increased groundwater pumping.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Justice Kagan’s majority respected the Master’s facts with a presumption of correctness while independently reviewing and retaining responsibility.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: Justice Kagan’s majority opinion gave the special Master's factual findings a "presumption of correctness" (treated them as presumptively right). But the Court reviewed them independently and kept final responsibility for the decision.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Original jurisdiction between sovereigns was equitable, substituting for diplomacy or force.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: "Original jurisdiction" here (the Supreme Court hearing a case first) between sovereign states was "equitable," meaning the Court could use flexible remedies. It replaces the diplomacy or force independent nations would use.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Within them, remedies could protect rights and deter abuse; congressional approval also made breach a violation of federal law implicating public interest.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: Within the compact's terms, remedies could protect Kansas's rights and deter abuse. Because Congress approved the compact, a breach (violation) of it was also a violation of federal law, which involves the public interest.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: The Court agreed that Nebraska knowingly exposed Kansas to substantial risk and recklessly disregarded its rights, while retaining the Master’s finding that it had not purposefully set out to breach.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: The Court agreed that Nebraska knowingly exposed Kansas to a substantial risk and recklessly disregarded its rights. It kept the special Master’s finding that Nebraska had not purposefully set out to breach (break) the compact.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: The discussion of deliberate breach in the Restatement did not erase distinctions among purpose, conscious disregard, and negligence; conscious disregard supported relief in this interstate setting.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: The Restatement's discussion of deliberate breach did not erase the differences among acting on purpose, "conscious disregard" (knowingly ignoring a risk), and negligence. Conscious disregard was enough for relief (a remedy, here giving up some gain) in this dispute between states.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Those developments and deterrence also defeated a cognizable danger of recurrence needed for an injunction.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: An injunction requires a "cognizable" (legally real) danger that the violation will recur. Nebraska's reforms plus the deterrence (discouraging effect) of paying meant no such danger remained.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: The Court did not license profitable breach; it found additional preventive relief unnecessary.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: The Court was not allowing a state to breach a compact whenever it pays. It simply found that further "preventive relief" (a court order to stop future violations) was unnecessary.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: On accounting, Thomas distinguished mistaken expression of an actual bargain from mistaken belief that deliberately chosen procedures would work well.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: On the water-accounting issue, Thomas distinguished a mistake in writing down the parties' actual bargain (their real deal), which courts may fix, from a mistaken belief that procedures they deliberately chose would work well, which they may not.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: Rescission might address a basic-assumption mistake, though nobody sought it.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: Rescission (cancelling the agreement) might be the remedy for a mistake about a basic assumption, though nobody asked for it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: He urged restraint under ordinary contract principles, found disgorgement unsupported for nondeliberate breach, considered $1.8 million arbitrary rather than reasonably measured profit, and opposed absorbing litigation expense contrary to fee rules.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: Thomas urged restraint under ordinary contract rules. He found "disgorgement" (giving up the breaching party's profits) unsupported for a breach that was not deliberate, saw the $1.8 million as arbitrary rather than a reasonable measure of profit, and opposed shifting lawyers' costs against the usual fee rules.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.sentence: The Court overruled all exceptions and adopted the Master’s recommendations: $3.7 million compensation, $1.8 million partial disgorgement, no injunction, and accounting reform.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-005.plain: The Court "overruled all exceptions" (rejected every objection) to the special Master's report and adopted it: $3.7 million for Kansas's losses, $1.8 million in partial "disgorgement" of Nebraska's gains, no injunction, and corrected water accounting.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: The president denied ordering or buying these particular skins and said he promptly wrote Harding that they were unfit and held subject to Hobbs’s directions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: The company's president said he never ordered this shipment and quickly wrote to Harding that the skins were no good and the company was holding them until Hobbs said what to do with them. That would be a rejection, if it reached Hobbs.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: The company argued that notice to Harding was notice to Hobbs.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: The company argued that Harding acted as Hobbs's agent, so telling Harding about the rejection legally counted as telling Hobbs.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: Agency went to the jury under unchallenged instructions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: Agency (whether Harding acted as Hobbs's agent) went to the jury under instructions neither side challenged.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: Another instruction allowed a plaintiff’s verdict if the company remained silent while having reason to believe the sender understood it was accepting the skins.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: Another instruction told the jury it could return a plaintiff’s verdict (find for Hobbs) if the company stayed silent while having reason to believe Hobbs understood it was accepting the skins.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: Given the verdict and the quality instruction, the appellate court treated the shipment as conforming and Hobbs as having received no rejection notice.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: Given the verdict for Hobbs and the instruction barring recovery for poor-quality skins, the appeals court treated the shipment as "conforming" (meeting the requirements) and Hobbs as never having received a rejection notice.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: The company’s own testimony supported a standing offer for suitable skins of the stated size.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: The company's own testimony (its witnesses' evidence) supported a "standing offer," an ongoing offer to buy any suitable skins of the stated size.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: Even if sending alone did not complete the bargain, the prior transactions warranted a conforming shipment and called for action on receipt.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: Even if sending skins did not by itself complete the bargain (the contract), the parties' past dealings entitled Hobbs to send a "conforming shipment" (skins meeting the terms) and required the company to act on receiving it, such as by rejecting it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: Silence combined with retention for an unreasonable period permitted an inference of assent despite an undisclosed contrary intention.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: Silence plus keeping the skins for an unreasonable time allowed an "inference" (a reasonable conclusion) that the company assented (accepted), even if it privately intended otherwise and never said so.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: On March 1, 1893, the Supreme Judicial Court overruled the exceptions and left Hobbs’s verdict in place.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: On March 1, 1893, the Supreme Judicial Court (Massachusetts's highest court) overruled the company's exceptions, its objections to the trial rulings, and left Hobbs's verdict in place.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.sentence: The court did not let a stranger impose a purchase simply by shipping goods, or decide an unpreserved challenge to the agency instructions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B1-058.plain: The court did not let a stranger force a purchase just by shipping goods. Nor did it decide an "unpreserved" challenge to the agency instructions, one not properly raised at trial.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: Eugene H. Emmick retained attorney L. S. Hamm for consideration to prepare a will and codicils.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: Emmick paid lawyer Hamm to write his will and later amendments to it.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: They contended that timing violated California’s then-existing perpetuity and alienation restrictions.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: They argued the trust's timing broke California's then-existing "perpetuity and alienation restrictions," rules against tying up property, or blocking its transfer, for too long.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: A third count concerned Hamm’s later representation of executors in a testamentary-capacity contest.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: A third claim involved Hamm's later work for the executors when relatives brought a "testamentary-capacity" contest, a challenge claiming Emmick lacked the mental ability to make a valid will.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: The trial court sustained a general demurrer to the second amended complaint without further leave and dismissed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: The trial court sustained a "general demurrer" (ruled the complaint stated no legal claim even if its facts were true) to the second amended complaint, refused further leave to amend, and dismissed the case.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: Carrying out a client’s testamentary directions foreseeably benefits intended recipients, while the estate ordinarily suffers no corresponding loss when they miss their gifts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: Carrying out a client's "testamentary" directions (instructions for a will) obviously benefits the people meant to receive gifts. But if they miss their gifts, the estate usually suffers no matching loss, so unless they can sue, nobody can.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: A contract expressly for a third person’s benefit excluded incidental beneficiaries but required no formal recital naming them or direct delivery of services.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: A contract made expressly to benefit a third person could be enforced by that person, though not by "incidental beneficiaries" who merely happen to benefit. It needed no formal recital (statement) naming them, nor direct delivery of services to them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: The court disapproved contrary language in earlier decisions requiring the promisor personally to intend the benefit.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: The court disapproved (rejected) language in earlier decisions requiring that the promisor, the one making the promise (here, the lawyer), personally intend to benefit the third party.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: Absent a special undertaking, an error on a question competent lawyers could reasonably consider doubtful did not establish liability.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: Without a "special undertaking" (a lawyer's specific promise of a result), getting wrong a question competent lawyers could reasonably find doubtful did not establish liability for malpractice.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.sentence: Because the five years ran from a distribution order, invalidity depended on the remote possibility of distribution being delayed beyond a life in being plus sixteen years.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-030.plain: The trust's five years ran from the court's distribution order.
