brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: Under the FSIA (the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act), an exception to immunity gave the court "subject-matter jurisdiction" (power over this type of case). But § 1330(b) made "personal jurisdiction" over Sudan depend on proper service under § 1608.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: Section 1608(a) required a hierarchy for foreign states: special service arrangement, then applicable international convention, then prescribed mailing, and finally diplomatic channels through the Secretary of State if mailing could not be completed within thirty days.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: Section 1608(a) set a required order for serving a foreign state: any special arrangement, then any applicable treaty, then mail sent as prescribed, and last, if mail failed within thirty days, "diplomatic channels" through the Secretary of State.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: The question was whether naming that person at the Washington embassy sufficed, not whether likely actual notice excused the statutory method.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: The question was whether addressing the papers to the foreign minister at the Washington embassy satisfied the statute. It was not whether Sudan's likely "actual notice" (really learning of the suit) excused the statute's method.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: Section 1608(b), for agencies or instrumentalities, expressly allowed reasonable-actual-notice measures and specified agents, including domestic recipients.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: Section 1608(b), for "agencies or instrumentalities" (state-owned entities, not countries themselves), expressly allowed methods reasonably likely to give actual notice and service on specified agents, including recipients in the U.S.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: Reopening a later default was no substitute for proper initial service.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: Sudan's ability to come in later and challenge the default judgment does not make up for failing to serve it properly in the first place.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: Its interpretation of diplomatic inviolability under the Vienna Convention informed context, but the Court did not decide that interpretation independently; statutory construction avoided the potential conflict.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: The State Department's reading of embassy "inviolability" (protection from intrusion) under the Vienna Convention gave context, but the Court did not decide it. Its "statutory construction," requiring mail to the ministry abroad, avoided any conflict.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: On the Vienna Convention, he distinguished physical inviolability from immunity to judicial authority; ordinary service mail did not invade premises.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: On the Vienna Convention, Thomas separated physical "inviolability" of embassy premises from immunity to courts' authority. Ordinary service by mail did not invade the premises.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.sentence: He added that, even if conflict existed, the later FSIA would control.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-089.plain: He added that, even if a conflict existed, the FSIA, enacted later than the treaty, would control as a matter of U.S. law.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: It also required a showing that exculpatory results would have prevented conviction and that the request would not unreasonably delay punishment.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: The law also required showing that "exculpatory" results (pointing to innocence) would have prevented conviction, and that the request would not unreasonably delay punishment.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: It affirmed the second denial on the no-fault requirement, accepting counsel’s earlier choice as reasonable strategy.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: The court affirmed (upheld) the second denial on the "no-fault" requirement, that untested evidence not be the prisoner's fault. It accepted his trial counsel's earlier choice not to test as a reasonable strategy.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: The district court dismissed under circuit precedent requiring habeas for such requests; the Fifth Circuit affirmed.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: The district court dismissed the suit under circuit precedent (earlier rulings of its regional appeals court) requiring such requests to go through habeas. The Fifth Circuit affirmed.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: Counsel explained that he challenged the DNA statute as authoritatively construed, rather than seeking federal appellate reversal of particular state judgments or adjudication of prosecutorial misconduct.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: Counsel explained that Skinner challenged Texas's DNA statute as authoritatively construed (interpreted) by the state's top criminal court. He was not seeking federal appellate reversal of particular state judgments, or a ruling on prosecutorial misconduct.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: An independent constitutional attack on the governing statute or rule could proceed even if a state court had already considered a related question.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: An independent constitutional challenge to the governing statute or rule itself could go forward even if a state court had already considered a related question.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: Even if Skinner could have raised his federal theory earlier, Rooker-Feldman was not preclusion under another name.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: Whether Skinner lost his claim by not raising it earlier is a separate question under the rules against relitigating issues (preclusion). Rooker-Feldman does not answer that, and the lower court could take it up on remand.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: Section 1983 could not provide relief whose success necessarily implied an outstanding conviction or sentence was invalid.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: Section 1983 (the civil-rights suit law) could not provide relief whose success would necessarily mean an outstanding conviction or sentence was invalid; that challenge belongs in habeas.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: A postconviction Brady claim was different: suppression of favorable material evidence includes prejudice and necessarily undermines a conviction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: A postconviction Brady claim, that prosecutors suppressed helpful evidence, is different. It requires the evidence be "material" and shows "prejudice" (harm to the outcome), so it necessarily undermines the conviction.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: Allowing attacks on the process through § 1983 could evade habeas exhaustion and deference.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: Thomas worried that allowing attacks on the process through § 1983 could let prisoners evade habeas "exhaustion" (using state courts first) and deference (respect for state-court rulings).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.sentence: That functional point differed from whether a testing request counted as collateral review under a particular federal tolling statute.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-270.plain: That practical point differed from whether a testing request counts as "collateral review" (a later challenge outside the direct appeal) under a particular federal "tolling" statute, which pauses a filing deadline.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.sentence: No records or executed releases had been produced when Selective moved to compel them, but the thirty-day response period had not expired.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.plain: No records or "executed releases" (signed permission forms) had been produced when Selective "moved to compel" them, asking the court to order production. But Pyle's thirty-day response period had not yet expired.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.sentence: Selective then asked the court to compel cooperation or alternatively excuse all electronically stored information production.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.plain: Selective then asked the court either to order cooperation on search methods or to excuse it from producing all "electronically stored information," such as emails and electronic files.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.sentence: Expected timely compliance was not yet a failure warranting an advance production order.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.plain: Pyle's expected "timely" (on-time) compliance was not yet a failure that justified an order requiring production in advance.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.sentence: Selective could return to court if Pyle failed to comply when the materials became due; the court did not approve permanent withholding or resolve a particular privilege objection.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.plain: Selective could return to court if Pyle failed to comply when the materials came due. The court did not approve withholding them forever or decide any particular privilege objection (a claim the records were legally protected).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.sentence: It resolved a refusal to participate in methodology, leaving the parties to perform their discovery duties.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-376.plain: The court resolved only the refusal to take part in working out the search method, leaving the parties to perform their discovery duties (exchanging evidence).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: The district court denied preliminary relief, and the merger proceeded May 1, 1956, under an agreement preserving separate books and Kinney’s asset identity.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: The district court denied preliminary relief (a temporary order blocking the merger), and the merger went ahead May 1, 1956. An agreement kept separate books and preserved Kinney's assets, so the merger could still be undone.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: It found unlawful threats from vertical foreclosure and greater retail concentration, permanently prohibited Brown’s interest in Kinney, and ordered full divestiture.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: The court found unlawful threats from "vertical foreclosure" (Brown shutting rival makers out of Kinney's stores) and greater retail concentration. It permanently barred Brown's interest in Kinney and ordered full divestiture (selling it off).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Both sides wanted immediate Supreme Court review, but their agreement could not confer jurisdiction.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: Both sides wanted immediate Supreme Court review, but their agreement could not confer jurisdiction; only law can give a court power to hear a case.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: The Expediting Act then allowed direct Supreme Court appeal from final district-court judgments in government civil antitrust suits, without a general interlocutory route to the courts of appeals.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: The Expediting Act then allowed a "direct Supreme Court appeal" from final district-court judgments in government civil antitrust suits. There was no general interlocutory route (appeal of non-final rulings) to the courts of appeals.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Its current objections concerned condemnation of the merger, not whether complete divestiture would follow if unlawful.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: Brown's objections concerned the ruling that the merger was illegal, not whether complete divestiture (selling off Kinney) should follow if it was unlawful.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Neither collateral-order analogies nor exceptional execution orders fit, and Brown had already been allowed to merge rather than suffering irreparable harm from waiting.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: Harlan said neither "collateral-order" analogies (the narrow exception for early appeals) nor rare orders on carrying out judgments fit. And Brown had already been allowed to merge, so waiting caused it no "irreparable harm" (harm that cannot be fixed later).

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Having accepted jurisdiction, the Court read the 1950 amendments to reach anticompetitive tendencies in their incipiency, including vertical acquisitions.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: Having accepted jurisdiction, the Court read the 1950 amendments (changes to the antitrust law) to reach "anticompetitive" tendencies (threats to competition) in their "incipiency," their early stage, including vertical acquisitions between suppliers and customers.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: The standard was reasonable probability in the industry’s setting, neither certain future monopoly nor remote possibility.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: The standard was "reasonable probability" of harm to competition in the shoe industry's real setting. It did not require a certain future monopoly, and a remote possibility was not enough.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Practical indicators such as uses, customers, price, facilities, and industry recognition could establish submarkets.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: Practical signs such as product uses, customers, price, production facilities, and industry recognition could establish "submarkets," narrower groups of products treated as their own market.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: A manufacturer’s acquisition of outlets could foreclose rivals, especially if those outlets shifted purchasing toward the acquirer.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: When a manufacturer buys stores, rival manufacturers may lose those stores as customers, especially if the stores start buying mainly from their new owner.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Existing competition did not immunize acceleration of a harmful trend.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: That the shoe industry was still competitive did not save the merger; the law aims to stop mergers that speed up a trend toward less competition.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: Internal growth could add capacity and opportunities; absorbing an existing seller or buyer eliminated an independent choice.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: A company that grows by opening new stores adds options for consumers. A company that grows by buying an existing business removes an independent competitor from the market.

brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.sentence: The decision itself concerned an unconditional liability and basic-remedy determination with implementation outstanding; it did not authorize immediate review whenever delay seemed inconvenient.
brief-CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501.plain: The decision concerned a final, unconditional finding of liability (that the merger was illegal) and of the basic remedy, with only carrying it out left. It did not allow immediate review whenever waiting seemed inconvenient.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: His lawyer Barry Croland explained distribution and alimony exposure and the need for fairness, disclosure, and independent counsel.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: Antonio's lawyer, Barry Croland, explained what he could owe in property distribution (dividing marital property) and alimony in a divorce. He also explained that the agreement needed fairness, full disclosure, and independent counsel for Francesca.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: After a plenary trial, an October 25, 1996 order upheld the bargain, finding no coercion, fairness measured in 1985, and no credible proof of Francesca’s claimed 1989 mutual cancellation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: After a "plenary trial" (a full trial), an October 25, 1996 order upheld the bargain (agreement). It found no coercion (improper pressure), measured fairness as of 1985, and found no credible proof of Francesca’s claim that they agreed to a "mutual cancellation" in 1989.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: The appellate court upheld the no-cancellation finding because substantial credible evidence supported it, including failure to establish that Antonio destroyed a signed cancellation document.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: The appellate court upheld the finding that the agreement was never canceled, because substantial believable evidence supported it, including her failure to prove Antonio destroyed a signed cancellation document.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: Judge D’Annunzio’s unanimous Appellate Division opinion distinguished premarital choice and adversarial settlement of a marriage both parties considered over.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: Judge D’Annunzio’s unanimous Appellate Division opinion distinguished this from a premarital agreement, where one can simply decline to marry, and from a hard-fought settlement between parties who both see the marriage as over.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: Genuine reconciliation agreements supplied a closer analogy, requiring a substantial marital rift, fairness, good faith, and attention to conditions at enforcement.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: Genuine "reconciliation agreements" (deals to save a troubled marriage) were a closer comparison. They require a serious marital rift, fair terms, good faith (honest dealing), and attention to conditions when the agreement is enforced.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: Considering actual tax consequences differed from deducting speculative taxes.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: A court may account for taxes that will really be owed. But the trial court wrongly subtracted taxes on hypothetical sales of property, when nothing showed the divorce required selling anything.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: Continuing contributions as mother, homemaker, and helpmate could support later prosperity, just as diminished wealth could make enforcement unfair to an obligor.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: A wife's continuing work as mother, homemaker, and helpmate can support later prosperity, so fairness may be judged at enforcement. Likewise, shrunken wealth could make enforcement unfair to an "obligor," the spouse who must pay.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.sentence: Antonio’s $166,000 interim-support credit request against the now-unenforceable payment and his recording objection became moot.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-033.plain: Antonio's request for a $166,000 credit for "interim-support" (temporary support paid during the case) against the now-unenforceable payment, and his objection to the recordings, became moot, meaning there was nothing left to decide.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: The trial court sustained a demurrer without leave to amend and dismissed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: The trial court sustained a demurrer, ruling that even if her allegations were true she had no legal claim. It gave no leave (permission) to amend and dismissed the case.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: On appeal, the court accepted properly pleaded material allegations but did not treat new assertions in briefing as established facts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: On appeal, the court accepted the material facts properly pleaded in her complaint as true, but did not treat new assertions made only in briefing (written arguments) as established facts.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: In the majority’s view, the latter permission did not allow contracting away personal obligations of marital status.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: The majority said spouses may make contracts about property, but cannot turn the personal duties that marriage already imposes, like caring for each other, into something bought and sold.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: A promise of compensation for that performance supplied no new consideration and offended public policy.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: Promising pay for that performance, care a spouse already owed, gave nothing new in return, so it lacked consideration. It also offended public policy, the values courts protect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: Support’s personal elements made it nondelegable in a way comparable to fidelity and respect.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: The personal side of a spouse's duty of support made it "nondelegable," meaning it cannot be handed off to someone else, like the duties of fidelity and respect.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: Older precedent reflected coverture and a division of male financial support and female domestic labor.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: The dissent said older precedent (earlier rulings) reflected "coverture," the old rule merging a wife's legal identity into her husband's, and a split of male earning and female housework.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: His second note declined to resolve possible statute-of-frauds and property-transmutation problems because the complaint alleged defendants were estopped to invoke them.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: The dissent's second note did not resolve possible "statute-of-frauds" (a required writing) or property-transmutation (changing property's ownership) problems, because the complaint alleged defendants were "estopped" (barred by their own conduct) from raising them.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.sentence: Those denials were not a state Supreme Court merits opinion adopting every part of the majority’s reasoning.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-035.plain: Those denials of review were not a state Supreme Court opinion on the merits adopting every part of the majority’s reasoning; the court simply declined to hear the case.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: On appeal, Evergreen argued the outside-fill promise lacked consideration because Milstead already owed the work.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: On appeal, Evergreen argued its promise to pay for outside fill dirt lacked consideration (nothing given in exchange), because Milstead already owed that work under the contract.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: Maryland’s exception to the preexisting-duty rule could apply even if precautions might have prevented surprise.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: Usually a promise to pay more for work already owed is unenforceable. Maryland makes an exception when unforeseen difficulties arise, and the court said it applied even if better planning might have avoided the surprise.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: If excluded, the promise purchased additional work; if ambiguous, experienced representatives’ agreement, records, and written approval persuasively showed their interpretation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: If the contract excluded outside fill, the promise bought additional work. If the contract was ambiguous (unclear), the experienced representatives' agreement, records, and written approval persuasively showed they understood it as extra.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: Even assuming admission was proper, exclusion caused no harm: both sides’ witnesses and the trial court treated thirty working days as reasonable, matching the legally implied time.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: Even assuming admission of the oral-deadline evidence was proper, excluding it caused no harm. Both sides' witnesses and the trial court treated thirty working days as reasonable, matching the "implied" time, the deadline the law supplies when none is set.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: An operating history could support reasonably certain profits, but a new enterprise presented greater speculation.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: An established business's operating history could support reasonably certain lost profits. But a "new enterprise" has no track record, so its claimed profits involve more speculation (guesswork).

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: The court distinguished deliberate, willful breach from good-faith substantial performance, where price less deviation allowances could avoid giving the owner retained labor and materials without payment.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: The court separated deliberate "willful breach" from good-faith "substantial performance" (honestly doing nearly all the work). In the latter, the contract price minus allowances for the shortfall keeps the owner from getting the labor and materials free.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.sentence: No clear error appeared in treating the work as subordinate, its omission as nonwillful, and a calculable deduction as adequate protection.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-031.plain: There was no "clear error" (obvious mistake) in finding the unfinished work a minor part of the job, its omission "nonwillful" (not on purpose), and a calculable deduction from the price enough to protect Evergreen.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.sentence: A jury awarded damages on a third-party-beneficiary contract theory.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.plain: A jury awarded damages on a "third-party-beneficiary" contract theory: the motorist, though not a party to the contract, was someone it was meant to benefit, so his widow could sue for its breach.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.sentence: Justice Hopkins’s opinion regarded the service evidence as sufficient to support breach but held the personal-injury and death losses outside the contemplated contractual responsibility.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.plain: Justice Hopkins’s opinion found the evidence about the service enough to show breach. But it held the personal-injury and death losses were outside the responsibility the parties contemplated (could foresee) when contracting.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.sentence: It recognized particular benefits for motorists, including regulated charges and refunds for overcharges, while rejecting this consequential recovery under contract foreseeability principles.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.plain: It recognized specific benefits for motorists, such as regulated (set) charges and refunds for overcharges. But it rejected this "consequential recovery" (damages for losses flowing from the breach) under contract "foreseeability" rules.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.sentence: Its majority affirmed expressly for Hopkins’s reasons, rather than issuing a new extended analysis or adopting Justice Martuscello’s separate appellate concurrence.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.plain: The majority of New York's highest court affirmed expressly for Hopkins’s reasons, without writing a new extended analysis or adopting Justice Martuscello’s separate appellate concurrence.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.sentence: Relying on Restatement (Second) of Agency § 354, he reasoned that an agent undertaking necessary protective action could be liable for physical harm caused by reliance and an unexcused failure to act creating a foreseeable unreasonable risk.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.plain: Relying on Restatement (Second) of Agency § 354, the dissent reasoned that an agent who takes on needed protective action can be liable for physical harm when others rely on it and an unexcused failure to act creates a foreseeable, unreasonable risk.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.sentence: Fuchsberg would have reversed and remitted to the Appellate Division for consideration of the facts.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-094.plain: Fuchsberg would have reversed and "remitted" (sent back) the case to the Appellate Division, the lower appeals court, to consider the facts, which New York's highest court generally does not review itself.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.sentence: Late in 1975, Westinghouse wrote seventeen utilities claiming commercial impracticability excused delivery of approximately eighty million promised pounds.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.plain: Late in 1975, Westinghouse wrote to seventeen utilities claiming "commercial impracticability," that the huge price rise made performance so unreasonably costly the law excused it, for about eighty million pounds of promised uranium.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.sentence: With court approval, Westinghouse arranged to deliver its available uranium subject to later determination.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.plain: The court let Westinghouse deliver the uranium it had while everyone's rights were held open until the court decided who owed what.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.sentence: Denial of a complete excuse and openness to remedial adjustment were separate steps: the latter did not itself rewrite every obligation, fix damages or declare that the utilities were entitled to nothing.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.plain: Denying a complete excuse (release from the contracts) and being open to adjusting the remedy were separate steps. The second did not itself rewrite every obligation, set damages, or say the utilities would get nothing.

brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.sentence: Submissions addressing damages and an equitable adjustment followed.
brief-CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B4-113.plain: The parties then filed arguments on damages (what Westinghouse owed) and on an "equitable adjustment," a court-ordered fair sharing of the unexpected loss instead of full enforcement.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: The ordinary grace period continued coverage for thirty-one days after a due date, but the policy allowed US Life to extend it through written notice specifying when coverage would end.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The usual "grace period" kept coverage in force for thirty-one days after a missed due date. But the policy let US Life extend it by written notice stating when coverage would end.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: Evidence of insurability and written approval were generally required, but the evidence requirement did not apply within thirty-one days after the grace period ended.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: "Evidence of insurability" (proof he was still a good risk) and the insurer's written approval were generally needed to revive the policy. But the evidence requirement did not apply within thirty-one days after the grace period ended.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: The Maryland appellate court reviewed legal summary-judgment rulings de novo and explained that refusal to reconsider legal error was also an abuse of discretion.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The Maryland appellate court reviewed the summary-judgment rulings (decisions on legal questions without a trial) "de novo," deciding them fresh. It said refusing to reconsider a "legal error" was itself an "abuse of discretion."

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: The policy was delivered and premiums paid in Illinois, and the parties agreed that Illinois substantive law governed; Maryland and Illinois agreed on the dispositive principles.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The policy was delivered and premiums (payments) made in Illinois, and the parties agreed Illinois "substantive law" (the rules deciding rights) governed. Maryland and Illinois agreed anyway on the "dispositive" (deciding) principles.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: The later lapse notice could not unilaterally add a health-application or receipt condition contrary to the policy.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The insurer's later "lapse" notice (warning the policy would end) could not on its own add a health-application or payment-receipt condition contrary to the policy.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: Neither the later contractual deadline nor a tender first effective after death could insure an already realized loss.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: Neither the later contractual deadline nor a "tender" (offer of payment) that took effect only after Griffith's death could buy coverage for a loss that had already happened.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: The court discussed construing ambiguities against the drafter as a last resort but did not need that doctrine to choose between two equally plausible readings.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The court discussed construing (interpreting) unclear terms against the drafter, the side that wrote the contract, as a last resort. It did not need that tiebreaker, because the two readings were not equally plausible.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: It used unilateral-contract analysis to describe the promised revival upon performance, while reserving requests requiring evidence of insurability and affirmative approval.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The court used "unilateral-contract" analysis, an offer accepted by doing something rather than by promising, to describe revival of coverage upon performance (timely payment). It left open requests that need "evidence of insurability" and the insurer's affirmative approval.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: The mailbox rule could apply to authorized remittance as performance, not only to a mailed promise.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: The "mailbox rule" (an acceptance counts when sent, not when received) could apply to a payment sent by an authorized method as performance, not only to a mailed promise.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: Viewed favorably to defendants, Griffith could still countermand the July 23 instruction.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: Viewing the facts in the light most favorable to the defendants (the insurer and AMAIA), Griffith could still "countermand" (cancel) his July 23 instruction to his bank, so it did not yet count as sending payment.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: An otherwise payable check could be charged before its printed date unless the customer supplied the specified notice of postdating.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: A check otherwise payable could be charged to the account before the date printed on it, unless the customer gave the bank the required notice of "postdating" (dating a check later than it was written).

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: US Life’s alternative claim of a genuine factual dispute appeared first in its appellate reply after the opposite position below.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: US Life’s alternative claim that the facts were genuinely disputed appeared first in its appellate reply brief, after it had taken the opposite position below, in the trial court.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: AMAIA could receive premiums and deny claims as agent for a disclosed principal without assuming the principal’s promise to pay.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: AMAIA could collect premiums and deny claims as agent for a "disclosed principal" (an openly named company it acted for) without taking on that principal's promise to pay.

brief-CT-CB-0263.sentence: Because undisputed cross-motions squarely presented that issue, AMAIA was entitled to judgment, not merely vacatur of Wilson’s award against it.
brief-CT-CB-0263.plain: Because both sides' "cross-motions" (competing requests for judgment) on undisputed facts squarely raised that issue, AMAIA was entitled to judgment outright, not just "vacatur" (cancellation) of Wilson’s award against it.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: The administrative law judge found no demonstrated bias affecting judgment, regarded the allowances as sound, and found no need to alter the rules after detailed questioning.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: The "administrative law judge" (the agency's hearing officer) found no proven bias affecting the expert's judgment and regarded the recommended allowances as sound. After detailed questioning, he found no need to change the rules.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: Section 501(b) expressly required amendments implementing the new law to use Administrative Procedure Act section 553.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: Section 501(b) of the new law expressly required that amendments (rule changes) carrying it out use Administrative Procedure Act section 553, meaning notice-and-comment rulemaking: publishing proposals and taking public comments first.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: The agency answered only in April 1977, asserting good cause because Congress had already dictated the changes and rejecting renewed formal hearings.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: The agency answered only in April 1977. It claimed "good cause" to skip public comment because Congress had already dictated the changes, and it refused to hold renewed formal hearings.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: Saying rules had been revised in recognition of Congress explained the action, not omission of public participation.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: Saying the rules were revised in recognition of what Congress did explained why FDA acted. It did not explain why FDA left out public participation, which is what good cause requires.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: Impracticability, unnecessary procedure, and public interest were narrow exceptions.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: An agency may skip notice and comment only in narrow situations: when it is impracticable, truly unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: This was a new regulatory judgment, not technical deletion of forbidden words, and the urgent petition demonstrated public interest.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: This was a new "regulatory" judgment (a fresh policy choice), not a technical deletion of words Congress had forbidden. The urgent petition showed public interest in commenting.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: The FDA need not reopen issues previously available but unraised, rejected without appeal, or already resolved in its favor unless the legislation gave them a significantly new aspect.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: In the new comment process FDA did not have to reconsider old objections that people skipped, lost without appealing, or lost in court, unless the new law changed them significantly.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: The new provision applied where qualified experts did not generally recognize safety under intended conditions, invoking approval requirements.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: The new provision applied when qualified experts did not "generally recognize safety" of an ingredient under its intended conditions of use, triggering the approval requirements for food additives.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: The court found no categorical incompatibility between food and food additive: a food could become another food’s component without generally recognized safety.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: The court found nothing making "food" and "food additive" categorically incompatible. A food could become a component of another food without "generally recognized safety" in that use, and so count as an additive.

brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.sentence: Petitioners had received participation on that provision; invalidated cross-references were assumed removed, and untimely collateral attacks were declined.
brief-LRS-CLOSURE-015.plain: Petitioners (the challengers) had already been allowed to comment on that provision. The court assumed cross-references to invalidated rules would be removed, and declined "untimely" (late) collateral attacks that should have been raised earlier.

cp-bnsf.sentence: The Montana Supreme Court consolidated review and upheld general jurisdiction on two grounds: it read FELA’s 45 U.S.C. § 56 to authorize jurisdiction wherever a railroad did business and found BNSF a person “found within” Montana under state Rule 4(b)(1).
cp-bnsf.plain: The Montana Supreme Court consolidated review (decided both cases together) and upheld "general jurisdiction" (power over any claim) on two grounds: FELA’s 45 U.S.C. § 56 authorized jurisdiction wherever a railroad did business, and BNSF was "found within" Montana under state Rule 4(b)(1).

cp-bnsf.sentence: Justice McKinnon dissented, separating venue and subject-matter competence from personal jurisdiction and concluding Daimler applied.
cp-bnsf.plain: Justice McKinnon dissented. She separated venue (where suit is filed) and "subject-matter competence" (which courts may hear such cases) from personal jurisdiction (power over a particular defendant), and concluded Daimler's limit applied.

cp-bnsf.sentence: Rejecting a federal statutory basis would not itself dispose of the independent state-rule ground, which Montana had expressly decided.
cp-bnsf.plain: Even if the federal statute gave Montana no jurisdiction, Montana's own rule was a separate basis, so the Supreme Court also had to decide whether using it violated the Constitution.

cp-bnsf.sentence: Congress commonly states venue by where an action may be brought and personal jurisdiction by service-of-process authorization.
cp-bnsf.plain: Congress usually sets venue (the proper place) by saying where an action "may be brought," and grants "personal jurisdiction" (power over a defendant) by authorizing where legal papers may be served.

cp-bnsf.sentence: Plaintiffs’ construction of the predecessor would implausibly permit a diversity plaintiff to force litigation in the plaintiff’s own district despite no defendant or controversy connection.
cp-bnsf.plain: Plaintiffs' reading of the older law would oddly let a "diversity plaintiff" (one suing a citizen of another state) force the case into the plaintiff's own home district, even with no link to the defendant or the dispute.

cp-bnsf.sentence: That described shared subject-matter power, responding to a Connecticut decision treating FELA cases as exclusively federal.
cp-bnsf.plain: That sentence described shared "subject-matter power" (state and federal courts may both hear FELA cases). Congress added it after a Connecticut decision treated FELA cases as "exclusively federal."

cp-bnsf.sentence: With no claim-specific Montana connection, these suits required general jurisdiction over unrelated claims.
cp-bnsf.plain: Because the workers' injuries had nothing to do with Montana, Montana could hear the cases only if BNSF could be sued there on any claim at all.

cp-bnsf.sentence: Those contacts could support specific jurisdiction over related injuries, but not these unrelated claims.
cp-bnsf.plain: BNSF's Montana contacts (its activities there) could support "specific jurisdiction" over injuries related to them, such as those on Montana track, but not these unrelated claims.

cp-bnsf.sentence: She criticized measuring local activity against nationwide operations because greater size elsewhere could insulate a company despite major local business.
cp-bnsf.plain: Sotomayor objected that comparing a company's in-state business to its total business lets big national companies avoid general jurisdiction everywhere but their home states, even where they do huge business.

cp-bnsf.sentence: Plaintiffs separately asserted consent, but Montana had not addressed it, so the Supreme Court left it open.
cp-bnsf.plain: The plaintiffs also argued BNSF had agreed to be sued in Montana. Montana's courts had not ruled on that, so the Supreme Court did not either.

dave-gustafson.sentence: Section 8.9 allowed deductions for each weather working day beyond the deadline or an approved extension and described them as agreed compensation rather than punishment.
dave-gustafson.plain: Section 8.9 let the State deduct a set amount for each "weather working day" (a day with workable weather) beyond the deadline or an approved extension. It called the deductions agreed compensation, not punishment.

dave-gustafson.sentence: The trial court upheld the assessment as liquidated damages.
dave-gustafson.plain: The trial court upheld the daily charge as "liquidated damages," a valid estimate of the State's losses agreed to in advance.

dave-gustafson.sentence: The contractor appealed on the sole question whether it was instead an unenforceable penalty.
dave-gustafson.plain: The contractor appealed on one question only: whether the charge was instead a penalty (a punishment for lateness), which is unenforceable in court.

dave-gustafson.sentence: With one, the agreed measure replaced factual quantification even when actual loss was greater or smaller.
dave-gustafson.plain: If the clause is valid, the agreed amount is used instead of proof of actual losses, even if the real losses turn out higher or lower.

dave-gustafson.sentence: At formation, harm had to be difficult to estimate, the parties had to make a reasonable effort at fair compensation, and the sum had to bear a reasonable relation to probable damages.
dave-gustafson.plain: Judged at formation (when the contract was made): the harm had to be hard to estimate, the parties had to try reasonably to set fair compensation, and the sum had to bear a reasonable relation to probable damages (expected losses).

dave-gustafson.sentence: Hanson characterized the latter discussion as unnecessary dictum and unrealistic about effects on municipalities, travelers, and adjoining owners.
dave-gustafson.plain: Justice Hanson called that earlier discussion unnecessary "dictum," remarks not needed to decide the case and so not binding. He also found it unrealistic about how delays affect cities, travelers, and neighboring owners.

dave-gustafson.sentence: The court expressly overruled that portion, leaving the no-contractor-fault determination intact and not discarding all decisions invalidating penalties for readily measurable losses.
dave-gustafson.plain: The court expressly overruled (officially rejected) that part of the earlier case, keeping its finding that the contractor was not at fault. It did not discard decisions striking down penalties for losses that are easily measured.

dave-gustafson.sentence: The result rested on the statutes and test the court applied in 1968, distinguishing an unknown actual amount from proof that an agreed provision operated as a penalty.
dave-gustafson.plain: The decision applied the statutes and test in force in 1968. Under them, the State's not knowing its exact losses did not show the agreed daily charge was a penalty; uncertain losses are exactly why such clauses exist.

hamer.sentence: The later arrangement concerned what the uncle would do with money now belonging beneficially to the nephew, a distinction that becomes decisive when limitations is raised.
hamer.plain: Once the nephew performed, the money was in substance his. The later deal was about the uncle holding it for him, which matters because it can turn a stale debt claim into a timely trust claim.

hamer.sentence: Hamer obtained judgment at Special Term, the trial level of the New York Supreme Court.
hamer.plain: Hamer obtained judgment (won) at Special Term, the trial level of the New York Supreme Court; in New York, the "Supreme Court" is the trial court.

hamer.sentence: The court’s authorities describe consideration as either a benefit to the promisor or a requested forbearance, detriment, or undertaking by the promisee.
hamer.plain: The court's authorities describe "consideration" as either a benefit to the promisor (the one promising), or a forbearance (giving up a right), detriment, or undertaking (commitment) by the promisee, done at the promisor's request.

hamer.sentence: The executor’s authorities concerned different defects: unwritten surety promises within the Statute of Frauds; moral obligation invoked to support a later promise; an executory deed covenant based on love and affection; and performance of a pre-existing obligation.
hamer.plain: The executor’s authorities failed for other reasons: oral "surety" promises (to pay another's debt) needing a writing under the Statute of Frauds, moral duty used to support a later promise, an "executory" (unperformed) deed promise based on love, and performance of a duty already owed.

hamer.sentence: The court recognizes that the original oral agreement was not to be performed within one year and thus fell within the Statute of Frauds.
hamer.plain: The court recognizes that the original oral agreement could not be performed within one year, so the law required it to be in writing under the Statute of Frauds.

hamer.sentence: It also supplies an independent pleading reason: the bar did not appear on the face of the complaint, so the executor had to plead it in the answer to rely on it, and did not.
hamer.plain: It also gives a separate pleading reason. The bar did not appear "on the face of" the complaint (from the complaint itself), so the executor had to plead (raise) it in the answer, its written response, to rely on it, and did not.

hamer.sentence: The court says an action founded on the original contract would be time-barred under the pleaded Statute of Limitations.
hamer.plain: The court says a suit founded on the original contract alone would be "time-barred" (filed too late) under the pleaded (formally raised) Statute of Limitations.

hamer.sentence: It therefore asks whether the uncle and nephew remained merely debtor and creditor or became trustee and beneficiary.
hamer.plain: So the court asks whether the uncle and nephew stayed merely "debtor and creditor" (the uncle simply owed the nephew money) or became "trustee" and beneficiary (the uncle held identifiable money for the nephew in trust). A trust would avoid the deadline problem.

hamer.sentence: But the reversal order did not state that it rested on the facts.
hamer.plain: Because the intermediate court did not say it reversed on factual grounds, the top court had to treat the trial court's factual findings as settled.

hamer.sentence: On April 14, 1891, Judge Parker’s unanimous court reverses General Term’s order and affirms the Special Term judgment, with costs payable from the estate.
hamer.plain: On April 14, 1891, Judge Parker’s "unanimous" court (no judge disagreed), New York's highest court, reverses the order of the "General Term," the intermediate appeals court. It "affirms" (upholds) Hamer's trial "judgment" from the Special Term, the trial-level court, and orders court costs paid from the uncle's estate.

klocek.sentence: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil required an initial evidentiary showing comparable to the movant’s summary-judgment burden: Gateway first had to support existence of an enforceable arbitration agreement.
klocek.plain: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil required Gateway, as the "movant" (the side asking for arbitration), to first offer evidence, much as a party seeking summary judgment must first support its motion. Gateway first had to show that an "enforceable" (legally binding) arbitration agreement existed.

klocek.sentence: The Federal Arbitration Act enforces agreements; policy favoring arbitration and rules resolving doubts about a clause’s scope could not create assent to the clause itself.
klocek.plain: The Federal Arbitration Act enforces arbitration agreements people actually made. Its pro-arbitration policy, and the rules that resolve doubts about how far a clause reaches, could not create "assent" (actual agreement) to the clause itself.

klocek.sentence: In this diversity case, Kansas choice-of-law principles looked to the place of the last act necessary to contract formation.
klocek.plain: This was a "diversity case": it was in federal court because the parties were from different states. So the court used Kansas rules for choosing which state's law applies, and those look to where the last act needed for "contract formation" (the contract coming into being) happened.

klocek.sentence: A South Dakota choice-of-law clause in the disputed insert could not prove enforceability of the very document containing it.
klocek.plain: The disputed insert in Gateway's box had a "choice-of-law clause" saying South Dakota law applied. But that clause could not prove the "enforceability" (binding force) of the very document it was printed in; that would be circular.

klocek.sentence: Ordinarily the purchaser makes an offer and the vendor accepts by completing the sale, promising shipment, or shipping.
klocek.plain: Ordinarily the buyer makes the offer by ordering, and the "vendor" (seller) accepts by completing the sale, promising to ship, or shipping. So the contract is formed before the box arrives.

klocek.sentence: On the assumed Kansas and Missouri analysis, Gateway’s insert operated as an acceptance or written confirmation proposing additional terms under Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) § 2-207.
klocek.plain: On the court's assumed Kansas and Missouri analysis, Gateway’s insert was not the deal itself. Under Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) § 2-207, it was an "acceptance" or written confirmation that proposed "additional terms," meaning new terms sent after the contract was already made.

klocek.sentence: Under § 2-207(1)’s conditional-acceptance proviso, Gateway needed clearly to communicate unwillingness to proceed without assent to its added terms.
klocek.plain: Under § 2-207(1)'s conditional-acceptance "proviso" (an exception built into the rule), Gateway could make its terms a condition of the sale only by clearly telling Klocek it would not go ahead without his "assent" (agreement) to them.

klocek.sentence: Because Klocek was not a merchant, § 2-207(2)’s rules for automatic inclusion between merchants did not apply.
klocek.plain: Klocek was not a "merchant" (a business dealing in such goods), so § 2-207(2) did not apply. That rule lets some added terms become part of a contract automatically between merchants; here the terms needed Klocek's express agreement.

klocek.sentence: Treating the insert as a proposed § 2-209 modification likewise failed under the authorities applied because express assent was still absent.
klocek.plain: Treating the box terms as a proposed "modification" (change) to the existing contract under § 2-209 also failed under the cases the court applied. "Express assent," Klocek's clear agreement to the change, was still missing.

klocek.sentence: General allegations of larger claims against Gateway did not establish the amount against Hewlett-Packard, and procedural joinder rules supplied no independent subject-matter jurisdiction.
klocek.plain: General "allegations" (claims not yet proved) of larger claims against Gateway did not show the claim against Hewlett-Packard met the federal minimum amount. And "joinder" rules, which let a plaintiff sue both together, did not by themselves give the court "subject-matter jurisdiction," its power to hear the HP claim.

klocek.sentence: His requested writ of certiorari sought access to a state-court record through a device that did not turn the federal district court into that court’s appellate reviewer.
klocek.plain: Klocek asked for a "writ of certiorari," an order calling up another court's records, to get a state court's record. But that "device" (legal tool) could not turn the "federal district court," a trial court, into an "appellate" reviewer of the state court's work.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: The four papers refused to bargain, asserting independent-contractor status.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: The four newspapers "refused to bargain," meaning they would not negotiate with the newsboys' union. They claimed the newsboys had independent-contractor status, as independent business people rather than employees, so the labor law did not cover them.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: Subsequent unfair-labor-practice proceedings produced cease-and-desist and bargaining orders.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: Later "unfair-labor-practice" proceedings, in which the Board found the refusal to bargain illegal, produced "cease-and-desist" orders (orders to stop the illegal conduct) and orders to bargain with the union.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: The Ninth Circuit, with one judge dissenting, independently applied what it considered common-law employment standards and set aside the orders.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: The Ninth Circuit, the federal appeals court, made its own judgment, with one judge "dissenting" (disagreeing). It applied what it saw as "common-law" employment standards, the traditional court-made tests for who is an employee, and "set aside" (canceled) the Board's orders.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: Using local rules would give otherwise similar workers different coverage under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), a national response to national labor problems.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: If "local rules" (each state's own definition of 'employee') controlled, otherwise similar workers would be covered in one state and not another under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA). That makes no sense for a national law answering national labor problems.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: It identified an intermediate zone between clear employment and clear entrepreneurship.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: Some workers are clearly employees and some clearly run their own businesses; for the in-between cases, the statute's goals should guide the answer.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: Applying a broad term initially to a specific economic relationship, however, fell within the Board’s experienced administration of industries, workers, and bargaining disputes.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: Courts decide what the statute means. But applying a broad word like 'employee' in the first instance to a specific economic relationship fell within the Board's experience running the law across industries, workers, and "bargaining" disputes (fights over negotiating with unions).

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: The Court did not defer merely because the agency said “employee”; it assessed the factual findings against its own understanding of the statutory purposes before sustaining the application.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: The Court did not defer to the "agency" (the Board) merely because it used the word "employee." It checked the Board's "factual findings" against its own view of the "statutory" purposes, meaning the goals of the law, before "sustaining" (upholding) the Board's application of the term.

lrs-i-hearst.sentence: Statutory references to employees of different employers protected cross-employer union organization, not agency conversion of nonemployees into employees.
lrs-i-hearst.plain: Justice Roberts said the "statutory" references to employees of other employers, words in the law itself, only protected union organizing across companies. They did not let the "agency," the Board, turn people who are not employees into employees.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: A Social Security Administration administrative law judge, or ALJ, had to decide what other work his limitations permitted and whether significant numbers of those jobs existed nationally.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: To deny benefits, a Social Security Administration "administrative law judge," or ALJ (the agency's hearing judge), had to decide what other work Biestek's limitations still allowed. The ALJ also had to decide whether significant numbers of those jobs existed in the national economy.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: The District Court rejected Biestek’s argument that requested-but-withheld data necessarily deprived the expert testimony of substantial evidentiary value.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: The District Court, the federal trial court, rejected Biestek’s argument about the "expert testimony" at his hearing. He argued that because the expert withheld data he asked for, her job numbers necessarily lost their "evidentiary" value, their worth as substantial evidence.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: Biestek distinguished substantive sufficiency from a freestanding right to discovery.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: Biestek separated two ideas: "substantive" sufficiency, meaning whether the evidence was actually enough, and a freestanding right to "discovery," the process of demanding documents from the other side. He claimed only the first.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: Under 42 U.S.C. § 405(g), supported agency fact findings are conclusive.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: Under 42 U.S.C. § 405(g), a section of the Social Security Act in the United States Code, the agency's factual findings are "conclusive" (courts must accept them) as long as substantial evidence supports them.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: Substantial evidence exceeds a scintilla and is evidence a reasonable mind could accept as adequate.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: "Substantial evidence" is more than a "scintilla" (a tiny trace). It is evidence a reasonable mind could accept as adequate to support the conclusion.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: The threshold was not high, but admissibility did not establish sufficiency.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: The standard was not hard to meet. But "admissibility," evidence being allowed into the hearing, did not by itself establish sufficiency, meaning that the evidence was enough to support the decision.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: Conversely, an unexplained refusal of readily available material could support an adverse inference, especially without other grounds for confidence.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: On the other hand, an expert's unexplained refusal to share material she could easily provide could support an adverse "inference," a conclusion that the material would not back her up. That is especially so when nothing else gives reason to trust her testimony.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: It read the petition as seeking only the categorical rule and deliberately did not apply the standard afresh to this record.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: The Court read Biestek's petition as asking only for a "categorical rule," a blanket rule that withheld data always makes such testimony insufficient. It deliberately did not apply the standard afresh to the evidence in his particular case.

lrs-n-biestek.sentence: The agency bore the pertinent burden to identify other work, and the ALJ had to develop the nonadversarial record.
lrs-n-biestek.plain: In Justice Sotomayor's dissenting view, the agency bore the relevant "burden" (the duty to prove) of identifying other work Biestek could do. Because these hearings are "nonadversarial," with no one arguing against the claimant, the ALJ had to develop the record himself.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: FDA used that number to describe allowable contamination and guide enforcement, but had not adopted it through the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice-and-comment procedures.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: FDA used the 20-parts-per-billion figure to describe allowable contamination and guide enforcement. But it had not adopted that figure through the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice-and-comment process, publishing a proposed rule for public comment, which binding rules require.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: That ruling made the procedural challenge moot in the circuit’s view and prompted reconsideration of blending.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: That "ruling" (the appeals court's first holding that FDA had to set formal limits anyway) made the procedural challenge "moot" in the court's view, leaving nothing live to decide. It also led to "reconsideration" of blending contaminated corn with clean corn.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: FDA acknowledged that its action levels were rules under the Administrative Procedure Act, but invoked the exception for interpretative rules and general policy statements.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: FDA admitted its action levels were "rules" under the Administrative Procedure Act. But it invoked the exception for "interpretative rules" and general policy statements, which only explain the agency's views or plans and do not need public comment.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: Judges Mikva and Edwards applied the circuit’s American Bus precedent, which examined whether a pronouncement created a presently binding norm and genuinely left agency decisionmakers free to exercise discretion.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: Judges Mikva and Edwards applied the circuit’s American Bus "precedent," an earlier decision of that appeals court. It asked whether a pronouncement created a binding norm now, or truly left "agency" officials free to use their "discretion" (judgment) in each case.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: The regulations’ word “may” left the agency free to establish a level; it did not make an established level optional.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: The regulations said the "agency" (FDA) "may" set an action level. That word let FDA choose whether to set one; it did not make a level, once set, merely optional.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: Taken together, the agency’s words and conduct sufficiently constrained its own enforcement discretion to give the level substantive effect.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: Taken together, the agency’s words and conduct limited its own "enforcement discretion" (its freedom to decide case by case whom to pursue) enough to give the level "substantive" effect, the force of a real legal rule.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: Under that test, a legislative rule allows the agency to enforce a standard by showing its application and violation; policy requires independent justification of the standard under the governing statute and facts.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: Under the test Judge Starr preferred, a "legislative rule" (a binding rule) lets the agency enforce by showing only that the rule applies and was violated. A policy statement requires the agency to justify the standard anew under the statute and the facts. Since FDA still had to prove adulteration, he saw the limit as a policy statement.

lrs-n-community-nutrition.sentence: The Supreme Court’s Heckler v. Chaney decision and related circuit precedent treated certain decisions not to enforce as committed to agency discretion.
lrs-n-community-nutrition.plain: The Supreme Court’s Heckler v. Chaney decision and related circuit precedent treated certain decisions not to enforce as "committed to agency discretion." That means the law leaves those choices to the agency, so courts generally cannot second-guess them.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: The Fifth Circuit sustained a preliminary injunction on notice-and-comment and substantive immigration-law grounds, treating benefits eligibility as more than unreviewable nonenforcement.
lrs-n-regents.plain: The Fifth Circuit, a federal appeals court, upheld a "preliminary injunction," an order blocking the 2014 programs while the case went on. It found they needed public comment and conflicted with immigration law ("substantive" grounds). Because they made people eligible for benefits, they were more than "unreviewable" nonenforcement, a choice not to enforce that courts cannot review.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: In 2016, an equally divided Supreme Court affirmed without a controlling explanatory opinion.
lrs-n-regents.plain: In 2016 the Supreme Court was "equally divided" (split 4 to 4), so it "affirmed" the lower court's ruling. It issued no controlling "opinion" explaining why, so the ruling set no national precedent.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: The government requested certiorari before judgment in all three cases.
lrs-n-regents.plain: The government requested "certiorari before judgment," asking the Supreme Court to take all three cases right away, before the appeals courts had finished deciding them.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: The Court left broader questions about general nonenforcement policies open but held that DACA was more than passive nonenforcement.
lrs-n-regents.plain: The Court left open whether courts can review every general "nonenforcement" policy, meaning a policy of not enforcing the law. But it held DACA was more than passive nonenforcement: an active program with applications and approvals, so ending it could be reviewed.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: Section 1252(b)(9) concerned claims arising from action or proceedings to remove a person; these plaintiffs were not contesting removal proceedings.
lrs-n-regents.plain: Section 1252(b)(9) of the immigration law limits court review of "claims" (legal challenges) arising from action or proceedings to remove, meaning deport, a person. These plaintiffs were challenging the end of a program, not contesting any removal proceedings, so that limit did not apply.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: It could not retain an original decision while adding rationales as though they had always supported it.
lrs-n-regents.plain: An agency that gave weak reasons can either explain those same reasons better or make a new decision. It cannot keep the old decision and attach new reasons after the fact.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: The majority rejected a distinction between later explanations by lawyers and agency officials: timing, not the speaker, caused the problem.
lrs-n-regents.plain: The "majority" (the Justices whose view controlled) rejected a distinction between after-the-fact explanations from government lawyers and from agency officials. The problem was timing, not the speaker: the reasons still came after the decision.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: Deferring removal was distinct from lawful-presence designations for specified benefits, and relevant regulations allowed separation.
lrs-n-regents.plain: Deferring removal, meaning choosing not to deport someone, was distinct from designating them lawfully present for specified benefits. The relevant "regulations" (agency rules) allowed the two to be separated, so the agency could have ended the benefits while keeping the deportation protection.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: Disclaimers of substantive rights and two-year terms could reduce reliance’s weight but did not erase it.
lrs-n-regents.plain: DACA's "disclaimers" that it created no substantive rights, and its two-year terms, could make recipients' reliance count for less. But they did not erase that reliance, so the agency still had to consider how people had built their lives around the program.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: Roberts’s Part IV, joined only by Ginsburg, Breyer, and Kagan, found the pleaded animus theory implausible while assuming rather than deciding whether Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee barred it.
lrs-n-regents.plain: Roberts’s Part IV, "joined" (signed onto) only by Ginsburg, Breyer, and Kagan, found the "pleaded" animus theory, the complaints' claim of hostility toward Latinos, implausible. They assumed, rather than decided, whether Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, an earlier precedent limiting such claims, barred it.

lrs-n-regents.sentence: He also considered it an improperly promulgated legislative rule.
lrs-n-regents.plain: Thomas also considered DACA an improperly "promulgated" (formally issued) legislative rule: in effect a binding rule that should have gone through public notice and comment, and had not.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: Under procedures implementing Office of Management and Budget Circular A-76, it compared public costs with private bids.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: Under procedures carrying out Office of Management and Budget Circular A-76, a federal outsourcing policy, the Navy compared what it would cost government workers to keep running the ships with what private companies bid.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: It found plaintiffs outside the wage statute’s zone because they did not represent the successful contractor’s workers and regarded A-76 as internal management without private protected interests.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: The trial court found the "plaintiffs" (the unions suing) outside the zone the wage "statute" protects, because they did not represent the winning contractor's workers. It also regarded A-76 as internal government management that gives outsiders no protected interest they can sue over.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: Applying Hunt, the panel required member standing, germaneness, and no need for individual participation.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: Applying Hunt, the panel required three things for a union to have "standing" (the right to sue) for its members: some members could sue themselves, the case is "germane" (related) to the union's purpose, and individual members need not take part.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: Mere dissent did not establish improper representation.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: Mere "dissent," some members disagreeing with the lawsuit, did not by itself show the union was improperly representing them.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: Lost employment was real injury, but the causal and remedial chain from absent schedules was speculative.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: Losing jobs was a real injury. But the "causal" chain, the claim that the missing wage schedules caused the loss and that fixing them would change who won the contract, was only speculation.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: The panel rejected this claim for Article III traceability and redressability, expressly leaving the statutory zone issue undecided.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: The panel rejected this claim under Article III of the Constitution, which requires "traceability" (the harm came from the challenged act) and redressability (winning would fix it). It expressly left undecided whether the "statutory" zone, the group the wage law protects, included the unions.

lrs-n-standing-maritime.sentence: The court assumed remaining zone, cause-of-action, and justiciability issues because the claims failed even under the less demanding proposed review standard on undisputed facts.
lrs-n-standing-maritime.plain: On the remaining claims, the court assumed the threshold questions (the statute's zone, whether a "cause-of-action" existed, meaning a legal right to sue, and justiciability) were met. The claims failed on undisputed facts even under the easier review standard the unions proposed.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: The Supreme Court later had to assume the alleged retaliatory motive for the posture before it; it did not independently find that motive proved.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: Because of the case's "posture," dismissed before trial, the Supreme Court had to assume the "alleged" (claimed but unproved) retaliatory motive: that Thompson was fired to punish his fiancée. It did not independently find that motive proved.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: The full appellate court then affirmed the district court, 10–6.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: The full "appellate court," all the judges of the appeals court, then "affirmed" the "district court" (the federal trial court), siding with the company, 10–6.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: The en banc majority reasoned that Thompson had not himself engaged in protected activity, either for himself or for Regalado, and therefore was outside the class Congress authorized to sue for retaliation.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: The "en banc" majority (the full appeals court sitting together) reasoned that Thompson had not himself engaged in "protected activity," such as complaining, for himself or for Regalado. So he was outside the group Congress authorized to sue for retaliation.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: The question was whether the employer’s conduct could dissuade a reasonable worker from making or supporting a discrimination charge.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: The question was whether the employer's conduct could dissuade a reasonable worker from making or supporting a "discrimination charge," a formal complaint of job discrimination.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: Title VII nevertheless authorized suit by a person aggrieved, requiring a separate question about Congress’s intended cause of action.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: Even with enough harm to satisfy the Constitution, Title VII only lets "a person aggrieved" sue. That raised a separate question about Congress’s intended "cause of action": whether Congress meant to give someone like Thompson the right to sue.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: The Court looked to the Administrative Procedure Act’s use of aggrieved and adopted the zone-of-interests approach: interests arguably protected by the statute sufficed, while interests marginally related to or inconsistent with its purposes fell outside.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: The Court looked to the Administrative Procedure Act’s use of "aggrieved" and adopted the "zone-of-interests" test: a person may sue if the statute arguably protects their interest, but not if that interest is only marginally related to, or inconsistent with, the statute's purposes.

lrs-n-standing-thompson.sentence: He did not qualify merely because third-party harm was foreseeable; his injury played an intentional role in the retaliation itself.
lrs-n-standing-thompson.plain: Thompson did not qualify merely because "third-party" harm, harm to someone other than the target, was "foreseeable" (predictable). He qualified because hurting him was the intended means of the "retaliation" itself, the way the company allegedly chose to punish his fiancée.

lrs-s-field.sentence: Beginning January 1, 1892, its reciprocity provision directed the President to suspend that treatment for a producing country whose exactions on American products he found reciprocally unequal and unreasonable.
lrs-s-field.plain: Beginning January 1, 1892, the "reciprocity" provision (requiring fair treatment in return) directed the President to suspend duty-free treatment for a producing country if he found its "exactions," its taxes and charges on American products, reciprocally unequal and unreasonable.

lrs-s-field.sentence: The importers also alleged that a tobacco-rebate provision passed both Houses but disappeared from the enrolled Act.
lrs-s-field.plain: The importers also "alleged" (claimed) that a tobacco-rebate section passed both Houses of Congress but was missing from the "enrolled Act," the final official copy of the law, so the law was never properly enacted.

lrs-s-field.sentence: Attestation by both Houses’ presiding officers, presidential approval, and public deposit established the enacted text against this proposed contradiction through journals and related papers.
lrs-s-field.plain: "Attestation," the signatures of both Houses’ "presiding officers" (their leaders), plus the President's approval and filing with the Secretary of State, established the "enacted" text. Congressional journals and related papers could not be used to contradict it.

lrs-s-field.sentence: Working journals could contain errors and omissions; allowing collateral impeachment endangered settled laws.
lrs-s-field.plain: Congress's working journals could contain errors and omissions. Allowing "collateral impeachment," attacking a law's validity indirectly through such records, would endanger settled laws.

lrs-s-field.sentence: Harlan relied on Aurora, which sustained statutory operation contingent on a presidential proclamation of later circumstances.
lrs-s-field.plain: Harlan relied on Aurora, an 1813 case that upheld a "statutory" provision, part of a law, that took effect only when the President proclaimed that certain later circumstances had occurred.

lrs-s-field.sentence: Harlan located the decision that suspension should occur in Congress, while the President determined when its conditions existed.
lrs-s-field.plain: Congress itself made the policy choice to suspend duty-free status for unfair trading partners; the President only determined when that condition was met, so no lawmaking power was handed over.

lrs-s-field.sentence: Breadth of affected American products and duration discretion made the assignment legislative rather than mere identification of an ascertainable event.
lrs-s-field.plain: Lamar's dissent said the breadth of American products affected, and the President's "discretion" (freedom of judgment) over how long suspensions lasted, made the task lawmaking, not merely identifying an event anyone could ascertain.

lrs-s-field.sentence: The question was whether Congress evidently would not enact valid provisions without the challenged ones.
lrs-s-field.plain: To decide whether the rest of the law survives, the Court asked whether Congress clearly would not "enact" (pass) the valid parts, such as the import duties, without the challenged sugar payments. It found no such dependence, so the duties stood.

lrs-s-schechter.sentence: Section 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act allowed the President to approve fair-competition codes proposed by representative trade or industry groups.
lrs-s-schechter.plain: Section 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act let the President approve "fair-competition codes," rules for an industry proposed by groups representing that trade or industry. Once approved, the codes became binding law.

lrs-s-schechter.sentence: A violation in a transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was a misdemeanor carrying a fine up to $500, with each additional day potentially a separate offense.
