cp-boyle.plain: That the defense could be raised in a "diversity suit" (a case in federal court because the parties are from different states) did not mean every suit against a contractor automatically belonged in federal court.

cp-boyle.sentence: If the evidence under the proper rule could not support a reasonable verdict for the estate, judgment for Sikorsky could be entered.
cp-boyle.plain: If the evidence, under the proper rule, could not support a reasonable "verdict" for Boyle's estate, then "judgment" for Sikorsky could be "entered" (formally issued) without a new trial.

cp-boyle.sentence: The Fourth Circuit’s statement that Sikorsky satisfied the defense might have meant the evidence was conclusive under a proper sufficiency test, or might have reflected its own resolution of factual disputes.
cp-boyle.plain: The Fourth Circuit’s statement that Sikorsky met the "defense" was unclear. It might have meant the evidence was conclusive under a proper "sufficiency" test (no jury could disagree), which is allowed, or that it had decided factual disputes itself, which is not.

cp-boyle.sentence: Erie left only narrow areas of federal common law, and a private victim’s tort claim against a private manufacturer was collateral to a federal contract.
cp-boyle.plain: Brennan said that after Erie, "federal common law," judge-made federal law, covers only narrow areas. A private victim's "tort" (injury) claim against a private manufacturer "was collateral to," only loosely connected to, a federal contract.

cp-boyle.sentence: Creating a new liability restriction balancing a major public program against individual compensation went beyond ordinary interstitial adjudication.
cp-boyle.plain: Stevens said creating a new limit on liability, balancing a major public program against individual compensation, went beyond ordinary "interstitial" decision-making, the small gap-filling courts usually do. That choice was for Congress.

cp-mullane.sentence: A decree settling an account conclusively bound everyone interested in the fund or its participating trusts on the matters disclosed.
cp-mullane.plain: A "decree" (court order) approving the bank's account of the fund conclusively bound everyone with an interest in the fund or its participating "trusts" on the matters disclosed, so no one could later sue over them.

cp-mullane.sentence: When each trust joined the fund, Central Hanover mailed a statutory notice to known beneficiaries of full age and sound mind entitled to income or, if the relevant event had occurred, principal.
cp-mullane.plain: When each trust joined the fund, Central Hanover mailed a notice required by statute to known adult, mentally competent beneficiaries entitled to the trust's income, or to the principal (the trust property itself) if that right had already arisen.

cp-mullane.sentence: Such a guardian protects people absent or unable to act for themselves, but neither the bank nor the appointed guardian was required or apparently expected to warn the beneficiaries individually.
cp-mullane.plain: A special "guardian" protects people who are absent or unable to act for themselves. But neither the bank nor the appointed guardian, Mullane, was required or apparently expected to warn the beneficiaries individually.

cp-mullane.sentence: Mullane appeared specially, limiting his appearance to a challenge to the court’s authority rather than submitting to it.
cp-mullane.plain: Mullane "appeared specially," limiting his "appearance" in court to challenging the court's power over the absent beneficiaries, without submitting to that power.

cp-mullane.sentence: Mullane appealed to the Supreme Court through the route then available when a state’s highest court sustained a state statute against federal constitutional attack.
cp-mullane.plain: Mullane appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court through the route then available as of right when a state's highest court "sustained" (upheld) a state "statute" against a federal constitutional challenge.

cp-mullane.sentence: Mullane first drew on Pennoyer v. Neff, the earlier personal-jurisdiction decision: because the accounting resolved beneficiaries’ personal rights to surcharge the trustee rather than title or possession of particular property, he characterized it as an in-personam action that could not bind nonresidents lacking personal service within New York.
cp-mullane.plain: Mullane relied on Pennoyer v. Neff, the earlier "personal-jurisdiction" case. The "accounting" decided beneficiaries' personal rights to "surcharge the trustee" (make it pay for mismanagement), not "title" (ownership) of property, so it was "in-personam" and could not bind "nonresidents" not personally served in New York.

cp-mullane.sentence: Fourteenth Amendment requirements could not depend on labels so elusive and variable among states.
cp-mullane.plain: Fourteenth Amendment due-process requirements could not depend on labels like "personal" or "property-based" that are so slippery and differ from state to state.

cp-mullane.sentence: New York’s interest in closing trusts created under its laws and supervised by its courts justified determining all beneficiaries’ interests, wherever they lived, if they received a full opportunity to appear and be heard.
cp-mullane.plain: New York had a strong enough interest in wrapping up its own trusts to decide every beneficiary's rights, even those living elsewhere, but only if they were given a real chance to take part.

cp-mullane.sentence: A hearing opportunity means little when a person cannot learn that a matter is pending and decide whether to contest it.
cp-mullane.plain: A "hearing," the chance to be heard, means little if a person cannot learn that the case is pending and decide whether to contest it.

cp-mullane.sentence: The chosen means must resemble what a person actually trying to inform the absentee would reasonably use.
cp-mullane.plain: The notice method chosen must be what someone genuinely trying to inform the "absentee," the person not present, would reasonably use.

cp-mullane.sentence: That standard has two branches: notice reasonably certain to inform, or, when circumstances do not reasonably permit that, a substitute not substantially less likely to succeed than feasible and customary alternatives.
cp-mullane.plain: That standard has two branches. Notice must be reasonably certain to inform, or, if circumstances do not reasonably allow that, a substitute about as likely to work as other "feasible" (practical) and customary methods.

cp-mullane.sentence: Publication sometimes supplements seizure of a ship or chattel or legal entry onto land, events likely to alert an owner or caretaker.
cp-mullane.plain: Newspaper notice sometimes works alongside seizure of a ship or "chattel" (movable personal property) or legal entry onto land. Those events tend to alert an owner or caretaker; nothing like that happened here.

cp-mullane.sentence: Here, beneficiaries had not abandoned their interests, and the trustee ordinarily protecting them had become their adversary in seeking release from liability.
cp-mullane.plain: Here the beneficiaries had not abandoned their interests. And the "trustee," the bank that normally protected them, had become their "adversary" (opponent) by seeking "release" from liability to them.

cp-mullane.sentence: The Court likewise allowed publication for conjectural or future interests and for persons discoverable only through investigation whose interests had not become known in the ordinary course of administration.
cp-mullane.plain: The Court likewise allowed newspaper notice for "conjectural" or "future interests" (rights that may or will arise later), and for people "discoverable" only through special investigation whose interests had not come to light in the "ordinary course" of running the fund.

cp-mullane.sentence: Drawing on McDonald v. Mabee, the Court resisted letting legal fiction displace the facts needed for fair play.
cp-mullane.plain: Drawing on McDonald v. Mabee, the Court refused to let a "legal fiction," a pretense the law treats as true (here, that newspaper notice informs people), displace the facts needed for fair play.

cp-mullane.sentence: That explanation depends on the shared interests characteristic of this representative proceeding; it is not a general license to overlook individual notice in ordinary two-party suits.
cp-mullane.plain: That reasoning depends on the shared interests that mark this representative proceeding. It is not a general license to skip "individual notice" in ordinary two-party lawsuits.

cp-mullane.sentence: Personal service outside New York could also inform perfectly well even if it supplied no coercive jurisdiction, further illustrating why notice and adjudicatory power are distinct.
cp-mullane.plain: Handing papers to someone outside New York could inform them perfectly well even if it gave the court no "coercive" jurisdiction, power to compel them. That shows why notice and "adjudicatory power" (power to decide the case) are separate.

cp-mullane.sentence: Failure to reach every individual was not itself the constitutional flaw; choosing a poorly calculated method when a feasible superior one existed was.
cp-mullane.plain: Failing to reach every individual was not itself the constitutional flaw. The flaw was choosing a poorly designed method when a "feasible" (practical) better one, mail, existed.

cp-mullane.sentence: Mullane’s distinction between power and notice means that a court with jurisdiction can still violate due process through defective notice.
cp-mullane.plain: Mullane separates power from notice. So a court with "jurisdiction" (power over the case) can still violate due process if its notice is defective.

cp-mullane.sentence: Fiduciary accountings had received several labels, this proceeding combined features of both categories, and intangible property had blurred distinctions inherited from a different property system.
cp-mullane.plain: "Fiduciary" accountings (reports by trustees managing others' money) had been labeled different ways, this one mixed features of both categories, and "intangible property," like fund shares with no physical location, had blurred the old property categories.

cp-strawbridge.sentence: Strawbridge and other complainants brought a bill in chancery against Curtiss and additional defendants in the federal Circuit Court for Massachusetts.
cp-strawbridge.plain: Strawbridge and other "complainants" (plaintiffs) brought a "bill in chancery," an equity suit seeking court orders, against Curtiss and other "defendants" in the "federal Circuit Court" for Massachusetts, the old federal trial court.

cp-strawbridge.sentence: Marshall read it through the persons representing each distinct interest: when an interest was joint, every person concerned had to be competent to sue or liable to be sued in federal court.
cp-strawbridge.plain: Marshall read the statute by looking at who represented each distinct interest. When an interest was shared, every person involved had to be qualified to "sue" or be sued in federal court.

cp-strawbridge.sentence: Its reasoning construed Congress’s jurisdictional grant, without declaring that Article III itself barred every case lacking complete diversity.
cp-strawbridge.plain: The Court "construed" (interpreted) Congress's "jurisdictional" statute, the grant of power to federal courts. It did not declare that Article III of the Constitution itself barred every case lacking complete diversity.

cp-strawbridge.sentence: The case became associated with the complete-diversity rule, under which no plaintiff shares state citizenship with a defendant under the later general diversity statute.
cp-strawbridge.plain: The case became tied to the "complete-diversity" rule under the later general diversity statute: no plaintiff may share state "citizenship" with any defendant.

cp-strawbridge.sentence: The Court expressly reserved the different arrangement in which parties represented several distinct interests and only some qualified.
cp-strawbridge.plain: The Court expressly "reserved" (left open) a different situation, where parties on one side represented separate, distinct interests and only some of them qualified.

cp-taxicab.sentence: To obtain a federal forum applying a different general-common-law rule, Brown & Yellow’s shareholders organized a Tennessee corporation of the same name in September 1925, transferred the Kentucky company’s business and property, and dissolved it.
cp-taxicab.plain: To get a federal "forum" (court) applying a different "general-common-law" rule than Kentucky's, Brown & Yellow’s "shareholders" formed a Tennessee "corporation" of the same name in September 1925. They moved the Kentucky company's business and property to it and "dissolved" (ended) the old company.

cp-taxicab.sentence: The railroad cooperated in this deliberate creation of diversity.
cp-taxicab.plain: The railroad, supposedly the other side, cooperated in this deliberate creation of "diversity," the different-state citizenship that put the case in federal court.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Justice Butler applied Judicial Code § 37, requiring dismissal for absence of a real substantial federal controversy or improper or collusive party creation or joinder.
cp-taxicab.plain: Justice Butler applied Judicial Code § 37. It required dismissal if there was no real, substantial dispute within federal jurisdiction, or if parties were improperly or collusively created, or added by "joinder," to get into federal court.

cp-taxicab.sentence: The forum-seeking motive did not invalidate otherwise unimpeached incorporation and ownership.
cp-taxicab.plain: The motive of seeking a federal court did not invalidate a company whose formation and ownership were otherwise "unimpeached," genuine and unchallenged.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Butler answered that it construed no particular charter term and instead stated general law.
cp-taxicab.plain: Butler answered that the Kentucky decision "construed" (interpreted) no particular "charter term" of the railroad, which federal courts would follow. It stated "general law," which federal judges could decide for themselves under Swift.

cp-taxicab.sentence: The railroad owed no onward carriage from the station, and independent transfer companies had no inherent right to its premises for parking or solicitation.
cp-taxicab.plain: The railroad's duty as a carrier ended at the station, so letting one taxi company use its property was not favoritism in its carrier business.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Because those rulings rested on common-law policy rather than a governing statute or constitutional provision, the majority treated validity as general law.
cp-taxicab.plain: Kentucky's "rulings" rested on "common-law" policy (judge-made law), not a governing statute or the state constitution. So the "majority" treated the contract's validity as "general law," which under Swift federal courts could decide for themselves.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Finding no land-title issue, governing local statute or constitution, or ancient fixed usage, it invoked Swift and subsequent cases allowing federal judges to consult the same sources and independently decide general-law questions.
cp-taxicab.plain: "Finding" no land-title issue, no governing local statute or constitution, and no long-fixed local "usage" (custom), the Court invoked Swift and later cases. Those let federal judges consult the same sources and decide "general-law" questions independently.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Rules enforced within a State derived authority from that State, whose highest court spoke authoritatively just as its legislature did.
cp-taxicab.plain: Holmes argued that law in a state gets its force from that state, so its highest court's decisions are state law just as much as its statutes are.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Holmes cited historical research challenging Swift’s interpretation of the Rules of Decision Act, but expressly proposed leaving Swift itself undisturbed while preventing expansion into new fields.
cp-taxicab.plain: Holmes cited historical research showing Swift misread the Rules of Decision Act, the 1789 statute telling federal courts when to follow state law. But he expressly proposed leaving Swift itself in place, only stopping its spread into new areas.

cp-taxicab.sentence: He also offered a narrower answer: use of Kentucky land by a Kentucky-chartered railroad, subject to over thirty-five years of settled state policy, was sufficiently local.
cp-taxicab.plain: Holmes also gave a narrower answer: how a Kentucky-chartered railroad (one formed under Kentucky law) used Kentucky land, under more than thirty-five years of settled state policy, was local enough that Kentucky law should control.

cp-taxicab.sentence: Those later treatments explain the case’s instructional role but are not holdings of its 1928 majority, whose framework Erie subsequently rejected.
cp-taxicab.plain: Those later discussions explain why casebooks teach this case. But they are not holdings of its 1928 "majority," whose Swift framework Erie later rejected.

cp-taxicab.sentence: The premise was independent judgment about general common law, not unanimity across jurisdictions.
cp-taxicab.plain: The premise was federal judges' "independent judgment" about the general common law, not that all "jurisdictions" (states) agreed on it.

cp-tickle.sentence: Tickle first attempted service through the West Virginia Auditor under a nonresident-motorist statute covering accidents on public streets, roads, or highways.
cp-tickle.plain: Tickle first tried "service," formal delivery of the court papers, through the West Virginia Auditor under a "nonresident-motorist statute." That law covered only accidents on public streets, roads, or highways.

cp-tickle.sentence: Barton filed a plea in abatement challenging that service because the accident had occurred on private property.
cp-tickle.plain: Barton filed a "plea in abatement," a formal objection that would halt the case, challenging that service because the accident happened on private property, outside the statute.

cp-tickle.sentence: On December 5, 1955, one of Tickle’s lawyers obtained alias process and delivered it to a deputy sheriff.
cp-tickle.plain: On December 5, 1955, one of Tickle's lawyers obtained "alias process," a fresh summons replacing the first, and gave it to a deputy sheriff to serve.

cp-tickle.sentence: Tickle demurred, asking whether the pleaded facts were legally sufficient even if true.
cp-tickle.plain: Tickle "demurred": he argued that the facts Barton "pleaded" (stated in his plea) were not legally enough to void the service, even if true.

cp-tickle.sentence: The Circuit Court overruled the demurrer.
cp-tickle.plain: The Circuit Court, West Virginia's trial court, "overruled" (rejected) the demurrer, ruling that Barton's facts, if proved, would be enough.

cp-tickle.sentence: At both sides’ request, it certified that ruling to the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals.
cp-tickle.plain: At both sides' request, the trial court certified that "ruling" to the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals, the state's highest court, to answer the legal question before going further.

cp-tickle.sentence: The reviewing court therefore considered the well-pleaded material allegations as true.
cp-tickle.plain: So the "reviewing court" treated Barton's "well-pleaded" material allegations, specific factual claims properly stated, as true without deciding whether they were.

cp-tickle.sentence: Judge Haymond’s majority adopted the generally recognized rule that a litigant may not obtain personal service on an otherwise unreachable nonresident through fraud, trickery, artifice, or a wrongful device inducing entry into the jurisdiction.
cp-tickle.plain: Judge Haymond’s "majority" adopted the common rule: a "litigant" cannot get "personal service" (papers handed over in person) on an otherwise unreachable "nonresident" by using fraud, trickery, "artifice" (a cunning scheme), or a wrongful "device" to lure them into the "jurisdiction," the state.

cp-tickle.sentence: Physical presence might ordinarily place a person within the court’s power, but courts should not exercise that power to aid a party who wrongfully manufactured the opportunity for service.
cp-tickle.plain: Being physically in the state normally puts a person within its courts' power. But courts should not use that power to help a "party" who wrongfully manufactured the chance to serve them.

cp-tickle.sentence: Tickle was legally responsible for his lawyer’s conduct.
cp-tickle.plain: A lawyer acts as the client's agent, so the lawyer's trick would count against Tickle himself.

cp-tickle.sentence: Treatise qualifications distinguished inducing entry through fraud from taking advantage of voluntary entry, even where misinformation later created an opportunity to serve.
cp-tickle.plain: "Treatise" writers (legal scholars) distinguished "inducing" entry, luring someone into the state through "fraud," from taking advantage of a voluntary visit, even if misinformation later created a chance to serve.

cp-tickle.sentence: Tickle remained free to file a proper replication denying the plea and to contest it with competent evidence.
cp-tickle.plain: Tickle could still file a proper "replication," a formal reply denying Barton's "plea," and contest it with "competent evidence" (evidence a court can properly consider).

cp-tickle.sentence: The decision did not conclusively establish fraud, finally quash service after a factual hearing, resolve the initial Auditor service, dismiss the injury action, or decide liability.
cp-tickle.plain: The decision did not conclusively find "fraud," finally void the service after a factual "hearing," resolve the first Auditor service, "dismiss" the injury "action" (lawsuit), or decide "liability."

cp-walker.sentence: Oklahoma treated service as commencement for limitations, allowing timely filing to relate back only if service followed within sixty days.
cp-walker.plain: Oklahoma treated service, not filing, as "commencement" of a suit for the deadline. A "timely" filing could "relate back," counting as the start date, only if service followed within sixty days.

cp-walker.sentence: Walker argued that filing therefore tolled the state limitation, while expressly conceding the suit would be barred in state court.
cp-walker.plain: Walker argued that under the federal rule his filing "tolled" (paused) Oklahoma's deadline. Yet he expressly admitted the suit would be "barred" (too late) in state court.

cp-walker.sentence: This was not uncertainty about whether state law would defeat his claim; it was whether federal filing displaced that law.
cp-walker.plain: Everyone agreed Oklahoma law would bar the claim; the only question was whether the federal rule overrides that law in federal court.

cp-walker.sentence: The district court found service integral to Oklahoma’s limitation scheme and applied Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co., rejecting Walker’s claim that Hanna had implicitly overruled it.
cp-walker.plain: The "district court" found service a built-in part of Oklahoma's deadline scheme. It followed Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co., rejecting Walker's claim that Hanna had implicitly "overruled" (overturned) it.

cp-walker.sentence: Hanna itself had distinguished, not overruled, Ragan.
cp-walker.plain: Hanna itself had distinguished Ragan as a different situation; it had not "overruled" it.

cp-walker.sentence: Hanna’s analysis applies only after interpreting a Federal Rule to cover the issue.
cp-walker.plain: Hanna's rule, that a valid Federal Rule wins, applies only if the Rule, properly read, actually addresses the question at hand.

cp-walker.sentence: Rule 3 here marked the starting point for federal procedural timing, without stating that filing tolled every state limitation.
cp-walker.plain: Rule 3 here only marked when a federal case starts for the court's own procedural timing. It did not say that filing "tolled" (paused) every state deadline for suing.

cp-walker.sentence: The Court required plain meaning; a genuinely governing Rule would trigger Hanna’s validity inquiry.
cp-walker.plain: The Court required "plain meaning," reading Rule 3 by its ordinary words. A Rule that truly governed the issue would then trigger Hanna's question of whether the Rule is valid.

cp-walker.sentence: Oklahoma’s service requirement served repose and preservation of evidence by telling a defendant that liability remained contested.
cp-walker.plain: Oklahoma's service requirement served "repose," letting a defendant not served in time stop worrying about an old claim. It also preserved evidence by telling a served defendant that liability was still contested.

cp-walker.sentence: It was part of the substantive limitation, not an unrelated formality.
cp-walker.plain: The service requirement was part of Oklahoma's rule about when claims expire, which is a substantive policy federal courts must follow, not mere paperwork.

cp-walker.sentence: With no governing federal conflict, Erie and Ragan required state limitations law.
cp-walker.plain: Since no federal rule actually conflicted, Erie and Ragan required the federal court to apply Oklahoma's deadline rule.

cp-walker.sentence: Even without actual forum-shopping intent, allowing this suit would give a diverse plaintiff an advantage over an otherwise identical state-court plaintiff, producing inequitable administration.
cp-walker.plain: Even without any real "forum-shopping" intent (choosing a court for advantage), allowing this "suit" would give an out-of-state plaintiff an edge over an identical state-court plaintiff. Erie calls that "inequitable administration" of the laws.

cp-walker.sentence: The Court reserved Rule 3’s tolling effect on federal claims, whether their periods came from federal law or borrowed state law.
cp-walker.plain: The Court "reserved" (left open) Rule 3's "tolling" effect on federal claims, whether their deadlines came from federal law or were borrowed from state law.

cp-walker.sentence: It also declined to decide whether a hypothetical Rule expressly controlling this tolling issue would violate the Enabling Act or Congress’s constitutional power.
cp-walker.plain: It also declined to decide whether a hypothetical Rule expressly controlling this "tolling" question would violate the Rules Enabling Act or exceed Congress’s constitutional power.

klar.sentence: The parcel room conceded ordinary negligence but asserted that the printed condition limited its responsibility to $25.
klar.plain: The parcel room admitted ordinary "negligence" (carelessness) in giving the package to the wrong person. But it argued the printed condition on the ticket limited its responsibility to $25.

klar.sentence: The Appellate Term reduced recovery to $25 because it considered the printed limitation adequately communicated and contractual.
klar.plain: The Appellate Term, the first appeals court, cut the recovery to $25. It considered the printed limit adequately communicated and "contractual," part of a binding agreement.

klar.sentence: A bailee for hire owed ordinary care and, without an effective special agreement, answered for the reasonable value of negligently lost property.
klar.plain: A "bailee for hire," a business paid to hold someone's property, owed ordinary care. Without a valid special agreement, it owed the "reasonable value" of property it carelessly lost.

klar.sentence: The parcel room bore the burden of showing reasonable notice and assent.
klar.plain: The parcel room "bore the burden" (had to prove) that the customer got "reasonable notice" of the $25 limit and agreed to it.

klar.sentence: A ticket used to identify property did not necessarily signal a change in substantive rights.
klar.plain: A ticket used to identify property did not necessarily signal a change in "substantive rights," the customer's actual legal rights.

klar.sentence: Words printed on the check followed by acceptance did not compel a finding of agreement as a matter of law.
klar.plain: Terms printed on the claim check, followed by the customer's "acceptance" of it, did not force a "finding" of agreement "as a matter of law," meaning one no judge could reject.

klar.sentence: Whether this acceptance manifested assent was therefore for the trial judge.
klar.plain: So whether this "acceptance" of the ticket showed agreement to its terms was a question for the trial judge, who found it did not.

klar.sentence: In those circumstances, he regarded the failure to read as inexcusable.
klar.plain: The dissenting judge thought the CONTRACT label was obvious enough that the customer should be held to the terms whether or not he read them.

klar.sentence: On May 15, 1947, the New York Court of Appeals affirmed with costs and without an opinion, supplying no additional written rationale.
klar.plain: On May 15, 1947, the New York Court of Appeals, the state's highest court, affirmed with costs and without an "opinion," giving no written explanation of its own.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: The National Firearms Act defined a machinegun by its capacity to fire automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, through a single function of the trigger.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: The National Firearms Act defined a machinegun as a weapon able to fire more than one shot automatically, without manual reloading, through "a single function of the trigger."

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: In 2018, ATF issued a final rule interpreting a single trigger function to include a single pull and analogous motions, and describing the devices as self-regulating mechanisms that produced continuous fire.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: In 2018, ATF, the federal firearms agency, issued a "final rule" (a binding regulation) reading "a single function of the trigger" to include one pull and similar motions. It described bump stocks as self-regulating "devices" producing continuous fire.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: He surrendered them under protest and sued the Attorney General and other federal officials under the Administrative Procedure Act, contending that ATF lacked statutory authority.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: Cargill turned in his bump stocks "under protest," without giving up his objection. He sued the Attorney General and other officials under the Administrative Procedure Act, arguing ATF had no power under the statute to treat them as machineguns.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: The rule’s origin explained the litigation, but neither an absolute prohibition on agency interpretive changes nor a defect in notice and comment became the basis of the Supreme Court’s holding.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: The rule's origin explains the lawsuit. But the Supreme Court's holding did not rest on any absolute ban on agencies changing their interpretations, or on a flaw in "notice and comment" (public input before a rule); it rested on what the statute means.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: A majority at least agreed that the statute was ambiguous and that lenity required resolving the uncertainty in Cargill’s favor.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: A majority of the full appeals court at least agreed the "statute" was ambiguous (unclear). They held that "lenity," the rule that unclear criminal laws are read in the defendant's favor, required resolving the doubt for Cargill.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: Thus, affirming the en banc judgment did not necessarily mean adopting lenity as the Supreme Court’s own rationale.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: So "affirming" (upholding) the full appeals court's "judgment" did not necessarily mean the Supreme Court adopted "lenity" as its own reason.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: The Court gave two distinct reasons: separate trigger functions remained necessary for separate shots, and, alternatively, the additional ongoing input prevented multiple shots from occurring automatically through a single trigger function.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: The Court gave two separate reasons. Each shot from a bump-stock rifle still needs its own trigger action. And even if not, the shooter must keep pushing the gun forward, so the shots do not happen 'automatically'.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: The device assisted rapid repetition without turning those separate engagements into one mechanical function.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: The "device," the bump stock, helped the shooter repeat trigger actions quickly. But it did not turn those separate trigger actions into one mechanical function.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: Even assuming the sequence could be attributed to one function, the majority found that the disputed device required ongoing input beyond that function.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: Even assuming the burst could count as one trigger function, the "majority" found the disputed "device" required ongoing input beyond it: the shooter had to keep pushing the gun forward, so the fire was not automatic.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: ATF invoked the presumption against ineffectiveness: a court should resist an interpretation that permits easy evasion of a law’s evident objective.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: ATF invoked the "presumption against ineffectiveness": courts should resist reading a law in a way that lets people easily get around its obvious goal, and bump stocks mimic machineguns.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: Congress could choose a line narrower than the broadest imaginable statement of the statute’s purpose.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: Congress could draw a line narrower than the broadest imaginable statement of the "statute's" purpose.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: Those classifications did not become binding law or estop the agency from changing position; they supported the majority’s response to the purposive argument.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: ATF's earlier rulings that bump stocks were legal did not become binding law or "estop" the agency (block it) from changing its view. But they supported the "majority’s" reply to its "purposive" argument, the claim that leaving bump stocks out defeats the law's purpose.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: Footnote 9 supplied a further answer to reliance on the ordinary label “machinegun”: an express statutory definition normally governs even if it differs from broader ordinary usage.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: Footnote 9 gave a further answer to relying on the everyday meaning of "machinegun": when a statute expressly defines a word, that definition normally controls, even if ordinary usage is broader.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: It held that ATF exceeded the authority supplied by the enacted definition, on both the single-trigger-function and automatic-fire grounds.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: The Court held that ATF went beyond the power given by the "enacted" (passed) definition, on both grounds: the single-trigger-function point and the automatic-fire point.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: She offered these as evidence of contemporary word usage, rather than only evidence of general legislative policy.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: Sotomayor offered the 1934-era sources as "evidence" of how people then used the words, their "usage," not only as evidence of Congress's general policy goals.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: She found no textual reason to make dispositive the fact that the disputed accessory performed externally a process other weapons performed internally.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: She found nothing in the statute's words making it "dispositive" (decisive) that the bump stock did from outside the gun a process other weapons do inside.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: She charged the majority with shifting perspectives: counting internal mechanical actions for one requirement, then turning to the shooter’s conduct for the other.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: She said the majority was inconsistent: it looked at the gun's moving parts to count trigger functions, but at the shooter's actions to decide whether firing was automatic.

lrs-k-cargill.sentence: The judgment did not adjudicate a Second Amendment right, decide mechanical spring-operated devices, or settle every federal or state rule governing other rapid-fire accessories.
lrs-k-cargill.plain: The "judgment" did not "adjudicate" (decide) any Second Amendment right, rule on mechanical spring-operated devices, or settle every federal or state rule on other rapid-fire accessories.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The parties arranged a multistep deal called the Bedrock Transaction to bring the loans current.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The bank and borrowers arranged a multistep deal called the Bedrock Transaction to bring the overdue loans current, meaning up to date on payments.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The governing statute, 12 U.S.C. § 1818(e), required misconduct, harmful effect or personal benefit by reason of that misconduct, and specified culpability.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The governing "statute," 12 U.S.C. § 1818(e), required three things to remove and ban a banker: misconduct, harm to the bank or personal gain caused by that misconduct, and a specified "culpability," a serious level of fault.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The Board found unsafe or unsound practices and rejected a requirement that Calcutt proximately cause the harm.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The FDIC Board found "unsafe or unsound practices" (imprudent banking). It rejected any need to show that Calcutt "proximately caused" the harm, meaning caused it directly in the legal sense.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: It attributed the $30,000 charge-off to his extensive involvement, but only part of the $6.4 million losses because some loss probably would have occurred anyway.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The appeals court attributed the $30,000 "charge-off," a loan written off as uncollectable, to Calcutt's heavy involvement. But it attributed only part of the $6.4 million in losses to him, since some loss probably would have happened anyway.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: Despite narrowing the harms and changing the standard, a 2–1 panel affirmed the sanctions on substantial-evidence grounds.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: Even after narrowing the harms and changing the legal test, a 2–1 "panel" (three judges, two agreeing) upheld the "sanctions" (penalties) because substantial evidence supported them.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The Board had never applied proximate cause or decided whether those same sanctions were warranted on the corrected basis.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The Board had never applied "proximate cause" (direct legal causation) or decided whether the same "sanctions" were justified on the corrected, smaller harms.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The Court’s unsigned opinion applied Chenery, the earlier decision requiring agency action to be reviewed on the agency’s stated grounds.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The Court's "unsigned opinion," with no named author, applied Chenery: "agency action" must be "reviewed" by courts on the reasons the agency itself gave.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: If those grounds fail legally, a reviewing court ordinarily must remand for explanation or investigation rather than substitute its own discretionary decision.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: If those reasons fail legally, a "reviewing court" ordinarily must "remand" (send the case back) for the agency to explain or investigate further. It should not substitute its own "discretionary" decision, the agency's judgment call.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The Sixth Circuit had relied on Wyman-Gordon, an earlier agency-review case recognizing that remand can be an idle formality when the outcome is certain.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The Sixth Circuit had relied on Wyman-Gordon, an earlier agency-review case recognizing that a "remand" can be an idle formality, a pointless step, when the outcome is certain.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: Here, however, whether to sanction Calcutt and how severely called for contextual discretion and multiple culpability considerations.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: Here, however, whether to "sanction" (penalize) Calcutt and how severely required case-specific "discretion" (judgment) and weighing several "culpability" (fault) factors, so the outcome was not certain.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: Calcutt had not received final exoneration, and the FDIC was not barred from reaching the same outcome through lawful reconsideration.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: Calcutt had not been finally cleared. The FDIC was not "barred" (prevented) from reaching the same result through lawful "reconsideration" using the correct test.

lrs-o-calcutt.sentence: The Supreme Court retained that narrow exception, including a situation where law required one agency action despite a mistaken rationale.
lrs-o-calcutt.plain: The Supreme Court kept that narrow exception, including where the law permits only one "agency action" even though the agency gave a mistaken reason.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Disability insurance required insured status and a medically determinable impairment preventing substantial gainful work, considering age, education, and work experience.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: "Disability insurance" required insured status (paying into Social Security long enough) and a "medically determinable impairment," a medically provable condition, preventing substantial paid work given age, education, and work experience.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: After termination came reconsideration, an evidentiary hearing before an administrative law judge, possible Appeals Council review, and judicial review.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: After benefits stopped came "reconsideration" (the agency looking again), a full evidentiary hearing before an "administrative law judge" (an agency hearing judge), possible Appeals Council "review," and finally review by a court.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Eldridge accepted the overall system if payment continued until that hearing; his objection concerned the earlier interruption.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: Eldridge did not object to the process as such; he objected to having his payments cut off before he got a live hearing.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: A failure to exhaust, the Secretary argued, blocked judicial consideration under the Social Security Act.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: The Secretary argued that Eldridge's "failure to exhaust," skipping the agency's own appeal steps, blocked a court from hearing his case under the Social Security Act.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Justice Powell’s opinion distinguished claim presentment from exhaustion within § 405(g)’s final-decision requirement.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: Justice Powell's "opinion" split § 405(g)'s final-decision requirement in two: presenting the claim to the agency at all, and "exhaustion," going through every agency appeal step.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Section 405(h), as construed in Salfi, foreclosed ordinary federal-question jurisdiction over the benefits denial.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: "Section 405(h)" of the Social Security Act, as read in the Salfi case, ruled out ordinary "federal-question jurisdiction," the usual route to federal court over a federal-law issue, for this benefits denial.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: His constitutional issue was collateral to substantive eligibility: later success on the medical question would not answer whether a hearing had been required sooner.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: His constitutional claim "was collateral," separate from whether he was still eligible for benefits. Winning later on the medical question would not answer whether he deserved a hearing sooner.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: He also colorably alleged interim harm retroactive money could not fully repair.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: He also "colorably" (plausibly) alleged harm in the meantime that "retroactive" money, back pay, could not fully repair.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: The Secretary accepted that continued statutory benefits were a protected property interest.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: The Secretary agreed that continued "statutory" benefits, ones the law provides, were a protected "property interest," so the Constitution requires fair procedures before taking them.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: The Court asked what procedures were due, weighing the private interest, the risk of error and probable value of added safeguards, and government interests including fiscal and administrative burdens.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: To decide how much process was required, the Court weighed three things: how much the person stands to lose, how likely mistakes are and how much extra steps would help, and what those steps would cost the government.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Goldberg’s means-tested welfare program identified recipients at the margin of subsistence; disability insurance did not establish need in that way.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: Goldberg's welfare program went only to people proven needy, at the edge of survival. "Disability insurance" did not establish need that way, so the Court saw less risk of desperate hardship.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Some cases involved credibility, yet procedural design was assessed across the generality of cases.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: A live hearing helps most when someone's honesty is in question. Some disability cases are like that, but the Court judged the procedures by how they work in typical cases.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Amici’s reversal statistics were relevant but inconclusive because denominators differed and later proceedings could add evidence or examinations.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: "Amici," outside groups filing briefs, showed many cutoffs were later reversed. Those numbers were "relevant" but inconclusive, because the statistics measured different groups and later stages could add new evidence or exams.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: The holding rejected an additional Goldberg-type hearing before cutoff, not every form of advance participation.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: The holding rejected only an extra, Goldberg-type live hearing before benefits stop, not every form of participation in advance, such as written responses.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Jurisdiction and defeat on the merits coexist: a colorable delay injury permitted adjudication of a claim that ultimately failed.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: "Jurisdiction" (the power to hear a case) and losing "on the merits" can coexist. Eldridge's "colorable" (plausible) claim of harm from delay let the court decide his claim, which ultimately failed.

lrs-o-mathews.sentence: Section 405(g) nevertheless supplied review here because presentment was nonwaivable while exhaustion could yield in appropriate circumstances.
lrs-o-mathews.plain: Even so, § 405(g) gave review here. Presenting the claim to the agency was "nonwaivable" (could never be skipped), while finishing every agency appeal could be excused in proper cases.

nelson-hazel.sentence: Nelson remodeled the Hazels’ home and initially sued to foreclose a mechanic’s and materialman’s lien.
nelson-hazel.plain: Nelson, the contractor, remodeled the Hazels' home and first sued to foreclose a "mechanic’s and materialman’s lien," a legal claim on the house for unpaid labor and materials, which could force its sale.

nelson-hazel.sentence: The work was not workmanlike, substantial performance was absent, and the lien could not be enforced.
nelson-hazel.plain: The work was not "workmanlike" (done with ordinary skill), "substantial performance" (doing close enough to what was promised) was missing, and the lien could not be enforced.

nelson-hazel.sentence: Justice Smith’s opinion distinguished enforcement of the contract and lien from quasi-contractual recovery of an excess benefit.
nelson-hazel.plain: Justice Smith’s "opinion" separated enforcing the contract and lien, which failed, from "quasi-contractual" recovery: being paid for any value the work added beyond the harm it caused, so the owners are not unfairly enriched.

nelson-hazel.sentence: Contract damages compensate injury; they do not necessarily let owners retain every valuable improvement by a defaulting contractor without paying a net balance.
nelson-hazel.plain: "Contract damages" compensate for injury. They do not necessarily let owners keep every valuable improvement made by a "defaulting contractor," one who broke the contract, without paying the leftover balance.

nelson-hazel.sentence: Building contracts furnished an exception to the usual rule against recovery by a defaulting party because improvements remain with the landowner.
nelson-hazel.plain: Usually a "defaulting party," one who broke the contract, cannot recover. Building contracts are an exception because the improvements stay with the landowner whether or not the owner pays.

nelson-hazel.sentence: Avoiding forfeiture supported payment of that excess.
nelson-hazel.plain: Avoiding "forfeiture," Nelson losing everything for work that still benefited the Hazels, supported paying that leftover value.

nelson-hazel.sentence: For remediable defects, the market cost of completion or correction ordinarily measured the offset.
nelson-hazel.plain: For "remediable" (fixable) defects, the market "cost of completion" or correction ordinarily measured the "offset," the owners' damages subtracted from what the builder is owed.

oglebay.sentence: Oglebay sought declaratory relief in April 1986; Armco eventually counterclaimed unenforceability.
oglebay.plain: In April 1986 Oglebay sought "declaratory relief," a court statement that the contract still bound both sides. Armco eventually "counterclaimed" (sued back) that the contract was unenforceable.

oglebay.sentence: Armco said independent rates were no longer public, and the trial court quashed nonparty rate subpoenas.
oglebay.plain: Armco said independent shipping rates were no longer published, and the "trial court" quashed (canceled) "subpoenas," court orders that would have made outside companies hand over their rates.

oglebay.sentence: For future seasons the parties had to notify it of impasse; a mediator would be appointed and chief executives required to meet toward a rate.
oglebay.plain: For future seasons, the companies had to tell the court if they reached an impasse on price. A "mediator," a neutral helper, would be appointed and their chief executives required to meet to agree on a rate.

oglebay.sentence: The Ohio Supreme Court treated the questions as mixed law and fact and asked whether competent, credible evidence supported critical findings.
oglebay.plain: The Ohio Supreme Court treated the questions as "mixed law and fact." It asked whether "competent, credible evidence," reliable and believable evidence, supported the trial court's key findings.

oglebay.sentence: Restatement § 33 and its comments permitted an otherwise binding bargain to gain definition from usage, dealing, implication, or a legally supplied term.
oglebay.plain: Restatement § 33 and its comments let an otherwise binding "bargain" get its missing details from industry practice, past dealing between the parties, implication, or a reasonable term supplied by law.

oglebay.sentence: A market or third-party measure that never materializes could support reasonable completion, paralleling Uniform Commercial Code § 2-305.
oglebay.plain: When a market or "third-party" price measure never materializes, a court may set a reasonable price to complete the contract, just as Uniform Commercial Code § 2-305 does for sales of goods.

oglebay.sentence: Those concrete comparisons and history justified reasonable completion; the Court did not authorize any midpoint between bargaining demands.
oglebay.plain: The court could set a price because real market comparisons supported it, not by simply splitting the difference between the two sides' demands.

oglebay.sentence: Restatement § 362 required sufficiently certain obligations for specific relief, but ordinary interpretation and supplied terms had to be tried before finding fatal uncertainty.
oglebay.plain: Restatement § 362 required sufficiently certain duties before "specific relief," a court order to perform. But ordinary interpretation and supplied terms had to be tried before any "finding" that uncertainty was fatal.

oglebay.sentence: Changing markets and decades of duration made future damages too speculative.
oglebay.plain: Money damages would not work because no one could reliably predict losses over decades of changing markets, so ordering continued performance was appropriate.

oglebay.sentence: The case distinguishes uncertainty in an existing contract’s machinery from uncertainty over whether a binding agreement was ever made.
oglebay.plain: A broken price-setting method in a real contract can be repaired by a court; that is different from a case where the parties never actually agreed.

renner.sentence: Following an October 1983 bench trial, the trial court entered findings and an order in January 1984 allowing rescission for mutual mistake and failure of consideration.
renner.plain: After an October 1983 "bench trial" (no jury), the trial court entered "findings" and an "order" in January 1984 allowing "rescission," undoing the sale. Its grounds were mutual mistake about the water and "failure of consideration," the buyers not getting what they bargained for.

renner.sentence: Because appellants had responsibility for an adequate record, the reviewing court presumed substantial support for the findings and a proper exercise of discretion.
renner.plain: The "appellants," the sellers who appealed, were responsible for providing an adequate record and did not. So the "reviewing court" presumed the evidence supported the findings and the judge used "discretion" properly.

renner.sentence: Adequate water was therefore a material basic assumption, not an incidental preference.
renner.plain: Adequate water was therefore a material "basic assumption," a fundamental premise of the deal, not a minor preference. That made the shared mistake serious enough to undo the contract.

renner.sentence: Its second footnote emphasized that failure to investigate thoroughly did not itself defeat rescission when the risk had not been allocated and the shared mistake concerned a material basic assumption.
renner.plain: Its second footnote stressed that the buyers' failure to investigate thoroughly did not by itself defeat "rescission." The contract had not put that risk on them, and the shared "mistake" concerned a material "basic assumption."

renner.sentence: Reimbursing all development losses in this fault-free mutual-mistake setting would shift the entire risk to the sellers.
renner.plain: In this "mutual-mistake" setting, where no one was at fault, repaying all the buyers' development losses would shift the entire risk to the sellers.

renner.sentence: The court rejected the former measure here, while preserving restitution under § 376 to prevent unjust enrichment.
renner.plain: The court rejected the full-reimbursement measure here. But it kept "restitution" under § 376, returning benefits the sellers received, to prevent "unjust enrichment," the sellers ending up unfairly better off.

renner.sentence: They were entitled to their down payment and any enhancement in the returned property’s value attributable to their work, less the fair rental value of their occupancy.
renner.plain: The buyers were entitled to their down payment and any "enhancement" (increase) in the returned land's value from their work, minus the "fair rental value" of their time using it.

renner.sentence: On June 25, 1986, Gordon, Holohan, Hays, Cameron, and Feldman unanimously affirmed the trial court in part and reversed in part, approved the appellate decision in part and vacated it in part, and remanded under that formula.
renner.plain: On June 25, 1986, Justices Gordon, Holohan, Hays, Cameron, and Feldman "unanimously" affirmed the trial court in part and "reversed in part." They approved the "appellate" court's decision in part, "vacated" (canceled) it in part, and "remanded" (sent back) the case under that formula.
